question: A boat glides into a black grotto at Waitomo, on New Zealand's North Island, and the lamps go out. The cave roof blazes with thousands of tiny blue-green sparks, like a whole galaxy hanging in the rock. What tiny living creatures make the glow?
context: New Zealand's glowworms (Arachnocampa luminosa) cling to the ceiling of Waitomo's Glowworm Grotto by the thousand; in the pitch dark their blue-green points look exactly like a starry sky. It is one of New Zealand's most-visited natural wonders — about 500,000 people came each year before the pandemic. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave

question: Guides at Waitomo keep every boat silent and dark as it drifts through the grotto: no talking, no lamps. The rule protects the living lights on the ceiling, because a burst of noise or light provokes a swift reaction in their blue-green glow. How do the lights react?
choices: they flash from blue to red
context: Boats glide along the underground Waitomo Stream through the Glowworm Grotto while guides keep everyone silent; noise and light make the glowworms' glow fade, so darkness and quiet keep the living constellation bright. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave

question: Local Māori had known the dark mouth of the Waitomo cave for generations and never gone inside. Then, in 1887, Fred Mace, a surveyor from England, and the chief Tāne Tinorau poled in together on a raft of flax stems, guided only by candlelight. In Māori tradition, what did that cave mouth mark?
choices: the lair of a taniwha, a water-monster
a place made tapu, or forbidden
a path for the spirits of the dead
context: Māori had known the Waitomo cave-mouth for generations but treated it as an entrance to the underworld and left it unexplored. In December 1887 the local chief Tāne Tinorau and English surveyor Fred Mace built a flax raft and poled inside by candlelight, following the Waitomo Stream where it vanishes underground — their first find was the glittering Glowworm Grotto. (Māori tradition.) Source: explorersweb.com/natural-wonders-waitomo-glowworm-caves; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave  (Legend.)

question: Chief Tāne Tinorau and his wife Huti opened the Waitomo caves to travelers in 1889, guiding visitors by candlelight themselves. For most of the next century the government ran the caves — until a landmark 1989 decision changed who owned them. What did that decision do?
answer: returned the caves to the founding family's heirs
choices: returned the caves to the founding family's heirs
sold the caves to a private tourism company
declared the caves a protected national park
handed the caves to a university for research
context: By 1889 Tāne Tinorau and his wife Huti were guiding travelers through the caves for a small fee — about 500 visitors came in the first two years, one of the earliest Māori-run tourism ventures. In 1989 the caves were returned to their descendants, who own and run them today; a 1990 Deed of Settlement grants the family a share of the revenue. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitomo_Glowworm_Cave

question: Thousands of living lights hang from the Waitomo ceiling, and every one is the glowworm Arachnocampa luminosa. Tasmania's Marakoopa cave, across the Tasman Sea, shines with the same blue-green light from its own cave roof. Where does Arachnocampa luminosa live in the wild?
answer: in New Zealand and nowhere else
choices: in New Zealand and nowhere else
context: Arachnocampa luminosa is endemic to New Zealand: it lives naturally in the country's caves and wet forests and nowhere else on Earth. Its nearest relatives live in Australian caves, for example Arachnocampa tasmaniensis in Tasmania's Marakoopa and Gunns Plains caves, but they are separate species that never crossed the Tasman. Source: inaturalist.org/taxa/125921-Arachnocampa-luminosa; caveanimals.com.au/glow-worms

question: Dionisio Pulido, a farmer, was in his cornfield near Paricutin, Mexico, in February 1943 when the ground cracked open and started spitting ash. A brand-new volcano was being born at his feet. How tall was Pulido's volcano by the end of that first day?
context: Within 24 hours the new cone stood about 50 m (160 ft) tall; it kept climbing to its final 424 m by 1952, then fell silent forever. Dionisio Pulido had witnessed something almost no human ever has -- a volcano's birth from its very first minute. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paricutin'; IUGS Geoheritage, 'Paricutin Volcano'.

question: Paricutin burst from the ground in 1943, and for nine years its lava crept across the Mexican countryside until it swallowed the whole town of San Juan Parangaricutiro. The town lies under a frozen sea of black rock, all but one structure still jutting up out of the hardened lava. What is it?
choices: The roof of the town hall
context: Only the church of San Juan Parangaricutiro survived, its bell tower and altar rising out of the black rock. Locals call the surviving altar a miracle; it is still used for occasional services, and pilgrims walk out across the lava to reach it. Source: Atlas Obscura, 'Viejo San Juan Parangaricutiro'; Wikipedia, 'Paricutin'.

question: An undersea volcano built Surtsey, a brand-new island off Iceland's south coast, between 1963 and 1967. Scientists closed it to the public and watched over it to study how life first reaches new land. One year they found a healthy tomato plant growing there, sprouted from a researcher's own buried waste. What did the scientists do about their surprise tomato?
answer: Pulled it up, to keep the island pristine
choices: Pulled it up, to keep the island pristine
Fenced it off and studied its growth
Celebrated it as Surtsey's first crop
Left it alone as a natural experiment
context: The tomato was pulled up at once to keep Surtsey pristine. Only scientists may land there; the first plant to arrive on its own, sea rocket, sprouted in 1965. Surtsey is a UNESCO-protected natural laboratory for watching how life colonizes new land. Source: Wikipedia, 'Surtsey'.

question: Three people died at Paricutin, in Michoacan, Mexico, though in nine years of eruption its slow lava never caught anyone. They were killed not by lava or falling rock but by a violent weather hazard that the volcano's own churning ash cloud brewed in the sky overhead. What killed those three people?
context: Volcanic ash clouds build up enormous static charge and crackle with lightning. Three people near Paricutin were killed by that lightning, even though the creeping lava itself claimed no lives in nine years of eruption. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paricutin'.

question: A small new islet rose from the Pacific beside Nishinoshima, an island about 1,000 km south of Tokyo, in an undersea eruption in 2013. Eruption after eruption the lava piled up, until the islet merged with the old island, which grew to about twenty times its old size. Japanese officials watched each new eruption with quiet delight. What did the eruptions do for Japan?
answer: Added brand-new national territory to its map
choices: Added brand-new national territory to its map
Opened a rich new deep-sea fishing ground
Built a natural harbor for its navy
Raised a sunken island back above the sea
context: The new lava enlarged Nishinoshima to roughly 4.1 sq km -- about twenty times its old size -- literally adding fresh land, and the surrounding waters, to Japan's territory. Undersea eruptions are still redrawing the map today. Source: Wikipedia, 'Nishinoshima (Ogasawara)'.

question: Four seated giants of the pharaoh Ramesses II guard the front of Abu Simbel, in far southern Egypt, shoulder to shoulder. Each is about 20 m tall, as high as a six-story building. What is most unusual about how the temple was made?
answer: Cut directly into a solid sandstone cliff
choices: Cut directly into a solid sandstone cliff
Built up from sun-dried mud brick
context: Abu Simbel is entirely rock-cut: instead of stacking blocks, workers under Ramesses II chiseled the whole temple -- facade, halls, and the four 20-m colossi -- straight into a living sandstone cliff, so it is really one carved mountain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel; egymonuments.gov.eg/archaeological-sites/abu-simbel.

question: Lake Nasser was rising behind Egypt's new Aswan High Dam in the 1960s, creeping toward Abu Simbel, Ramesses II's temple with its four giant statues, to drown it forever. Nations around the world sent engineers to save it. What did the international team do?
answer: Sawed it into over a thousand blocks and moved it uphill
choices: Sawed it into over a thousand blocks and moved it uphill
Raised the whole temple straight up on hydraulic jacks
Floated it whole on giant sealed pontoons to safety
Ringed it with a new dam to hold the lake back
context: Behind the new Aswan High Dam, Lake Nasser was rising to swallow the temple. From 1964-1968 an international team sawed Abu Simbel into 1,036 numbered blocks (807 for the Great Temple, 235 for the Small) and rebuilt it on higher ground. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel.

question: Right beside the giant Great Temple at Abu Simbel stands a second, smaller temple that Ramesses II carved for his queen, Nefertari. Unusually, her statues on its front rise as tall as the pharaoh's own. To which goddess did he dedicate the queen's temple?
context: Hathor was the Egyptian goddess of love, joy, and music. Nefertari's temple is one of very few where the queen's statues on the facade stand as tall as the pharaoh's -- and she is shown as Hathor herself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel.

question: One of the four giant Ramesses statues at Abu Simbel had lost its head and shoulders to an earthquake in ancient times. When the temple was rescued and rebuilt in the 1960s, the engineers made a deliberate choice about that broken colossus. What did they do with the fallen head?
answer: Left it lying at the statue's feet
choices: Left it lying at the statue's feet
Rebuilt it from fresh matching sandstone
Sent it to a museum in Cairo
Replaced it with a copy in concrete
context: An ancient earthquake toppled the head and torso of the second colossus. When they rebuilt the temple in the 1960s, the restorers deliberately left the broken pieces lying at its feet, exactly as they had fallen. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel.

question: The rescue team lifted Abu Simbel 65 m up the cliff and set it about 208 m back from the rising lake. Then the massive carved blocks of a 3,200-year-old temple had to be fitted back into their old places. How closely did the rebuilders match the original?
choices: To within about half a meter
context: The team raised Abu Simbel 65 m and moved it about 208 m back from the water, reassembling the blocks to a tolerance of only about 5 mm so the ancient sunrise alignment would still work. The seams are almost invisible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel.

question: Deep inside Abu Simbel, four gods sit carved into the back wall at the end of a pitch-dark corridor about 60 m long. Twice a year, around February 22 and October 22, the rising sun spears straight down the passage at dawn and lights three of the four faces, while one god alone stays in shadow. Which one?
context: The three lit figures are Ra-Horakhty, Amun-Ra, and the deified Ramesses; Ptah, linked to the underworld, is the one left in darkness. Many hold that the ancient builders designed the alignment deliberately. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Simbel; corroborated egymonuments.gov.eg and worldhistory.org/image/15453.

question: Engineers rebuilding Abu Simbel on higher ground in the 1960s labored to keep its famous sunrise alignment. Twice a year the dawn sun still floods the sanctuary and lights the gods, but it is often said the modern builders could not quite match the ancient ones. What is the small imperfection?
answer: The sunlit days shifted by about one day
choices: The sunlit days shifted by about one day
The beam now lights all four gods, not three
The sunbeam reaches only halfway down the hall
The sunrise now misses the sanctuary in winter
context: It is widely reported that the original illumination fell on about February 21 and October 21, and that after the 1960s move the dates slipped by roughly a day -- a reminder that modern engineers couldn't perfectly reproduce 3,200-year-old astronomy. Source: egiptoexclusivo.com/en/blog/solar-alignment-at-abu-simbel; suryatara.com/abu-simbel-sun-festival.  (Legend.)

question: A steep cliff curves in a horseshoe nearly 76 m tall above a bend of the Waghora River in Maharashtra, western India. Along its face stand about 30 Buddhist prayer halls and monasteries, full of pillars, painted shrines and carved ceilings, which monks began over 2,000 years ago. How was the whole Ajanta complex made?
answer: carved directly out of the solid cliff
choices: carved directly out of the solid cliff
built up course by course in fired brick
assembled from precisely fitted stone blocks
framed and roofed in carved teak beams
context: Not one block was stacked at Ajanta: every pillar, doorway, and ceiling was cut away from the living basalt of the gorge, so the finished halls stand inside the hollowed rock. The horseshoe cliff bends about 76 m above the Waghora river in Maharashtra. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; worldhistory.org/article/849/the-ajanta-caves/

question: Princes, dark-eyed queens, elephants and dancers crowd the dim walls inside the Ajanta caves, painted in ochre and deep blue and still glowing after some 1,500 years. It is the largest surviving body of ancient Indian painting, and nearly every scene tells one of the Jataka tales. What do the Jataka stories tell?
choices: the ten avatars of the god Vishnu
the daily rituals of the resident monks
context: Jataka tales tell of the Buddha's earlier births -- as princes, animals, even a great six-tusked elephant -- each life teaching a virtue such as generosity or patience. Nowhere else on earth survives so much ancient Indian painting as on these cave walls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; asi.nic.in/pages/WorldHeritageAjantaCaves

question: Beside the shrine of Cave 1 glows the most beloved image at Ajanta: a tall prince with lowered eyes and a jeweled crown, his head tilted in quiet kindness, holding a single blue lotus. He is a bodhisattva, one who stays in the world to help others toward release. What is this gentle Cave 1 bodhisattva called?
context: Padmapani means 'the lotus-bearer,' a form of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. On the opposite side of Cave 1's shrine stands his sterner companion, Vajrapani, 'the thunderbolt-bearer.' The Padmapani mural is the single most reproduced image of Ajanta. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; asi.nic.in/pages/WorldHeritageAjantaCaves

question: Captain John Smith, a British army officer, was out hunting in the Deccan hills in April 1819 when he glimpsed a dark cave mouth through the trees. A local boy led him inside to the painted halls of Ajanta, lost to the jungle and forgotten for over a thousand years since its monks left. What had the officer been chasing?
context: The officer was Captain John Smith of the Madras army, and the date was 28 April 1819. Inside Cave 10 he scratched his own name and the date over a 1,500-year-old painting -- graffiti that can still be read on the pillar today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; livehistoryindia.com/story/monuments/how-ajanta-caves-were-rediscovered

question: Five of the caves at Ajanta are chaityas, tall prayer halls, and the ancient Cave 10 is one of them. The monks carved each hall around one object at its far end, so that pilgrims could walk around it as they prayed. What stands there?
context: A chaitya-griha is a worship hall built around a stupa, a solid domed shrine, so that pilgrims could circle it in prayer; the monks lived in viharas, square halls ringed with small cells. Five of Ajanta's caves are chaityas (9, 10, 19, 26 and 29) and the rest viharas; Cave 10, the oldest, is a chaitya. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; asi.nic.in/pages/WorldHeritageAjantaCaves

question: Harishena, the Vakataka emperor, sponsored a second dazzling wave of carving at Ajanta around 460-480 CE, nearly 600 silent years after the first caves were cut in the 2nd-1st century BCE. It gave the site its grandest halls and its finest murals. What is true of many of Harishena's second-phase caves?
choices: they were each carved by a single monk
they copied the plan of the early caves
they were meant as palaces, not temples
context: When Harishena's Vakataka dynasty collapsed soon after his death, the carvers downed their tools mid-work. Several of the grand later caves still stand half-made -- roughed-out pillars, blank plastered walls, and figures only partly cut from the living rock, frozen at the moment the carving stopped. The first, far smaller phase belongs to the Satavahana era around the 2nd-1st century BCE, when Cave 10, the oldest, was cut. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves; worldhistory.org/article/849/the-ajanta-caves/

question: Ships sailing into Santorini's bay pass between cliffs about 300 m high, a broken ring around deep blue water some 12 km long. The island, Thera to the ancient Greeks, wraps around it like a bowl's rim. What do geologists call this kind of feature?
context: Santorini's bay is a caldera -- the basin a volcano leaves when its emptied magma chamber collapses. This drowned crater is about 12 by 7 km across, ringed by cliffs near 300 m high and up to about 385 m deep. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santorini_caldera

question: Archaeologists digging down through Santorini's ash reached Akrotiri, a town from the Minoan world whose stone houses still stand two and three stories tall, with paved lanes and clay drainpipes. People nickname it 'a second Pompeii.' Compared with Pompeii, when was Akrotiri buried?
context: The buried town is Akrotiri, part of the Minoan world. It was sealed roughly 1,600 years before Pompeii (destroyed 79 CE) -- back in the Bronze Age -- yet its houses still stand two and three storeys high with paved streets and clay drains, so visitors can walk through their upper floors. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrotiri_(prehistoric_city)

question: Pompeii's ash preserved thousands of bodies frozen where they fell. Akrotiri, on Santorini, lies buried under volcanic ash the same way, yet archaeologists found almost no bodies there, no crowds of the dead at all. What is the leading explanation for the empty town?
answer: the townspeople felt earthquakes and fled in time
choices: the townspeople felt earthquakes and fled in time
the acidic ash slowly dissolved the bones away
the survivors came back and buried their dead
floods later washed the bodies out to sea
context: Archaeologists report 'no uninterred human skeletal remains' at Akrotiri. Warning earthquakes seem to have driven the townspeople out in good order before the blast -- and they carried their valuables with them, which is why the houses were found nearly bare. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrotiri_(prehistoric_city)

question: Excavators found the houses of Akrotiri, on Santorini, stripped almost bare, but in 1999 they lifted out one treasure tucked inside a wooden box within a clay chest: the one object of solid gold ever found in the whole town. What was this lone treasure?
context: The lone gold object is a small ibex (wild goat) figurine, found in 1999 inside a wooden box within a clay chest, beside a pile of animal horns. That the whole town yielded just this single precious piece is itself the clue that its people left in an orderly evacuation, taking their wealth. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/image/1358/gold-ibex-akrotiri/

question: Diggers at Akrotiri on Santorini uncovered the 'Spring Fresco' in 1970: swallows swooping over clusters of red lilies on rocky volcanic ground, finished well before 1600 BCE. It became an instant landmark in the study of Aegean art. What set it apart from every earlier fresco find?
answer: it was the first fresco found still on its original wall
choices: it was the first fresco found still on its original wall
it was the oldest fresco ever dug up in the Aegean
it was rebuilt from thousands of tiny scattered fragments
it was the first fresco ever hung whole in a museum
context: Uncovered in 1970, the Spring Fresco -- swallows swooping over red lilies on a rocky volcanic landscape -- was the first Aegean wall-painting ever found perfectly preserved on the very wall where it was painted, not pieced together from fallen fragments. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/673/akrotiri-frescoes/

question: Giant stone pillars crowd a field at Aksum, in northern Ethiopia, each carved with rows of blind windows and a false door at its foot, floor stacked upon floor. What was each Aksum stele carved to imitate?
context: Aksum's stelae are single blocks of stone carved to look like the tall, multi-storey tower-houses that Aksumites actually built -- complete with rows of false windows on every 'floor' and false doors detailed right down to imitation door-locks. The Obelisk of Axum shows nine storeys; the fallen Great Stele depicts thirteen. Source: Wikipedia, 'Obelisk of Axum.'

question: Aksum's traders sent ivory, tortoise-shell and gold out from the kingdom's Red Sea ports, and the empire grew rich as the great middleman between inland Africa and the Roman Mediterranean. In return, costly goods came in by sea. Which luxuries did Aksum bring in?
context: Aksum was the principal supplier of African goods to the Roman world: ivory, tortoise-shell, and gold went out, while silk and spices came in from as far away as India. Sitting between inland Africa and the Red Sea, this middleman trade made Aksum one of the great commercial powers of the ancient world. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kingdom of Aksum.'

question: Quarry workers at Gobedra Hill, four kilometres west of Aksum, freed each of the city's stelae as a single block of rock. The biggest weigh hundreds of tons, and the builders had no saws big enough to cut them out. How did the workers crack each colossal block free from the bedrock?
answer: soaked wooden wedges until they swelled and split it
choices: soaked wooden wedges until they swelled and split it
heated the rock, then cracked it with cold water
drilled it out with hardened iron chisels
levered it free with long bronze bars
context: The stelae were quarried as single blocks from nepheline-syenite at Gobedra Hill, about 4 km west of Aksum. Workers cut grooves into the rock, drove in wooden wedges, and soaked them with water; as the wood swelled it split the giant block free. Teams of laborers then dragged the colossal stones to the burial field. Source: Metropolitan Museum and archaeological sources on the Gobedra quarry.

question: King Endybis ruled Aksum around 270 AD, when the kingdom's ships traded with Rome and India. He began something that ancient rulers treated as a mark of true sovereignty, the sign of a kingdom beholden to no greater ruler. What did he have Aksum do, as only a handful of kingdoms in his day did?
answer: mint its own gold and silver coins
choices: mint its own gold and silver coins
build a fleet of ocean-going warships
cut a great canal to the Red Sea
context: Around 270 AD, King Endybis of Aksum began minting coins in gold, silver, and bronze, the first state in sub-Saharan Africa to do so. Minting one's own coinage was one of the ancient world's classic marks of a sovereign power, and Aksum was one of the very few kingdoms of its age to do it. Aksumite coins circulated across the Red Sea trade world.

question: The first Church of St Mary of Zion rose at Aksum under King Ezana in the 4th century AD, one of the oldest churches in Ethiopia. For many centuries afterward one great ceremony of the Ethiopian empire could take place lawfully only there. What ceremony?
context: For centuries, an Ethiopian ruler could be crowned legitimate emperor only at Aksum, in a service tied to the Church of St Mary of Zion. The original church, founded under King Ezana in the 4th century AD, is among the oldest in Ethiopia. Source: Wikipedia, 'Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion.'

question: Under King Ezana, around 340 AD, the images stamped on Aksum's coins changed, and those little metal discs record one of the great turning points in the kingdom's story. The old royal symbols were dropped, and a new emblem appeared that makes Aksumite money some of the earliest anywhere to carry it. What new symbol appeared on the coins?
context: Under King Ezana in the 330s-340s AD, Aksum became one of the first kingdoms anywhere to adopt Christianity, and its money records the change. Around 340 the coins' older pagan crescent-and-disc gives way to the cross, making Aksumite coinage some of the earliest in the world to bear a Christian cross. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kingdom of Aksum.'

question: A single monk keeps watch over a small, closely guarded chapel beside the Church of St Mary of Zion at Aksum; he is chosen for life and never allowed to leave the grounds. Ethiopian Orthodox tradition holds that inside rests one of the most sacred relics of the whole Bible, carried long ago from King Solomon's Jerusalem by Prince Menelik. Held on faith, what does Aksum claim to guard here?
context: The Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion claims to guard the Ark of the Covenant -- in the Hebrew Bible, the chest that held the tablets of the Ten Commandments. By Ethiopian tradition, Prince Menelik I, son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, brought it from Jerusalem; only a single guardian monk, appointed for life and forbidden ever to leave, may see it. This is a sacred belief, held on faith -- neither proven nor disproven. Source: Wikipedia, 'Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion.'  (Legend.)

question: The Pharos, Alexandria's great lighthouse and one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, burned a fire at its summit to guide ships through the night. But sailors could catch its signal even in full daylight, centuries before electricity. How did the Pharos warn ships by day?
answer: It flashed sunlight from a huge polished mirror.
choices: It flashed sunlight from a huge polished mirror.
It sent up a tall column of black smoke.
It rang an enormous bronze harbor bell.
It raised bright banners along the tower.
context: By day a polished mirror at the top of the Pharos threw the sun's light out to sea; the flash was said to be visible nearly 47 km from shore, from a tower rising perhaps 100-130 m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria; britannica.com 'Lighthouse of Alexandria'.

question: Alexandria rose on the coast of Egypt where Alexander the Great chose the spot in 331 BC, and he named the new city after himself. It would grow into the greatest city of the ancient world. What happened to Alexander and the city that carries his name?
answer: He never returned to see the city finished.
choices: He was crowned Egypt's pharaoh in the city's temple.
He never returned to see the city finished.
He personally dug the city's first harbor channel.
He raised his statue at the city's main crossroads.
context: Alexander's architect Dinocrates laid the city out on a grid of broad avenues crossing at right angles, but Alexander himself marched off to Persia within months and never saw the finished city that carries his name. Source: worldhistory.org/alexandria/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Alexandria.

question: Royal keepers ran the Library of Alexandria, founded under Ptolemy II, Egypt's Greek pharaoh, around 285 BC, and they set it one bold mission. Ships docking in the harbor were searched, scrolls were copied by hand, and hall after hall filled with papyrus rolls. What did the Library set out to collect?
answer: A copy of every book in the world.
choices: A copy of every book in the world.
The holy scriptures of every religion.
A map of every land ever charted.
The verses of every Greek poet.
context: Chasing a copy of every book in existence, the Library gathered tens of thousands of scrolls (ancient estimates range wildly, from 40,000 to several hundred thousand) to become the greatest library of the ancient world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Alexandria.

question: As Alexander the Great marked out Alexandria's walls in 331 BC, the story goes he had no chalk to draw the lines on the dark Egyptian soil. So he traced the whole city outline in pale barley meal instead. Then something happened that scared him badly, until his seers talked him back to calm. In the legend told by Plutarch, what happened to Alexander's barley-meal outline?
answer: Flocks of birds swooped down and ate every grain.
choices: Flocks of birds swooped down and ate every grain.
A sudden desert wind scattered it to nothing.
A night rainstorm washed the pale lines away.
Stray dogs trampled the outline into mud.
context: Plutarch (Life of Alexander 26) tells it: the birds terrified Alexander, but his seers read a good omen in it, saying the city would feed and nourish peoples from many nations. Framed here as legend. Source: livius.org (Plutarch, Life of Alexander 26).

question: Sultan Qaitbay, the Mamluk ruler, raised a squat stone fortress around 1480 on the rocky point at the mouth of Alexandria's harbor, and it still guards the water today. Centuries earlier the towering Pharos lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders, had risen on that same point; by Qaitbay's day it lay nearby in earthquake-shattered ruins. Where did the stone for his fort come from?
answer: Salvaged from the fallen ruins of the ancient Pharos.
choices: Salvaged from the fallen ruins of the ancient Pharos.
Shipped up the Nile from the Aswan quarries.
Hauled across the sea from the isle of Cyprus.
Cut fresh from the cliffs of the western desert.
context: Earthquakes in AD 956, 1303, and 1323 brought the Pharos down; around 1477-1480 Sultan Qaitbay reused its fallen stones to raise Fort Qaitbay on the exact spot, and the fort still stands there today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria; britannica.com 'Lighthouse of Alexandria'.

question: Scribes at the Library of Alexandria copied out by hand the books carried up to them from the harbor, where every ship that docked was searched by royal decree. The city's hunt for scrolls had turned ruthless. Once the scribes finished, what did the Library do with the borrowed scrolls?
answer: It kept the original scrolls and gave owners the copies.
choices: It kept the original scrolls and gave owners the copies.
It kept the copies and gave owners the original scrolls.
It kept both versions and paid the owners in silver.
It kept neither, returning every scroll untouched.
context: These were catalogued as 'books of the ships'; the Library kept the originals and gave owners the copies. Its great book-collecting rival was the Library of Pergamon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Alexandria (citing Galen).

question: Beneath the streets of modern Alexandria wind the Catacombs of Kom el Shoqafa, Roman-era burial halls cut deep into the rock and then lost and forgotten for more than a thousand years. In 1900 they were stumbled upon entirely by accident. How were the catacombs of Kom el Shoqafa found again?
answer: A donkey fell through the ground into the shaft.
choices: A donkey fell through the ground into the shaft.
A well-digger's bucket dropped into the void.
A flood tore open a long-sealed doorway.
A farmer's plough snagged on a buried statue.
context: Inside, three cultures meet in one carved tomb: the Egyptian god Anubis stands in Roman legionary armor, a wall shows the Greek myth of Persephone's abduction, and statues wear Egyptian poses in Roman dress. 'Kom el Shoqafa' means 'Mound of Shards,' after the broken feast-pottery mourners left behind. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs_of_Kom_El_Shoqafa.

question: Eratosthenes, chief scholar at Alexandria's great library around 240 BC, heard that on the longest day of the year the noon sun stood straight over a deep well at Syene and cast no shadow. At that moment in Alexandria an upright pole cast a short shadow. From the difference and the distance between the cities he calculated one number, right to within about 1 percent. What did he measure?
answer: The distance around the whole Earth.
choices: The distance around the whole Earth.
The distance from the Earth to the sun.
The width of the Moon's grey disc.
The height of the dome of the sky.
context: The Alexandria shadow measured about 7.2 degrees, exactly 1/50 of a circle; multiplying the Syene-to-Alexandria distance by 50 gave Earth's circumference within roughly 1% of the true value. Jealous rivals nicknamed the brilliant Eratosthenes 'Beta,' the second letter, sneering that he was second-best at everything. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eratosthenes.

question: The Golden Temple of Amritsar, holiest shrine of the Sikh faith, sits on a small island in a vast square pool of sacred water. Rich or poor, every pilgrim reaches it the same way. What is the one link between the shore and the island?
context: The one crossing is the marble Guru's Bridge (Guru da Pul), about 202 feet long and 21 feet wide, the sole way in and out, so the shrine seems to float alone on the water. Source: SGPC (sgpc.net/sri-harmandir-sahib); Wikipedia (Golden Temple).

question: Pilgrims bathe in the sacred pool around the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the holiest shrine of the Sikh faith, which stands on a small island at its centre. At dawn the still water blazes as though it had caught fire, the shrine's reflection burning orange across the surface. What gives the shrine this fiery glow?
answer: its dome and towers are covered in real gold
choices: its dome and towers are covered in real gold
its walls are faced with polished brass
its roof is laid with sheets of copper
its surface is coated in gold-colored paint
context: Maharaja Ranjit Singh had the sanctum overlaid, marble and copper around 1809, then gilded with roughly 400 kg of gold leaf about 1830. The low sun strikes that gold and pours its fire down into the pool, the Amrit Sarovar, below. Source: Wikipedia (Golden Temple); Incredible India (Sri Harmandir Sahib).

question: At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, pilgrims from every land wade down the steps into the great square tank at dawn and cup the water to their lips. They come not merely to wash, but because of what this particular water is held to be. What do the faithful believe the pool holds?
answer: nectar that heals body and soul
choices: nectar that heals body and soul
the tears of a grieving saint
context: The pool is the Amrit Sarovar, 'amrit' meaning nectar and 'sar' a pool, and the city of Amritsar takes its very name from it. Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh Guru, had the great tank completed around 1577; its water is revered as amrit, nectar believed to heal body and soul. Source: Wikipedia (Golden Temple / Amrit Sarovar).  (Legend.)

question: Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, built the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar the opposite way from the great temples and mosques of his day. They rose high above the streets, and worshippers climbed long flights of steps to reach the holy place; he set the shrine's entrance low, so pilgrims walk down steps to enter. What did Guru Arjan mean this downward entrance to teach?
answer: that God is found with the humble, not the proud
choices: that God is found with the humble, not the proud
that all who enter shed their rank at the door
that the shrine must bow before its sacred pool
that the way to God sinks low before it climbs
context: Guru Arjan also gave the Harmandir Sahib a door on each of its four sides, open to every caste and faith, from every direction, while other shrines faced only one way. Asked why he built low when others built high, he is remembered as replying that God is found with the humble, those who bow, and not with the proud. Source: sikhism.net.in (Golden Temple); SGPC (sri-harmandir-sahib).

question: Volunteers in the langar, the vast dining hall beside the Golden Temple in Amritsar, cook around 50,000 free meals on an ordinary day, for anyone at all, of any faith or caste, prince or pauper. To make plain that all who eat there are equals, the langar keeps one firm rule at every meal. What is that rule?
answer: everyone sits together on the floor to eat
choices: everyone sits together on the floor to eat
everyone eats standing, in a single line
everyone brings a bowl from home
context: The langar (Guru Ka Langar) is called the world's largest free kitchen: around 50,000 meals on an ordinary day, well over 100,000 on festivals, cooked by roughly 500 volunteer sevadaars working nearly around the clock, about 12,000 kg of flour and 13,000 kg of lentils daily, with a machine turning out some 200,000 rotis. All sit on the floor as equals, so that no one who comes to the Guru's door is turned away hungry. Source: The National (2023); goldentempleamritsar.org (langar).

question: Engineers dug rings of canals across Amsterdam's marshy ground in the 1600s to build a whole new city centre, leaving about 90 tiny islands stitched together by even more bridges than Venice has. About how many bridges cross Amsterdam's canals today?
context: Over 1,200 bridges span Amsterdam's 100-plus kilometres of canals, linking its roughly 90 islands — a denser web of bridges than Venice itself. The showpiece is the 17th-century 'canal ring' (grachtengordel) around the old core, dug in planned phases and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: Wikipedia (Amsterdam — Geography; Canals of Amsterdam / grachtengordel; UNESCO WHC 1349).

question: Fishermen settled around 1270 at the mouth of a small tidal river called the Amstel, but North Sea tides kept surging in and drowning the marsh they meant to farm. To shut the tide out they built one water-work across the river's mouth, and a mighty city grew behind it. What kind of water-work was it?
context: Here is the delight the question kept back: 'Amstel-dam' — a dam across the little River Amstel — is exactly what the name 'Amsterdam' records. Historians date the dam to about 1264–1275, and Amsterdam first appears in an official record in 1275. Dam Square, the busy plaza at the city's heart, still stands on the spot where that first dam held back the tide. Source: Wikipedia (Amsterdam — Etymology/History; Dam Square).

question: The builders of Amsterdam's Royal Palace, a giant of solid sandstone, drove 13,659 poles straight down through soaked peat and clay to a firm bed of sand far below, then stood the whole palace on their tops. By rights it should sink slowly into the mud, but it has not. What are those 13,659 poles?
context: The 13,659 piles are whole softwood tree trunks — fir and spruce shipped from Scandinavia — driven about 12 metres down to the first firm layer of sand beneath the peat. A mountain of stone floating on a buried forest: the poet Constantijn Huygens called the building 'the world's Eighth Wonder.' It opened in 1655 as Amsterdam's city hall and became a royal palace only in 1808. Sources: Wikipedia (Royal Palace of Amsterdam — 13,659 wooden piles); dutchamsterdam.nl.

question: Water constantly seeps up into the fields and streets of Amsterdam, for parts of the city and much of the Netherlands lie below the level of the sea. It must be lifted out and flung over the dikes, a task that never ends. Long before electric pumps, the Dutch did this lifting with tens of thousands of one kind of machine. Which machines pumped the Netherlands dry?
context: The classic Dutch windmill was often a water pump, not a flour mill: its sails turned an Archimedes' screw or scoop-wheel that lifted seepage up and over the dikes, tirelessly. Electric and diesel pumping stations later took over the job. Much of Amsterdam's centre sits about 2 metres below sea level, kept dry only by this constant pumping. Sources: Wikipedia (Amsterdam — elevation about −2 m below sea level; polders); incredibleamsterdam.com.

question: Johannes Hudde, the mayor of Amsterdam, ordered careful water-level readings after a big flood in 1675, and those readings hardened into a single fixed zero mark for measuring how high land stands above or below the sea. It became the Amsterdam Ordnance Datum. For how large an area did this city's flood mark become the official zero height?
context: Mayor Johannes Hudde's benchmark grew into the NAP (Normaal Amsterdams Peil), which became the reference 'zero' for elevation across much of Western Europe — so a mountain's height in several countries is still measured up from a mark first set in flood-prone Amsterdam. Source: Wikipedia (Normaal Amsterdams Peil; Amsterdam — polders).

question: Along Amsterdam's canals the tall, narrow brick houses famously lean, and much of that lean was built in on purpose. Many tilt forward, their top edge jutting out beyond the base, in a style the Dutch call 'op de vlucht.' Why did their builders tip the whole front wall forward?
answer: so goods hoisted up the front wouldn't scrape the wall
choices: so goods hoisted up the front wouldn't scrape the wall
so rain would run off the front instead of the windows
so the top-floor rooms would catch more sun
so the tall house would look grander from below
context: Because the staircases were too tight for big furniture, Amsterdammers hauled loads up the OUTSIDE, using a hoisting hook and beam — the hijsbalk — still seen at the top of many gables; the forward tilt kept the swinging load from scraping the facade. Not every lean is intentional, though: houses that tilt SIDEWAYS, leaning unevenly into their neighbours, are usually truly sinking — their wooden piles have begun to rot where a falling groundwater level let air reach the wood. Sources: expatica.com, dutchreview.com (Amsterdam canal houses); amsterdamian.com (hijsbalk); commonedge.org (rotting piles).

question: Angel Falls leaps off a sheer cliff in the Venezuelan rainforest and drops 979 metres, Earth's tallest waterfall, over half a mile of it in one plunge. In the dry season the water does something strange on the way down. What does it do?
answer: it breaks apart into a drifting mist and blows away
choices: it breaks apart into a drifting mist and blows away
it freezes into a hanging sheet of ice
it splits into a braid of smaller streams
it doubles back and sprays upward in the wind
context: Angel Falls is the tallest waterfall on Earth: 979 m in all, with a single uninterrupted plunge of 807 m, more than half a mile of free fall. The drop is so vast that much of the water vaporizes into mist and swirls away in the turbulent air, especially in the dry season, before it ever reaches the valley floor. Source: geology.com highest-waterfall; simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls.

question: At the foot of Angel Falls, deep in the jungle-covered tablelands of southeastern Venezuela, the water gathers into the small Churún River and runs on into the wider Carrao. In the end those two streams carry the falls' water into one of South America's mightiest rivers. Which one?
context: Angel Falls drops from Auyán-tepui in Canaima National Park; the water that survives the plunge flows out as the Churún, into the Carrao, and finally into the mighty Orinoco — not the Amazon, whose basin lies to the south. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls.

question: The Pemón people have lived under the cliff of Angel Falls for centuries, and they already had their own name for it: Kerepakupai Merú. The falls' English name comes from Jimmie Angel, an American aviator who spotted them from his small plane in 1933, but in 2009 Venezuela's government officially adopted the Pemón name. What does 'Kerepakupai Merú' mean?
answer: the waterfall of the deepest place
choices: the waterfall of the deepest place
context: The Pemón name Kerepakupai Merú (also rendered Parakupá Vená) means 'waterfall of the deepest place.' Venezuela formally adopted the Pemón name in 2009, after President Hugo Chávez championed it. The English name honors bush pilot Jimmie Angel, who made the falls famous abroad — but the Pemón had always known them; he did not 'discover' them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls; simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls.

question: Jimmie Angel, an American bush pilot, was hunting a rumored bed of gold when he first flew over the falls that now carry his name. In 1937 he tried to land his plane on the mountain's flat summit, but the wheels sank into the boggy ground and stuck fast, and he and his companions had to climb down the cliffs on foot. What became of the plane he left behind?
answer: it stayed stranded on the summit for 33 years
choices: it stayed stranded on the summit for 33 years
it was hauled down for scrap within a year
it slid over the cliff edge in the next storm
it was carried off piece by piece by looters
context: Angel's plane, named 'El Río Caroní,' sat marooned on the summit of Auyán-tepui for 33 years. In 1970 the Venezuelan Air Force lifted it off in sections by helicopter; it was restored and is now displayed at the airport in Ciudad Bolívar. Angel's climb down after the crash took 11 days. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_Falls; jimmieangel.org 'Operation Auyantepui 1970'; countryreports.org.

question: Across southern Venezuela stand dozens of sheer-walled table mountains, whose flat tops rise high and lonely above the rainforest. They are built of some of the oldest rock exposed anywhere on Earth. How do geologists explain these isolated flat-topped giants?
answer: erosion wore away a vast highland, leaving these hard stumps
choices: erosion wore away a vast highland, leaving these hard stumps
lava flows piled up and cooled into flat sheets
an ancient seabed was thrust up and planed flat
desert sand dunes hardened and were lifted high
context: The tepuis are the eroded stumps of a once-continuous sandstone plateau. Their layered quartzite and sandstone — the Roraima Supergroup, roughly 1.7-1.9 billion years old — sit on the Precambrian Guiana Shield, among the oldest exposed rock on Earth. Source: geologyscience.com on Roraima geology; Grokipedia Auyán-tepui (Roraima Supergroup ~1.87 Ga).

question: King Suryavarman II ordered Angkor Wat built in Cambodia about 900 years ago as a temple and a model of the Hindu universe. Its towers, moats, walls and courtyards cover about 400 acres, so huge that Guinness World Records gives it a world title. Which title does it hold?
answer: the largest religious monument in the world
choices: the largest religious monument in the world
the largest building in the world
the largest fortress in the world
the largest palace in the world
context: Guinness lists Angkor Wat as the largest religious structure on Earth — note the word 'religious': it is not the largest building overall, but no house of worship anywhere covers more ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat

question: A royal advisor, not a king, built Banteay Srei, a miniature jewel-box of a temple at Angkor in deep pink-red sandstone; no other great Angkor temple has that story. Its carvings are so crisp, deep and delicate that they seem impossible to cut in hard stone by hand. What does its Khmer name, 'Banteay Srei,' mean?
context: Consecrated in 967 CE and built by the courtier Yajnavaraha rather than a king, Banteay Srei ('Citadel of the Women') is famed for carving so fine it is compared to goldsmith's work or woodcarving. In 1923 the future French writer Andre Malraux was arrested for stealing statues from it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banteay_Srei

question: A carved scene about 49 metres long runs along Angkor Wat's eastern gallery, the largest stone telling of this Hindu myth found anywhere on Earth. A long row of gods and a long row of demons grip a giant serpent and haul it back and forth, spinning the Sea of Milk like a butter churn. In the myth, what magical prize were they struggling to churn up from the ocean?
choices: the first rays of the sun
context: The 'Churning of the Sea of Milk' (Samudra Manthan): gods and demons use the serpent Vasuki as a rope to spin Mount Mandara and churn the ocean for amrita, the nectar of immortality. Angkor Wat's is the largest carved telling in the world. Source: https://www.wmf.org/news/churning-sea-milk-gallery-angkor-cambodia  (Legend.)

question: Monsoon rains drench Angkor for months and then the long dry season sets in, so the Khmer dug colossal rectangular reservoirs by hand to hoard the water and feed their rice fields. The greatest of them, about 7.8 kilometres long, still holds water 900 years on. What is it called?
context: This is the West Baray, a man-made reservoir about 7.8 by 2.1 km with a small island temple, the West Mebon, at its center. It was part of Angkor's immense water grid of canals, moats and embankments spread over roughly 1,000 sq km, and reservoirs like it caught the monsoon rains to irrigate rice through the dry months and supply a city of hundreds of thousands.

question: Archaeologists flew a tight grid over the jungle around Angkor, firing millions of laser pulses at the ground and timing each echo, a technique called LiDAR, to map the earth hidden under the canopy. Only Angkor's stone temples had ever shown above the trees. Stripped of its forest, the map revealed what Angkor truly had been. What did the survey show Angkor to be?
answer: the largest city of the pre-industrial world
choices: the largest city of the pre-industrial world
the oldest walled city in all of Asia
a chain of forts guarding a gold route
a ring of tombs around a sacred lake
context: LiDAR fires laser pulses from a plane and times their return to map ground hidden under vegetation. The 2013 surveys revealed not a lone temple but a planned grid of roads, canals and neighborhoods stretching for miles — the largest city of the entire pre-industrial world. Source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1306539110

question: Scientists reading the growth rings of Angkor's ancient cypress trees found the record of its fall. Angkor slowly emptied across the 1300s and 1400s until the jungle swallowed it, and the rings tie its end to the breakdown of one vast engineered system that Angkor, unlike other medieval cities, had been built entirely around. Which system failed?
context: Angkor was a 'hydraulic city' utterly dependent on its canals and reservoirs. Tree-ring studies of old cypress trees revealed two prolonged megadroughts in the mid-1300s and early 1400s, broken by unusually fierce monsoons, as the climate shifted toward the Little Ice Age. The droughts starved Angkor's reservoirs while the violent rains choked its canals with debris, wrecking the water network and forcing the city's gradual abandonment.

question: At the exact center of Angkor Thom, the walled Khmer capital, rises the Bayon, a temple-mountain of dozens of stone towers packed close together. One thing is carved on those towers over two hundred times, each turned a different way, and it made the Bayon world-famous. What is carved again and again across its towers?
context: These are the famous smiling faces of the Bayon, nicknamed 'the smile of Angkor.' More than 200 survive on the roughly three dozen towers still standing (sources disagree on the original tower count, citing about 49, 54, or 59). When the French writer Pierre Loti reached the temple the faces unnerved him: 'all of a sudden my blood curdled as I saw an enormous smile looking down on me... then three, then five, then ten, appearing in every direction.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon; smarthistory.org/bayon-temple-angkor-thom; cambodgemag.com (quoting Pierre Loti, 'Un pelerin d'Angkor').

question: A woman gives birth, cooks tend open-air fires and people pick lice from one another's hair on the Bayon's lower galleries. Where most ancient temples show gods, kings and battles, these walls show everyday Khmer life. In one scene a ring of men leans in, shouting and placing bets. What contest are they gambling on?
context: The Bayon's outer galleries are famous for carving daily life rather than only gods: a market with women selling fish, a game of chess, and bookies taking bets at a cockfight. They are one of the richest windows we have into how ordinary people actually lived in the medieval Khmer Empire. Sources: factsanddetails.com/southeast-asia/Cambodia (Bayon reliefs); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon.

question: Giant stone faces gaze out in every direction from the towers of the Bayon, and no one can say for certain whom they portray. Many scholars read them as a single holy being repeated hundreds of times; others believe they are the god-king Jayavarman VII himself, watching over every corner of his realm, and some say they are both. Which Buddhist figure do scholars most often see in the faces?
choices: Maitreya, the Buddha yet to come
context: The faces are usually identified with Avalokiteshvara (Lokeshvara), the Mahayana bodhisattva of compassion, but because there is no clear inscription, scholars still debate whether they also portray Jayavarman VII as a god-king, his face broadcast in every direction. The Bayon was the last great state temple built at Angkor, and Jayavarman VII made it Mahayana Buddhist, where Angkor Wat had begun as a Hindu temple. Sources: smarthistory.org/bayon-temple-angkor-thom; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon.

question: The five great gate-towers into Angkor Thom rise nearly 23 m above the moat. At the foot of each tower, on either side of the passage, a huge stone beast rears up with a god riding on its back, its head lowered toward a pool of lotus blossoms. Which of the gods' mounts stands watch over the gateways of the city?
context: The beast is Airavata, the three-headed elephant of the god Indra, its trunks reaching down to pluck lotus flowers while Indra rides on its back. Each of the five gates rises about 23 m and is crowned with four faces pointed to the cardinal directions, so the whole 9-square-km walled city is watched over from its edges inward. Sources: helloangkor.com (Angkor Thom gates); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Thom.

question: Fleets of crowded war canoes ram one another along one of the Bayon's longest panels, while warriors pitch overboard into water thick with fish and crocodiles and a victory feast is carved beneath the fighting. The panel records a real war, not a myth. On which body of water did the Khmer fight this great naval battle?
context: The battle is the Khmers' war against the Chams (from the kingdom of Champa, in what is now central Vietnam), fought on the Tonle Sap, the vast lake at the heart of Cambodia. The Cham warriors can be picked out by their distinctive head coverings. The Bayon carves this real history on the same walls as its gods and myths. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon; lonelyplanet.com (Bayon).

question: Cambodia's flag has a bright red stripe across the middle with blue bands above and below, and on the red one white silhouette: the five stone towers of a temple the Khmer built about 900 years ago, on the flag since 1863. Which temple is it?
context: The five lotus-bud towers on the flag are the silhouette of Angkor Wat, the vast Khmer temple on the plain north of Siem Reap. It sits at the very center of Cambodia's national flag, a white temple silhouette on a broad red band, and has appeared on Cambodian flags since 1863. The temple stayed at the heart of Cambodian identity even as the empire that raised it faded into the jungle.

question: A moat 190 metres wide and more than five kilometres around encircles Angkor Wat. It helped defend the temple -- but on Angkor Wat's stone map of the Hindu universe, this great ring of water was built to stand for something far vaster at the rim of the world. What does the moat of Angkor Wat represent?
context: In Hindu cosmology Mount Meru stands at the center of creation, surrounded by a vast cosmic ocean. Angkor Wat's builders recreated that image: the central towers are Meru and the broad moat is the primordial ocean encircling it. The moat is about 190 m wide and over 5 km around. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat (moat 190 m wide, ~5 km perimeter, representing the cosmic ocean around Meru).

question: The jungle swallowed most of Angkor's temples after the empire faded, splitting them apart with strangler-fig roots and leaving them in ruins. Yet Angkor Wat itself stayed nearly whole. Historians credit one community that never left, keeping up worship inside its walls without a break for some 800 years. Who kept Angkor Wat alive?
context: After the Khmer court shifted toward Phnom Penh in the 1400s, Angkor's other temples were abandoned to the forest, but Theravada Buddhist monks kept living and worshipping at Angkor Wat unbroken for roughly 800 years. That continuous care is a key reason the temple survived far more intact than its neighbours. Source: worldhistory.org/Angkor_Wat (continuous Buddhist worship preserved the temple).

question: One of the most famous carvings in all of Asia runs along a 49-metre gallery of Angkor Wat. Eighty-eight gods grip the head of a giant serpent while 92 demons haul on its tail, straining against each other in a colossal tug-of-war with the snake stretched between them like a living rope. Which Hindu myth is carved here?
answer: the Churning of the Ocean of Milk
choices: the Churning of the Ocean of Milk
the Descent of the River Ganges
the Burning of the Three Cities
the Slaying of the Buffalo Demon
context: This is the Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra Manthan). To win amrita, the nectar of immortality, gods (devas) and demons (asuras) churn the cosmic sea, using the serpent Vasuki as their rope wound around Mount Mandara. Angkor Wat's relief shows 88 devas and 92 asuras -- and in the story, the moment they succeed they fall to fighting over the prize. Source: penang-traveltips.com (49 m relief, 88 devas / 92 asuras); britannica.com/topic/churning-of-the-ocean-of-milk.  (Legend.)

question: King Suryavarman II gave Angkor Wat a main gate facing west, toward the setting sun, where nearly every other Khmer temple opens toward the sunrise. Its long wall carvings also run counter-clockwise, the reverse of the usual order. Scholars read these two choices as a clue to a purpose beyond worship. What was Angkor Wat most likely built to be?
context: West is the direction of the setting sun and, in Hindu belief, of death and the god Yama. Angkor Wat's westward orientation and its counter-clockwise (prasavya) reliefs -- the reverse of the auspicious order -- lead many scholars to conclude that Suryavarman II built it as his own funerary temple and mausoleum. He was known after death as Paramavishnuloka, 'he who has gone to the supreme world of Vishnu.' Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Angkor_Wat (west = death, funerary temple, prasavya reliefs).  (Legend.)

question: Angkor Wat's great carving of gods and demons hauling on a serpent shows a disaster in the making: the mountain they are spinning with it begins to sink into the ocean, threatening to ruin everything. To rescue it, the god Vishnu plunges beneath the waves in the shape of a giant animal and bears the mountain up from the depths. Into what creature does Vishnu transform?
context: The turtle is Kurma, the second avatar of Vishnu. As the churning drags Mount Mandara down into the Ocean of Milk, Vishnu becomes the great turtle Kurma and supports the mountain on his shell from the sea-floor; at the very center of Angkor Wat's relief he appears again in human form, steadying it. Source: penang-traveltips.com (Vishnu's turtle avatar Kurma supporting Mount Mandara).  (Legend.)

question: The Khmer builders of Angkor Wat needed as many as ten million blocks of sandstone, some weighing a tonne and a half apiece, and no stone like it lies near the temple. They quarried every block from a single holy mountain about 50 kilometres away and floated them to the site along a network of canals. From which mountain did all that sandstone come?
context: The sandstone came from Phnom Kulen (Mount Kulen), a plateau some 40-50 km to the northeast that the Khmer revered as the birthplace of their empire. Workers cut 5-10 million blocks and floated them to Angkor along purpose-built canals -- one of the great logistical feats of the ancient world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat (Kulen sandstone, 5-10 million blocks up to 1.5 t, canal transport).

question: The wind at one spot on Earth averages about 80 km/h across a whole year: not a rare gust, but the everyday average. Its blizzards have torn past 240 km/h, and Guinness World Records calls it the windiest place of all. Which place is it?
context: Commonwealth Bay, on the coast of East Antarctica -- and Cape Denison on its shore, where Douglas Mawson built his hut -- is listed by Guinness World Records and the National Geographic Atlas as the windiest place at sea level on Earth. The cause isn't a passing storm: freezing air pours off the high inland ice sheet and funnels down to this exact stretch of coast almost without pause, so the yearly AVERAGE wind speed is already a gale. Death Valley is the hottest place, the Atacama the driest non-polar desert, and Vostok the coldest -- each holds a different record. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Bay

question: Douglas Mawson and his Australasian Antarctic Expedition wintered in a hut at Cape Denison in 1912, on what turned out to be the windiest coast on Earth. When Mawson wrote the story of those brutal years, he gave the book a title that has clung to the place ever since. What did he call it?
choices: The Worst Journey in the World
context: Mawson published The Home of the Blizzard in 1915, and the name stuck to Cape Denison. His Australasian Antarctic Expedition of 1911-14 had pitched camp, without knowing it, on the windiest coast on Earth, where freezing air pours down off the high ice sheet to the sea almost without pause. The expedition's wooden main hut still stands on that shore, kept as a historic site. Source: antarctica.gov.au -- 'Home of the Blizzard' book; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mawson%27s_Huts

question: High on the frozen East Antarctic plateau, about 3,488 m up and far from any coast, one lonely research station took its reading on 21 July 1983: -89.2 °C, the coldest air temperature ever recorded at a weather station anywhere on Earth. A home freezer sits at about -18 °C. Which station holds that record?
context: Vostok Station, a Russian base, sits about 3,488 m (11,444 ft) up on the East Antarctic ice sheet, roughly 1,300 km from the South Pole -- the great height and the distance from any warming ocean are why the air there turns so brutally cold. One careful detail: -89.2 C is the coldest AIR temperature ever measured at a weather station. Satellites later spotted even colder ICE-SURFACE patches on the plateau (about -94.7 C in 2010), but those are surface readings, not official air records, so both facts stay true. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_Station

question: Drills bored nearly 4 km down through the ice of East Antarctica and reached a liquid freshwater lake about 250 km long and 50 km wide, about the size of Lake Ontario, sealed away from sunlight and air for roughly 15 million years. It is the largest of some 675 lakes known to hide beneath the frozen continent's ice. What is this buried lake called?
context: It is Lake Vostok -- the largest of Antarctica's roughly 675 known subglacial lakes, about 250 km long by 50 km wide, sealed beneath some 4 km of ice for perhaps 15 million years. On 5 February 2012 Russian scientists finished drilling the longest ice core ever (about 3,768 m) and finally broke through to its surface, water no light had touched in millions of years. Lakes Whillans, Ellsworth, and Concordia are other real subglacial lakes, but far smaller. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Vostok

question: Wind scours Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys so hard that snow evaporates before it can settle, leaving the largest bare, ice-free stretch of the continent, where parts may not have seen rain in nearly two million years. NASA has tested rovers and drills there since the 1970s as Earth's closest match to one other world. Which world?
context: The same katabatic winds that hammer the coast keep the McMurdo Dry Valleys -- about 4,500 sq km, the largest ice-free region in Antarctica -- swept clear of snow, leaving cold, rainless, almost lifeless ground. Since the Viking program, NASA has used the valleys as its closest earthly stand-in for the Martian surface. Taylor Glacier here also feeds 'Blood Falls,' a five-storey outflow stained red by iron-rich brine. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMurdo_Dry_Valleys

question: The Transantarctic Mountains run across Antarctica and split its ice in two, a larger sheet and a smaller one. The larger is so vast that if it alone melted, seas around the world would rise by more than 50 metres. What is this larger ice sheet called?
context: The East Antarctic Ice Sheet holds most of Antarctica's ice: melted completely, it would raise global sea level by about 52 metres. The far smaller West Antarctic Ice Sheet lies on the other side of the Transantarctic Mountains, while the Ross and Ronne are floating ice shelves along the coast, not ice sheets. Source: grokipedia.com/page/East_Antarctic_Ice_Sheet

question: An ice sheet kilometres thick buries a continent at the bottom of the world. It holds roughly 90% of the planet's ice and about 70% of its fresh water, more than every river, lake and glacier elsewhere combined. Which is Earth's greatest freshwater store?
context: Antarctica holds about 90% of all the ice on Earth and roughly 70% of the planet's fresh water — by far Earth's greatest freshwater store. Greenland's ice sheet is a distant second; Lake Baikal is the largest single body of liquid fresh water but tiny beside the frozen continent. Source: British Antarctic Survey Antarctic factsheet; Wikipedia: Antarctica.

question: Antarctica is buried in ice, yet its frozen interior almost never sees new snow: barely 150 mm of moisture falls there in a year, less than in the Sahara. Geographers judge land like this by how little water falls, not by heat. That makes the continent the world's largest what?
context: A desert is defined by how little precipitation it gets, not by heat. Antarctica's interior receives only about 150 mm (6 in) a year — drier than the Sahara — making the frozen continent the largest desert on Earth. Source: Wikipedia: Antarctica ('a polar desert... about 150 mm of water per year').

question: Researchers come and go from Antarctica's research stations, but no one lives there for good, and the continent has no native people. In 1959 twelve nations signed a landmark treaty on its future. Under that Antarctic Treaty, who owns Antarctica?
answer: No nation owns it, only science and peace
choices: No nation owns it, only science and peace
The twelve treaty nations, as joint owners
The United Nations, as a neutral trustee
Each nation, in the sector it once claimed
context: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze every territorial claim and set the whole continent aside for peace and science, banning military bases, mining, and nuclear weapons. No country owns Antarctica; only about 1,000–5,000 scientists live there seasonally, with no permanent residents. Source: Wikipedia: Antarctica (Antarctic Treaty System).

question: A slow trickle the deep red of blood seeps from the snout of Taylor Glacier in East Antarctica and spreads across the pure white ice. Robert Falcon Scott's men stumbled onto it in 1911 and were unsettled, for the crimson stain looked like a wound cut into the glacier. It is not blood at all. What stains the water at Blood Falls that eerie red?
answer: Iron-rich brine that rusts in the air
choices: Iron-rich brine that rusts in the air
Red algae blooming in the meltwater
Fine red dust blown off the rocks
Pink minerals dissolved from the ice
context: Blood Falls flows from the snout of Taylor Glacier. Iron-rich saltwater, sealed beneath the ice and cut off from air and sunlight for about 1.5–2 million years, oxidizes — literally rusts — the instant it reaches the surface, staining the ice blood-red. Source: Wikipedia: Blood Falls.

question: Scientists have measured the Antarctic ice sheet all across the frozen continent with radar; under its snow and glaciers lies ordinary bedrock, but reaching it would mean drilling through an astonishing depth of ice. The ice is thickest of all in Terre Adélie, the French-claimed sector facing the Southern Ocean. How deep does it go there?
context: Antarctica's ice averages about 1.9 km thick and reaches its greatest measured thickness of roughly 4,776 m — nearly 3 miles — in Terre Adélie. Source: British Antarctic Survey Antarctic factsheet; Wikipedia: Antarctica.

question: Gales pour across the coast of Antarctica at up to about 300 km/h, among the fiercest winds on Earth, and along some stretches they blow almost every day of the year, summer and winter alike. Geographers call them katabatic winds. What drives them?
answer: cold, heavy air sliding downhill off the ice sheet
choices: cold, heavy air sliding downhill off the ice sheet
warm sea air rushing inland to fill a gap
storms circling endlessly round the Southern Ocean
jet-stream winds dragged down to the ground
context: Katabatic winds (from the Greek katabasis, 'descent') form as cold, dense air on the high plateau slides downhill under gravity, reaching about 300 km/h. At Commonwealth Bay, explorer Douglas Mawson (1911–14) endured such ceaseless katabatic gales that he titled his account 'The Home of the Blizzard'; Guinness rates it the windiest place on Earth. Source: Wikipedia: Katabatic wind / Commonwealth Bay.

question: The weight of Antarctica's ice sheet, trillions of tons, has crushed the continent's bedrock far below sea level: at the Bentley Subglacial Trench the buried rock lies 2,555 m down, the lowest land on Earth not under the ocean. If the ice were somehow stripped away, what would the bedrock do over the thousands of years that followed?
answer: It would slowly rise back upward
choices: It would slowly rise back upward
It would slowly sink even deeper
It would stay fixed at its crushed depth
It would crack apart and drift out to sea
context: The ice's colossal weight has pressed Antarctica's bedrock below sea level in many places — the Bentley Subglacial Trench, 2,555 m down, is the lowest land on Earth not covered by ocean. Freed of the ice, the crust would slowly rebound upward over millennia (in places by roughly 1,500 ft), a balancing of load and buoyancy that geologists call isostasy. Source: Wikipedia: Bentley Subglacial Trench; UAF Geophysical Institute.

question: Leaves of the extinct Glossopteris tree, which grew more than 260 million years ago, lie fossilized in the rocks of Antarctica, Africa, South America, India and Australia. Those matching fossils were the first sign that all these southern lands had once been joined into one huge supercontinent. What was that lost landmass called?
context: Glossopteris fossil forests over 260 million years old show Antarctica was once a green corner of Gondwana, the great southern supercontinent (with today's Africa, South America, India, and Australia). Growing through months-long polar light and dark, the trees slammed from summer growth into winter dormancy in as little as a month. Source: ScienceDaily / National Geographic: Antarctic Gondwana fossil forests (Gulbranson & Isbell).

question: Families at Çatalhöyük, a town in central Turkey almost 9,000 years ago, lived in mud-brick houses packed together wall to wall like a giant honeycomb, with no streets between them and no doors on the sides. How did families get inside their homes?
answer: They climbed down a ladder through a hole in the roof.
choices: They climbed down a ladder through a hole in the roof.
They crawled through a low tunnel linking house to house.
They walked in from a shared central courtyard.
They pushed aside a mat over a ground-level door.
context: The flat rooftops were Çatalhöyük's real streets -- its walkways and gathering places -- and every home had a hole in the ceiling with a ladder leading down into one main room. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Çatalhöyük.

question: When someone died at Çatalhöyük, one of the world's earliest towns, on the plain of south-central Turkey about 9,000 years ago, the family folded the body tightly, knees drawn up to the chest, and sometimes wrapped it in a reed mat before burial. Where did families lay their dead to rest?
answer: Under the floors and sleeping platforms of their homes.
choices: Under the floors and sleeping platforms of their homes.
Out in a walled cemetery on the edge of town.
Deep in caves in the hills beyond the fields.
Down in pits dug out in the open fields.
context: So every family slept directly above its own buried ancestors. Years later they sometimes dug a skull back up, plastered it, and painted the face with red ochre to bring back the features of the dead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Çatalhöyük.

question: A painter at Çatalhöyük decorated a wall about 8,600 years ago with what looks like a town seen from above and a two-peaked volcano erupting behind it, and the picture is often called the world's oldest map. But Stephanie Meece, an archaeologist, argued that the shape everyone reads as a volcano is really something ordinary. What did she say it was?
context: Meece's rival reading is a leopard skin above an abstract geometric panel -- not a map at all -- and the debate is still open. Fifty years on, geologists tested pumice from Hasan Dağ and confirmed it really did erupt between about 9,500 and 8,400 years ago, overlapping the painting's age; that revived the 'oldest map' reading without proving it. Source: sci.news/archaeology and pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (Schmitt et al.).  (Legend.)

question: A flat-topped limestone rock rises about 70 metres out of the streets of Athens, a natural fortress in the middle of the city. Marble temples built roughly 2,500 years ago still crown its summit, in sight from almost anywhere in town. What is this rock called?
context: 'Acropolis' means 'high city' (from Greek akron, 'highest point,' + polis, 'city'). This flat-topped limestone rock rises about 70 m above Athens (156 m above the sea) and spans roughly 300 by 150 m on top -- a natural citadel that Athenians crowned with their greatest temples. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acropolis_of_Athens ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Acropolis/

question: Visitors climbing to the Parthenon in Athens, the temple raised for the goddess Athena around 440 BC, expect its white marble to shine chalk-white in the strong Greek sun. But tiny traces of iron inside the stone slowly react with air and sun. What does the Parthenon's marble do instead?
context: Pentelic marble carries a faint trace of iron; as it weathers, the iron oxidizes and tints the stone a warm honey-gold, so the Parthenon seems to glow in the sun and at dusk. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentelic_marble

question: The Athenians built the Parthenon, their great marble temple, to honour the goddess Athena, and named it after one of her own titles: Athena Parthenos. What does the Greek word parthenos mean?
context: Parthenos means 'maiden' or 'virgin' -- a title of Athena, who in myth never married. Her temple, the Parthenon, is literally the house of the maiden goddess. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_Parthenos ; https://www.worldhistory.org/article/785/athena-parthenos-by-phidias/

question: Socrates would stop passersby with his endless questions in the busy open square below the great rock of Athens, where people came to trade, gossip and argue. It was the public heart of the ancient city. What was this open square called?
context: 'Agora' means 'gathering place.' The Athenian Agora was the city's civic center -- markets, law courts, and shrines -- and the stage on which its democracy and philosophy played out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Agora_of_Athens

question: A Doric temple from the 400s BC stands on a low hill above the old marketplace of Athens, still almost completely intact, its roof, columns and walls all in place, while the ruined Parthenon looms on the rock above. Which temple is this, the best-preserved in all of ancient Greece?
context: The Temple of Hephaestus (the Hephaisteion), god of the forge and metalworkers, was built around 450 BC on the western edge of the Agora. Never destroyed like the Parthenon, it still stands almost whole -- roof and all -- making it the most complete ancient Greek temple in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Agora_of_Athens

question: Iktinos and Kallikrates, the architects of the Parthenon, hid a subtle trick in its marble: the temple looks flawlessly straight and rectangular, yet hardly a line in the whole building is actually straight. What did they do to its columns?
answer: they made the columns swell in the middle and lean slightly inward
choices: they made the columns swell in the middle and lean slightly inward
they made the columns taper to a sharp point near the top
they made the columns twist in a slow spiral toward the roof
they made the columns lean slightly outward, over the viewer
context: This is entasis: the columns bulge gently at the middle and tilt inward (their axes would meet more than a kilometer overhead), while the marble floor rises a few centimeters at its center. These deliberate curves trick the eye so the temple LOOKS perfectly straight and alive rather than stiff. Source: https://archeyes.com/the-parthenon-architectural-excellence-of-ancient-greece/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon

question: Teams hauled some 20,000 tons of white marble roughly 19 km to build the Parthenon in the 400s BC, by ox-cart, sled and sheer human muscle, and dragged every block up onto the sacred rock of Athens. All of it came out of one single mountain, and Greek quarrymen gave the marble itself that mountain's name. From which mountain did the Parthenon's marble come?
context: The marble came from Mount Pentelicus (Penteli), source of the fine white 'Pentelic' marble that built the Parthenon. An estimated 20,000-22,000 tons were quarried and dragged some 19 km down to Athens and up onto the Acropolis. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentelic_marble ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon_Frieze

question: The Erechtheion, a smaller temple beside the Parthenon in Athens, holds up the marble roof of one porch not on plain columns but on six calm, graceful stone women, each carrying the weight on her head. What are these sculpted figures called?
context: They are the Caryatids -- six marble maidens on the Erechtheion's Porch of the Maidens (about 421-406 BC). The weathered originals now shelter inside the Acropolis Museum, with copies outdoors; Lord Elgin carried one away to the British Museum in London, where it still stands apart from its sisters. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erechtheion

question: Phidias, the sculptor, made an image of the goddess Athena nearly 12 m tall, and in 438 BC it was dedicated inside the Parthenon. It was a treasure so valuable that it was later stripped bare and finally lost forever. What two costly materials was this colossal statue made of?
context: This was the Athena Parthenos, made by Phidias of gold and ivory over a wooden frame -- a technique called chryselephantine. About 11.5 m tall, it wore some 40 talents of pure, removable gold and held a small winged Victory in its hand. The statue vanished in antiquity; only small Roman copies survive. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_Parthenos ; https://greekreporter.com/2023/09/02/statue-athena-parthenos-acropolis/
