question: A Venetian army was besieging the Ottoman garrison on the rock of Athens in 1687, during the Morean War, when one of its mortars scored a direct hit on the Parthenon. The temple had stood nearly whole for more than 2,000 years, serving in turn as a Greek temple, a Christian church and finally a mosque. What had the Ottoman soldiers stored inside it?
context: On September 26, 1687, a Venetian mortar fired by Francesco Morosini from the nearby Hill of Philopappos struck the gunpowder the Ottomans had stored inside the Parthenon. The explosion blew off the roof, collapsed the temple's center, killed about 300 people, and brought down three-fifths of its carved frieze -- ending more than 2,000 years of near-wholeness in a single instant. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon

question: About fifty low, rounded hills rise one by one out of the streets and parks of Auckland, New Zealand's biggest city: Mount Eden, One Tree Hill and dozens more. All of them are the same kind of landform. What are they?
context: Auckland sits on the Auckland Volcanic Field — roughly 53 separate volcanic centres of scoria cones, craters, and lava hills scattered across the city. It is a live basaltic field, still capable of erupting. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_volcanic_field

question: On sunny weekends tens of thousands of small yachts and dinghies crowd the harbour of Auckland, New Zealand's largest city, their white triangles filling the view. Its people own more boats per person than almost anyone else on Earth. What nickname has Auckland been given?
context: Auckland was officially dubbed the 'City of Sails' in 1985. It has long had more boats per head than almost anywhere on Earth — once about one boat for every three households — with tens of thousands moored around its harbours. Source: ahi.auckland.ac.nz/2021/12/11/whats-in-a-name-calling-auckland-through-time/

question: An island volcano rose straight out of the sea off Auckland only about 600 years ago, the biggest and youngest volcano of the whole area, with a near-perfect cone. What is this young island volcano called?
context: Rangitoto rose from the sea around 1450 CE and is so young its lava makes up about 41% of everything the whole field has ever erupted. Its near-perfect symmetrical shield-cone silhouette is the iconic backdrop to Auckland's harbour. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangitoto_Island

question: Archaeologists digging on the island of Motutapu, off Auckland, worked down between layers of volcanic ash that the neighbouring island volcano had dropped on it in a fresh eruption. There they found a startling trace of the Māori who had lived beside the volcano. What did they find preserved in the ash?
context: On Motutapu, next to Rangitoto, human footprints were found preserved between layers of Rangitoto's volcanic ash — Maori walking across the fresh ashfall, the clearest evidence that people witnessed the eruption within living memory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangitoto_Island

question: The fifty-odd hills of Auckland, Mount Eden and One Tree Hill among them, belong to a volcanic field that can still erupt. Geologists call it a monogenetic field, and that one word shapes their forecast. Where do they think Auckland's next eruption will start?
answer: at a brand-new vent no one can yet pinpoint
choices: at a brand-new vent no one can yet pinpoint
inside Rangitoto, the youngest of the cones
beneath Mount Eden, the isthmus's highest cone
in the oldest cone, long overdue to erupt
context: A monogenetic field erupts each new volcano at a new vent, then abandons it forever (Rangitoto is the lone repeat, in two phases about 50 years apart). Because of this, geologists expect Auckland's next eruption to break out not from an old crater but at a brand-new, presently unknown location. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_volcanic_field

question: Long before European sailors arrived, Māori lived on the narrow neck of land where Auckland now stands, squeezed between two harbours, and fought over it because it was such rich ground for kumara gardens, fishing and trade. In their language they knew the place as Tāmaki Makaurau. What does that Māori name mean?
context: Tamaki Makaurau is usually translated 'Tamaki desired by many' (or 'Tamaki of a hundred lovers'). Its fertile volcanic soils and two harbours made it the most sought-after and fought-over ground in the north. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland

question: King U-Thong founded Ayutthaya, the royal capital of Siam, where three rivers meet, safely above the reach of the ocean tides, so that no enemy warship could sail up and attack it. What kind of landform did this river-guarded capital stand on?
context: Set on its river island, Ayutthaya was founded in 1350 by King U-Thong (crowned Ramathibodi I) and grew so laced with canals that European traders nicknamed it 'the Venice of the East.' The ring of water was chosen partly because the site sat above the reach of the Gulf of Siam's tides, so enemy seagoing warships could not sail straight up to the walls. Source: UNESCO Historic City of Ayutthaya (whc.unesco.org/en/list/576); Wikipedia, Ayutthaya Kingdom.

question: In the ruins of Wat Mahathat rests the single most photographed sight in all of Ayutthaya, sitting right at ground level. It is something serene and beautifully carved, held tight in the twisting roots of an old fig tree that grew up around it across the centuries. What do the roots cradle?
context: The image is old sandstone. A strangler fig earns its name: it begins as a seed a bird drops high in another tree, then sends aerial roots creeping down the host's trunk that thicken into a lattice and slowly envelop it — here embracing a lost Buddha head. How the head came to rest here is uncertain; by tradition it was simply left among the rubble as the old temple fell into ruin, and the fig did the rest. Thais treat the spot as sacred. Source: Wikipedia, Ayutthaya Historical Park; Britannica, strangler fig; thailand-highlights.com.  (Legend.)

question: A Buddha 42 metres long, longer than a blue whale, lies stretched on his side at Wat Lokayasutharam in Ayutthaya, his head propped on one hand, calm with eyes half-closed. The great reclining pose marks one exact moment in the Buddha's life. Which moment does it show?
choices: his birth in a grove of trees
the day he gives his first sermon
context: A reclining Buddha traditionally depicts the parinirvana — the Buddha lying on his right side at the end of his earthly life, passing into final Nirvana. This one, of brick and stucco, faces west and is among the largest reclining images in Thailand. Source: thaizer.com; renown-travel.com, Wat Lokaya Sutha.

question: Three tall, bell-shaped stone chedis stand in a perfect line at Wat Phra Si Sanphet, once the grandest royal temple inside Ayutthaya's palace — today the postcard image of the whole ruined city. These towers were all raised for the same solemn purpose. What do they hold?
choices: the crown jewels of old Siam
context: The three chedis are royal reliquaries: they hold the ashes of King Borommatrailokkanat and two of his royal successors. Wat Phra Si Sanphet housed no monks — it was the private royal chapel of the palace. Source: thailandforvisitors.com, Wat Si Sanphet; renown-travel.com.

question: Merchant ships sailed in from far away to Ayutthaya around 1700, when it was one of the largest cities on Earth, perhaps home to nearly a million people, more than London. Portuguese, Dutch, Chinese and Japanese traders all did business there. How did this river capital house its foreign communities?
answer: each nation had its own riverside quarter
choices: each nation had its own riverside quarter
all foreigners shared one walled compound
foreigners could stay only aboard their ships
traders lived inside the royal palace walls
context: Each foreign community kept its own district strung along the rivers. The Japanese village, Ban Yipun, held about 1,000 people under the mercenary Yamada Nagamasa, whom the king raised to noble rank (Okya Senaphimuk); and a Greek adventurer, Constantine Phaulkon, rose from common sailor to become one of King Narai's most powerful ministers. The near-million population figure (per researcher George Modelski) is an estimate. Source: Wikipedia, Ayutthaya Kingdom; southeastasianarchaeology.com.  (Legend.)

question: Along the brick galleries of Ayutthaya's ruined temples, long rows of stone Buddhas still sit in meditation, but almost every statue is broken in exactly the same way. That is the mark left by Burmese soldiers who overran and looted the capital in 1767. What did the soldiers do to the statues?
context: The invaders decapitated the sacred images and prised the gold from them; the long rows of headless Buddhas are among the ruins' most haunting sights. Source: Wikipedia, Ayutthaya Historical Park; thailand-highlights.com.

question: Six honey-gold limestone columns still rise in a row from Jupiter's temple at Baalbek, in the mountains of Lebanon, after nearly two thousand years. They are the tallest columns the Romans raised on any temple in their empire. About how tall is one of them?
answer: as tall as a six-story building
choices: as tall as a single-story cottage
as tall as a six-story building
as tall as a fifteen-story tower
as tall as a thirty-story skyscraper
context: Each of the six survivors stands about 19.9 m (65 ft) tall and nearly 2.5 m thick -- the largest temple columns anywhere in the Roman world. The Temple of Jupiter once had 54 of them, ten across each end and nineteen down each side; earthquakes and stone-robbers toppled the rest. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Jupiter_(Baalbek)

question: Three giant blocks, the Trilithon, sit in the western wall of the temple at Baalbek exactly where Roman builders placed them two thousand years ago, each about 800 tonnes and over 19 m long. One thing about them still astonishes visitors today. What is it?
answer: the blocks fit so tightly no knife blade slips between them
choices: the blocks were floated to the site down a river canal
the blocks fit so tightly no knife blade slips between them
the blocks are carved with the names of the men who cut them
the blocks are hollow inside to reduce their great weight
context: A knife blade still won't slide into the joints between the three Trilithon blocks, set in the western podium wall over 4 m up. They rest on a lower course of about two dozen 'smaller' foundation stones -- each of those still weighs around 300 tonnes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Jupiter_(Baalbek)

question: In the quarry just outside Baalbek lies a colossal cut block of about 1,000 tonnes that Roman workers shaped but abandoned -- it was never dragged to the temple. For centuries local people have known this stranded giant by a vivid nickname. What is it called?
answer: the Stone of the Pregnant Woman
choices: the Stone of the Pregnant Woman
context: The 'Stone of the Pregnant Woman' (Hajar al-Hibla) still lies in the quarry, roughly 1,000 tonnes (some estimates up to 1,200). Folk legends say a pregnant woman, or a race of giants, once lifted it -- but in truth it was simply left where Roman quarrymen carved it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baalbek_Stones

question: Archaeologists at Baalbek, in Lebanon, long knew that the Romans broke ground on Jupiter's enormous temple around 16 BC, but no one could pin down when it was finished. The answer, about AD 60 under the emperor Nero, was settled not by any grand imperial inscription but by a small, surprising clue an ordinary workman left on the stones. What was that clue?
answer: a line of graffiti scratched by a worker
choices: a hoard of coins buried in the foundation
a dedication carved in the emperor's honor
a line of graffiti scratched by a worker
a sundial set into the temple floor
context: The completion date was fixed from a scratch of graffiti a worker left on one of the topmost column drums -- so the temple took roughly 75 years to raise. Everyday marks like this often date ancient buildings more precisely than grand official inscriptions. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Jupiter_(Baalbek)

question: Baalbek's builders had already set 800-tonne blocks into the temple wall -- but in 2014 a German Archaeological Institute team found an even greater one at the ancient site: a single limestone block roughly 19.6 m long and about 1,650 tonnes. What record does the Baalbek block hold?
answer: the largest stone block ever cut by human hands
choices: the largest stone block ever cut by human hands
the largest stone block ever polished by human hands
the largest stone block ever moved by human hands
the largest stone block ever raised by human hands
context: A German Archaeological Institute team led by Jeanine Abdul Massih measured the block at about 19.6 m long, 6 m wide, 5.5 m high, and roughly 1,650 tonnes -- the largest stone ever cut by people anywhere on Earth. It was carved but never dragged from the quarry: flawed limestone at one edge meant it might crack if anyone tried to move it, so it still lies exactly where the quarrymen shaped it -- which is why it holds the record for the largest block ever CUT, not moved or raised. Source: heritagedaily.com; smithsonianmag.com; archaeology.org

question: Jean-Pierre Adam, an engineer, took on the puzzle of how Rome's crews moved Baalbek's 800-tonne Trilithon stones, which lie inside a temple Roman builders raised. He calculated that about 512 men could drag a stone of more than 500 tonnes across the ground. In his reconstruction, what did those men rely on?
context: No one has proved exactly how Rome's crews shifted the 800-tonne Trilithon, and that open question is genuine -- but the answer is human, not alien: the megaliths lie beneath a temple Roman builders demonstrably raised. Engineer Jean-Pierre Adam calculated that about 512 men working capstans (rope-winding drums) and pulley blocks could drag a 557-tonne stone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baalbek

question: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon, raised by King Nebuchadnezzar II around 575 BC, glowed deep blue. Its glazed bricks were fired to match the most prized blue stone of the ancient world, mined in the distant mountains of Afghanistan. Which stone did it imitate?
context: Facing an entire city gate in the color of lapis lazuli -- one of the ancient world's most treasured stones -- announced Babylon's wealth to everyone who approached. Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ishtar_Gate/

question: Babylon's ruins, the remains of a city of ziggurats and the blue Ishtar Gate, lie in Iraq about 85 km south of Baghdad. The city rose right on the bank of one of the two great rivers of its plain. On which river did ancient Babylon stand?
context: Babylon stood near the modern Iraqi town of Hillah, and the Euphrates ran through the very heart of the city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon

question: Rows of golden animals stride across the Ishtar Gate's deep-blue walls: wild bulls, lions, and a stranger scaly beast called the mushhushshu, with a serpent's head and a flicking forked tongue. The lions belonged to the goddess Ishtar. The dragon was the sacred beast of which of Babylon's gods?
context: Marduk was Babylon's supreme god, and the mushhushshu was his guardian creature; the wild bulls on the gate honored the storm-god Adad. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishtar_Gate

question: The mushhushshu, the sacred dragon striding across the Ishtar Gate, is stitched together from several animals. It has a snake's scaly body and forked tongue, a horned and crested head, and powerful front legs taken from a lion. Its two hind feet come from a very different creature. What are the mushhushshu's back feet?
context: This snake-lion-eagle mix made the mushhushshu one of the strangest monsters in all of ancient art; its Sumerian name means roughly 'furious serpent.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mushhushshu

question: The Babylonians called their city Bab-ilim, two Akkadian words spoken more than three thousand years ago in what is now Iraq. They, and the later scholars who read their clay tablets, took the two words together to name something grand and holy, fit for a city full of temples and ziggurats. What was Bab-ilim traditionally taken to mean?
context: Modern scholars think this is a folk etymology laid over an older, forgotten name -- but for the ancients, Babylon was the gate of the gods. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylon

question: King Nebuchadnezzar II, who raised the Ishtar Gate around 575 BC, left a proud inscription carved on it. He wrote that he had set wild bulls and fierce dragons upon the gate for one reason above all others. By his own words, why did he cover the gate in beasts?
answer: so that people might gaze on them in wonder
choices: so that people might gaze on them in wonder
so that no enemy would dare approach
so that the gods would guard the city
so that his name would never be forgotten
context: His dedication reads that he adorned the gateways 'with luxurious splendor so that people might gaze on them in wonder.' Source: https://www.worldhistory.org/Ishtar_Gate/

question: Archaeologists dug up the shattered bricks of Babylon's Ishtar Gate in the early 1900s and carried them thousands of miles away from Iraq. There they rebuilt the gate, 14 metres high, indoors in a world-famous museum, where visitors pass through it today. In which museum does the Ishtar Gate stand?
context: The archaeologist Robert Koldewey excavated the gate's bricks between 1902 and 1914, and the reconstruction was finished in Berlin in 1930. Even so, only the smaller front gate was rebuilt -- the original was a far larger double gate. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishtar_Gate

question: A grand ceremonial road ran straight out through Babylon's Ishtar Gate toward the city's great temple, its high walls glazed with rows of striding golden lions that seemed to march along beside every traveller. The Babylonians gave this Processional Way a proud, boastful name in their own tongue: 'Aibur-shabu.' What did that name mean?
choices: The sun shall never set here
The road shall shine with gold
context: The road ran over half a mile out to the Bit Akitu, the New Year festival house; each spring the statue of the god Marduk was carried in procession down it and out through the gate. Source: https://madainproject.com/processional_street

question: A colossal stepped temple-tower, a ziggurat, once rose over Babylon, and its name meant 'the foundation of heaven and earth.' It most likely stood behind the Bible's tale of the Tower of Babel, a great tower built to reach the sky. What was this real ziggurat called?
context: Etemenanki was dedicated to Marduk and rebuilt by Babylon's kings. Centuries later Alexander the Great ordered the crumbling tower torn down to be rebuilt grander -- but he died in 323 BC before the work was done. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etemenanki

question: Robert Koldewey, the archaeologist who uncovered the Ishtar Gate, saw that its lions and bulls were plainly real animals, and he began to wonder about the mushhushshu dragon striding among them. In 1918 he suggested the strange beast might be modeled on a real creature known only from fossils. What did Koldewey compare the mushhushshu to?
context: Koldewey reasoned that if the gate's lions and bulls were real animals, the dragon might be too -- perhaps a dinosaur remembered in legend. Most scholars, though, think the mushhushshu was always a purely mythical guardian. Source: https://new-cryptozoology.fandom.com/wiki/Sirrush

question: Stephanie Dalley, an Oxford scholar, argues that Babylon's most famous wonder, the Hanging Gardens, was real but bloomed in a different city entirely. The gardens were counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, yet they have left no ruins and no foundation anywhere in Babylon's soil. Which city does Dalley name?
context: Legend said King Nebuchadnezzar II built the gardens for his homesick wife, Queen Amytis, who missed her green mountain homeland -- but the Hanging Gardens are the only one of the Seven Wonders whose site has never been confirmed. Dalley argues the real gardens were built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib at Nineveh. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging_Gardens_of_Babylon

question: Hot-air balloons float over the plain of Bagan in Myanmar at dawn, and temple spires poke from the trees in every direction. Kings and nobles raised them along the Irrawaddy about a thousand years ago, to earn merit for the next life. About how many still stand?
context: Over 2,200 brick temples and pagodas still stand on the Bagan plain today, scattered along a bend of the Irrawaddy River. The famous dawn balloons -- Balloons Over Bagan has flown the dry-season skies since 1999 -- drift over the whole misty field as the sun comes up. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagan)

question: The kings of the Pagan Kingdom ruled from Bagan between 1044 and 1287 and covered its plain with monuments. The ones that still stand today are only the leftovers. How many temples, pagodas and monasteries had been built across the plain at the kingdom's peak?
context: At its height, more than 10,000 temples, pagodas, and monasteries rose on the Bagan plain during the Pagan Kingdom (1044-1287). Centuries of neglect, looting, and earthquakes have since thinned them to the roughly 2,200 that survive. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagan)

question: Four gilded Buddhas, each over 9 metres tall, stand in the dim inner corridors of Bagan's most beloved temple, one facing each point of the compass. The whitewashed shrine, crowned with a golden spire, was completed in 1105 under King Kyansittha. By what name is it known?
context: The Ananda Temple, finished in 1105 under King Kyansittha, is Bagan's best-loved shrine. Its four standing gilded Buddhas each rise 9.5 m (31 ft) and face north, south, east, and west; the spires were re-gilded for the temple's 900th anniversary in 1990. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ananda_Temple)

question: King Narathu raised Bagan's largest temple, the brooding Dhammayangyi, around 1167. Legend says he had murdered his own father and brother to seize the throne, and that guilt drove him to demand masonry so flawless that no gap could be found between the great blocks; any mason whose work fell short was executed. According to the legend, what was Narathu's test for a tight-enough joint?
answer: Whether a needle could pass between two blocks
choices: Whether a needle could pass between two blocks
Whether water could seep through the seam
Whether a hair could be drawn through the gap
Whether daylight showed through the joint
context: Dhammayangyi (built about 1167-1170) is the largest temple on the Bagan plain, and its brickwork really is famously tight. Legend says King Narathu, atoning for murdering his father and brother, had masons executed wherever a needle could be pushed between two bricks -- historians treat this as folklore. Its inner sanctums were later bricked up, for reasons still unknown. (Source: havecamerawilltravel.com/field-notes/dhammayangyi-temple-bagan-myanmar)

question: A magnitude-6.8 earthquake rippled across the plain of Bagan on 24 August 2016, cracking spires and toppling temple tops among its roughly 3,250 monuments. Bagan sits in an active earthquake belt, and quakes like it have thinned its temples for centuries. When the shaking stopped, how many monuments had been damaged?
context: A magnitude-6.8 earthquake struck central Myanmar on 24 August 2016, damaging nearly 400 of Bagan's roughly 3,250 monuments in a single day. Bagan sits in an active seismic zone, and repeated quakes over the centuries are one reason so few of the plain's thousands of original temples still stand. (Source: phys.org/news/2016-08-quake-scores-myanmar-heritage-bagan.html)

question: From a dawn balloon, the Bagan plain glows a warm red-brown -- spire after spire the colour of rust stretching to the horizon, quite unlike the pale grey monuments of many other great temple cities. What is almost every one of Bagan's temples built from?
context: Almost every structure at Bagan is brick, not the carved stone of Cambodia's Angkor Wat or Java's Borobudur -- which is why the plain reads as a forest of red-brown spires rather than grey stone towers. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagan)

question: The caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the Tigris in 762 and named it Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. He set his palace and the main mosque at the dead centre, with four gates opening toward distant cities, and gave the whole capital one bold shape rarely used for a city. What shape was it?
context: Al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 and named it Madinat al-Salam, the 'City of Peace.' His perfectly round capital took about 100,000 workers and roughly 18 million gold dinars to build, with four gates named for the roads to Kufa, Basra, Damascus, and Khorasan and the caliph's palace at the exact center. Nothing of the Round City survives today -- its circular walls have left virtually no trace. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_City_of_Baghdad

question: The ancient Greeks gave one famous name to the land cradled between two great rivers of what is now Iraq: the Tigris, which flows past Baghdad, and the Euphrates. The world's first cities and first writing were born there. What did the Greeks call it?
context: Mesopotamia is Greek for 'the land between the rivers' (mesos, 'middle,' and potamos, 'river'). This region between the Tigris and Euphrates -- now Iraq -- is called the cradle of civilization: the world's first cities, the first writing (cuneiform), and the wheel appeared here, and far older cities like Babylon, Ur, Uruk, and Nineveh rose in the same land. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesopotamia

question: Caliph al-Ma'mun filled Baghdad's House of Wisdom with scholars early in the 800s, and there they turned Aristotle, Euclid and the Greek doctors into Arabic. Legend says the caliph rewarded every finished translation with one remarkable prize. What is he said to have paid for a completed book?
context: By legend, al-Ma'mun (ruled 813-833) loved learning so much that he paid a translator the weight of each finished book in gold. Under him Baghdad's House of Wisdom became the greatest repository of books in the world, carrying Greek, Persian, and Indian works -- Aristotle, Plato, Euclid, Hippocrates, Galen, and the Indian astronomer Brahmagupta -- into Arabic. Source: https://www.1001inventions.com/house-of-wisdom/

question: Al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician in Baghdad, wrote a founding book on solving equations around 820 and helped spread a new way of writing numbers. Two everyday English words trace back to him: one comes from his book's title, the other from his own name. Which two words are they?
context: Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780-850) wrote 'Al-Jabr' around 820; its title word al-jabr ('restoration') became ALGEBRA, and he is called the father of algebra. His own name, Latinized as 'Algoritmi,' became ALGORITHM. He also introduced the Hindu-Arabic numerals and the decimal place-value system -- the digits and the zero we still use -- which reached Europe through 12th-century Latin translations. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi

question: Hulagu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, led his Mongols into Baghdad in 1258 and destroyed the libraries that had made it the world's capital of learning. A famous chronicler wrote that what the Mongols hurled into the Tigris stained the river for days. According to that account, what did the Tigris run with?
answer: black with the ink of books
choices: black with the ink of books
red with the blood of the slain
white with the ash of scrolls
context: Hulagu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, sacked Baghdad in February 1258. So many books were thrown into the Tigris that chroniclers said the river 'ran black with ink' -- a dramatic traditional claim some modern historians dispute. The last Abbasid caliph, al-Musta'sim, was rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses on 20 February 1258, because the Mongols had a taboo against spilling royal blood on the ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(1258)  (Legend.)

question: On the bank of the Tigris in Baghdad, one college of the Abbasid caliphs still stands, though al-Mansur's first capital and the House of Wisdom are long gone. Founded in 1227, it was old enough to live through the Mongol sack of 1258, and it ranks among the oldest universities still standing on Earth. A modern Baghdad university revived its name in 1963. What is this rare survivor?
context: The Mustansiriya Madrasa was founded by Caliph al-Mustansir in 1227 and survived the 1258 Mongol sack, making it among the oldest universities on Earth still standing. Its name was revived by a modern Baghdad university in 1963. With the Round City and the House of Wisdom gone, the Mustansiriya and the Tigris/Mesopotamia setting are among the few pieces of golden-age Baghdad you can still visit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mustansiriya_University

question: On Bali's south coast, the Uluwatu temple clings to a sea-cliff high above the waves. What does the name 'Uluwatu' mean in Balinese?
context: The name joins two Balinese words - 'ulu' (tip, edge, or head) and 'watu' (rock or stone) - so Uluwatu means the very end of the rock, the temple perched where Bali's land drops away into the sea. Source: Wikipedia, 'Uluwatu Temple'.

question: Tanah Lot, a Hindu sea-temple on Bali's southwestern shore, sits alone on a great rock at the water's edge. Its Balinese name means 'land in the sea,' and twice a day the ocean around it changes. What happens to Tanah Lot when the tide comes in?
answer: the rising sea cuts it off as an island
choices: the rising sea cuts it off as an island
the waves break clean over its shrine roof
its hidden sea-caves boom and throw up spray
a rolling mist rises and hides it from shore
context: Tanah Lot means 'land in the sea'. Perched on a lone rock offshore, it is one of Bali's guardian sea-temples, meant to be seen and worshipped from the water; at high tide the sea closes around it, and it can only be reached on foot once the tide falls again. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tanah Lot'.

question: As the sun sets on the Uluwatu cliff, up to 150 bare-chested men pack into a circle. By firelight they chant 'cak-cak-cak' and act out an ancient story. This famous Balinese fire-dance, the Kecak, is missing something almost every other dance has. What is it?
choices: there is no costume of any kind
there is no leader to cue them
context: The interlocking 'cak' of the chorus does the work of a whole gamelan - no drum, no gong, no strings, just up to 150 voices as the entire orchestra. The Kecak was shaped in the 1930s by Balinese dancer Wayan Limbak with German painter Walter Spies, built around an older trance ritual to retell the Ramayana epic. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kecak'.

question: Below Bali's volcanoes, whole hillsides are carved into glowing green rice terraces. For over a thousand years, water running down from the peaks has been shared among farmers by a network of canals, weirs, and small water-temples. Groups of 50 to 400 growers meet to agree on who gets each drop. The United Nations honored this living system in 2012. What is it called?
context: The Subak dates back to the 9th-11th century; today around 1,559 of them cover Bali, each led by an elected chairman called a 'pekaseh' who makes sure every member farmer gets a fair share of the water. UNESCO named the Subak landscape a World Heritage Site in 2012 (Cultural Landscape of Bali Province, #1194). Sources: Wikipedia, 'Subak (irrigation)'; UNESCO World Heritage List #1194.

question: Balinese farmers work their terraced rice paddies in some of the richest volcanic soil on Earth, below Mount Agung, the still-active volcano that is the island's highest peak at 3,031 metres. Every so often the mountain erupts violently and coats the countryside below. What does the volcano give the fields that makes them so fertile?
answer: the ash it showers on the fields
choices: the ash it showers on the fields
the minerals dissolved in its springs
the pumice it scatters down its slopes
the clay left by its old lava flows
context: Volcanic ash weathers into some of the most fertile soil on Earth, which is why farmers cluster around volcanoes worldwide. At 3,031 m, Mount Agung is Bali's highest peak, and the Balinese revere it as a replica of Mount Meru, the cosmic mountain and home of the gods. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Agung'.

question: High in Bali's cool northern mountains, Lake Batur, the island's largest lake and its chief source of water, fills part of an ancient volcanic basin ringed by highlands. The still-smoking cone of Mount Batur rises from the same basin floor, and the lake-goddess temple Pura Ulun Danu Batur stands on the shore. What do geologists call this kind of large landform?
context: A caldera is the huge bowl left behind when a volcano's summit collapses into the emptied magma chamber below - far larger than an ordinary summit crater. Batur's caldera measures about 10 by 13 kilometres. Cradled inside it, Lake Batur is Bali's largest lake and the chief source of the island's water, and on its shore stands Pura Ulun Danu Batur, dedicated to Dewi Danu, goddess of the lake, honoured as the wellspring that feeds every rice terrace below. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Mount Batur'; 'Pura Ulun Danu Batur'.

question: Across Bali's terraced rice-lands, each small water-temple stands exactly where a spring first rises or where one channel forks in two, the very points that decide who downstream receives water. The Balinese set them there by a philosophy of harmony among three things: people, nature and the divine. What is that guiding philosophy called?
context: Tri Hita Karana means 'the three causes of well-being' - harmony among people (pawongan), nature (palemahan), and the divine (parhyangan). Because the divine and the land must stay in balance, the water-temples sit precisely at the springs and forks that govern the flow, turning the whole terraced valley into a single machine of faith and farming. Sources: UNESCO World Heritage List #1194; Wikipedia, 'Subak (irrigation)'.

question: Bangkok answers to a ceremonial name of 168 letters, one Thai word that Guinness World Records counts as the longest name of any place on Earth. In daily speech Thais shorten it to its first two words, Krung Thep. What do those two words mean?
context: Krung Thep is only the start of Krungthepmahanakhon, the 168-letter name that opens 'City of angels, great city of immortals...' Centuries ago foreign traders found the older village name 'Bangkok' easier to pronounce, so the world kept it while Thais use the grand one. Source: Guinness World Records; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangkok

question: Old Bangkok was threaded with canals called khlongs: most people travelled by wooden boat, and vendors paddled between floating markets. Western visitors in the 1800s borrowed a nickname for it from a famous canal city in Italy. Which city did they compare Bangkok to?
context: 'The Venice of the East,' Westerners called it. Floating markets still sell fruit and goods from boats on the water, and the Chao Phraya River remains the city's great watery highway. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chao_Phraya_River

question: Thailand's most sacred image, the Emerald Buddha, sits high on a golden altar in the royal chapel of Bangkok's Grand Palace. For all its name, the figure is not carved from emerald at all; the word describes only its deep-green colour. From what single block of stone was it carved?
context: It is one block of deep-green jade (nephrite); 'emerald' describes only its color. Legend credits the sage Nagasena with making it in 43 BCE, but scholars date the carving to about the 15th century. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Buddha

question: Across the Chao Phraya River from the Grand Palace rises Wat Arun, the 'Temple of Dawn.' Its steep central spire climbs about 70 metres above the water. Up close the tower glitters, because builders coated it in millions of bits of an unexpected material. What is it?
context: The shards were broken Chinese porcelain that had reached Bangkok as ballast weighting empty trading ships; masons pressed the colorful pieces into the spire's plaster. The temple is named for Aruna, the Hindu god of the dawn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Arun

question: Pilgrims in the royal chapel of Bangkok's Grand Palace crane their necks toward a towering gilded altar, where the Emerald Buddha sits perched high over the crowds. It is the most sacred and most fiercely guarded image in Thailand, and visitors expect a figure grand enough to match its shrine. How tall is it, head to crown?
context: Just 66 cm (26 inches) tall, the Emerald Buddha is dwarfed by the vast golden hall around it — a reminder that in Thailand this image's power lies in its holiness, not its size. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Buddha

question: A short walk from the Grand Palace, inside Bangkok's Wat Pho, a single gilded Buddha lies stretched on its side, 46 metres head to toe — so vast that visitors must walk its full length to take it all in. The glowing giant looks like solid gold, but that is only a skin of gold leaf. What is the huge statue built from underneath?
context: The Reclining Buddha measures 46 metres long and 15 metres high — brick and plaster covered in gold — among the largest Buddha images in Thailand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Pho

question: At each turn of the seasons in Bangkok's Grand Palace, the Emerald Buddha is solemnly re-dressed in one of its three golden costumes: one for the hot season, one for the rainy, one for the cool. By custom, one person in all Thailand holds the duty of climbing up to change them. Who is it?
context: The King of Thailand changes the costume himself at each change of season, or sends a senior royal to stand in for him, in a solemn ceremony. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerald_Buddha

question: King Rama I laid out his new royal capital in 1782 on an island in Thailand's Chao Phraya River, around a small village that already stood there, called Bang Makok. That humble name, the root of the word 'Bangkok' the whole world still says, was plain Thai and named a fruit tree that grew on the spot. What did Bang Makok mean?
context: 'Makok' is the olive-plum tree, so 'Bang Makok' meant the place where it grew. Rama I ringed the island with canals and named the new royal district Rattanakosin, 'Jewel of Indra,' after the Emerald Buddha it would come to house. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rattanakosin_Kingdom

question: The Reclining Buddha of Wat Pho ends in two colossal flat feet, each sole five metres long and divided into 108 squares. Every square holds a sacred emblem of a Buddha: lotus flowers, white elephants, dancers, and tigers. What shimmering material is used to decorate these 108 panels?
context: Each sole is inlaid with 108 mother-of-pearl panels showing the lakshanas — the auspicious signs by which a Buddha is recognized. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Pho

question: Around the courtyards of Bangkok's Wat Pho, the lessons of one traditional Thai art are carved on stone tablets and figures, and the temple still teaches it as the place where it was born. Graduates of its school now practise in 145 countries. Which art is it?
context: Wat Pho's stone tablets and figures recording the body's healing lines make it the acknowledged home of Nuad Thai (traditional Thai massage); its school has trained more than 200,000 therapists who now practice in 145 countries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Pho

question: Builders laid the first stone of Antoni Gaudí's great spired church in Barcelona in 1882, and they are still at work on it more than 140 years later. Millions come every year to watch it rise over the city. What is this famous unfinished church called?
context: The Sagrada Família's first stone was laid on 19 March 1882. For over 140 years it remained a working building site — one of the longest construction projects in human history — as generation after generation of Barcelonans carried on Gaudí's design. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sagrada Família' (corroborated by Grokipedia).

question: For the last forty years of his life Antoni Gaudí gave himself to the Sagrada Família, living on the building site and turning down every other paid job. A tram struck him in 1926, and he was buried beneath his unfinished church. What fond nickname did Barcelona give him?
context: Antoni Gaudí (1852–1926) grew so single-mindedly devoted to the Sagrada Família that he became known as 'God's Architect.' He lies buried in a crypt beneath the basilica he never saw finished — at his death, less than a quarter of it had been built. Source: Wikipedia, 'Antoni Gaudí.'

question: Workers in Barcelona lifted the last arm of a giant cross onto the Sagrada Família's central tower in February 2026, and it became the world's tallest church. The old record had stood since 1890, held by another towering church. Which church did the Sagrada Família pass?
context: The Tower of Jesus Christ tops out at 172.5 m, edging past Germany's Ulm Minster (161.5 m), which had reigned as the world's tallest church since 1890. The tower first overtook Ulm on 30–31 October 2025; the top arm of its cross was set in place on 20 February 2026 — exactly 144 years after building began. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Sagrada Família' and 'List of tallest church buildings'; My Modern Met (2026).

question: When Antoni Gaudí fixed the final height of the Sagrada Família's tallest tower, he set himself a strange and humble rule. The tower had to stop one metre short of the top of Montjuïc, the tallest natural hill inside Barcelona. Why would the devout architect let his tower rise no higher than that hill?
answer: so no work of man would rise above the work of God
choices: so no work of man would rise above the work of God
so the tower would better survive strong sea winds
so it would not overshadow Barcelona's old cathedral
so sailors could still sight Montjuïc from far out at sea
context: Gaudí capped his central tower one metre below the summit of Montjuïc, Barcelona's highest natural hill, because he believed the work of man should never stand taller than the work of God. Even now, as the world's tallest church, the Sagrada Família bows to Barcelona's own hill. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Sagrada Família'; ArchDaily (2026).  (Legend.)

question: Inside the Sagrada Família, Gaudí's stone columns lean apart as they rise and branch high overhead into slimmer shafts that carry the roof with no heavy supports outside. Gaudí said he had not built a plain hall of pillars at all, but a stone version of one kind of natural place. What did he mean his interior to be?
context: Gaudí conceived the nave as a stone forest: the branching, tree-like columns carry the vaults from within, so the Sagrada Família needs none of the external flying buttresses that prop up the walls of a Gothic cathedral. Source: Wikipedia, 'Antoni Gaudí' (corroborated by Grokipedia).

question: Hunting for curves that would let the heavy stone arches of his Sagrada Família stand without cracking or toppling, Antoni Gaudí hung little bags of birdshot from a web of cords until they sagged into perfect natural loops. Then, to read his design, he did one surprising thing to the whole sagging model. What did he do?
answer: he turned the whole model upside down
choices: he turned the whole model upside down
he froze it solid over one winter
he traced its shadow onto a wall
he studied it only in a mirror
context: The shape a chain makes when it hangs freely is called a catenary. Flipped upside down, that same curve lets stone stand in pure compression — no tension, no cracking. Gaudí built these hanging birdshot models for the Colònia Güell church and used the principle throughout the Sagrada Família. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Antoni Gaudí'; Grokipedia, 'Sagrada Família.'

question: Ildefons Cerdà, an engineer, drew the Eixample across Barcelona in 1859, the vast grid of streets where the Sagrada Família now stands. From above, his grid looks unlike an ordinary checkerboard: every single city block has its four corners sliced flat, so each block becomes an octagon. Why did Cerdà cut the corner off every block?
answer: to open up light, air, and sightlines at every crossing
choices: to open up light, air, and sightlines at every crossing
to trace the line of the old city walls
to let rainwater drain straight to the sea
to echo the floor plan of Catalan cathedrals
context: Those cut-off corners are called chamfers. Cerdà's chamfered (octagonal) blocks let in more light and air, opened up sightlines, and — in the horse-and-carriage era — gave vehicles room to turn at each junction. The Eixample's octagon blocks are one of the most recognizable city grids on Earth. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eixample.'

question: A batik artist on the island of Java draws a design on plain cloth in hot melted wax, dripped from a small copper tool with a spout. Then the whole cloth goes into a bath of coloured dye. Why does the artist lay down the wax before the dye?
answer: It blocks the dye, so the covered areas stay uncolored
choices: It blocks the dye, so the covered areas stay uncolored
It soaks up the dye, so the covered areas turn darkest
It stains the covered areas a brighter shade
It softens the cloth so the dye spreads more evenly
context: This is wax-RESIST dyeing, the heart of batik. The wax is not paint and adds no color of its own — it simply protects the cloth so those lines can't take the dye. When the wax is later removed, the hidden pattern surfaces pale against the colored ground. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batik

question: The finest batik on Java is drawn by hand with a tool called the canting. It is a tiny copper cup of hot wax with a thin spout, held on a handle and trailed over the cloth like a pen. The trouble is that the hot wax keeps hardening and clogging the narrow tip. To clear it and keep drawing, what does the artisan often do?
answer: Blow through the tip to push the wax out
choices: Blow through the tip to push the wax out
Dip the tip in cold water to loosen it
Scrape the tip clean with a knife blade
Tap the cup sharply against the wax pan
context: Hand-drawn batik is 'batik tulis' — written batik — and the canting (say 'chan-ting') is its pen: a copper reservoir (the nyamplung) ending in a spout (the cucuk) on a wooden handle. A quick puff of breath through the spout clears a clog without interrupting the line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canting

question: Drawing every wax line by hand with the canting can take a Javanese artist weeks or months for a single cloth. In the 1800s, workshops found a way to make batik far faster: instead of drawing the wax line by line, they pressed the whole pattern on in one go. What tool made that possible?
context: The stamp is the 'cap' (pronounced 'chop'), and cloth made this way is 'batik cap.' One press lays down a whole repeating block of the pattern, so a workshop can produce in a day what hand-drawing would take weeks to do. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batik

question: When the last dye bath is over, a Javanese batik cloth looks a mess, its pattern hidden under a hard crust of dyed wax. One final step, called nglorod, brings the design out at last. What is done to the cloth in nglorod?
answer: Boiling the cloth so the wax melts away
choices: Boiling the cloth so the wax melts away
Scrubbing the cloth with sand and stones
Peeling the hardened wax off by hand
Freezing the cloth so the wax cracks off
context: In nglorod the cloth is boiled in hot water, often with soda ash (sodium carbonate), to melt off every trace of wax and reveal the once-hidden pattern. Because the wax can be laid on thick, this washing-out can take days. Source: iwarebatik.org/batik-production-process/

question: At the royal courts in Yogyakarta and Surakarta on Java, only the sultan and his family could wear the grandest batik designs, such as the diagonal parang, and the court could punish any commoner caught in one. A single length of cloth showed at a glance who was royal. What were these royalty-only patterns called?
context: These reserved patterns were the larangan — literally 'forbidden.' The parang was the classic example, and it came ranked by scale: the grandest, Parang Barong, belonged to the reigning sultan alone, while the smaller, more delicate Parang Klitik was worn by the royal princesses. In 1785 Sri Sultan Hamengku Buwono I of Yogyakarta declared Parang Rusak a larangan motif. Source: sonobudoyo.jogjaprov.go.id; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parang_(batik)

question: Sultan Agung, the great king of Mataram in the 1600s, once sat meditating at Parangtritis on Java's southern coast, a Javanese legend says, and there he designed the parang pattern. Watching one thing hour after hour, he shaped its endless diagonal chain. What was he watching, in the story?
answer: The waves crashing against the cliffs
choices: The waves crashing against the cliffs
A column of soldiers on the march
context: This is a legend, not documented history. The parang is a row of interlocking S-shapes running on a diagonal; the name comes from the Javanese 'pereng' (a slope or cliff), and the unbroken chain is said to symbolize continuity — striving that never stops, like the sea forever chopping at the rocks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parang_(batik)

question: The diagonal parang, born in the royal courts of Java, runs in an unbroken chain of S-shapes that reads like a blade chopping without pause, the pattern of kings and warriors. Because of that warlike spirit, Javanese tradition warns guests never to wear parang to one particular celebration. Which one?
context: By tradition the parang's battle-energy — its endless 'chopping' — is believed to foreshadow conflict, so wearing it to a wedding is thought to risk strife between the newly married couple. This is folk belief, not fact: the very S-chain that symbolizes a king's unceasing struggle is what makes it feel wrong at a celebration of union. Source: seasia.co/2025/10/07/the-paradox-of-parang-why-a-noble-batik-is-taboo-at-weddings  (Legend.)

question: At the center of Beijing stands the largest palace complex on Earth. It covers 72 hectares and holds about 8,700 rooms and 980 halls, wrapped in a moat 52 metres wide. For five centuries, emperors ruled from inside, and ordinary people were kept out. What is this vast walled palace called?
context: Begun in 1406 and finished in 1420 under the Ming Yongle Emperor, the Forbidden City housed 24 emperors until 1924. It sprawls across 72 hectares with about 980 surviving buildings and roughly 8,700 rooms -- the largest and best-preserved palace complex in the world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City

question: From any high point in old Beijing, the emperor's buildings stood out by the colour of their glazed roof tiles. One shade was reserved by law for the throne, and a commoner caught using it on a private roof faced harsh punishment. Which colour glowed on the imperial roofs?
context: Golden-yellow was the emperor's exclusive color, so the Forbidden City's roofs shine gold while common Beijing roofs stayed grey. One grand exception: the Temple of Heaven's Hall of Prayer wears deep-blue tiles to echo the sky. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City

question: The builders of Beijing's imperial palace stopped at 9,999 and a half rooms, a famous legend says, leaving it one half-room shy of ten thousand on purpose. In old China, ten thousand was a sacred number. According to the tale, why would no emperor let his palace reach a full 10,000 rooms?
answer: ten thousand rooms belonged to Heaven's palace alone
choices: ten thousand rooms belonged to Heaven's palace alone
ten thousand was a number that invited bad luck
the workers ran out of timber before finishing
imperial law forbade counting rooms past 9,999
context: In the tale, the full 10,000 rooms belonged to the Jade Emperor's palace in Heaven, so an earthly ruler stopped at 9,999 1/2 rather than match the gods. A 1973 on-site survey actually counted about 8,707 rooms (980 buildings, 8,886 bays) -- the 9,999 figure is folklore, not fact. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City; chinahighlights.com/beijing/forbidden-city/  (Legend.)

question: The grand south gate of Beijing's imperial palace rises about 38 metres from a red U-shaped wall, crowned with five watchtower pavilions. Only the emperor himself was allowed to walk through the tall central archway at its base. What is this great front gate called?
context: The Meridian Gate (Wumen), nicknamed the Five-Phoenix Tower for its five pavilions, is the tallest and grandest of the Forbidden City's gates. Only the emperor could use the central archway; officials and princes filed through the smaller side passages. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_Gate

question: Carpenters and engineers still travel to Beijing's Temple of Heaven to study the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, a round tower of wood 38 metres tall beneath three stacked roofs, first raised in 1420. One feature of how it was put together draws them there. What is that feature?
answer: it stands without a single nail
choices: it stands without a single nail
it is the tallest timber tower in China
it is the oldest surviving hall in Beijing
it was raised in a single year
context: The 38-m Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests is joined entirely by interlocking wooden brackets and slotted joints -- not one nail. The building standing today is a faithful nail-free rebuild after lightning burned the original to the ground in 1889. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Heaven

question: Narrow grey lanes called hutong still wind through old Beijing, lined with courtyard homes. The first were laid out in the 1200s, when the Mongol Yuan dynasty made the city its capital, and their name began as a Mongolian word naming the thing each cluster of homes was built around. What did that word mean?
context: 'Hutong' derives from a Mongolian word for 'water well' -- the well being the shared heart of each neighborhood. The lanes are formed by siheyuan, four-sided courtyard homes, joined wall-to-wall. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutong

question: In the imperial gardens outside Beijing, China's Empress Dowager Cixi finished rebuilding a grand boat at the edge of the Summer Palace's Kunming Lake in 1893. It stands two stories tall and 36 metres long, with wide decks and even a pair of paddle-wheels on its sides. In over a century it has never once left the shore -- and it never will. Why can this boat never sail?
answer: it is carved from solid marble
choices: it is carved from solid marble
the shallow lake would run it aground
its hull was never fitted with a rudder
imperial law forbade it to leave the dock
context: The Marble Boat is a 36-m pavilion carved from stone to look like a paddle-steamer, right down to its stone 'paddle wheels' -- a boat that can never float. The original wooden pavilion here was destroyed in 1860 and later rebuilt in marble. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Palace

question: Imperial labourers dug out the whole basin of Kunming Lake at Beijing's Summer Palace by hand, 2.2 square kilometres of open water. Rather than cart the earth away, they piled every basket of it into one hill that still rises beside the lake. Which hill did the diggers raise from the mud?
context: Kunming Lake covers 2.2 km2 (540 acres) and is entirely hand-dug; the excavated soil was heaped up to raise the 60-m Longevity Hill on its shore, so the lake and the hill are two halves of one enormous earthwork. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Palace

question: Tour guides at Beijing's Temple of Heaven, built in the 1400s for China's emperors to pray for good harvests, gather crowds every day beside a smooth circular wall of polished glazed brick around the small round Imperial Vault of Heaven. The wall's perfect curve does something strange to sound, and the guides show off its one uncanny power. What does the wall do?
answer: it carries a soft whisper all the way around its curve
choices: it carries a soft whisper all the way around its curve
it makes each footstep ring out like a temple bell
it swallows every sound so the yard stays silent
it hums on its own when the north wind blows
context: This is the Echo Wall, a smooth circular wall around the Imperial Vault of Heaven that works as a 'whispering gallery': sound skims along the curved stone so a murmur travels its full length. Nearby the emperor prayed as the 'Son of Heaven.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Heaven

question: Along the shore of the Summer Palace's Kunming Lake runs a covered walkway called the Long Corridor. It stretches 728 metres and is roofed over 273 bays. Every single crossbeam overhead is hand-painted with a different scene: birds, legends, landscapes, flowers. Roughly how many separate painted pictures cover it?
context: The Long Corridor stretches 728 m in 273 bays, every crossbeam painted with a different scene -- more than 14,000 in all. In 1990 Guinness World Records named it the longest painted corridor on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Corridor; guinnessworldrecords.com

question: On a Chinese palace roof, a little procession of glazed mythical beasts marches down each corner ridge, and the grander the building, the more beasts it is allowed, with nine the strict maximum for any roof in the empire. Yet one hall in Beijing's imperial palace carries a tenth beast, a sword-wielding, monkey-faced immortal named Hangshi found on no other roof in China. Which hall wears it?
context: Roof-ridge beasts were capped at nine for the highest rank. The Hall of Supreme Harmony -- the throne hall at the empire's ceremonial heart -- is the only building in China permitted a tenth figure, the immortal Hangshi. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall_of_Supreme_Harmony

question: One ceremonial spine runs straight through Beijing's imperial palace, from the Bell and Drum Towers in the north to the Yongdingmen gate 7.8 kilometres to the south, and the city's grandest monuments stand in line along it. It is a model of cosmic order, and in 2024 the United Nations' cultural agency added it to the World Heritage List. What is this line called?
context: Beijing's Central Axis runs 7.8 km from the Bell and Drum Towers south through the Forbidden City to Yongdingmen, with the city's monuments arranged symmetrically along it. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site on 27 July 2024 -- China's 59th. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/1714/

question: Along Bergen's old harbor on Vagen bay leans a row of tall, narrow, pointed wooden houses. Their gable ends are painted in warm reds, browns, and yellows. It is the picture-postcard face of the whole city. What is this famous old harbor front called?
context: Bryggen -- literally 'the wharf' -- is Bergen's old Hanseatic quarter, and its leaning colorful gables are the emblem of the city, drawing visitors to Vagen bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryggen ; grokipedia.com/page/Bergen

question: Behind the colourful gables of Bergen's old wharf, foreign merchants ran a walled trading post for about four hundred years. They held a tight grip on Norway's most valuable export, the dried cod called stockfish. Which merchant power controlled the wharf?
context: German merchants of the Hanseatic League held their Bergen privileges from the mid-1300s until 1754, trading grain and goods for the stockfish that fed much of Catholic Europe on fast days. Their walled post was called a Kontor. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bergen ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryggen

question: From Bergen's harbor, boats set out into Norway's grandest scenery, where huge arms of the sea reach up to 200 km inland between vertical rock walls, and one of them runs deeper than the ocean just offshore. Bergen is famed as the gateway to these inlets. What is this kind of deep coastal sea inlet called?
context: Fjords are valleys that Ice-Age glaciers gouged far below sea level; when the ice melted, the sea flooded in. Sognefjord is the world's longest and deepest at 1,308 m. Sitting between it and Hardangerfjord, Bergen is Norway's 'gateway to the fjords.' Source: en.visitbergen.com/about-bergen/facts-about-bergen ; grokipedia.com/page/Bergen

question: Bergen sits in a bowl ringed by mountains, and the 18th-century playwright Ludvig Holberg fixed its fond nickname, 'the city of seven mountains.' He chose seven on purpose, to make his rainy home echo a far grander city celebrated for its seven hills. Which city was Bergen made to imitate?
context: Ludvig Holberg -- Bergen-born and a leading writer of the Dano-Norwegian Enlightenment -- modeled the nickname on Rome, the classical 'city of seven hills.' To this day Bergeners cheerfully argue over exactly which seven of their peaks should count. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen ; planetware.com  (Legend.)

question: Bergen, on Norway's west coast, is often named Europe's wettest city: in a typical year it sees rain on roughly two days in every three, and its people boast that a real Bergener scorns umbrellas and just pulls up his hood. What wrings so much water out of the sky over the town?
answer: wet sea winds forced up over its mountains
choices: wet sea winds forced up over its mountains
warm fjord water steaming up and falling back
cold air sliding off the glaciers inland
sea fog trapped in the harbour basin
context: Bergen's rain is orographic rainfall (from Greek oros, 'mountain'): moist Atlantic winds hit the ring of mountains around the city, rise, cool and drop their water on the town, about 2,250 mm across some 240 wet days a year. Bergen is widely reckoned Europe's rainiest city, though the world's crown belongs to Mawsynram in India. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bergen ; gofjords.com

question: Medieval merchants of one great trading league kept four overseas posts, called Kontors, at Novgorod, London, Bruges and Bergen. In 1979 the United Nations listed Bergen's old wharf as a World Heritage Site for something none of the other three Kontors could offer. What was it?
answer: it alone still stands, rebuilt on its medieval plan
choices: it alone still stands, rebuilt on its medieval plan
it alone was the birthplace of the whole League
it alone was the largest of the four Kontors
it alone traded in Russian furs and beeswax
context: Of the League's four Kontors -- Novgorod, London (the Steelyard), Bruges, and Bergen -- only Bryggen still stands. Its wooden buildings date mostly from the rebuilding after the great fire of 1702, which kept to the old medieval plots and lanes, as earlier rebuildings had after fires such as that of 1476. UNESCO listed it in 1979 as the last preserved Hanseatic Kontor in the world. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Bryggen ; hanse.org/en/the-medieval-hanseatic-league/die-kontore

question: In a quiet town in the Indian state of Bihar, pilgrims gather beneath a single fig tree called the Bodhi tree. Buddhist tradition says the prince Siddhartha Gautama meditated under this very tree until he awoke to the truth and became the Buddha. What is the town called?
context: Bodh Gaya sits in Bihar, India, on the bank of the Falgu River (also called the Niranjana or Lilajan). In the Buddha's own day the place was known as Uruvela. Pilgrims come from across the Buddhist world to the single sacred fig that marks the spot of his enlightenment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodh_Gaya  (Legend.)

question: Beside the sacred fig at Bodh Gaya, where the prince Siddhartha meditated until he became the Buddha, stands a polished stone slab. Ashoka, the emperor who championed Buddhism, set it there around 250 BCE to mark the spot where the Buddha is said to have sat. By what name is this stone seat known?
context: The stone seat is the Vajrasana, Sanskrit for 'Diamond Throne.' Emperor Ashoka set it beside the tree around 250 BCE and built the first shrine at the site — the earliest known royal monument marking the spot. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabodhi_Temple

question: The Mahabodhi Temple rises 55 metres over the sacred tree at Bodh Gaya. The tower went up about 1,500 years ago, in the Gupta era, and it ranks among the oldest religious towers standing in India. Almost all of it is built from one common, everyday material. Which material is it?
context: The Mahabodhi Temple rises 55 metres (180 ft) and dates to the Gupta era (5th-6th century CE) — one of the oldest and most imposing structures in India built entirely of brick, and still standing. Its complex was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabodhi_Temple

question: Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta, a Buddhist nun, carried a cutting of the Bodh Gaya tree across the sea to Sri Lanka around 288 BCE, according to the chronicles, and King Devanampiya Tissa planted it in his royal capital. Called the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, it is the oldest human-planted tree with a known planting date, and it grows there still. In which ancient city?
context: The tree is the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi. Its planting date is 'known' because it was recorded in the Sri Lankan chronicle the Mahavamsa; Ashoka's daughter, the nun Sanghamitta, is said to have carried the cutting, planted by King Devanampiya Tissa around 288 BCE. Now over 2,300 years old, it stands raised on terraces and was ringed by a golden fence in 1969. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaya_Sri_Maha_Bodhi

question: A storm killed the last ancient tree at Bodh Gaya in 1876, leaving the site of the Buddha's enlightenment without its tree. Five years later Alexander Cunningham, the British archaeologist, planted a new one in its place, drawn from a remarkable source. What did he plant?
answer: a cutting from the tree's own descendant in Sri Lanka
choices: a cutting from the tree's own descendant in Sri Lanka
a wild fig dug from the banks of the Falgu River
a sapling raised from seeds of the original dead tree
a young fig sent as a gift by a Nepalese monastery
context: The original Bodh Gaya tree had been destroyed and regrown several times over the centuries, and the last old tree died in an 1876 storm. In 1881 Alexander Cunningham replanted the site from the Sri Lankan lineage — so the tree at the world's most famous enlightenment site is a descendant of a cutting once sent abroad. The parent survives through its own child. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodhi_Tree

question: From the ground, Borobudur on the island of Java looks like a stepped mountain of grey stone. From high above, its six square and three round terraces nest around a central dome in one vast, balanced plan that pilgrims walk on their way to the top. What sacred design is the monument built as?
context: A mandala is a symbolic map of the cosmos used in Buddhist and Hindu meditation, and Borobudur is a mandala built to be climbed. Its square base runs about 123 m (404 ft) on each side, rising through nine stacked platforms (six square, then three round) to a central dome about 35 m (115 ft) high. Borobudur's clockwise pilgrimage is called pradakshina; spiralling up its terraces, a pilgrim symbolically travels from earthly desire to enlightenment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: Pilgrims at Borobudur, on the island of Java, never step inside: the temple has no rooms, nowhere to gather within its walls. They take in the monument by moving over it, from the bottom to the very top. How does a pilgrim make the climb?
answer: by spiraling clockwise up its open-air terraces
choices: by spiraling clockwise up its open-air terraces
by climbing a single staircase straight to the top
by ascending ladders fixed to its outer walls
by riding a ramp built for royal processions
context: Following every gallery to the summit means walking more than 5 km (3 miles), always clockwise, with the monument on the pilgrim's right. There is no shortcut and no shrine to reach -- the long climb is itself the pilgrimage, a slow rise from the everyday world at the base toward enlightenment at the peak. Source: sacredsites.com; britannica.com/topic/Borobudur

question: At the crown of Borobudur, 72 bell-shaped stupas of grey stone ring the three round terraces, each pierced all over with small openings like a cage. A pilgrim who peers through the gaps can just glimpse something in the shadow within. What is hidden inside each stone bell?
context: These 72 latticework shells are called perforated stupas, and each cradles a seated Buddha making the 'turning the wheel of dharma' gesture -- teachings a pilgrim glimpses but never fully sees. Counting these plus 432 Buddhas in open niches on the terraces below, Borobudur was built with 504 Buddha statues in all. Reaching a hand through the lattice to touch the Buddha inside is a local luck tradition. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: Local villagers never forgot the stones of Borobudur, but for some 800 years after it was abandoned around 1000 CE the monument all but vanished from the wider world. It stood almost whole on Java the entire time, smothered under jungle and thick grey drifts until crews began clearing it in the 1800s. What had buried it?
context: After centuries of use the monument was abandoned; layer by layer, eruptions of the surrounding volcanoes dusted it in ash while tropical jungle grew over the mound until it looked like an ordinary forested hill. It lay lost to the wider world for hundreds of years. Clearing began in 1814 under Thomas Stamford Raffles, with Hermann Cornelius directing about 200 workers over two months -- the local villagers had always known it was there. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: Borobudur's three stacked tiers each stand for a plane of the Buddhist cosmos, and a pilgrim crosses them one by one on the way to the summit. The three circular terraces at the very crown mark the last stage of the whole spiritual ascent. What name do these highest terraces carry?
choices: Svarga, the heaven of the gods
context: The three worlds are Kamadhatu (desire) at the hidden base, Rupadhatu (form) on the square terraces carved with gods and stories, and Arupadhatu (formlessness) on the round summit, where the carvings stop and only the stupas remain. The climb dramatizes the soul's rise from worldly craving toward release. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur; britannica.com/topic/Borobudur

question: The fertile Kedu Plain of Central Java, where Borobudur rises, lies in a restless landscape crowded with volcanoes, the same landscape that made the stone the monument is built from. One smoking peak still looms above it today, among the most active volcanoes on Earth. Which volcano is it?
context: Mount Merapi is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. The volcanic ash that once buried Borobudur, the fertile Kedu Plain it sits in, and the andesite stone the temple is built from all come from this restless volcanic landscape; Merapi's 2010 eruption dusted the temple in acidic ash once more. Source: britannica.com/topic/Borobudur; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: Borobudur hides a secret storey. A Dutch engineer looking over the monument in 1885 found that its builders had walled up the very base, sealing away 160 carved panels that ordinary pilgrims never see. The panels were photographed and walled up again, with one corner left open. What do these buried carvings show?
answer: how good and evil deeds are repaid
choices: how good and evil deeds are repaid
how the Sailendra kings were crowned
how the great monument was built
context: The hidden base holds the Karmawibhangga reliefs, carvings of the Buddhist law of karma -- good deeds and their rewards, cruel deeds and their punishments, shown through scenes of everyday 9th-century Javanese life. Buried when the base was encased in stone (perhaps to buttress the slumping base), they were discovered in 1885 and photographed in 1890, then covered again; only the southeast corner is left visible. Source: photodharma.net; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karmawibhangga_Museum

question: The 72 latticed stone bells crowning Borobudur do not all look the same up close. As a pilgrim climbs from the lower round terraces to the highest one, the little openings in the stone change in a deliberate pattern, so that what lies within grows harder and harder to make out. How do the openings change?
answer: from diamond-shaped holes to square holes
choices: from diamond-shaped holes to square holes
from square holes to round holes
from wide holes to no holes at all
from few holes to many small holes
context: On the two lower circular terraces the openings are diamond-shaped (rhombic); on the highest terrace they become square. The change is symbolic: as the pilgrim nears the formless summit, the Buddha grows harder to glimpse -- form itself dissolving as enlightenment approaches. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur; britannica.com/topic/Borobudur

question: One great stone dome crowns the very peak of Borobudur, the goal of the whole climb, larger than the 72 latticed bells around it and walled shut on every side. Theodoor van Erp, the Dutch engineer who restored the temple from 1907 to 1911, found something strange buried in the dirt inside it. What was it?
choices: a golden reliquary of the Buddha's tooth
a hoard of gold and jewelled offerings
a sealed stone jar of royal ashes
context: Van Erp found the main stupa otherwise empty, with only this rough-hewn, unfinished Buddha in the dirt inside; it is now kept in the Karmawibhangga Museum at the site. Where it first stood is disputed. Van Erp took it for a failed statue that had been thrown away; others argue it belonged inside the stupa all along, its roughness perhaps deliberate, an image of an enlightenment beyond all shape. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unfinished_Buddha

question: Rainwater soaking the earthen hill packed inside Borobudur had left the monument crumbling badly by the twentieth century, its terraces bulging and sliding. A huge international rescue in the 1970s and 1980s, led by a United Nations cultural agency, took the most drastic step possible for a wonder 1,100 years old. What did the engineers do to Borobudur?
answer: took it entirely apart and rebuilt it block by block
choices: took it entirely apart and rebuilt it block by block
sealed the whole monument inside a glass dome
moved it stone by stone to higher, drier ground
injected the inner hill with concrete to freeze it
context: Between 1975 and 1982, more than a million stone blocks were numbered, lifted off, cleaned, and set back in place on a new hidden foundation of concrete and drainage layers to stop the terraces collapsing -- a technique called anastylosis. The rescue cost about US$6.9 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur

question: President Juscelino Kubitschek set out to draw Brazil inland, away from Rio de Janeiro, its old capital on the crowded Atlantic coast. On bare highland scrub his government built a whole new capital, Brasília, which opened in 1960. How long did the city take to build?
context: Rio de Janeiro handed over the role of capital in 1960. Ground was broken in the mid-1950s and the whole city rose from bare cerrado scrub in just 41 months, inaugurated on April 21, 1960 -- a national capital conjured from empty ground to opening day in under four years. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasilia; clickpetroleoegas.com.br, 'Brasilia was born in just 41 months')

question: Lúcio Costa laid out the whole of Brasília on paper before a single brick was set, so the capital never sprawled at random like older cities. Seen from high overhead, the finished city famously resembles one big object. What is Brasília most often said to look like?
context: The master plan, the Plano Piloto, was designed by urban planner Lucio Costa, who won a national competition for it in 1957. From the air the layout reads like a giant airplane (some also say a bird or dragonfly): two gently curved 'wings' hold the housing while a long straight 'fuselage' holds the government buildings. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasilia; free-map.org, 'Brasilia: The Airplane-Shaped Capital')

question: Oscar Niemeyer built the Cathedral of Brasília from sixteen curved white concrete columns that lean together and lift a glass roof toward the sky, nothing like an old stone church. Brazilians named it after one object from the crucifixion of Jesus. What do they call it?
context: Oscar Niemeyer's Cathedral of Brasilia is a hyperboloid of 16 curved concrete columns, each about 90 tons, dedicated on May 31, 1970. Niemeyer said they were like two hands reaching toward heaven; Brazilians dubbed the soaring white ring a 'crown of thorns.' The glass roof opens the interior to the sky. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_of_Brasilia; en.wikiarquitectura.com)

question: Whatever Brasília's outline looks like from the air, its planner, Lúcio Costa, insisted the design carried one deliberate meaning. He said the plan grew from an ancient, simple gesture: the mark a person scratches on bare ground to stake a claim to a place. What did Costa say the shape of Brasília stood for?
context: Lucio Costa wrote that the plan was 'born of a primary gesture of one who marks or takes possession of a place, two axes crossing at right angles, the very sign of the Cross.' The east-west Monumental Axis holds the government; the curved north-south Residential Axis holds the housing -- so the famous 'airplane' is, by its designer's own account, really a cross. (Costa's Pilot Plan proposal, via wiki.acervolima.com and archdaily.com/1041821)

question: Sailboats dot Lake Paranoá, the wide blue lake that curls around Brasília, and lakeside palaces line its shores, though the capital sits on a high, dry plateau hundreds of miles from any coast. It is no natural lake: the planners made it on purpose to give their inland city a waterfront. How did the engineers conjure the lake out of the dry plateau?
answer: they dammed a river and flooded the valley
choices: they dammed a river and flooded the valley
they lined a huge basin with concrete and filled it
they piped rainwater down from distant mountains
they pumped up groundwater to fill a hollow
context: Engineers dammed the Paranoa River to flood the artificial Lake Paranoa, wrapping the dry inland capital in water. The dam opened on September 12, 1959 -- President Kubitschek's birthday -- and Niemeyer shaped the lake's edge as a 'dynamic curve, like the ocean waves.' (artsandculture.google.com, 'The History of Lake Paranoa'; e-geos.it, 'Brasilia, Paranoa Lake')

question: Two identical slim towers rise side by side in Brasília, flanked by a pair of giant white concrete bowls. One bowl opens upward to the sky like a shallow saucer; the other is turned over into a solid dome. It is the city's most photographed building. Which landmark is it?
context: The National Congress sets two twin towers between two great concrete bowls: the upturned, open bowl (opening to the sky) shelters the Chamber of Deputies -- 'open to the people' -- while the domed, upside-down bowl covers the Senate, symbolizing reflection and deliberation. It stands at the tip of the plan's 'fuselage' on the Praca dos Tres Poderes. Brasilia became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 for its modernist architecture and urban design. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Congress_of_Brazil; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasilia; whc.unesco.org/en/list/445)
