question: A single musician at a wooden keyboard in the 83-metre Belfry over the market square of Bruges strikes its levers with hands and fists. Near the tower's top hang 47 tuned bronze bells, and the music peals out over the whole city. What is this bell instrument called?
context: The Belfry (Belfort) climbs 83 metres over the Markt, and 366 steps reach the carillon of 47 tuned bells — about 27.5 tonnes of bronze, the great bourdon alone near 11,000 pounds — still played by a carillonneur from a hand-and-fist keyboard. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfry_of_Bruges

question: Bruges grew rich as one of medieval Europe's greatest ports, its ships reaching the North Sea through a tidal channel called the Zwin. Over the 1400s the Zwin silted shut with sand and mud, stranding Bruges inland with no way to the sea. Which nearby city seized the sea-trade and rose to lead the Low Countries in its place?
context: The Zwin, a tidal channel torn open by a great storm in 1134, had made inland Bruges one of medieval Europe's foremost ports. When it choked with silt around 1500, the sea-trade and prosperity passed to Antwerp, which became the economic flagship of the Low Countries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zwin

question: Bruges today looks almost untouched by time, a beautiful maze of canals, cobbled lanes, and stepped-gable brick houses. Other great trading cities of Europe tore their medieval quarters down long ago and rebuilt in grander styles. What kept the old city of Bruges whole while its rivals lost theirs?
answer: It grew too poor to tear down and rebuild, so the medieval city simply survived.
choices: It grew too poor to tear down and rebuild, so the medieval city simply survived.
A ruling duke decreed that its medieval streets be preserved forever.
It was carefully rebuilt as a replica after being flattened in wartime.
The townsfolk restored the old quarter on purpose to draw in pilgrims.
context: At its height around 1350 Bruges held some 46,000 people and the richest money-market in the Low Countries; once the Zwin closed, the impoverished city could not afford to demolish and rebuild, so its medieval streets survived almost whole. The historic centre became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruges

question: Thousands of tall, thin stone spires crowd shoulder to shoulder on the floor of Bryce Canyon in southern Utah, more than in any other place on the planet, and at sunrise they glow rose and orange. What are these Bryce rock formations called?
context: Bryce holds the largest concentration of hoodoos found anywhere on Earth, crowded densest inside the Bryce Amphitheater. Hoodoos are tall, thin rock spires that rise from arid basins, bulging thicker and thinner along their height like totem poles. (NPS 'Geologic Formations', nps.gov/brca; brycecanyoncountry.com)

question: Of all the stone spires in Bryce Canyon, Utah, one about 150 feet tall is the single most photographed spot in the park, and its likeness turns up on postcards and guidebooks. What is this famous spire named?
context: Thor's Hammer -- a slab of harder rock perched on a slender stone neck, standing roughly 150 feet tall -- is Bryce's most famous single hoodoo. (Wildland Trekking 'Hoodoos of Bryce'; desertusa.com 'Hoodoos of Bryce Canyon')

question: Ebenezer Bryce, a Mormon pioneer, built a cabin below the cliffs of southern Utah in 1875 and grazed his cattle among the tangle of spires that now carries his name. Asked what he made of the bewildering stone maze, he gave a dry reply that park signs still quote. What did he reportedly say?
answer: A hell of a place to lose a cow.
choices: A hell of a place to lose a cow.
A garden the Lord left half-finished.
The finest cattle range in all Utah.
A cathedral no man's hand could build.
context: The park is named for Ebenezer Bryce, a Mormon pioneer who homesteaded below the cliffs in 1875. He reportedly called the maze of spires 'a hell of a place to lose a cow.' (Wikipedia 'Ebenezer Bryce'; brycecanyoncountry.com 'The History of Bryce Canyon's Namesake')

question: At dawn the stone spires of Bryce Canyon in southern Utah blaze rose, orange and deep red, a band of rock so vivid that early American mappers labelled it the Pink Cliffs. Yet scraped clean, the stone itself is a pale, almost whitish limestone. What paints Bryce's rock all those warm colours?
choices: red desert sand blown onto it
context: The rock is the pink Claron Formation limestone, about 50-60 million years old. Iron oxide staining the stone gives it its rose, orange, and red glow -- the band early mappers named the 'Pink Cliffs.' (Grand Canyon Trust 'Steps of Grand Staircase-Escalante'; geology.utah.gov 'The Pink Cliffs')

question: No river ever cut Bryce Canyon in southern Utah, and that makes its name a puzzle, for a true canyon is a valley that a river saws downward through solid rock. What is Bryce, in geological terms?
answer: a set of amphitheatres eroded into a plateau's edge
choices: a set of amphitheatres eroded into a plateau's edge
a deep basin scooped out by a moving glacier
a wide crater blasted out by a meteor strike
a rift valley where the earth's crust pulled apart
context: Bryce isn't a true canyon: no central river carved it. Its bowl-shaped amphitheatres were eaten backward (headward erosion) into the eastern edge of the high Paunsaugunt Plateau. (Wikipedia 'Bryce Canyon National Park'; brycecanyoncountry.com 'Erosion in Bryce Canyon')

question: Bryce Canyon's thin stone spires in southern Utah look as if desert gales sandblasted them into shape. Yet geologists say wind does little here: the spires do not even line up with it. Something else pries the rock apart, flake by flake. What is the real sculptor?
answer: water freezing and swelling in its cracks
choices: water freezing and swelling in its cracks
salt crystals growing in its pores
tree roots wedging into its joints
summer heat cracking its outer skin
context: The real sculptor is frost wedging: temperatures dip below freezing on more than 200 nights a year, and water seeping into cracks freezes and swells about 9%, prying the rock apart. Slightly acidic rain then dissolves the limestone's cement between freezes. Wind does little: the hoodoos don't line up with the prevailing winds, and crusted, plant-anchored soil gives it no loose grains to blast with. (desertusa.com 'Hoodoos of Bryce Canyon'; NPS 'Hoodoos', nps.gov/brca; Wildland Trekking)

question: Two neighbouring spires at Bryce can crumble at wildly different speeds: one may still stand tall centuries after the other has melted into a slope. The difference lies in the armour each one wears. What gives a long-lasting spire its staying power?
answer: a hard caprock shielding the softer stone beneath it
choices: a hard caprock shielding the softer stone beneath it
a core of solid granite running up its centre
a hard iron shell coating its entire surface
a dense slab of rock anchoring it at the base
context: Each hoodoo owes its totem-pole shape to a caprock -- a layer of harder dolomite or limestone on top that shelters the softer mudstone beneath, so the protected column erodes far slower than the rock around it. (Wildland Trekking 'Hoodoos of Bryce'; desertusa.com)

question: Long before geologists studied Bryce, the Paiute people told their own story of its crowd of red spires: the rocks were once the Legend People, birds, lizards and beasts in human shape, whom a trickster froze into stone as punishment for their greed. In the Paiute stories, which trickster turned them to stone?
context: To the Paiute the hoodoos are the Legend People (To-when-an-ung-wa) -- beings who 'looked like people' but were birds, animals, and lizards -- turned to stone by the trickster Coyote for their misdeeds; the Paiute call the rocks Anka-ku-was-a-wits, 'red painted faces.' In one telling Coyote invited the greedy Legend People to a grand banquet and, as they sat down in their finest paint and clothing, cast the spell that froze every one of them into stone before a single bite was taken. (NPR 'A Paiute Take On Bryce Canyon's Hoodoos', Paiute elder Indian Dick, 1936; brycecanyoncountry.com 'Native American Lore')

question: From Bryce Canyon's Pink Cliffs, the top step, the Grand Staircase falls away to the south in a giant flight of cliffs, each step a different band of coloured rock, dropping more than 6,000 feet over 100-plus miles of Utah and northern Arizona. What world-famous landform forms the very bottom step?
context: Bryce sits at the very top of the Grand Staircase -- a giant flight of cliffs climbing more than 6,000 vertical feet over 100-plus miles -- whose lowest step, far to the south, is the Grand Canyon (its north-rim Kaibab Limestone is the bottom tread). Zion, a middle step, sits between them. (Grand Canyon Trust 'Geology Rocks: Steps of Grand Staircase-Escalante'; Wikipedia 'Grand Staircase')

question: Hilly, castle-topped Buda faces flat, bustling Pest across the Danube, the two halves of Hungary's capital. For a very long time no permanent bridge linked them, until one great span opened in 1849, the first bridge ever fixed across the Danube in Hungary. What is it called?
context: Buda (hilly, crowned by the royal castle) and Pest (flat and commercial) were separate towns until the Szechenyi Chain Bridge -- the first permanent bridge over the Hungarian Danube -- opened on 20 November 1849; the two sides formally united into 'Budapest' in 1873. The Liberty, Margaret, and Elisabeth Bridges are all real Budapest crossings built later. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szechenyi_Chain_Bridge

question: On a snowy Budapest day, steam rolls off a grand outdoor pool where bathers soak chest-deep, some hunched over chessboards floating on the water as snow settles in their hair. The bright yellow, palace-like bathhouse, said to be the largest medicinal bath in Europe, is fed by a spring drilled far below ground. Which bathhouse is it?
context: The Szechenyi Baths (opened 1913), a neo-Baroque bath-palace, is called Europe's largest medicinal bath -- 3 outdoor and 15 indoor pools fed by a spring drilled 1,256 m down that surfaces near 77C. The winter chess matches on floating boards in the steaming outdoor pool are a real, much-photographed tradition, not a legend. The Gellert, Rudas, and Kiraly are other famous Budapest baths. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szechenyi_thermal_bath

question: Hot water wells up all over Budapest, yet no volcano stands anywhere near the city. Its springs rise along the edge where the wooded Buda hills drop suddenly to the flat Pest plain. Where does the water get its heat?
answer: rain sinks deep along a fault and the Earth warms it
choices: rain sinks deep along a fault and the Earth warms it
a hidden pocket of magma lies under the Buda hills
sun-baked rock on the hills warms the seeping rain
limestone gives off heat as the water dissolves it
context: Budapest's heat is not volcanic: the city lies on the Buda thermal fault zone, where the Buda hills meet the Pest plain and the karst rock drops about 1,000 m under the Pest side. Rainwater sinks deep, is warmed by the Earth's inner heat, and rises back to the surface along the fault. Source: pangea.stanford.edu (Geothermal Budapest, Toth 2020)

question: More than 200 caves riddle the limestone beneath Budapest's Buda hills -- one of the largest cave systems of its kind anywhere on Earth. Caves like these can be dissolved out of limestone in several very different ways. What carved the maze of caves under Buda?
answer: hot mineral water rising from below
choices: hot mineral water rising from below
the surf of an ancient sea
context: Warm, mineral-rich water rising from deep below dissolves limestone into caves from the bottom up -- the reverse of ordinary rain-fed caves, which form from the top down as rainwater seeps in from the surface. This bottom-up 'thermal karst' has produced over 200 caves under the Buda hills, one of Earth's largest thermal-water cave systems, fed by the same deep water that surfaces in the city's baths. River caves, sea caves, and glacier caves are all real cave types, but none of them carved the Buda caves. Source: vilagorokseg.e-epites.hu (Caves of the Buda Thermal Karst); atlasobscura.com

question: Beneath Buda Castle hill runs a labyrinth of caves, and during the siege of Budapest in 1945 a secret hospital there, built for about 60 patients, took in more than 600 wounded soldiers and civilians. Later, in the Cold War, the Hungarian government quietly refitted the same rock tunnels for a new purpose. What did they become?
context: This is the 'Hospital in the Rock' (Sziklakorhaz), part of a roughly 3.3 km cave-and-cellar labyrinth cut into the soft limestone under Buda Castle hill. Built for 60-70 patients, it took in more than 600 wounded during the 1945 siege of Budapest, and was later secretly refitted as a Cold War nuclear-fallout bunker; it is a museum today. A radio post, a police prison, and a fuel depot are the kinds of hidden facilities Cold War states really did build underground, but not what this one became. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_in_the_Rock

question: Hungary's neo-Gothic Parliament stretches 268 metres along the Pest bank of the Danube, its spires mirrored in the dark water at night. It rises exactly 96 metres, a coded tribute to 896, the year tradition gives for the Magyar settlement of the land, and by old custom nothing in central Budapest stands taller. One other great landmark was deliberately built to that very same 96-metre height. Which is it?
context: Both the Hungarian Parliament and St. Stephen's Basilica rise to exactly 96 metres -- a matched height often said to symbolise that worldly and spiritual power stand equal in Hungary -- and 96 nods to 896, the traditional date the Magyars settled the Carpathian Basin. By long custom no building in central Budapest rises above 96 m. Matthias Church, Buda Castle, and Fisherman's Bastion are other real Budapest landmarks, none built to that height. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Parliament_Building; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Stephen's_Basilica_(Budapest)

question: A cave found in 1984 deep under Budapest's József Hill has walls bristling with glittering needles of aragonite crystal. It did not form the ordinary way: a gas rising from deep below turned into a powerful acid and slowly ate the cavern out of solid limestone. Which acid carved it?
context: The Jozsef-hegy Cave (found 1984) is famed for its needle-like aragonite crystals. It formed by 'sulfuric-acid speleogenesis': hydrogen-sulfide gas (the rotten-egg smell) rising with the thermal water oxidised into sulfuric acid, which dissolved the limestone -- the same rare process that carved Carlsbad and Lechuguilla Caverns in the USA. Ordinary caves are carved by weak carbonic acid from rainwater. Source: researchgate.net (Minerals and speleothems of the Jozsef-hegy Cave, Budapest)

question: Immigrants, dockworkers and sailors packed into the tenements of La Boca, the dockside quarter of Buenos Aires, began dancing a smouldering new partner dance in its bars in the 1880s, long before it reached the grand ballrooms of Europe. What is this dance?
context: Tango grew up in La Boca's port arrabales -- the tenement courtyards, cantinas and dance halls of Buenos Aires's poorest immigrant districts -- in the 1880s, danced by dockworkers and sailors long before it conquered the ballrooms of Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tango

question: Pedestrians crossing the avenue through downtown Buenos Aires often need two or three green lights, for it runs about 110 metres from kerb to kerb, with up to seven lanes of traffic each way. Guinness World Records counts it the widest avenue in the world. What is it called?
context: Avenida 9 de Julio is recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's widest avenue. Its name honours the 9th of July, 1816 -- the day Argentina declared its independence from Spain -- so the broadest avenue on Earth is essentially a boulevard named after a birthday. The white Obelisco stands at its centre. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenida_9_de_Julio

question: Along Caminito, a short lane in the dockside La Boca district of Buenos Aires, the tin-walled houses are splashed in clashing blues, reds, greens and yellows, no two walls alike. The poor workers who built the little shacks could not afford proper house paint. Where did all that colour come from?
answer: leftover paint scraped from the harbour ships
choices: leftover paint scraped from the harbour ships
coloured clay dug from the riverbank
reject batches from a paint factory
old tiles shipped over from Italy
context: La Boca's shipyard workers finished their corrugated-tin homes with whatever paint was left over from the boats in the harbour, so each wall ended up a different colour. The dockside painter Benito Quinquela Martin later turned the barrio into a deliberate open-air canvas, and Caminito became one of Buenos Aires's most photographed streets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Boca

question: Thousands of marble mausoleums stand shoulder to shoulder above the ground in one wealthy district of Buenos Aires, set in blocks along little streets and squares like a miniature city of stone. Eva Perón, known as Evita, is buried here among the elite. What is this famous burial ground called?
context: La Recoleta Cemetery holds 4,691 above-ground mausoleums laid out in blocks like a small city of the dead, and is regularly ranked among the most beautiful cemeteries in the world. Eva Peron -- 'Evita,' Argentina's famous first lady -- rests in her family's tomb here, one of its most visited graves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Recoleta_Cemetery

question: In the La Boca district, the football club Boca Juniors plays in a stadium with three steeply stacked tiers on three sides and one oddly flat wall on the fourth. Fans boast that it 'does not shake, it beats,' because the packed stands pulse up and down when tens of thousands of them leap at once. By what warm nickname is this stadium known?
context: La Bombonera -- 'the chocolate box' -- earned its nickname from its unusual shape: three steep tiers and one flat vertical stand make it look like an open box of bonbons. Its close, steep walls trap and amplify the roar of Boca Juniors' fans, and the stands really do flex when the crowd jumps, giving rise to the saying 'La Bombonera no tiembla, late' -- it does not shake, it beats. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Bombonera

question: The Río de la Plata, the great river between Argentina and Uruguay, never runs blue or green beside Buenos Aires. From one bank clear to the other it stays a steady, murky brown the whole year round. What gives the river its permanent brown colour?
context: The Rio de la Plata's brown comes from the immense load of fine sediment -- silt and mud -- that it carries and holds in suspension, staining the whole estuary the colour of milky coffee from one bank to the other. Tannins, algae or dissolved minerals turn other rivers brown, but here the cause is plain suspended sediment washed down off the land. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_la_Plata

question: From the Buenos Aires waterfront, the brown Río de la Plata carries the waters of the Paraná and the Uruguay out to the Atlantic, and geographers still argue whether it is a river at all or an estuary. Counted as a river, which record does it hold?
answer: the widest river in the world
choices: the widest river in the world
the muddiest river in the world
the deepest river in the world
the saltiest river in the world
context: Near Buenos Aires the Rio de la Plata already spans more than 40 km, and it flares to roughly 220 km wide where it meets the Atlantic -- so vast it looks like a muddy brown sea with no far shore. Counted as a river it is the widest in the world, though geographers debate whether so broad a brackish body should count as a river or an estuary at all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_la_Plata

question: A slender brick tower about 45 metres tall has risen over the old Silk Road city of Bukhara, in Uzbekistan, since 1127. Bands of patterned brick wrap its round shaft from the base to the top. What kind of tower is it?
context: This is the Kalyan ('Great') Minaret, about 45.6 m tall (nearly 48 m to the tip), completed in 1127. A minaret is the tower from which a mosque sounds the call to prayer; the Kalyan has done so for close to 900 years. A belfry is a Christian bell-tower, a pagoda a tiered East Asian temple tower, and a ziggurat an ancient Mesopotamian stepped temple. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyan_Minaret

question: Genghis Khan rode into Bukhara in 1220 to burn it, legend says, and tipped his head so far back to see the top of the Kalyan tower that his hat fell off. Stooping for it, the conqueror who boasted he had never bowed to any man was so struck by the tower that he made a strange choice. What did he do?
answer: He ordered the minaret spared as the city burned.
choices: He ordered the minaret spared as the city burned.
He had the minaret pulled down before all else.
He made his archers shoot down from its gallery.
He renamed the towering minaret after himself.
context: The tale is a favourite of Bukhara guides but is historically unverified. What is real: the Kalyan minaret did survive the Mongol sack of 1220, when much of the city was destroyed. Genghis Khan (c. 1162–1227) led the Mongol conquest of Central Asia. Sources: https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/kalyan-minaret ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyan_Minaret  (Legend.)

question: As the sun moves over Bukhara's Samanid Mausoleum, a nearly perfect cube about nine metres on each side, the basketweave and chequerboard patterns of its walls seem to shift, so the same wall looks different at dawn and at dusk. What single material is the whole tomb built from?
context: Each side is about 9.4 m. The tomb's beauty is famous precisely because it is achieved in plain baked brick alone — no coloured tile — laid so that raised and angled bricks throw shifting shadows through the day. It is one of the oldest surviving monuments of Central Asian Islamic architecture. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samanid_Mausoleum

question: When the Mongols stormed Bukhara in 1220, they smashed nearly every big building. Yet the Samanid Mausoleum came through untouched, and people still admire it a thousand years later. It escaped for one surprising reason. Why did the Mongols leave this tomb standing?
answer: Flood silt and sand had long buried it, so they never found it.
choices: Flood silt and sand had long buried it, so they never found it.
They honoured it as the tomb of their own ancestors.
A wide belt of marsh made it impossible to reach.
Its keepers paid the raiders richly to pass it by.
context: The Samanid Mausoleum survived the Mongol sack because, over the centuries before 1220, floods had heaped mud and sand over it until it was hidden from view; the raiders simply never saw it. It was dug back out much later. The tomb, in effect, was saved by being lost. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samanid_Mausoleum

question: The people of Bukhara called the Kalyan tower, the slender giant beside the Great Mosque, by a grim nickname into the early 1900s: the Tower of Death. What did the city's rulers do at the tower to earn it that name?
answer: Flung condemned prisoners from its top gallery to the square below.
choices: Flung condemned prisoners from its top gallery to the square below.
Chained rebels in iron cages to starve high above the crowd.
Burned executed enemies on a pyre built atop its roof.
Sealed plague victims inside its shaft until the sickness passed.
context: The custom is real: for centuries, and into the early 1900s, the condemned in Bukhara were led to the minaret's high gallery and thrown to their deaths on the pavement below. The Scottish traveller Fitzroy Maclean, who visited in 1938, recorded that men were cast down from 'the delicately ornamented gallery which crowns it.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyan_Minaret ; Fitzroy Maclean, 'Eastern Approaches' (1949).

question: Bukhara's emirs ruled until 1920 from the Ark, a huge mud-brick citadel whose walls run nearly 800 metres around. The whole fortress stands lifted about 20 metres above the plain on a vast mound. What is that great mound made of?
answer: The rubble of its own earlier forts, rebuilt again and again.
choices: The rubble of its own earlier forts, rebuilt again and again.
A natural outcrop of bedrock rising from the plain.
An artificial hill of packed clay hauled in by hand.
The buried ruins of an ancient Greek fortress-town.
context: Each time the citadel was destroyed or decayed, its rulers levelled the ruins and built again on top — so the Ark literally sits on roughly 20 m of its own former selves. Its walls run about 790 m around and rise 16–20 m; it was the seat of Bukhara's emirs for over a thousand years, until 1920. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ark_of_Bukhara

question: A rich merchant raised Chor Minor on a quiet Bukhara side street in 1807, as the gateway to a madrasa long since vanished. Each of its four sky-blue domed turrets is decorated in its own way, and some scholars see a hidden meaning in the four designs. In that reading, what do the turrets stand for?
choices: the four seasons of the year
the four winds of the desert
context: Chor Minor — Persian for 'four minarets' — was built in 1807 by a wealthy merchant, Khalif Niyaz-kul, as the gateway to a madrasa (an Islamic school) that has since vanished, leaving only the gate. Some scholars read the four differing motifs on its turrets as hints of different faiths — seeing suggestions of a cross, a fish, and other symbols. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chor_Minor

question: People still live, pray and trade among some 140 mosques, tombs, madrasas and domed bazaars in Bukhara's old town, a working place and no dead ruin, and in 1993 the United Nations' cultural agency added it to the World Heritage List. With so much old architecture packed into one living town, Bukhara carries a two-word nickname. What is it often called?
context: About 140 monuments crowd Bukhara's historic centre, yet it stays a lived-in, working town — which is what makes its nickname a small surprise: it is called a 'museum city.' UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre of Bukhara as a World Heritage Site in 1993. The rival nicknames belong to other cities: the 'Eternal City' is Rome, the 'Forbidden City' is Beijing's imperial palace complex, and the 'Golden City' is Prague. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukhara ; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/602/

question: Phoenician sailors from Byblos, an ancient harbour on the coast of Lebanon just north of Beirut, spread a writing tool around 1000 BCE so simple and useful that almost every nation now uses a version of it. What did Byblos give the world?
context: Byblos -- called Gebal by the Phoenicians -- has been lived in without a break since about 5000 BCE, one of the oldest cities on Earth. Its Phoenician traders carried the 22-letter alphabet by sea, and nearly every alphabet in use today descends from it. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byblos; /Phoenician_alphabet)

question: The little stone harbor of Byblos, in Lebanon, has been lived in without a break since about 5000 BCE. It is one of the oldest towns on Earth. Long before the Greeks named it Byblos, the Phoenicians had their own name for it. What did they call the city?
context: 'Gebal' is thought to mean 'mountain town' or 'frontier town.' Excavations begun in 1860 revealed settlement layers running from the Neolithic all the way to the Ottoman era, plus five Byblian royal inscriptions dated roughly 1150-950 BCE. (worldhistory.org/Byblos; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byblos)

question: A merchant of Byblos could write with just 22 signs, where Egyptian writing needed hundreds. The Phoenician letters managed it by leaving out one of the two basic kinds of speech sound, which readers filled in from memory; it works because Semitic languages pack their meaning into the other kind. Which kind of sound did Phoenician leave out?
context: A script that writes only consonants and leaves the vowels to the reader is called an abjad -- Semitic languages carry their meaning mostly in the consonants, so it works. Centuries later the Greeks would borrow this alphabet and add signs for the vowels. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet)

question: Ships out of Byblos, Tyre and Sidon carried the Phoenicians' 22 letters to ports from the Middle East to Spain. The Romans would later spread their own letters through war, but the Phoenicians spread theirs through the everyday thing their ships were built for. What was it?
context: With only a couple dozen signs to learn -- versus years of training for hieroglyphs or cuneiform -- a merchant could master the alphabet, not just a priest. Phoenician ships carried it across North Africa and southern Europe, so it spread by trade rather than conquest. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet)

question: A landslide at Byblos in 1923 ripped open a row of royal tombs, and ten metres down one shaft Pierre Montet, a French archaeologist, found a stone coffin covered in writing. Its 38-word text, from about 1000 BCE, is the oldest long Phoenician inscription ever found. Whose coffin was it?
context: French archaeologist Pierre Montet found the coffin in 1923 after the landslide exposed the royal tombs; the burial shaft ran ten meters deep. The Ahiram sarcophagus now rests in the National Museum of Beirut, and UNESCO listed Byblos's Phoenician alphabet inscriptions in its 'Memory of the World' register in 2005. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahiram_sarcophagus)

question: Around the lid of a royal coffin at Byblos runs the oldest long text in Phoenician letters, and it is neither a hymn nor a king's boast but a curse on any later king who drags the coffin from its tomb. What fate did the curse promise him?
answer: his own royal scepter would snap in two
choices: his own royal scepter would snap in two
his firstborn son would die before him
his name would be chiseled off every stone
his bones would lie unburied on the shore
context: The inscription warns that if any king disturbs the coffin, 'his imperial scepter shall break... the throne of his kingship shall overturn, and peace shall depart from Byblos.' It is the oldest substantial Phoenician text known -- a 38-word warning from about 1000 BCE. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahiram_sarcophagus)

question: Egyptian papyrus, the paper the Greeks wrote and read on, poured through Byblos in such quantity that the Greeks named the paper itself byblos after the harbour, a single scroll a biblion, and a whole collection of them ta biblia, the books. Which famous sacred book takes its name from that phrase?
context: The same root gives us 'biblio-' words -- a bibliophile is a book-lover, a bibliography a list of books -- all tracing back to a Lebanese harbor's papyrus trade. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byblos; etymonline.com/word/Byblos)

question: A Phoenician scribe at Byblos writes aleph, the first of the 22 letters. Each of them started out as a tiny sketch of something from daily life and took that thing's name, and a capital A turned upside down still shows the horns of the creature aleph drew. What animal was aleph?
context: This is called acrophony: a letter's picture was named for a thing, and the first sound of that thing's name became the letter's sound -- 'aleph' (ox) gave the 'a' sound. Aleph became Greek alpha and then our A. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet; ancient-hebrew.org/ancient-alphabet/aleph.htm)

question: A Phoenician ship out of Byblos carried the 22 letters across the sea, among them the sign mem that later became our zig-zag capital M. Like every Phoenician letter it was named for the plain thing it once drew, and that name survives almost unchanged as the Hebrew word mayim. What everyday thing did mem first picture?
context: Other letters still hide their pictures too: 'bet' was a house (Hebrew 'bayit'), 'dalet' a door, 'ayin' an eye (Hebrew 'ayin' still means eye), 'kaph' a palm of the hand, and 'resh' a head. Each letter's name was the thing it once drew. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet)

question: From Phoenician Byblos the letters crossed to Greece and then sailed on to Italy. There a people famous for the painted tombs they left in the hills north of Rome took the Greek letters, reshaped them and passed them to the Romans in the 600s BCE, giving Rome the letters of Latin. Which people handed the letters on to Rome?
context: The full trail runs Phoenician -> Greek -> Etruscan -> Latin, so the ABCs of English are great-great-grandchildren of a Lebanese trading script. The Romans borrowed the letters from the Etruscans around the 7th century BCE. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_alphabet)

question: Traders of a desert nation carved the rose-red temples of Petra in Jordan, and they wrote with letters descended from those of Byblos. Another branch of the same family grew into Aramaic and later Hebrew; theirs grew into the flowing Arabic writing used across the world today. Which people carried the family line toward Arabic?
context: The same Phoenician root branched east into Aramaic, and from Aramaic into Hebrew and -- by way of the Nabataean script -- Arabic. Scholars say nearly every alphabet on Earth either descends from this first Semitic alphabet or was inspired by one of its descendants. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_alphabet)

question: The people of Cahokia, on the far bank of the Mississippi from today's St. Louis, raised more than a hundred flat-topped mounds a thousand years ago, the tallest as high as a ten-storey building, without using a single stone. What did they pile up, load by load, to build them?
context: The greatest were 'platform mounds' -- flat-topped earthen pyramids that served as raised bases for temples and the halls of chiefs. Basket by basket, Cahokia's builders moved an estimated 55 million cubic feet of soil, in about 120 mounds all told. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cahokia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia.

question: Monks Mound, the centrepiece of Cahokia, rises in four wide steps to about 30 metres, all of it carried up by hand. Its base covers about 13 acres, almost the same ground as one of the ancient world's most famous monuments. Which monument does Monks Mound match in size?
context: Its base -- about 291 by 236 m -- rivals the Great Pyramid's ~13-acre footprint, making Monks Mound the largest earthwork in the Americas and the largest pyramid north of Mexico. It only matches Giza at the base: the stone pyramid still rises more than four times higher. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monks_Mound.

question: Across the river from today's St. Louis stood Cahokia, the greatest city north of Mexico, but its builders left no writing, so their own name for it is lost. They had raised over a hundred earthen mounds and were gone by about 1350. Where does the name Cahokia come from?
answer: a neighboring people who arrived long after
choices: a neighboring people who arrived long after
a great chief buried in its biggest mound
a river that flows right past the site
an old Spanish word for the mounds
context: When French explorers reached the area in the 1600s, they named the long-abandoned ruins after the Cahokia, an Illiniwek people then living nearby -- who had not built the city and arrived centuries after it emptied. The builders left no writing, so their own name for their metropolis is unknown. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cahokia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia.

question: In Cahokia's Grand Plaza, huge crowds gathered to watch the city's favorite sport. A player would roll a smooth stone disc across the packed dirt. Then he would throw a wooden spear to land where the stone stopped. What was this popular Cahokian game called?
context: The game was chunkey, and it mattered so much that beautifully polished chunkey stones were buried as elite treasures. Crowds packed the Grand Plaza to cheer these contests of skill. Source: Gilder Lehrman / World History Commons Cahokia essays; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72.

question: Ten thousand or even twenty thousand people may have lived at Cahokia around 1100 CE, at the city's height, and no city in what became the United States would top it until Philadelphia passed 40,000 in the 1780s. For that moment it was probably bigger than one great European capital of the same century. Which capital did Cahokia outnumber?
context: The population is an estimate -- 'may have held' 10,000-20,000 at its ~1100 CE peak -- but that likely put Cahokia ahead of the London of the same century. That no U.S. city surpassed it until Philadelphia passed ~40,000 in the 1780s shows Cahokia was a true metropolis, not a scattered village. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cahokia.

question: Shiny sea shells, some as wide as a man's hand, and hammered copper from the Great Lakes have turned up in Cahokia's graves and workshops, hundreds of miles from any coast, carried there by its traders across half a continent. From which distant shoreline did the traders bring the big shells?
context: Cahokia sat at the hub of a continent-spanning trade web: lightning-whelk and conch shells came up the Mississippi from the Gulf of Mexico, copper from the Great Lakes, and Mill Creek chert hoes from quarries in southern Illinois. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Cahokia.

question: A barrier two miles long, with guard towers standing out along its length, walled off Cahokia's sacred heart, Monks Mound and the Grand Plaza. It came down and went up again three or four times over two centuries. What was this great wall made of?
context: This was a palisade -- a two-mile stockade of 15,000-20,000 oak and hickory logs, each about a foot thick and 20 feet tall, with guard-tower 'bastions' roughly every 85 feet, rebuilt several times over about two centuries. Source: gilderlehrman.org Cahokia essay; cahokiamounds.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia.

question: Just west of the largest earthen pyramid at Cahokia, its people set up great rings of upright red-cedar posts, lined up with the sunrises of the seasons and known today as Woodhenge. A watcher standing at the centre at dawn on the spring or fall equinox sees one striking thing happen. What does the rising sun seem to do?
answer: rise straight out of Monks Mound itself
choices: rise straight out of Monks Mound itself
set Monks Mound's summit ablaze with light
split into twin beams above the plaza
cast a long shadow across the whole ring
context: The circle is nicknamed 'Woodhenge' -- the best-studied ring (~1000 CE) had 48 red-cedar posts and spanned about 410 feet. At the equinox the rising sun appears to emerge from the front of Monks Mound half a mile away, as if the mound itself gives birth to the dawn -- a striking effect of careful alignment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia_Woodhenge.  (Legend.)

question: Deep inside Mound 72 at Cahokia, archaeologists uncovered a powerful young man laid out on a glittering bed of some 20,000 polished shell beads. The beads were not scattered but carefully arranged into the outline of a single creature, its head under his head and its body spread out beneath his arms and legs. Which creature did the beads form?
context: This is the 'Birdman' burial: the beads formed a falcon, its head beneath his head and wings and tail beneath his limbs -- a falcon-warrior symbol of a powerful ranked society. Bead counts vary in the sources (Wikipedia ~10,000; Grokipedia and popular accounts ~20,000). He did not lie alone: Mound 72 held over 270 burials, many of them sacrificed attendants -- evidence of rulers who held power of life and death. Radiocarbon dates it to about 1030 CE. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Mound_72; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_72.  (Legend.)

question: Cahokia stood silent and nearly empty by about 1350 CE, and scholars still argue over why its thousands drifted away. One old idea blamed the Cahokians themselves: they cut so many trees for building and fuel that they stripped the land and caused the very floods that ruined their farms. When researchers studied the ancient flood layers in 2021, what did they find about this self-inflicted collapse?
context: A 2021 Washington University study of the flood layers found scant evidence that local logging caused the flooding, challenging the old self-destruction idea. The real cause is still genuinely debated: a great Mississippi flood around 1200 buried farmland in silt, and Little Ice Age drought and resource stress are also blamed. Cahokia became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982 -- one of only a handful in the U.S. Source: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1501904112; source.washu.edu (2021).

question: The ancient Greeks named Seven Wonders of the World, sights every traveller longed to see. Over the centuries six of the seven crumbled or vanished, and only one still stands, more than 4,500 years after it was built. Which wonder is the last one standing?
context: Six of the Seven Wonders -- the Colossus of Rhodes, the Lighthouse of Alexandria, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the Statue of Zeus, the Temple of Artemis, and the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus -- are long gone. Only the Great Pyramid of Giza, on the desert edge of Cairo, still stands after about 4,500 years -- the last survivor of the ancient world's Seven Wonders. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza

question: The Egyptians built the Giza pyramids, beside today's Cairo, and nearly every grand royal tomb on the west bank of the Nile, never the east. To them the west was the land of the dead, the fitting side for a grave. What made the west the side of death in their eyes?
answer: it was where the sun died each evening
choices: it was where the sun died each evening
it was where the Nile's flood began each year
it was where the desert winds blew hottest
it was where their enemies' lands lay
context: Egyptians watched the sun set and 'die' in the west each evening, then be reborn in the east at dawn, so they made the west bank the realm of the dead and placed their royal tombs -- including the Giza pyramids -- there. Source: egypttoursportal.com; inside-egypt.com

question: Archaeologists digging beside the Great Pyramid, on the desert edge of Cairo, uncovered a big graveyard of the pyramid's own workers and a whole planned town built to house and feed thousands of them. For centuries people had assumed that slaves raised it. Who does this evidence show actually built the Great Pyramid?
answer: paid Egyptian workers, free and proud
choices: paid Egyptian workers, free and proud
enslaved captives seized in foreign wars
prisoners condemned to years of hard labor
foreign engineers hired from distant lands
context: The builders were skilled, paid Egyptians, not slaves: their tombs sat honorably beside the king's pyramid, their work-gangs bore proud names like 'Friends of Khufu' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure,' and about 10,000 workers were fed some 21 cattle and 23 sheep every single day. Source: guardians.net/hawass; cbc.ca

question: Students have been taught at one mosque in medieval Cairo without a break for over a thousand years, ever since the Fatimid rulers founded it around 972, which makes its school one of the oldest running universities on Earth. Which Cairo mosque is it?
context: Al-Azhar's mosque was founded by the Fatimids between 970 and 972 AD; the teaching that grew around it makes al-Azhar one of the oldest continuously operating universities in the world. It stands in the medieval quarter of 'Islamic Cairo,' near the Citadel of Saladin (begun 1176 AD). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Azhar_University

question: Thousands of families in Cairo cook, sleep and send their children to school among the tombs of a huge old cemetery, about 6 kilometres long, on the city's eastern side. Their homes, shared with the graves, have electricity and running water. What is this lived-in cemetery called?
context: Cairo's City of the Dead (al-Qarafa) is a necropolis roughly 6.4 km (4 miles) long where families live among the tombs, some for generations -- a working neighborhood of graves and homes with schools, water and electricity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_the_Dead_(Cairo)

question: An emir built a walled inn for travelling traders in the middle of medieval Cairo around 1382, and over the centuries it grew into a maze of covered alleys packed with lantern-makers, spice sellers, goldsmiths and coppersmiths. It has traded without stopping for more than 600 years. What is this famous bazaar called?
context: Khan el-Khalili was founded around 1382, when the emir Jaharkas al-Khalili built a large khan (a merchants' caravanserai) here; it grew into one of Cairo's greatest bazaars and still bustles today in the medieval heart of the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_el-Khalili

question: When the Fatimid general Jawhar founded a brand-new royal capital in Egypt in 969 AD, he named it after a planet that was rising in the sky at that very moment -- a planet the Arabs called al-Najm al-Qahir, 'the Conquering Star.' From that name comes Cairo's Arabic name, al-Qahira, 'the Victorious.' After which planet was Cairo named?
context: Cairo's Arabic name, al-Qahira ('the Victorious' or 'the Vanquisher'), comes from al-Najm al-Qahir, 'the Conquering Star' -- the planet Mars -- which was rising in the sky as the Fatimid general Jawhar founded the city in 969 AD. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo  (Legend.)

question: On many days a low white cloud gathers on the level top of Table Mountain, behind Cape Town, and spills slowly over its front edge, hanging there for hours before the sun burns it off. Capetonians gave this cloud a fond nickname long ago. What do they call it?
context: That draping cloud is Cape Town's beloved 'tablecloth,' formed when moist sea air is forced up the slope and cools into cloud right at the rim, then spills over and vanishes in the warmer air below. Locals say the mountain has 'laid its tablecloth.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain; hiketablemountain.co.za.

question: Jan van Hunks, a retired pirate, sat smoking on Table Mountain, an old Cape Town legend says, when a stranger dared him to a smoking contest. For days they puffed away until their smoke piled into a huge white cloud, and only too late did van Hunks see who his rival really was. Who was it?
context: In the folktale the stranger was the Devil, and a lightning bolt ended their duel; when the 'tablecloth' pours over Table Mountain, Capetonians joke that Jan van Hunks and the Devil are at it again. It is legend, not history. Source: awoltours.co.za; the-legends.fandom.com/wiki/Jan_van_Hunks.

question: A round, plump little mammal with no tail, about the size of a big guinea pig, naps on the sun-baked rocks at the top of Table Mountain, above Cape Town, and visitors who ride up nearly always meet it. What do the locals call it?
context: The dassie, or rock hyrax, is a plump, tail-less little mammal that lives in colonies among the warm summit rocks and is the animal visitors spot most often on top of Table Mountain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain; awoltours.co.za.

question: Most visitors ride to the top of Table Mountain by cableway, first opened in 1929, in cars that glide up the cliff in under five minutes carrying 65 people at a time. Few cableways anywhere match them, thanks to one strange thing the cars do on every trip. What is unusual about them?
answer: the floor rotates a full turn
choices: the floor rotates a full turn
the two cars pass midway up
the roof opens for the view
the cabin is walled in glass
context: Since 1997 the cableway's 'Rotair' cars have a floor that spins a full 360 degrees during the climb, so all 65 passengers see the whole panorama without moving — one of only a handful of rotating cableways on Earth. The cableway first opened on 4 October 1929. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain_Aerial_Cableway.

question: The cableway sets visitors down near one end of Table Mountain's flat top, but that spot is not quite the mountain's highest. The true summit lies a little higher, out across the broad plateau, and reaching it means a walk of a few kilometres over the level rock. By what name is this true high point of Table Mountain known?
context: Maclear's Beacon, a stone cairn about 1,086 m (3,563 ft) high, is the true summit of Table Mountain — a little higher than the upper cableway station. Sir Thomas Maclear built it in 1865 as a trigonometrical survey station. Devil's Peak, Lion's Head and Signal Hill are the neighbouring heights around the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain.

question: Low, tough bushes and bright wildflowers, not tall forest, cover the rocky slopes of Table Mountain above Cape Town, blooming in a hundred shapes and colours. The Dutch-descended settlers of the Cape gave this shrubland its own Afrikaans name. What is it called?
context: Fynbos — Afrikaans for 'fine bush' — is the fine-leaved, flower-rich shrubland that makes up about 80% of the Cape Floral Kingdom and cloaks most of Table Mountain. Chaparral, maquis and matorral are its cousins in California, the Mediterranean and Chile. Source: wwf.panda.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fynbos.

question: Botanists have counted about 2,200 kinds of wild flowering plants on Table Mountain above Cape Town, though its flat top is only a few square miles across. The island of Britain, hundreds of times larger, has its own well-known list of native flora. How does Table Mountain's plant count stack up against Britain's?
answer: it beats the whole of Britain's flora
choices: it beats the whole of Britain's flora
it holds about half of Britain's flora
it holds about a tenth of Britain's flora
it matches one English county's flora
context: Table Mountain National Park holds over 2,200 flowering-plant species — more than the roughly 1,490 native species of all Great Britain — with about 90 of them found nowhere else on Earth. Source: nature-reserve.co.za; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain_National_Park.

question: The Cape around Cape Town has a whole floral kingdom to itself: botanists divide all the plant life on Earth into six of them, and one belongs to the Cape alone. Among the six, the Cape Floral Kingdom holds one record all its own. Which record is it?
context: The Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of Earth's six floral kingdoms (with the Antarctic, Australasian, Boreal, Neotropic and Palaeotropic), yet the richest for its size; the wider Cape Floristic Region became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. Source: wwf.panda.org; southafricatourism.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Floristic_Region.

question: A pale, very hard sandstone armours the flat crown of Table Mountain. Geologists date it to roughly half a billion years ago, when its sand was settling on an old sea floor and one whole great branch of life had not yet made its home on dry land anywhere on Earth. Which group of living things had not yet moved onto land?
context: Table Mountain Sandstone is hard quartzitic rock laid down in the Ordovician period, roughly 450-510 million years ago. Land plants were only just beginning to green the continents; the first animals would not crawl ashore for tens of millions of years yet. Hundreds of millions of years of erosion then planed the summit dead flat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_Mountain.

question: From the top of Table Mountain a low, flat island can be seen out in the bay off Cape Town. South Africa's apartheid government used it as a prison and held Nelson Mandela there for 18 of his 27 years in jail, made to labour in a limestone quarry whose glare hurt his eyes, before he walked free in 1990. What is the island called?
context: Robben Island — Dutch for 'seal island' — sits in Table Bay within sight of the summit. The apartheid government imprisoned Nelson Mandela there for about 18 of his 27 years, forcing him to labour in a glaring limestone quarry that damaged his eyes; he walked free in 1990 and became South Africa's first democratically elected president. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robben_Island; history.com.

question: A whole city carved deep underground lay forgotten for centuries beneath Derinkuyu, a town in central Turkey's Cappadocia. In 1963 a local man broke into a dark space inside his own home and stumbled into it. What was he doing when he found it?
answer: knocking down a wall in his basement
choices: knocking down a wall in his basement
digging out a deeper water well
chasing a stray goat into a crack
context: In 1963 a resident of Derinkuyu, renovating his home, knocked through a basement wall and found a passage leading into a vast underground network no one had used for centuries. The site opened to visitors in 1969, and more than 600 tunnel entrances have since been found in the area. Source: interestingengineering.com/culture/derinkuyu-underground-city-turkey

question: People in Cappadocia carved whole homes and churches into the pale volcanic rock with simple hand tools, because it is soft when freshly cut. Stranger still is what a new surface does once the air reaches it. What happens to the rock then?
choices: it crumbles back into loose ash
it swells up and seals its own cracks
context: Freshly cut tuff is soft enough to carve with hand tools, but exposure to the air hardens its surface into durable stone -- ideal for rooms meant to last. Cappadocia's tuff came from three ancient volcanoes, Mount Erciyes, Mount Hasan, and Golludag, which buried the region in ash millions of years ago. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia

question: A hand-cut passage leaves Derinkuyu, deep beneath Cappadocia in central Turkey, and runs for some eight kilometres through solid volcanic rock, far past the city's outer edge. Most of the city's tunnels link only level to level and room to room. What lies at the far end of the long passage?
context: The tunnel leads to Kaymakli, a second underground city -- so Derinkuyu was never alone. Roughly 8 to 9 kilometers of hand-cut passages join the two, letting people travel from one buried city to the other without ever surfacing. Kaymakli holds its own marvels, including a single block of hard andesite drilled with 57 holes, used to cold-work copper ore deep underground. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaymakli_Underground_City

question: Raiders who broke into Derinkuyu, the city carved beneath Cappadocia in central Turkey, could still be shut out level by level. Its defenders needed a barrier they could close from within in seconds, one no attacker could shove open from the far side. What kind of door did they devise?
answer: a huge round stone rolled across the passage
choices: a huge round stone rolled across the passage
a thick oak slab banded with iron bars
a heavy portcullis of iron-tipped stakes
a hinged gate cast from solid bronze
context: Each level of Derinkuyu could be blocked by a great disc of stone, like a millstone -- up to about 1.5 meters across and weighing around half a ton -- rolled across the tunnel from the inside, so raiders could not pull it open. A small hole cut through the center let defenders jab spears out at anyone trying to force through. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city; loveexploring.com; thetravelbunny.com

question: Thousands of people and their animals could crowd into the deepest levels of Derinkuyu, beneath Cappadocia in central Turkey, and stay hidden for weeks at a time. So far below ground, the air should have grown stale and deadly. What kept fresh air flowing all the way down to the lowest floors?
answer: a hidden network of shafts running up to the surface
choices: a hidden network of shafts running up to the surface
great fires kept burning to draw out the stale air
gangs of workers pumping air down with huge bellows
hollow reed pipes running out to the hillsides
context: More than 50 narrow ventilation shafts pulled fresh air down to Derinkuyu's lowest floors. One shaft, about 55 meters deep, doubled as a well -- and it could be sealed off from below, so an enemy laying siege from above could not reach or poison the defenders' water. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city; interestingengineering.com/culture/derinkuyu-underground-city-turkey

question: Whole valleys in Cappadocia, in central Turkey, bristle with pale stone cones taller than houses. Many still wear a single dark boulder on top, like a hat. What do the locals call these cones?
context: Their Turkish name is peri bacalari, 'fairy chimneys.' Some rise as tall as about 40 m (130 ft). Source: Smithsonian, 'Turkey's Fairy Chimneys' (smithsonianmag.com/travel/fairy-chimneys-turkey-180956654/).

question: Families in Cappadocia have lived inside its pale cliffs and stone cones for centuries. Their kitchens, bedrooms, stables and even hidden churches are cool rooms in the rock, and some now serve travellers as cave hotels. How did people first make these rooms?
answer: by carving the rooms into solid rock by hand
choices: by walling off the mouths of natural caves
by carving the rooms into solid rock by hand
by tunneling into old collapsed lava tubes
by digging pits and roofing them with slabs
context: Cappadocia's soft rock let people hollow homes and churches straight out of the cliffs by hand; many of those rock rooms are now cave hotels. Source: Much Better Adventures, 'How Cappadocia's Fairy Chimneys Formed' (muchbetteradventures.com/magazine/cappadocia-fairy-chimneys/).

question: Mount Erciyes and Mount Hasan buried Cappadocia in central Turkey under deep layers of ash millions of years ago. Over long ages the ash hardened into a pale stone, soft, yet firm enough to hold up a 40-metre cone for many centuries. What do geologists call this hardened ash rock?
context: The rock is tuff -- compacted volcanic ash. Mount Erciyes, central Anatolia's tallest peak at 3,916 m, was one of its sources. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cappadocia' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia).

question: Dawn breaks over Cappadocia in central Turkey, and dozens of great coloured bulbs of fabric lift off the valley floor together, swelling over roaring burners. They drift above the pale stone cones while riders in wicker baskets watch the land glow at sunrise. What fills the dawn sky here?
context: Cappadocia is one of the world's top spots for hot-air ballooning, letting visitors see the same soft-rock cones from above. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cappadocia' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia).

question: Among Goreme's rock-cut chapels, one is nicknamed the 'Dark Church' for its single tiny window. That gloom once seemed a defect, but it proved a gift: the church's 11th-century Byzantine frescoes are the best-preserved in all Cappadocia, still glowing in blue, red and gold. Why did being so dark protect them?
answer: sunlight never reached the pigments to fade them
choices: sunlight never reached the pigments to fade them
raiders could not find the chapel in the gloom
cool dark air kept mould from ever taking hold
lamp smoke sealed the paint under a hard glaze
context: The Dark Church (Karanlik Kilise) in the Goreme Open-Air Museum: its lack of windows kept out the sunlight that fades pigment, so its mid-11th-century frescoes stayed vivid. Source: Peter Sommer Travels, 'Goreme' (petersommer.com/blog/archaeology-history/goreme).

question: When invading armies swept through Cappadocia, its people climbed down with their animals into Derinkuyu, a city cut deep into the soft volcanic rock. It was far more than a cellar, with stables, wells, chapels, storerooms and rooms for pressing wine and oil. Roughly how many people could it shelter?
context: Derinkuyu could shelter around 20,000 people plus their animals and food, with stables, wells, wine and oil presses, cellars, chapels, and a barrel-vaulted room used as a religious school. Source: Wikipedia, 'Derinkuyu' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derinkuyu_underground_city).

question: Six great pyramids of packed earth rise from Peru's dry Supe Valley. The town around them, Caral, was built about 2600 BC, while Egypt's first pyramids were going up across the world. Among all the ancient towns of the Americas, what is Caral known as?
answer: the oldest city in the Americas
choices: the oldest city in the Americas
the largest city in the Americas
the highest city in the Americas
the driest city in the Americas
context: Radiocarbon dating of the reeds and the woven 'shicra' carrying-bags used to haul stone puts Caral's building at about 2627 BC — as old as, or older than, Egypt's Step Pyramid of Saqqara — yet the two civilizations rose with no contact between them. Caral lies about 182 km north of Lima and only 23 km from the Pacific, and was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009. Source: Wikipedia, 'Caral'.

question: A few thousand people built Caral around six great earthen pyramids in Peru's dry Supe Valley about 2600 BC. Archaeologists there keep coming up empty on one thing that turns up in almost every other city its size. What has never been found at Caral?
context: Archaeologists have found no defensive walls, no weapons, and no mutilated bodies at Caral — no signs of war. Important: this is an absence of EVIDENCE, not proof that Caral was ever perfectly peaceful; it means these particular signs simply have not turned up. Source: Wikipedia, 'Caral'.  (Legend.)

question: A stash of 32 small objects lay in the ruins of Caral, a city of pyramids and plazas that rose near Peru's dry Pacific coast about 5,000 years ago. Each was carefully carved from the wing and leg bones of condors and pelicans, and they date to about 2170 BC. What were they?
context: The 32 bone flutes were accompanied by 37 cornetts (a kind of horn) carved from deer and llama bone. They are among the oldest wind instruments ever found in the Americas, and mark Caral as a deeply musical, ceremonial city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Caral'.

question: Crowds at Caral, in Peru's Supe Valley, gathered for ceremonies in front of the city's two biggest earthen pyramids. Each meeting place was a wide ring dug down into the ground, with a low wall around it, big enough for the whole town to fit inside. What is this signature Caral space called?
context: Caral has two of these sunken circular plazas — round courts dug below ground level: one at the foot of the Great Pyramid's staircase, and a second fronting the Pyramid of the Amphitheatre. Ringed by low walls, they let crowds gather for ritual below the towering earthen mounds. Source: Popular Archaeology, 'Caral: America's Oldest City'.

question: Diggers at Caral, a city in Peru's Supe Valley with no pottery at all, uncovered what may be the oldest known example of a special counting device. Some 4,000 years later the Inca used the same kind of device to track their people, taxes and records across a whole empire without an alphabet. What is it called?
context: A quipu (also spelled khipu) is a set of knotted cotton or wool cords, where the position and type of each knot recorded numbers and information. Remarkably, Caral had no pottery at all — a 'preceramic' city that left almost no art — yet its people knotted cords to keep records. Archaeologist Ruth Shady said the find points to a knotted 'writing' tradition in the Andes lasting some 4,500 years. Sources: gogeometry.com; Wikipedia, 'Norte Chico civilization'.  (Legend.)

question: The people of Caral traded with the Pacific coast, only 23 kilometres from their city in Peru's dry Supe Valley, and hauled dried anchovies and sardines back up the valley. One crop, above every other, was the backbone of that trade. Which crop was it?
context: Caral's economy ran on cotton — but not for eating. The people grew it to make fishing nets and textiles, then traded the cotton (alongside crops like squash and beans) down to Pacific fishers for their catch of anchovies and sardines. Unlike most later American civilizations, Caral was not built on maize. Source: Wikipedia, 'Norte Chico civilization'.

question: Stone Age farmers near Carnac, on France's Brittany coast, cut more than 3,000 granite pillars about 6,000 years ago and dragged them across the fields to stand upright. It is the biggest field of standing stones on Earth. How do the stones stand?
context: Near the little town of Carnac in Brittany, more than 3,000 menhirs — a menhir is a single upright standing stone — march across the fields in long parallel rows, not in a ring like Stonehenge. It is the largest field of standing stones anywhere on Earth, hewn from local granite by Neolithic farmers. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnac_stones

question: More than 3,000 huge upright rocks stand at Carnac on France's Brittany coast, dragged into place by early Neolithic farmers one generation after the next, starting even before they had metal tools. Set beside the world's other famous ancient sites, where does Carnac fall in time?
answer: raised long before Egypt's pyramids and Stonehenge
choices: raised long before Egypt's pyramids and Stonehenge
built in the same age as the pyramids and the Sphinx
raised a few centuries after Britain's Stonehenge
younger than Rome's Colosseum and aqueducts
context: The Carnac stones were raised during the Neolithic, roughly 4500-3300 BC, by some of Europe's earliest farming people — centuries before Stonehenge's great circle and before the Egyptian pyramids. Standing among them, you are looking at monuments older than almost any other famous wonder on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnac_stones

question: Alexander Thom, a Scottish engineer, surveyed the stones of Carnac for years in the 1900s. More than 3,000 tall granite pillars stand there on France's Brittany coast, set up by Stone Age farmers about 6,000 years ago. Thom came away with one bold idea about why, and other scholars still argue over it. What did he think Carnac was built to be?
answer: an observatory for the sun and moon
choices: an observatory for the sun and moon
a great market for trading tribes
context: Scottish engineer Alexander Thom spent years surveying Carnac and argued that its rows form a giant ancient observatory, with stones aligned to key sunrises and moonrises at the solstices. It is the most famous theory about the site — but it is disputed and has never been proven. In truth no one knows why Neolithic people raised thousands of menhirs in rows: an astronomical calendar, ceremonial processions, territory markers, and honoring the ancestors have all been proposed, and the purpose remains genuinely unsolved. Source: https://cparici.com/en/carnac-alignments-guide/; https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/antiquity/article/abs/lunar-observatory-hypothesis-at-carnac-a-reconsideration/

question: A short way from Carnac, at Locmariaquer, Neolithic people raised the Grand Menhir — at nearly 21 metres tall and around 330 tons, the largest single standing stone any prehistoric people ever set upright. Yet a visitor today never sees it looming over the fields. Why not?
answer: it lies toppled, broken into four huge pieces
choices: it lies toppled, broken into four huge pieces
it slowly sank deep into the coastal marsh
later builders carried it off for their stone
an earthquake toppled it into the open sea
context: At Locmariaquer, a short way from Carnac, Neolithic people around 4700 BC raised the Grand Menhir Brise — about 20.6 m (68 ft) tall and roughly 330 tons, the largest single standing stone any prehistoric people ever set upright. Its name means 'the Great Broken Menhir': a few centuries later it fell and shattered into four huge pieces, and today it lies toppled on the ground. Whether it was deliberately pulled down or thrown by an earthquake is still argued. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locmariaquer_megaliths; https://www.worldhistory.org/Locmariaquer/

question: Archaeologists digging into the great burial mounds beside Carnac, on France's Brittany coast, found polished ceremonial axe-heads of green jade laid beside the region's most powerful dead. The mounds were raised more than 6,000 years ago. Where had the green stone for those axes come from?
answer: from the Alps of central Europe
choices: from the Alps of central Europe
from the beaches of Carnac itself
from Egyptian traders across the sea
context: Beside Carnac rises the Saint-Michel tumulus, the largest burial mound in continental Europe. Inside its chambers the high-status dead were buried with treasures carried from far away: polished axe-heads of jade from the Alps, and beads and pendants of green callais (variscite) from Iberia. Moving such prized stone hundreds of miles shows these were powerful, hierarchical peoples more than 6,000 years ago. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Michel_tumulus; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnac_stones

question: Saint Cornelius, a holy man of Breton legend, had one miracle left to work, and an old tale says he spent it on the fields of Carnac, where thousands of standing stones rise today. According to the legend, what are those stones?
answer: a pagan army turned to stone as it marched
choices: a pagan army turned to stone as it marched
a forest of trees turned to stone long ago
a company of giants turned to stone at dawn
a wedding party turned to stone mid-dance
context: This is folklore, not history. A Breton Christian legend says Saint Cornelius (Saint Cornely), fleeing a whole pagan Roman army, reached the shore and turned the soldiers to stone — which is why the menhirs stand in ranks like marching men. A local variant credits the wizard Merlin with petrifying a Roman legion. Both are folk tales invented to explain the strangely orderly rows, not real accounts of how the stones were raised. Source: https://www.solosophie.com/carnac-stones/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnac_stones

question: The Spanish ringed the old town of Cartagena, on Colombia's Caribbean coast, with 11 kilometres of thick stone wall to keep out raiding pirates. The tops of those walls are so wide that Cartagenans use them in daily life. What do the tops serve as today?
context: Las Murallas took shape in stages from 1614 to 1796, and the ramparts are so thick that their tops became public space to walk and gather on. Cartagena's walled old town and forts were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Colombia

question: Pirates prowled the Caribbean around Cartagena, on the coast of Colombia, and Spain closed the city in behind rings of stone and a fort that guarded every side. All those walls guarded one thing every pirate craved. What waited in the harbour for the yearly fleet home to Spain?
choices: gold from the West African coast
context: Cartagena was Spain's treasure vault on the Caribbean: American silver was gathered here for the yearly fleet home, which is exactly why the crown walled and fortified the city so heavily — the treasure drew the pirates. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Colombia

question: Above Cartagena stands Castillo San Felipe, often called the greatest fort the Spanish ever built in the New World. Its walls rise about 41 meters tall. To build it, the Spanish used a stone found right around Cartagena, not shipped from Europe. What is San Felipe mostly built of?
context: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, on the Hill of San Lazaro, rises about 41 m (135 ft) and is widely called the greatest fortress the Spanish built in the New World. Much of it was raised from coral mined out of the region's reefs, its walls wide at the base and narrowing to the parapet. Source: https://www.frommers.com/destinations/cartagena/attractions/el-castillo-de-san-felipe-de-borajas/

question: Narrow tunnels ran through the heart of Castillo San Felipe, the great hilltop fort the Spanish built in the 1600s to guard Cartagena, on Colombia's Caribbean coast, from pirates. The builders shaped those tunnels so well that the guards had one strange edge over any attacker. What could the defenders do because of them?
answer: hear approaching enemies through the stone
choices: hear approaching enemies through the stone
keep the powder magazine cool and dry
hide troops to spring a counterattack
context: San Felipe is riddled with galleries built so that sound carried along them; by tradition, defenders could hear an enemy's footsteps coming. Some chambers were even mined so they could be blown up to bury attackers who broke inside. Source: https://www.frommers.com/destinations/cartagena/attractions/el-castillo-de-san-felipe-de-borajas/  (Legend.)

question: Blas de Lezo, the Spanish admiral at Cartagena, faced a huge British fleet of nearly 200 ships in 1741. The harbour had two sea gates, a wide one and a narrow one called Bocachica, and he funnelled the fleet into the narrow gate under his guns. To block that channel, what did he do?
answer: sank his own ships across it
choices: sank his own ships across it
threw a bridge of boats across it
packed it with rafts of burning tar
context: The Spanish sealed the wide Bocagrande and forced attackers through the narrow Bocachica, straight under the 49 guns of Fort San Luis. In the channel Blas de Lezo scuttled ships and strung a chain boom across it to obstruct the passage. His garrison of roughly 3,000 held off Admiral Edward Vernon's fleet of nearly 200 ships and some 25,000 men, who withdrew to Jamaica with heavy losses. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cartagena_de_Indias

question: Ships carrying captive Africans unloaded at Cartagena's docks on Colombia's Caribbean coast, for Spain let only a few ports in the Americas sell enslaved Africans, and Cartagena was one. Over a million captives were landed there. In which of Cartagena's squares, now a pleasant tourist plaza, were they bought and sold?
answer: the triangular Plaza de los Coches
choices: the triangular Plaza de los Coches
the broad Plaza de la Aduana
the church-side Plaza de Santo Domingo
context: The Spanish crown authorized only a few American ports to sell enslaved Africans, and Cartagena was one of them; well over a million captives were landed at its docks over the city's history. The market centered on the triangular Plaza de los Coches, now a tourist square; nearby, the Jesuit Pedro Claver met the arriving ships to minister to the captives. Source: https://www.mirandakaufmann.com/bbchistorymagcartagena.html

question: Rain falling on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula eats away at the soft limestone for ages, hollowing out long caves full of groundwater. Nobody digs the round pools called cenotes: they form on their own. Then, all at once, one cave is thrown open to the sky. What happens?
context: This is classic 'karst' collapse: slightly acidic rainwater dissolves the limestone into caverns, and when a cave roof finally falls in, the cool groundwater below is exposed as a natural open well. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: The Maya of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula peered into the still, dark water of a cenote, the sky mirrored on its black surface, and believed they gazed at the threshold of another world. To them a cenote was far more than a well. In Maya belief, where did its deep water lead?
answer: down to Xibalba, the land of the dead
choices: down to Xibalba, the land of the dead
up to the Flower Mountain of the sun
back to the roots of the world tree
context: The Maya held that a cenote's deep water was a doorway to Xibalba, the watery underworld, and a home of Chaac, the rain god — the pools were thresholds to the afterlife, not merely wells. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote  (Legend.)

question: The asteroid that blasted out the Chicxulub crater, now buried beneath Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, was about 10 kilometres wide by geologists' estimate: not a boulder but a rock the size of a mountain. If it were set upright next to Mount Everest, the highest mountain on Earth, how would the two compare?
answer: the asteroid towering over the summit
choices: the asteroid towering over the summit
the asteroid reaching only halfway up
the asteroid level with the base camp
the asteroid barely clearing the foothills
context: The Chicxulub crater is about 180-200 km wide, and the impactor was roughly 10 km (6 mi) across — so large that, set on end at sea level, it would have risen higher than Mount Everest (about 8.8 km). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_crater

question: Near Tulum, cave divers spent years mapping two flooded cave systems, Sistema Sac Actun and Sistema Dos Ojos. In 2018, they announced a discovery that made headlines among cave explorers around the world. What had the divers found deep in the drowned passages?
answer: a flooded tunnel joining the two systems
choices: a flooded tunnel joining the two systems
a sunken chamber piled with Maya gold
an unknown kind of blind white cave-fish
a lost stone staircase built by the Maya
context: In 2018 divers confirmed a flooded connection between Sistema Sac Actun and Sistema Dos Ojos near Tulum, merging them into a single system of over 370 km of passage — one of the longest underwater caves on Earth. (The current record-holder is nearby Sistema Ox Bel Ha, surveyed to about 541 km.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_Sac_Actun

question: Far from the Yucatan, in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas, a flooded pit called El Zacaton drops more than 300 metres straight down — one of the deepest water-filled sinkholes on Earth. Its odd name comes from something strange that covers its surface and shifts about in the wind. What is it?
context: El Zacaton, in Tamaulipas, is one of the deepest known water-filled sinkholes on Earth — about 339 m (1,112 ft) deep — and is named for the free-floating islands of 'zacate' grass that drift across its surface in the wind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zacaton

question: NASA lowered an autonomous swimming robot into El Zacatón, a deep, dark flooded shaft in Mexico's state of Tamaulipas, in 2007. The robot was not there mainly to study the sinkhole: it was rehearsing for a much stranger future mission. What did its designers want it to explore one day?
answer: the ocean under the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa
choices: the ocean under the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa
the sea under the ice of Saturn's moon Enceladus
the methane lakes on Saturn's moon Titan
the deep trenches of Earth's own oceans
context: In 2007 NASA sent an autonomous diving robot called DEPTHX (Deep Phreatic Thermal Explorer) into El Zacaton as a testbed for exploring the ocean beneath the ice of Jupiter's moon Europa; it mapped the flooded pit and discovered new kinds of bacteria. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zacaton

question: In a dry canyon in what is now New Mexico, the Ancestral Puebloans raised huge stone houses. The largest held about 650 rooms, rose four stories tall, and covered nearly two acres. Until the 1800s, it was the biggest building in North America. What is this greatest of the Chaco great houses called?
context: Pueblo Bonito ('beautiful village' in Spanish) is the largest and most famous great house at Chaco; at its height it held roughly 650 rooms in a great D-shaped sweep four storeys tall, and its scale rivaled the Roman Colosseum. Chetro Ketl is a neighboring Chaco great house; Casa Rinconada is Chaco's great kiva (a huge circular ceremonial room); Cliff Palace is the famous cliff dwelling at Mesa Verde. The builders were the Ancestral Puebloans (an older name, 'Anasazi,' is now avoided; today's Pueblo peoples are their descendants), who lived at Chaco from about 850 to 1150 CE.
