Source: Wikipedia, Chaco Culture National Historical Park; WebSearch (Pueblo Bonito).

question: About 200,000 pine and fir trees went into the great houses of Chaco Canyon, yet the canyon and its surroundings held almost no big timber. The heavy roof beams came from mountain forests up to 70 miles away. How did the Ancestral Puebloans move them across that distance?
choices: dragged them along the ground on ropes
context: There were no wheels and no horses, oxen, or other heavy draft animals anywhere in the pre-Columbian Americas, and no navigable river reaches Chaco, so human porters shouldered the beams the entire way. Archaeologists note the timbers show almost no drag marks, evidence they were carried rather than dragged or rolled. Some 200,000 trees' worth of straight pine, fir, and spruce beams were cut, cured, and hauled roughly 110 km (70 miles) by hand from ranges such as the Chuska Mountains. Source: Wikipedia, Chaco Culture National Historical Park.

question: Skilled craft workers at Chaco Canyon, in New Mexico's high desert, shaped one prized stone into beads and jewels, and traders carried them for hundreds of miles across the Southwest. Diggers have recovered about 200,000 worked pieces of it. Which stone was Chaco famous for cutting?
context: That stone is turquoise, and Chaco was the great turquoise-working center of the ancient Southwest: roughly 200,000 worked pieces have come out of the ruins, cut and polished in specialized workshops and traded across a network reaching hundreds of miles. Rough turquoise was carried in from distant mines, shaped at Chaco into beads and mosaics, and sent out again as finished ornaments. Source: Wikipedia, Chaco Culture National Historical Park.

question: Wide, well-made roads run out from Chaco Canyon for tens of kilometres, some about 30 feet across, linking it with roughly 30 far-off villages. Researchers still cannot fully explain why the Ancestral Puebloans chose the paths they did. What was special about the routes the Chaco roads took?
context: The Chaco roads hold astonishingly straight bearings, driving across mesas, ridges, and canyons rather than bending around them. The 'Great North Road' runs about 35 miles almost due north. Because a dead-straight line is rarely the easiest route, many researchers think the roads were laid out for ceremonial or symbolic reasons more than for easy travel; over 400 miles of these engineered roads have been mapped across the wider Chacoan world. Source: Wikipedia, Chaco Culture National Historical Park; WebSearch (Chaco Research Archive; SAH Archipedia).

question: Chaco Canyon fell quiet around 1130 CE: its builders suddenly stopped work, and its people drifted away. Tree rings in the region's old timbers show why. A drought had struck, and not an ordinary dry spell but the worst in the whole thousand-year record. About how long did this megadrought grind on?
context: Tree-ring dating shows great-house building at Chaco stopped around 1130 CE, right as a punishing megadrought — lasting roughly 50 years, from about 1130 to 1180 — settled over the Southwest; it was the most intense drought in the North American record for that thousand-year span. In this high desert, where farming always hung on scarce, unreliable rain, a dry spell half a century long was ruinous, and the Ancestral Puebloans migrated away to resettle across the wider Southwest, their descendants becoming today's Pueblo peoples. Chaco had flourished from about 850 to 1150 CE. Source: WebSearch (worldhistory.org; Crow Canyon 'A.D. 1130-1180 Megadrought'; SERC Carleton tree-ring lab).

question: High on Fajada Butte, a rocky tower rising from the floor of Chaco Canyon, an ancient spiral is pecked into the cliff behind three tall leaning slabs of stone. On just one day each year, at midday, sunlight slipping between the slabs forms a thin blade of light that slices straight down through the exact center of the spiral. On which day does this 'Sun Dagger' pierce the spiral's heart?
context: Artist Anna Sofaer first noticed the Sun Dagger in 1977 while recording rock art on Fajada Butte, and the next year founded the Solstice Project to study it. At the summer solstice a single dagger of light bisects the spiral through its center; at the equinoxes two daggers appear; and at the winter solstice two daggers bracket the spiral like bookends, so the marker tracks the whole solar year. Accuracy note: by 1989 erosion (largely from modern foot traffic loosening the soil) had shifted one slab, so the dagger no longer crosses the exact center at solstice; the site was stabilized and closed to visitors in 1990. This describes the alignment as documented in the 1970s. Source: WebSearch (Solstice Project / Anna Sofaer; PlanetQuest; Ancient Origins).

question: The Ancestral Puebloans aligned Chaco's great houses and its great kiva, Casa Rinconada, with the compass directions and with the rising and setting sun. But researchers studying the buildings found they also line up with a far slower rhythm of the sky, one that takes 18.6 years to complete a full cycle, far longer than the sun's yearly round. Which slow celestial cycle did the Chacoans build their walls to track?
choices: the path of the planet Venus
context: This 18.6-year rhythm is the lunar standstill, the slow swing in how far north and south along the horizon the moon rises and sets. Researchers with the Solstice Project found that Chaco's great houses and the great kiva of Casa Rinconada align not only to the cardinal directions and the sun but to the extremes of this lunar cycle. It is a rhythm so slow that no one could watch a full cycle in the prime of life, so the builders had to hand their sky-knowledge down across generations. Scholars still debate how deliberate every alignment was, but the precision at Chaco is striking. Source: WebSearch (worldhistory.org; Solstice Project; Casa Rinconada).  (Legend.)

question: The Chimu built Chan Chan on Peru's dry northern coast, near modern Trujillo. Its walls, plazas, and royal courts covered about 20 square kilometers. That made it the largest city in ancient South America. The whole desert city, even its towering walls, was built from just one thing. What was it?
context: Chan Chan sprawled over roughly 20 sq km near modern Trujillo -- the largest city of pre-Columbian South America and the largest earthen (adobe) city ever built in the Americas. Its ten-metre walls were shaped from millions of hand-made mud bricks, and they survived only because it almost never rains on this desert coast. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/366 ; worldhistory.org/Chan_Chan ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan_Chan

question: The towering walls of Chan Chan, the Chimu capital on the dry desert coast of northern Peru, still run on for kilometres, every surface carved with the same reliefs repeated over and over. What did the Chimu sculpt again and again across the walls of their desert capital?
context: The Chimu were an ocean people who lived off the Pacific's rich fisheries, and they carved the sea across their city: friezes of fish, waves, and seabirds such as pelicans cover the walls, with endless cross-hatching thought to picture a fisherman's net. Source: worldhistory.org/Chan_Chan ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan_Chan

question: Chan Chan, the Chimu capital on Peru's desert coast, was crowded with tens of thousands of people when a rising empire swept down the coast around 1470. It seized the city, took the last Chimu king prisoner for life, and marched Chan Chan's celebrated goldsmiths off to work its own treasuries. Which empire absorbed the Chimu?
context: Around 1470 CE the Inca conquered Chan Chan and absorbed the Chimu into their empire, keeping the last Chimu king, Minchancaman, a lifelong prisoner in the Inca capital Cuzco and carrying off the city's renowned goldsmiths. Source: worldhistory.org/Chan_Chan ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan_Chan

question: Five hundred workers set 1,000 screw-jacks under Chicago's six-story Tremont House hotel in 1861, to fit new sewers beneath the swampy city. They turned all the jacks together and raised the whole building about six feet. Who never moved out during the lift?
answer: the paying guests, still in their rooms
choices: the paying guests, still in their rooms
the digging crews, down in the trench
the city mayor, there on a dare
context: The Tremont House was raised while fully open for business. One guest is said to have watched the view from his window climb several feet without ever realizing the hotel was moving. In the 1850s-60s Chicago jacked up hundreds of buildings this way to slip sewers beneath them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_of_Chicago  (Legend.)

question: Crews jacked all of downtown Chicago up on giant screws in the 1850s and 1860s to drain its muddy streets. Wooden buildings in the way were not knocked down, and a visiting Scot said he saw what happened to them almost daily. What did the crews do with these houses?
answer: rolled them down the streets to new lots
choices: rolled them down the streets to new lots
buried them under the new roadbed
context: The visiting Scot, David Macrae, wrote that scarcely a day passed that he 'did not meet one or more houses shifting their quarters.' Whole wooden buildings were rolled through the streets on logs to new lots instead of being demolished. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_of_Chicago

question: After the Great Fire of 1871 leveled wooden Chicago, the rebuilt city climbed upward. In 1885, William Le Baron Jenney finished a ten-story tower that weighed only a third as much as a stone building its size. Its outer walls held up nothing, hanging like a curtain. What carried the whole weight instead?
choices: a hidden core of poured concrete
a lattice of heavy oak timbers
deep stone piers under each floor
context: Jenney's Home Insurance Building is widely credited as the world's first skyscraper, though the claim is genuinely debated. Its iron-and-steel frame carried the load, so a building's height was no longer limited by the thickness of its walls. It rose 10 stories (later 12) and was demolished in 1931. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Insurance_Building  (Legend.)

question: Chicago's elevated trains, or 'the L,' run downtown on a rectangle of tracks that was finished in 1897. That rectangle of rails circles the whole business district. The circling tracks gave the neighborhood its one-word nickname. What is downtown Chicago called?
context: The 'L' is short for 'elevated.' The downtown ring of elevated track, the Union Loop, was completed in 1897 and financed by transit magnate Charles Tyson Yerkes; the loop of rails literally names the neighborhood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_%22L%22

question: Chicago drank from Lake Michigan, but the Chicago River carried the city's sewage straight into that same lake. In 1900, after digging the Sanitary and Ship Canal, engineers broke the last dam at dawn on January 2. The river then did something no major river had done before. What happened to the Chicago River?
choices: it vanished into a covered tunnel
it stilled into a wide lagoon
context: Reversing the river sent Chicago's sewage down toward the Mississippi watershed instead of into its own drinking-water lake. Workers broke the final dam at dawn on January 2, 1900, and the full reversal was complete by January 17; the American Society of Civil Engineers later called it a 'Monument of the Millennium.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Sanitary_and_Ship_Canal

question: The slaughterhouses of the Union Stock Yards on Chicago's South Side, the world's biggest meatpacking district for nearly a hundred years from 1865, dumped their waste into one dead-end branch of the Chicago River for decades. It became a stagnant, reeking industrial sewer. What nickname, still used by Chicagoans, did that fouled branch earn?
context: The branch is the South Fork of the Chicago River, nicknamed 'Bubbly Creek' because so much rotting stockyard waste sank into it that decomposition gases bubbled up through the surface. It was one of the horrors that pushed Chicago toward its great sanitation projects. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_River

question: Aaron Montgomery Ward, the mail-order tycoon, was furious at schemes to build on Chicago's Lake Michigan shore. Starting in 1890, he won four Illinois Supreme Court cases to keep the lakefront open to the public, though in most big cities private high-rises fill the finest waterfront. What fills that protected shore today?
answer: a long chain of public parks
choices: a long chain of public parks
a public boat harbor and docks
context: An 1836 canal-commissioners' map had marked the ground 'A Common to Remain Forever Open, Clear and Free of Any Buildings.' Aaron Montgomery Ward, the 'watchdog of the lakefront,' won four Illinois Supreme Court cases to enforce it, and Daniel Burnham's 1909 Plan of Chicago made it doctrine, declaring the lakefront by right belongs to the people. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Montgomery_Ward

question: When Chicago's Sears Tower (now the Willis Tower) topped out in 1973 at 1,451 feet, it was the world's tallest building — a title it held about 25 years. Engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan built its frame not as one solid block but as nine separate square 'tubes.' How did he arrange those nine tubes?
choices: stacked one on top of another
context: The 108-story tower's nine bundled square tubes stop at different heights, giving its stepped silhouette and bracing one another against Chicago's wind. Its glass Skydeck 'Ledge' boxes jut out over the street about 1,350 feet up. It remained the world's tallest building until 1998. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willis_Tower

question: Streets run startlingly flat across Chicago, with barely a rise for miles. That flatness is the smooth, level floor of something vast that filled this basin at the end of the last Ice Age, then drained away about 13,000 years ago. What is the city built on the bed of?
context: The vanished water was Glacial Lake Chicago, the meltwater ancestor of Lake Michigan, which formed as the glaciers retreated about 13,000 years ago. The city's flatness is its fossil lakebed, and sandy ridges like Ridge Road trace its ancient beaches. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Chicago

question: Chicago sits at a low, swampy gap early settlers called 'Mud Lake' — a six-mile portage where, in high water, a canoe could slip across from one great water system to another. In 1673 Louis Jolliet and Jacques Marquette crossed it, and Jolliet saw its huge value: a short canal here would join two watersheds. Which two water systems does the Chicago Portage link?
answer: the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River
choices: the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River
the Missouri and the Ohio rivers
the St. Lawrence and the Atlantic coast
context: The Chicago Portage is a low gap in the subcontinental divide between the Great Lakes and Mississippi watersheds; settlers called its marshy middle 'Mud Lake.' Jolliet's idea for a canal there became the Illinois & Michigan Canal (opened 1848), which made Chicago the hub of the Midwest. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Portage

question: Beneath Chicago, giant bores driven hundreds of feet underground, up to 33 feet across, feed reservoirs that hold more than 17 billion gallons of storm water and sewage that would otherwise foul Lake Michigan. Begun in 1975 and still unfinished, it is one of Earth's largest engineering projects. What blunt two-word nickname do Chicagoans give it?
context: The system is the Tunnel and Reservoir Plan (TARP), or 'Deep Tunnel': about 109 miles of tunnels as much as 350 feet underground and up to 33 feet across, feeding reservoirs like Thornton (7.9 billion gallons). With over 17 billion gallons of capacity and decades and billions of dollars invested, it is among the largest civil-engineering works ever built. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunnel_and_Reservoir_Plan

question: The Maya built El Castillo, the step pyramid at the heart of Chichen Itza, as a calendar in stone. Its four staircases and the last step onto the temple platform add up to 365 steps in all, matched to one great cycle. Which cycle is it?
answer: the days of the solar year
choices: the days of the solar year
the days of the ritual round
the days of the Venus cycle
the days of the lunar year
context: 91 steps on each of the four staircases make 364, and the step onto the top platform makes 365 — the length of the Haab', the Maya solar year, a calendar carved in stone. The other options are real cycles the Maya counted separately: the 260-day Tzolk'in ritual round and the 584-day Venus cycle. This is the widely accepted reading; because some steps are eroded, the total is counted 'including the top platform.' Source: Wikipedia, 'El Castillo, Chichen Itza' (91x4 + top platform = 365, matching the Haab').  (Legend.)

question: Twice a year, on the spring and autumn equinox, the late afternoon sun hits the stepped edge of El Castillo's north staircase. Seven triangular shadows link into one long, rippling body. For about half an hour, a great serpent seems to slither down the stairs to the carved stone snake head at the base. Which god do the Maya show coming down the pyramid?
context: The effect is real and deliberately engineered by the builders: broken by the pyramid's stepped northwest edge, the equinox sun casts seven triangles of light down the north balustrade (alfarda), so a body of light and shadow ripples down to the great carved serpent-head at the base — the descent of Kukulkan, the Feathered Serpent. (Quetzalcoatl is the related Aztec god; Chaac is the rain god; Itzamna a creator.) It shows for roughly half an hour, about 4:30-5:10 pm. Sources: mayan.org Chichen Itza guide; Wikipedia, 'El Castillo'; yucatanmagazine.com.

question: High on the walls of Chichen Itza's Great Ball Court hang two heavy stone rings, carved with twined feathered serpents, set about 26 feet above the ground. Teams kept a solid rubber ball moving using only their hips, knees, and elbows. To score, what did a team have to make the ball do at one of these rings?
answer: send it up through the ring
choices: send it up through the ring
knock the ring off the wall
circle the ball around the rim
bounce it off the ring's face
context: Driving a heavy rubber ball up through a vertical stone ring 8 m (26 ft) overhead — with no hands or feet — was so hard that a single goal could end the game. The rings are carved with intertwined feathered serpents. At about 168 m by 70 m, with walls 8 m high and 36 m apart, this is the largest ancient ball court in all the Americas. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Chichen Itza'; World History Encyclopedia.

question: Carved stone panels run the length of Chichen Itza's Great Ball Court, spelling out the game's deadly stakes. On one, a defeated ball-player kneels — beheaded. From his severed neck the Maya sculptor sent not plain blood but seven shapes bursting upward, one of them blossoming into a plant, as if blood were becoming life. What did the carver shape those streams into?
context: The relief ties the ballgame to sacrifice and fertility: from the decapitated captain's neck spring seven streams carved as serpents, one of them turning into a plant — blood becoming new life. Several such panels line the Great Ball Court. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Chichen Itza'; World History Encyclopedia (Great Ball Court reliefs).

question: Behind a plaza bristling with carved stone pillars rises Chichen Itza's Temple of the Warriors. At its summit lies a stone man leaning back on his elbows, knees drawn up, head turned sharply aside, with a shallow dish resting on his belly to hold offerings. Maya and Toltec builders set this same reclining figure atop temples across old Mexico. What is it called?
context: A Chac Mool is a reclining stone figure — head turned 90 degrees, a bowl or disk on its belly to receive offerings — found at Toltec and Maya sites across central Mexico and the Yucatan. This one crowns the Temple of the Warriors, fronted by the Group of a Thousand Columns. (An atlante is a pillar carved as a standing warrior; a stela a carved standing slab; a zoomorph a boulder carved as a creature.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Chichen Itza.'

question: At the northern edge of Chichen Itza the ground opens into the Sacred Cenote, a sheer-walled pit about 60 metres across whose cliffs drop some 27 metres to still green water. In times of drought the Maya threw gold discs, carved jade, balls of copal incense and human offerings into this pool, and Edward Thompson dredged them up after 1904. Which hook-nosed god of rain were they begging?
context: This is the Sacred Cenote (Cenote Sagrado), about 60 m across with cliffs dropping ~27 m to green water. Into it the Maya cast gold, jade, copal incense and human offerings to petition Chaac, the hook-nosed Maya rain god. (Tlaloc is the Aztecs' rain god; Kukulkan the feathered serpent; Itzamna a creator.) Between 1904 and 1910 the American consul Edward Herbert Thompson dredged and dived the pool, raising gold, jade, pottery, incense and human bones — many of children and young adults offered in droughts. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chichen Itza' (Cenote Sagrado; Thompson 1904-1910).  (Legend.)

question: El Castillo hides a secret: it was raised right over an older, smaller pyramid, sealed whole inside it. In April 1935, archaeologists tunneling into the buried temple came upon a stone throne shaped like a crouching beast. It was painted brilliant red, with two spheres of jade for its eyes and white shell for its fangs. What animal was this hidden throne carved as?
context: Sealed inside El Castillo is an older pyramid; tunneling in during April 1935, archaeologists found the inner temple's throne carved as a jaguar — the Maya emblem of kingship — painted bright red (the 'Red Jaguar Throne'), its spots inlaid jade discs, its eyes jade spheres, its fangs white shell. A reclining Chac Mool with mother-of-pearl eyes guarded it. Source: Wikipedia, 'El Castillo, Chichen Itza' and 'Red Jaguar Throne.'

question: A quiet word spoken at the temple on one end of Chichen Itza's Great Ball Court carries plainly to a friend at the temple on the far wall, more than 135 metres off across open stone. The court is a stone avenue 168 metres long between two high parallel walls, and a few cathedral domes are famous for the same trick. What is this kind of acoustic space called?
context: The Great Ball Court is a natural whispering gallery: a soft word at one end temple carries clearly to the far temple over 135 m (about 450 ft) away, and a single handclap in the court sets off a booming flutter echo between the parallel walls. Popular guides exaggerate the effect (claiming it works 'in any wind'), but the long-distance whisper transmission is real and measured. Sources: Acoustical Society of America, 'Acoustics of the Great Ball Court at Chichen Itza' (JASA); ResearchGate, 'Whispering gallery at Chichen Itza's Great Ballcourt.'  (Legend.)

question: Across the whole Yucatan Peninsula there is scarcely a river or lake on the surface, yet the great Maya cities all cluster around deep, water-filled sinkholes. The reason lies in the bedrock: the peninsula is a vast slab of soft limestone, and rain does something to it that leaves the surface bone-dry. What happens to the rain?
answer: it soaks straight down into the rock
choices: it soaks straight down into the rock
it evaporates in the tropical heat
it is drunk up by jungle roots
it runs off quickly to the coast
context: The Yucatan is a flat slab of porous limestone (a karst landscape): rain sinks straight through it, so there are almost no surface rivers or lakes. Groundwater gathers below, and where the limestone roof collapses it exposes the water table as a sinkhole — a cenote (Maya ts'ono'ot, 'water deposit'). Cenotes were the region's only reliable fresh water, which is exactly why the Maya built their cities beside them. Sources: Britannica, 'cenote'; Monroy-Rios (Northwestern), Yucatan karst speleogenesis; chichenitza.com.

question: Beside the pyramids at Chichen Itza stands El Caracol, a round tower on a broad platform, named 'the snail' for the spiral stair coiling up inside. Its narrow windows and the sight lines across its corners are no accident. They point to the horizon spots where one sky-body rises and sets at the ends of its 8-year cycle, the one the Maya watched to time planting and war. Which sky-body did El Caracol track?
context: El Caracol ('the snail,' for its inner spiral stair) is an observatory: about 20 of its 29 identified sightlines — through narrow windows and along wall corners — point to the horizon extremes where Venus rises and sets across its 8-year cycle (five Venus cycles are close to eight years). The Maya tracked Venus closely to time planting and warfare. Source: Aveni et al., 'The Caracol Tower at Chichen Itza,' Science 188:977 (1975); Wikipedia, 'El Caracol.'

question: A single handclap at the foot of El Castillo's great staircase at Chichen Itza comes back from the steps as a strange downward chirp, a rapid ringing note that slides from high to low. David Lubman, an acoustic engineer who first measured the effect in 1998, found the echo uncannily like the piping call of one bird the Maya held sacred. Which bird does the pyramid seem to echo?
context: The chirp is a real, measurable effect, not magic: the evenly spaced stone steps act like a diffraction grating — a 'picket fence' that reflects a clap back as a rapid run of tones sliding high to low, close to the piping call of the quetzal, the bird the Maya held sacred. California acoustic engineer David Lubman first documented it in 1998; Declercq and colleagues explained the physics in 2004. Sources: Nature News 2004, 'Mystery of chirping pyramid decoded'; Declercq et al., JASA 116(6):3328 (2004); Lubman, Acoustical Society of America.

question: Cone-shaped hills rise across a plain in central Bohol, in the Philippines, each so alike in shape and size that the field looks laid out to one plan. They are not a dozen odd mounds but a crowd. About how many of these cones stand there?
context: The cones -- about 1,268 counted -- spread across more than 50 square kilometers around the towns of Carmen, Batuan and Sagbayan, and rise mostly 30 to 120 meters, the tallest as high as a 30-story building. A local legend even claims two feuding giants made them, hurling sand and boulders at each other for days until they tired, made peace, and left the mounds scattered behind. Sources: UNESCO Bohol Island Global Geopark; Wikipedia 'Chocolate Hills'; GeologyScience 'Chocolate Hills Philippines'.

question: Every dry season, Bohol's Chocolate Hills in the Philippines turn a deep chocolate brown across the whole plain. Yet the stone inside a hill is no brown rock at all, only pale grey limestone. What actually dries out and browns, painting the hills their famous colour?
answer: A blanket of coarse cogon grass
choices: A blanket of coarse cogon grass
A carpet of moss and lichen
context: The color is the grass, not the rock: the hills are pale grey limestone, and only the coarse cogon grass (Imperata cylindrica) blanketing them dries brown in the dry months -- so when the rains return, the same hills green up again. That seasonal brown coat is exactly what earned them the name 'Chocolate Hills.' Sources: GeologyScience 'Chocolate Hills Philippines'; Wikipedia 'Chocolate Hills'.

question: The pale grey cones of the Chocolate Hills rise across a broad inland plain on the Philippine island of Bohol, green in the wet season and chocolate brown in the dry. Their limestone, split open, is crowded with tiny fossils. What kind of fossils are they?
context: The pale limestone still holds proof it was underwater: fossil shells of foraminifera, coral, mollusks and algae from a sea that covered Bohol in Pliocene-to-Pleistocene times. The cone shape has its own label -- 'cone karst' or 'cockpit karst.' The hills became a National Geological Monument in 1988, and in 2023 Bohol was named the Philippines' first UNESCO Global Geopark. Sources: GeologyScience 'Chocolate Hills Philippines'; UNESCO Bohol Island Global Geopark; Wikipedia 'Chocolate Hills'.

question: A bare, stony limestone plateau rises in southwest Slovenia, above the sea near Trieste. It is pocked with sinkholes and with streams that drop into the ground. Geographers took this plateau's own name and now use it worldwide for every place where water drains like this. What is that term?
context: The plateau is the Kras (German 'Karst'); English borrowed the word in the late 1800s, and its pre-Indo-European root simply means bare, stony rock — the land literally named after being rock without soil. From this one tableland above Trieste, 'karst' spread worldwide to name any limestone country where water drains underground. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karst)

question: Rain falling on Slovenia's bare Kras plateau is slowly eating the rock. Each drop takes in a gas as it falls through the air and turns into a mild acid, strong enough over the ages to hollow caves and sinkholes out of solid limestone. Which acid does plain rain become?
context: The gas is carbon dioxide: raindrops dissolve it to form weak carbonic acid, which slowly eats the limestone and tunnels downward. That is why karst has so few surface streams or lakes — its drainage runs underground. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karst)

question: In southwest Slovenia, the Reka River rolls along like any ordinary river, wide enough to swim. Then, near one village, its whole flow pours off the land and into the rock, and the river vanishes from sight. Into what does the Reka disappear?
context: The Reka starts as an ordinary surface stream ('Big Creek') on Mount Snežnik, then at the village of Škocjan plunges off the surface into the Škocjan Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reka_(river))

question: Underground, the Reka thunders through Hanke's Channel, a rock-walled void inside Slovenia's limestone so vast that its ceiling is lost in the dark far overhead. In fair weather the river is a modest ribbon on the cavern floor, but downstream the passage pinches to a gap that can plug like a bottleneck. After a heavy storm, about how high up the walls can the trapped flood climb?
context: Hanke's Channel is a giant rock-walled canyon inside the Škocjan Caves — about 3.5 km long, 10–60 m wide, and over 140 m from the black water up to the ceiling. In heavy rain the trapped water can rise more than 100 m when a downstream siphon cannot drain the flood fast enough, nearly filling the void. It ranks among the largest underground river canyons known. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Škocjan_Caves)

question: Unseen, the Reka River races through Slovenia's limestone for about 34 kilometres after it sinks underground. Then it bursts out into the daylight near the Adriatic coast by Trieste, rising from the ground as a cluster of springs under a brand-new name. As what river does the Reka come back to the sea?
context: After some 34 km underground, the Reka resurges as the Timavo springs near San Giovanni di Duino, flowing only about 2 km in the open before reaching the Gulf of Trieste. Roughly a third of the Timavo's water is the sunken Reka; the rest is rain soaked straight into the plateau. Virgil's Aeneid described the river bursting from the mountain in many mouths. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Škocjan_Caves)

question: Boats drift across Lake Cerknica in Slovenia in the wet season, when it spreads wide enough to be the country's largest lake and locals fish it. By midsummer farmers are cutting hay on the same ground, for the lake lies in a polje, a karst basin with a flat floor. How does the lake empty?
answer: it drains down holes in its own floor
choices: it drains down holes in its own floor
it dries up in the long summer heat
a dam upstream cuts off its rivers
context: A polje is a flat-floored karst plain. Lake Cerknica fills to about 38 km² in the wet season, then drains away through swallow-holes, called ponors, in its own bed, so locals fish it when it is full and farm the dry bed when it empties. Valvasor described it to London's Royal Society in 1687; once (1834–35) it stayed dry for over a year. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Cerknica)

question: High on a mountain ridge in Costa Rica sits Monteverde. Drifting mist wraps it so constantly that water beads up and drips from the leaves, even on days when no rain falls at all. Foresters have a special name for this kind of misty mountain woodland. What is it?
context: Monteverde, high on Costa Rica's Cordillera de Tilaran, sits so constantly inside the passing clouds that its leaves drip even in dry weather. A tropical mountain forest bathed in near-permanent cloud is a cloud forest -- not just any misty wood. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monteverde_Cloud_Forest_Reserve ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_forest

question: Whole hanging gardens of moss, orchids and bromeliads sprout straight from the branches in Costa Rica's Monteverde cloud forest, rooted in no soil at all. Botanists call such plants epiphytes. What share of all Monteverde's plant species grow this way?
context: With the trees always soaked, plants grow with no soil at all, perched right on the branches -- mosses, orchids and bromeliads called epiphytes, or 'air plants,' from the Greek epi ('upon') + phyton ('plant'). At Monteverde they make up about 29% of the flora, some 878 species. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monteverde_Cloud_Forest_Reserve ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphyte

question: The Inca did not build Machu Picchu on a bare, dry peak. They chose a green ridge on the eastern slopes of the Andes, wrapped almost every morning in cloud, its stonework kept damp by moisture climbing endlessly up from a huge lowland below. Which lowland's rising damp feeds those clouds?
context: Machu Picchu stands about 2,430 m up on the eastern Andean slope, inside a montane cloud forest. Moisture rising off the Amazon basin keeps humidity at 80-90% and wraps the ruins in morning mist. The Inca chose this milder, well-watered ridge deliberately, below their cold high capital of Cusco. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machu_Picchu

question: Higher than any tree can grow, on the cold misty grasslands that crown the tropical Andes above the cloud forest, one strange plant rules the slopes. It grows as a giant leaf rosette atop a thick trunk, wrapped in a shaggy coat of pale dead leaves and fuzz. Whole hillsides look dotted with woolly green statues standing in the fog. What is this signature Andean plant called?
context: The frailejon (Espeletia) rules the high Andean grasslands -- a giant rosette on a shaggy, furry trunk. Its look-alikes -- Africa's giant lobelias and groundsels, the Andes' own puya -- are giant rosettes of other tropical high mountains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A1ramo

question: High in the northern Andes, above the cloud forest, the trees give out and the páramo begins: a cold, wet grassland where frost bites on many nights and fog soaks the slopes by day. Bogotá and Quito, below it, depend on the páramo for one thing above all. What does it give them?
choices: cool air in the hot season
context: Above the cloud forest the trees stop and the páramo takes over: a cold, wet, tropical-alpine grassland roughly 3,000-4,800 m up, with mean temperatures of only 2-10 C and a daily freeze-and-thaw. Its spongy plants and soils soak up rain and fog and let the water out slowly, feeding the water supplies of Bogotá and Quito. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A1ramo

question: The mangroves of the Sundarbans stand in the tide where the Ganges meets the Bay of Bengal, and they steadily change the coastline of Bangladesh. Most trees just sit on the land where they are rooted. What are these mangroves doing that almost no other forest can?
answer: Building brand-new land out into the sea.
choices: Building brand-new land out into the sea.
Marching slowly inland as the sea rises.
Draining the delta's swamps into farmland.
Splitting the Ganges into a hundred rivers.
context: By slowing the tide and combing silt out of the water, the Sundarbans' mangrove roots trap sediment and build new land seaward -- and that same dense root tangle absorbs wave energy, blunting a cyclone's storm surge and even tsunamis so the delta villages behind the forest flood far less. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangrove

question: Off the cold Atlantic coast at the very tip of South Africa sways the Great African Sea Forest, a golden underwater woodland tall enough to dive through and the setting of the film 'My Octopus Teacher'. Yet its towering, tree-like fronds are not trees at all -- and not even plants. What is a giant kelp, really?
context: Kelp only looks like a plant. A giant kelp is a brown alga (a seaweed); its body is called a thallus, not a plant with true roots, stems, and leaves. The Great African Sea Forest fringes Cape Town and runs over 1,000 km up the cold coast toward Namibia -- said to be the only forest of giant 'sea bamboo' (Ecklonia maxima) on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelp_forest ; seachangeproject.com/great-african-seaforest/

question: In the giant-kelp forests off the coast of California, each frond starts on the seabed in dim light and must race upward through the water to reach the sunlight. Giant kelp is one of the fastest-growing living things on the whole planet. On a good day, how much taller can one frond grow between sunrises?
context: Giant kelp can shoot up 30-60 cm -- up to about two feet -- in a single day, among the fastest growth of any living thing, as it races sunlight to the surface. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelp_forest

question: Acre for acre, the tidal mangrove forests of the Sundarbans, on the coast of Bangladesh and India, lock away several times more carbon than a tropical rainforest does, and scientists call it blue carbon. Where do these mangroves keep most of it?
answer: in the airless mud beneath them
choices: in the airless mud beneath them
in their thick and waxy leaves
in the tidal water around them
context: Most of a mangrove forest's carbon lies not in its wood but in the mud: in waterlogged, airless soil, fallen leaves and dead roots barely rot, so their carbon stays buried for centuries. A major study of mangrove forests across the Indo-Pacific found that the soil held roughly half to almost all of each forest's carbon. Carbon stored this way by coastal ecosystems, the mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes, is called blue carbon. Source: nature.com/articles/ngeo1123 (Donato et al. 2011)

question: Northern Chile's Atacama Desert runs right down to the Pacific, yet some of its weather stations have gone years with no measurable rain. A cold current sweeps up the coast from the far south and chills the air above the water, so that it cannot rise, form clouds or rain. Which current is it?
context: Cold water chills the air just above it, and cold air cannot rise to form rain — so the Humboldt breeds fog but almost never a downpour. The sea off this coast sits near 16°C (61°F) when tropical seas usually top 25°C. The current is a MAIN cause of the aridity, working alongside the sinking air of the subtropical high and the Andes rain shadow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current.

question: Villagers in the rainless hills above Chungungo, on Chile's Atacama coast, hang huge mesh screens across the ridgetops. Called atrapanieblas, or fog catchers, they comb drinking water out of the drifting sea mist. A mesh screen looks good for a trickle at best, yet the biggest arrays near Huasco proved far richer. About how much water can such a fog farm wring from the mist on a good day?
context: Tens of thousands of liters. Large fog-catching towers near Huasco were reported to yield 10,000–50,000 liters of water a day, and the village of Chungungo once ran 94 nylon-mesh atrapanieblas to supply about 300 people. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog_collection.

question: Fog off the cold Benguela Current cloaks Namibia's northern Atlantic shore so thickly that sailing ships lost their bearings and ran aground in the murk. Their rusting hulks still lie half-buried in the sand as the dunes slowly swallow them, and Portuguese sailors called this shore 'The Gates of Hell'. By what name is the coast known today?
context: The Skeleton Coast — named both for the whale and seal bones that once littered it and for the skeletal hulks of wrecked ships. The dunes still hold named wrecks: the Eduard Bohlen (now stranded far inland as the sand advanced), the Otavi (1945), the Dunedin Star, and the Portuguese Bom Jesus, aground since the 1530s and one of the oldest shipwrecks ever found in sub-Saharan Africa. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeleton_Coast.

question: Alfred Wegener, a German scientist, saw in 1912 how Brazil's bulge tucks into the coast of West Africa, and made a bold claim. All of today's continents, he said, had once been fused into one giant landmass, ringed by a single world ocean. What name did Wegener give that lost supercontinent?
context: Pangaea is Greek for 'all Earth', and the single ocean surrounding it was Panthalassa, 'all sea'. It assembled about 335 million years ago and began breaking apart about 200 million years ago, first splitting into a northern half, Laurasia, and a southern half, Gondwana. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea

question: Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews, two British scientists, published magnetic readings from the Carlsberg Ridge, in the Indian Ocean, in 1963. On either side of the ridge the sea floor's magnetism lay in matching, mirror-image stripes. Alfred Wegener's drifting continents had waited decades for someone to show what moved them. What did those stripes finally prove was happening?
answer: New seafloor forms at the ridge and spreads out both sides.
choices: New seafloor forms at the ridge and spreads out both sides.
The whole Earth is slowly swelling and cracking its crust.
The continents plough forward through the solid ocean floor.
Meteor strikes shattered the crust into the moving plates.
context: The mirror-image magnetic stripes showed that fresh crust forms at the ridge, records Earth's magnetic field as it hardens, and is carried away on both sides as the seafloor spreads, as Harry Hess had proposed. Matthews had surveyed the ridge from HMS Owen in 1962, and the Canadian Lawrence Morley reached the same idea on his own, so it is often called the Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis. It gave Wegener's continents their engine, and the theory took its modern name, plate tectonics, in the 1960s. Source: Vine and Matthews, 'Magnetic Anomalies over Oceanic Ridges', Nature 199 (1963); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drummond_Matthews

question: The Indian subcontinent is still ploughing north into the rest of Asia, pushing the Himalayas higher as it goes. Geologists like to say it creeps along at almost exactly the pace of one familiar thing that grows. What grows at about the same speed?
context: India drifts north at roughly 5 cm a year — about the rate fingernails grow — and because the collision is unfinished, the Himalayas are still being pushed upward today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_plate

question: Nanga Parbat soars 8,126 m over the mountains of northern Pakistan, standing at the sharp western corner of the Himalayan arc where India's plate drives hardest into the crust. Guinness World Records lists this single peak for one geological superlative. Which is it?
choices: the most isolated mountain on Earth
context: Guinness World Records lists Nanga Parbat as the fastest-rising mountain; thermochronology puts its uplift near 7 mm a year, concentrated at the western Himalayan syntaxis where India's push is squeezed into a knot. Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/fastest-rising-mountain  (Legend.)

question: At the top of the Himalayas lies rock that was once the bed of a real ocean. That sea lay between India and Asia until the two continents slammed together and squeezed it shut, around 50 million years ago. What was the vanished ocean called?
context: The seafloor now atop the Himalayas was the bed of the Tethys Ocean, the sea that once separated India from Asia; as India rammed north the Tethys closed (final closure ~50-60 million years ago) and its floor crumpled into the peaks. Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012821X16306707

question: In the folded ranges of western Iran, the same kind of continent-against-continent collision that raised the Himalayas is unfolding today. A whole plate grinds north into Eurasia at about 25 mm a year, crumpling up the Zagros Mountains. Which plate is doing the pushing?
context: The Arabian plate drives into Eurasia at about 25 mm a year, still crumpling up Iran's Zagros Mountains — a live continent-continent collision, the same engine that built the Himalayas and the Alps. Source: https://www.geolsoc.org.uk/science-and-policy/plate-tectonic-stories/zagros-ramge/

question: India is a slab of light continental rock, and it has kept ramming into Asia for some 50 million years without vanishing. Ocean floor that collides with a continent dives down into the mantle and is destroyed; India has not. What has India's leading edge been doing all that time?
answer: forcing its way in under Asia
choices: forcing its way in under Asia
piling up as a coastal range
context: Because India is thick, buoyant continental crust it could not subduct like ocean floor; it forced partway under Asia, roughly doubling the crust's thickness there and buckling the surface up into the Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayan peaks. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/why-mount-everest-can-grow-and-shrink-plate-tectonics

question: Coral on Australia's Great Barrier Reef glows gold, green and pink, yet strip away its tenants and the coral animal itself is pale, almost see-through. Its bright colours come from millions of tiny partners crowded inside its tissue. What are these hidden lodgers?
context: Those partners are microscopic algae called zooxanthellae. They live inside the coral's tissue and use sunlight to make food, feeding the coral and painting it its brilliant colors; the coral animal itself is nearly colorless. (Wikipedia, 'Coral bleaching')

question: A marine heatwave struck Australia's Great Barrier Reef in 2016. The reef runs some 2,300 kilometres, so vast that one hot summer might seem too little to harm it badly, yet later surveys counted how much of all its coral had died in that single event. What share did they find?
context: Back-to-back marine heatwaves in 2016 and 2017 brought the worst bleaching the Great Barrier Reef had then known. The 2016 event alone killed an estimated 29 to 50 percent of the reef's coral, and the northern reefs, where the water was hottest, lost the most. Reefs can recover from one hot year, but not when struck again before they heal. (Wikipedia, 'Coral bleaching'; Hughes et al., Nature 2018)

question: Low coral islands ring a calm turquoise lagoon at Enewetak, far out in the Pacific, with open ocean on every side and no larger island rising in the middle. Some 440 coral rings like it are scattered across the oceans, most of them in the Pacific. What is such a formation called?
context: This is an atoll, a ring of coral reef enclosing a lagoon with no island in the middle, like Enewetak in the Pacific. Most of the world's roughly 440 atolls lie in the Pacific Ocean. Charles Darwin reasoned that each began as a reef fringing a volcano that slowly sank while the coral kept building upward. (Wikipedia, 'Atoll')

question: Mount Mazama once towered over Oregon's Cascade Range, until a huge eruption about 7,700 years ago left a hole where its summit had been. Crater Lake now fills that bowl, some 8 to 10 kilometres across. What do geologists call such a basin?
context: A caldera forms when a volcano empties its underground magma chamber and its summit collapses into the void -- far larger than a crater, the smaller pit around a volcano's vent. Mount Mazama's collapse about 7,700 years ago left the caldera that Crater Lake now fills. Source: USGS, Geology and History Summary of Mount Mazama and Crater Lake (usgs.gov).

question: High in Oregon's Cascades, Crater Lake holds some of the cleanest water on Earth, a clear sapphire blue with almost no sediment in it. The whole lake is replaced only about once every 150 years. What keeps it filled?
context: With no muddy river flowing in, sunlight sinks deep into the clear water and the blue wavelengths scatter back to the eye -- the source of that intense color. Crater Lake's whole volume renews only about every 150 years, kept full by the deep winter snows of the Cascades. Source: Crater Lake (en.wikipedia.org).

question: Crater Lake lies nearly 6,200 feet up in Oregon's Cascade Range, a broad blue sheet some 20 square miles across, filling the hollow left when Mount Mazama fell. Its clear sapphire water is famous the world over. Which United States record does it hold?
answer: the deepest lake in the United States
choices: the deepest lake in the United States
the oldest lake in the United States
the largest lake in the United States
the highest lake in the United States
context: At 1,949 feet (594 m), Crater Lake is the deepest lake in the United States and one of the deepest on Earth, though Lake Baikal and Lake Tanganyika plunge far deeper. It sits high in the Cascades, spreads about 20 square miles and fills a young caldera. Source: Crater Lake (en.wikipedia.org).

question: Scientists on Crater Lake lowered a white disc on a rope and watched it sink. In an ordinary lake such a disc vanishes into the murk within a few feet, but here it stayed clearly visible far below the surface. About how far down could they still see it?
context: The white disk is called a Secchi disk. In 1997, researchers measured clarity of 142 feet (43 m) at Crater Lake -- among the clearest freshwater ever recorded. With almost no sediment or algae to cloud it, sunlight drives deep, feeding the lake's legendary blue. Source: Crater Lake (en.wikipedia.org).

question: William Gladstone Steel, a champion of Oregon's Crater Lake, gave a name in 1885 to the small young volcano rising from its waters. Fresh eruptions had built the cinder cone on the sunken floor left when Mount Mazama collapsed, until it broke above the surface. What did Steel call it?
context: Wizard Island is a small cinder cone that grew inside the caldera AFTER Mount Mazama collapsed -- a young volcano rising from the floor of the ruined old one. Early Crater Lake champion William Gladstone Steel named it in 1885 because its cone reminded him of a sorcerer's (wizard's) pointed hat. Source: William Gladstone Steel (en.wikipedia.org).

question: A whole hemlock log known as Old Man of the Lake, kept sound by the cold, pure water, has drifted on Crater Lake since at least 1896. The tree is now centuries old, yet what makes visitors stare is its curious behaviour. What is so strange about the way this log rides the water?
answer: It floats upright, standing straight up like a post.
choices: It floats upright, standing straight up like a post.
It floats fully submerged, gliding just below the surface.
It spins slowly in place, turning like a compass needle.
It freezes into the winter ice and thaws free each spring.
context: The 'Old Man of the Lake' stands about 1.2 m (4 ft) proud of the surface and has bobbed vertically since it was first noted in 1896 -- over 130 years upright. The frigid, mineral-poor water preserves the wood so well that carbon dating puts the tree at 450+ years old. In a 1938 study, John Doerr found it wandered at least 62 miles (100 km) around the lake in a single summer, moving most on windy days. Source: Old Man of the Lake (en.wikipedia.org).

question: Mount St. Helens flattened whole forests when it erupted in 1980. Yet the eruption that destroyed Mount Mazama about 7,700 years ago, leaving the hollow that Crater Lake fills, was the largest the Cascade Range has produced in a million years. Roughly how many times more powerful was Mazama's great blast?
context: Mazama poured out roughly 50 cubic km of magma, and the blast is often rated about 42 times as powerful as St. Helens in 1980. Its pale 'Mazama ash' settled across the Pacific Northwest and beyond, and geologists still dig up that single bright layer as a natural time-stamp; traces have been found as far away as Greenland. Source: Crater Lake National Park (NPS), as quoted by the USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory; oregonencyclopedia.org/articles/mt_mazama/

question: The Klamath people were living near Mount Mazama when it erupted, and their oral tradition may preserve an eyewitness memory of it. In their story Llao, spirit of the underworld, dwelt beneath the mountain while Skell ruled the sky, and the two waged a furious battle. How does the Klamath account say it ended?
answer: Skell hurled the mountaintop down onto Llao, sealing him deep below.
choices: Skell hurled the mountaintop down onto Llao, sealing him deep below.
Llao buried Skell's people under a river of fire and ash.
The two spirits made peace and agreed to share the mountain.
Skell fled across the western sea and never returned.
context: This is Klamath ORAL TRADITION, not written history -- but because the Klamath lived in this land when Mazama fell about 7,700 years ago, many regard the story as a genuine memory of the eruption, carried down across thousands of years. In the tale, the mountain's collapse seals Llao in the underworld beneath what is now Crater Lake. Source: The Creation of Crater Lake, Klamath tradition (traveloregon.com).  (Legend.)

question: In the small Italian city of Cremona, around 1700, Antonio Stradivari built stringed instruments by hand. A single one of them can now sell for millions, and many call his work the finest ever made. What kind of instrument is Cremona famous for?
context: Antonio Stradivari (c.1644-1737) spent almost his whole long life in Cremona, and any instrument he made is called a 'Stradivarius.' He built violas and cellos too, but it is his violins the world calls the finest ever made. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stradivarius.

question: Antonio Stradivari marked every instrument that left his workshop in Cremona in the late 1600s and early 1700s. The mark named him in Latin, with the word 'Cremonensis,' meaning 'of Cremona,' and the year he made it. What did he use to sign his work?
context: The label read, in Latin, 'Antonius Stradivarius Cremonensis Faciebat Anno' and the year - 'Antonio Stradivari of Cremona made this in the year ___.' He glued one inside every instrument that left his house on Cremona's Piazza San Domenico (today Piazza Roma). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Stradivari.

question: More than a thousand instruments came out of Antonio Stradivari's workshop in Cremona over some 75 years of work. Three hundred years of wars, fires and hard daily use have passed since then. About how many of his instruments are still around today?
context: Over roughly 75 years Stradivari made about 1,100 instruments (scholars count near 1,116). Around 650 survive today, and a single violin can now sell for millions of dollars. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stradivarius.

question: The Lady Blunt, a violin Antonio Stradivari built in Cremona in 1721, came up for auction in June 2011 and fetched $15.9 million, the highest price ever paid for any violin. Yet the sale is remembered less for the record than for what became of the money. Where did it all go?
answer: it all went to Japanese tsunami relief
choices: it all went to Japanese tsunami relief
it endowed a violin museum in Cremona
it was divided among the seller's heirs
it funded a search for lost Stradivari violins
context: The 'Lady Blunt' - named for Lord Byron's granddaughter, Lady Anne Blunt - sold for a record $15.9 million in a 2011 online auction. Its owner, the Nippon Music Foundation, gave every penny to relief for Japan's 2011 earthquake and tsunami. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Blunt_Stradivarius; bloomberg.com 2011-06-20.

question: The most celebrated Stradivarius of all, the 1716 'Messiah' from Cremona, now rests in Oxford's Ashmolean Museum. After three centuries it still looks nearly brand-new. The varnish shows no wear whatsoever, and the carved edges remain unusually crisp and sharp. Why does this violin still look untouched?
answer: it has been played almost never
choices: it has been played almost never
it was restored just a few years ago
it was kept locked in a bank vault
it is a careful modern copy
context: The 'Messiah' got its name from a violinist's joke: because everyone talked about it but no one ever saw it, Jean-Delphin Alard quipped it was 'like the Messiah of the Jews: one always expects him but he never appears.' Barely played, it now sits in Oxford's Ashmolean Museum as a yardstick for future makers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messiah_Stradivarius.

question: A long cold spell, the Little Ice Age, gripped Europe from roughly 1645 to 1750, during Antonio Stradivari's long life in Cremona. No one has fully proven why his violins sound so glorious, but one leading theory credits the cold. According to it, how did the cold help make such perfect violin wood?
answer: Alpine trees grew slowly, making dense spruce
choices: Alpine trees grew slowly, making dense spruce
frost split the logs into thin, light panels
the cold thickened the varnish as it dried
snowmelt soaked the wood and softened its tone
context: It's only a theory. Tree-ring study traces Stradivari's spruce to the high forests of Val di Fiemme in Trentino, Italy, and the cold 'Maunder Minimum' would have made those trees grow slowly and evenly, giving dense, even-grained wood. A rival theory points to chemistry instead - traces of aluminum, copper and calcium hint at treatments like borax (to kill woodworm) or sodium silicate. Neither is proven. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stradivarius.  (Legend.)

question: Niccolo Paganini, the great violinist, prized one instrument above all others, and it was not a Stradivarius. It was a 1743 violin by Giuseppe Guarneri, Stradivari's rival in Cremona, and Paganini nicknamed it for the overpowering force of its sound. What did he call it?
context: Paganini's favorite was a 1743 violin by Giuseppe Guarneri 'del Gesu' - a nickname from the sacred 'IHS' Christogram Guarneri stamped on his labels. Paganini called the violin 'Il Cannone,' the Cannon, for its powerful tone. Fewer than 200 Guarneris survive; one, the 'Vieuxtemps,' later sold for about $18 million (2013). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Guarneri.

question: Ten world-class soloists put on welder's goggles in Paris in 2012, so they could not see what they were holding, and played priceless old Stradivari violins from Cremona against brand-new ones. For 300 years people had believed a Stradivarius simply sounds better. What did the players decide?
answer: most of them preferred a brand-new violin
choices: most of them preferred a brand-new violin
every soloist singled out a Stradivarius
they judged all the violins identical
they refused to trust their own ears
context: In the 2012 Paris test, run by Claudia Fritz and Joseph Curtin, 6 of the 10 soloists picked a new violin as their favorite, and the new violins outscored the old Italians overall. A 2017 listening study found audiences also couldn't reliably tell old from new - and judged the new violins to project better across a hall. The Stradivarius 'secret' has never actually been proven. Sources: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1619443114; theviolinchannel.com 'The Paris Experiment.'

question: Scribes at the temple storehouse of Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia, tallied grain, sheep and cattle on the oldest tablets yet found, around 3300 BC. Among the very first things ever written down were daily rations of bread and jugs of what?
context: Beer and bread were the twin staples of Sumer, both brewed and baked from barley, and the temple paid its workers in both. The earliest Uruk tablets are ration lists and receipts -- writing was invented for accounting, not literature. Source: worldhistory.org/cuneiform/

question: Around Uruk, the Mesopotamian city that left the world's oldest writing, the flat land offered almost no stone to carve and very little wood to spare. Its scribes could not record their words the way other peoples did. What did they write on instead?
context: Mesopotamia had almost no stone or timber, but endless river mud. Scribes shaped clay into a tablet, wrote while it was damp, then let it dry in the sun or baked it hard. Clay is the reason so much Sumerian writing survives today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform

question: The tablets of Mesopotamian cities such as Nineveh have outlasted nearly all the paper and papyrus of the ancient world, and some half a million survive. They came through a disaster that struck city after city, one that ought to have destroyed them. What was it?
context: Fire destroys paper but bakes clay: a burning city fired its clay tablets exactly like a kiln fires pottery, turning soft mud into near-indestructible ceramic. The greatest cuneiform libraries -- like Nineveh's -- survived precisely because they were put to the torch. Source: britishmuseum.org/blog/how-write-cuneiform

question: Mesopotamian bookkeepers tracked debts in three dimensions long before the first tablet: each sheep, jar or measure of grain was a small token, and the tokens for one deal were sealed inside a hollow ball called a bulla. Scholars think writing began when someone did what to the tokens?
answer: stamped their shapes on the outside
choices: stamped their shapes on the outside
strung them onto a knotted cord
context: Instead of breaking open a sealed bulla to check the count, accountants began stamping each token's shape onto the outside of the ball -- and eventually skipped the tokens entirely, drawing the shapes straight onto a flat tablet. Three-dimensional counters had become two-dimensional signs. Source: metmuseum.org/essays/the-origins-of-writing

question: At Uruk, around 3300 BC, a new script was invented to record one people's everyday tongue. Over the next 3,000 years, dozens of completely unrelated peoples across the Near East borrowed its signs to write down their own speech. Whose language did cuneiform first write?
context: Cuneiform began at Uruk around 3300 BC as a way to write Sumerian, but a script is only a set of signs -- so unrelated peoples could borrow it for their own tongues. Over three millennia Akkadians, Babylonians, Elamites, and Hittites all wrote their completely different languages in the same wedges, exactly the way the same alphabet today writes English, Spanish, and Vietnamese. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform

question: The scribes of ancient Sumer counted not in tens but by a much larger base number, over 4,000 years ago. Two habits still come from them: a full circle has exactly 360 degrees, and a clock runs in strange counts instead of clean hundreds. Which number did their arithmetic count by?
context: The Sumerians counted in base-60 (sexagesimal), probably because 60 divides so evenly, by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and more. The 60-second minute, the 60-minute hour and the 360-degree circle all come down, by long tradition, from their clay-tablet maths. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexagesimal  (Legend.)

question: Ashurbanipal, king of Assyria, gathered over 30,000 tablets into his library at Nineveh, sending scribes across his empire to hunt down and copy old texts. He took special pride in one personal skill that set him apart from other kings of his day. What was it?
answer: he could read the ancient scripts himself
choices: he could read the ancient scripts himself
he had his own laws carved in stone
he could recite long poems from memory
he never lost a single battle
context: In an age when literacy was a scribe's specialized craft and most kings kept scribes to read for them, Ashurbanipal could personally read both Akkadian and the already-ancient Sumerian. His Nineveh library, dug up in the 1850s, preserved the fullest surviving copy of the Epic of Gilgamesh. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Ashurbanipal

question: Buried in Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, on twelve tablets, lay the oldest great story humanity has recovered: the Epic of Gilgamesh. When scholars finally read the eleventh tablet in the 1870s, they got a shock. It told a tale that Jewish and Christian readers thought began in the Book of Genesis, only written centuries earlier. What ancient story does that tablet tell?
context: Tablet XI describes a god-sent flood that drowns the world, survived by one man in a great boat -- matching Noah's flood, but recorded before Genesis was written. The discovery stunned Victorian Britain and made cuneiform tablets front-page news. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh  (Legend.)

question: George Smith, an engraver by training who had taught himself cuneiform on his lunch breaks, was bent over a scorched tablet from Nineveh in the British Museum in 1872 when its signs revealed a lost tale no one had read in over 2,000 years. His colleagues said the normally reserved Smith then did something wildly out of character. What did he do?
context: Smith reportedly grew so excited that he 'began to remove articles of his clothing' and ran round the room shouting in delight. He had taught himself cuneiform on his lunch breaks and was the first modern person to read the tablet after more than two millennia of oblivion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(Assyriologist)  (Legend.)

question: High on a limestone cliff at Behistun in western Iran, about 100 metres up, King Darius the Great had a giant cuneiform inscription carved around 500 BC. In the 1830s and 40s the scholar Henry Rawlinson spent years copying it sign by sign -- a dangerous feat, since the carving sits on a sheer rock face far above the ground. How did Rawlinson reach it to copy it?
answer: he hung from ropes on the cliff
choices: he hung from ropes on the cliff
he cut a stairway in the rock
he copied it through a telescope
context: Rawlinson began scaling the Behistun cliff in 1835 and had accurate copies in Europe by 1847, at one point using an agile local boy to cross the most dangerous stretch. His years of perilous work made Behistun the single most important source for reading the lost script -- cuneiform's 'Rosetta Stone.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behistun_Inscription

question: Darius the Great had his boast of nineteen battles won in a single year carved into the cliff at Behistun three times over, side by side, each in a different language of his empire. Why did that triple carving finally let scholars read cuneiform?
answer: one script was nearly an alphabet
choices: one script was nearly an alphabet
one version was carved in Greek letters
the tablet came with a scribe's dictionary
the signs were labeled with small pictures
context: The three scripts were Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian. Old Persian was by far the simplest -- almost an alphabet, and close to later Persian -- so scholars deciphered it first, then used that reading to unlock the far more complex Elamite and Babylonian. Nothing at Behistun could be read in advance; the key was that one text appeared in three scripts, and one of them was simple enough to break into. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behistun_Inscription

question: A scribe in Nineveh, the great city on the Tigris, pressing a line of words into wet clay, often set a determinative beside one of them: a sign that was written but never read aloud. Scholars reading his tablets some 2,700 years later still lean on it. What did that silent sign tell the reader?
answer: what kind of thing the word named
choices: what kind of thing the word named
how the word should be sounded out
which language the word came from
where a new sentence was to begin
context: Determinatives were silent signs written just before or after a word to show its category: a god, a place, a man, or something made of wood, so that a town would not be mistaken for a person of the same name. Cuneiform signs juggle three jobs, standing for a whole word, for a sound, or as a silent category marker, and one sign can do any of them depending on context. That triple duty is a big reason the script took scholars decades to crack. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform

question: Guides at Sacsayhuaman, above Cusco, show tourists how tightly its giant limestone blocks fit without mortar. They try to slide one thin everyday object into the seam between two blocks, and it will not go in. What do they try to slide in?
context: The chronicler Pedro Cieza de Leon wrote in 1553 that not even a rial -- a Spanish silver coin -- could be slipped between two of Sacsayhuaman's stones. The Inca cut and re-cut each block until it hugged its neighbours exactly, with no mortar of any kind. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuam%C3%A1n

question: Sacsayhuaman crowns the hill above Cusco as the head of the crouching puma that the city's plan is said to trace. Its three mighty terrace walls climb the ridge one above the next, high over the city. Which part of the puma's head are those walls said to be?
context: Sacsayhuaman's terraces climb the hillside in three great walls of sharp saw-tooth angles -- its most striking feature -- long imagined as the bared teeth of the puma whose head the fortress forms above Cusco. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuam%C3%A1n

question: Thousands of people crowd the grassy field below Sacsayhuaman, above Cusco, every 24 June to watch a costumed royal parade in honour of the Inca god Inti. The old festival was banned for nearly four hundred years after the Spanish conquest. Which Inca festival is staged there?
context: The festival is Inti Raymi, the Inca Festival of the Sun. Once the empire's grandest ceremony, it is reenacted every 24 June on the esplanade below Sacsayhuaman, drawing tens of thousands of spectators. Source: intiraymiticket.com/blog/inti-raymi-sacsayhuaman/

question: The giant limestone blocks of Sacsayhuaman, above Cusco, some weighing over 100 tons, are fitted so perfectly, with no mortar at all, that some visitors insist aliens or a lost super-technology must have raised them. Archaeologists disagree, pointing to the marks real Inca tools left across every block face. How did Inca workers shape the blocks?
answer: by pounding them with harder hammerstones
choices: by pounding them with harder hammerstones
by grinding them with wet sand
by cracking them with fire and cold water
by carving them with bronze chisels
context: Inca workers pounded the blocks into shape with jiwayas -- dense, harder river cobbles used as hammerstones -- using no iron tools at all. The faces still carry thousands of tiny impact dimples from the hammering. No aliens or lost technology were involved. Source: machupicchualtitude.com

question: The largest block in Sacsayhuaman's walls is a limestone monster estimated at well over a hundred tonnes -- heavier than a fully loaded lorry. The Inca quarried it about 35 km away and somehow brought it all the way to the hilltop fort. How did Inca crews move such a colossal stone across the mountains?
answer: dragged by teams of workers on log rollers
choices: dragged by teams of workers on log rollers
floated on a raft down a river
hoisted by a tall wooden crane
rolled along on giant stone wheels
context: The largest limestone block is estimated at anywhere from about 128 to 200 tonnes (the weights are estimates, not exact measurements). Inca crews dragged it roughly 35 km from the quarry at Rumicolca on ramps and log rollers, hauled by hundreds of workers -- without wheels or draft animals. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuam%C3%A1n

question: The Inca emperors ruled from Cusco, high in the Peruvian Andes, and called their stone capital Qosqo. The name is traditionally translated as a part of the human body, for to the Inca the city was that part of the world. Which part?
context: Qosqo is traditionally translated 'the navel' -- the still center from which the empire's four quarters radiated. The half-Inca chronicler Garcilaso de la Vega popularized 'navel of the world' in his Royal Commentaries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco; studycountry.com.

question: Travellers who fly into Cusco from sea level, about 3,400 metres up in the Peruvian Andes, often grow dizzy and short of breath in the thin air. Andean people have eased it for thousands of years by chewing one local plant's leaves. Which plant?
context: The coca leaf is the traditional Andean remedy for soroche (altitude sickness), chewed or brewed as tea for thousands of years. Cusco stands about 3,400 m (11,200 ft) up, near the Sacred Valley and the Urubamba River. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco.

question: From the great central plaza of Cusco, four royal roads shot outward, one to each of the four quarters of the empire. The Inca named their entire realm after this fourfold shape, since all four parts met at the capital. By what name did the Inca know their empire?
context: Tawantinsuyu means 'the four parts together' (tawa = four). Four great roads split from Cusco to the quarters -- Chinchaysuyu, Antisuyu, Qullasuyu, and Kuntisuyu -- all meeting at the capital. Chachapoyas, Chinchorro, and Tiwanaku were other real Andean cultures. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawantinsuyu.

question: The emperor Pachacuti rebuilt Cusco during the 1400s, one tradition says, to trace the body of a sacred Andean animal. The hilltop fortress of Sacsayhuaman was its head, two meeting rivers its tail. Which animal was the city said to trace?
context: Scholars treat the puma layout as a tradition, not settled fact: Sacsayhuaman is said to form the puma's head and the meeting of the Saphi and Tullumayo rivers its tail, from Pachacuti's 1400s rebuild. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacsayhuaman; terandes.com.  (Legend.)

question: Visitors crowd a narrow lane in old Cusco called Hatunrumiyoc to see one block in an Inca palace wall. The Inca built without mortar, cutting each stone to lock into its neighbours, and Peru prints this one on postcards as the symbol of their stonework. What makes this stone so famous?
context: The Twelve-Angled Stone is a single greenish-diorite block cut with twelve corners that lock into its neighbors without mortar, set in Inca Roca's old palace wall (now the Archbishop's Palace). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_angle_stone.

question: Stone roads ran out from Cusco across the Inca empire to villages a thousand miles away, and urgent news could travel up to about 150 miles along them in a single day. The Inca had no wheels and no horses at all. How did they move news so fast across the mountains?
context: These relay runners were the chasquis, posted at short intervals along the royal roads; each sprinted his own stretch at full speed and handed off to the next, so a message could cover up to about 240 km (150 miles) in a day. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Inca_road_system; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_road_system

question: The earthquake of 1950 wrecked more than a third of Cusco, and the Spanish church of Santo Domingo cracked and fell. The old Inca walls beneath it came through unharmed, and the wreckage even laid bare the Inca temple below. What lets Inca walls ride out quakes that flatten what is built on top of them?
answer: the fitted stones shift, then settle back
choices: the fitted stones shift, then settle back
the walls are simply too thick to crack
a deep bed of sand cushions the shaking
flexible mortar bends with the ground
context: Inca blocks are trapezoidal and lean slightly inward, and because they are dry-fitted without mortar they can shift during a tremor and resettle rather than shatter. The 1950 quake wrecked the Santo Domingo church and laid bare the undamaged Inca masonry of Coricancha beneath. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qorikancha; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusco.

question: The Spanish who reached Cusco were stunned by Coricancha, the Temple of the Sun and the city's holiest shrine. Their chroniclers described a garden in its courtyard of life-size corn, flowers and llamas, models crafted by the empire's finest artisans, and walls faced in sheets of one shining metal. Which metal covered Coricancha's walls?
context: Coricancha (Quri Kancha, 'the golden enclosure') had gold-sheathed walls and a garden of gold-and-silver plants and animals. The gold is gone because the Spanish stripped it -- much went to the 1533 ransom of the captured emperor Atahualpa, and the Dominicans built the Church of Santo Domingo on the temple's Inca walls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qorikancha.

question: Quechua families near the Apurimac River, in the Peruvian Andes, tear down Q'eswachaka, the last Inca rope bridge still in use, every year and rebuild it by hand across the gorge. The Inca hung such swaying bridges wherever their stone roads crossed a deep canyon. What are the bridge's great cables twisted from?
context: Q'eswachaka spans about 45 m over the Apurimac River and is the last surviving Inca rope bridge, rebuilt each year from braided ichu grass by the Quechua communities who keep it. The Inca road network, the Qhapaq Nan, ran without the wheel or horses, its cargo carried by llama caravans. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_road_system.

question: Cyril and Methodius, two Greek brothers, gave the Slavs their first letters in the 800s; today about 250 million people use Cyrillic, from Moscow to Belgrade. The brothers grew up in one big city of the Byzantine world. Which city was their childhood home?
context: The brothers grew up in Thessalonica (Thessaloniki), the Greek port where their father Leo served as a Byzantine military officer (a droungarios) of the theme of Thessalonica. Cyril was born Constantine (826/827) and Methodius born Michael (815-820); together the two are honored as the 'Apostles to the Slavs.' Reputable estimates put Cyrillic's readers today at roughly 250-350 million across 50-plus languages. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saints_Cyril_and_Methodius

question: Cyril and Methodius travelled north in 862 to Great Moravia, a Slavic kingdom in what is now Central Europe, to teach Christianity. A monk writing as Hrabar later recorded that, until the brothers arrived, the Slavs had no alphabet and kept their records a rougher, older way. What did they use?
context: The account came from a monk who signed himself Chernorizets Hrabar ('Hrabar the Brave'), whose treatise 'On the Letters' (O pismeneh) defended the new Slavic alphabet. He recorded that before Christianity 'the Slavs did not have their own letters, but read and communicated by means of strokes and incisions' -- tallies and rough sketches. He credited Saint Constantine (Cyril) with later composing 'thirty-eight letters ... suitable to express Slavic sounds.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernorizets_Hrabar  (Legend.)

question: Saint Cyril died in Rome in 869, before the neater script that bears his name existed; he and Methodius had made Glagolitic. His followers built the new script later, at the Preslav school, so the name Cyrillic honours a man who never made it. In which realm did the Preslav scholars work?
context: Constantine took the monastic name 'Cyril' only weeks before he died in Rome on 14 February 869 -- so the alphabet honors a name he held only at the very end of his life, and one he never made.
