The equinoxes are the two days when daylight and darkness are equal. Where does the dawn light fall inside Mnajdra on those two mornings?
choices: onto the edges of the flanking stones
context: Mnajdra's builders aligned it to the sky over 5,000 years ago: at the spring and autumn equinox the sunrise runs straight down the central axis, while at the summer and winter SOLSTICES the first light instead strikes the edges of the two great stones flanking the doorway -- so this one temple tracks the entire solar year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mnajdra

question: Sebastian Steudtner, a German surfer, rode one wave at Praia do Norte, the beach at Nazaré on Portugal's Atlantic coast, in October 2020. Guinness World Records ratified a world record for that single ride in 2022. What record does he hold?
context: Steudtner's wave measured 26.21 m (86 ft) - about as tall as an eight-storey building - and was ratified in May 2022 as the largest wave ever surfed. It broke the mark set at the same beach, Praia do Norte, by American surfer Garrett McNamara, whose 23.8 m ride in November 2011 first made Nazaré famous. (Source: guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/78115-largest-wave-surfed-unlimited)

question: Nazaré in Portugal, like Jaws off Maui and Mavericks in California, throws up its giant waves at the very same spot on every big swell, whatever the weather. Off Praia do Norte, the beach at Nazaré, an ordinary Atlantic swell of maybe fifty feet can rear up into a hundred-foot wall. What stands Nazaré's giants up at that one spot?
context: Nazaré's giants stand up over the Nazaré Canyon - the largest submarine canyon in Europe, about 230 km long and up to 5,000 m deep - whose head comes within roughly 1 km of Praia do Norte. It delivers the open-ocean swell to shore with almost no loss of energy, while the shallow shelf on either side saps ordinary waves; on perfectly lined-up days the wave can even triple. It is the shape of the sea floor, not the wind, that decides where a giant wave is born: Nazaré has its canyon; at Jaws an underwater ridge trips the incoming swell, and at Mavericks a sloping rock ramp slows part of the wave while the deep water beside it races on, bending the crest into a U-shape that collapses onto one spot. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazaré_Canyon; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mavericks,_California)

question: Sailors swore for generations that a lone wall of water could rear out of an ordinary sea and swallow a ship, and scientists dismissed it as myth. Then on New Year's Day 1995 a laser pointed down from the Draupner platform off Norway caught one: a single wave 25.6 metres tall, more than twice as tall as the waves around it. What is such a sudden lone giant called?
context: That was the Draupner wave - the first 'rogue wave' ever captured by an instrument, proving the sailors right. The sea around the platform that day averaged only about 12 m, so at 25.6 m the wave reared more than twice as high, and steeper, than its neighbours. The rig had been engineered to survive a 1-in-10,000-year 20 m wave; the rogue beat even that. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draupner_wave)

question: On the north coast of County Antrim, Northern Ireland, the Giant's Causeway steps down into the sea as a natural pavement of about 40,000 dark stone columns set edge to edge. Most of the columns share the same cross-section shape. What shape are they?
context: Not every column is a perfect hexagon -- some have four, five, seven or even eight sides -- but six-sided columns dominate because hexagons pack together with the least wasted space and the shortest cracks as the cooling rock shrinks. The tallest columns rise about 12 metres (39 ft). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant's_Causeway

question: The Giant's Causeway is laid so neatly along the Antrim shore that its legend credits a giant with setting every stone. Yet it all formed in a single natural event, long before anyone walked that coast. What made its 40,000 columns?
answer: A sheet of molten lava that cooled and cracked
choices: A sheet of molten lava that cooled and cracked
A glacier that ground the coast into blocks
Beds of seashells slowly pressed into stone
Wind-blown sand dunes hardened over ages
context: As a thick sheet of basalt lava cooled, it shrank and fractured from the top surface downward, splitting into tall columns -- a process geologists call columnar jointing. The very same thing crazes drying mud into tiles, only here on a slow, giant scale. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant's_Causeway; https://www.nps.gov/subjects/volcanoes/columnar-jointing.htm

question: Dark columns step out of the sea at the Giant's Causeway, and more of them wall Fingal's Cave in the cliffs of Scotland's Staffa. In Iceland whole beaches glitter with jet-black sand. All three are made of one heavy volcanic stone that hardens quickly from cooling lava. Which rock is it?
context: Basalt is the dark, iron-rich rock that runny volcanic lava freezes into -- the most common rock beneath the world's oceans. Because basalt lava is thin and flows far before cooling, it can spread into the broad, even sheets that crack into column fields like the Causeway. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant's_Causeway

question: Lava once flooded the coast where the Giant's Causeway now meets the sea, yet no cone-shaped volcano poured it out. About 60 million years ago it welled straight up from the ground across the whole region, from no single peak. Geologists tie that outpouring to one dramatic thing happening to the crust beneath this coast. What was it?
choices: An ocean floor was sinking into a trench
Two plates were sliding past each other
context: As Europe (carrying Ireland and Britain) pulled away from Greenland and North America, the stretching crust tore and floods of basalt poured out along the widening cracks -- geologists call the whole outpouring the North Atlantic Igneous Province. Into that growing rift a vast new ocean, the North Atlantic, began to flood, and the same slow spreading still widens the Atlantic by a few centimetres a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant's_Causeway

question: Across the sea from the Causeway, on the tiny Scottish isle of Staffa, tall stone columns frame the mouth of Fingal's Cave -- a sea cave about 85 metres deep, walled and roofed in pillars and floored by the open Atlantic. Reaching it is famously awkward. How do visitors get inside?
answer: By small boat, riding in on the swell
choices: By small boat, riding in on the swell
By a spiral staircase cut down the cliff
Through a tunnel bored under the island
Across a rope bridge slung at the mouth
context: The bold can also scramble in along a ledge of broken column-tops beside the water, but there is no dry path -- the sea fills the floor. Inside, the arched roof soars about 20 to 23 metres high. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingal's_Cave

question: Benandonner, the huge Scottish giant of the best-loved Causeway legend, came thundering across the stone road to fight Finn McCool. One look at his rival's size left Finn terrified. Finn's wife saved him with a single trick. What did she do?
answer: She dressed Finn as a giant baby in a cradle
choices: She dressed Finn as a giant baby in a cradle
She dug a deep pit and hid it under turf
She dared Benandonner to a riddle he could not answer
She baked hard stones into loaves to crack his teeth
context: Seeing the size of the 'baby,' Benandonner panicked at how gigantic its father must be and fled home, ripping up the causeway behind him so Finn could not follow -- which, in the story, is why the columns plunge into the sea and rise again at Staffa. Weathered rocks at the site carry folk names too: the Giant's Boot (a stone the legend calls a size 93.5), the Organ, and the Chimney Stacks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant's_Causeway; https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/northern-ireland/giants-causeway/history-of-giants-causeway

question: Fingal's Cave on Staffa, some 120 kilometres across open sea from the Giant's Causeway, is walled in the same dark columns, much as the legend of a giant's road running on beneath the waves would have it. Geologists in the 1800s worked out the real link between the two sites. What is it?
answer: They erupted from one and the same lava flow
choices: They erupted from one and the same lava flow
They were carved out by one and the same glacier
They were raised long ago by the same builders
They stand on the slopes of the same volcano
context: Both are surviving scraps of the North Atlantic Igneous Province -- one immense outpouring of basalt about 60 million years ago that once blanketed the whole region. Erosion has stripped away the rest, leaving the Causeway and Staffa as matching ends of a road that, in rock at least, really does cross the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingal's_Cave

question: The Atlantic swell booms and echoes down the columned hall of Fingal's Cave like a vast pipe organ, which is why its Gaelic name, Uaimh Bhinn, means 'the cave of melody.' In 1829 the sound so gripped a seasick 20-year-old visitor, the composer Felix Mendelssohn, that a theme came to him on the spot. It grew into one of his most famous concert overtures. Which one?
context: Mendelssohn jotted the opening bars into a letter to his sister Fanny, saying the Hebrides had 'affected me extraordinarily.' The finished overture (Op. 26) is nicknamed the 'Fingal's Cave' overture. The cave drew a roll-call of Romantic-era admirers -- Queen Victoria, Wordsworth, Keats, Jules Verne, Walter Scott, and the painter J.M.W. Turner, who painted it in 1832. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingal's_Cave; https://www.classical-music.com/features/works/mendelssohns-hebrides-overture-fingals-cave

question: Big Rock lies alone on the flat prairie west of Okotoks, Alberta: a quartzite boulder longer than a blue whale, some 16,500 tonnes, split in two. Its stone is a plain mismatch for the ground beneath it. What do geologists call such a boulder?
context: 'Erratic' comes from the Latin errare, 'to wander' — a boulder that wandered far from home. Big Rock, about 8 km west of Okotoks (whose name is the Blackfoot word for 'rock'), is the largest known glacial erratic on Earth: roughly 41 by 18 metres, 9 metres high, some 16,500 tonnes of quartzite left stranded when the ice melted. A moraine, drumlin, and esker are glacial landforms too, but each is built of piled-up debris, not a single travelled boulder. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Rock_(glacial_erratic)

question: The Blackfoot tell how Big Rock came to lie in two great slabs on the Alberta prairie. Napi the trickster laid his robe on it as a gift, snatched it back when rain threatened, and the angry rock tore loose and rolled after him across the plains. In their story, what caught the rolling rock and split it in two?
answer: a swarm of bats that dived at it
choices: a swarm of bats that dived at it
a river that rose up to block it
a herd of bison that charged it
a bolt of lightning that struck it
context: This is Blackfoot oral tradition, not literal history. In the story the diving bats that split the rock got their flattened faces in the bargain — one tale explaining two wonders at once. The real crack is a natural fracture through a roughly 16,500-tonne quartzite boulder. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Rock_(glacial_erratic)  (Legend.)

question: From Big Rock on the Alberta prairie, a trail of matching quartzite boulders runs about 930 kilometres south along the eastern edge of the mountains into Montana, and Big Rock is the largest of them. A single Ice Age glacier dropped each one as it crept along. What is this vast line of boulders called?
context: Big Rock is the biggest boulder of the Foothills Erratics Train, a line of quartzite blocks a glacier ferried about 930 km south along the Rockies' eastern edge into northern Montana. The quartzite began as a landslide in the Athabasca River valley during the Pleistocene, then rode the ice for hundreds of kilometres before being set down. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Rock_(glacial_erratic)

question: The Madison Boulder rests in the New Hampshire woods, a granite slab 83 feet long and heavier than 5,000 tonnes, on flat ground with no cliff in sight it could have tumbled from. Yet geologists can name the ledge it was torn from: Whitten Ledge, less than two miles to the northwest. With no one there to watch, how did they trace it to that ledge?
answer: its rock is an exact match for the stone of that ledge
choices: its rock is an exact match for the stone of that ledge
long scratches in the bedrock point straight back to the ledge
the ledge still bears a boulder-shaped hollow where it broke off
the ledge sits straight up the glacier's known flow path
context: Because an erratic's rock can be matched to a distant parent, each boulder is a signpost of where the vanished ice came from — and, traced across a whole region, which way it flowed. The Madison Boulder is Conway granite torn from Whitten Ledge less than two miles to the northwest: a giant that barely travelled, unlike Big Rock, which rode the ice about 930 km. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Boulder

question: On the hillside at Norber in the Yorkshire Dales, dark boulders lie scattered across a floor of pale limestone. Each dark boulder perches on its own little pedestal of pale limestone, a hand's-width tall, as though someone had set it on a pillar. What lifted each boulder up on its own column of rock?
answer: each boulder sheltered the limestone beneath it from the rain while the ground around it wore down
choices: each boulder sheltered the limestone beneath it from the rain while the ground around it wore down
the sheer weight of each boulder pressed the soft limestone up into a column beneath it
meltwater froze beneath each boulder and slowly jacked it upward on a hidden plug of ice
each boulder ground the limestone away all around itself but never right beneath it
context: The dark boulders are Silurian greywacke about 430 million years old; the pale pedestals are younger Carboniferous limestone — a startling case of OLDER rock resting on YOUNGER. Rain slowly dissolves bare limestone, but each boulder shielded the stalk beneath it, so the protected columns now stand up to 30 cm proud of a surface that lowers about 25 mm every 1,000 years. The Norber erratics sit on Ingleborough's southern slopes near the village of Austwick. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norber_erratics

question: Louis Agassiz stood before Swiss naturalists at Neuchâtel on 24 July 1837 and pointed to granite boulders that had come from the distant Alps, scattered over the pale limestone of the Jura, and to the polished, scratched bedrock beneath them. A great ice age, he argued, had once buried the whole land. What had the stranded boulders long been blamed on?
context: In his 'Discours de Neuchatel' (24 July 1837), later expanded in 'Etudes sur les glaciers' (1840), Louis Agassiz argued from erratics and polished, striated bedrock that great glaciers, not the biblical Flood, had once buried the land. It set off a real fight: some still credited the Flood, and Charles Lyell argued that icebergs drifting over a drowned land had dropped the boulders, while Agassiz's 'glacialists' credited moving ice sheets. His field evidence eventually won. https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-Agassiz ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lyell

question: Grey stone castles crowd the imperial city of Gondar, up in Ethiopia's northern mountains, their towers and turrets like a slice of medieval Europe dropped onto the African highlands. The sight earned Gondar a nickname from King Arthur's legendary court. What is the city called?
context: Camelot was King Arthur's legendary castle-court, so the nickname captures a traveler's shock at finding turreted stone castles high in the Ethiopian highlands -- the last place you'd expect a 'slice of medieval Europe.' Source: thecandytrail.com/castles-gondar-ethiopia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondar.

question: Emperor Fasilides built a stone castle at Gondar in 1636 and stayed put, ending centuries in which Ethiopia's emperors ruled with no capital city and their court kept moving from place to place. Through those roving centuries, what did the wandering court use for a home?
context: Fasilides settled at Gondar in 1636 and made it Ethiopia's first permanent capital -- a role it held for about 200 years, until the mid-1800s -- ending centuries in which the emperor's court roamed the land in movable tented camps. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondar; thecandytrail.com/castles-gondar-ethiopia.

question: A visitor who steps into Debre Berhan Selassie, a small 17th-century church in Gondar, and looks straight up finds about 80 painted faces covering the whole wooden ceiling in neat rows, each slightly different, all gazing down at once. The ceiling is famous across Africa. Whose faces fill it?
context: The church is Debre Berhan Selassie ('Trinity at the Mount of Light'), built in the late 1600s under Emperor Iyasu I (reigned 1682-1706). The ceiling's winged cherub faces -- a widely cited count of about 80, though some guides say up to 135 -- are each painted differently and are meant to show that God sees everywhere. It is one of the most famous church interiors in Africa. Source: iccrom.org (angel ceiling); sacred-destinations.com/ethiopia/gondar-debre-birhan-selassie-church.

question: Beside Gondar's castles lies Fasilides' Bath, a large stone pool with a small turreted tower on an island at its center. For most of the year it sits completely empty and dry -- then, on a single day, it is filled to the brim for one great celebration. For which festival is the pool flooded each year?
choices: Meskel, the Finding of the Cross
context: Fasilides' Bath fills just once a year, on 19 January, for Timkat -- Ethiopia's Epiphany. Tens of thousands of Ethiopian Orthodox pilgrims plunge into the blessed water to renew their baptism, joyfully re-enacting Christ's baptism in the River Jordan. Source: brilliant-ethiopia.com/fasilides-bath; blogs.loc.gov (Timkat in Gondar).

question: Near Fasilides' Bath in Gondar, Emperor Yohannes I raised a modest stone tomb in the late 1600s. It holds no king and no saint: he built it out of grief for a beloved companion he could not bear to lose. What did the emperor honour with this royal tomb?
context: The horse was named Zobel, and Emperor Yohannes I loved his warhorse so much that he built Zobel's Mausoleum in stone near Fasilides' Bath -- a royal tomb for a favourite mount. Source: brilliant-ethiopia.com/fasilides-bath.

question: A raiding army swept into Gondar in 1888 and burned its churches, all but one: Debre Berhan Selassie still stands. Local tradition credits a miracle. As the raiders reached its wooden gates, something came pouring out of the old church and drove them back in terror. What is said to have poured out?
context: In 1888 the Mahdist (Sudanese Dervish) army sacked Gondar and burned every church but Debre Berhan Selassie. Local tradition holds that a swarm of bees poured from the church and stung the raiders into flight -- and that the Archangel Michael himself stood before the wooden gates with a drawn flaming sword. Told as legend, not record. Source: brilliant-ethiopia.com/debre-birhan-selassie-church; local-tradition corroboration.

question: On the tiny island of Gorée, two kilometres off Dakar, stands a pink-and-ochre building called the House of Slaves. It is the world's best-known memorial to the slave trade. Guides lead visitors to a narrow upstairs doorway called the 'Door of No Return.' What lies just beyond it?
context: Step through the Door of No Return and there is nothing ahead but the sea -- for those sold into slavery, the last African ground under their feet before the ships. The two-storey pink-and-ochre house was built around 1776 by the Pepin family; curator Boubacar Joseph Ndiaye turned it into a museum in 1962 and led its tours by hand for decades. Source: Wikipedia, 'House of Slaves.'

question: Dutch traders who seized the little island off Dakar in 1588 called it Goede Reede, and over the centuries the phrase wore down into Gorée, a name that now sounds French. What were those Dutch sailors praising about the place?
answer: its safe water for anchoring ships
choices: its safe water for anchoring ships
context: 'Goede Reede' is Dutch for 'good roadstead' -- a roadstead being a sheltered stretch of water where ships can lie safely at anchor. The Portuguese had reached Gorée first, in 1444, but it was the Dutch, who held the island from 1588, whose name wore down over the centuries into 'Gorée.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Gorée.'

question: The Portuguese, Dutch, English and French captured and recaptured Gorée about seventeen times between 1588 and 1814, in the age of the Atlantic slave trade, though the island off Dakar is barely 18 hectares of rock, smaller than many an American farm. What made this scrap of an island worth so many wars?
answer: its harbour controlled the coast south of Cap-Vert
choices: its harbour controlled the coast south of Cap-Vert
its cannon controlled the mouth of the Senegal River
its quarries held the coast's only building stone
its springs were the region's only fresh water
context: One account calls Gorée's harbour 'the key to accessing the trade of the entire coast south of the Cap Vert' -- whoever held this speck of rock held the gateway to the Atlantic corner of West Africa. That is why it changed hands about seventeen times before France took firm control from 1677. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Gorée'; BlackPast.org, 'Gorée Island, Senegal.'

question: Guides at Gorée's House of Slaves long told visitors that more than a million enslaved people had passed through its door, and some said fifteen to twenty million. The historian Philip Curtin, in his 1969 census of the Atlantic slave trade, disputed that story. On what grounds?
answer: he argued only a few hundred a year shipped from the island
choices: he argued only a few hundred a year shipped from the island
he argued the trade there had lasted only a few decades
he argued the captives were brought in from the Americas
he argued the famous house was a much later forgery
context: Curtin -- whose 1969 census reshaped the field -- bluntly called the popular story 'phony,' pointing out that the House was really a wealthy merchant's home, and that most captives in the region left not from Gorée but from busier depots at the mouths of the Senegal and Gambia rivers. Abdoulaye Camara of the island's own Historical Museum has even called the Slave House a 'distorted account... created with tourists in mind.' Yet scholars on both sides agree the memory Gorée carries is real: it works like a 'tomb of the unknown soldier,' holding the memory of a trade that spanned centuries and thousands of miles of coast, whatever the exact count through this one door. Sources: History News Network, 'The Myth of Gorée Island'; Philip Curtin, 'The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census' (1969); The Chronicle of Higher Education.  (Legend.)

question: Nelson Mandela, freshly released after 27 years behind bars, came on pilgrimage to Gorée's House of Slaves. Standing among the cells where captives had been held, he did something that startled those watching, then walked back out with tears in his eyes. What did Mandela do?
answer: he folded himself into the tiny punishment cell under the stairs
choices: he folded himself into the tiny punishment cell under the stairs
he knelt and kissed the threshold of the Door of No Return
he read aloud the names carved into the cellar walls
he refused to step through the seaward doorway
context: Mandela squeezed into the cramped punishment cell under the stairs, where those who resisted their chains had been confined, and came out with tears in his eyes. Gorée became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978 -- one of the original twelve on Earth, and the first in all of Africa -- and its Door has since drawn Pope John Paul II and US presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama, who in 2013 called it 'very powerful.' Sources: IBTimes UK; CBS News; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Island of Gorée.'  (Legend.)

question: At sunset the Alhambra, on its ridge above Granada in southern Spain, takes on a warm glow, for its great walls were rammed together from earth and iron-rich local clay. The palace's Arabic name, al-Hamra, describes that colour. What does al-Hamra mean?
context: al-Hamra means 'the red one' (full form al-Qal'at al-Hamra, 'the red fortress'). The walls are rammed earth packed with iron-oxide-rich local clay that glows reddish, especially at sunset, and the palace-city sits on the Sabika ridge above Granada. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra

question: Pools mirror the Alhambra's courtyards and fountains murmur in its halls, yet the palace crowns a high, dry ridge above Granada with no stream of its own. Nasrid engineers fed it through a canal, the Acequia Real, that carried water onto the plateau. Where does all that water begin?
answer: the Darro river, about 11 km upstream
choices: the Darro river, about 11 km upstream
the Genil river, south of the city
a spring high on the Cerro del Sol
a deep well at the foot of the ridge
context: The water comes from the Darro: the Acequia Real (the Royal Canal, or Sultan's Canal) taps the river about 11 km upstream and carries it by gravity along the northern flank of the Cerro del Sol, past the Generalife's orchards, before devices raise it the last stretch onto the plateau. Before the canal, the older fort had to survive on a rainwater cistern and water hauled up from the Darro below; the canal is what turned a defensive fort into a garden palace-city. Source: https://www.alhambra-patronato.es/en/elemento-del-mes/the-royal-canal ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra

question: A low marble fountain stands at the heart of the Alhambra's most famous courtyard, and its round basin rests on no ordinary base: the carved backs of a ring of white marble beasts, shoulder to shoulder, water spilling from their mouths. Which animal did the Nasrid sculptors carve to hold it up?
context: They are lions — twelve of them, carved from white Macael marble, ringing the low fountain at the heart of the Court of the Lions, built by sultan Muhammad V (begun 1362). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_the_Lions

question: Water spills from a fountain in the courtyard Sultan Muhammad V began at the Alhambra in 1362, and four narrow channels carry it across the marble floor, one toward each point of the compass, to the four halls around the court. That cross-shaped plan is the mark of the classic Islamic garden. In that tradition, what do the four channels stand for?
choices: the four seas that ring the world
the four seasons of the year
context: The four channels picture the four rivers of the paradise garden, flowing out toward the four points of the compass (an image of paradise's rivers shared with Christian tradition too). The fountain itself rests on twelve marble lions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_the_Lions

question: In the Generalife, the Nasrid summer retreat beside the Alhambra, a stone stairway of four flights climbs the hillside. Its builders ran cold mountain water through the stair itself, and it still cools a climber on a hot day. Down which part of the stair does the water actually run?
choices: down a channel between the flights
down grooves cut into each step
down a pipe beneath the paving
context: The water runs down the hollowed stone banisters of the Generalife's Escalera del Agua ('Water Staircase'), a four-flight stair whose handrails are cut into little channels, so cold canal water runs beside a climber's hand, and the old Nasrid water gardens still run it today. The Generalife (Arabic Jannat al-'Arif) was the Nasrid summer estate next to the Alhambra. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalife

question: Inside the Alhambra's Hall of the Two Sisters, muqarnas fill the dome overhead: at least five thousand tiny cells drip down in tiers from its peak and bloom into sixteen little domes, like a stalactite cave turned to lace. What did the Nasrid craftsmen build those cells from?
context: The dome over the Hall of the Two Sisters is muqarnas, honeycomb or 'stalactite' vaulting built from tiers of small cells of carved plaster (stucco), at least 5,000 of them unfolding from a central summit into sixteen miniature domes around its rim. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muqarnas ; https://www.alhambradegranada.org/en/info/nasridpalaces/hallofthetwosisters.asp

question: Granada, the last Muslim-ruled city in Spain, passed from its sultan Boabdil to Ferdinand and Isabella on 2 January 1492, ending nearly eight centuries of al-Andalus. A great palace is usually looted and burned when its city falls, yet the Alhambra still stands almost untouched. What spared it?
answer: the city surrendered on agreed terms, so no army stormed it
choices: the city surrendered on agreed terms, so no army stormed it
a truce ended the siege before the fighting reached it
the attackers valued it too much to let it be harmed
it stood in the hills, beyond reach of the siege guns
context: Granada surrendered by treaty, not by storm, so the Alhambra was never sacked. When the last Nasrid sultan Muhammad XII (Boabdil) handed the city to Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile on 2 January 1492, Christian troops moved in quietly in case of resistance; none came, and the new rulers preserved the palace — which is why it survives almost intact. It ended nearly 800 years of al-Andalus (Muslim rule had begun in 711). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War

question: The curving granite walls of Great Zimbabwe, some higher than a house, have stood for more than 600 years. The builders' secret lies in the joints between their millions of hand-shaped blocks. How did the Shona masons make the walls hold?
answer: By fitting the stones so tightly no mortar was needed
choices: By fitting the stones so tightly no mortar was needed
By cementing the blocks with lime-and-ash mortar
By pinning the blocks together with iron cramps
By binding the courses with mud and cattle dung
context: Great Zimbabwe was built entirely of dry stone — millions of shaped granite blocks stacked without a drop of mortar or cement, held for over 600 years by nothing but their tight fit and gravity. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; news.artnet.com/art-world/huge-great-zimbabwe-ruins-2531265

question: The Shona raised a great walled city on the plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, from the 11th to the 15th century. Modern Zimbabwe took its name from the Shona words for a place like this: dzimba dza mabwe. What does the phrase mean?
context: 'Dzimba dza mabwe' is Shona for 'houses of stone' (also read as 'dzimbahwe,' venerated or chief's houses). When the country won independence in 1980 it took the name Zimbabwe straight from these ruins. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe

question: Great Zimbabwe's oldest quarter crowns a granite hill strewn with house-sized boulders, first settled around the 11th century. The Shona builders did not clear that jumble of giant rocks away; they did something cleverer with it. What did they do?
answer: Wove their granite walls in and around the standing boulders
choices: Wove their granite walls in and around the standing boulders
Rolled the boulders downhill to pave a grand avenue
Hollowed the boulders out into cool storage chambers
Split the boulders into blocks for the walls below
context: The boulder-strewn Hill Complex (or 'acropolis') is the oldest part of the city, settled from about the 11th to 13th centuries, its dry-stone walls woven right into the standing granite of the kopje. The whole ruin field sprawls over roughly 7 sq km. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; britannica.com/place/Great-Zimbabwe

question: Inside the Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe rises a solid granite cone about 9 metres tall. It has no door, no window and no chamber inside. Its true purpose is still debated, but one idea is widely favoured. What is the cone most likely thought to represent?
answer: A giant grain bin marking the king's bounty
choices: A giant grain bin marking the king's bounty
A fertility pillar honouring royal ancestors
A boundary stone between sacred and common ground
An altar for burning offerings to the spirits
context: The Conical Tower is a solid dry-stone cone about 5.5 m across and 9 m tall. Its meaning is genuinely debated; the leading interpretation reads its grain-bin shape as a symbol of the king's granary — and so of his power to provide — but this is interpretation, not proven fact. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; britannica.com/place/Great-Zimbabwe  (Legend.)

question: A visitor entering the Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe through its one narrow gate is funnelled into the Parallel Passage, a curving corridor about 55 metres long, pinched between the towering outer wall and a second wall just inside it. Where does this long stone corridor lead everyone who walks it?
answer: To the foot of the Conical Tower
choices: To the foot of the Conical Tower
Up onto the crest of the outer wall
Out to the terraced fields beyond the gate
Down into an underground water cistern
context: The Parallel Passage runs about 55 m between the outer wall and an inner wall of the Great Enclosure, funnelling anyone who enters toward the Conical Tower. Source: greatzimbabweguide.com/walking-around-great-zimbabwe-monument

question: High along the outer wall of Great Zimbabwe's Great Enclosure runs a band stretching tens of metres, the one famous ornament on walls that are otherwise mostly plain. It was made not with paint or carving but purely by the way the granite blocks are set. What pattern do they form?
answer: A zig-zag chevron, laid like herringbone
choices: A zig-zag chevron, laid like herringbone
A row of jutting stone teeth
A running spiral of set stones
context: The chevron band is the site's most famous ornament — a herringbone frieze of set granite tens of metres long, running along the top of the Great Enclosure's outer wall (its southern arc). It is widely read as a symbol of water and fertility, though that meaning is an interpretation. Source: zimfieldguide.com/masvingo/great-enclosure-great-zimbabwe-photographs-2025; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe

question: Eight birds carved from soapstone, each standing atop its own tall pillar, once looked out from the walls of Great Zimbabwe. To the Shona they were spirit-messengers between the living and their ancestors, and one still spreads its wings at the centre of Zimbabwe's national flag. Which real bird of the African skies do these carvings represent?
context: Eight soapstone birds, each on a tall monolith, once perched on Great Zimbabwe's walls. They represent the bateleur eagle, a good omen and spirit-messenger in Shona belief; today the Zimbabwe Bird is the national emblem on the country's flag and coat of arms. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe  (Legend.)

question: Great Zimbabwe swallowed millions of granite blocks, yet no chisel its builders owned could cut such stone cleanly. The Shona masons, it is thought, split the tough granite into stackable slabs another way, with no metal tool at all. What was their method?
answer: Heat the rock in a blaze, then throw cold water on it to crack it
choices: Heat the rock in a blaze, then throw cold water on it to crack it
Drive dry wooden wedges into cracks, then wet them to swell
Pound the rock for days with heavier hammer-stones
Let water freeze in the seams on cold nights until it burst
context: Lacking metal tools hard enough to cut granite, the builders are thought to have quarried by fire-setting — heating the rock in fires, then dousing it with cold water so it cracked along the grain into brick-like slabs (a commonly reported technique; some detail is debated). Source: news.artnet.com/art-world/huge-great-zimbabwe-ruins-2531265

question: Karl Mauch, a German explorer, reached the ruins of Great Zimbabwe in 1871 and could not accept that Africans had raised such a city. He whittled a sliver from a roof beam, decided it smelled like Lebanese cedar, and announced 'proof' of who the true builders were. Whom did Mauch wrongly credit?
choices: The lost legions of ancient Rome
context: Karl Mauch reached the ruins on 5 September 1871 and refused to believe Africans built them. He declared the site the biblical Ophir and the palace of the Queen of Sheba, 'proving' it by whittling a roof beam and deciding the wood was Lebanese cedar like Solomon's Temple. He was wrong on every count — the builders were the ancestral Shona. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Mauch; pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/mysteries-of-great-zimbabwe  (Legend.)

question: Archaeologists digging through the floors of Great Zimbabwe, hundreds of kilometres inland, unearthed proof that the city was linked to trade reaching the far side of the world. It had grown rich sending gold and ivory down to the ports of the Swahili coast. What did they find pressed into the dirt?
answer: Chinese porcelain and Persian glass beads
choices: Chinese porcelain and Persian glass beads
Roman coins and Greek wine jars
context: Great Zimbabwe grew rich exporting gold and ivory down to the Swahili-coast ports of Kilwa and Sofala. Chinese porcelain (Longquan celadon and blue-and-white) and Persian glass beads dug from its floors prove it traded across the Indian Ocean. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe; metmuseum.org/essays/great-zimbabwe

question: Peter Garlake and other archaeologists had proved beyond doubt by the 1970s that the ancestral Shona built Great Zimbabwe themselves, with no help from outside. Rhodesia's white-minority government would not accept it. What did the government order done about the finding?
answer: Ordered writers to give the foreign-builder myths equal space
choices: Ordered writers to give the foreign-builder myths equal space
Ordered the ruins closed to all foreign archaeologists
Ordered the oldest walls bulldozed to bury the evidence
Ordered the site renamed after a European explorer
context: After 1965, Rhodesia's white-minority government required any article crediting Africans with building Great Zimbabwe to give equal space to claims it was built by Phoenicians, Portuguese, or the Queen of Sheba. Archaeologist Peter Garlake, who proved Shona authorship, was forced out of the country in 1970. When the nation won independence in 1980, it took its very name from these once-suppressed ruins. Source: thezimbabwean.co/2012/01/dr-peter-garlake-archaeologist-who; tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0067270X.2012.682779

question: In the Palawan rainforest of the Philippines, tourists ride a boat deep into a dark mountain cave. They follow the Puerto Princesa river as it winds through the rock. This underground river is famous for where it ends up. Where does the river finally flow?
answer: into the open sea just offshore
choices: into the open sea just offshore
into a wide, muddy river delta
context: The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River in Palawan runs 8.2 km straight through a limestone mountain and empties into the sea — the world's longest navigable underground river, with boat trips reaching about 4.3 km into the dark. Because it meets the sea, its lower half is brackish: seawater pushes roughly 6 km inland and the tides reach inside the mountain, so a thin layer of fresh water floats on the salty water below. It was named one of the New 7 Wonders of Nature in 2012 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Princesa_Subterranean_River_National_Park

question: Sightseeing boats have carried tourists over Florida's Silver Springs since 1878, across water so clear that the bottom shows straight through it. One brand-new kind of boat was invented right there, and later copied at beaches around the world. What was it?
context: At Florida's Silver Springs — one of the largest artesian springs in the world — the glass-bottom boat was invented so tourists could peer straight down through the crystal-clear spring water. Boats have carried sightseers there since 1878, making Silver Springs Florida's oldest commercial tourist attraction. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Springs_(attraction)

question: The Amazon pours a huge flood of fresh water across South America toward the sea. Yet the Amazon and every other river and lake on Earth together hold almost none of the planet's unfrozen fresh water; about 99 percent is stored out of sight. Where does nearly all of it actually sit?
answer: soaked into underground rock and sand
choices: soaked into underground rock and sand
drifting through the sky as water vapor
context: This hidden water is called groundwater. About 99% of Earth's unfrozen fresh water isn't in rivers or lakes at all — it's soaked into rock and sand below the surface, filling the tiny spaces the way water fills a sponge. Groundwater supplies roughly half the world's drinking water and about 40% of its irrigation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundwater

question: Divers have hauled prehistoric bones from the sandy floor of Florida's Wakulla Springs since 1850. On its biggest day the spring poured out 1.2 billion gallons of clear water, a record, from a maze of flooded limestone caves that form the longest surveyed underwater cave in the United States. Whose ancient bones did the divers find?
context: Where water-soaked rock (an aquifer) meets the surface, groundwater bursts out as a spring; Wakulla Springs is one of the world's largest and deepest, once gushing a record 1.2 billion gallons in a single day (April 11, 1973). Divers and fossil-hunters, working since the bones were first spotted in 1850, have pulled mastodon bones and at least ten kinds of extinct mammal from the spring's floor. Its flooded cave — about 32 miles surveyed — is the longest known underwater cave in the United States. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakulla_Springs

question: Cattle stations and small towns in Australia's outback sit hundreds of kilometres from the nearest river, under skies that can stay rainless for months. Yet at scattered desert mound springs, fresh water bubbles up out of the ground, enough to keep people and cattle alive. Where does the water in these springs come from?
choices: an underground river flowing from distant hills
context: The Great Artesian Basin is the largest and deepest artesian groundwater basin on Earth — about 1.7 million km², underlying 22% of Australia and reaching 3,000 m deep. Rain that fell on far-off highlands seeps underground for thousands (up to ~2 million) years, then rises to the surface on its own at desert mound springs — the only water for hundreds of dry kilometres. 'Artesian' means water pushed up under its own pressure with no pump; the word comes from Artois, a province of northern France where such self-flowing wells were famously drilled. The water often comes up scalding: at Birdsville it emerges near 98°C — hot enough that the town runs a geothermal power station on it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Artesian_Basin

question: Wells across the American Great Plains tap the Ogallala Aquifer, which lies under parts of eight states and waters about a third of all crops that U.S. groundwater irrigates. Almost none of it is today's rain: it is fossil water, soaked into the rock in one long-gone age, and once pumped out it will not return for thousands of years. From which age does most of it date?
context: The Ogallala (High Plains) Aquifer underlies parts of eight states (~174,000 sq mi) and yields about 30% of the groundwater the U.S. uses for irrigation. Much of it is 'fossil water' banked since the Ice Age that barely refills. In places, pumping has dropped the water table more than 5 feet in a single year — faster than a lifetime can replace it. Once drained, the Ogallala would take over 6,000 years to refill naturally. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogallala_Aquifer

question: Muammar Gaddafi called it the Eighth Wonder of the World: 2,820 kilometres of buried concrete tubes, wide enough to stand inside, the largest underground network of pipes on Earth, carrying fresh water to Libya's coastal cities since the 1980s, though the country lies almost entirely inside the Sahara. Where does all this desert water come from?
answer: an ancient aquifer deep beneath the Sahara
choices: an ancient aquifer deep beneath the Sahara
desalinated water from the Mediterranean Sea
floodwater held behind a giant Nile dam
rain-fed reservoirs high in the mountains
context: An aquifer is the water-soaked rock or sand that holds groundwater; the water table is the top of that saturated zone. Libya's water comes from the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer — the world's largest store of fossil water (~2 million km² under Libya, Egypt, Sudan and Chad), filled tens of thousands of years ago when the Sahara was green. The 'Great Man-Made River' pumps it to the coast through 2,820 km of buried concrete pipe 4 metres wide — the world's largest underground pipe network — mining water that will not return. Muammar Gaddafi called it the 'Eighth Wonder of the World.' Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubian_Sandstone_Aquifer_System ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Man-Made_River

question: In the downtown parks of Gyeongju, South Korea, grassy mounds as big as houses rise among the walking paths -- 23 of them in Daereungwon park alone. They look like natural hills, but every one was raised by human hands about 1,500 years ago. What are these green mounds?
context: These grassy 'hills' are the earth-covered royal burial mounds of Silla kings and queens, some about 1,500 years old. Daereungwon park alone holds 23 of them among its paths, and downtown Gyeongju is so thick with mounds that surveys count roughly 35 royal tombs and 155 tumuli in the city center, with about 421 more in the outskirts -- rising between houses, roads and rice fields. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daereungwon

question: Gyeongju's Silla kings were buried in solid-gold crowns, gold belts and gold rings, so much treasure that people called Silla 'the land of gold.' Almost everywhere else in the ancient world, robbers dug up royal gold like this within a few generations, yet Gyeongju's lay untouched for 1,500 years. What protected it?
answer: a deep cap of piled stones over the coffin
choices: a deep cap of piled stones over the coffin
a curse carved above every tomb door
a moat of water ringing each mound
context: Silla was known as 'the land of gold.' Each royal mound was a wooden chamber piled over with a mountain of stones and then earth -- with no doorway or passage a robber could tunnel through. So while almost every other ancient royal treasure was looted, Gyeongju's gold crowns, jade comma-beads and gold belts survived intact for 1,500 years. Source: smarthistory.org/gold-crown-gold-belt-north-mound-hwangnamdaechong-tomb/

question: Archaeologists who opened a Silla king's tomb at Gyeongju in 1973 found him laid among about 11,500 treasures. The rarest was a painted flap of white birch bark, one of the only paintings from the whole Silla kingdom to survive, and its picture gave the tomb its nickname. What creature is painted on it?
context: The mound is Cheonmachong, the 'Heavenly Horse Tomb,' opened in 1973. The painted birch-bark mudguard shows the Cheonma, a mythical white 'sky horse' -- one of the very few Silla paintings that survive. Inside lay about 11,500 objects: a gold crown, gold bracelets and rings, and a 98 cm sword. The mound itself is 47 m across and 12.7 m high. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheonmachong  (Legend.)

question: Silla astronomers once watched and recorded the stars, sun and moon from Cheomseongdae, a curved, bottle-shaped tower of pale granite raised in a Gyeongju field in the 630s under Queen Seondeok. The tower holds a record no other observatory in East Asia can claim. What is it?
choices: the tallest one in all of Asia
the most accurate one of its age
context: Cheomseongdae, built in the 630s under Queen Seondeok, is the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia. Many read it as a calendar in stone: by one count about 362 blocks (near the days of the lunar year; another count gives 365, the days of the solar year) stacked in 27 layers, said to honour Seondeok, Silla's 27th ruler. It stands 9.17 m tall, and its small window has 12 layers of stone above and 12 below, often linked to the 12 months. Source: worldhistory.org/Cheomseongdae/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheomseongdae

question: High on Mount Toham above Gyeongju, a stone dome shelters the Seokguram Grotto: a serene granite Buddha, 3.5 m tall, carved in the 8th century by the minister Kim Daeseong. The builders aimed the whole shrine with great care so that the Buddha looks out at one exact thing. What does the Buddha face?
answer: the first light of sunrise over the sea
choices: the first light of sunrise over the sea
the summit of the sacred mountain behind
the roofs of the royal tombs below
the gate of the temple down the slope
context: The Seokguram Grotto (begun 751) was aimed east so the Buddha catches the first light of sunrise over the East Sea, about 750 m above the water. Its builders used no mortar at all -- the domed roof is locked together with carved stone rivets, and its proportions follow careful geometry, the golden rectangle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seokguram

question: Below Seokguram stands Bulguksa temple, finished in 774, where two stone pagodas face each other across the courtyard -- one plain, one richly carved. In 1966 workers opened the plain pagoda, Seokgatap, and found a Buddhist scroll that had lain sealed inside for over 1,200 years. Why did that scroll astonish the world?
answer: it is among the oldest printed texts ever found
choices: it is among the oldest printed texts ever found
it is the first text printed with movable metal type
it is the oldest printed text with a known date
it is the oldest text ever written by hand
context: The scroll is the Great Dharani Sutra, printed from carved wooden blocks around 704-751 CE -- among the world's oldest surviving printed texts, though scholars still debate the exact date. (Movable metal type came far later, with Korea's Jikji of 1377; the oldest printed text bearing its own date is the Diamond Sutra of 868 CE.) Bulguksa (finished 774) is famous for its twin pagodas: plain Seokgatap, which hid the scroll, and ornate Dabotap, so beloved it is engraved on South Korea's 10-won coin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulguksa

question: Gyeongju served Silla's kings as their capital for nearly a thousand years, from 57 BCE to 935 CE, and their works still crowd the old city: more than 600 ancient tombs, old stone pagodas, temple terraces and carved Buddhas. That wealth of monuments has earned Gyeongju a famous nickname. What is the city called?
choices: the city of a thousand kings
the gate to the eastern sea
context: Gyeongju was the Silla capital for nearly a thousand years, from 57 BCE to 935 CE. So many tombs, pagodas, temples and Buddhist carvings still stand across the open valley that the city is nicknamed 'the museum without walls.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongju

question: The Jade Emperor, in a Vietnamese legend, sent a Mother Dragon and her children swooping down from the sky to defend the coast from northern invaders. Ha Long, the bay's name, means 'descending dragon.' In the legend, how did the dragons raise the islands that walled the enemy fleet out of the bay?
answer: They spat jewels of jade and emerald that sank and turned to stone
choices: They spat jewels of jade and emerald that sank and turned to stone
They lashed the water with their tails until the waves froze into rock
They breathed fire that hardened the sea into blackened peaks
They dove beneath the waves and their scales sank and turned to stone
context: The bay's name, 'descending dragon,' comes from this legend: the Jade Emperor sent a Mother Dragon and her children to defend Vietnam, and the jewels of jade and emerald they spat into the sea turned to stone and became the islands that walled out the invaders. Source: SciTechDaily, 'Bai Tu Long Bay and the Legend of the Mother Dragon'; Grokipedia, 'Ha Long Bay'.

question: Faintly acidic rain spent millions of years dissolving a thick slab of limestone in northern Vietnam into a maze of steep stone pinnacles, a landscape geologists call tower karst. Today those pinnacles stand as islands in the open sea. What turned the karst hills of Ha Long into a bay full of islands?
answer: Rising seas after the Ice Age drowned the valleys between them
choices: Rising seas after the Ice Age drowned the valleys between them
A powerful earthquake dropped the whole plain below the sea
Ancient rivers carved deep channels that the tide slowly filled
Old volcanoes blasted craters that later filled with seawater
context: Ha Long's islands are 'tower karst': faintly acidic rain dissolved a thick slab of limestone into steep pinnacles, then after the last Ice Age rising seas drowned the valleys between them, leaving only the tops above water. The tallest towers rise up to about 400 meters straight out of the sea. Source: UNESCO/IUCN evaluation via Grokipedia, 'Ha Long Bay'; NASA Earth Observatory, 'The Emerald Isles of Ha Long Bay'.

question: One slender pillar among Ha Long Bay's stone towers is called Dinh Huong, the Incense Burner, and it is so loved that Vietnam put its picture on an everyday object millions of people see each day. On what everyday object does Dinh Huong appear?
context: Dinh Huong — the 'Incense Burner' islet — is so iconic it appears on Vietnam's 200,000-dong banknote. A nearby twin-rock called Trong Mai, the 'Fighting Cocks,' is a national symbol of Vietnamese tourism. Source: Vietnam.travel, 'Ha Long Bay's most mesmerizing islets'; thenewway.vn, 'Dinh Huong Islet'.

question: In Ha Long Bay's Bo Hon cluster, a narrow crack in a limestone tower leads inward before opening into a hall the size of a cathedral. It is about 500 meters long and 30 meters high, and its ceiling is hung with giant stalactites. When French explorers first mapped this hidden chamber in 1901, what did they name it?
choices: The Cave of the Dragon King
The Grotto of a Thousand Lamps
context: French explorers mapped this cave in 1901 and named it 'Grotte des Surprises' — the Cave of Surprises — for the way its narrow entrance opens into a vast inner hall. In Vietnamese it is Sung Sot, 'Surprise Cave'; it runs about 500 meters long and up to 30 meters high, hung with giant stalactites. Source: Oxalis Adventure, 'Explore Sung Sot Cave'; Vietnam Discovery, 'Surprise Cave'.

question: Some of Ha Long Bay's islands hide a secret in their very center: a perfectly still lake sits deep inside the island, ringed on every side by sheer limestone walls, with the open sea nowhere in sight. There is only one way to reach such a hidden lake. What is it?
answer: By paddling a small boat through a low sea-cave tunnel
choices: By paddling a small boat through a low sea-cave tunnel
By climbing over the cliff walls with ropes and ladders
By a stone staircase carved down through the rock
By a hidden footpath winding up and over the ridge
context: These sealed lakes are drowned sinkholes — dolines — trapped inside the rock. Ba Ham Lake, inside Dau Be island, is a chain of three ringed by cliffs; the tunnel in runs about 152 meters with a ceiling only 1.5-2.8 meters high, passable only at low tide. Dau Be island alone hides six such enclosed lakes. Source: HalongBayLux Cruises, 'Ho Ba Ham Islet'; UNESCO/IUCN evaluation via Grokipedia, 'Ha Long Bay'.

question: Korean writers once had to master thousands of Chinese characters, until King Sejong swept them aside with an alphabet of his own, Hangul. How many basic letters does Hangul use today?
context: Modern Hangul has just 24 basic letters — 14 consonants and 10 vowels; the original 1446 system had 28 (17 consonants, 11 vowels). Those few simple letters replaced the thousands of Chinese characters (Hanja) scholars once had to memorize. Hangul was created in 1443 and formally published in 1446. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hangul; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunminjeongeum.

question: King Sejong of Korea could already read Chinese, like every nobleman at his court. Yet in the 1440s he spent years designing a brand-new alphabet called Hangul. His own scholars fought him on it. Why did Sejong say he created it?
answer: so ordinary people could finally read and write
choices: so ordinary people could finally read and write
so the army could send its orders in secret code
so Buddhist monks could copy their sutras faster
so merchants could keep neater trade accounts
context: Sejong introduced Hangul to his court in 1443 (published 1446) precisely so commoners and women — over 99% of whom could not read the borrowed Chinese characters — could finally read and write for themselves. Unlike most alphabets, which grew slowly over centuries, Hangul was a single, deliberate royal invention. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hangul; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul.

question: The scholar Jeong Inji marvelled at how quickly King Sejong's new Hangul letters could be learned. A wise man, he wrote, could master the whole script in a single morning. How long would even the slowest, dullest learner need?
context: The line comes from Jeong Inji's postface to the Hunminjeongeum Haerye (1446): a wise man could learn the script in one morning, 'even a stupid man' in ten days. It is often misattributed to King Sejong himself, but the boast was Jeong Inji's. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunminjeongeum_Haerye; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul.  (Legend.)

question: Sejong's scholars drew each Hangul consonant as a tiny diagram, a design no other major alphabet shares, and every one pictures the same kind of thing. The square 'm', the angular 'k' and the letter for 'n' are each a little picture of what?
answer: a speaker's mouth and tongue making that sound
choices: a speaker's mouth and tongue making that sound
an object from nature whose name opens with that sound
a stroke borrowed from the matching Chinese character
a musical note marking the sound's pitch
context: Hangul is the only major 'featural' alphabet — its consonant shapes diagram the speech organs. ㅁ (m) is a closed square like sealed lips, ㄴ (n) shows the tongue tip at the ridge behind the teeth, ㅅ (s) pictures a pointed tooth, ㅇ the round open throat, and ㄱ (k) the tongue root blocking the back of the mouth. Linguist James McCawley called Hangul 'the most ingeniously devised writing system that exists.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul; grokipedia.com/page/Hangul.  (Legend.)

question: When King Sejong designed Hangul's vowels, he built every one from just three simple marks, a tiny model of the universe drawn from an old Korean cosmology: a round dot for the heavens, a flat line for the earth, and a single upright stroke. What does that last mark represent?
context: The three vowel marks encode a tiny cosmology from the Hunminjeongeum Haerye: a round dot ㆍ for heaven, a flat line ㅡ for earth, and an upright line ㅣ for the standing human — combined to build every Korean vowel. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hangul; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul.  (Legend.)

question: Choe Manri, a senior scholar in King Sejong's own Hall of Worthies, sent the king a blistering petition in 1444, the year after Hangul appeared, demanding he scrap it and keep the classical Chinese characters. What did Choe warn that a homegrown Korean script would do?
answer: drag the kingdom down to the level of the northern barbarians
choices: drag the kingdom down to the level of the northern barbarians
empty the treasury that paid the royal scribes
anger the spirits who guarded the old characters
let commoners forge the king's own decrees
context: In his 1444 petition Choe Manri (Ch'oe Malli), a deputy in the Hall of Worthies, argued that only barbarians — the Mongols, Jurchens, Tanguts, Japanese and Tibetans — invent their own scripts, so a Korean script would make Joseon 'alike to the barbarians.' Elite yangban scholars long sneered at Hangul as eonmun ('vulgar script'), keeping Chinese characters for themselves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choe_Manri; grokipedia.com/page/Hangul.  (Legend.)

question: A small people who had never had an alphabet of their own chose in 2009 to write their language in Korea's Hangul, the script scholars often call one of the most scientific ever invented. No non-Korean language had ever adopted it before. Which people made that choice?
answer: the Cia-Cia of Buton Island, Indonesia
choices: the Cia-Cia of Buton Island, Indonesia
the Hmong of the Vietnamese highlands
the Chamorro of the island of Guam
context: In 2009 the Cia-Cia people (about 40,000 speakers) of Buton Island, Indonesia, adopted a modified Hangul to write their language, which had no script of its own: the first non-Korean language to take up Hangul. Early lessons went well, but by 2020 the Latin alphabet had pushed Hangul back into a supporting role. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Hangul.

question: Scooters weave through the 36 Streets, the maze of narrow lanes at the heart of Hanoi's Old Quarter, where Hàng Bạc, Hàng Thiếc and Hàng Mã have worn the same names for centuries. What does each of those names record?
answer: The goods once sold along the lane
choices: The family that first settled the lane
The temple standing at the lane's end
The goods once sold along the lane
The emperor who first paved the lane
context: The word 'Hàng' means 'merchandise', so each 'Hàng + product' name is a fossil of the guild that clustered there after the 11th century: Hàng Bạc = Silver Street, Hàng Thiếc = Tin Street, Hàng Mã = Paper-Offerings Street, Hàng Gai = Silk Street. Roughly 76 lanes survive today, many still wearing the name of a vanished trade. Source: lasiestahotels.com/mamay/hanoi-old-quarter-streets-name.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanoi

question: Emperor Lê Lợi, in the legend of Hanoi's Hoàn Kiếm Lake, drove the Ming Chinese army out of Vietnam with a magic sword. One day, as he boated across the lake, a great animal broke the surface and demanded the blade back for its true owner, the Dragon King. What creature rose to reclaim it?
context: In the legend the golden turtle god Kim Quy reclaimed the sword the Dragon King had lent Lê Lợi to expel the Ming; the grateful king renamed the lake Hoàn Kiếm, 'Returned Sword'. A crumbling islet still holds Tháp Rùa, Turtle Tower, and giant softshell turtles really did live in the lake — the last famous one died in 2016. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoàn_Kiếm_Lake

question: Emperor Lý Thái Tổ moved his royal seat to the Red River delta of northern Vietnam in 1010 and gave the new city, today's Hanoi, a grand, auspicious name it would carry for centuries. What was that first name?
answer: Thăng Long, 'City of the Ascending Dragon'
choices: Thăng Long, 'City of the Ascending Dragon'
Đại La, 'City of the Great Rampart'
context: By tradition Lý Thái Tổ saw a golden dragon rise over the Red River as he arrived, and named his capital Thăng Long, 'City of the Ascending Dragon' — the 1010 founding and the name are settled history, while the dragon vision is the founding legend. Đại La, Đông Đô, and Cổ Loa are all real early names of the Hanoi area. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanoi

question: Families in Hanoi's Old Quarter built their shop-houses just 2 to 4 metres wide at the street, then ran them 20 to 60 metres straight back, and people call them tube houses. Why did the families build them so thin in front and so long behind?
answer: Tax was charged by a house's width along the street
choices: The lanes were too cramped to build any wider
Guild law capped how wide each shopfront could be
Tax was charged by a house's width along the street
Yearly floods pushed homes onto narrow dry ridges
context: Because the tax on a house was set by how wide it stood along the street, families built 'tube houses' (nhà ống) just a few metres wide but 20-60 metres deep — rarely up to 100 m. The narrow front was the shop; the family lived down the long tail and upper floors, with tiny interior courtyards pulling in light and air. Source: academia.edu (Tube houses in Hanoi Old Quarter); lasiestahotels.com/mamay/hanoi-old-quarter-streets-name.html

question: The walls of Emperor Lý Thái Tổ's new citadel kept crumbling, the legend says, until he prayed to Long Đỗ, Hanoi's guardian spirit, at the shrine that is now the Old Quarter's oldest temple. An animal then appeared and traced a great loop around the site; when the king built his ramparts along that trail, the walls at last held firm. What animal's path did the king follow?
context: The temple is named Bạch Mã — 'White Horse' — after this very legend; it is the oldest in the Old Quarter and honors the city-god Long Đỗ. By legend the white horse galloped the very loop the king's citadel walls then traced. Source: vinpearl.com/en/bach-ma-temple; authentiktravel.com (Bạch Mã Temple)

question: Hanoi grew up along the Red River where it spreads across its broad delta toward the sea. In 1831 the emperor Minh Mạng renamed the city Hà Nội, a name that pins exactly where it lies. What does 'Hà Nội' literally mean?
context: 'Hà Nội' means 'inside the river' — the city is cupped in a curve of the Red River (Sông Hồng). A delta is the fan of fertile land a river builds from dropped silt as it nears the sea; a dike is a raised earth wall that holds water back — the low, flood-prone city is ringed with them. Minh Mạng adopted the name in 1831, replacing the old Thăng Long. ('Land of Nine Dragons', Cửu Long, is the name of the far-southern Mekong delta.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanoi; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_Delta

question: Behind a single stone wall pierced by just five gates, Harar in eastern Ethiopia packs 368 twisting alleys into barely one square kilometre, so tight a maze that people simply call it one. The walled town also has an ancient name of its own. What is Harar's old town called?
context: The single stone ring wall that wraps Harar's old town gives it the name the Jugol — about 3.5 km around and 4-5 metres high, pierced by just five historic gates, it squeezes the entire fortified town into barely one square kilometre. Inside, 368 narrow, twisting alleyways make the old town so dense it is often simply called a maze behind the wall; UNESCO lists the site as Harar Jugol, the Fortified Historic Town. Source: UNESCO WHC list/1189; nationalparks-worldwide.com/eaf/ethiopia/cities/harar/harar.html.

question: Eighty-two mosques and over a hundred saints' shrines crowd inside the walls of Harar, a small town in eastern Ethiopia, and give it the name City of Saints. Many Muslims rank it the fourth-holiest city of Islam, just behind three others. Which three are they?
context: Mecca (the Kaaba) and Medina (the Prophet's city) are Islam's two holiest sites, with Jerusalem's Al-Aqsa third; the fourth-holiest claim for Harar is widely held rather than a universal ranking. Inside Harar's one square kilometre stand 82 mosques — three of them from the 10th century — and 102 saints' shrines; its Arabic name Madinat al-Awliya means 'City of Saints.' Source: UNESCO WHC list/1189; ovpm.org/city/harar-jugol-ethiopia/.

question: A lone man settles in the darkness just outside Harar's stone wall every night and does something almost no one else on Earth would dare. The custom goes back to Yusuf Mume Saleh, around the 1950s or 1960s, and his son Abbas Yusuf keeps it up. What is the nightly practice?
answer: Feeding wild spotted hyenas raw meat by hand
choices: Feeding wild spotted hyenas raw meat by hand
Juggling lit torches for passing caravans
Wrestling a leopard to the ground for crowds
Walking barefoot across a bed of hot coals
context: Every night outside Harar's wall, a 'hyena man' hand-feeds strips of raw meat to wild spotted hyenas that slip into town through gaps called 'hyena doors' — sometimes offering the meat off a stick held in his own mouth. Yusuf Mume Saleh began the nightly feeding around the 1950s-60s, reportedly to stop the hyenas raiding his goats, and his son Abbas Yusuf carries it on. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotted_hyenas_in_Harar; nationalgeographic.com/photography/article/this-man-lives-with-hyenas.

question: Inside one of Harar's tall old gey gar townhouses, the walls glow bright red above a raised sitting platform, with little display niches set into them. The townsfolk fill those niches with the craft they are famous for. What decorates a Harari home's walls?
context: Harar's 'gey gar' (city houses) have brightly painted interiors built around a raised platform called a nadaba, with wall niches (taqet) that display hung Harari basketry — a colourful woven craft that gives the homes an interior style unlike the usual layouts of Muslim countries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harar; UNESCO WHC list/1189.

question: Richard Burton, the English explorer, got inside Harar in January 1855, though the walled city had shut out outsiders for centuries and local legend warned it would fall the day a Christian passed its gates. He was the first European known to enter. How did Burton get through the gates?
choices: Under a sultan's letter of safe-conduct
By bribing a gatekeeper with coffee
Over the wall through a hyena hole
context: Richard Burton slipped into Harar in disguise in January 1855, the first European known to enter, and told the story in 'First Footsteps in East Africa' (1856); he had earlier used disguise to reach Mecca as well. The old belief that a Christian's entry would doom the city was local legend — Harar did not fall. Source: Richard F. Burton, 'First Footsteps in East Africa' (1856), burtoniana.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harar.

question: Arthur Rimbaud wrote his dazzling poetry as a teenager, gave it up for good by about 21, and spent 1880 to 1891 inside the walls of Harar as a caravan trader on the old route down to the coast. In that market town, what goods did Rimbaud deal in?
context: Arthur Rimbaud, who wrote his revolutionary poetry as a teenager and abandoned it by about 21, spent 1880-1891 as a merchant in Harar dealing in coffee, hides, and musk along the great caravan route to the coast; a grand house in the town is now kept as the Rimbaud museum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harar.

question: Top fashion brands around the world sell Harris Tweed, a thick wool cloth from Scotland's storm-lashed Outer Hebrides, yet by law every true length must be woven in just one kind of place on the islands. Where is real Harris Tweed woven?
context: By law, every genuine length of Harris Tweed is handwoven by the islanders in their own homes on foot-powered treadle looms — never in a factory, and with no electricity. It is famous as a world-class cloth still made this cottage way, on the windswept Outer Hebrides of Lewis, Harris, the Uists, Benbecula and Barra. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed

question: Mainland mills were selling cheap machine-made cloth as Harris Tweed by the early 1900s, so in 1909 the islanders of the Outer Hebrides registered a trademark to guard the real thing. Inspectors still stamp it on every true length. What is this famous mark called?
context: The mark is the Orb — a globe topped with a cross, registered in 1909 after islanders fought back against machine-made knock-offs. It is the oldest British certification mark still in use, stamped on the cloth only once inspectors confirm each length was handwoven in the Outer Hebrides. Source: wipo.int/web/wipo-magazine/articles/from-the-croft-to-the-catwalk-the-harris-tweed-certification-mark-38379; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed

question: The weavers of Lewis and Harris have worked since 1993 under a rarer shield than an ordinary trademark. It fixes what their cloth must be: pure new wool, dyed and spun in the Outer Hebrides and woven by hand by the islanders themselves. What kind of shield is it?
choices: a royal warrant from the Crown
a worldwide patent on the weave
context: The protection is the Harris Tweed Act 1993 — a UK Act of Parliament passed for this one cloth. It defines Harris Tweed in law as fabric handwoven by the islanders at their homes in the Outer Hebrides, finished there, and made from pure virgin wool dyed and spun in the Outer Hebrides. Source: legislation.gov.uk/ukla/1993/11/enacted; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed

question: Independent weavers on Lewis and Harris, in the Outer Hebrides, still weave Harris Tweed at home on a small single-width loom driven by nothing but their own feet on the pedals, with no motor and no electricity. This old English-built loom has served island weavers for generations. What is it called?
context: The loom is the Hattersley, the single-width treadle loom that independent island weavers still use in their own homes on Lewis and Harris. Weavers who work for the mills use a newer double-width loom, the Bonas-Griffith rapier loom, also in their own homes, and by law both must be worked by the weaver's own power for the cloth to earn its Orb mark. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed; annstweed.com/pages/the-process-of-weaving-tweed-on-a-hattersley-loom

question: Islanders across the Outer Hebrides gathered a natural dye called crottle by hand and boiled it with the wool, giving the old Harris Tweed its deep, muted reds and purple-browns and a faintly earthy scent. What kind of living thing is crottle?
context: Crottle is a lichen (Parmelia saxatilis) that islanders scraped from the rocks of Lewis and Harris. Boiled with the wool, it dyed Harris Tweed its deep reddish purple-brown and left the cloth with a distinctive earthy scent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_tweed

question: Families stroll and fish along Havana's 8-kilometre stone sea wall on calm evenings, but when winter storms blow in off the sea, giant waves burst clean over the wall and flood the whole road behind it. What is this famous seafront walk called?
context: The Malecón, begun in 1901, runs 8 km from the mouth of Havana Harbor in Old Havana, past Centro Habana and Vedado, to the mouth of the Almendares River. Built to hold back the sea, it turns into a wall of thundering spray during the winter frentes fríos (cold fronts), sending waves clear over the road. Source: Wikipedia, 'Malecón, Havana.'

question: Pirates raided and burned Havana again and again in the 1500s. So Spain sent an Italian builder, Battista Antonelli, to raise a huge stone castle at the harbor mouth. Work began in 1589 to guard the narrow gap. What is this fortress called?
context: El Morro — Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro — was designed by Battista Antonelli and begun in 1589. With its sister fort La Punta directly across the channel, it helped make Havana one of the safest ports in the Americas; a lighthouse, the Faro del Morro, was added in 1846 and still marks the entrance. Source: Wikipedia, 'Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro'; Encyclopedia.com, 'El Morro (Havana).'

question: Havana's harbor opens to the sea through one narrow channel, with a stone fort on each side. The Spanish wanted no pirate slipping in at night. So every night they dragged a barrier across the water, from one fort to the other, until dawn. What did they pull across each night?
context: The 'boom defence' — a heavy chain strung each night from El Morro across to the fort of La Punta on the far side — could be raised to snag and damage any ship that tried to force the entrance. Together with the forts it closed Havana's port from dusk to dawn, and helped make the bay one of the safest anchorages in the New World. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'El Morro (Havana)'; Wikipedia, 'Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro.'

question: The great stone fortress of La Cabaña stands guard high above the mouth of Havana's harbor in Cuba. Every night at nine o'clock the same signal is given from its walls, a custom that dates from colonial times. Long ago it warned Havana's citizens that the city gates were about to close for the night. What marks nine o'clock in Havana?
context: El cañonazo de las nueve, the nine o'clock cannon, is fired every night from the Fortaleza de San Carlos de la Cabaña, a custom from colonial times, when one gun signalled the closing of the gates in the city walls and another, before dawn, their opening. Accounts of its history differ: one dates the ceremony at La Cabaña to the fortress's opening in 1774, another says a warship in the harbour long fired the signal, and the evening shot is said to have moved from eight o'clock to nine over the years. Source: oncubanews.com/cronicas/y-nos-dieron-las-nueve-240-anos-de-canonazos; ecured.cu/Cañonazo_de_las_nueve; Wikipedia, 'Fortaleza de San Carlos de la Cabaña.'

question: Spanish ships carried silver mined across the Americas to one Caribbean port, Havana, where two convoys met and waited, then crossed the Atlantic to Spain together under armed guard. The Crown ringed the harbour with stone forts to protect them. What was this yearly convoy called?
context: French privateers sacked Havana in the 1550s, and Spain answered by ringing the harbour with stone forts. Each year the two treasure fleets, one loaded at Veracruz in Mexico and one at Cartagena on the South American coast, met in Havana's bay and sailed for Spain together in one heavily armed body, which is why the Crown guarded this single harbour so heavily. Source: Wikipedia, 'Spanish treasure fleet'; Wikipedia, 'Havana.'

question: The Spanish Crown, which raised Havana to the rank of a city in 1592, also gave it a grand official title, since whoever held its harbour held the sea-road between the Americas and Europe, and it is a name the city still carries on its coat of arms. What did the Crown call Havana?
answer: the Key to the New World
choices: the Key to the New World
context: The Spanish Crown, which made Havana a city in 1592, officially styled it 'Key to the New World and Rampart of the West Indies' (Llave del Nuevo Mundo y Antemural de las Indias Occidentales); one account dates that decree to 1634. A golden key still appears on the city's coat of arms, a reminder that whoever locked or unlocked this harbor commanded the whole route to Spain's Atlantic empire. Source: Wikipedia, 'Havana'; crouchrarebooks.com (1634 decree).

question: Kool Herc, a Bronx DJ, set up his turntables in the rec room of his own building one night in August 1973 for his sister Cindy's summer party. That party is now called the birth of hip-hop. What was the building's address?
context: The party is usually dated August 11, 1973. Herc's sister Cindy Campbell had rented the rec room to raise money, and the night ran until 4 a.m. 1520 Sedgwick is the most-credited birthplace but not the only one: historians note hip-hop 'developed slowly in several places' in the 1970s Bronx, so this is best remembered as the famous origin party, not the sole birthplace. In 2021 the U.S. Senate passed a resolution recognizing the Bronx and the building as hip-hop's birthplace, and Herc called it 'the Bethlehem of hip-hop culture.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1520_Sedgwick_Avenue  (Legend.)

question: Cindy Campbell, DJ Kool Herc's teenage sister, rented a West Bronx rec room for $25 in 1973 and charged a small fee at the door for the party that launched hip-hop. No record label or club was behind it. Why did Cindy throw the party?
answer: to raise money for back-to-school clothes
