choices: to raise money for back-to-school clothes
to raise money for a new sound system
to welcome new neighbors to the building
context: Cindy Campbell charged 25 cents for girls and 50 cents for boys; the party ran from 9 p.m. to 4 a.m., and the Campbells' parents supplied the refreshments. She was saving for new back-to-school clothes — and ended up helping bankroll the birth of a global culture. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1520_Sedgwick_Avenue

question: DJ Kool Herc saw the dancers at his Bronx parties go wildest during the break, the short, pounding drum stretch of a record. So he found a way to keep the break going as long as the crowd wanted. How did he stretch it?
answer: He spun two copies of the record and switched between them
choices: He spun two copies of the record and switched between them
He lifted the needle back to the break's start each time
He spliced the break onto one long loop of tape
He had a live drummer play the break along with him
context: Herc called his trick the 'Merry-Go-Round': with two copies of the same record on two turntables, he cued the break on one copy while the other played, then switched back and forth 'with no slack.' His favorite break records were conga-heavy tracks like 'Apache' and 'Bongo Rock' by the Incredible Bongo Band, and 'Apache' became known as hip-hop's national anthem. Looping the break was the foundation the whole music grew from. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DJ_Kool_Herc  (Legend.)

question: Bronx DJs carried their parties out of doors in the 1970s, to public parks and schoolyards for free summer block parties, where there was no outlet for a big, pounding sound system. So they tapped city power right off the street, for free. What did they open up and plug into?
context: With no promoters and no outlets, DJs would pop open the base of a street lamppost and wire their sound systems into it for free power — a signature image of early Bronx hip-hop. Herc's own rig, the 'Herculords,' ran two turntables into a booming Shure 'Vocal Master' PA with tall speaker columns, so loud that people came just to stand and watch. Early park home bases included '63 Park and Boston Road. Source: https://www.nycgovparks.org/about/history/hip-hop  (Legend.)

question: Coke La Rock took up the microphone while his friend DJ Kool Herc worked the turntables at their early-1970s Bronx parties, hyping the dancers with playful shout-outs and chants over the beat. He is remembered as the first person to work a mic this way at a hip-hop party. What vocal art, now the voice of hip-hop worldwide, was he the first to perform?
context: Coke La Rock (born April 24, 1955, in the Bronx) rapped alongside DJ Kool Herc and is widely credited as hip-hop's first MC — 'MC' stands for Master of Ceremonies. He had no stage name and often performed out of the crowd's sight, so at first no one knew who was doing the rhyming. His shout-outs to friends in the room were the seed of what became rapping. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coke_La_Rock

question: When DJ Kool Herc looped the beat at his Bronx park jams, certain dancers dropped low and attacked the floor — spinning, flipping, and freezing in sharp poses to outdo their rivals. Whole crews battled each other move for move on the concrete. What is this Bronx-born dance called?
context: DJ Kool Herc named the dancers 'b-boys' and 'b-girls,' the 'b' usually said to stand for 'break' — they saved their wildest moves for the looped break. Breaking has four move families: toprock (standing steps), downrock or footwork (hands on the floor), power moves (spins like the windmill, backspin, and headspin), and freezes (holding a pose off the ground). Herc even gave a second story for the word: 'this man broke... he went to the breaking point,' dancing himself into a frenzy. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakdancing  (Legend.)

question: Grandmaster Flash, a younger Bronx DJ than Kool Herc, treated the turntable like a science. Where Herc looped records by ear and the beat often slipped, Flash worked the record with his fingertips and the crossfader to cut, repeat and stretch a tiny slice of a song dead on the beat. What did Flash name this precise method?
context: Grandmaster Flash — Joseph Saddler, born January 1, 1958, in Barbados and raised in the Bronx — turned DJing into a precise science with his 'Quick Mix Theory,' using a fingertip on the vinyl and the crossfader to cut, repeat, and extend a tiny piece of a record exactly on the beat. To make it possible he also invented the DJ slipmat — a felt-and-waxed-paper pad that let a record spin or stop freely under his hand — and used 'punch phrasing,' jabbing short horn hits over a running beat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash

question: Grand Wizzard Theodore, a Bronx DJ of about 12, was spinning records at home around 1975 when his mother yelled at him to turn it down. He pressed his hand on the record to quiet it and made a new sound no DJ had used on purpose, then built a whole move around it. What did Theodore invent that day?
context: Grand Wizzard Theodore (Theodore Livingston) is credited with inventing the scratch — now one of the most recognizable sounds in music — around 1975, when he was about 12. Holding the record still under his hand, he rubbed it back and forth against the needle and fell in love with the rhythmic sound it made. The legend is that he discovered it while his mother stood in the doorway telling him to turn the music down. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Wizzard_Theodore

question: The Black Spades were among the biggest and most feared street gangs of the 1970s Bronx. From their ranks grew a new movement that drew young people away from gang fights toward DJing, dancing and art, and went on to carry hip-hop around the world. What was this movement called?
context: The movement is the Universal Zulu Nation. It grew in the 1970s out of the reformed Black Spades, joined by members of other former gangs, and its members organised parties and cultural events for the young. From the early 1980s it set up branches abroad, in Japan, France, Britain, Australia and South Africa among other places. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Zulu_Nation  (Legend.)

question: At the block parties of the 1970s Bronx, hip-hop grew into far more than music. Its followers still count four 'elements' that make up the culture: DJing on the turntables, MCing on the mic, dancing on the floor, and one more. What is hip-hop's fourth element?
context: Hip-hop's four elements are usually given as DJing, MCing, breaking and graffiti, the spray-painted 'writing' that covered New York's subway trains and walls in the 1970s. The Universal Zulu Nation spread this picture of hip-hop as a whole culture and later added a fifth element, knowledge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Zulu_Nation; https://grokipedia.com/page/Universal_Zulu_Nation  (Legend.)

question: Bronx teenagers invented an acrobatic floor dance at their 1970s park jams, and over the next fifty years it spread across the whole world. In 2024 it earned an honour no other dance born on a city street had ever received. What happened to the dance in 2024?
answer: it became an official Olympic sport
choices: it became an official Olympic sport
it became a UNESCO heritage tradition
it became a Broadway dance musical
it became a professional world league
context: Breaking — the dance the Bronx b-boys and b-girls created — became an official Olympic sport at the 2024 Paris Summer Olympics. Japan's Ami Yuasa won the first-ever women's gold and Canada's Philip Kim won the men's title. A dance once powered by electricity tapped from Bronx lampposts had reached the Olympic Games. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakdancing

question: In the heart of Hiroshima stands one broken ruin. It is kept just as it was on the morning of 6 August 1945: a hollow brick shell topped by a bare metal frame. It was the only building near the blast that kept its shape. What does the city call it?
context: Genbaku Dome means 'Atomic Bomb Dome' in Japanese. Of all the structures near the center of the blast, this one alone kept its shape while everything around it was flattened, and its skeletal shell still stands at the heart of the city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial.

question: The Hiroshima bomb flattened wood and brick alike for miles around. Yet one building just 160 meters from the center kept its walls and dome frame up. Why did this one place survive when all around it fell?
answer: the blast burst high overhead, pressing its walls down from almost straight above
choices: the blast burst high overhead, pressing its walls down from almost straight above
its brick-and-concrete walls were built far sturdier than the wooden shops nearby
the wide river beside it soaked up much of the blast's outward energy
taller buildings clustered around it took the first force of the shockwave
context: The bomb detonated about 600 meters up and almost directly above the building, so the shockwave bore down through its vertical brick-and-concrete columns instead of striking them from the side -- which is why its shape held while the city flattened for kilometers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial.

question: Paper cranes sent by children around the world all but bury one monument in Hiroshima's Peace Park. It honours Sadako Sasaki, who was two when the bomb fell; later she got leukemia and folded paper cranes by the hundreds, trusting a legend that a thousand cranes grant a wish. She died at twelve. What does the bronze figure crowning the monument show?
answer: a girl lifting a folded crane high overhead
choices: a girl lifting a folded crane high overhead
a girl kneeling to fold a crane in her lap
a boy cupping a paper crane in both hands
a mother shielding a small child from the flames
context: Unveiled on 5 May 1958, the Children's Peace Monument is topped by a bronze girl holding a folded crane above her head. Its inscription reads, 'This is our cry, this is our prayer: for building peace in the world.' Children from around the world still send origami cranes by the thousand, gathered in glass cases around its base. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children%27s_Peace_Monument + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadako_Sasaki.  (Legend.)

question: Jan Letzel, a visiting Bohemian architect, drew the plans for a domed building in Hiroshima that opened in 1915, its copper dome and European lines standing out over the low wooden shops, long before it became a ruin. What was the building first built to be?
context: It opened in 1915 as the Hiroshima Prefectural Commercial Exhibition Hall -- about 25 meters tall, its brick reinforced with concrete and crowned with an oval copper dome. Its Czech designer, Jan Letzel (1880-1925), left Japan for Prague in 1923 and died there in 1925, twenty years before his cheerful exhibition hall became the world's most famous ruin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Letzel.

question: Hiroshima's shattered domed ruin was nearly torn down after the war, but the city kept it braced and never patched or rebuilt it, a warning for the world. In late 1996, after long debate, the ruin won a famous title. What did it become?
choices: one of the New Seven Wonders
context: The Atomic Bomb Dome was nearly demolished in the years after the war, but Hiroshima resolved to keep it, and in December 1996 UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site -- listed as a stark reminder of the destructive force humankind can unleash, and a symbol of hope for lasting peace. Mayor Shinzo Hamai had championed saving the shell; a permanent-preservation resolution passed the city council in 1966, and the dome stands guarded from collapse but never repaired. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial.

question: The people of flattened Hiroshima expected their city to lie dead for years, yet on 9 August 1945, only three days after the bomb, one part of its transport was already moving again, waving stunned survivors aboard for free. What had started running again so soon after the blast?
context: On 9 August 1945 a Hiroden streetcar ran again between Koi and Tenma-cho, astonishing survivors who had thought the city finished. Two of the cars damaged that day, numbered 651 and 652, still carry passengers through Hiroshima today. Source: Japan Tourism Agency (mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/en) + gethiroshima.com.

question: Experts warned that Hiroshima's poisoned ground would stay barren for decades after the blast, and that at first not even grass would grow at the very centre. Yet in the spring of 1946, trees that had stood within a kilometre of the explosion did something the survivors had thought impossible so soon. What did these scorched trees do?
answer: put out fresh green buds and new leaves
choices: put out fresh green buds and new leaves
bloomed out of season, months too early
shed their scorched bark in long black strips
leaned and slowly toppled as the soil shifted
context: These A-bombed survivors are called hibaku jumoku, 'survivor trees.' Fresh leaves the next spring became living proof the city would recover; by 2011 about 170 trees that had lived through the bombing still grew in Hiroshima, roughly a dozen within 1,000 meters of the blast. Because it flowered so fiercely in the ruins, the oleander was chosen as Hiroshima's official flower. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibakujumoku.

question: Hoi An's Japanese Covered Bridge, a roofed wooden footbridge more than 400 years old, has a carved dog guarding one end and a carved monkey the other. Right at the centre of the span it holds something no one expects a bridge to hold. What is built into its middle?
context: The Japanese Covered Bridge (Chua Cau) has spanned Hoi An for over four centuries with a tiny temple built right into its middle. By legend the mismatched guardians -- a dog at one end, a monkey at the other -- mark the zodiac years the work began (Year of the Monkey) and finished two years later (Year of the Dog). Source: Vietnam Discovery, Japanese Covered Bridge; corroborated by Atlas Obscura.

question: Once a month the old town of Hoi An, on Vietnam's central coast, switches off its electric lights and glows only with silk lanterns, while paper ones drift down the Thu Bon River carrying wishes. The town sets no calendar date for it; it waits on the moon. On which phase of the moon does lantern night fall?
context: Hoi An holds its lantern night on the 14th day of every lunar month -- the eve of the full moon -- then darkens its streets anyway, so the lanterns become the only glow on the brightest night of the month. Families hang silk lanterns and float paper ones down the Thu Bon carrying wishes. Source: Hoi An Guidebook, Lantern Festival guide; corroborated by Klook Hoi An lanterns guide.

question: Ships from China, Japan, India and Europe crowded Hoi An for 400 years, when it was one of Southeast Asia's busiest trading ports. Then the merchant fleets stopped coming, the trade shifted about 30 kilometres north to Da Nang, and the town sat almost untouched for centuries. War and politics were not to blame; the Thu Bon River was. What did the river do to Hoi An's harbour?
answer: silted up until big ships couldn't dock
choices: silted up until big ships couldn't dock
swung its course away from the town
swept the old docks out to sea
dropped too low for ships to enter
context: Mud carried by the Thu Bon slowly filled Hoi An's port with silt, so ocean-going ships shifted to the deeper harbor at Da Nang and the merchant town was left behind. That very decline preserved it: UNESCO listed Hoi An in 1999 as an exceptionally well-kept small-scale trading port (Western traders once knew it as 'Faifo'). Sources: UNESCO World Heritage #948; La Siesta Hoi An history.

question: Pilgrims at Prayagraj, in northern India, watch the pale, silty Ganges meet the clearer blue-green Yamuna, the two colours sliding side by side in a sharp seam for a stretch before they mix. What do geographers call this kind of spot?
context: At the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj (Allahabad), the silt-laden Ganges and the clearer Yamuna meet, and their different colors stay visibly separate in a line before mixing — the classic picture of a river confluence. A delta or estuary instead forms where a river meets the sea; a tributary is a stream that feeds a larger river. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triveni_Sangam

question: Some 660 million pilgrims bathed at Prayagraj's Sangam in 2025, by the organisers' count the largest crowd ever. Legend says the gods once churned the sea, and drops of a wondrous liquid spilled from a pitcher onto four places on earth, Prayagraj among them. What was the liquid said to be?
choices: the poison of the churned sea
the blood of a slain demon
the waters of the sacred Ganges
context: Legend says the four Kumbh Mela sites, Prayagraj, Haridwar, Nashik and Ujjain, were sanctified when drops of amrita, the divine nectar of immortality, fell there during the mythological churning of the ocean. At the 2025 Maha Kumbh the organisers counted more than 660 million bathers at the Sangam, far beyond the 400 million they had planned for, which would make it the largest gathering on Earth, though some observers doubt the total. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumbh_Mela; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Prayag_Maha_Kumbh

question: The Jordan River runs only about 250 kilometres from its snow springs on Mount Hermon, but from its start it drops into a long trench in the Middle East whose floor sinks far below sea level. What slow force carved out this deep valley?
answer: two plates grinding sideways past each other
choices: two plates grinding sideways past each other
two plates crashing head-on into each other
a glacier gouging a trough in the Ice Age
a river cutting down through soft rock
context: The Jordan runs down the Jordan Rift Valley, which follows the Dead Sea Transform, a great fault where the Arabian plate grinds north past the African plate, by more than 100 km so far. Where the fault steps aside, the crust between is pulled apart into deep basins that sink below sea level, so this one short river passes the lowest freshwater lake and ends at the lowest dry land on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea_Transform

question: On its way south the Jordan widens into a broad blue lake, fished for thousands of years and known as the Sea of Galilee, Lake Tiberias or the Kinneret. Among all the freshwater lakes on Earth, what record does it hold?
context: The Sea of Galilee — also called Lake Tiberias or the Kinneret — sits about 210 m below sea level, the lowest freshwater lake on the planet (its level drifts between roughly 209 and 215 m). The Jordan flows in from the north and out to the south toward the Dead Sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Galilee

question: Hong Kong has more skyscrapers than any other city on Earth: Guinness counted 669 towers of 150 metres or more there in 2025, packed one behind another in a wall of glass and steel. Why did the city build so high?
answer: its steep mountains leave almost no flat land
choices: its steep mountains leave almost no flat land
its swampy ground cannot carry wide buildings
typhoon floods keep homes off the low ground
colonial law banned building beyond the harbour
context: Steep mountains drop straight into the sea across Hong Kong, leaving it almost no flat land, so the city had nowhere to build but up. As of 30 January 2025 Guinness World Records counted 669 buildings at least 150 m tall there, more than any other city on Earth; Shenzhen was second (626), New York third (434) and Dubai fourth (424). Source: https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/505189-city-with-the-most-buildings-150-m-or-taller

question: The Peak Tram began hauling passengers up Victoria Peak by cable in 1888, on a slope reaching 48 percent, toward the 552-metre summit above Hong Kong Island. What claim did the Peak Tram make when it opened?
answer: the first funicular railway in Asia
choices: the first funicular railway in Asia
the steepest cable railway in the world
the first electric railway in Asia
the highest hillside railway in Asia
context: A funicular is a cable railway on a steep slope where two cars are joined by a cable over a wheel at the top, so each car counterweights the other as one climbs and the other descends. The Peak Tram opened on 30 May 1888 as the first funicular in Asia, climbing nearly 400 m up a grade reaching 48% in about five minutes. Victoria Peak, 552 m, is the highest point on Hong Kong Island. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_Tram ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Peak

question: Boats at the Aberdeen shore loaded one sweet-smelling cargo all through the Ming and Qing dynasties and carried it away across the region, and the best-known story says that is how the place came to be called heung gong in Cantonese, Fragrant Harbour: Hong Kong. What was that cargo?
context: 'Hong Kong' (heung gong) means 'Fragrant Harbour.' During the Ming and Qing dynasties, agarwood and other fragrant incense woods were shipped out of the Aberdeen-area harbour, and the explanation most often told is that the boat people named the port for them; others link the fragrance to the sweet fresh water of the Pearl River. Source: https://www.lungfushannaturalist.hku.hk/post/the-origin-of-the-name-hong-kong; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong

question: Some 33,000 people once lived jammed into Kowloon Walled City, a single block of leaning towers whose lower alleys sunlight never touched. Hong Kong demolished it between 1993 and 1994, then opened something new on the cleared block. What did the city open there?
context: By 1987 about 33,000 people lived in Kowloon Walled City, packed into 2.6 hectares -- a density near 1.2 million people per square kilometre, for a time one of the densest places humans have ever lived. It was demolished between March 1993 and April 1994, and Kowloon Walled City Park, a quiet classical Chinese garden, opened on the site in December 1995. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon_Walled_City

question: Passengers riding the Peak Tram up Victoria Peak after dark watch the glittering skyscrapers outside do something impossible. A 2013 University of Hong Kong study by Chia-huei Tseng traced the illusion to a mismatch between the tram's seats and its straight window frames, which tricks the brain. What do the towers appear to do?
answer: lean far over, as if toppling
choices: lean far over, as if toppling
context: University of Hong Kong researcher Chia-huei Tseng documented the illusion in a 2013 study: the tram's tilted seats and its straight window frames trick the brain about which way is 'up,' so the passing skyscrapers appear to lean and even topple. The effect is strongest at night and weakens when a rider stands up. Source: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/06/130620162848.htm

question: Bridges, shared stairs and roofed alleys laced the roughly 350 towers of Kowloon Walled City into one tangle, raised without architects or building codes. People boasted that the whole block could be crossed from one end to the other without once doing what?
context: Kowloon Walled City was so densely interconnected by staircases and passageways that a person could reportedly travel from the north end to the south end of the whole block without ever touching solid ground. Its roughly 350 buildings, mostly 10-14 stories, were fed by only about 8 water pipes and built with no architects and no building codes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kowloon_Walled_City  (Legend.)

question: The largest ocean ships anchor right beside the towers of Hong Kong in Victoria Harbour, deep, calm water winding between steep green hills. Geographers class it with the drowned inlets of Galicia, in Spain, whose local name the type now carries. What kind of coastal feature is it?
context: Victoria Harbour is a ria, a river valley drowned by the sea: after the last Ice Age, rising seas flooded the low ground between Hong Kong's hills. The word comes from the rias of Galicia, in Spain, where such drowned inlets line the coast. (A fjord is a valley carved by a glacier and then drowned.) The deep, sheltered water is why Hong Kong became one of the world's great natural ports. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ria ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Harbour

question: One volcano on Hawaii's Big Island, sitting right over the hotspot, kept its lava running for 35 straight years, 1983 to 2018, among the longest lava flows ever, and it still ranks among Earth's most active volcanoes. Which restless volcano is it?
context: Kilauea, on the Big Island's southeastern flank, is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth and still erupts today; its 1983-2018 flow ran about 35 years, one of the longest eruptions ever documented. The volcano itself is young -- only about 210,000 to 280,000 years old -- because it sits almost directly over the hotspot, while the older islands to the northwest have long gone cold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%ABlauea

question: At the far northwest end of Hawaii's main islands lies an island whose volcanoes died long ago. Over 5 million years, rain has carved its slopes into deep green canyons and knife-edge ridges. Which Hawaiian island is this ancient, deeply eroded one?
context: Kauai, at about 5 million years old (roughly 5.1-5.5 million), is the oldest of Hawaii's main islands. The plume that built it moved on long ago, leaving it extinct while rain carved its deep canyons and knife-edge ridges. The younger islands lie to the southeast, closer to the still-burning hotspot. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_hotspot

question: The Hawaiian hotspot has built at least 129 volcanoes over about 85 million years. Yet only a handful still stand above the waves as islands today. What became of the other 120 or so once the plate carried them away from the hotspot?
answer: they sank into drowned seamounts and atolls
choices: they sank into drowned seamounts and atolls
they fused into one enormous island
they blew apart and vanished completely
they drifted back over the hotspot
context: As the plate hauls each volcano off the hotspot it cools, stops erupting, and slowly sinks -- worn down until it drowns as a flat-topped seamount or a ring-shaped coral atoll. Over its ~85-million-year history the Hawaiian hotspot has built at least 129 volcanoes; more than 123 are now extinct. The whole chain is a graveyard of islands the plate carried away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_hotspot

question: Beyond the last of Hawaii's main islands the chain does not simply stop: it runs on beneath the sea as more than 80 dead undersea volcanoes, stretching about 6,200 kilometres almost to Russia. To geologists, this immense trail is a fossil record of what?
answer: the path the Pacific plate has drifted
choices: the path the Pacific plate has drifted
the boundary where two plates collide
the rim of a vast sunken crater
the shoreline of a lost continent
context: Because the hotspot stays put while the Pacific plate slides over it, the plate prints a volcano, then carries it away -- so the whole Hawaiian-Emperor chain, read backward from Hawaii, traces exactly where the plate has traveled. It runs about 6,200 km (3,900 mi) and holds more than 80 dead undersea volcanoes: a fossil record of the plate's entire path. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian%E2%80%93Emperor_seamount_chain

question: An undersea volcano once called Loihi, now Kamaehuakanaloa, is already erupting about 35 kilometres off the Big Island's southeast coast, though its summit still lies some 975 metres beneath the waves. After another 10,000 to 100,000 years of eruptions, what should it finally do?
answer: rise above the sea as Hawaii's next island
choices: rise above the sea as Hawaii's next island
collapse into a deep undersea trench
drift away and go extinct like the older islands
merge quietly with the Big Island's coast
context: Kamaehuakanaloa -- renamed from Loihi in 2021 -- sits over the leading edge of the Hawaiian hotspot, about 35 km off the Big Island's southeast coast, its summit still ~975 m (3,200 ft) underwater. Its last known eruption was in 1996, during a swarm of about 4,070 earthquakes. In another 10,000 to 100,000 years it is expected to break the surface as Hawaii's newest island. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C5%8D%CA%BBihi_Seamount

question: The Galapagos ride their own hotspot, but here the age pattern runs east to west. The eastern islands are the oldest and going quiet, while one young western island under 700,000 years old sits right over the plume and is the whole chain's most active volcano. Which fiery western island is this?
context: The Galapagos hotspot lies to the west, so Fernandina (under 700,000 years old) is the youngest and most volcanically active island, erupting often. The older eastern islands -- San Cristobal (~4 million years) and Espanola (~3.2 million) -- have drifted off the plume and gone quiet. It is the same conveyor as Hawaii, just read the other direction. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernandina_Island

question: The Hawaiian-Emperor chain of volcanoes, far to the northwest of Hawaii, stops trending northwest and swings almost due north at a sharp elbow in the seafloor, some 47 to 50 million years old. What does this famous kink in the chain most likely record?
answer: a change in the direction of the plate's motion
choices: a change in the direction of the plate's motion
the collision of two ancient continents
the impact site of a giant meteorite
the boundary of a drowned ice sheet
context: The elbow -- dated to about 47-50 million years ago, where the northwest-trending Hawaiian ridge kinks to the north-trending Emperor seamounts -- was long read as the moment the Pacific plate swung course by roughly 60 degrees. It is one of the most striking features on the entire ocean floor, though whether the plate alone changed direction is now debated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian%E2%80%93Emperor_seamount_chain

question: The oldest surviving link in the whole hotspot chain, Meiji Seamount, about 82 million years old, has nearly finished its long ride: it now sits at the edge of the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench off Russia. What is happening to this ancient seamount there?
answer: it is being pulled down into the earth and destroyed
choices: it is being pulled down into the earth and destroyed
it is rising once more into a brand-new island
it is drifting slowly back toward Hawaii's hotspot
it is tearing open along a mid-ocean ridge
context: Meiji Seamount, at about 82 million years the oldest surviving link in the Hawaiian-Emperor chain (nearby Detroit Seamount is confirmed at ~81 Myr), has ridden the Pacific plate all the way to the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench. There the plate dives beneath Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula in a process called subduction, dragging the ancient seamount down to be destroyed -- the conveyor delivering its cargo to its end. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Seamount

question: Geologists explained the great elbow in the Hawaiian-Emperor chain, some 47 to 50 million years old, one neat way for decades, by the movement of the Pacific plate alone. Newer research argues the seafloor evidence fits better if something else was moving too over those millions of years. What does this view propose was also drifting?
answer: the hotspot plume itself was drifting south
choices: the hotspot plume itself was drifting south
the mid-ocean ridge was creeping northward
the Earth's spin axis had wandered
a nearby plate boundary was jumping
context: The classic explanation credited a ~60-degree change in Pacific-plate motion for the bend. But newer research argues the plume beneath Hawaii itself drifted south by hundreds of kilometers before about 47 million years ago. Today many scientists think the bend records a MIX of both -- a moving plate and a moving plume -- not a single settled cause. A good reminder that even textbook geology still has open questions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian%E2%80%93Emperor_seamount_chain

question: India slid over a deep plume, the Réunion hotspot, about 66 million years ago, and the ground tore open. Floods of runny basalt poured out again and again, burying much of western India under layers more than 2 kilometres thick across an area the size of a country. What is this vast staircase of ancient lava called?
context: The Deccan Traps buried much of India in basalt -- over 500,000 sq km, a volume near 1 million cubic km, with layers more than 2 km thick -- erupting right at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary (~66 million years ago), the same moment the dinosaurs died out. That timing has tempted scientists to blame the eruptions, but most now credit the Chicxulub asteroid impact as the main killer, with the Deccan volcanism a debated accomplice. The same Reunion plume that flooded India still builds the volcanic island of Reunion today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deccan_Traps  (Legend.)

question: People crossing the bridges of Hue, the old imperial city of central Vietnam, can smell the river below them each autumn, for the Song Huong, the Perfume River, truly turns fragrant then. What drifts down on its current to give it that sweet scent?
answer: Orchard blossoms drifting down from upstream hills
choices: Orchard blossoms drifting down from upstream hills
Incense drifting down from riverside pagodas
Perfume workshops that once crowded its banks
Lotus flowers carpeting the river's surface
context: The Perfume River (Sông Hương) runs about 30 km from where its two source branches, the Ta Trach and Huu Trach, meet at the Bang Lang fork in the Annamite Range. Each autumn, blossoms from fruit orchards far upstream fall into the current and drift down, scenting the whole river - the real origin of its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfume_River

question: Emperor Gia Long, having reunified Vietnam after years of civil war, began raising a great walled citadel at Hue beside the Perfume River in 1804. For the palace-city inside, with its yellow-tiled roofs and moats, he consciously copied the plan of one grand foreign palace-city. Which one did he copy?
context: Gia Long, founder of the Nguyen dynasty, laid out Hue in 1804; his son Minh Mang finished the core in the 1830s. The plan copied Beijing's Forbidden City but was adapted to Vietnamese feng shui - its back to Ngu Binh Mountain, its face to the Perfume River. The Nguyen ruled from here until the last emperor, Bao Dai, abdicated in 1945. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Imperial_City_of_Hu%E1%BA%BF

question: Behind a wall of its own at the heart of the Hue citadel lay the emperor's private household. Besides the emperor and his family, only one kind of servant could live and work within those inner walls. Who were they?
context: The Forbidden Purple City took its name from Beijing's Forbidden City, whose Chinese name means 'Purple Forbidden City' - the 'purple' evoking the pole-star enclosure of heaven, home of the celestial emperor. Only the emperor, his family, and his castrated eunuch servants could pass within; the eunuchs alone were trusted to serve so close to the imperial women. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Imperial_City_of_Hu%E1%BA%BF

question: Emperor Gia Long ordered nine great bronze guns, the Nine Holy Cannons, cast at Hue in 1803, each named for a season or an element, to guard his imperial throne forever, yet none of them was ever fired. What bronze did he melt down to make them?
answer: The weapons of the defeated Tay Son dynasty
choices: The weapons of the defeated Tay Son dynasty
Temple bells collected from across the kingdom
Old bronze coins withdrawn from circulation
Cannon captured from foreign trading ships
context: Gia Long had the Cuu Vi Than Cong cast in 1803-1804 from the melted-down bronze weapons of the Tay Son dynasty he had just overthrown - four cannons named for the seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter) and five for the elements (metal, wood, water, fire, earth). Meant as the throne's eternal guardians, they were never once fired. Source: https://www.vietnam.vn/en/cuu-vi-than-cong-tuyet-tac-nghe-thuat-duc-dong-cua-trieu-nguyen

question: In the pine hills around Hue, each Nguyen emperor raised himself a grand garden-tomb of pavilions, lotus ponds and stone stelae. The strangest belongs to Emperor Tu Duc, who finished his in 1867 - then did what no one expects of a tomb's owner. What did Tu Duc do with his own tomb?
answer: He moved in and lived there for years before dying
choices: He moved in and lived there for years before dying
He sealed it and never set foot there again
He handed it over to shelter Buddhist monks
He had it demolished and rebuilt twice over
context: Tu Duc built his tomb in 1864-1867 and used it as a pleasure-retreat while still alive - boating on Luu Khiem lake, reclining in the Xung Khiem Pavilion to compose poetry among his concubines. He had 104 wives and concubines but, left sterile by smallpox, never fathered a son, and he wrote his own tomb epitaph, an act traditionally thought a bad omen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_T%E1%BB%B1_%C4%90%E1%BB%A9c

question: Emperor Tu Duc's lavish garden-tomb at Hue draws crowds today, yet it hides a startling secret: his body was never actually buried inside it. By tradition his real grave was dug elsewhere in Hue and kept hidden forever by one grim measure. What became of the roughly 200 servants who buried him?
answer: They were all beheaded on their return
choices: They were all beheaded on their return
They were exiled from the kingdom for life
They were sworn to lifelong silence
They were buried alive beside him
context: This is legend, not documented fact: by the traditional account the roughly 200 servants who carried out Tu Duc's secret burial were all beheaded on their return, so none could ever reveal the true grave - which has never been found. Tu Duc's grand tomb thus honours an emperor who is not actually buried in it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_T%E1%BB%B1_%C4%90%E1%BB%A9c

question: A hurricane is on the way, forecasters in Miami warn. That same week weather offices in the Philippines track a storm they call a typhoon, and fishermen off India brace for a cyclone. From a satellite all three look alike: a huge spinning wheel of clouds. How are these storms related?
answer: They are one and the same storm, just named by region.
choices: They are one and the same storm, just named by region.
They are three separate storms, ranked by wind speed.
They are three separate storms, one for each ocean.
They are the same storm seen at three life stages.
context: One storm, three names. The spinning tropical cyclone is called a hurricane over the Atlantic and northeastern Pacific (around the Caribbean), a typhoon over the northwestern Pacific (around the Philippines), and a cyclone over the Indian Ocean and South Pacific (around India and Australia). Same beast, three regional names. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone

question: Hurricane Hunter pilots fly straight into an Atlantic hurricane, battering through a towering wall of cloud toward the eye at its very centre, a circle some 30 to 65 kilometres across. What do they find when they burst into the eye?
answer: a sudden calm, often with blue sky above
choices: a sudden calm, often with blue sky above
the storm's strongest winds of all
the storm's heaviest rain of all
a knot of tornadoes whirling together
context: Inside the eye the air sinks, so it is calm and often cloud-free, a circle typically 30-65 km across. The fiercest winds and heaviest rain lie just outside it, in the ring called the eyewall. Observed eyes have ranged from just 3 km wide to a giant 370 km. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone

question: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration finds that water, not the shrieking wind most people fear, causes nearly 90% of tropical-cyclone deaths. On low coasts like the U.S. Gulf Coast, which watery hazard is the single biggest killer as a hurricane comes ashore?
context: Water, not wind, is the great killer: NOAA reports water causes nearly 90% of tropical-cyclone deaths, and from 1963-2012 about half of U.S. landfalling-cyclone deaths came from storm surge -- a wall of seawater the storm shoves ashore (that share fell to about 11% in 2013-2023 as warnings improved). Source: https://www.noaa.gov/stories/storm-surge-deadliest-threat-from-tropical-cyclones

question: An Atlantic hurricane that moves inland fades within hours, and forecasters can predict where one will grow and where it will fade, because these storms draw all their power from a single source. Without it they quickly starve. What do they need to keep growing?
context: These storms only spin up over ocean warmer than about 26.5 C (80 F) -- the warm deep water is their fuel -- which is why they weaken quickly over land or cooler seas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone

question: The Bhola cyclone, the deadliest tropical cyclone ever recorded, struck East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, in November 1970, and an estimated 300,000 to 500,000 people died beneath a surge over 10 metres high. A shallow, funnel-shaped coast squeezed the water higher as the storm rammed it ashore. Up which body of water did the storm drive that killer surge?
context: The 1970 Bhola cyclone struck the low-lying delta of East Pakistan (now Bangladesh) on 12 November 1970. An estimated 300,000 to 500,000 people died, mostly in a storm surge about 10.5 m (35 ft) high, because the funnel-shaped, densely populated Bay of Bengal magnifies the surge as the coast narrows. The toll is only an estimate -- there were no census records. The World Meteorological Organization ranks it the deadliest tropical cyclone in modern history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Bhola_cyclone

question: An Atlantic hurricane rated Category 5 sits at the top of five categories, the most feared of all, yet its rating comes from just one number, and that number takes no account of how much damage a storm actually does on the ground. What does the Saffir-Simpson scale measure?
context: The Saffir-Simpson scale rates hurricanes 1 to 5 strictly by wind speed, not by damage. A Category 5 means sustained winds of 157 mph (252 km/h) or more, the top of the scale. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saffir%E2%80%93Simpson_scale

question: U.S. Air Force crews flew some 60 missions into one typhoon over the western Pacific in October 1979 just to chart it: the storm spanned about 2,220 kilometres from edge to edge, nearly half the width of the lower United States, the largest tropical cyclone ever measured. Which typhoon was it?
context: Typhoon Tip (October 1979) is the largest tropical cyclone ever measured -- about 2,220 km (1,380 mi) across, with gale-force winds spanning some 3.8 million square km. It also set the world record for lowest sea-level pressure, 870 hPa, with peak winds of 190 mph. U.S. Air Force crews flew about 60 reconnaissance missions into it. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoon_Tip ; https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/largest-tropical-cyclone-

question: The first Category 5 hurricane on record to strike the United States hammered the Florida Keys on Labor Day 1935 with 185-mph winds. Its surge swept a whole rescue effort away and drowned more than 400 people, many of them stranded work crews. The storm also wrecked the pioneering route out across the open shallows to Key West, never rebuilt in its original form. What did it destroy?
context: The 1935 Labor Day hurricane hit the Florida Keys with a pressure of 892 mb and winds near 185 mph. A relief train sent to evacuate stranded World War I veterans was swept off its tracks by the surge; more than 400 people died. The storm destroyed the Overseas Railroad to Key West, which was never rebuilt as a railway -- its route was later replaced by the Overseas Highway (U.S. 1). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_Labor_Day_hurricane

question: Super Typhoon Haiyan tore into the central Philippines in November 2013 as a Category 5 storm with winds near 315 km/h, among the strongest ever to make landfall anywhere. Its surge, more than 7 metres high, swallowed one low-lying coastal city almost whole, and roughly 6,300 people died. Which Philippine city did Haiyan's surge devastate?
context: Super Typhoon Haiyan (November 2013) struck the central Philippines as a Category 5 storm with winds near 315 km/h and a storm surge up to about 7.5 m that flattened the coastal city of Tacloban. It killed roughly 6,300 people and left millions homeless, among the strongest storms ever to make landfall. Source: https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/2013-state-climate-record-breaking-super-typhoon-haiyan

question: A fully organised spiral storm struck the coast of southern Brazil in March 2004 and broke a rule forecasters had long held: that no true hurricane could form in the South Atlantic, where the water runs too cool and the winds up high too strong. It is still the only confirmed South Atlantic hurricane. What was this rule-breaking storm named?
context: Hurricane Catarina (March 2004) was the first hurricane ever confirmed in the South Atlantic, a basin where the cool water and strong wind shear were thought to make hurricanes impossible. It made landfall in Brazil's Santa Catarina state -- which is how it got its name -- killing about 3 people. It remains the only confirmed South Atlantic hurricane. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Catarina

question: One typhoon spun up barely 1.5 degrees north of the equator near Singapore in December 2001, closer to the line than any tropical cyclone has ever been seen to form. The belt within a degree or two of the equator had long been thought off-limits to such storms, and such a fluke is reckoned to come perhaps once in centuries. What was this record-breaker named?
context: Typhoon Vamei (December 2001) formed only about 1.5 degrees north of the equator near Singapore -- roughly 150 km (95 mi) from the line -- the closest to the equator a tropical cyclone has ever been observed to form. Because the Coriolis force (which gives storms their spin) is nearly zero that close to the equator, such a storm is reckoned to be a once-in-centuries freak. Source: https://weather.com/news/weather/news/2024-12-24-on-todays-date-typhoon-vamei-near-equator

question: Across eastern Washington sprawls a dry maze of bare rock canyons called the Channeled Scablands. The land lies stripped to bare black basalt across some 2,000 square miles. What carved this vast scarred badland?
context: The Scablands were torn open by the Missoula floods — dozens of ice-age megafloods that stripped away the soil and scoured the basalt bare in a matter of days, not the slow ages geologists long assumed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channeled_Scablands

question: A barrier some 2,000 feet tall, higher than the Empire State Building, plugged Montana's Clark Fork valley and held back Glacial Lake Missoula: 500 cubic miles of water, as much as Lakes Erie and Ontario together. When the barrier gave way, the water burst free. What was this colossal dam made of?
context: The dam was a lobe of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet plugging the Clark Fork River. Because ice floats and leaks, it failed and re-formed again and again — at least 25 times — each collapse unleashing a megaflood. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_Lake_Missoula

question: The people of Missoula, Montana, live on the floor of a huge ice-age lake that has since drained away. The mountains ringing the city still carry the vanished lake's mark on their slopes, faint but there for anyone who looks up from the streets. In what form does that mark show?
answer: Level shorelines cut into the slopes
choices: Level shorelines cut into the slopes
Deep canyons gouged down the slopes
context: These are the wave-cut shorelines of Glacial Lake Missoula, etched where its surface stood for long spells at different heights. From across the valley they look like faint horizontal terraces climbing hundreds of feet up the mountainsides. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_Lake_Missoula

question: Row after row of long, evenly spaced ridges, some up to 50 feet high, march across parts of eastern Washington's Channeled Scablands. What are these giant ridges?
answer: Ripple marks left by rushing water
choices: Ripple marks left by rushing water
Dunes heaped up by desert wind
context: They are current ripples, the same marks water leaves in a sandy streambed, but 3 to 49 feet tall and spaced like rows of hills. Only from the air is the rippled pattern visible; on the ground a walker would never guess. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channeled_Scablands

question: Glacial Lake Missoula's dam failed at least 25 times: each time it sealed shut, the lake refilled and burst out again. At each flood's peak the torrent tore across the countryside as fast as 65 miles an hour. Roughly how many Amazon Rivers' worth of water did each peak carry?
context: At peak discharge a Missoula flood moved water at roughly 13 times the Amazon's flow — among the largest freshwater floods known on Earth — and did it over and over as the ice dam re-formed and failed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missoula_Floods

question: Not a drop of water runs over Dry Falls today. The curving rock wall, 400 feet high and three and a half miles wide in the desert of eastern Washington, has deep round basins gouged at its foot. At the peak of the ice-age floods it was a waterfall. Set beside Niagara Falls, how big was it?
answer: About five times wider than Niagara
choices: About five times wider than Niagara
About the same width as Niagara
About half the width of Niagara
context: At the Missoula floods' peak, Dry Falls was among the greatest waterfalls on Earth by flow — roughly five times the width of Niagara. Today it is bone dry, the abandoned lip of a vanished megaflood. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dry_Falls

question: As the great Laurentide Ice Sheet melted back, its meltwater pooled into a single inland sea. That sea spread across 440,000 square kilometers of central North America, larger than all five of today's Great Lakes combined. Then it drained and mostly vanished. What was this greatest of all North American lakes called?
context: Lake Agassiz, named for scientist Louis Agassiz, was bigger than all the Great Lakes combined. Its flat, silt-rich bed is now the ultra-fertile Red River Valley farmland on the US-Canada border, and Lake Winnipeg is a surviving remnant of it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Agassiz

question: A 15-ton lump of iron from space came to rest in Oregon's green Willamette Valley: the Willamette Meteorite, the largest ever found in the United States. No crater marks the spot, and it most likely fell hundreds of miles away, in Montana or western Canada, then somehow crossed the mountains to Oregon. How did this iron giant make the trip?
answer: Carried inside an iceberg on a great flood
choices: Carried inside an iceberg on a great flood
Rolled the whole way by a creeping glacier
Dragged across the land by early hunters
Hurled westward by a volcanic eruption
context: The meteorite most likely landed on ice in Montana or western Canada and was locked into a glacier, then rafted hundreds of miles inside an iceberg on a Missoula flood, grounding in the Willamette Valley when the ice melted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willamette_Meteorite; pbs.org/wgbh/nova/megaflood/scab-14.html

question: J Harlen Bretz argued in 1923 that the Scablands of eastern Washington were carved fast, in a catastrophe. His colleagues, sure that landscapes change only slowly, mocked him for about 40 years. What kind of evidence helped vindicate him at last?
answer: Photographs taken from aircraft and space
choices: Photographs taken from aircraft and space
Fossil bones found deep in the canyons
context: Joseph Pardee's evidence for Glacial Lake Missoula backed Bretz, and photographs from aircraft and then, in the 1970s, NASA satellite images showed the giant flood channels plainly from above. Bretz won geology's top Penrose Medal in 1979 at age 96, telling his son, 'All my enemies are dead, so I have no one to gloat over.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J_Harlen_Bretz

question: The Northern Hemisphere was warming out of the last ice age some 12,900 years ago when it plunged back into deep ice-age cold. One debated idea blames a vast meltwater lake in North America that burst into the sea, its cold fresh water stalling the ocean's warm currents. What do scientists call this abrupt return to the cold?
context: The Younger Dryas is named after Dryas octopetala, an Arctic wildflower whose pollen surges back into ancient mud when the cold returned. The plunge was brutal — Greenland cooled by up to 10 degrees C, some of it within a few years. The Agassiz trigger is a debated hypothesis; some argue the meltwater instead escaped down the Mackenzie River. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Younger_Dryas

question: Lake Bonneville, an ice-age lake in Utah with no outlet, kept rising with meltwater until, about 17,500 years ago, it brimmed over Red Rock Pass in Idaho, a low gap in its northern rim. The soft pass crumbled, and the lake tore loose in one of the largest floods known. Down which river did that flood pour?
context: When Lake Bonneville overtopped Red Rock Pass, the Bonneville Flood roared down the Portneuf and Snake rivers, and on into the Columbia, at roughly a million cubic meters per second, carving canyons and stranding house-sized boulders still seen along the Snake today. It sent almost 5,000 km3 of water downstream and dropped the lake's level by roughly 410 feet, among the largest floods known in Earth's history. It happened because a closed, overfilled basin finally found an escape over its rim. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Bonneville

question: From a ship's deck in the North Atlantic an iceberg can look small, which is what makes it deadly: most of its ice hides below the water. English speakers made the sight into a phrase for a small visible clue to a much bigger hidden problem. What is the phrase?
context: Freshwater ice weighs about 920 kg per cubic meter and seawater about 1,025, so a berg must sink roughly nine-tenths of its bulk just to float — only about a tenth shows above the surface. That hidden mass is why 'the tip of the iceberg' came to mean the small visible piece of a much bigger problem. Source: NOAA / US Coast Guard Navigation Center (navcen.uscg.gov); Wikipedia, 'Iceberg.'

question: Two kinds of ice float in the waters off Greenland: thin sea ice, which forms when the ocean's surface freezes each winter, and towering icebergs that drifted down from the glaciers. A thirsty sailor soon learns the two are not the same. What is true of an iceberg's ice, but not of sea ice?
answer: It's fresh water you could drink
choices: It's fresh water you could drink
It's saltier than the sea around it
It is barely a year old
It never melts, even in warm water
context: An iceberg is glacier ice — snow pressed down over thousands of years on land — that 'calved' (broke off) from the end of a glacier or ice shelf and floated away, which makes it fresh water. Sea ice is completely different: it's the ocean's own surface frozen into a salty crust each winter. The word 'iceberg' even comes from the Dutch ijsberg, 'ice mountain.' Source: NOAA (oceanservice.noaa.gov); Wikipedia, 'Iceberg.'

question: Ice spotters watching the shipping lanes off Newfoundland call a floating chunk an iceberg only if it is more than about 15 metres long. The most dangerous small ones, about the size of a truck, ride barely a metre above the water and hide from radar in rough seas. What nickname do sailors give them?
context: To count as a true 'iceberg,' floating ice must be more than about 15 meters long. Smaller pieces have their own names: a 'bergy bit' stands about 1-5 meters out of the water, and a 'growler' — named for the growling sound of air hissing out of the melting ice — rises less than a meter, about the size of a truck or a piano. Low and dark, growlers are notoriously hard for ships' radar to catch. Source: International Ice Patrol size classes; Wikipedia, 'Iceberg.'

question: The iceberg B-15 broke from the Ross Ice Shelf of Antarctica in 2000, a flat-topped tabular giant of the kind that calves off the continent's floating ice shelves, the largest icebergs ever measured. It was so vast that scientists reached for an island to describe its size. Which island was B-15 as big as?
context: B-15 calved from Antarctica's Ross Ice Shelf in March 2000, measuring roughly 295 by 37 km — about 11,000 square kilometers, the size of Jamaica. Antarctica's flat-topped 'tabular' bergs, wider than they are tall, calve off floating ice shelves and dwarf Arctic bergs. Another giant, A23a, broke from the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in 1986, grounded on the seabed for about 30 years, then finally drifted free in 2020. Source: Wikipedia, 'Iceberg B-15' and 'A23a'; British Antarctic Survey.

question: Sailors off Antarctica sometimes meet an iceberg that glows an eerie, deep sapphire blue all the way through, like a floating jewel, though most bergs look white or pale. That colour is a clue to the history of the ice. What does a deep-blue iceberg reveal about its ice?
answer: It is thousands of years old
choices: It is thousands of years old
It is barely a year old
It is still full of trapped air
It is really salty sea ice
context: Fresh glacier ice is full of tiny trapped air bubbles that scatter light and look white. But after thousands of years, the sheer weight of the ice squeezes those bubbles out; with nothing left to scatter the light, the dense ice absorbs the red and yellow wavelengths and reflects deep blue back to your eye — so a blue berg is old ice. Rarer still, a few Antarctic bergs glow jade green, colored by iron-rich dust frozen into the ice. Source: NOAA (oceanservice.noaa.gov); National Geographic.

question: Red-hot magma keeps welling up under Iceland, a small island in the North Atlantic with some 30 active volcanic systems. Over the last five centuries this one island has poured out a startling share of all the lava on Earth. About how much of Earth's lava has come from Iceland?
context: Over the past 500 years Iceland's volcanoes have produced roughly a third of all the lava erupted on the whole planet -- astonishing for one small island that packs in around 30 active volcanic systems. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanism_of_Iceland

question: Iceland's Reykjanes peninsula had lain quiet for about 800 years when Fagradalsfjall, one of its volcanoes, erupted in 2021, and it caused no panic. About 700,000 visits were logged as crowds streamed out to it. What did they hike across the lava fields to do?
choices: Soak in the warm ash pools
context: Fagradalsfjall began erupting on March 19, 2021 -- the area's first eruption in about 800 years. Rather than forcing evacuations, it became a spectacle: roughly 700,000 visits were logged across the 2021-2023 eruptions as people hiked out to watch fresh lava. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagradalsfjall

question: Iceland stands where the world's longest mountain range, hidden for almost its whole length beneath the oceans, climbs above the waves as dry land. All along this undersea range the sea floor splits and spreads apart. Which spreading ridge surfaces in Iceland?
context: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a divergent boundary -- the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart along it. Almost everywhere it lies deep undersea, but in Iceland it rises onto dry land, so the country is literally splitting. Iceland also sits over a hotspot; both feed its volcanoes, and the plates here diverge -- they never collide. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanism_of_Iceland

question: A rift runs right across Iceland, and along it the island is slowly splitting in two: its western half rides one of Earth's great plates and its eastern half another, drifting about 2 centimetres farther apart each year. Which two plates meet and pull apart beneath Iceland?
answer: The North American and Eurasian plates
choices: The North American and Eurasian plates
context: Iceland straddles the seam between the North American and Eurasian plates. They drift apart about 2 cm a year, so Iceland grows a little wider annually -- the western half riding with North America, the eastern half with Eurasia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanism_of_Iceland

question: At one national park in Iceland, visitors walk a path down into a gorge whose tall western wall is the very edge of a tectonic plate; across the sunken rift valley beyond lies the edge of the next. Nearly everywhere else on Earth such a boundary lies hidden far beneath the sea. What is this rift-valley park called?
context: At Thingvellir National Park the path drops into the Almannagja gorge, the largest fault crossing the rift: its western wall is the edge of the North American plate, and the Eurasian plate's edge lies across the sunken rift valley to the east, at the Hrafnagja fault. Thingvellir also hosted the Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments, founded in 930 AD, but the geological wonder is the rift itself. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thingvellir ; https://icelandtravelguide.is/locations/almannagja/

question: Divers come to Silfra, a flooded crack in Iceland's rift valley, to swim in the gap that is opening between two of Earth's great plates as they pull apart. Silfra draws divers from around the world for one more reason. What is it famous for?
context: Silfra lies in the Thingvellir rift valley, between the edges of the North American and Eurasian plates, and divers swim down its flooded crack. Its glacial meltwater is filtered for decades through porous lava rock, giving over 100 meters (328 ft) of visibility, said to be the clearest water on Earth. Source: https://www.padi.com/dive-site/iceland/silfra/  (Legend.)

question: Eyjafjallajokull erupted under its Icelandic glacier in April 2010 and hurled fine glassy ash into the sky, and winds carried it across Europe. That kind of ash can wreck jet engines, so airlines grounded flights across the continent: over 100,000 were cancelled and about 10 million people stranded. It was the worst shutdown of European air travel since which event?
context: The 2010 Eyjafjallajokull ash plume rose about 9 km and, blown southeast by a steady jet stream, blanketed Europe. Most European airspace closed April 15-20; over 300 airports in about 20 countries stopped flights, more than 100,000 flights were cancelled and roughly 10 million passengers were stranded -- the worst air-travel disruption since World War II. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_eruptions_of_Eyjafjallaj%C3%B6kull

question: Just after midnight in January 1973, a volcano split open Heimaey, a small Icelandic island, less than a mile from its sleeping town. Within about six hours, in the dark of a winter night, nearly all 5,300 residents had been carried to safety. How were they evacuated so quickly?
choices: Across a causeway to the mainland
On a troopship sent from Denmark
context: When Eldfell's fissure tore open barely a kilometer from Heimaey's town center in the early hours of January 23, 1973, nearly all of the 5,300 residents were safe on the mainland within about six hours. Most left on the island's fishing boats, much of the fleet happening to be in the harbor that night; a few, mainly the elderly and hospital patients, were flown out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldfell

question: The Eldfell eruption on Heimaey dragged on for months, and a slow wall of black lava crept toward the mouth of the harbour, the lifeline of this fishing town. If it sealed the harbour, the town was finished. For weeks the islanders and their helpers fought to chill the lava solid. What did they pump onto it to freeze it in place?
context: To stop Eldfell's lava from sealing off the harbor, townspeople and crews pumped about 7.3 million cubic meters of seawater onto the flow, through 32 pumps brought from the United States, each able to move up to 1,000 liters a second, cooling it solid. They saved the harbor, and the hardened lava even improved it by forming a new breakwater. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldfell

question: At Iguazu, on the Argentina-Brazil border, the river splits around forested islands and spills over a long curved cliff as many separate falls. Guides give visitors a headline number for how many falls that makes, and most first-timers are surprised. About how many is it?
context: Iguazú isn't one waterfall but a system of roughly 275 cascades strung along a 2.7-km (1.7-mile) arc — and the count actually shifts with the water, from about 150 in the dry season toward 300 in flood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: Eleanor Roosevelt, First Lady of the United States, first stood at the edge of Iguazu Falls, on the Argentina-Brazil border, in the 1940s. Its curved cliff runs nearly three kilometres, almost three times wider than Niagara. She reportedly summed up the whole sight in one tart remark. What did she say?
context: Iguazú's arc is nearly three times as wide as Niagara, and Niagara is the shorter drop too — so the pity was earned. 'Poor Niagara!' is the line everyone repeats about Eleanor Roosevelt's first visit. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls (width corroborated by https://www.cnn.com/travel/article/iguazu-falls-bucket-list)

question: At the centre of Iguazu's long arc, about fourteen separate falls converge in a U-shaped chasm and drop some 82 metres in one plunge, hurling up a permanent tower of mist. This most violent part of the falls carries a fittingly sinister name. What is it called?
context: In Spanish it's the Garganta del Diablo — the Devil's Throat. About fourteen cascades pour together into this one U-shaped chasm and drop roughly 82 metres, the tallest and loudest part of the whole falls. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devil%27s_Throat,_Iguazu_Falls

question: A metal walkway at Iguazu, on the Argentina-Brazil border, leads visitors out to the rim of a deep U-shaped gorge at the centre of the falls, where the river folds in on itself with a roar heard from far away. About how much of the whole river do they watch pour into that one gorge?
context: That gorge is the Devil's Throat, and it hogs about half of the Iguazú River's entire flow — funnelling it into a chasm roughly 82 m high, 150 m wide, and 700 m long. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devil%27s_Throat,_Iguazu_Falls

question: The Guarani people lived along the river at Iguazu long before Europeans came, and the name they gave it is still used today. They joined two everyday words of their language, 'y' and 'ûasú', to capture what towered in front of them. What does 'Iguazú' mean?
context: In Guaraní, 'y' means water and 'ûasú' means big — Iguazú is simply 'big water.' The Guaraní named the river for the obvious long before any European saw it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: A jealous forest snake-god wanted a girl named Naipi for himself, a Guarani legend of Iguazu says, but she fled downriver in a canoe with her love, Taroba. In his fury the god created the falls in an instant. What did he do?
answer: he sliced the river in two
choices: he sliced the river in two
he turned their canoe to stone
context: This is told as legend, not history. In the Guaraní tale the serpent-god, robbed of Naipí, slashed the river into a cliff so the fleeing canoe would plunge — condemning Naipí and Tarobá to fall forever. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: A priest, captured and tied to a wooden cross, goes tumbling over Iguazu Falls in the opening scene of a 1986 epic about Jesuit missionaries among the Guarani. The film won the Palme d'Or, and an Oscar went to its cinematography. What is the film called?
context: The film is The Mission (1986), which took the Palme d'Or at Cannes and an Oscar for cinematography — much of it shot at Iguazú, including the martyred priest sent over the cataracts lashed to a cross. Source: https://about.new7wonders.com/2011/05/30/the-mission-at-iguazu-falls/

question: Great dusky swifts spend the daylight hours snatching insects from the mist above Iguazu's cascades. At dusk the whole flock streams back to one roost, a place so hard to reach that few predators dare follow. Where do these little birds tuck their nests?
answer: on ledges behind the falling water
choices: on ledges behind the falling water
on cliff shelves above the gorge
on rock stacks amid the rapids
in crevices deep in the canyon wall
context: Great dusky swifts really do fly straight through the curtain of falling water to reach ledges on the bare rock behind it — the sheet of water walls their nests off from predators. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/birds/great-dusky-swift

question: The river at Iguazu leaps from a hard black lip that is no ordinary bedrock. It is the top of a giant stack of ancient lava flows, piled up to a kilometre thick across the Parana Plateau when this corner of South America lay buried under erupting lava. What do geologists call such a vast sheet of stacked, hardened lava?
context: It's flood basalt — the Serra Geral formation of the Paraná Plateau, a stack of old lava flows up to about 1,000 m thick. The whole river simply tumbles off the edge of that ancient lava sheet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: Iguazu Falls is creeping upstream, just as Niagara does. Beneath its hard rock lip the softer rock washes out, the overhang cracks and drops away, and the whole cliff moves a couple of centimetres farther upriver every year. What do geographers call this slow migration of a waterfall?
context: It's headward erosion. Undercutting strips the soft rock from beneath the hard basalt cap, the ledge collapses backward — and so the whole waterfall slowly migrates toward the river's source, about 1.4 to 2.1 cm a year, the same slow retreat that is dragging Niagara upstream too. Undercutting, plunge-pool scour and hydraulic action are the mechanisms doing the work; 'headward erosion' is the name for the migration itself. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguazu_Falls

question: Blue domes ring the huge central square of Isfahan, in central Iran. A Persian proverb boasts that seeing this one city is like seeing a huge share of everything on Earth worth seeing. How much of the world does the proverb say Isfahan is?
context: The proverb runs 'Isfahan nesf-e jahan ast' -- 'Isfahan is half the world.' Shah Abbas the Great made Isfahan his capital around 1600 and packed it with wonders to earn the boast. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isfahan)  (Legend.)

question: Shah Abbas the Great laid out a huge rectangular plaza in Isfahan around the year 1600. It runs about 560 metres end to end, among the largest public squares on Earth, and mosques, a palace and a bazaar gate frame all four sides. What is this vast plaza called?
context: Naqsh-e Jahan means 'Image of the World.' About 160 x 560 m (~89,600 m2), it was built 1598-1629 and is protected by UNESCO as 'Meidan Emam, Esfahan.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naqsh-e_Jahan_Square)

question: The Safavid shahs used Isfahan's great central square as a royal polo field, galloping after the ball while the court watched from a palace terrace. It was a marketplace and a parade ground as well. Four hundred years on, what from those polo games still stands at each end of the square?
context: The marble goalposts said to date from the Safavid games still stand at the square's north and south ends, some 400 years later. The shah watched from the terrace of the Ali Qapu Palace on the west side. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naqsh-e_Jahan_Square)  (Legend.)

question: On the east side of Isfahan's great square sits the small Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, a gem of Safavid tilework. Unlike almost every other grand mosque, it has no towering minaret and no open courtyard at all. What explains these missing features?
answer: it was the shah's private family mosque
choices: it was the shah's private family mosque
it was left unfinished when Shah Abbas died
it was originally a royal library
it was meant only for winter use
context: Because it was the shah's private family mosque rather than a public one, it needed no minaret to summon crowds and no courtyard to hold them. It was named in 1622 after Sheikh Lotfollah, Shah Abbas's revered father-in-law. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Lotfollah_Mosque)

question: Crowds still gather at dusk under the arcades of Isfahan's Si-o-se-pol, whose 33 stone arches carry it nearly 300 metres across the Zayanderud river. Its Safavid builders gave it a clever second purpose that a plain bridge could never serve. What was it?
answer: it held the river back as a dam
choices: it held the river back as a dam
it cooled the palace with piped water
context: The 33-arch Si-o-se-pol ('bridge of 33 arches') was built 1599-1602 under the Safavid commander Allahverdi Khan; it could pond the Zayanderud upstream like a dam, and its arcades are still where people of Isfahan meet at dusk. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si-o-se-pol)

question: Shah Abbas II built a garden pavilion in Isfahan around 1647 and named it Chehel Sotoun -- 'Forty Columns.' Yet a visitor who counts the slender wooden columns holding up its porch finds only twenty. Where are the other twenty columns?
answer: mirrored in the pool out front
choices: mirrored in the pool out front
painted as a trick on the back wall
context: By tradition the twenty columns double to 'forty' in the long reflecting pool laid before the pavilion -- the name is a poetic count, not a literal one. Chehel Sotoun was finished under Shah Abbas II around 1647. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chehel_Sotoun)  (Legend.)

question: The great blue dome of Isfahan's Shah Mosque glows across the square in turquoise and cobalt, its whole surface a skin of glazed tiles. To cover so vast a dome quickly, its Safavid craftsmen perfected a faster tile-glazing method that broke with the older, painstaking mosaic style. What was their shortcut?
answer: painting many colors onto each tile before firing
choices: painting many colors onto each tile before firing
firing each tile once for every color
pressing gold leaf over the glaze
carving the design into wet plaster
context: The method is called haft-rangi -- 'seven colors' -- because up to seven glaze colors were painted onto a single square tile and fired together, far faster than cutting and fitting single-color mosaic pieces. It gave Isfahan's domes their glowing skin. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah_Mosque_(Isfahan))

question: Sweden's High Coast, on the Gulf of Bothnia, keeps climbing out of the sea faster than any other land known on Earth: about 300 metres over the past ten thousand years, and still roughly 8 mm every year. What is lifting this whole coastline?
answer: An ice-age glacier that pressed the crust down has now melted away
choices: An ice-age glacier that pressed the crust down has now melted away
A plume of hot magma is slowly rising beneath the whole region
Two tectonic plates are colliding and crumpling the coast here
Ages of river sediment have piled up along the whole shore
context: The crust floats on the soft, dense mantle below. A great ice sheet — here about two miles thick — pressed the land down like a hand pushing into a mattress; now that the ice has melted, the land is slowly springing back up. This is 'isostatic rebound.' Sweden's High Coast (Hoega Kusten) has risen about 300 m since the ice melted and still rises ~8 mm a year — Wikipedia calls it the highest known isostatic rebound on Earth. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 2000, joined in 2006 with Finland's Kvarken archipelago) precisely because it shows the process live, and it is where post-glacial rebound was first recognised and studied. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Coast ; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/898/

question: Around Hudson Bay in Canada, the heart of the old Laurentide Ice Sheet, which vanished only about 8,000 years ago, sensitive instruments still pick up a real anomaly. One everyday measurement comes out noticeably lower there than almost anywhere else on Earth. Which one?
answer: Gravity — a scale shows you weigh a hair less
choices: Gravity — a scale shows you weigh a hair less
Air pressure — a barometer reads a touch lower
The magnetic field — a compass pulls a bit weaker
The temperature — a thermometer runs a shade colder
context: Where the ice pressed hardest, the crust is still slightly 'dented' and has not fully risen back, so there is a little less mass beneath you — and gravity reads measurably weaker: about 0.3 milligals below normal, meaning you would weigh roughly 0.005% (about a tenth of an ounce) less at Hudson Bay than elsewhere. Honest caveat: incomplete rebound explains only about a quarter to a half of this gravity low; the rest comes from slow, deep mantle flow, not the vanished ice. The Laurentide Ice Sheet was about 3.2 km thick (up to ~3.7 km over the bay) and weighed on the order of 10 trillion tons; the land there still rises about 1 cm a year and has roughly 650 more feet to rebound over the next ~5,000 years. Sources: https://earthlymission.com/hudson-bay-quebec-gravity-anomaly-explained/ ; https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1029/92GL00687

question: At Finland's Kvarken archipelago, on the Gulf of Bothnia, the maps go out of date within a single human lifetime: the coastline visibly moves from one decade to the next. What is happening to this shore?
answer: Fresh land keeps rising from the sea, gaining new meadows each year
choices: Fresh land keeps rising from the sea, gaining new meadows each year
The coast is steadily sinking, drowning its old fishing villages
Fierce storms are tearing the shoreline back a little each year
Great tides scour the flat shores bare twice every single day
context: The land at Kvarken rises about 8-9 mm a year, so the shallow sea keeps turning into ground: roughly 700 hectares of fresh land — about twice the size of New York's Central Park — surface every year (around one square kilometre annually). New islands and meadows appear within a human lifetime, and old harbours are left stranded far inland: Vaasa's harbour grew too shallow to use, and after the town burned in 1852 it was rebuilt 6-7 km closer to the sea (the fire triggered the move, but the retreating shoreline is why they rebuilt seaward). Geologists expect the shallow Kvarken seabed to surface within about 2,000 years, pinching the Gulf of Bothnia into a southern gulf and a northern lake. (The Baltic here is nearly tideless, so the 'great tides' option was a red herring.) Sources: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/uplift-underway-in-finlands-kvarken-archipelago-153740/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kvarken

question: Ferries crowd the narrow saltwater channel that splits Istanbul down the middle, with half the city in Europe and half in Asia. Istanbul is the only big city on Earth that sits on two continents at once. What is that channel called?
