context: The Bosphorus is about 31 km long and pinches to just ~700 m at its narrowest — a saltwater strait, not a river. Istanbul is the only major city built across two continents, and ferries and bridges knit its European and Asian halves together. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosphorus

question: The emperor Justinian finished a huge domed building around the year 537, after just under six years of work. Its dome was so wide, and had so many windows, that it seemed to float on light. Which Istanbul landmark, still standing after nearly 1,500 years, is this?
context: Justinian I ordered Hagia Sophia raised after riots destroyed the earlier church; it went up in just 5 years and 10 months (532–537 AD), designed by two scholars — the mathematician Anthemius of Tralles and the geometer Isidore of Miletus. It remained the largest cathedral on Earth for nearly a thousand years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia

question: A quarter-million people bargain every day in a covered market in the heart of old Istanbul, a roofed maze of about sixty streets and over four thousand shops. Mehmed the Conqueror first built it in the 1450s. What is this huge covered market called?
context: The Grand Bazaar has around 61 covered streets and over 4,000 shops, begun under Mehmed II in the 1450s–60s. Between 250,000 and 400,000 people pass through it every day — one of the oldest and largest covered markets anywhere. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Bazaar,_Istanbul

question: Beneath Istanbul's busy streets, 336 marble columns rise from the shallow water of the Basilica Cistern, the dim, echoing reservoir the emperor Justinian built 1,500 years ago. Two of the columns stand not on plain bases but on huge carved heads hauled from an older ruin. Whose face is carved there?
context: The Basilica Cistern (Turkish Yerebatan Sarayı, 'Sunken Palace') was built under Justinian in the 6th century, about 138 m by 65 m, its 336 columns standing over the shallow water. Two columns rest on huge carved Medusa heads dragged from an older Roman building — one set upside down, the other on its side. No one knows for certain why they were placed that way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_Cistern

question: Turkey's new secular republic reopened Istanbul's great domed cathedral of 537 in 1935 as something belonging to no single faith. It had been an Orthodox Christian cathedral, then a mosque after Mehmed II took the city in 1453, and today it is a mosque once more. What did it become in 1935?
context: Hagia Sophia lived four lives: an Orthodox cathedral from 537, a mosque after Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, a museum from 1935 under the secular Turkish Republic, and a working mosque again from 2020. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia

question: Greek settlers from Megara founded a small town on the site of Istanbul around 660 BC. Centuries later, in 330, Constantine the Great made it the Roman Empire's capital, and for the next thousand years it was called Constantinople. What was that first Greek town called?
context: Settlers from Megara founded Byzantium around 660 BC. Constantine the Great refounded it as the Roman capital in 330 AD, and it became Constantinople; the name 'Istanbul' — from the Greek phrase 'stin poli,' 'to the City' — became official only in 1930. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_Istanbul

question: Genoese settlers raised the stout stone Galata Tower on Istanbul's northern shore in 1348, and it still stands. Hezarfen Ahmed Celebi, a famous legend from 1638 says, crossed the whole strait that splits the city, from the European side to the Asian shore. How does the legend say he made the crossing?
answer: he glided across on home-made wings
choices: he glided across on home-made wings
he swam the whole way across
he crossed on a single tightrope
he rowed over in a tiny skiff
context: The Galata Tower (~67 m) was raised by Genoese settlers in 1348 and called the 'Tower of Christ,' once the tallest building in the city. The 1638 tale of Hezarfen Ahmed Çelebi gliding on home-made wings across the Bosphorus is a beloved legend, not documented fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galata_Tower

question: For a thousand years Constantinople's triple Theodosian Walls, a deep moat backed by two lines of stone ramparts, turned back every attacking army. Then in 1453 the young sultan Mehmed II broke through with one fearsome weapon, built just for the siege and so massive that teams of oxen hauled it into place. What was this weapon?
context: Mehmed II's Hungarian founder Orban cast a giant bronze bombard, the 'Basilic,' about 9 m long, which hurled stone balls of roughly 500 kg; accounts say teams of oxen dragged it to the walls. The 5.7-km triple Theodosian Walls had guarded the city for a thousand years before falling on 29 May 1453. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1180/1453-the-fall-of-constantinople/ ; https://worldhistoryedu.com/walls-of-constantinople/

question: The strait that splits Istanbul curls through the city like a river and is only about 700 metres wide where it pinches tightest. One great sea has no other natural passage out to the Mediterranean except through this single gap. Which sea is bottled up behind it?
context: The Bosphorus is the only sea-gate out of the Black Sea, linking it through the Sea of Marmara to the Mediterranean. About 31 km long and only ~700 m wide at its narrowest, it is a true strait, not a river. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosphorus

question: The Ottoman sultans ruled their empire for nearly four hundred years from one sprawling palace on a wooded point of Istanbul, where the strait meets the Sea of Marmara. Mehmed the Conqueror began it in 1459, and it stayed the seat of Ottoman power until the mid-1800s. Which palace was it?
context: Mehmed the Conqueror began Topkapı Palace in 1459 on Seraglio Point, where the Bosphorus meets the Sea of Marmara. It housed the sultans for about 400 years, until they moved to the new Dolmabahçe Palace in 1853. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topkap%C4%B1_Palace

question: Sultan Ahmed I raised his great mosque in Istanbul between 1609 and 1616 and gave it six slender minarets. That set off a scandal: the Great Mosque of Mecca, the holiest in all Islam, also had exactly six, and nothing was supposed to rival Mecca. How, according to legend, did the sultan settle the uproar?
answer: he funded a seventh minaret added at Mecca
choices: he funded a seventh minaret added at Mecca
he had one of his six minarets torn down
he left his sixth minaret unfinished
he renamed his mosque to honour Mecca
context: The six-minaret Sultan Ahmed Mosque (1609–1616), nicknamed the 'Blue Mosque' for its tens of thousands of blue İznik tiles, faces Hagia Sophia across a square. Legend says Ahmed I paid for a seventh minaret at Mecca's Great Mosque to settle the rivalry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_Ahmed_Mosque

question: Visitors who step through the gates of Jaipur's walled old town, in India's desert state of Rajasthan, find the reason for its nickname all around them. Each of Rajasthan's four most famous cities has a nickname earned from its signature look. What is Jaipur nicknamed?
context: The whole walled old town of Jaipur is washed a single terracotta pink — the traditional colour of welcome — which earned it the name the 'Pink City.' Its Rajasthan neighbours wear their own nicknames: Jodhpur is the Blue City, Jaisalmer the Golden City, and Udaipur the City of Lakes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur

question: Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II had every building in Jaipur's old town painted one shade in 1876, the traditional colour of welcome, and the city has worn it ever since. It was a grand gesture to honour one important visitor arriving in the city. Whom was Jaipur dressed up to greet?
answer: the visiting Prince of Wales, Britain's future king
choices: the visiting Prince of Wales, Britain's future king
Queen Victoria, newly proclaimed Empress of India
the Viceroy of India, the Queen's deputy in Delhi
the Nizam of Hyderabad, a great Indian prince
context: The guest was Albert Edward, the Prince of Wales, on his 1875–76 royal tour of India; he would later be crowned King Edward VII. Pink was the colour of hospitality, so Ram Singh II had the whole old town washed in it to welcome him — and Jaipur has stayed pink ever since. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur

question: Sawai Jai Singh II, a Kachhwaha Rajput ruler, founded Jaipur in 1727 as a brand-new capital and named the city after himself. He is remembered as much for one personal passion as for the city he built. What was Jai Singh's ruling passion?
context: Jai Singh II was a serious astronomer who built great stone observatories in Jaipur, Delhi, and other cities. He named his capital 'Jaipur' — the City of Jai — and founded it on 18 November 1727. His love of the sky shaped the city, from its careful plan to its climbable observatory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur

question: Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, Jaipur's planner, drew the whole city on paper in 1727 before a single house was built, then laid it over the ground in one bold geometric shape. Most of India's old cities had grown slowly over the centuries into tangled mazes of winding lanes. What overall shape did he give Jaipur?
answer: a rectangular grid of nine blocks
choices: a rectangular grid of nine blocks
a star of eight avenues from the palace
a cross of four great roads
context: Vidyadhar Bhattacharya's grid split Jaipur into nine rectangular blocks — two reserved for the palace and state buildings, seven for the public — cut by broad main streets about 34 metres wide. It made Jaipur one of India's first fully planned cities, and in 2019 UNESCO listed the walled city for its blend of Hindu, Mughal, and Western planning. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaipur ; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1605/

question: An astronomer at the Jantar Mantar, the open-air observatory finished in Jaipur in 1734, took his readings of the sun or a star from its 19 instruments in a way that still surprises visitors. How did he read them?
choices: by peering through a brass telescope
by floating a magnetic needle in water
by reading a printed star almanac
context: Instead of small handheld tools, Jai Singh built his 19 astronomy instruments as huge masonry structures — ramps, bowls, and towers you climb — all for naked-eye observation of the sky. The Jantar Mantar was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jantar_Mantar,_Jaipur

question: The Samrat Yantra towers about 27 metres over Jaipur's Jantar Mantar, roughly the height of a nine-storey building, the largest single instrument there. Yet it is precise enough to tell local time to within about two seconds. Among the world's great historic time-telling devices, what does that make the Samrat Yantra?
context: The Samrat Yantra ('Supreme Instrument') is the world's largest stone sundial, about 27 metres (88–90 feet) tall. Its shadow is so big it visibly creeps along at roughly 1 mm per second — about a hand's breadth every minute — so you can actually watch the sun's motion with your naked eye. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jantar_Mantar,_Jaipur

question: Royal women once looked down on the busy street, without being seen, from 953 tiny latticed windows in the five-storey front of Jaipur's Hawa Mahal, built in 1799. The palace earned the name Palace of Winds for what a breeze does when it is forced through hundreds of such tiny gaps, which keeps the rooms cool inside. What does the breeze do?
answer: it speeds up into a brisk, rushing draft
choices: it speeds up into a brisk, rushing draft
it slows into a soft, gentle drift
it splits into many fine, criss-crossing streams
it swirls into slow, circling eddies
context: Those 953 tiny openings work like a natural air-conditioner: squeezing a breeze through so many small gaps speeds the air up — a Venturi (or chimney) effect — and the faster draft cools the rooms behind, which is exactly how the 'Palace of Winds' got its name. The Hawa Mahal was built in 1799 by Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawa_Mahal ; https://www.cnn.com/travel/article/india-hawa-mahal-palace-of-the-winds/index.html

question: Lal Chand Ustad designed Jaipur's Hawa Mahal in 1799 to rise in a tall, tapering front of latticed screens that grows narrower toward the top. He shaped this pyramid-like profile on purpose, to echo the crown worn by one beloved Hindu god. Whose crown does the Palace of Winds imitate?
context: The Hawa Mahal's tapering, pyramid-like shape was designed to resemble the mukut — the tall crown — of Lord Krishna. It was commissioned by Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh and built in 1799. Source: https://www.yatrapur.com/hawa-mahal/

question: Thousands of tiny convex mirrors, each backed with coloured foil, encrust the walls and ceiling of the Sheesh Mahal, a hall inside Amber Fort above Jaipur. Suppose you shut its doors in the dark and light just one small candle. What happens?
answer: the whole hall blooms into a sky of stars
choices: the whole hall blooms into a sky of stars
the room seems to stretch on forever
your reflection splinters into a thousand faces
the walls shimmer with a shifting rainbow
context: The Sheesh Mahal (Mirror Palace) is covered in thousands of tiny convex mirror pieces set with coloured foil, so the light of a single candle flame reflects and glitters across the whole hall like a starlit sky. Amber Fort, begun by Raja Man Singh I, mirrors itself in Maota Lake below — the palace's main water source — and was inscribed by UNESCO in 2013 as part of the 'Hill Forts of Rajasthan.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amer_Fort

question: In New Orleans, when a brass band comes swinging down the street, a crowd of strangers falls in behind it, twirling parasols and waving handkerchiefs. Anyone at all is welcome to join in the dancing behind the band. What is this dancing crowd called?
context: The band and family up front are the 'main line'; the crowd of dancers who fall in behind — parasols twirling, handkerchiefs waving — are the 'second line,' and anyone can join. Second lines roll at both street parades and jazz funerals, and it is one of New Orleans's most beloved traditions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_funeral

question: A brass band marches to a New Orleans cemetery playing slow, sad songs at a jazz funeral. Once the body is laid to rest, the band bursts into hot, joyful music for the dance back home. Which upbeat song most famously rings out on that jubilant march home?
choices: "Just a Little While to Stay Here"
context: On the way to the grave the band plays dirges like 'Nearer My God to Thee' and 'Just a Closer Walk With Thee.' Once the body is entombed, it 'cuts the body loose' and swings into joyous numbers — most famously 'When the Saints Go Marching In' (or 'Oh, Didn't He Ramble') — for the dancing march home. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_funeral

question: Enslaved people in old New Orleans gathered on Sundays, their one day of weekly rest, in a public square that was in effect the only spot in the country where they could drum, sing and dance in the open. There they kept alive the rhythms that would later grow into jazz. What was the square called?
context: Under the French slave code, the Code Noir, Sunday was a day of rest, and Congo Square became effectively the only place in the United States where open African drumming survived. Those rhythms seeded jazz; the square now sits inside Louis Armstrong Park in the Tremé neighborhood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_Square

question: Louis Armstrong, an eleven-year-old New Orleans boy, fired his stepfather's pistol into the air to celebrate New Year's Eve in 1912 and was sent to a home for wayward boys. There a teacher, Peter Davis, put an instrument in his hands and made him bandleader. What instrument did young Armstrong first learn to play?
context: The reform school was the Colored Waif's Home. Instructor Peter Davis handed Armstrong a cornet — the trumpet's stubbier cousin — and made him bandleader. 'Satchmo' would go on to remake jazz around the improvising soloist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong

question: Early jazz pianists in New Orleans found their steadiest work, night after night, in the saloons and brothels of a legal red-light district of the city, which ran from 1897 to 1917. When the U.S. Navy forced it shut in 1917, many musicians rode the riverboats up the Mississippi and carried jazz north to Chicago. What was the district called?
context: Storyville was named for alderman Sidney Story, who wrote the ordinance creating it and was mortified that the vice quarter forever bore his name. Secretary of War Newton Baker had the Navy close it at midnight on November 12, 1917, to clear vice from near military bases — and the musicians' exodus helped carry New Orleans jazz up the Mississippi. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storyville,_New_Orleans

question: Drums, gourds and banjos pounded beside European fiddles and tambourines when enslaved Africans gathered in a public square in old New Orleans on their one free day. Their most celebrated dance set the whole crowd stamping in unison, and its name still echoes in New Orleans music today. What was the dance called?
context: The bamboula — named for the bamboo-headed drum that drove it — along with dances like the Calinda and Juba, filled Congo Square on Sundays. That blend of African drums with European strings still surfaces in New Orleans second lines and Mardi Gras Indian parades. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_Square

question: Louis Armstrong's lyric sheet fluttered to the floor in the middle of a 1926 recording of 'Heebie Jeebies,' the story goes. Rather than stop the band, he kept the tune rolling by improvising made-up sounds where the words should have been, and the record became a surprise hit that spread the style. What is this wordless, improvised way of singing called?
context: Armstrong didn't invent scat, but 'Heebie Jeebies' helped make it famous. The dropped-sheet-music tale is likely a legend Armstrong enjoyed telling; either way, scat means singing improvised nonsense syllables as if the voice were a horn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong

question: Louis Armstrong of New Orleans reshaped jazz in the 1920s with his Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings. One part of a jazz performance became the beating heart of the music, and every jazz musician after him would be measured against him by it. What did Armstrong make the centrepiece of jazz?
context: Critics say Armstrong 'almost single-handedly created the role of the jazz soloist,' building his lines on the song's chords rather than just its melody. From his Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings on, the improvised solo became the art at the heart of jazz. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong

question: Critics mocked a New Orleans pianist who had started out at fourteen playing in the city's brothels, for he claimed to have invented jazz back in 1902. Yet in 1915 he really did publish one of the very first jazz compositions ever put into print. What was this landmark tune called?
context: The braggart was Jelly Roll Morton, who started playing piano in Storyville brothels at fourteen. Critics mocked him for 'exaggerating his worth,' but his 'Jelly Roll Blues' (1915) truly was among the first jazz compositions ever published. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelly_Roll_Morton

question: A white New Orleans group, the Original Dixieland Jass Band, cut the first jazz record ever to reach the shops in February 1917, and it was pure novelty: its instruments honked and squealed like farm animals, all for laughs. It became a runaway national hit. What was this first jazz record called?
context: The band was the Original Dixieland Jass Band — note the early spelling 'Jass' — a white New Orleans group, even though Black New Orleans musicians had been creating the music for years. Their barnyard-noise novelty introduced jazz to a national audience. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_Dixieland_Jass_Band

question: One New Orleans horn player blew so loud and so wild around 1900 that listeners swore his horn carried clear across the city on a still night, before anyone had ever recorded jazz. His fans hailed him as the first King of the new music, yet not one recording of him is known to survive. Who was he?
context: Buddy Bolden's career ended in 1907, at age 30, when he suffered a mental collapse and was committed to the state asylum in Jackson, Louisiana, where he died in 1931. His signature tune, 'Buddy Bolden's Blues' — once the scandalous 'Funky Butt' — was so wild that clarinetist Sidney Bechet remembered 'the police put you in jail if they heard you singing that song.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Bolden  (Legend.)

question: A walker can cross Jerusalem's Old City, a small walled square of pale golden stone, from one end to the other in about an hour. Inside its walls lie four named neighbourhoods, each with its own community and holy places. What are these four quarters called?
answer: the Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Armenian Quarters
choices: the Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Armenian Quarters
the Jaffa, Damascus, Zion, and Herod Quarters
the Greek, Latin, Coptic, and Syriac Quarters
the Roman, Crusader, Ottoman, and British Quarters
context: The whole walled Old City fits inside about 0.9 square kilometres — smaller than many city parks — yet it is split into the Muslim Quarter (the largest and most crowded), the Christian Quarter, the Jewish Quarter, and the Armenian Quarter (the smallest, roughly 0.13 sq km). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_City_(Jerusalem)

question: In Jerusalem's Old City, worshippers fold tiny slips of paper with written prayers on them. They press these into the cracks between the huge stone blocks of one holy wall. Families have kept up this custom for hundreds of years. Which sacred site is filled with these paper prayers?
context: Jews call it simply the Kotel — 'the Wall.' It is the holiest place where Jews gather to pray, and for centuries visitors have tucked folded prayers into the gaps between its ancient stones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Wall

question: Honey-coloured stone walls about 12 metres high ring Jerusalem's Old City, and many visitors take them for the work of some ancient king. In truth they are barely 500 years old, built in just five years on one ruler's orders. Which ruler built the walls that still stand today?
context: The walls you see today were raised in just five years, from 1537 to 1541, by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent — about 4 km around and some 12 metres high. Herod, Hadrian, and Saladin all shaped Jerusalem in far earlier centuries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walls_of_Jerusalem

question: Through the narrow, twisting lanes of Jerusalem's Old City runs a path about 600 metres long. Christian tradition marks it as the route Jesus walked, carrying his cross, toward his crucifixion. Pilgrims still follow it on foot, stopping to pray at 14 marked stations. What is this route through the city called?
context: Via Dolorosa means 'the Way of Sorrows.' The route is marked by 14 Stations of the Cross, each recalling a moment of the Passion; the final five stations lie inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where the route ends. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Dolorosa

question: Abd al-Malik, a caliph of the Umayyad line, had a shrine raised on Jerusalem's central platform around 691, and its bright gilded cap now stands as the emblem of the whole city. Scholars regard it as the oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture anywhere. What is this monument called?
context: The Dome of the Rock was built around 691 CE by the caliph Abd al-Malik, making it the oldest surviving Islamic building in the world. Its golden dome shelters the Foundation Stone, an exposed slab of bedrock that Jews, Christians, and Muslims all hold sacred. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome_of_the_Rock

question: Just east of Jerusalem's walls, across the deep Kidron Valley, rises a long ridge whose city-facing slope has served as a Jewish burial ground for roughly 3,000 years. Around 150,000 graves step down the hillside, making it one of the oldest cemeteries on earth still in daily use. What is this ridge called?
context: The Mount of Olives faces the Old City across the Kidron Valley. Its western slope holds roughly 150,000 graves and has been a Jewish cemetery for about 3,000 years. At its foot lies the Garden of Gethsemane, where some gnarled olive trees are believed to be many centuries old. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_of_Olives

question: In the eastern wall of Jerusalem's Old City, facing the Kidron Valley, stands a double-arched gate. It was deliberately bricked up in 1541 and has stayed sealed ever since. In part, this is because Jewish tradition holds that the Messiah will one day enter Jerusalem through this very gate. Which sealed gate is this?
context: The Golden Gate (also called the Gate of Mercy) was sealed in 1541 and has stayed bricked up ever since. Jewish tradition teaches that the Messiah will enter Jerusalem through this eastern gate, coming from the Mount of Olives across the valley. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate_(Jerusalem)  (Legend.)

question: Jewish worshippers pray beside a great wall of huge stones in Jerusalem's Old City, yet it is not a wall of the Jewish Temple at all, a fact that surprises many visitors. Its giant lower stones survive from a vast building project that the Judean king Herod the Great carried out around 19 BCE. What is the wall a surviving side of?
answer: the huge platform Herod built to enlarge the Temple Mount
choices: the huge platform Herod built to enlarge the Temple Mount
the fortress Herod built to guard the Temple courts
the aqueduct Herod built to carry water to the city
the royal palace Herod built on the western hill
context: Herod the Great didn't rebuild only the Temple — around 19 BCE he raised an enormous artificial platform around the sacred hill to enlarge it, and the Western Wall is a surviving retaining wall holding up one side of that platform. The Temple building itself was later destroyed; the exposed prayer section of the retaining wall rises about 19 metres. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Wall

question: King Hezekiah's workers cut a tunnel more than 500 metres through solid rock as the Assyrians advanced, to bring the water of the Gihon spring from outside Jerusalem's defences safely inside the walls. An inscription the workers carved themselves, found in 1880, boasts of one feat. What did the diggers achieve?
answer: they cut from opposite ends and met in the middle
choices: they cut from opposite ends and met in the middle
they finished the entire tunnel in a single night
they carved it in a perfectly straight underground line
they cut it wide enough to march soldiers through
context: The Gihon Spring was ancient Jerusalem's only reliable water source. Around 700 BCE, with the Assyrians advancing, King Hezekiah's engineers tunneled over 500 metres through bedrock. The Siloam inscription, found in 1880, was carved by the workers to record the moment the two teams — digging toward each other from opposite ends — broke through and met underground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gihon_Spring

question: Six Christian communities share the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, which stands where tradition places Jesus's crucifixion and tomb, and their quarrels over the building can turn bitter. Yet the key to its front door, and the daily job of unlocking and locking it, have belonged to the same keepers for centuries. Who holds them?
context: For centuries, two Muslim families have safeguarded the door so that no single Christian group can control it: the Joudeh family keeps the roughly 30-centimetre iron key, and the Nuseibeh family unlocks and locks the door each day. Tradition traces the arrangement to Saladin, who granted it in 1187. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Holy_Sepulchre

question: A plain wooden ladder rests on a stone ledge high on the front of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, beneath an upper window above the main doors. Visitors have puzzled over it for generations, and it has become one of the church's most famous sights. What is this ladder called?
context: The 'Status Quo,' fixed in 1757, governs the six Christian communities that share the church; because nothing can change without all of them agreeing, a wooden ladder propped on a façade ledge has not moved for roughly 300 years — earning it the name the 'Immovable Ladder.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Holy_Sepulchre  (Legend.)

question: One town in Jiangxi province, packed with porcelain kilns, glowed so fiercely at night that travellers said the whole place looked on fire. For over a thousand years it has made the world's finest porcelain. Which town is it?
context: Jingdezhen, in Jiangxi province, has produced porcelain for over 1,000 years and is called China's 'Porcelain Capital.' The French Jesuit Pere d'Entrecolles wrote in 1712 that arriving at night, 'one thinks that the whole city is on fire, or that it is one large furnace with many vent holes.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen; gotheborg.com (Letters of Pere d'Entrecolles).  (Legend.)

question: So much porcelain reached Europe from Jingdezhen's kilns that English speakers named the ware after the Asian country it came from, and by the 1650s the name had shrunk to one short everyday word. What is that word?
context: English called porcelain 'China dishes' in the 1570s, 'China-ware' by the 1630s, and simply 'china' by the 1650s -- the ware named for the land it came from. Source: etymonline.com/word/china; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcelain.

question: When Jingdezhen's porcelain reached Europe, Italians gave it the name porcellana, after a glossy little seashell that its shiny surface brought to mind, and English took the word porcelain from it. Which shell gave porcelain its name?
context: In Italian, porcellana meant a cowrie shell; the smooth, glassy surface of the new ware resembled the shell, so the glossy porcelain borrowed its name. Source: etymonline.com/word/porcelain; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcelain.

question: Jingdezhen's potters gave their porcelain its pure white body with a special clay dug from a nearby hill known as High Ridge. Potters everywhere now call this white clay by a word taken straight from the hill's own name. Which clay is it?
context: The clay is kaolin, and its name comes straight from the hill: the Chinese called it Gaoling -- gaolingtu, 'High Ridge earth' -- a hill and village near Jingdezhen. The word reached English in 1727 through Pere d'Entrecolles' 1712 report, and the mineral kaolinite was later named from it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaolinite.  (Legend.)

question: Boats carried Jingdezhen's porcelain away from the town, because the brittle ware could not survive a jolting overland cart ride. The town had fine clay, porcelain stone and pine forests for kiln fuel all close by. On which river did Jingdezhen float its porcelain to the world?
context: Jingdezhen sits on the Chang River, whose boats carried the brittle porcelain far more safely than jolting carts could. The town also lay beside China's finest porcelain-stone deposits and was ringed by pine forests for kiln fuel -- clay, stone, fuel, and a river, all in one place. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen_porcelain.

question: For years European potters tried and failed to copy Jingdezhen porcelain. Without the right white clay, their pieces slumped and cracked in the kiln. A Jingdezhen merchant told the French priest d'Entrecolles they had left out half of what porcelain needs, comparing its two raw materials to two parts of a living body. Which pair?
context: Chinese potters called kaolin clay the 'bones' of porcelain and the ground porcelain-stone its 'flesh.' The merchant said Europeans failed because they tried to make 'a body in which the flesh would be supported without bones' -- plenty of stone, but no kaolin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen; gotheborg.com (d'Entrecolles).  (Legend.)

question: At Jingdezhen the emperor kept a private imperial kiln of his own, and one painted design belonged to him alone. Under the Qing, it is said, a painter who put it on porcelain for anyone else could be killed along with his whole family. What was the emperor's design?
context: The five-clawed dragon signified the emperor himself: under the Yuan, five claws marked the emperor and four marked princes, and by the Ming, using the five-clawed dragon outside the imperial circle counted as treason. The tale of a painter executed with his family is a traditional account. Source: sothebys.com (Enter the Dragon); taliesinantiques.com.  (Legend.)

question: Jingdezhen's potters knew their white clay would not hold together in the fire on its own, so they mixed it with a second local rock that melts into glass in the kiln and fuses everything into hard-paste porcelain. The town sat right beside the finest deposits of that rock in all the land. What is it called?
context: The second ingredient is petuntse, also called China stone or porcelain stone; fired with kaolin at very high heat, it supplies what the clay lacks to form true hard-paste porcelain. Jingdezhen's nearby deposits were the finest in China. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen_porcelain.

question: The Ming court sent Jingdezhen a single order in 1433 for porcelain painted with dragons and phoenixes, not to sell but purely to give away as gifts to officials and foreign envoys. The number of pieces demanded in that one order was staggering. About how many did it call for?
context: A single 1433 imperial order called for 443,500 pieces of Jingdezhen porcelain in dragon-and-phoenix designs, all destined as court and diplomatic gifts -- a glimpse of the imperial kilns' astonishing output. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen_porcelain.

question: Zhenzong, the Song emperor, so loved the thin white porcelain of Jingdezhen around 1004 that he had pieces stamped with something of his own and renamed the whole town after it. Most Chinese towns take their names from a river, a mountain or a compass direction, so Jingdezhen is a rare exception. After what did he name the town?
context: Emperor Zhenzong's 'Jingde' era ran 1004-1007. Enchanted by the local ware, he ordered pieces marked 'made in the Jingde period' and changed the town's name from Changnanzhen to Jingde-zhen -- 'Jingde town' -- a rare Chinese city named for an emperor's reign-title. Source: kupi.com (Jingdezhen history); chano-yu.com.  (Legend.)

question: Père d'Entrecolles, a French Jesuit living beside Jingdezhen's kilns, sent home in 1712 the first full description to reach the West of a recipe that European kings had spent fortunes for two centuries trying to learn. They gave that guarded formula a mysterious, magical-sounding name, as if it were a wizard's spell. What did Europeans call this secret?
context: Europe called the porcelain secret the 'Arcanum.' d'Entrecolles mailed the first detailed Western account of Jingdezhen's methods in 1712 (a second letter followed in 1722), spreading the recipe and later helping found France's Sevres works. Germany's Meissen had in fact already achieved hard-paste porcelain around 1708-10 using local kaolin, so the letters did not give Europe its first porcelain -- they revealed the recipe to the wider West. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francois_Xavier_d'Entrecolles; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain.

question: Climbers on K2, high on the Pakistan-China border, face a peak steeper and colder than taller Everest, and it kills them far more often. George Bell, a climber on the American expedition of 1953, gave it a chilling nickname that stuck. What nickname did Bell give K2?
context: American climber George Bell coined the 'Savage Mountain' nickname after the 1953 expedition, saying, 'It's a savage mountain that tries to kill you.' At 8,611 m (28,251 ft), K2 stands second only to Everest's 8,849 m, rising in the Karakoram range on the China–Pakistan border. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: K2, on the Pakistan-China border, stands too remote to have earned a common local name, while peaks such as Annapurna and Nanga Parbat keep names passed down for centuries. Its label is not a word in any language and means nothing in the tongues of the people who live nearest it. Where does 'K2' come from?
context: In 1856 the British surveyor Thomas Montgomerie, working on the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, labelled the Karakoram peaks K1, K2, K3 and so on — the 'K' standing for Karakoram. K1 later reverted to its local Balti name, Masherbrum, but K2 sat so deep in the range that no common local name reached the mapmakers, so the survey code stuck. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: Hundreds of climbers stand on top of Everest each year, and few of them die trying. K2, the second-highest peak, on the Pakistan-China border, kept a far darker tally for decades. About how many climbers reached its summit for every one who died on the mountain?
context: For decades K2 counted roughly one death for every four climbers who reached its top, a fatality rate above 20%, which is why the peak, not taller Everest, earns its dread; the ratio has fallen as more climbers have summited in recent years. By comparison, Annapurna is usually ranked the deadliest 8,000er by death-to-summit ratio, historically closer to one in three. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: Near the very top of K2 lies the most feared stretch in all of mountaineering: a short but brutally steep gully of snow and ice that every summit climber must cross. Worse, it sits right below a wall of hanging ice cliffs, called seracs, that can break loose without warning. What is this dreaded passage on K2 called?
context: The Bottleneck, a couloir around 8,200 m, funnels climbers directly under a band of hanging seracs. On 1–2 August 2008, a serac collapse there sheared the fixed ropes and eleven climbers died — K2's worst single disaster. Lower on the mountain lie other named cruxes like House's Chimney and the Black Pyramid. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: K2 threw back climber after climber until 31 July 1954, when an Italian team led by the geologist Ardito Desio finally put two men on the summit. The route they cut that day proved so reliable that most climbers have followed the same line up K2 ever since. What is this classic route called?
context: Italians Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli reached the summit on 31 July 1954 via the Abruzzi Spur, on the expedition led by geologist Ardito Desio. The ascent stayed controversial because support climber Walter Bonatti and porter Amir Mehdi were forced to bivouac in the open above 8,000 m. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2

question: During a fierce storm high on K2 in 1953, an American team was struggling to lower a desperately sick teammate when six roped-together climbers slipped at once and began sliding toward a deadly plunge. In a heartbeat, one of them, Pete Schoening, stopped the whole falling chain with a single move that mountaineers still speak of simply as 'The Belay.' How did Schoening save all six?
answer: wedged his ice axe behind a rock
choices: looped the rope around his shoulders
wedged his ice axe behind a rock
caught the rope with his bare hands
anchored them with a tent stake
context: Pete Schoening braced a single ice axe behind a boulder and held all six of his roped teammates during the 1953 American expedition's storm-battered retreat — a save mountaineers still simply call 'The Belay.' The sick climber they were lowering, Art Gilkey, was later swept away and died. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2  (Legend.)

question: Ten climbers stood together on the frozen summit of K2 on 16 January 2021, singing their national anthem. For decades the mountain had thrown back every winter attempt in cold near minus 40 and hurricane winds, the one 8,000-metre peak nobody had climbed in winter. Whose team made this first winter ascent of K2?
context: The ten Nepali climbers deliberately regrouped about ten metres below the top so that no one would be first, then stepped onto the summit together while singing Nepal's national anthem. The team was led by Nirmal 'Nimsdai' Purja and Mingma Gyalje Sherpa; of the ten, only Purja climbed without supplemental oxygen. Sources: https://www.planetmountain.com/en/news/alpinism/k2-nepalese-mountaineers-claim-historic-first-winter-ascent.html ; https://www.ukclimbing.com/news/2021/01/first_winter_ascent_of_k2_made_by_all-nepali_team-72688

question: A former shrine dancer named Izumo no Okuni led an all-female troupe in a wild new dance-drama around 1603, out in the open on the dry, pebbled bed of a river running through Kyoto. It grew into kabuki, Japan's theatre of painted faces. On which river's dry bed did kabuki first take shape?
context: The river is the Kamo (Kamo-gawa), and the exact spot — its wide, dry, pebbled bed in central Kyoto — is remembered as the Shijogawara. There, around 1603, Izumo no Okuni, a former miko (shrine maiden) by tradition linked to the great Izumo Taisha shrine, drew crowds with a flashy, avant-garde dance-drama that grew into kabuki. In a famous irony, the theatre a woman founded on this riverbed would ban women within a generation and become entirely male. The other choices are real rivers of the Kyoto region: the Kamo, Katsura, and Uji all feed the Yodo River system. Source: Grokipedia 'Kabuki'; Wikipedia 'Kabuki'.

question: Flashy young rebels called the kabukimono swaggered through the streets of Kyoto and Edo in the early 1600s in mismatched clothes, defying every custom, and kabuki takes its name from them. Their nickname grew from an old Japanese verb, kabuku. What did kabuku first mean?
context: The verb kabuku literally meant to tilt or lean off-center, and from it came kabukimono — roughly 'the tilted, crooked ones' — a nickname for the outrageously dressed show-offs of the early 1600s who flouted every rule of proper dress. Only later were the three kanji 歌 (song), 舞 (dance), 伎 (skill) chosen to write 'kabuki' — a clever phonetic fit that also happens to describe the art. Source: Grokipedia 'Kabuki'; Wikipedia 'Kabuki'.

question: At the most thrilling moment of a kabuki play in Edo, or old Tokyo, the hero suddenly slams to a halt, with every muscle locked, one foot stamped down, and both eyes crossed hard toward the nose. He holds the statue-still pose while a fan in the crowd bellows out his stage-name. What is this frozen, cross-eyed climax pose called?
context: The frozen pose is the mie; the crossed-eye glare freezes a moment of peak emotion (and, by tradition, wards off evil). As the actor holds it, a devoted fan shouts his stage-name — a cry called kakegoe. The mie and the bold makeup style were pioneered by the great actor Ichikawa Danjuro I (1660–1704). keren are spectacular stage tricks and chunori is 'flying' on wires above the crowd; aragoto is Edo's bombastic superhuman-hero style. Source: Grokipedia 'Kabuki'; Wikipedia 'Kabuki'.

question: Namiki Shozo, an Osaka playwright, built a bold new device into the kabuki stage around 1758, in a city whose theatres kept outdoing one another with new stage machinery. Western stages would not copy it for more than a century, and playhouses worldwide still use it today. What did he add to the Osaka stage?
answer: the mawari-butai, a giant revolving turntable
choices: the mawari-butai, a giant revolving turntable
the hanamichi, a raised walkway into the crowd
the seri, a set of trapdoor stage elevators
the chunori, a rig for flying actors on wires
context: The device is the mawari-butai (revolving stage), a giant turntable set into the stage floor and credited to the Osaka playwright Namiki Shozo around 1758 — the world's oldest revolving stage, predating similar machinery in Western theatres by well over a century, and still standard in playhouses today. Kabuki loved such spectacle: seri trapdoors lifted actors and whole sets up through the floor, chunori ('riding in the sky') hoisted an actor over the audience on wires, and the hanamichi was a raised walkway that carried actors dramatically through the crowd. But the spinning stage was Osaka's own. Source: Wikipedia 'Namiki Shozo I' & 'Revolving stage'; Playbill 'History of the Theatrical Turntable'; KABUKI WEB.

question: Kano, one of West Africa's oldest cities, guarded its trans-Saharan trade behind walls that ran about 11 miles around the town and rose as much as 30 feet high. King Gijimasu began them around 1100, and later kings built them taller. What were Kano's mighty walls built from?
context: The walls, called the Ganuwa in Hausa, were begun by Sarki (King) Gijimasu around 1095-1134 and extended by his successors over the following centuries. By 1851 the explorer Heinrich Barth recorded them as roughly 10-11 miles around and up to 30 feet high; after the British conquest in 1903, General Frederick Lugard said he had 'never seen anything like it in Africa.' Sources: Wikipedia, 'Ancient Kano City Walls' & 'Kano (city).'

question: In one corner of Kano, deep clay pits brim with near-black indigo, and cotton cloth has been dipped and re-dipped there by hand since around 1498 - the oldest indigo-dyeing pits still worked anywhere in Africa. These pits sit beside one of Kano's old city gates and take its name. Which gate is it?
context: The Kofar Mata dye pits are the oldest indigo-dyeing pits still in use in Africa: cloth has been coloured in the same clay pits for more than five centuries. (Wikipedia says 'more than 500 years'; the specific date of about 1498 comes from Kohan Textile Journal and other textile-trade sources.) The dye uses just three natural ingredients - indigo-plant leaves, wood ash, and potash - left to ferment in the pits for weeks. In its prime Kano had some 270 pits; only a few dozen still work today. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Kofar Mata Dye Pits'; Kohan Textile Journal.

question: King Muhammad Rumfa opened the Kurmi Market in Kano, on the southern edge of the Sahara, in the 1400s. Camels carried the city's goods across the desert to Timbuktu and beyond. What was Kano most prized for across the desert?
context: By 1851 Kano was exporting on the order of 10 million pairs of leather sandals and 5 million tanned hides a year, and its indigo cloth and leather reached as far as Timbuktu, Tripoli, Lake Chad, Morocco, and Europe. The Kurmi Market itself was established by the reforming king Muhammad Rumfa (reigned about 1463-1499). Source: Wikipedia, 'Kano (city).'

question: Karnak, the vast temple complex of Amun-Re at ancient Thebes, sprawls over more than two square kilometres on the east bank of the Nile in southern Egypt. Its own Egyptian builders gave it a proud name, Ipet-isut. What did that name mean to them?
choices: the House of a Million Years
the Horizon of the Two Lands
the Throne of the Rising Sun
context: 'Ipet-isut' means 'the Most Select of Places' — the ancient Egyptians' own boast that Karnak was the finest, holiest ground in all of Egypt. It stood at Thebes (modern Luxor) on the Nile's east bank, dedicated above all to Amun-Re, king of the gods. Source: discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple; Britannica /place/Karnak.

question: Egyptologists are so struck by Karnak's scale that they don't call it simply a temple. Beside the Nile at ancient Thebes it grew over two thousand years into the largest religious complex ever built, a walled spread of chapels, courts and gateways around a sacred lake of its own. What is Karnak often called?
context: Karnak is the largest religious complex ever built — a whole 'city of temples' that grew for two thousand years until it sprawled across more than 2 square kilometres. It is not one building but a walled expanse of temples, chapels, pylons, courts, and its own sacred lake, so vast that the single word 'temple' no longer fits it. Guinness World Records lists Karnak as the largest ancient Egyptian temple site. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com; discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple; britannica.com/place/Karnak.

question: A forest of 134 stone columns fills Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall, and down its central aisle stand twelve giants about 21 metres tall, as high as a six-storey building, their tops flaring open like blossoms. The twelve were carved to imitate a single plant that grew thick along the Nile. Which plant?
context: The twelve central columns of Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall stand about 21 m (69 ft) tall — a six- to seven-storey building — carved as papyrus stalks crowned with open-blossom tops. Papyrus was Egypt's own plant: it grew thick along the Nile, and its stalks were pressed into sheets to write on. The 122 shorter outer columns (roughly 10–15 m) wear closed papyrus-bud tops. At about 5,000 sq m, the hall is the largest room of any religious building in the ancient world. Source: memphis.edu/hypostyle; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnak.

question: Courts, pylons and halls piled up at Karnak over nearly two thousand years in clashing styles, their walls out of line, each generation of builders adding onto the last. No single plan ever guided them. Who were the builders who kept enlarging Karnak across twenty centuries?
answer: a long line of Egypt's pharaohs
choices: a long line of Egypt's pharaohs
the temple's guild of master masons
context: About thirty different pharaohs added to Karnak between roughly 2000 BCE (the Middle Kingdom) and 204 BCE (the Ptolemies) — nearly two thousand years. No king ever declared it finished; each simply built onto, or right over, the work of the one before. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnak; discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple.

question: For the great festivals, priests carried the god Amun's statue out of Karnak in a slow procession, down a broad avenue guarded on both sides by more than a thousand stone sphinxes with the heads of rams. Where did this Avenue of Sphinxes lead?
context: The Avenue of Sphinxes — the 'Rams' Road' — ran about 2.7 km from Karnak south to Luxor Temple, lined by over 1,000 sphinxes; the ram-headed ones honoured Amun, whose sacred animal was the ram. Buried for centuries, it was re-excavated and reopened on 25 November 2021 with a torch-lit pharaonic parade through Luxor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_of_Sphinxes; timesofisrael.com.

question: Beside the temples at Karnak lies a great rectangular stone-lined lake, about 120 metres long, its water rising from the Nile's own water table. Each day, before performing the god's rituals, the temple's priests walked down its steps. What did they do there?
answer: bathed to purify themselves for ritual
choices: bathed to purify themselves for ritual
launched boats bearing the god's statue
drew the drinking water for the city
washed the temple's fine linen robes
context: Karnak's Sacred Lake — about 120 m by 77 m and 4 m deep, the largest at any Egyptian temple — was dug on the orders of the warrior-pharaoh Thutmose III. Priests bathed in its water to purify themselves before serving the god. The fallen half of Hatshepsut's broken obelisk now lies on the ground nearby. Source: madainproject.com/karnak_sacred_lake; discoveringegypt.com/karnak-temple/karnak-temple-sacred-lake.

question: Queen Hatshepsut had an obelisk almost 30 metres tall hauled 200 km down the Nile from the pink granite pits at Aswan to Karnak, where it still stands, the tallest ancient obelisk upright in Egypt. From how much stone was this 300-tonne pink needle cut?
answer: a single unbroken block of granite
choices: a single unbroken block of granite
a granite shell over a brick core
context: Hatshepsut's obelisk at Karnak — about 29–30 m tall and over 300 tonnes — was cut from ONE block of pink Aswan granite, floated downriver, and raised upright: the tallest ancient obelisk still standing in Egypt. Its twin broke and now lies on its side near the Sacred Lake. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precinct_of_Amun-Re; exploreluxor.org/hatshepsut-obelisk.

question: Karnak's builders never finished its grandest gateway, the First Pylon, a pair of sloping stone towers 113 metres wide. Against its inner wall they left behind the very thing they had used to lift massive stone blocks dozens of metres into the air. What still stands there today?
answer: a long ramp of mud brick
choices: a long ramp of mud brick
a crane of rope and timber
a spiral of carved stone steps
context: Karnak's First Pylon — about 113 m wide and 43 m high, the largest pylon in Egypt — was never completed. Against its inner face the builders' great mud-brick construction ramp still stands: workers dragged the huge stones up such earthen ramps to build ever higher, then removed them when the job was done. Here, the work unfinished, the ramp was simply left behind. Source: madainproject.com/first_pylon_karnak_temple; digitalkarnak.ucsc.edu/1st-pylon.

question: Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall once lay in permanent twilight under its stone roof, a forest of giant columns, the tallest flaring open at the top like blossoming flowers. To the temple's priests, the whole shadowy hall stood for one watery place out of Egyptian myth. Which one?
answer: the marsh where the creator-god first rose from the water
choices: the marsh where the creator-god first rose from the water
the field of reeds where the blessed dead lived forever
the papyrus swamp where the infant Horus hid from Seth
the underworld river the sun-god sailed each night
context: The papyrus columns — the twelve central ones opening like blossoms — turned the hall into a stone image of the primeval marsh: the watery chaos of Nun from which the creator-god Atum first rose on the mound of creation at the beginning of the world. Colossal 70-tonne stone architraves once roofed it over, keeping it in permanent twilight, like a real marsh at dusk. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hypostyle_Hall.

question: Workers digging in one of Karnak's courtyards in 1903 broke through into a deep hidden pit. Inside lay a staggering hoard that the temple's own priests had buried there in ancient times, then sealed away and forgotten. What had they hidden underground?
answer: a mass of stone and bronze statues
choices: a mass of stone and bronze statues
a chest of gold and silver
a tomb of the high priests' mummies
context: Karnak's 'Cachette' — a pit in the Cachette Court opened in 1903 — held roughly 900 stone statues and many thousands of bronze figures. Over the centuries the temple filled with donated statues; rather than throw sacred images away, the priests reverently buried the old ones in this pit. It remains one of the greatest single finds of Egyptian sculpture ever made. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precinct_of_Amun-Re.

question: Weavers at their wooden looms in Ghana turn out bright strips of kente only about four inches wide, then sew them edge to edge into one broad cloth. Which town is the famous home of kente weaving?
context: Bonwire, in Ghana's Ashanti Region, has been the heart of kente weaving for centuries and is still one of West Africa's most important weaving centers. Each cloth is built from narrow strips, only about four inches wide, sewn edge to edge into one wide piece. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: The first kente weavers, deep in the Ghanaian forest, watched one small creature build with great care, an Ashanti legend says, and copied its work with silk and cotton. Its details vary from one teller to the next. Which creature does it say taught people to weave?
context: The trickster spider of Ashanti folklore is Anansi (Ananse), and tradition credits him with teaching people to weave. In the fuller tale, hunters watched a spider spin its web in the forest around 1720 and reproduced it at home. Because the story is passed down orally, the weavers' names change between tellings — it is remembered as legend, not fixed history. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: A Ghanaian weaver works kente in narrow strips of tight, interlaced weave; the cloth's older Akan name, nwentoma, means simply 'woven cloth'. The newer name is thought to come from the Akan word kenten, for a common household thing with the same tight, woven look. What is a kenten?
context: 'Kente' is thought to come from the Akan word kenten, 'basket,' because the cloth's tight, interlaced weave looks basket-like. The Asante's own older name for it, nwentoma, means simply 'woven cloth.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: Kings and queens of the Ashanti in Ghana wore robes stitched from kente's narrow, bright strips, and in kente every colour carries its own meaning. A band of black is no sign of mourning, as it might be elsewhere in the world. Among the Ashanti, what does black cloth stand for?
context: In kente's language of color, every shade carries meaning: gold for royalty and wealth, blue for peace and harmony, green for growth and renewal, red for the blood of the ancestors, and black for maturity and the ancestral spirits. A cloth can be 'read' as much as worn. (Source: explorekumasi.com/history-and-symbolism-of-kente)

question: Opoku Ware I, the Asantehene, founded a royal weaving workshop in the 1700s, and at his court in Kumasi only kings and chiefs could wear the richest kente. A great chief wore his cloth in one customary way. How was a chief's kente traditionally worn?
answer: Over one shoulder, like a toga
choices: Over one shoulder, like a toga
Wound around the head as a turban
Tied at the waist as a skirt
Draped over the head as a veil
context: Kente was long reserved for royalty. In the 1700s the Asantehene Opoku Ware I set up a weaving workshop to develop the craft, and only kings and chiefs could wear the richest cloths — draped over one shoulder, toga-style. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: A master weaver in Ghana's Ashanti Region dares to give a cloth the name Adweneasa only once in a great while. It belongs to the most intricate kente of all, woven with extra heddles on its loom, and it commands the very highest price. Translated from the Akan, what boast does the name make?
context: Adweneasa means roughly 'I have exhausted my skill' — the name a master weaver gives a cloth only when he has poured every technique he knows into it. The most decorated of all kente patterns, it needs extra heddles on the loom and commands the highest price. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth)

question: Ghana's first leader, Kwame Nkrumah, was not himself Ashanti, yet when the country won its independence in 1957 he chose the royal Ashanti cloth, kente, to stand for the whole new nation. In 1960 he presented a kente cloth to hang inside one of the world's most famous buildings, where a version still hangs today. Which building received it?
context: Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's first leader after independence in 1957, was not himself Asante, but he chose kente to represent the whole new nation. In 1960 he gave a kente cloth to hang at the United Nations in New York (a replacement still hangs there), helping make kente a worldwide symbol of African heritage and pride. (Source: npr.org/sections/goatsandsoda/2020/06/11)

question: Minnesota calls itself the Land of 10,000 Lakes, though the real count is 11,842. Most are small round ponds that a huge ice sheet left dotted across the plains as it melted back, about 12,000 years ago. Each of them has one odd trait that most lakes on Earth lack. What is that trait?
answer: It has no river flowing in or out.
choices: It has no river flowing in or out.
It fills the crater of an extinct volcano.
It is saltier than the open sea.
It is a thin ribbon in a mountain valley.
context: Minnesota's slogan says '10,000,' but the counted tally of lakes at least 10 acres in size is 11,842 — hollows the retreating Wisconsin ice sheet, in places over a kilometer thick, left as it pulled back roughly 12,000 years ago. The tell of these ice-born ponds is that no river feeds them and none drains them; they fill with rain and groundwater alone. Source: Geography of Minnesota; Kettle (landform), Wikipedia.

question: Thousands of small round ponds, no more than 10 metres deep, dot the plains of Minnesota. They were left behind about 12,000 years ago, at the end of the last ice age, as a giant continental glacier slowly melted back across the whole region. How does such a pond form?
answer: A block of buried glacier ice melts and the ground over it caves in.
choices: A block of buried glacier ice melts and the ground over it caves in.
A looping river bend gets cut off and stranded as a curved pond.
Groundwater dissolves the limestone below until the surface sinks in.
A meteor slams down and punches a round crater into the plain.
context: This collapse pit is called a KETTLE — literally the footprint of a melted ice block. As the glacier that dimpled Minnesota pulled back, meltwater streams buried a stranded block of 'dead ice' under sand and gravel; when it finally thawed, the ground heaped on top slumped into a rounded, riverless basin. The other three make real lakes too — an oxbow from a cut-off river bend, a sinkhole pond in dissolving limestone, a crater from a meteor — but none is born from buried ice. Source: Kettle (landform), Wikipedia.

question: Henry David Thoreau built his cabin on the north shore of Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts, in 1845. The pond is small and steep-sided and plunges over 100 feet deep, its water so clear that Thoreau imagined a hidden spring feeding it from the bottom. What kind of lake is Walden Pond?
context: Walden Pond covers about 64.5 acres yet plunges to roughly 102 feet - a small, steep-sided kettle that a buried glacier block left about 10,000 to 12,000 years ago. With no inlet or outlet, Thoreau guessed a hidden bottom spring fed its famously clear water. Source: Walden Pond, Wikipedia.

question: Two lobes of the great ice sheet met in Wisconsin's Kettle Moraine, and the same vanished ice that left its pits also heaped up the opposite landform right beside them: rounded mounds of sand and gravel, some standing 300 feet above the lakes. What are these glacial mounds called?
context: The Kettle Moraine formed where two great tongues of the Laurentide Ice Sheet met - the Green Bay Lobe on the west and the Lake Michigan Lobe on the east - dumping sediment between them. Its kettles hold water from 3 to 200 feet deep, while kames of piled gravel rise as much as 300 feet above them: pits and mounds from the very same ice. Source: Kettle Moraine, Wikipedia.

question: More than half of North America's migrating ducks and geese hatch in a huge belt of shallow, round ponds that stretches from the Dakotas up into Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, which is why the region is nicknamed the duck factory. What are these ponds called?
context: This belt of glacial kettle wetlands - the Prairie Pothole Region - spreads across roughly 800,000 square kilometers of the northern Great Plains. Though it holds only about a tenth of the continent's waterfowl breeding habitat by area, more than half of North America's migratory waterfowl hatch among its potholes, earning it the nickname 'the duck factory.' Source: Prairie Pothole Region, Wikipedia.

question: Silk Road merchants heading west stopped at Khiva, an oasis city ringed by tall mud walls in Uzbekistan, to top up their water skins and feed their camels one last time. Beyond its western gate lay a brutal 400-km slog across shifting sand dunes toward Persia. Which desert did they have to cross?
context: Khiva was the final fortified stop before the Karakum ('black sand') desert crossing to Persia (Iran) on the Silk Road. The Kyzylkum lies the other way, toward Bukhara; the Taklamakan and Gobi are far to the east, in China and Mongolia. Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/543/

question: Muhammad Amin Khan meant his wide, blue-and-green-tiled tower in Khiva to be the tallest minaret in the Muslim world, yet it stops at just 29 metres, and its name, Kalta Minor, means 'short'. Why did the tower never rise to its planned height?
choices: an earthquake sheared off its top
the soft ground could bear no more
the royal treasury ran out of money
context: Muhammad Amin Khan began the Kalta Minor in 1851, intending a minaret of 70-80 m (legend says 110 m); when he was killed in 1855, the work simply stopped and was never resumed. 'Kalta' means 'short,' and its turquoise majolica is said to be 'still as bright as in 1855.' Khiva's tallest FINISHED tower is the later Islam Khodja minaret (1908-10), about 57 m — nearly double the stubby Kalta Minor. Sources: https://www.advantour.com/uzbekistan/khiva/kalta-minor.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaltaminor

question: Only a few shafts of daylight light the low, dim hall of Khiva's Djuma, or Friday, Mosque, which has a flat roof instead of the tiled domes and towering arches of most great Central Asian mosques. What fills the whole interior and holds up that flat roof?
answer: a forest of carved wooden columns
choices: a forest of carved wooden columns
a grid of ancient granite piers
a cage of riveted iron beams
a rank of glazed brick pillars
context: The Djuma Mosque's flat roof rests on a forest of about 212 carved wooden columns set in 17 rows, each cut from karagach (black elm). Roughly 25 are ancient (10th-16th centuries) and four date to the 10th-11th century — over a thousand years old. The mosque was founded in the 10th century and rebuilt in 1788-89. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juma_Mosque,_Khiva ; https://www.orexca.com/uzbekistan/khiva/juma_mosque.htm

question: Mosques, madrasas, minarets, palaces and tombs stand shoulder to shoulder inside the walls of Khiva's Itchan Kala, a town just 650 by 400 metres across. Most old towns have one great church or palace that people line up to see. About how many old monuments are packed into this one?
context: Within its walls Itchan Kala packs over 50 historic monuments — about 20 mosques, 20 madrasas and 6 minarets, plus palaces and mausoleums — alongside some 250 old houses (mostly 18th-19th century), so complete that the whole town looks frozen in time. UNESCO calls it 'a coherent and well-preserved example of the Muslim architecture of Central Asia.' Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/543/

question: A huge snowcapped volcano lifts its head above the flat plains of northeast Tanzania, near the Kenyan border, almost 6,000 metres high: Kilimanjaro. Trekkers from all over the world spend a week walking up to its summit, Uhuru Peak, the Roof of Africa. Of all the mountains on Earth, what record does Kilimanjaro hold?
choices: the tallest peak in the tropics
context: Kilimanjaro isn't the highest mountain on Earth (Everest wins that), but because it stands alone and rises about 4,600 m straight from the plains, it's the tallest free-standing mountain in the world -- one giant, not a peak in a crowded range. Source: andbeyond.com/destinations/africa/tanzania/kilimanjaro; climbing-kilimanjaro.com/interesting-kilimanjaro-facts.

question: Safari-goers in one Kenyan wildlife park regularly photograph elephants and zebras with the snowy peak of Kilimanjaro, Africa's tallest mountain, floating in the sky behind them across the border in Tanzania. Which park is it?
context: Amboseli National Park in southern Kenya is famous for exactly this view: flat, dusty plains with snow-topped Kilimanjaro -- actually across the border in Tanzania -- floating on the horizon. Source: amboseli.ke/mount-kilimanjaro-the-majestic-backdrop-of-amboseli-national-park; earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/2720/mount-kilimanjaro-tanzania.

question: Heat bakes the savanna below Kilimanjaro all year long, where thorny acacias dot the dry plains and lions and elephants roam, for the mountain stands almost right on the equator. Yet trekkers who climb for a week to its summit, Uhuru Peak, find it always covered by what?
context: Kilimanjaro's summit sits only about 3 degrees south of the equator, yet Uhuru Peak wears permanent glaciers and snow -- ice in the tropics, high enough that it never fully melts. Source: education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/kilimanjaro; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro.

question: Climbers on Uhuru Peak, the Roof of Africa, stand 5,895 metres up on the youngest and tallest of the three volcanic cones that built Kilimanjaro, in northeast Tanzania. Time has worn the two older cones down into jagged spires and a flat plateau. What is the name of this tallest cone?
context: Kibo is the youngest, tallest cone and holds Uhuru Peak; jagged Mawenzi (5,149 m) is extinct and, unlike Kibo's walk-up, a technical rock climb; old Shira collapsed long ago into a flat plateau. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro; climbmountkilimanjaro.com/about-the-mountain/location-geology-appearance.

question: Hans Meyer, a German geographer, made the first ascent of Kilimanjaro in 1889 and gave its highest point a grand German name. When Tanganyika won its freedom in 1961, the peak was renamed Uhuru, Swahili for 'freedom.' What had Meyer first named the Roof of Africa?
context: After his 1889 ascent, Hans Meyer named the summit 'Kaiser Wilhelm Peak' for the German emperor. When Tanganyika (now Tanzania) won independence in 1961, Lt. Alexander Nyirenda climbed up and lit the Uhuru ('freedom') Torch on the roof of Africa, and the peak became Uhuru Peak. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_Torch; ultimatekilimanjaro.com/the-true-meaning-of-uhuru-peak.

question: Richard Reusch, a missionary pastor, found the body of a leopard near the frozen summit of Kilimanjaro in 1926, a leopard that had somehow wandered that high. Even after years lying near the top it had not rotted away, and Ernest Hemingway later wove the strange find into a famous short story. Up in the harsh, freezing, thin summit air, what had happened to the leopard's body?
answer: it had freeze-dried into a mummy
choices: it had frozen inside a glacier
it had freeze-dried into a mummy
context: Pastor Richard Reusch found the freeze-dried leopard at about 5,600 m on Kibo's rim; no one knows why it climbed so high (he guessed it chased a goat). Ernest Hemingway made it famous in 'The Snows of Kilimanjaro' (1936), and the spot is now called Leopard Point. Source: earthtouchnews.com/discoveries/discoveries/the-amazing-story-of-the-frozen-leopard-atop-mount-kilimanjaro; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Snows_of_Kilimanjaro_(short_story).  (Legend.)

question: Kilimanjaro's summit ice lived through a brutal global drought, its ice cores show: the same dry catastrophe that helped topple the Akkadian Empire in Mesopotamia. Climatologists have a formal name for this event. What is it called?
context: About 85% of the ice present in 1912 is gone. An ice core shows melting on this scale hasn't happened in roughly 11,700 years -- even that 300-year drought left the ice intact. Scientists project the cap could vanish around 2050, though the exact timing is debated. Source: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0906029106 (Thompson et al.); ultimatekilimanjaro.com/mount-kilimanjaros-glaciers-estimated-to-be-gone-by-2050.

question: Scientists pushed a probe just 30 cm beneath the floor of the inner crater on Kilimanjaro's highest cone, expecting frozen rock so near the icy 5,895-metre summit, and the reading stunned them. The summit looks dead and frozen, but that cone is only dormant, not extinct. What temperature did the probe find?
context: Nested inside Kibo's summit crater is the inner Reusch Crater, whose ash pit still steams with sulphurous fumaroles. A probe pushed just 30 cm under the crater floor read 78.5 C (173 F) -- scalding rock a stone's throw from the equator's highest ice. Kibo is not dead, only sleeping. Source: ultimatekilimanjaro.com/reusch-crater-the-ash-pit-on-kilimanjaro; markhorrell.com/blog/2017/a-brief-introduction-to-kilimanjaros-volcanic-crater.

question: Trekkers climbing Kilimanjaro rise through five climate zones in a single week, from tropical foothills at its base to an arctic summit far above. One belt partway up is unmistakable, studded with giant groundsels and giant lobelias, oversized plants that tower over the trail. Which of the mountain's five zones is this?
context: This is Kilimanjaro's heath and moorland zone, the belt famous for its giant groundsels and giant lobelias. It is one of five zones a climber crosses in a few days -- cultivated farmland (bananas, coffee, maize), tropical rainforest, heath and moorland, stark alpine desert, and the arctic summit -- so a single week's walk feels like traveling from the equator to the pole. Source: kilimanjaropark.org/climate-ecological-zones; climbing-kilimanjaro.com/mount-kilimanjaro-climate-zones.

question: Damp trade winds sweep in off the Indian Ocean and meet Kilimanjaro's broad southern flank, which drinks in 2,000 to 3,000 mm of rain a year and grows a dense belt of rainforest, even as the far higher summit stays a near-desert. Kilimanjaro is so vast it makes its own weather. What is this kind of rainfall called?
context: This is orographic rainfall: a mountain forces moist air upward until it cools and drops its water on the windward slope. Kilimanjaro's southern rainforest belt collects 2,000-3,000 mm a year, while the far higher summit -- in the mountain's own rain shadow -- gets barely 100 mm, mostly as snow. Source: altezzatravel.com/articles/kilimanjaro-climate-zones; ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5569136.

question: A small island off the coast of Tanzania, reachable only by boat, was no fishing village in the Middle Ages. It was one of the richest cities of the Indian Ocean, home to perhaps more than ten thousand people who traded African gold for Chinese porcelain. Which Swahili-coast island city was it?
context: Kilwa Kisiwani — the name means 'Kilwa on the island' in Swahili — sat on the southern Swahili coast of what is now Tanzania. From the 1100s to the 1400s it was the leading trading city of the East African coast, home to an estimated 10,000-plus people dealing in gold, ivory, and luxuries carried across the Indian Ocean. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kilwa Kisiwani'; Grokipedia (Kilwa Kisiwani).

question: Kilwa's Great Mosque and its cliff-top palace rise in neat grey blocks, cut and squared like any rock from a quarry. Builders up and down the Swahili coast, at Zanzibar and Lamu as at Kilwa, used the same signature stone. What were Kilwa's walls built from?
context: Swahili cities built in coral stone: blocks of coral limestone cut from the reef and squared into coursed masonry, often finished with a fine coral-lime plaster. Kilwa, Zanzibar's Stone Town and Lamu all share this pale coral stonework, the signature material of the East African coast. Source: Wikipedia, 'Great Mosque of Kilwa' and 'Kilwa Kisiwani'.

question: Sultan al-Hasan gave Kilwa's Great Mosque, one of the oldest still standing on the East African coast, a feature no building on that coast had had before, and it stayed the biggest of its kind there until the 1800s. The mosque had no open courtyard. What did the sultan raise over it?
context: The oldest sections of the Great Mosque date to the 11th-12th century; Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman added its great dome in the early 1300s. It was the first true dome raised on the East African coast and remained the largest dome on the coast until the 19th century; the traveller Ibn Battuta described the dome after his 1331 visit. Source: archnet.org/sites/3779; Wikipedia, 'Great Mosque of Kilwa'.

question: Kilwa had no gold mines of its own, yet it grew fabulously rich on gold. The secret was control of a single coastal harbour, the one place where all the gold carried out of the deep African interior reached the sea. Kilwa seized that harbour and taxed every shipment bound for Arabia and India. Which port made Kilwa the gatekeeper of African gold?
context: Sofala, on the coast of what is now Mozambique, was the outlet for gold mined in the far interior of southern Africa. Kilwa controlled Sofala and taxed the gold, ivory, and goods flowing through it toward Arabia and India — growing rich as the middleman without ever mining an ounce of gold itself. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kilwa Sultanate'.

question: Small copper coins turn up in the ruins of Kilwa, struck at the island's own mint from the 1100s onward. Each was stamped with the ruling sultan's name and one odd extra flourish. What did Kilwa's coins carry, besides the sultan's name, that almost no other coins of the age did?
answer: a line of Arabic rhyming verse
choices: a line of Arabic rhyming verse
the name of the mint town
context: Kilwa began minting its own coins in the 1100s under Sultan Ali bin al-Hasan — mostly copper, with occasional silver and gold — each inscribed with the ruling sultan's name and a short Arabic rhyming couplet. Very few sub-Saharan African cities struck their own coinage; Kilwa's mint marks how sophisticated and independent the city-state had become. Source: EBSCO Research Starters; CNG Coins; Numista Kilwa catalogue.

question: High on a cliff above the Indian Ocean at Kilwa stand the ruins of Husuni Kubwa, built by Sultan al-Hasan with more than a hundred rooms around sunken courtyards, said to be the largest building in all of sub-Saharan Africa before modern times. One of its luxuries still amazes visitors today. What did the sultan build into his cliff-top palace?
context: Husuni Kubwa ('the big fort/palace') was raised by Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman around 1310-1333 on a sandstone cliff over the sea. Its 100-plus rooms, sunken courtyards and octagonal bathing pool are said to have made it the largest building in sub-Saharan Africa before the modern era, and part of it doubled as a warehouse, with terraces and a staging area for loading goods onto trading ships. Source: archnet.org; worldhistory.org; Wikipedia, 'Kilwa Kisiwani'.

question: Ali ibn al-Hassan, a Persian prince from Shiraz, bought the site of Kilwa from its local king for enough coloured cloth to stretch all the way around it, Kilwa's founding legend says. When the king came back to reclaim his land, he could not reach it: the newcomers had done one thing that put Kilwa forever beyond him. What had they done?
answer: dug away the land bridge to the mainland
choices: dug away the land bridge to the mainland
burned every boat drawn up on the shore
walled off the whole neck of land
flooded the low approaches with seawater
context: The Kilwa Chronicle tells that Ali ibn al-Hassan of Shiraz bought the island for enough cloth to ring it, then — when the local king tried to take it back — the settlers had already dug away the land bridge, so Kilwa was now a true island beyond his reach. It is a founding legend, not documented history, but it captures how Kilwa's island setting protected its wealth. Source (legend): Wikipedia, 'Ali ibn al-Hassan Shirazi'; the Kilwa Chronicle.

question: Archaeologists digging in the ruins of a great kingdom deep in the African interior, hundreds of miles from any coast, pulled a copper coin from Kilwa's own mint out of the soil, hard proof of how far the little island port's trade reached across the continent. In whose ruins was the Kilwa coin found?
