context: At least one copper coin minted at Kilwa has been excavated at Great Zimbabwe (accounts give one or two), the dry-stone-walled kingdom of the southern African interior whose gold flowed down to the Swahili coast. The find is physical proof of a trade web binding a tiny Indian Ocean island to a kingdom hundreds of miles inland: gold flowing out to the coast, and Kilwa's own money carried back in. Source: Wikipedia, 'Kilwa Kisiwani'; Huffman (1972), cited at eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/142682; EBSCO Research Starters.

question: When a treasured tea bowl breaks in Japan, a mender can glue the pieces back together with tree-sap lacquer, then trace every crack with sparkling metal dust, so the old breaks shine as bright lines across the bowl. The craft is called kintsugi. Which metal does the classic kintsugi repair dust into the cracks?
context: Kintsugi means 'golden joinery' — kin, 'gold,' plus tsugi, 'joinery.' The shards are bonded with urushi, a lacquer tapped from a Japanese tree, and the seams are dusted or mixed with powdered gold so the repair is meant to be seen, not hidden — usually becoming the most striking feature of the whole piece. Gold isn't the only choice: silver dust makes a variant called gintsugi, and platinum is used too. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintsugi

question: A craftsman in old Japan could heal a broken tea bowl with kintsugi, piecing the shards together with tree-sap lacquer and fine metal dust, so the mended bowl came out crisscrossed with shining seams along every old crack. A rumour, legend rather than history, says some tea collectors loved these glowing seams too much. What were they said to do to their own perfect pots?
answer: smash them deliberately, shattering the perfect glaze
choices: smash them deliberately, shattering the perfect glaze
boil them fast so the sudden heat crazed the glaze
chill them in ice water until the glaze cracked through
bury them for a year so the damp soil crazed the glaze
context: This one is a LEGEND, not settled fact: some tea collectors were said to love gold-mended pottery so much that they deliberately smashed prized pieces just to have them repaired with glittering seams. It fits the Japanese ideas behind kintsugi — wabi-sabi, the beauty found in imperfect and impermanent things, and mottainai, a hatred of waste — where a bowl's break becomes part of its story and makes it more treasured, not less. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintsugi

question: Ashikaga Yoshimasa, a shogun who ruled Japan in the 1400s, had a favourite Chinese tea bowl, and when it cracked he sent it back to China for mending, one old story says, hoping craftsmen there could return it as beautiful as before. It came home mended, but the fix was so ugly that it pushed Japan to invent a lovelier way, the craft of kintsugi. In the story, how had the Chinese repaired the bowl?
answer: clamped back together with metal staples
choices: filled in with a plug of coarse gray clay
clamped back together with metal staples
sealed under a thick, mismatched glaze
bound along the crack with waxed cord
context: This origin tale is a LEGEND, not documented history. As the story goes, in the late 1400s the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa sent a cracked tea bowl to China for a fix, and it returned merely clamped with ugly metal staples — so Japanese craftsmen sought a lovelier mend, and gold-lacquer kintsugi grew from that. A real bowl sits behind the legend: the 13th-century 'Bakohan' celadon tea bowl, sent to China for a replacement, came home fastened with big metal staples said to look like a locust — and it was prized more for them. It still wears those staples today in the Tokyo National Museum. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintsugi

question: Knossos rose on the island of Crete around 1900 BC, the grandest palace of Bronze Age Europe and home to thousands of people. Later Greeks wove the whole palace into their most famous legend. What did they remember Knossos as?
context: Knossos was the largest building of Minoan Crete, first built around 1900 BC and home to tens of thousands of people. Its floor plan of some 1,300 interconnecting rooms across as many as five floors so bewildered later Greeks that they reworked the palace itself into the legend of the Labyrinth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knossos.

question: The stone ruins of Knossos stand on the Greek island of Crete, more than 3,000 years old, where Greek legend places the palace of King Minos. In the story, Minos kept a fearsome beast caged deep in a twisting maze under the palace, so tangled that no one sent in ever found the way back out. Which monster lurked there?
context: The Minotaur -- a monster with a bull's head on a man's body -- was said to be caged in the labyrinth King Minos had his architect Daedalus build beneath the palace. Source: knossos-palace.gr/2023/08/24/the-myth-of-theseus-and-the-minotaur/.  (Legend.)

question: Theseus, the hero of the Greek legend, sailed from Athens to Crete to go down into the winding depths under Knossos and kill the monster caged there, though no one sent in had ever found the way back out. Princess Ariadne, the king's daughter, gave him one thing so he could trace his path and escape. What did she give him?
context: Theseus unspooled 'Ariadne's thread' as he went in, slew the Minotaur, then followed the thread back out to safety -- the thread that saved the hero. Source: knossos-palace.gr/2023/08/24/the-myth-of-theseus-and-the-minotaur/.  (Legend.)

question: Poseidon, the sea god, punished King Minos of Knossos by cursing his queen, the old Cretan legend says. Queen Pasiphae was driven into a wild, unnatural love for one particular animal that Poseidon had sent up out of the sea. A monster was born of it, half human and half beast. What animal did Pasiphae fall in love with?
context: In the myth, Queen Pasiphae's unnatural love for a white bull produced the Minotaur -- a monster with a bull's head and a man's body. To feed it, King Minos forced conquered Athens to send seven youths and seven maidens to Crete as tribute, until the hero Theseus killed the beast and ended the toll. Source: greekmyths-greekmythology.com (myth of Theseus and the Minotaur).  (Legend.)

question: Minoan artists at Knossos, on Crete, painted a bright fresco around 1450 BC that froze three young athletes mid-motion in a real and risky sport with a live, charging bull. Archaeologists found it on a wall of the ruined palace. What were the athletes doing in the scene?
choices: wrestling the bull to the ground
sacrificing the bull at an altar
context: Minoan painters used a strict color code -- men shown dark reddish-brown, women pale white -- so in this Bull-Leaping (Taureador) Fresco the two pale figures gripping the bull's horns and tail are women, and the dark figure vaulting its back is a youth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bull-Leaping_Fresco.

question: Sleek sea animals curve through the water, surrounded by darting little fish, on a bright blue fresco in the queen's rooms at Knossos, the great palace of Bronze Age Crete. It is one of the loveliest Minoan wall paintings to survive. Which sea animals star in this famous Knossos fresco?
context: The Dolphin Fresco decorated the Queen's Megaron (the royal apartments) -- leaping dolphins and small fish across the wall, one of the most charming images in all Minoan art. Source: odysseyadventures.ca (Knossos, Royal Apartments).

question: Archaeologists in the ruins of Knossos, the great Minoan palace on Crete, found one shape carved into the stone walls again and again. Later Greeks told stories of a Labyrinth there that trapped a monster, and many scholars now think the very word Labyrinth grew from the old Minoan name for this one symbol. Which symbol covers the walls?
context: The double axe was called 'labrys,' and 'Labyrinth' probably meant 'House of the Double Axe' -- so the palace's very name may come from the axe-marks carved on its stones. Source: worldhistory.org/Minoan_Civilization/.

question: The Minoans piped fresh water through Knossos in clay pipes nearly 3,700 years ago, and the pipes ran clear and never clogged, a feat Europe would not match for thousands of years. They managed it with one odd design choice. How was each clay pipe shaped where it joined the next?
choices: sealed with lead at each joint
pierced with holes at each joint
context: The narrowing sped the water up -- like a thumb over a hose -- and the faster flow scoured out sediment so the pipes never clogged. Source: toilet-guru.com/minoan/; goworldtravel.com/crete-palace-of-knossos/.

question: Diggers in the queen's rooms at Knossos found what may be Europe's oldest example of a fixture still found in homes today, built into the palace about 3,700 years ago with its own drain to the palace sewer, more than a thousand years before Rome. What was this fixture?
context: The seat sat over a drain to the sewer and was flushed by pouring in a jug of water -- what may be Europe's oldest flushing toilet, engineered roughly 3,700 years ago, over a millennium before Rome's aqueducts. Source: goworldtravel.com/crete-palace-of-knossos/.

question: Deep within Knossos survives the Throne Room, where a single carved gypsum seat still stands against the wall where the Minoans set it more than 3,000 years ago -- the oldest stone throne in all of Europe. Painted on the plaster to either side, a pair of guardian beasts sit facing it, watching over whoever once took the seat. Which creatures flank the throne of Knossos?
context: The gypsum throne is flanked by painted griffins -- mythical beasts with a lion's body and an eagle's head -- and is the oldest stone throne in Europe. Sir Arthur Evans called it King Minos's throne, but most archaeologists now think the room was sacred, used in 'epiphany' rituals in which a High Priestess appeared in the role of the goddess. Source: greekreporter.com (the mystery of the oldest throne in Europe at Knossos).

question: Sir Arthur Evans did not simply uncover Knossos: between 1905 and 1930 he rebuilt whole sections of the palace and repainted its fallen columns in vivid reds and blues. Critics say he partly invented what visitors see today, and call the site 'a museum of a museum.' Which material did Evans choose to raise his new walls?
context: The reinforced concrete let Evans permanently 'reconstitute' the palace, but froze his own guesswork into the ruins -- leaving what Mary Beard called 'a museum of a museum.' It was also Evans who coined the name 'Minoan,' after the legendary King Minos. Source: thearchaeologist.org (Palace of Minos: restoration vs preservation); lrb.co.uk (Mary Beard, 'Builder of Ruins').

question: Builders on India's east coast, beside the Bay of Bengal, raised a grand temple to Surya, the Hindu sun god, around 1250. Rather than build the usual boxy shrine, they shaped the whole structure, walls, base and terraces, into one sacred form. What is the Konark Sun Temple carved to look like?
context: The whole temple is Surya's cosmic war-chariot rendered in stone, the sun god shown forever riding it across the heavens. It was built around 1250 CE on the Odisha coast beside the Bay of Bengal and is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Konark_Sun_Temple

question: Sculptors at Konark gave the Sun Temple's platform a whole fleet of huge stone wheels, one row along either flank, and a team of straining stone horses to haul it. Another grand temple might show a carved wheel or two as decoration. How many wheels and how many horses did they carve in all?
context: The chariot rides on 24 wheels and is pulled by seven horses, and the numbers carry meaning: the seven horses are read as the seven days of the week, and the 24 wheels as the fortnights of the year, making the whole temple a giant 'wheel of time.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konark_Sun_Temple

question: Visitors at Konark can still read the giant stone wheels of the Sun Temple, each with a raised hub, wide spokes and a fine rim of beads that people long took for mere decoration. In truth every wheel is laid out as a real science tool. What kind of tool does a Konark wheel work as?
context: Every wheel is a working sundial. The shadow a spoke throws onto the beaded rim tells the hour, the eight broad spokes split the day into eight three-hour 'prahars,' and the fine beads between them let a careful reader tell the time down to a few minutes. Source: worldhistory.org/Konarak_Sun_Temple

question: The main spire of the Konark Sun Temple, on India's eastern coast in Odisha, once rose perhaps over 200 feet, but it collapsed into rubble centuries ago. Only one huge, richly carved section of the 13th-century temple still stands almost whole, the part visitors line up to photograph today. Which section survives?
context: The fallen tower was the deul, the main spire above the sanctum; what survives is the jagamohana, the great audience hall, about 39 m high. The original spire's height is debated: traditional accounts say roughly 68-70 m (over 200 ft), while some scholars estimate closer to 45 m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konark_Sun_Temple

question: For centuries, European sailors crossing the Bay of Bengal fixed their position by the towering Konark temple looming over the Odisha shore -- a seamark so dependable it was marked on their charts. To these foreign crews the Hindu temple went by a blunt, two-word English nickname that stuck for generations. What did the sailors call Konark?
context: Sailors paired it with the 'White Pagoda,' the bright Jagannath temple up the coast at Puri, using the two as landmarks in the Bay of Bengal. Konark's stone had weathered to a dark hue, which earned it the name 'Black Pagoda.' Source: grokipedia.com/page/Konark_Sun_Temple

question: Scholars point to poor-quality stone, a sinking foundation or a lightning strike to explain why the great spire of Konark's Sun Temple fell. An old sailors' legend blames a single powerful object once fixed at the summit, said to have lured passing ships to their doom on this coast, and the tale goes that taking it down toppled the whole tower. What does the legend say stood atop Konark?
context: This is legend, not history, and no record of the magnet survives. The story claims the summit lodestone threw ships' compasses into chaos and even held the temple's iron idol floating in mid-air, and that removing it doomed the tower. Scholars instead blame the poor khondalite stone, subsidence, or lightning. Source: orissapost.com

question: The loudest sound ever recorded on Earth burst from Krakatoa in August 1883, heard nearly 3,000 miles away, as the volcanic island blew itself apart. It stood in the narrow sea between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra. What is that narrow sea called?
context: Krakatoa sat on the Sunda volcanic arc — the chain of fire-mountains where the Indo-Australian plate dives beneath Southeast Asia — right in the Sunda Strait dividing Java from Sumatra. The 1883 eruption was heard across roughly a quarter of the planet. Source: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.

question: The final blast of Krakatoa, at 10:02 on the morning of 27 August 1883, was one of the most violent explosions Earth has ever produced. When the smoke and steam finally cleared, sailors looked to where the peak had towered. What had become of the island?
answer: Almost the whole island had vanished into the sea
choices: Almost the whole island had vanished into the sea
It had doubled in height from fresh lava
It had split into a ring of tall new peaks
A glowing lava lake had filled its crater
context: The climactic explosion destroyed most of the island, leaving a submarine caldera — a great crater below the sea — where the mountain had stood. Source: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.

question: The police chief on Rodrigues Island, near Mauritius, heard a far-off booming from the east about four hours after Krakatoa blew up on 27 August 1883. The sound had rolled 3,000 miles across the ocean, the farthest any sound has ever been heard on Earth. What did he and the colonists take it for?
answer: Distant naval guns firing out at sea
choices: Distant naval guns firing out at sea
Dynamite blasting at a faraway mine
The first tremors of a great earthquake
A violent thunderstorm over the horizon
context: On Rodrigues the police chief logged 'the roar of heavy guns' from the east; colonists nearly 5,000 km away truly thought warships were firing. The blast was also heard 3,110 km away in Perth, Australia — audible across about a thirteenth of the globe. Sources: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'; Live Science, 'Krakatoa Volcano'.  (Legend.)

question: The Royal Mail Ship Norham Castle was sailing about 64 km (40 miles) from Krakatoa when the shockwave of the explosion slammed into her. Her captain wrote in the log that the blast had done the same thing to more than half the men aboard. What had it done to them?
context: The blast reached roughly 180 decibels at the source. The captain of the Norham Castle, about 64 km away, recorded that the explosion had ruptured the eardrums of more than half his crew. Source: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.

question: Hardly any of the 36,417 people Krakatoa killed, by the official count, were burned by the volcano, though it was one of the deadliest eruptions in history. Something else did almost all the killing, wiping out whole coastal towns in minutes. What was it?
choices: A vast slide of hot mud
context: The collapsing volcano launched tsunamis up to 42 m (138 ft) high onto Java and Sumatra. Of the 36,417 official dead, more than 34,000 — about nine in ten — drowned. Sources: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'; NOAA/NCEI, 'On This Day: Historic Krakatau Eruption of 1883'.

question: The Dutch steam gunboat Berouw lay at anchor in the same strait as Krakatoa. When the volcano blew apart in 1883, the sea rose, seized the ship and left her somewhere no ship should ever be. Where did the Berouw end up?
answer: Carried far inland, stranded up a river valley
choices: Carried far inland, stranded up a river valley
Smashed to splinters on the outer reef
Dragged far out into the open sea
Flipped upside down at her mooring
context: The Berouw was swept about 2.5 km (over 1.5 mi) up a river valley and left stranded roughly 9 m above sea level; all 28 of her crew died. On nearby Sebesi island, every one of the ~3,000 inhabitants was killed. Sources: Live Science, 'Krakatoa Volcano'; VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'.

question: Krakatoa released about 200 megatons of energy when it blew apart in 1883, enough to hurl volcanic ash 50 miles into the sky. The largest nuclear weapon ever set off, the Soviet Union's Tsar Bomba, exploded above the Arctic in 1961. How did Krakatoa's single blast compare with it in raw power?
context: The eruption's energy — roughly 200 megatons of TNT — was about four times the yield of the largest nuclear weapon ever detonated. Sources: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'; VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'.

question: Krakatoa's blast punched a pulse of pressure into the atmosphere that spread outward like a ripple across the whole sky. Barographs at weather stations all over the world kept detecting it for five straight days as it swept past them. How many times did that single pressure wave circle the entire planet?
answer: About three and a half times
choices: About three and a half times
context: Barographs recorded the wave seven separate times over five days — four times heading away from Krakatoa and three times bouncing back — meaning it circled the Earth about three and a half times. Sources: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'; VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'.

question: A brand-new island pushed up out of the waves late in 1927, at the very spot where Krakatoa had stood before its eruption of 1883. Volcanoes there do not stay dead, and Indonesians gave the newcomer a name that said exactly what it was. What did they call it?
context: Anak Krakatau — Indonesian for 'Child of Krakatoa' — first broke the surface from the drowned crater in late December 1927 and became a permanent, ever-growing island by 1930. Sources: VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'; Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.

question: Sunsets around the world glowed blood-red for months after Krakatoa's eruption of 1883, lit by ash and sulphur high in the sky. One evening in New York, Poughkeepsie and New Haven the glow so alarmed the townspeople that they did something startling. What did they do?
answer: Called out the fire brigades to fight the red sky itself
choices: Called out the fire brigades to fight the red sky itself
Crowded into the churches, fearing the world had ended
Fled inland, sure a great wildfire was sweeping in
Read the blood-red glow as an omen of coming war
context: The dust veil turned skies blood-red worldwide for months; fire brigades in New York, Poughkeepsie, and New Haven were called out to 'fires' that were only the red evening sky. The same veil cooled the Northern Hemisphere's summer by about 0.4°C the next year. Source: Wikipedia, '1883 eruption of Krakatoa'.  (Legend.)

question: A young volcano had been quietly building itself up for decades where Krakatoa had stood before 1883. One December night in 2018, with no warning at all, disaster came back to the strait. What did the young volcano do that night?
answer: Its flank slid into the sea, raising a sudden tsunami
choices: Its flank slid into the sea, raising a sudden tsunami
It buried the coast under a metre of scalding ash
It split open and drained the strait into itself
It flung molten rock all the way to Java
context: In December 2018 the flank of Anak Krakatau collapsed into the sea, triggering a sudden, warning-free tsunami along the Sunda Strait that killed 437 people, injured more than 14,000, and displaced tens of thousands — the child echoing its parent 135 years later. Source: VolcanoDB, 'Krakatoa Eruption'.

question: A bronze dragon sits at the mouth of a limestone cave beneath Krakow's Wawel Hill, placed there by the sculptor Bronislaw Chromy in 1972. Every few minutes it does something that makes the waiting tourists jump. What does this Krakow dragon do?
answer: shoots a jet of real flame
choices: shoots a jet of real flame
puffs a cloud of cold mist
context: The bronze dragon was sculpted by Bronislaw Chromy and set at the cave mouth in 1972. A hidden gas nozzle lets it shoot a jet of real flame every few minutes, delighting the crowds below Wawel Castle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wawel_Dragon_(statue)

question: Visitors to the bronze Wawel Dragon below Krakow's royal castle need not wait for its next show. They can set it off themselves, in a modern way that would have astonished its sculptor when he made it in 1972. How can a visitor set off the show on command?
choices: toss a coin in a slot
context: It's true -- a hidden system lets visitors send a text message (SMS) to a special number and make the dragon spit fire on command, on top of the automatic burst it gives every few minutes. Source: https://www.thevintagenews.com/2018/03/09/wawel-dragon/

question: A chain of underground rooms runs beneath Krakow's Wawel Hill in the Dragon's Den, about 80 metres of it open to visitors, and it is no dug-out tunnel but a real natural cave. The hill above is soft limestone. What slow natural process hollows out such a cave?
choices: lava draining from a volcanic tube
a glacier grinding through the hillside
sea waves cutting into a cliff
context: Slightly acidic rainwater seeps into cracks and slowly dissolves soluble limestone, carving out caves, sinkholes and towers over thousands of years -- a landscape geographers call KARST. Wawel Hill is limestone, so the Dragon's Den (Smocza Jama) is a genuine karst cave; the whole thing runs about 270 m, with roughly 80 m open to visitors through three chambers. Legend put a fire-breathing dragon in it, but the cave itself is pure earth science. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smocza_Jama

question: St Mary's twin-towered Basilica, the Renaissance Cloth Hall and long rows of cafes frame Rynek Glowny, the market square laid out in Krakow in 1257, when the city was Poland's royal capital. Among all the town squares of medieval Europe, what makes Krakow's stand out?
context: Rynek Glowny was laid out in 1257 under Magdeburg law, each side running more than 200 m (about 3.8 hectares) -- the largest medieval town square in Europe. Krakow's Old Town, square and all, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978, among the very first sites ever listed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_Square,_Krak%C3%B3w

question: A terrible dragon, the Krakow legend says, lived in a cave beneath Wawel Hill above the Vistula River and ate the townsfolk's sheep and daughters. Knights in armour charged it with swords and lances, and none came back. Then Skuba, a humble shoemaker's helper, stepped forward with a quiet idea instead of a sword. What clever trap did Skuba set to kill the dragon?
choices: a pit lined with sharp stakes
a mirror to turn it to stone
context: In the popular version, Skuba stuffed a sheep with sulfur and left it outside the lair. The dragon gulped it down, and the burning sulfur gave it such a raging thirst that it drank from the Vistula River until it swelled up and burst. It's Krakow's best-loved legend -- the dragon is a story, but the Dragon's Den cave below Wawel is real. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wawel_Dragon

question: Three huge pale bones hang on chains above a doorway of Krakow's Wawel Cathedral, as they have since at least the 1500s. People long called them the bones of the slain Wawel Dragon and said they kept the city safe. A scholar from Jagiellonian University studied them in 1937. What did the 'dragon bones' turn out to be?
answer: a whale bone, a mammoth bone, a rhino bone
choices: a whale bone, a mammoth bone, a rhino bone
a whale bone, a walrus bone, a seal bone
a mammoth bone and two aurochs bones
context: A Jagiellonian University scholar identified the chained bones in 1937 as a whale bone, a mammoth bone and a rhinoceros bone -- Ice-Age and ocean giants, not a dragon. They have hung by the cathedral door since at least the 1500s, long believed to protect Krakow; one legend even warns that when the bones finally drop from their chain, the world will end. Source: https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/the-bones-of-the-wawel-dragon-krakow-poland

question: A live trumpeter leans out from the taller tower of St Mary's Basilica above Krakow's market square every hour and plays a short bugle call, the hejnal, toward each point of the compass. For centuries the tune has ended the same strange way, and that ending is what Poles find unforgettable. How does the hejnal always end?
answer: it breaks off abruptly in mid-note
choices: it breaks off abruptly in mid-note
it fades into a slow drumbeat
it rises to a triumphant blast
context: The live hejnal stops abruptly in mid-phrase every hour. Oral tradition says it marks a medieval watchman shot in the throat by an arrow as he trumpeted a warning -- a legend, not documented history. The trumpeter plays it four times, once toward each compass direction, and Polish national radio has broadcast the noon call live every single day since 1927. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary%27s_Trumpet_Call

question: Krakow's market square, its Cloth Hall and its Gothic churches came through World War II almost untouched, while Warsaw and most Polish cities lay in bombed-out ruins. One grim reason lay in what the German occupiers chose to make of the city. What did the Nazis use Krakow as?
answer: the capital of their occupation government
choices: the capital of their occupation government
a supply depot behind the front
a hospital city for the wounded
a prison camp for captured officers
context: The Nazis made Krakow the capital of the General Government, their occupation regime, and Governor-General Hans Frank ruled Poland from Wawel Castle itself. Because they meant to 'Germanize' the city rather than raze it, Krakow's medieval Old Town escaped the destruction that flattened Warsaw. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krak%C3%B3w

question: A medieval watchman, as nearly every Krakow guidebook tells it, was struck in the throat by an arrow while blowing his warning, and the city's hourly trumpet call, the hejnal, honours him. Historians say the arrow tale is no ancient memory at all but the work of one modern writer. Where did the popular story come from?
context: The broken tune is genuinely old, but the arrow-in-the-throat backstory was popularized by American author Eric P. Kelly in his 1928 children's novel 'The Trumpeter of Krakow,' which won the Newbery Medal -- Kelly admitted he spoke little Polish. A romantic tale, not a medieval record. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary%27s_Trumpet_Call  (Legend.)

question: A three-storey hall stands beside a still pond in northern Kyoto, its two upper floors wrapped in real gold leaf. On a calm day the whole golden building shows again in the water, upside down. What is this famous hall called?
context: This is Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion. The pond is called Kyoko-chi, 'Mirror Pond,' named for exactly this flawless reflection. Its sister temple, Ginkaku-ji, is the 'Silver Pavilion.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinkaku-ji

question: Visitors to Kyoto's Golden Pavilion photograph a hall rebuilt in 1955. The original had stood beside the same pond since about 1397, until it burned to ash one summer night in 1950, a loss that so shocked Japan that the novelist Yukio Mishima later wrote a famous book about it. How was the original lost?
answer: A troubled young monk deliberately set it ablaze
choices: A troubled young monk deliberately set it ablaze
A lantern left burning caught the old timber
A summer lightning strike ignited its roof
A fire spread to it from the burning city
context: The arsonist was Hayashi Yoken, a 22-year-old novice monk, who set the fire at 2:30 a.m. on 2 July 1950. The shock ran so deep that the novelist Yukio Mishima built his 1956 novel, 'The Temple of the Golden Pavilion,' around him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinkaku-ji

question: From across its pond, Kyoto's Golden Pavilion looks like one single shining hall, yet its three stacked floors each follow a different style of building. The ground floor is styled as a Heian noble's palace and the middle floor as a samurai's house. What kind of building does the gilded top floor copy?
context: The three styles are shinden-zukuri (Heian aristocrat) on the bottom, buke-zukuri (samurai) in the middle, and a Chinese Zen hall on top, gilded gold both inside and out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinkaku-ji

question: Hundreds of stone animals stand guard among thousands of bright orange gates at Fushimi Inari, the great Shinto shrine on the wooded hills south of Kyoto. They serve as messengers of Inari, the god of rice and grain harvests, and many carry a rice-store key in their mouths. What animal are they?
context: The foxes are called kitsune, believed to carry Inari's messages; the key in their mouths opens the rice granary, since Inari is the god of rice and prosperity. Fushimi Inari, founded in 711 CE by the Hata clan, is the head of some 32,000 Inari shrines across Japan. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fushimi_Inari-taisha

question: About 10,000 vermilion torii gates tunnel up Fushimi Inari's sacred Mount Inari, and the rows keep lengthening year after year. Each gate was paid for by a single business or person, whose name is painted right down its back. Why did these donors each put up a gate?
answer: To win a wish, or give thanks for one granted
choices: To win a wish, or give thanks for one granted
To mark the birth of a child in the family
As a fine for breaking the shrine's rules
In memory of a family member who had died
context: Every torii on Mount Inari was paid for by a business or a person, in hope of a wish coming true or in thanks for one the god had granted, with the donor's name painted down the back; the custom began in the Edo period, so the tunnels keep growing as new gates are donated. About 10,000 gates now climb the mountain, and the densest stretch, the Senbon Torii ('thousand torii'), holds roughly 800 by itself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fushimi_Inari-taisha ; gov-online.go.jp

question: At the foot of the Arashiyama hills west of Kyoto, a long bridge spans the river close to where the first one was built in the year 836. It carries the name Togetsukyo -- given, by tradition, after a retired emperor watched something one night. What did he see?
answer: The moon seemed to walk across it
choices: The moon seemed to walk across it
The sun set exactly beneath its arch
Cherry petals covered it like snow
Its lanterns doubled in the water
context: Togetsukyo means 'Moon-Crossing Bridge.' By tradition the name comes from a retired emperor who said the moon looked as though it were walking from one end to the other. The first bridge here, built in 836, stood a little upstream; today's span dates from 1934. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arashiyama; kanpai-japan.com/kyoto/togetsukyo-bridge-arashiyama

question: The wooden stage of Kyoto's Kiyomizu-dera stands thirteen metres, about four storeys, above a wooded hill, resting on tall pillars built without a single nail. 'To jump off the stage at Kiyomizu' became a Japanese saying for taking the plunge, and in the Edo era people really did leap from it. What did the records show about the jumpers?
choices: Only about 15 percent survived the fall
Fewer than half survived the fall
context: Records from the Edo period show that about 85 percent of those who leaped from the stage survived; the government banned the practice in 1872. The entire stage rests on its tall pillars without a single nail. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiyomizu-dera

question: Nishida Kitaro, a famous modern Japanese thinker, walked a quiet stone path beside a cherry-lined canal in east Kyoto every morning, deep in thought, on his way to work. The two-kilometre path is called Tetsugaku-no-michi, the Path of Philosophy, in his honour. Where was he headed?
context: Nishida Kitaro, one of Japan's most famous modern philosophers, was said to meditate along this canal on his daily walk to Kyoto University; the path took its name, Tetsugaku-no-michi, 'the Path of Philosophy,' from his habit. It runs from Ginkaku-ji, the Silver Pavilion, to Nanzen-ji temple. Source: japan-guide.com/e/e3906.html

question: Timber bamboo grows so tall and dense in the Arashiyama grove west of Kyoto that its paths feel like a green cathedral. Japan's environment ministry put the grove on a national list of 100 treasures worth preserving in 1996, chosen not for a sight but for something only the ear can catch. What did the list protect?
answer: The creak and hiss of wind through the bamboo
choices: The creak and hiss of wind through the bamboo
The birdsong echoing off the tall stalks
The temple bells drifting up the valley
The rush of the river below the grove
context: The 'Soundscapes of Japan,' one hundred sounds chosen by the Ministry of the Environment in 1996, are noises the nation judged worth protecting. Arashiyama earned its place for the eerie creaking and hissing of wind moving through its giant timber bamboo. Source: arashiyamabamboogrove.org

question: When UNESCO, the United Nations cultural body, came to add Kyoto to its World Heritage list in 1994, it faced roughly 1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines packed into the old imperial capital and its wooded hills. It made an unusual choice about exactly what to protect. What did UNESCO do?
answer: Grouped seventeen scattered sites into one listing
choices: Grouped seventeen scattered sites into one listing
Named the whole old city one protected zone
Chose its three greatest temples to represent all
Listed the imperial palace and its gardens alone
context: The listing, added in 1994, is called the 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto,' and it groups seventeen separate sites in and around the city into one World Heritage Site. Kyoto -- founded in 794 by Emperor Kanmu and Japan's capital until 1868 -- still holds roughly 1,600 Buddhist temples and about 400 Shinto shrines. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto

question: Kyoto came through World War II almost untouched, which is why its ancient temples still stand while cities like Tokyo and Osaka were rebuilt from ash. Yet in 1945 Kyoto sat near the very top of the United States' list of atomic-bomb targets. Why did the city survive?
answer: A US official struck it from the target list to save its treasures
choices: A US official struck it from the target list to save its treasures
The US war secretary had once honeymooned there and loved it
Thick mountain fog hid the city from the bombers for months
Japan surrendered before Kyoto's turn ever came up
context: The US Secretary of War, Henry Stimson, personally had Kyoto removed from the atomic-target list, arguing the ancient capital was a treasure-house of Japanese art and religion; Nagasaki was added in its place. A popular story claims Stimson spared Kyoto because he had honeymooned there, but the historian Alex Wellerstein could find no evidence for it: Stimson's known visits to Kyoto came in 1926 and 1929, and neither was a honeymoon. The documented reason was the city's cultural significance. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto ; blog.nuclearsecrecy.com/2023/07/24/henry-stimson-didnt-go-to-kyoto-on-his-honeymoon/

question: A single switchback road once linked La Paz, deep in an Andes canyon, with El Alto on the rim about 400 metres above, a 90-minute crawl. In 2014 the city opened a link that takes about 11 minutes. What kind of transit is it?
context: The answer is Mi Teleférico ('My Cable Car'), opened in 2014 and now the backbone of La Paz-El Alto transit: gondola cabins gliding over the rooftops in place of the old switchback crawl, with a new cabin departing about every 12 seconds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mi_Teleférico; theworld.org (PRX), 2025.

question: Riders on Mi Teleférico in La Paz change from line to line the way subway riders do in any big city, and its map reads like a subway map. Its ten lines are labelled the same way many subway systems label theirs. How are the ten lines named?
context: Each line carries a color: Red, Yellow, Green, Blue, Orange, White, Sky Blue, Purple, Brown, and Silver -- a cable-car metro map painted across the Andean sky. The Silver Line (Línea Plateada), opening 9 March 2019, completed what Guinness World Records certified as the world's largest public-transit cable-car network. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mi_Teleférico; Guinness World Records.

question: La Paz's grandest homes sit down low in the Zona Sur, while low-income families build high up the canyon walls, the reverse of most cities, where the rich pay for the high ground and its wide views. What makes the low ground the prized place to live in La Paz?
answer: the air is warmer and richer in oxygen there
choices: the air is warmer and richer in oxygen there
the ocean is visible from the lower streets
the oldest colonial palaces stand down there
the river keeps the low ground green and cool
context: In La Paz, altitude -- not the skyline view -- is the luxury. The affluent Zona Sur lies around 3,250 m in warmer, more breathable air, while lower-income neighborhoods climb past 4,000 m up the canyon walls, the reverse of the usual class map. When Mi Teleférico's gondolas linked these long-separated districts, an anthropologist noted they connected neighborhoods the road network had effectively kept apart. (Bolivia is landlocked, so no ocean is anywhere in sight.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz; theworld.org (PRX), 2025.

question: An airliner lines up for takeoff at El Alto International Airport, which serves La Paz from a flat plain about 4,058 metres up, the highest international airport on Earth. The air there is so thin that the plane's wings and engines have far less to grip as it gathers speed. What does the thin air force every airliner leaving El Alto to do?
answer: roll much farther before lifting off
choices: roll much farther before lifting off
burn much less fuel on the way up
lift off at a much steeper angle
context: Thin air means less lift and less engine thrust, so jets need long takeoff rolls and often fly with reduced loads out of El Alto. The airport sits above El Alto itself, which at roughly 4,000-4,150 m and about 885,000 people (2024 census) ranks among the highest big cities in the world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Alto.

question: Illimani's three snow-capped peaks fill nearly every view in La Paz, seen from streets all across the city. The mountain rises to 6,438 metres, the tallest peak of the Cordillera Real, and is the city's emblem. How does the Andean tradition of the region honour it?
answer: as a guardian spirit watching over the city
choices: as a guardian spirit watching over the city
as a volcano that once buried the valley
as the source of the canyon's river
as the tomb of an ancient Inca ruler
context: In Andean belief an apu is the protective spirit of a sacred mountain, and Illimani is revered as the guardian watching over La Paz. Its first recorded ascent was in 1898 by the British climber William Martin Conway with Italian guides. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illimani.

question: The Valle de la Luna, or Moon Valley, rises about 10 km south of La Paz as a bone-white forest of clay spires, so lunar that local tales credit Neil Armstrong with naming it after his Moon landing of 1969. Geographers put it in the same landform family found across the Dakotas and the dry American West. Which landform is it?
context: Badlands form where soft, poorly cemented rock -- here clay and sandstone -- erodes fast into a labyrinth of spires and gullies (karst instead needs soluble limestone). The Neil Armstrong naming story is a popular local tradition, not documented fact. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valle_de_la_Luna_(Bolivia).

question: Newcomers to La Paz often fall sick with soroche within a day, the headaches and nausea of altitude sickness at about 3,600 metres. Yet millions of people spend their whole lives there, and the drop in oxygen is not as steep as the misery suggests. Roughly what share of sea-level oxygen does each breath in La Paz still carry?
context: At La Paz's altitude the air carries only about two-thirds of the oxygen available at sea level -- enough of a drop that unacclimatized visitors get soroche within 6-24 hours, yet high enough that millions live and work here for life. This single fact underlies the city's long takeoff rolls and its upside-down class map. Source: biologyinsights.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz.

question: An entire neighborhood of wooden houses stands on tall stilts above the Lagos Lagoon, with no dry land beneath them. Residents paddle canoes from door to door, and visitors nickname it 'the Venice of Africa.' What is this famous stilt district of Lagos called?
context: The stilt district is Makoko, sometimes called 'the Venice of Africa.' It is really six villages — four floating on the lagoon and two on land — home largely to the Egun people, who came from Badagry and neighbouring Benin, and who live mainly by fishing the lagoon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Makoko.'

question: In Yoruba homes and markets across Lagos, people still call the city by a name far older than the one Portuguese sailors gave it in 1472. The Yoruba, one of Nigeria's largest peoples, knew the place by that name long before the sailors came, and it is still their everyday word for the city. What do Yoruba speakers call Lagos?
context: Yoruba speakers call the city Èkó, a name older than the Portuguese 'Lagos.' Its exact meaning is debated — some say a farmstead or hamlet, others a Benin war-camp — but Èkó is still the everyday Yoruba name for Lagos today. Source: Wikipedia, 'Lagos'; Pulse.

question: An 11.8-kilometre bridge strides clear across the Lagos Lagoon on tall concrete piers, one of several great spans that thread sprawling Lagos together over its waters. When it opened in 1990 it was the longest bridge in all of Africa. What is this record-setting Lagos bridge called?
context: The Third Mainland Bridge runs 11.8 km (7.3 mi) across the Lagos Lagoon. When it opened in 1990 it was the longest bridge in Africa, holding that title until Cairo's 6th of October Bridge overtook it in 1996. Source: Wikipedia, 'Third Mainland Bridge'; Institution of Civil Engineers.

question: Off the shore of Lagos, engineers are raising an entire new district on land reclaimed from the ocean, shielded by a colossal 8.5-km sea barrier nicknamed 'the Great Wall of Lagos.' While the lagoon's poorest families live out in stilt houses standing in the water, this gleaming district is being walled off from the sea instead. What is this new city-on-reclaimed-land called?
context: The reclaimed-land district is Eko Atlantic, rising off Victoria Island behind a sea wall of about 8.5 km nicknamed 'the Great Wall of Lagos.' The contrast is stark: while Makoko's families live out in the lagoon water, this luxury city is being walled off from the same sea. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eko Atlantic'; ekoatlantic.com.

question: The emperor Aurangzeb had a mosque of deep red sandstone raised in Lahore in just two years, across a wide plaza from the city's fort. It was finished in 1673, and for three hundred years no mosque on Earth was larger. What is it called?
context: The Badshahi ('Imperial') Mosque was commissioned by the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb and built in just two years, 1671–1673. Its four octagonal corner minarets each rise 60 metres (196 feet), and worshippers climb 22 steps just to reach its main gate. It remained the largest mosque on Earth for over three centuries, until the late 20th century, and its construction was overseen by Aurangzeb's foster brother Fidai Khan Koka, then governor of Lahore. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badshahi_Mosque

question: Shah Jahan built a small marble pavilion inside Lahore's fort around 1631, its walls and ceiling set with thousands of tiny mirrored tiles. A single candle lit there in the dark breaks into countless points of light across the ceiling, like a private galaxy of stars. What is this dazzling hall called?
context: The Sheesh Mahal ('Palace of Mirrors', about 1631–32) was built for the emperor Shah Jahan. Its mirror-work is a craft called ainakari, in which thousands of tiny convex mirror-tiles multiply a single flame into countless points of light. A semi-octagonal marble pavilion, it is also inlaid with pietra dura — precious stones set into the white marble — and pierced screens called jali, and is often called 'the jewel in the crown' of Lahore Fort. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheesh_Mahal_(Lahore_Fort)

question: Two huge round brick towers, fluted like giant drums, flank the high arch of the main entrance to Lahore's fort. The emperor Aurangzeb added this gateway, guarding the way into the royal fort, in 1674. What is this grand entrance called?
context: The Alamgiri Gate, the main entrance to Lahore Fort, was built by the emperor Aurangzeb in 1674 and is flanked by two huge semi-circular fluted bastions — one of the fort's most iconic faces. The fort as a whole holds 21 notable monuments spread across more than 20 hectares. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore_Fort

question: Three great terraces step down the land in the royal pleasure garden that Shah Jahan laid out in Lahore, each about four to five metres above the next. The emperor gave them poetic names meaning 'Bestower of Pleasure,' 'Bestower of Goodness' and 'Bestower of Life.' What is the garden called?
context: Shah Jahan's Shalimar Gardens step down in three descending terraces — Farah Baksh (upper), Faiz Baksh (middle) and Hayat Baksh (lower) — completed in 1642 after only about 17 months of work, and threaded with some 410 fountains that spray into wide marble pools. They are laid out as a charbagh, a Persian 'four-part paradise garden' quartered by water channels to picture an earthly Eden. The Lahore Fort and the Shalimar Gardens were jointly inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalimar_Gardens,_Lahore

question: Lahore came under Sikh rule in the early 1800s, after the Mughal empire crumbled, and the vast marble courtyard of Aurangzeb's great mosque lost its sacred use. Its new masters put that enormous walled space to a rough, worldly purpose. What did the Sikh forces turn the courtyard into?
context: After the Mughal empire declined, Lahore came under Sikh rule, and the vast courtyard of the Badshahi Mosque was used as a military stable while the surrounding cells (hujras) served as soldiers' quarters — a stark fall for what had been the largest mosque on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badshahi_Mosque

question: Hundreds of fountains and pools in Shah Jahan's royal garden at Lahore needed water without pause, out on the dry plain of the Punjab. The Mughal noble Ali Mardan Khan answered with one vast public work that carried water down from the distant foothills of Kashmir. What did he build to feed the garden?
context: To feed the hundreds of fountains of the Shalimar Gardens, the Mughal noble Ali Mardan Khan had a canal dug roughly 100 miles (about 160 km) to bring water from the foothills of Kashmir down to the dry Lahore plain — an enormous public work built just to keep a paradise garden flowing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalimar_Gardens,_Lahore

question: Elephants fight, camels gallop and polo matches rage across the outer face of Lahore's fort, a wall about 440 metres long covered edge to edge in glittering glazed tile and painted fresco. Painted angels appear among them, and so does a creature from Persian myth. Which mythical creature is worked in among the real animals of this Picture Wall?
context: The outer 'Picture Wall' of Lahore Fort runs about 440 metres (1,450 feet) long and up to 15 metres high, and is often called the largest mural in the world. Begun under the emperor Jahangir and decorated through the 1620s in glazed kashi-kari tile and fresco, it shows elephant fights, camels, horses, polo games and angels — and among them coil winged Persian dragons, a picture-book of Mughal court life laid across the fort's face. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore_Fort

question: A physician from Chiniot, who rose to become the royal doctor and then governor of Punjab, paid for a mosque in old Lahore that many call the most richly decorated of the whole Mughal age. Nearly every surface, inside and out, is sheathed in glazed tile of cobalt, green and gold. What is this mosque called?
context: The Wazir Khan Mosque (built 1634–1641) was paid for by Hakim Ilam-ud-din Ansari, a physician from Chiniot who rose to become the royal doctor and then governor of Punjab under the title 'Wazir Khan.' Nearly every surface, inside and out, is sheathed in kashi-kari faience tilework — cobalt blue, cerulean, white, green, orange, yellow, purple and red — with true-fresco painting; widely called 'the jewel of Lahore,' it is considered the most ornately decorated mosque of the entire Mughal era, its four minarets each rising about 107 feet. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wazir_Khan_Mosque

question: A crack in the crust of southern Siberia cradles Lake Baikal for more than 600 kilometres, in a trench so long and deep that the lake holds far more water than its outline on a map suggests. Which record does it hold among freshwater lakes?
answer: the largest freshwater lake by volume
choices: the largest freshwater lake by volume
the largest freshwater lake by area
the highest freshwater lake on Earth
the longest freshwater lake on Earth
context: By sheer volume Lake Baikal holds about 23,615 cubic kilometres of water — more than any other freshwater lake on Earth, and roughly a fifth of all the planet's unfrozen surface fresh water. Several lakes (Superior, the Caspian) spread across more surface area, but none matches Baikal's staggering depth-fed volume. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: Lake Baikal, in southern Siberia, has outlived countless other lakes. Most lakes slowly fill with mud and river silt and vanish within ten or twenty thousand years of forming, but Baikal has defied that fate on a scale that stuns geologists. Roughly how long has it held its water?
context: At an estimated 25 to 30 million years old, Baikal is by far the oldest lake in the world, while most lakes fill with sediment and disappear within 10,000 to 20,000 years. Baikal has existed since long before modern humans, or even the ape ancestors of humans, walked the Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: A weighted line dropped over the side of a boat on Lake Baikal just keeps going down. It sinks deeper than the floor of any other lake on Earth, into a rift in the crust that cuts far below sea level. Roughly how deep is Baikal at its deepest point?
context: Baikal's deepest point reaches 1,642 metres (5,387 feet) below the surface — the deepest lake on Earth, and deeper than four Eiffel Towers stacked end to end. Its floor lies well below sea level, cradled in one of the deepest continental rifts on the planet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: As many as 330 rivers and streams pour their water into Siberia's Lake Baikal, tumbling down from the surrounding mountains. Yet only a single river ever carries water back out of the lake, off toward the distant Arctic Ocean. Which river is that lone outlet?
context: As many as 330 rivers and streams flow into Baikal, but the Angara alone flows out, carrying the lake's water toward the Yenisei River and eventually the Arctic Ocean. In Buryat legend the Angara is Baikal's runaway daughter, fleeing to marry the Yenisei. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: Some 2,600 kinds of animals crowd the waters of Lake Baikal, from freshwater sponges growing in branching forests to snails and pale fish of the deep. Biologists who study them are struck by one fact about most of them. What is it?
answer: most of them live nowhere else on Earth
choices: most of them live nowhere else on Earth
most of them also live in the Arctic Ocean
most of them were carried in by human settlers
most of them die if the water ever freezes
context: About 80% of Baikal's roughly 2,600 known animal species live nowhere else on Earth — biologists call such one-place-only species 'endemic'. That staggering biodiversity, together with the lake's record age, depth and volume, earned Lake Baikal a place on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996, where it is celebrated as the world's oldest and most voluminous freshwater lake. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal; yichuans.me/datasheet/output/site/lake-baikal (inscribed 1996).

question: Twin marble peaks drop straight into Lake Baikal at Cape Burkhan, on Olkhon island, the spiritual centre of the Buryat people. Shamans held their rites there, and the Buryat long forbade ordinary people even to set foot on the spot. In Buryat belief, what is this rock?
answer: the home of the lake's guardian spirit
choices: the home of the lake's guardian spirit
the tomb of the first Buryat ruler
the gateway to the land of the dead
the anchor that steadies the island
context: Cape Burkhan, also called Shaman Rock, on Olkhon Island is among the holiest sites in Buryat shamanism, long held to be the dwelling of the lake's guardian spirit. Told here as belief, not settled fact. Source: msabelli.wordpress.com; pomexplores.com.  (Legend.)

question: Far inland in southern Siberia, more than 1,700 kilometres from the nearest ocean, Lake Baikal shelters creatures cut off from the sea, and it holds one claim that no other lake on Earth can match. What sets Baikal apart from every other lake?
answer: it is the only lake with a seal species of its own
choices: it is the only lake with a seal species of its own
it is the only lake ringed by active volcanoes
it is the only lake with ocean-like tides
it is the only lake that drains into two seas
context: The nerpa (Pusa sibirica) is the only seal species that lives entirely in fresh water, stranded more than 1,700 kilometres from the nearest ocean, probably cut off when Ice-Age meltwater rivers that once linked Baikal to the Arctic dried up. Finland's Lake Saimaa and Russia's Lake Ladoga hold landlocked seals too, but they are subspecies of the sea-going ringed seal, so Baikal is the only lake with a seal species of its own. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Baikal_seal; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saimaa_ringed_seal

question: Living creatures flourish more than a kilometre beneath the surface of Lake Baikal. In most very deep lakes the water that far down is a dead, lifeless zone where almost nothing survives. What unusual property of Baikal's water makes such deep life possible?
answer: it stays rich in oxygen down to the very bottom
choices: it stays rich in oxygen down to the very bottom
it stays warm down to the very bottom
it carries no trace of salt at any depth
it is fed by warm underground springs
context: In most very deep lakes the bottom water is starved of oxygen and nearly lifeless, but Baikal stays rich in oxygen all the way down, so creatures thrive more than a kilometre below the surface. Scientists credit powerful seasonal mixing that carries oxygen into the depths. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal.

question: Satellites watching Lake Baikal's winter ice since the 1990s have picked out strange dark circles on it, perfectly round and several kilometres wide. The rings puzzled scientists for decades until researchers traced them to something moving in the water far below. What forms these giant ice rings?
answer: warm water eddies spinning beneath the ice
choices: warm water eddies spinning beneath the ice
cold currents sinking from the surface
hot springs venting from the lakebed
context: These dark 'ice rings', several kilometres across, form when warm eddies of water swirl beneath the frozen surface and thin the ice from below. First spotted from space, they baffled scientists for years before the hidden underwater eddies were identified. Source: livescience.com/ice-rings-lake-baikal.html.

question: When a fierce Siberian winter locks Lake Baikal in ice, the wind-driven waves freeze mid-surge and shatter into jagged, glass-clear shards that jut as high as twelve metres, heaped along the shore like a field of broken glass. These transparent ice shards are famous for glowing what colour?
context: In a hard freeze, wind-driven waves lock into jagged, transparent 'hummocks' that can rear several metres high — the tallest to around twelve — and glow an unearthly turquoise where light passes through the clear ice. Source: mymodernmet.com/lake-baikal-russia-ice-hummocks.

question: Plants rot on the deep bed of Lake Baikal and give off a gas that streams up toward the surface. When the bubbles meet the underside of the winter ice they freeze in place, stacked into pearly white discs hanging in the crystal-clear ice like frozen strings of pearls. What gas is trapped in these columns?
context: Methane released by plants rotting on the deep lakebed rises in bubbles that freeze against the underside of the ice, stacking into pearly white discs that a skater on the ice can look straight down into. Source: apod.nasa.gov/apod/ap181218.html (Methane Bubbles Frozen in Lake Baikal).

question: Lake Natron spreads its shallow soda water across the floor of the East African Rift in northern Tanzania, glowing a deep red and orange that astronauts have picked out from orbit. Its water is so hot and harsh that almost nothing can live in it. What gives the lake its blood-red color?
answer: Salt-loving microbes whose red pigment dyes the water
choices: Iron-rich minerals dissolved out of the red desert rock
Salt-loving microbes whose red pigment dyes the water
Fine red dust blown in off the surrounding desert
Red soda crystals that crust the shallow lakebed
context: The red is alive, not a mineral: halophilic (salt-loving) cyanobacteria pack the scalding brine, and their red photosynthetic pigment dyes the whole lake. A 'soda lake' is one saturated with dissolved sodium carbonate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Natron ('The red accessory photosynthesizing pigment in the cyanobacteria produces the deep reds').

question: The ancient Egyptians, thousands of kilometres to the north, harvested a chalky white salt from lakes in their desert, the same salt that cakes the shores of Lake Natron in Tanzania. Called natron, it is mostly sodium carbonate, and it dries out anything it touches. What did the Egyptians use natron for?
answer: To dry out and preserve the dead as mummies
choices: To flavour and preserve their stored food
To make the blue glaze on temple tiles
To dry out and preserve the dead as mummies
To tan animal hides into leather
context: Natron -- sodium carbonate -- is the very salt ancient Egyptians packed around bodies to dry them out for mummification; Lake Natron is essentially a whole lake of embalming salt. Source: Smithsonian, 'Flamingos Find Life Among Death' ('a chemical once used in Egyptian mummification'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natron.

question: A wader in Lake Natron, in northern Tanzania, risks burned skin and eyes, for the water is packed with dissolved soda and can heat to around 60 C. In chemistry, the lake's water is a natural version of which harsh household substance?
answer: Lye, the caustic cleaner that unclogs drains
choices: Lye, the caustic cleaner that unclogs drains
Bleach, the cleaner that whitens laundry
Ammonia, the cleaner that washes windows
Baking soda, the powder that raises cakes
context: Natron's water is a natural lye, loaded with sodium carbonate and trona; its pH sits near 10.5 and can spike above 12 in the dry season, while temperatures reach about 40 C and can approach 60 C -- caustic enough to burn skin and eyes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Natron (pH 'can reach greater than 12'; highs near 60 C).

question: Nick Brandt photographed birds and bats from Lake Natron that look like blackened stone statues, and his haunting pictures fed a viral story that the lake turns animals to stone the instant they touch it. What is really happening to these creatures?
answer: The soda slowly coats creatures that had already died
choices: The caustic water petrifies them the instant they touch it
Minerals seep in and replace their bones with rock
The fierce heat bakes them into hardened clay shells
The soda slowly coats creatures that had already died
context: The 'turns animals to stone' story is sensationalized: the soda does not petrify the living on contact -- it slowly encrusts animals that have ALREADY died, sealing them in a hard soda-salt crust like natural mummies. Nick Brandt found and posed calcified birds and bats for his book 'Across the Ravaged Land.' Source: Smithsonian; NBC News, 'Lake That Turns Animals to Stone? Not Quite.'  (Legend.)

question: Lesser flamingos hatch by the million on low soda-crust islands far out in Lake Natron, up to 2.5 million birds, most of their kind on Earth. Foxes and jackals prowl the shore but almost never reach the nests. What keeps the predators away?
answer: A moat of scalding, caustic soda-water they will not cross
choices: Massed adult flamingos forming a wall around the chicks
A moat of scalding, caustic soda-water they will not cross
Tall mud nest-mounds too steep for a predator to climb
Parent birds carrying the chicks to safety each night
context: Natron hosts about 2.5 million lesser flamingos -- some 75% of the world population -- the most important breeding site on Earth for the species. The caustic water and the ring of scalding soda around the seasonal evaporite islands form a moat no fox or jackal will cross, so the nests are almost untouchable: the lake defends its own nursery. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Natron ('Its caustic environment is a barrier against predators'); Smithsonian.

question: South of Lake Natron rises Ol Doinyo Lengai, the only volcano on Earth that erupts carbonatite lava, so cool, at barely 500 C, that it flows out jet black instead of glowing red. Stranger still is what becomes of the black lava within hours of hardening on the slopes. What happens to it?
answer: It weathers to white powder that feeds the lake below
choices: It shatters into black glass all across the slopes
It slowly reheats from within and glows dull red
It weathers to white powder that feeds the lake below
It hardens into rock that never wears away
context: Ol Doinyo Lengai (Maasai for 'Mountain of God'), about 15 km south of the lake and 2,962 m tall, is the only active volcano erupting carbonatite (natrocarbonatite) lava. Because it is only about 500-600 C -- roughly half the heat of ordinary lava -- it pours out jet black, then within hours absorbs moisture from the air and weathers to white soda powder that rain washes downhill to feed Lake Natron its strange chemistry. Source: volcanosatlas.com/volcano/lengai-ol-doinyo; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natrocarbonatite.

question: The villagers in the valleys below Lake Nyos, a quiet crater lake in the highlands of Cameroon, went to sleep on the night of 21 August 1986, and 1,746 of them never woke. Thousands of cattle died too, yet no body bore a wound, and there had been no flood or fire. Something had welled silently up out of the lake. What invisible thing was it?
context: The killer was ordinary carbon dioxide (CO2), not a poison-gas attack, just invisible CO2 in a deadly amount. Because CO2 is about 50% denser than air, the cloud hugged the ground, rolled downhill and pooled in the valleys, smothering every breathing thing within about 25 km (16 miles) of the lake. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nyos_disaster; Britannica 'Lake Nyos disaster.'

question: Volcanic gas seeped for decades from magma deep under Lake Nyos, in Cameroon, and dissolved into the cold depths of the lake, until one night in 1986 it all burst out at once in a limnic eruption. Why had so much gas been able to build up down there?
answer: the deep water never mixed with the layers above
choices: the deep water never mixed with the layers above
a thick mat of floating weeds capped the lake
the gas froze into ice on the cold lakebed
the lake's outlet stream was choked with mud
context: The gas could pile up because Lake Nyos is layered: its cold, heavy deep water never mixes with the layers above, so carbon dioxide seeping in from the magma below stays trapped under pressure for years, like the gas in a sealed soda bottle. When something disturbed the water in 1986, the gas fizzed out all at once: a limnic eruption, from limne, Greek for lake. Scientists still are not sure what set it off; the leading guesses are an underwater landslide or a spell of cold rain that suddenly mixed the layers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nyos_disaster; Britannica 'Lake Nyos disaster.'

question: Engineers began sinking long pipes straight down into the deep water of Lake Nyos in 2001, to make the lake safe before its deadly gas could build up again. Once started, each pipe shoots a tall fountain of water into the air and keeps it going for years on its own, with no pump. What keeps the fountain rising by itself?
answer: the carbon dioxide bubbling out of the rising water
choices: the carbon dioxide bubbling out of the rising water
the heat of magma boiling the water from below
the inflow of mountain rivers feeding the lake
the wind funneling down the crater walls
context: As the deep water rises, the drop in pressure lets its dissolved gas fizz out of solution; the bubbles make the column lighter than the water around it, so it accelerates upward, a self-powered 'gas lift,' like a shaken soda bottle erupting the moment its cap comes off. The first degassing pipe went in in 2001, with two more added in 2011. Only three lakes on Earth are known to be able to erupt this way: Nyos and Monoun in Cameroon, and giant Lake Kivu on the Rwanda-Congo border, where about two million people live around the shores. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nyos_disaster; eos.org/science-updates/cameroons-lake-nyos-gas-burst-30-years-later.

question: Lake Superior, at the top of North America's five Great Lakes on the border between Canada and the United States, is so vast that a person standing on one shore cannot see the other. Among all the world's freshwater lakes, what record does it hold?
choices: the largest by total volume of water
context: Lake Superior covers about 82,100 km2 (31,700 sq mi) along the US-Canada border -- more surface than any other freshwater lake on Earth. It is largest by AREA; by sheer volume of water it ranks only third in the world, behind Siberia's Lake Baikal and Africa's Lake Tanganyika. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior; lakesuperior.com.

question: The five Great Lakes spread between the United States and Canada as the biggest system of freshwater lakes on Earth. Of every drop of fresh water lying on the planet's surface, in every lake, river and pond, these five lakes alone hold a huge share. About how much of it do they hold together?
context: The five Great Lakes -- Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario -- together hold roughly 21%, about one-fifth, of all the fresh water on Earth's surface (some six quadrillion gallons). Source: css.umich.edu Great Lakes factsheet; US EPA / NOAA.

question: Hundreds of ships have gone down in Lake Superior's storms over the centuries, and sailors have long said the lake 'never gives up its dead': the drowned from its wrecks are almost never found floating back to the surface. What property of Superior's deep water best explains this?
answer: it stays near freezing all the year round
choices: it stays near freezing all the year round
it is far deeper than a body could ever rise from
its currents drag the drowned out toward the middle
it is unusually heavy with dissolved minerals
context: Below about 200 m (110 fathoms), Superior stays a constant ~4 C (39 F) all year. That cold slows decay and the buildup of gases that would normally refloat a drowned body, so shipwreck victims tend to stay on the bottom -- the origin of the sailors' saying that Superior 'never gives up its dead.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior.  (Legend.)

question: A November storm battered the Great Lakes for days in 1913 with 90-mph gusts and 35-foot waves, wrecking 19 ships and killing more than 250 people. It was one of Lake Superior's 'Gales of November', the ferocious autumn storms that sink ships. What sets off these sudden November monsters?
answer: cold Canadian air crashing into warm, moist Gulf air
choices: cold Canadian air crashing into warm, moist Gulf air
leftover tropical hurricanes tracking up from the Gulf
a full-moon tide surging across the open lake
warm chinook winds pouring down off the Rockies
context: The fierce autumn 'Gales of November' form when cold, dry air from northern Canada slams into warm, moist air drawn up from the Gulf of Mexico; the lakes' still-warm water feeds the clash and the jet stream strengthens it. The Great Storm of 1913, the 'Big Blow' or 'Freshwater Fury', battered the lakes for days with gusts near 90 mph and waves over 35 feet, destroying 19 ships and killing more than 250 people. Source: canr.msu.edu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_Storm_of_1913.

question: Superior and its four sister lakes look ancient and eternal on the map of North America, yet their basins took their present shape only about 10,000 years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age. What carved these enormous hollows out of solid bedrock?
context: During the last Ice Age, ice sheets more than a mile thick crept south across North America, scraping and gouging the bedrock -- a process geologists call GLACIAL SCOURING -- to carve the five Great Lakes' basins. Meltwater filled them to roughly their present form only about 10,000 years ago, making these giant lakes geological newborns. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior; USGS Great Lakes.

question: The crust around Lake Superior is still springing slowly back up, thousands of years after the mile-thick ice of the last Ice Age melted off it, a rise geologists call isostatic rebound. What is that rise doing to the lake itself?
answer: tipping its water slowly toward the south shore
choices: tipping its water slowly toward the south shore
draining it slowly out toward the Atlantic
splitting its bed into two separate basins
warming its deep water slowly from below
context: Freed of the mile-thick ice that once pressed it down, the crust is slowly springing back up, a process called glacial isostatic adjustment, or isostatic rebound. Around Superior the north shore rises faster than the south, so the whole lake is slowly tipping, and its water creeps up the southern shore. Source: ijc.org; medium.com/the-environment.

question: Dark basalt about 1.1 billion years old lines Lake Superior's north shore and its wild Isle Royale. It poured out when North America itself began to tear apart along a crack that ran for thousands of kilometres, flooding the gash with lava, until the tearing stopped and the continent stayed whole. What is this ancient failed split beneath Lake Superior called?
context: Superior's north shore and Isle Royale rest on 1.1-billion-year-old flood basalt of the Midcontinent Rift, a buried scar some 2,000 to 3,000 km long by different counts, where the North American continent began to tear apart, then stopped. Lava filled the crack, and its copper-rich veins later made Michigan's Keweenaw Peninsula a legendary copper-mining district. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midcontinent_Rift_System; grokipedia.com/page/Midcontinent_Rift_System

question: A thin blue ribbon of water, Lake Tanganyika threads down eastern Africa as the shared border of four countries. It runs about 673 kilometres from tip to tip but is never wider than about 72. Among all the world's freshwater lakes, what record does its long, narrow shape earn it?
choices: the world's largest freshwater lake by area
context: Lake Tanganyika is the world's longest freshwater lake -- 673 km (418 miles) end to end but only 16-72 km wide, a thin ribbon threaded down the East African Rift Valley. Baikal (636 km) is deeper and older, and Superior is larger by area, but for sheer length Tanganyika wins. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/497936-longest-lake.

question: Fishing boats bob on Lake Tanganyika, above the deep crack in eastern Africa that holds it. Most of Earth's fresh water lies frozen in ice caps or buried underground, so only a thin slice is liquid and within reach at the surface. About how much of that reachable water sits in Tanganyika alone?
context: This single African lake holds about 16% -- roughly one-sixth -- of all the world's available (liquid, surface) fresh water. Because most of Earth's fresh water is frozen in ice caps or locked underground, the reachable share is small, so a sixth of it sitting in one lake is astonishing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika.

question: The cold, black bottom of Lake Tanganyika lies roughly 1,470 metres below its surface in East Africa, a freshwater abyss sunk well below the level of the distant Indian Ocean. Only one lake on Earth sinks deeper. Which lake is it?
context: Tanganyika's floor lies about 1,470 m (~4,800 ft) down, making it the world's second-deepest lake. Only Lake Baikal in Siberia goes deeper -- past 1,600 m. Malawi, Superior, and Victoria are all far shallower. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika; guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/497936-longest-lake.

question: Lake Tanganyika, in the East African Rift, has utterly defied the fate of most lakes. Elsewhere a glacier gouges out a hollow or a river shifts its course, and within a few thousand years silt and reeds choke the basin. About how long has Tanganyika's basin held water?
context: Lake Tanganyika is one of the oldest lakes on Earth -- its central basin began forming roughly 9-12 million years ago, when most of today's lakes did not yet exist. Ordinary lakes silt up and vanish within a few thousand years, but Tanganyika has endured for millions. Only a handful of lakes, such as Siberia's Lake Baikal, are older still. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika.

question: Geologists study the East African Rift, the huge crack in the crust that cradles Lake Tanganyika, as it opens a few millimetres wider every year with the continent slowly pulling apart. Some of them make a bold guess about the lake's far future. What do they think could become of it?
answer: it could flood and become part of a new ocean
choices: it could flood and become part of a new ocean
it could erupt into a long chain of volcanoes
it could crack apart into many smaller lakes
it could sink into the deepest dry basin on land
context: Tanganyika sits in the Albertine Rift, the western branch of the East African Rift, where the African plate is slowly splitting apart by a few millimetres a year, so it is a 'rift lake' (like Baikal). Some geologists think the rift could one day split eastern Africa from the rest and let the sea flood in, much as the Red Sea once opened between Africa and Arabia, though that could take tens of millions of years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Rift; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika.

question: Cichlid fish of more than 250 kinds, in bright colours and found nowhere else on Earth, crowd the sunlit top of Lake Tanganyika. Yet everything below about 100 metres, most of the lake by volume, is a black realm where almost nothing lives. What makes Tanganyika's vast deep so lifeless?
answer: the deep water holds no oxygen at all
choices: the deep water holds no oxygen at all
the deep water stays frozen the year round
the deep water is far too salty for life
the deep water is boiling hot near the bed
context: Tanganyika is 'meromictic': its layers almost never turn over (flushing time up to ~7,000 years). Below about 100 m the water holds no oxygen and is rich in toxic hydrogen sulfide, so life -- including its 250+ endemic cichlid species -- crowds the thin sunlit top while the huge, still deep lies dark and dead. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika; lakepedia.com/lake/tanganyika.html.

question: Steamboats and ferries carry passengers and goods between Peruvian and Bolivian ports across Lake Titicaca, though its shore lies about 3,812 metres up in the Andes, level with many mountain peaks elsewhere. Among all the world's lakes, what is Titicaca's claim to fame?
choices: the world's highest lake of any kind
context: Higher lakes and even ponds dot the Andes and Himalaya, but no full-size boats sail them -- so geographers use the careful phrase 'highest navigable.' Titicaca's steamers and cargo boats work a lake set higher than many mountain peaks. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Titicaca; britannica.com/place/Lake-Titicaca.

question: The Uros people build the very ground they stand on out on Lake Titicaca, some 60 floating islands that are home to about 1,200 people. When the bottom layer rots they lay fresh material on top. What do they weave the islands, their houses and their boats from?
context: Totora is a tall reed that grows thick in Titicaca's shallows. From this one plant the roughly 1,200 Uros make the island underfoot, the thatched house, and the curved boat with its animal-head prow -- ground, home, and craft from a single reed.
