Sources: smithsonianmag.com/travel/people-peru-live-manmade-islands-constructed-plants-180956218/; britannica.com/plant/totora.

question: Bolivia has no seacoast at all, yet it keeps thousands of sailors and a fleet of boats, based high in the Andes on Lake Titicaca. The country has drilled this navy for more than a hundred years. What does Bolivia dream its mountain-lake navy will someday accomplish?
answer: reach the open ocean from a coastline won back
choices: reach the open ocean from a coastline won back
carry an expedition down the Amazon to the Atlantic
patrol the lake frontier it shares with Peru
join a combined South American fleet at sea
context: Bolivia lost its Pacific coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879) and has been landlocked ever since. Its navy trains on Titicaca and the country still marks a yearly 'Day of the Sea,' keeping alive the hope of one day sailing from its own shore. Sources: observers.france24.com/en/20091126-Bolivia-landlocked-sea-navy-Chile-war-Pacific-ocean; britannica.com/place/Lake-Titicaca.

question: Rivers pour into Lake Titicaca, yet almost none of its water ever reaches the ocean. A single slow river, the Desaguadero, trickles south into small Lake Poopo, carrying off barely a tenth of it. Where does the other ninety percent go?
answer: it evaporates into the thin, sun-blasted mountain air
choices: it evaporates into the thin, sun-blasted mountain air
it seeps down into deep underground caverns
it freezes into glaciers along the frozen shore
it soaks away into the surrounding Altiplano marshes
context: A lake with no real outlet is called endorheic, or closed-basin. Titicaca's only drain, the Desaguadero River, carries off about 10% of its water to small Lake Poopo; the other ~90% evaporates under the fierce high-altitude sun and wind. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Titicaca.

question: Divers exploring the bed of Lake Titicaca have brought up sealed stone boxes that were lowered into the water as offerings to the gods some five centuries ago. Cracking one open, archaeologists found its gift perfectly preserved. What lay sealed inside these sacred stone boxes?
answer: a tiny llama figurine carved from spiny-oyster shell
choices: a tiny llama figurine carved from spiny-oyster shell
a clay tablet inscribed with an unknown script
the bones of a condor wrapped in fine cloth
a string of knotted cords that recorded tribute
context: Underwater archaeologists have raised more than a dozen sealed stone boxes from Titicaca's bed. One recovered intact held a tiny llama carved from Spondylus (spiny-oyster) shell -- hauled some 2,000 km from Ecuador -- beside a rolled sheet of gold, sunk about 500 years ago as a gift to the gods. Sources: sciencealert.com/an-ancient-llama-encased-in-stone-and-sunk-underwater-was-likely-a-gift-to-inca-gods; livescience.com/65126-lake-titicaca-offerings.html.

question: To the Inca, Lake Titicaca was the most sacred water in the world -- the place where creation began. In their accounts, the creator god Viracocha rose from the lake and called forth the sun, and from these same waters came Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo. According to Inca belief, who were Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo?
answer: the first Inca, sent to found their people
choices: the first Inca, sent to found their people
two mountain spirits who guard the lake's depths
the twin children of the moon and morning star
the priests who first built temples on the shore
context: In Inca belief, the creator Viracocha rose from Titicaca and made the sun, and the first Inca -- Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo -- emerged from its waters to found their people at Cusco. It is told as sacred origin, not history. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isla_del_Sol; chacanacenter.com/post/lake-titicaca-isla-del-sol.  (Legend.)

question: Farmers raise potatoes, quinoa and llamas in a mild belt right along the shore of Lake Titicaca, though the open Altiplano around it, at 3,812 metres, is so cold that little grows there. How does the huge lake let crops thrive on its shore where the bare plateau cannot?
answer: it soaks up the day's heat and releases it at night
choices: it soaks up the day's heat and releases it at night
it shelters the shore fields from the cutting plateau wind
it floods the shore each year with fertile mountain silt
it wraps the shore in mist that blocks night frost
context: The huge lake is a thermal buffer: it soaks up the day's intense sun and slowly releases that heat at night, warming a narrow shore belt enough to grow potatoes and quinoa and graze llamas where the frost-bitten Altiplano cannot. (The thin air here also holds about a third less oxygen than at sea level.) Sources: swallowsnotes.com/blog/lake-titicaca-and-high-altitude-geography; internationalparks.org/peru/Titicaca.

question: Fishing villages ring Lake Victoria, a freshwater sea of about 60,000 square kilometres, nearly as big as Ireland, shared by Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya. The lake sits almost exactly on the equator. Among all the world's lakes, what record does it hold?
answer: the largest tropical lake in the world
choices: the largest tropical lake in the world
the largest freshwater lake in the world
the deepest lake in the world
the oldest lake in the world
context: Lake Victoria covers about 59,947 km2 -- the largest lake in Africa and the largest tropical lake on Earth. But by surface area it is only the world's SECOND-largest freshwater lake; North America's Lake Superior is bigger. So 'largest tropical' and 'largest in Africa' are true, while 'largest freshwater' belongs to Superior. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria

question: An area the size of Ireland lies under the water of Lake Victoria, yet the lake breaks the pattern of great lakes like Baikal and Tanganyika, famous for their depths. Across most of its huge expanse, how deep is Victoria on average?
context: Victoria averages only about 40 m deep, with a maximum around 80-84 m -- astonishingly shallow for a lake the size of Ireland. Rift lakes like Tanganyika (~1,470 m) and Baikal (~1,600 m) sit in deep tectonic cracks; Victoria instead spreads thin across a broad, gently dished basin. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria

question: The Nile, the longest river on Earth, is born where Lake Victoria spills over its rim at a cataract, far to the south of Egypt, and runs some 6,600 km north to the Mediterranean. At which lakeside town does the Nile begin its journey?
context: The White Nile spills out of Lake Victoria at Jinja, Uganda -- historically at Ripon Falls, now drowned beneath the Nalubaale Dam -- and flows some 6,650 km to the Mediterranean, the longest river on Earth. Its other great branch, the Blue Nile, begins far away at Lake Tana in Ethiopia. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria

question: Lakes Tanganyika and Malawi, Victoria's deep neighbours, lie in giant cracks in the Great Rift Valley where the African continent is slowly splitting apart. Lake Victoria instead rests on stable old rock between the rift's two arms. How did its broad, saucer-shaped basin form?
answer: the land slowly warped and tilted, ponding rivers backward
choices: the land slowly warped and tilted, ponding rivers backward
a giant meteorite blasted the hollow out on impact
a huge volcano collapsed into a circular crater
an ice-age glacier scooped the basin out
context: Victoria sits on the stable ancient (Precambrian) shelf BETWEEN the Eastern and Western arms of the Great Rift Valley. As the plateau slowly tilted and back-warped, west-flowing rivers were ponded backward into a broad, shallow hollow -- a down-warped basin, not a rift crack. That is why it is so wide yet so shallow. Source: wldb.ilec.or.jp/Display/html/3586

question: Geologists drilling deep into the floor of Lake Victoria have pulled up cores of layered sediment. From them they judge that at least three times this enormous lake has done something almost unimaginable for so vast a body of water, most recently about 15,000 years ago. What happened to it?
answer: it dried up completely, its bed becoming dry land
choices: it dried up completely, its bed becoming dry land
it froze solid all the way to the bottom
it split apart into several separate lakes
it turned as salty as the ocean
context: Sediment cores suggest Lake Victoria has dried out completely at least three times, most recently drying up around 17,300 years ago and refilling about 14,700 years ago -- so the lake on today's bed is only a few thousand years old. Being so shallow makes it easy to lose in a long drought. (Framed as geologists' reconstruction; confidence is moderate.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria  (Legend.)

question: Fishermen on Lake Victoria, one of the most lightning-struck places on Earth, drown by the thousands every year; the Red Cross puts the toll at 3,000 to 5,000. The storms keep an eerie daily schedule, piling up over the surrounding land by afternoon and unleashing their full fury over the open water in the dead of night. What flips them out onto the lake after dark?
answer: the cooling land and still-warm lake pull the night winds together over the water
choices: the cooling land and still-warm lake pull the night winds together over the water
cold winds pour down off the surrounding highlands onto the lake at night
the moon's night-time pull drags the lake's humid air upward into storms
the lake vents warm gases after dark that spark the towering thunderheads
context: By day, thunderstorms build over the warm land around Victoria. At night the land cools but the lake holds its heat, so converging night winds drive the storms out over the water -- making Victoria one of the most thunderstorm- and lightning-active places on Earth, with the northern lake seeing storms 200-plus days a year. The Red Cross estimates 3,000-5,000 fishermen die here annually in the sudden waves. Source: science.nasa.gov (NASA Earth Observatory); nature.com/articles/ncomms12786

question: Red lava fountained from more than 130 vents in southern Iceland in June 1783, all strung along one line some 25 kilometres long at Lakagigar. What kind of eruption was it?
context: Laki's fissure -- Lakagigar, 'the craters of Laki' -- is a 25-km line of more than 130 vents that opened on 8 June 1783. A fissure eruption feeds lava up through a long crack in the crust instead of a single central cone, and Laki poured out one of the greatest lava floods in recorded history, roughly 14 cubic kilometres of basalt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: The great crack of Laki tore open across southern Iceland in 1783. Most eruptions people picture are quick and violent, a mountain that blows its top and falls quiet within days, but Laki welled up quietly and simply kept flowing. Roughly how long did it pour out lava before it stopped?
context: Laki opened on 8 June 1783 and did not stop until 7 February 1784 -- about eight months of near-continuous lava. Icelanders call the disaster the Skaftareldar, the 'Skafta Fires,' after the river valley the lava buried. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: Laki's lava burned only a handful of farms, yet within two years about four out of every five sheep in Iceland were dead. The animals were not killed by the fire itself, but by something the eruption spread across the pastures where they grazed. What killed the sheep?
answer: fluorine gas that settled on the grass
choices: fluorine gas that settled on the grass
volcanic ash that buried the grass
glacier floodwater that drowned the grass
freezing frost that killed the grass
context: About 8 million tonnes of fluorine drifted down onto Iceland's grass. Sheep that grazed it died of fluorosis -- brittle bones and swollen joints -- and roughly 80% of the island's sheep (about 190,000 animals) perished, along with about half its cattle and half its horses. The killer was the gas, not the lava. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: Iceland's people had almost nothing left to eat, with most of their sheep and about half their cattle and horses dead after Laki. The famine that followed, remembered as the Modhuhardindin or 'Mist Hardships,' swept the whole island. Roughly what share of Iceland's entire population did it kill?
choices: about one person in a hundred
context: The Modhuhardindin, the 'Mist Hardships,' killed roughly a fifth of everyone in Iceland -- about 20% of the population -- by 1785. Through poison gas and famine, a crack in the ground had come close to starving an entire nation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki

question: Benjamin Franklin puzzled over a pale bluish haze in the summer of 1783, a 'dry fog' that hung over Europe and part of North America so thick it dimmed the sun. He wrote that the sun's rays were so weak 'they would scarce kindle brown paper.' Where had the fog come from?
answer: sulfur gas carried south from Iceland
choices: sulfur gas carried south from Iceland
smoke from vast wildfires in Russia
dust blown from the Sahara desert
ash from an eruption of Italy's Vesuvius
context: Laki released about 120 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide -- roughly six times the amount from the huge 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption -- and winds carried it across Europe as a choking 'dry fog.' The English naturalist Gilbert White wrote that the sun 'looked as blank as a clouded moon, and shed a rust-coloured ferruginous light.' Franklin's guess at a distant volcanic cause was among the first times anyone tied a faraway eruption to Europe's weather. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki ; Benjamin Franklin, 'Meteorological Imaginations and Conjectures' (1784).

question: Jon Steingrimsson, the pastor at Kirkjubaejarklaustur, gathered his people in their small church in July 1783 as lava from Laki crept toward it, and preached his famous 'Fire Sermon.' By the time the service ended, the lava had stopped at the settlement's edge. Icelanders named the spot for the day it was saved. What do they call it?
context: The lava halted at the settlement's edge, and the spot has been called Eldmessutangi -- 'Fire Mass Point' -- ever since; eldmessa is Icelandic for the 'Fire Sermon' Reverend Jon Steingrimsson preached there on 20 July 1783. Whether the sermon truly stopped the flow or the lava simply reached a natural barrier, Icelanders have told the tale for more than two centuries, and Steingrimsson also kept a careful eyewitness diary of the whole disaster. Told as a legend. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki ; https://www.forbes.com/sites/robinandrews/2018/04/24/the-legend-of-the-icelandic-pastor-who-appeared-to-stop-a-lava-flow/

question: Laki's haze darkened France in 1783, and some writers link it to the cruel winters and poor harvests of the years that followed; in 1789 the hungry country exploded into revolution. They cast the volcano as a secret spark of the Bastille's fall, but historians are divided and warn that the leap risks a classic reasoning trap. Which trap is it?
answer: mistaking a striking coincidence in time for a proven cause
choices: mistaking a striking coincidence in time for a proven cause
mistaking one vivid example for proof of a general rule
mistaking a claim's popularity for evidence that it is true
mistaking the lack of any disproof for solid proof
context: The link is genuinely debated -- some serious historians argue Laki's ruined harvests deepened France's hunger and unrest, while others doubt it mattered much. The trap is treating the mere fact that the eruption came first as proof that it caused the Revolution; logicians call this 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' -- 'after this, therefore because of this.' A striking coincidence in time is a reason to investigate, never a finished proof. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laki ; https://news.climate.columbia.edu/2011/04/05/maybe-ben-franklin-was-wrong

question: Workers in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, around the 12th century, shaped eleven whole churches for King Lalibela out of the bedrock itself, still joined to the ground, with nothing but hammers and chisels. How did they carve every one of them out of the living rock?
answer: They chiselled down from the surface, cutting the rock away all around each church.
choices: They chiselled down from the surface, cutting the rock away all around each church.
They carved deep caves into a cliff face and smoothed the fronts into grand facades.
They hollowed long halls back into a hillside, roofed by the natural slope above.
They dug soft rock into a warren of hidden underground rooms and chapels.
context: The whole wonder of Lalibela is that these churches were EXCAVATED, not built: with hammers and chisels the workers cut straight down into one mass of volcanic rock, chipping away everything around each church until it stood as a single unbroken piece of the mountain -- no bricks, no mortar, and no foundation, because nothing was ever stacked up. Four of the eleven were freed on every side; the other seven still share one wall with the cliff. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela' (all 11 carved top-down from scoriaceous basalt with only hammers and chisels); Met Museum essay.

question: King Lalibela had eleven churches cut from solid volcanic rock in the highlands of Ethiopia some 800 years ago, and the town around them now bears his name. Who fills those churches now, day after day?
answer: White-robed Ethiopian Orthodox priests and pilgrims, gathered to worship.
choices: White-robed Ethiopian Orthodox priests and pilgrims, gathered to worship.
Archaeologists, sifting the floors for the buried treasure of the Zagwe kings.
Curators and ticketed tourists, filing past altars roped off behind glass.
A caretaker or two, guarding stone halls that emptied long ago.
context: These are still LIVING churches. Eight hundred years on, white-robed Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo priests hold daily worship, and thousands of pilgrims -- many wrapped in white cotton shawls called netela -- fill the site for festivals like Genna (Ethiopian Christmas) and Timkat/Timket (Epiphany). Lalibela was never abandoned to become a ruin. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela' (active Ethiopian Orthodox churches in daily use).

question: A visitor crossing the plain toward Bete Giyorgis, Lalibela's Church of St George, cannot see it at all until he reaches the rim of its deep pit and looks straight down onto its roof. The path down to it winds through a narrow canyon that turns into a tunnel. What shape is the roof?
answer: A Greek cross, with four equal arms.
choices: A Greek cross, with four equal arms.
A long rectangle, like a great hall.
A perfect circle, ringed by pillars.
context: Bete Giyorgis, the Church of St George, is carved from red volcanic tuff and stands roughly 15 m tall (some sources say ~12 m) inside a quarried pit whose trench measures about 25 m by 25 m. You approach unseen down a spiralling man-made canyon that becomes a tunnel, with sheer drops on every side, and first meet the church by looking down onto its Greek-cross roof. It was the last of the eleven built and is the best-preserved -- often called the 'Eighth Wonder of the World'; its three-tiered plinth is traditionally said to represent Noah's Ark. Source: Wikipedia, 'Church of Saint George, Lalibela.'

question: Saladin, the great Muslim general, captured Jerusalem from the crusaders in 1187, and the long pilgrimage from Ethiopia to the shrines of the Holy Land became hard and deadly. King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty answered by having eleven churches carved into the living rock of his highland capital. What did he want them to be?
answer: A new Jerusalem, a holy land his people could reach at home.
choices: A new Jerusalem, a holy land his people could reach at home.
A war-shrine, a blessing on the army sent to retake the city.
A monk's refuge, a haven for those fleeing the Holy Land.
A relic-treasury, a vault for what the faithful saved before the fall.
context: King Gebre Meskel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty (reigned about 1181-1221) built his New Jerusalem after Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187 and cut off the Ethiopian pilgrimage route to the Holy Land -- so he brought the Holy Land home in stone. Source: Met Museum essay, 'The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela'; Wikipedia.

question: Bete Medhane Alem stands open to the Ethiopian sky inside its own huge quarried pit at Lalibela, its columns and long halls all hewn from a single piece of rock. It is the grandest of the eleven churches, and its name means 'Saviour of the World.' Among all the churches on Earth, what record does it hold?
answer: It is the largest monolithic church in the world.
choices: It is the largest monolithic church in the world.
It is the oldest surviving church in all of Africa.
It is the only church ever cut in the shape of a star.
It is the highest church standing anywhere on Earth.
context: Bete Medhane Alem ('House of the Savior of the World') measures about 33.5 m by 23.5 m and is believed to be the largest monolithic (single-rock) church in the world -- an entire cathedral-sized building hollowed out of one mass of stone. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela.'

question: A channel cut through the rock at Lalibela divides the northern churches from the southern ones. King Lalibela's carvers shaped the ground between the churches to echo the geography of the Holy Land, and they gave this trench a sacred name. What did they call it?
context: The channel named the River Jordan divides the churches into a northern group of five and a southern group of five, with Bete Giyorgis standing on its own -- mirroring the Holy Land and symbolizing an earthly and a heavenly Jerusalem on either bank. The real Jordan is the river where Christians believe Christ was baptized. The churches are all linked by a maze of tunnels and trenches cut through the rock. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela.'

question: Heavy summer rains pound the highlands of northern Ethiopia, and at Lalibela every church sits at the bottom of an open pit in solid rock, a stone well the rain could fill like a bucket. To keep the sunken churches from flooding, what did the medieval carvers shape into the rock?
answer: Sloping roofs and drainage trenches, angled to run the water off.
choices: Sloping roofs and drainage trenches, angled to run the water off.
Sump pits gouged into each church floor to swallow the runoff.
Stepped terraces quarried above the pits to turn the rain aside.
A rock moat and carved spouts cut around each church.
context: Because the churches sit in pits below ground, the medieval carvers cut drainage channels and trenches to carry the highland rains away, and angled the free-standing roofs to shed rainwater -- everything shaped from the rock itself, nothing added on. Some of these original channels are now clogged with centuries of sediment, which is why water damage threatens the site today. Source: Met Museum essay, 'The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela.'

question: Medieval Ethiopians told a wondrous story to explain how the vast churches of Lalibela rose so fast. By day the workmen chiselled the rock; by night, the tradition holds, the carving went on without them, and each dawn found twice as much stone cut away. According to the legend, who worked the night shift?
answer: Angels, carving through the night to double each day's work.
choices: Angels, carving through the night to double each day's work.
The king himself, who could not rest until it was finished.
Pilgrims, who arrived in the dark from every corner of the land.
The spirits of the mountain the churches were cut from.
context: This is a devotional LEGEND, not history. King Lalibela's own medieval hagiography claims he completed all eleven churches in twenty-four years with the help of angels; some versions say angels finished an entire church in a single night while the men slept, doubling each day's work. The story is told as a sign of holiness -- and the churches' astonishing scale is the real wonder that inspired it. Source: hagiographic tradition, per africanarguments.org and ancient-origins.net.

question: Hawaii's Kilauea and Ethiopia's Erta Ale keep churning lakes of molten lava in their craters that never freeze over. Almost none of Earth's more than a thousand active volcanoes do the same. About how many hold a lava lake at any one time?
context: At any given time only about eight volcanoes on Earth hold a permanent, churning lava lake -- a truly exclusive club. The known set has included Nyiragongo (DR Congo), Erta Ale (Ethiopia), Kilauea (Hawaii), Erebus (Antarctica), Masaya (Nicaragua), Ambrym (Vanuatu), Mount Michael, and Villarrica (Chile). A lava lake is rare because the volcano must stay open and hot enough to keep the rock molten without erupting it all away or sealing over. Source: Wikipedia, 'Erta Ale' (only about eight lava lakes worldwide as of 2019).

question: A lake of molten lava churns and glows red in the wide crater of Mount Nyiragongo, which rises 3,470 metres over the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Just 12 km downhill, a crowded city of perhaps a million people sleeps every night in its glow. Which city lives in the shadow of Nyiragongo's fire?
context: Goma, home to perhaps a million people (estimates run from under 800,000 to more than two million) on the shore of Lake Kivu, sits about 12 km from Nyiragongo's summit crater and one of the largest lava lakes ever known. Living in the volcano's nightly red glow makes Goma one of the most dangerous city sites on Earth, which is why Nyiragongo was named a 'Decade Volcano' in 1991, singled out for urgent study because it is both very active and close to a huge population. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Nyiragongo'; Wikipedia, 'Goma.'

question: The crater wall of Mount Nyiragongo split open on 10 January 1977, and its whole lava lake drained out in under an hour. The flood tore downhill at about 60 km/h, faster than most people can run, though most lava creeps slowly enough for a person to walk away from it. Why does Nyiragongo's lava run so fast?
answer: Its lava is unusually thin -- very low in silica
choices: Its lava is unusually thin -- very low in silica
Its lava is unusually hot -- far hotter than most lava
Its lava is unusually gassy -- frothing with bubbles
Its lava is unusually acidic -- rich in sulfur
context: Nyiragongo's lava is unusually low in silica (alkali-rich, almost feldspar-free rock), which makes it extraordinarily thin and fluid -- thick, silica-rich lava barely creeps. So when the crater wall cracked on 10 January 1977, the lake drained in under an hour and raced downhill at up to about 60 km/h, the fastest lava flow ever recorded, killing at least 50 people. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Nyiragongo.'

question: On a continent buried under ice, one mountain keeps a lake of fire churning in its crater all year long. It rises over frozen Ross Island and is the southernmost active volcano on Earth. Its red glow flickers against the glaciers around it. Which volcano is this pool of fire on the ice?
context: Mount Erebus, on Ross Island, is the southernmost active volcano on Earth (3,792 m) and holds one of the world's few permanent lava lakes -- a pool of fire ringed by Antarctic ice, and the only volcano now erupting rare phonolite lava. Explorer James Clark Ross named it in 1841 after his ship HMS Erebus, itself named for Erebus, the Greek personification of underworld darkness -- so a volcano of fire on the ice carries the name of the dark realm of Hades. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Erebus.'

question: The volcano that keeps a lava lake burning amid Antarctica's ice breathes out a fine mist of something precious with its gases, about 80 grams of it every day. Tiny crystals of it ride the wind and settle in the snow up to 1,000 km from the crater. What treasure does the volcano breathe into the polar air?
context: Scientists estimate Mount Erebus releases roughly 80 grams of gold vapour a day, condensing out of its hot volcanic gases, and tiny gold crystals blown from it have been found in the snow up to 1,000 km away -- a volcano quietly gilding the Antarctic snow. Source: Wikipedia, 'Mount Erebus.'

question: The Maasai and Sonjo peoples have made their homes for centuries in the shadow of Ol Doinyo Lengai, the fire-mountain of northern Tanzania that erupts the world's strangest lava. The name they gave it long ago is the one everyone still uses. What does Ol Doinyo Lengai mean in the Maasai language?
context: In the Maasai language Ol Doinyo Lengai means 'the Mountain of God' -- to the Maasai and Sonjo peoples it is the earthly home of their creator deity, Engai, and they hold the fire-mountain sacred rather than fearful (their religious tradition, presented as they hold it). Source: Wikipedia, 'Ol Doinyo Lengai.'  (Legend.)

question: Hai Tong, a Buddhist monk, began carving a huge Buddha into a cliff at Leshan, China, in 713. The cliff stood high above the spot where three strong rivers crash together into one wild channel. What did he hope his giant Buddha would do?
answer: calm the deadly rapids that wrecked passing boats
choices: calm the deadly rapids that wrecked passing boats
hold back the river's destructive summer floods
drive off the water demons haunting the junction
win the region years of plentiful harvests
context: Hai Tong began the Leshan Giant Buddha around 713 CE, hoping the enormous holy figure gazing over the water would settle the deadly rapids that kept wrecking boats where the rivers met. Source: travelchinaguide.com (Hai Tong initiated the project around 713 CE, motivated by boat accidents at the confluence of three rivers).

question: A grown adult at the foot of the Leshan Giant Buddha barely reaches the top of one stone toe. Carved from a red sandstone cliff in Sichuan in the 8th century, the Buddha sits about 71 metres tall, as high as a 20-storey building. What is just one of his feet wide enough to hold?
answer: a crowd of over a hundred people
choices: a crowd of over a hundred people
a single row of parked market carts
a small grove of newly planted trees
a mere handful of people at a time
context: The Leshan Giant Buddha stands about 71 metres tall — the largest pre-modern stone Buddha ever carved — and it is built to a scale that shrinks any visitor: its instep runs roughly 8.5 metres across, broad enough for more than a hundred people to crowd onto a single foot, while each ear stretches some 7 metres long. Source: advantour.com (71 metres / 233 feet tall; largest stone Buddha in the world; foot platform ~8.5 metres across, holds over a hundred people; ears 7 metres long).

question: Three separate rivers slam together into one roiling flow below the cliff where the Leshan Giant Buddha sits in Sichuan, at what was once one of old China's most feared river crossings. The great stone figure gazes out over the churning junction. Which three rivers meet at the Buddha's feet?
answer: the Min, the Dadu, and the Qingyi
choices: the Min, the Dadu, and the Qingyi
the Yangtze, the Yellow, and the Wei
the Mekong, the Salween, and the Yalong
the Han, the Xiang, and the Gan
context: The Buddha sits exactly at the confluence of the Min, Dadu, and Qingyi rivers, and gazes across the water toward sacred Mount Emei — inspiring the local saying, 'The mountain is a Buddha and the Buddha is a mountain.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan_Giant_Buddha (confluence of the Min, Dadu, and Qingyi rivers; faces Mount Emei).

question: Sichuan's heavy monsoon rains have beaten on the Leshan Giant Buddha for more than 1,200 years, yet his soft red sandstone has barely worn away, though he is carved right into a cliff. What hidden work by his Tang-dynasty makers has kept the rain off him?
answer: a concealed system of drainage channels
choices: a concealed system of drainage channels
a concealed lining of waterproof lacquer
a concealed layer of lime-and-straw plaster
a concealed reservoir that stores the rainwater
context: The Tang builders cut concealed gutters and channels through the Buddha's coiled hair, its collar, its chest, and behind its ears; these quietly carry rainwater away from the soft sandstone, and the system has kept the statue from crumbling for over 1,200 years. Source: advantour.com (hidden drainage channels within the hair, collar, chest, and behind the ears to divert rainwater).

question: While the Leshan Giant Buddha was being carved, greedy local officials tried to seize the donation money the monk Hai Tong had gathered for the work. According to legend, Hai Tong stopped them with a single shocking act that shamed them into leaving the funds alone. What did he do?
answer: he gouged out one of his own eyes
choices: he gouged out one of his own eyes
he chained himself to the cliff face
he swore to fast until work resumed
he knelt in the rapids and prayed
context: The story goes that Hai Tong gouged out one of his own eyes to prove his sincerity, and the ashamed officials backed off. It is a legend rather than documented fact, but it captures the fierce devotion of the monk who began a Buddha he would never live to see finished. Source: advantour.com ('After he proved it by gouging out one of his own eyes, the officials felt ashamed').

question: The carvers of the Leshan Giant Buddha hacked a staggering amount of stone off the cliff face, and every block tumbled straight down into the three rivers below. Over the long decades of work, all that fallen rock did something to the very water the monks feared. What did the dumped stone do to the river?
answer: it reshaped the churning currents of the junction
choices: it reshaped the churning currents of the junction
it piled up a broad beach where boats could moor
it raised the riverbed and threw up new rapids
it split the flow around a new midstream island
context: Whether or not it soothed the river in the way its builders prayed for, the carving genuinely tamed the water: the enormous volume of rock hacked off the cliff and dumped below reshaped the currents where the three rivers met and made the crossing safer for boats — an accidental piece of river engineering. Source: advantour.com ('the enormous volume of stone was removed from the cliff and deposited into the river below... unintentionally altered the currents and made the waters genuinely safer for navigation').

question: White and red walls climb thirteen storeys up Marpo Ri, a hill above Lhasa, hiding more than a thousand rooms. For centuries the Dalai Lamas, the spiritual leaders of Tibetan Buddhism, spent their winters behind them. What is this huge landmark called?
context: The Potala Palace rises thirteen storeys on the Red Hill (Marpo Ri) above Lhasa, holding more than a thousand rooms. It was the Dalai Lamas' winter residence for centuries and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potala_Palace

question: The great palace on the Red Hill above Lhasa spreads 400 metres wide, its stone walls as much as five metres thick and some 200,000 statues inside. It stands some 3,700 metres above the sea. Which record does it hold among the world's palaces?
context: Though the Potala sprawls 400 m wide with more than a thousand rooms and some 200,000 statues, its true world record is altitude: standing about 3,700 m up on the Red Hill above Lhasa, it is widely called the highest palace on Earth, where the thin plateau air holds roughly a third less oxygen than air at sea level. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potala_Palace

question: Pilgrims travel for weeks or even months to pray at the temples of Lhasa, high on the Tibetan Plateau, the sacred heart of Tibetan Buddhism for over a thousand years. The city's name joins two Tibetan words, lha and sa. What does 'Lhasa' mean?
context: In Tibetan, lha means 'god' and sa means 'place' — so Lhasa is the 'Place of the Gods,' a fitting name for the sacred heart of Tibetan Buddhism high on the plateau. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhasa

question: One Dalai Lama began building the great white-and-red palace on the Red Hill above Lhasa in 1645, meaning it to unite his country under his rule and to stand as the seat of Tibetan power. It became the winter home of the Dalai Lamas. Which Dalai Lama began it?
context: The Great Fifth began the present Potala in 1645. Its outer shell rose in only about three years, but the painted and gilded interior took forty-five more years to finish — long after his own death. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potala_Palace

question: Two palaces stand joined as one on Marpo Ri above Lhasa, each named for its colour. The outer White Palace held Tibet's government offices and the Dalai Lama's own rooms; the inner Red Palace, finished around 1694, was built for sacred purposes alone. What lies at the heart of the Red Palace?
answer: the golden tombs of past Dalai Lamas
choices: the golden tombs of past Dalai Lamas
a vast library of Buddhist scriptures
the great assembly hall of monks
a shrine of a thousand buddhas
context: The Potala's halves are named for their colours: the White Palace (Potrang Karpo, 1649) for government and living quarters, the Red Palace (Potrang Marpo, 1690–1694) for chapels and the jewelled golden funerary stupas of past Dalai Lamas. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potala_Palace

question: About a kilometre east of the Potala, in the heart of old Lhasa, stands the site that Tibetan Buddhists revere above every other. Pilgrims who have travelled for months drop to the ground and stretch full-length toward its doors, again and again. Which sacred place is this?
context: The Jokhang, founded by King Songtsen Gampo around 640 CE, is the holiest shrine in Tibetan Buddhism. It enshrines the Jowo Shakyamuni, a gilded Buddha said to portray him at age twelve, brought to Lhasa by the Tang princess Wencheng — Tibet's single most revered statue. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jokhang

question: Tibetan Buddhists believe each Dalai Lama is a living embodiment of a great bodhisattva, an enlightened being who chooses to stay in the world to help others. The Dalai Lamas' palace in Lhasa, the Potala, takes its name from Mount Potalaka, said in Buddhist myth to be that bodhisattva's paradise-home. Which figure of Buddhist devotion is this?
choices: Maitreya, the buddha of the future
Amitabha, the buddha of pure light
context: 'Potala' comes from Mount Potalaka, the mythical mountain-paradise of Avalokiteshvara — Chenrezig in Tibetan — the bodhisattva of compassion whom the Dalai Lamas are believed to embody. The palace was thus imagined as his paradise made earthly on the Red Hill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Potalaka  (Legend.)

question: Desi Sangye Gyatso was regent in Lhasa when the Dalai Lama who began the great palace died in 1682, with its Red Palace still years from finished. The regent feared the work would halt if the news spread, so for more than a decade he kept a secret. What did he do?
answer: hid the death, saying the ruler was in long retreat
choices: hid the death, saying the ruler was in long retreat
said the ruler had gone on pilgrimage to India
sealed the palace gates until the work was done
announced the ruler had begun a lifelong silent vow
context: When the Great Fifth died in 1682 with the Red Palace unfinished, his regent Desi Sangye Gyatso concealed the death for some fifteen years, telling Tibet the ruler had withdrawn into a long meditation retreat, so that work on the Potala would not stop; on great occasions an old monk who resembled the Dalai Lama was even hired to pose in his place. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Potala_Palace; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5th_Dalai_Lama

question: An unbroken river of pilgrims shuffles from dawn along a stone-paved path about a kilometre long that circles the holiest temple at the heart of Lhasa. They spin handheld prayer wheels and keep the temple on their right as they walk it clockwise. What is this pilgrim circuit called?
context: The Barkhor is the middle of Lhasa's three sacred circuits (the inner Nangkhor, the middle Barkhor, and the outer Lingkhor). Pilgrims always walk it clockwise, keeping the holy Jokhang on their right, turning prayer wheels as they go. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barkhor

question: Niagara Falls throws up a huge cloud of spray as the river plunges over its cliff, and on a sunny day a bright rainbow glows among the millions of drifting droplets, though no rain is falling. What is really making the colors?
answer: Each raindrop bending the sunlight like a tiny glass prism
choices: Each raindrop bending the sunlight like a tiny glass prism
Sunlight bouncing off the flat river surface below
The droplets glowing with their own faint color
Sunlight scattering through colored dust in the air
context: Every clear, round droplet works like a miniature prism: sunlight refracts (bends) as it enters, reflects off the drop's back wall, then refracts again on the way out — fanning white light into its colors. Millions of drops doing this at once paint the arc you see. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: Suppose you stand on a viewing platform at Niagara Falls, facing the drifting spray on a sunny day. Where must the sun be for a rainbow to appear in the mist?
context: A rainbow always centers on the antisolar point — the spot directly opposite the sun — so the sun sits at your back and the bow appears ahead of you. The bright arc rides about 42 degrees out from that center point. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: A rainbow bends across the mist whenever the sun shines on the spray at Niagara Falls, where the river thunders over its cliff. At Niagara or anywhere else, the colors of every rainbow stack in the same order from the outer edge of the arc to the inner. Which color rides along the outer rim?
context: Red rides the outer edge and violet the inner, in every rainbow. Red light refracts (bends) the least as it passes through each drop, so it lands farthest out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: After a storm clears at Niagara, a second, fainter rainbow sometimes appears just outside the bright one — a 'double rainbow.' In that outer bow the light has bounced twice inside each drop instead of once. What has that done to its band of colors compared with the main bow?
answer: The color order reverses, with violet outside and red inside
choices: The color order reverses, with violet outside and red inside
The colors hold their usual order but the bow looks fainter
The colors blur together into one pale, whitish band
The bow keeps red outside but loses its blues and greens
context: The extra internal bounce flips the sequence: the secondary bow shows violet on the outside and red on the inside, a mirror of the primary. It looks fainter because light escapes at each reflection. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: When a double rainbow hangs over Niagara Falls, the ribbon of sky trapped between the bright inner bow and the faint outer bow looks noticeably darker than the sky on either side. This dark strip between the two bows has its own name. What is it called?
context: It is Alexander's band, after Alexander of Aphrodisias, the Greek philosopher who first described it around 200 AD. It looks dark because the raindrops send almost no light back to your eye from that in-between angle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

question: A hiker who catches a moonbow in the spray of Victoria Falls is often startled, for to the naked eye the arc looks ghostly and almost colorless, a pale bow in the dark. Yet a camera left open on a tripod records it in full rainbow color. Why does the eye see only white?
answer: Moonlight is far too dim to fire the eye's color-sensing cone cells
choices: Moonlight is far too dim to fire the eye's color-sensing cone cells
The eye's color cones cluster near the center, missing the wide arc
The eye adapts slowly to the dark, and color is the last sense to return
At such distance the eye can no longer separate one color from another
context: Color vision comes from cone cells, which need fairly bright light to respond. Moonlight is sunlight reflected off the moon and dimmed hundreds of thousands of times — below the cones' threshold — so only the rod cells (which see in gray) fire, and the moonbow reads as white. A camera's long exposure gathers enough light to record the real colors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonbow

question: One waterfall's steep gorge traps its mist so well that, alone in the whole Western Hemisphere, it shows moonbows on a dependable schedule when a bright moon hangs low and the wind cannot scatter the spray. Which waterfall is it?
choices: Iguazu Falls, on the Brazil–Argentina border
Niagara Falls, on the US–Canada border
context: It's Cumberland Falls in Kentucky, nicknamed the 'Niagara of the South' (about 68 ft high, 125 ft wide). Its narrow gorge traps the spray so the wind can't disperse it, making its moonbows uniquely reliable. Niagara once showed moonbows regularly too, but modern light pollution has drowned them out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_Falls

question: A damp grey sea fog coats Lima's streets each morning for half the year, though the city gets less than an inch of rain a year. It burns off by noon and gives Lima the nickname 'the grey city.' What do the locals call it?
context: The garúa is Lima's damp gray sea-fog. The city gets under 25 mm of rain a year -- one of the driest capitals on Earth -- yet humidity averages 84%, and from roughly May to November the low cloud-ceiling gives Lima its nickname 'the gray city.' The moisture usually burns off by afternoon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima (climate); geodiode.com/lima.

question: Glass towers and busy traffic surround a strange mound in Lima's smart Miraflores district, 22 metres high and built from millions of hand-made mud bricks. A coastal people raised this adobe pyramid around 500 AD, long before the Inca ever reached this coast. What is it called?
context: Huaca Pucllana in Miraflores is a seven-platform adobe pyramid about 22 m tall, raised by the pre-Inca Lima culture (~200-700 AD), roughly a thousand years before the Inca reached the coast. Archaeologists found benches and pits where its people made offerings of fish and sea creatures to their water gods. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huaca_Pucllana; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima_culture.

question: The builders of a great adobe pyramid in Lima stood their mud bricks on end and spaced them a little apart, like books on a shelf. This coast is among the most earthquake-shaken on Earth. When the ground heaves, what does the design let the pyramid do?
answer: flex and settle back into place
choices: flex and settle back into place
crack apart and spread along its base
context: The builders stood the adobe bricks on end and spaced them apart -- the 'librero' or bookshelf method. The air-gaps let the whole pyramid flex and settle rather than crack, which is how a mud-brick structure has ridden out about 1,500 years of earthquakes on one of the world's most seismic coasts. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huaca_Pucllana (construction).

question: Under the Basilica of San Francisco in old Lima runs a maze of catacombs. They served as the city's graveyard until 1810. As many as 70,000 of the colonial dead were buried down there, then forgotten. Workers reopened the tunnels in 1951. How did they find the bones laid out?
answer: sorted by type into neat geometric wells ringed with skulls
choices: sorted by type into neat geometric wells ringed with skulls
heaped in a jumbled pile where the tunnels once flooded
sealed one by one in small name-carved marble niches
burned to ash and kept in long rows of clay urns
context: The catacombs under the Basilica of San Francisco served as Lima's cemetery until 1810; an estimated 70,000 colonial dead lie there. Rediscovered in 1951, the bones are sorted and stacked in geometric designs, with skulls and femurs ringing circular wells. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_and_Convent_of_San_Francisco,_Lima.

question: Scribes at Knossos wrote their Linear B tablets on soft, sun-dried clay and wiped them clean for reuse within the year. Yet archaeologists dug them up 3,000 years later, perfectly legible, thanks to the very catastrophe that ended the palace. What destroyed Knossos?
context: The Linear B tablets were unbaked jottings meant to be wiped and reused within the year — but when the palace burned, the blaze fired the wet clay like a kiln, turning throwaway notes into near-indestructible bricks. The same palace fires preserved Linear B tablets at Pylos and Mycenae on the mainland. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B)

question: Sir Arthur Evans dug up the Linear B tablets at Knossos, and for fifty years no one could read them, while scholars dreamed they might hold lost poems or secret prayers of a forgotten faith. When the script was finally cracked in 1952, the truth proved far more ordinary. What was written on the tablets?
context: Linear B tablets are almost all palace accounts — inventories of sheep, wheat, olive oil, chariot wheels, spears and swords. A precious few record offerings to gods whose names we still know: Zeus, Poseidon and Athena, worshipped in the Aegean more than 3,000 years ago. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B)

question: A whole lost people came to light when Sir Arthur Evans dug at Knossos, with grand palaces and their own writing, yet history had kept no name for them. Evans borrowed the name of the Labyrinth's legendary king, who demanded tribute from Athens. What did he call this lost people?
context: Evans coined 'Minoan' after King Minos, the mythical Cretan king of the Labyrinth story. He also named the two scripts he dug up: Linear A (the older, the Minoans' own) and Linear B (the younger). (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans)  (Legend.)

question: Michael Ventris sounded out the signs of the Knossos tablets in 1952, when everyone took them for some lost, strange tongue, the private speech of a vanished people. The words that came back were ones scholars knew at once from far later writings. What language did Linear B turn out to be?
context: Ventris proved Linear B was an early form of Greek — the language of the Mycenaeans, the mainland Greeks who ruled Crete — pushing written Greek back some 500 years before Homer. He announced it on BBC radio on 1 July 1952; the broadcast drew the classicist John Chadwick in to help him. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B)

question: Like a wartime codebreaker, Michael Ventris sorted the signs of Linear B into a grid long before he knew what a single one meant. His way in was a gamble on a handful of words that recur across the Knossos tablets: if he guessed rightly what they stood for, their sound-values would crack open the whole grid. What did Ventris rightly bet these key words were?
context: Ventris reasoned that words found only on the Crete tablets must be Cretan place-names — and three of them, Knossos, Amnisos and Tulissos, became his 'wedge' into the grid, fixing real sound-values at last. He built on Alice Kober, an American scholar whose study of repeating word-endings (her 'triplets') proved the language changed word-forms like Greek or Latin; she died in 1950, before the solution. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decipherment_of_Linear_B)

question: Carl Blegen dug up a single tablet at Pylos, on the southern mainland, that gave the clinching proof Michael Ventris had read Linear B correctly. Beside a small drawing, Ventris's sound-values spelled out the word ti-ri-po-de, and the picture showed exactly the thing that word names. What was drawn beside it?
context: The 'tripod tablet' (PY Ta 641) was Ventris's clincher: ti-ri-po-de (Greek tripode, 'tripod') sat beside a three-legged pot, and a word he read as 'four-handled' sat beside a pot with four handles. Carl Blegen wrote that it fit so perfectly it seemed too good to be true. Our own word 'tripod' descends straight from that ancient one. (classics.cam.ac.uk; linearbknossosmycenae.wordpress.com)

question: The older script buried beneath Linear B at Knossos, Linear A, still defeats every scholar who tries it, though Michael Ventris made the younger one speak again. Its sounds are no obstacle: because Linear B borrowed its signs, scholars can read Linear A's syllables aloud with ease. One thing, never yet found, would finally crack it. What is that missing key?
context: Linear A records the Minoans' own, still-unknown language. Because Linear B borrowed its signs, scholars can even pronounce Linear A aloud — but sounding out words in a language nobody knows yields nothing but noise. Cracking it would take a bilingual inscription tying it to a language we already understand (the way the Rosetta Stone's Greek text unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs) — yet no such bilingual, no surviving relative language, and no other key has ever turned up. So the Minoans keep their silence. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_A)

question: Vasco da Gama sailed from the Belém docks at Lisbon's western edge with four small ships in the summer of 1497. The voyage made Lisbon a launch point of the Age of Discovery and little Portugal a great naval power. What did his fleet open for Europe?
choices: the first crossing to the Americas
the first voyage around the world
context: Vasco da Gama's fleet rounded Africa and reached India in 1498, opening the sea route that made small Portugal a maritime power and Lisbon a gateway of the Age of Discovery. The Belém Tower still guards the shore where the ships set out. (Source: Wikipedia, Belém Tower / Vasco da Gama 1497.)

question: Lisbon's churches were packed for All Saints' Day Mass on 1 November 1755 when an earthquake flattened much of the city, and about forty minutes later a tsunami surged up the Tagus from the Atlantic. What third disaster struck the city that day?
answer: a fire lit by toppled church candles
choices: a fire lit by toppled church candles
a plague carried by rats off the ships
a flood from a dam that burst upriver
a lava flow from a volcano out at sea
context: Candles lit for All Saints' Day were burning in the packed churches when the quake struck; toppled, they set fires that spread through the wrecked city and burned for days, after the tsunami that had swept in about 40 minutes after the shaking. Three disasters in a single morning. (Source: Wikipedia, 1755 Lisbon earthquake.)

question: Sailors on the Tagus docks had lived through the earthquake that wrecked Lisbon on All Saints' Day, 1755, but a giant wave was only minutes away. First the river did something strange, and any old salt on the wharves knew it at once for a terrible warning. What did the water do?
answer: it pulled back and bared the muddy seabed
choices: it pulled back and bared the muddy seabed
it rose slowly and swallowed the quays
it spun into a whirlpool off the river mouth
it turned glassy and eerily still
context: The retreating sea is the classic tsunami warning — the trough of the wave arrives before the crest, sucking the water out. Survivors described a plain of mud strewn with old shipwrecks and lost cargo, exposed for minutes before the water roared back in. (Source: Wikipedia, 1755 Lisbon earthquake.)

question: The great stone vault of Lisbon's medieval Carmo Convent crashed down on the congregation hearing Mass there on the morning of the 1755 earthquake. When the city rebuilt, it treated this one ruin differently from every other. What did Lisbon do with the Carmo Convent?
answer: left it roofless and open to the sky, as a memorial
choices: left it roofless and open to the sky, as a memorial
rebuilt it grander than before, crowned with a dome
cleared the ruins to open a new public square
hauled its stones away to build elsewhere
context: Lisbon never re-roofed the Convento do Carmo. Its skeletal Gothic arches still stand open to the sky in the city center as a memorial to 1 November 1755, and the shell now houses an archaeological museum. (Source: golisbon.com, Carmo Church; corroborated Grokipedia, Carmo Convent.)

question: On All Saints' Day, the Lisbon quake killed thousands of worshippers as they knelt at Mass. The most devout were struck down in the act of prayer, inside their own churches. Across Europe, the horror pushed thinkers like Voltaire to reopen one old, painful debate. Which debate did the Lisbon disaster thrust back to the center of European thought?
context: That so many faithful died at church on a holy day forced Europe to confront the 'problem of evil.' Voltaire pressed the question in his Poème sur le désastre de Lisbonne (1756) and mocked easy optimism through Dr. Pangloss in Candide (1759); Rousseau replied by blaming crowded cities. (Source: Wikipedia, Poème sur le désastre de Lisbonne; 1755 Lisbon earthquake.)

question: Sebastião de Carvalho, the king's minister and later Marquis of Pombal, sent every parish priest a list of questions after the 1755 earthquake. How long did the ground shake? Which way did the buildings fall? Did the sea rise or drop first? The answers earned him a founding place in one science. Which science did his survey help start?
context: Pombal's questionnaire asked how long the shaking lasted, which way walls fell, and whether the sea rose or fell first and how high. Archived at the Torre do Tombo, the priests' replies form the first large-scale objective survey of an earthquake — a founding document of modern seismology, the science of earthquakes. (Source: Wikipedia, 1755 Lisbon earthquake.)

question: Sebastião de Carvalho, the future Marquis of Pombal, rebuilt Lisbon's ruined lower town on a clean grid after the 1755 earthquake, determined that the new buildings would survive the next quake. Inside their thick masonry walls he hid a frame that let each building sway and absorb a tremor's shocks rather than shatter. Soldiers reportedly marched around scale models to test it. What was hidden inside those Pombaline walls?
answer: a cage of interlocking wooden beams
choices: a cage of interlocking wooden beams
a core of poured Roman concrete
a lattice of forged iron rods
a filling of packed sand and cork
context: The gaiola pombalina — a hidden three-dimensional timber cage inside the masonry — lets a Pombaline building flex and dissipate a quake's energy, one of the world's first deliberately earthquake-resistant systems. The story that troops marched around mock-ups to shake them is traditional and not firmly documented. (Source: Wikipedia, Gaiola (construction); Pombaline cage study, repositorio.ucp.pt.)

question: The pale-yellow earth of China's Loess Plateau crumbles in the hand into grains as fine as silt. It lies up to 200 to 300 metres deep across some 640,000 square kilometres, enough to bury whole hills, and its layers built up slowly through the ice ages. How did all this yellow ground get here?
answer: Blown in as dust on the wind
choices: Blown in as dust on the wind
Washed down and dropped by rivers
Ground up and dumped by glaciers
context: Loess is silt-sized dust that the wind carries and drops grain by grain. China's Loess Plateau — about 640,000 square kilometres, up to 200–300 m thick near the Liupan Mountains — is the largest such deposit on Earth, piled up over the ice ages from glacial 'rock flour' and fine dust off the cold Central Asian deserts (the Gobi region), not laid down by glaciers or rivers directly. Wind-dropped loess blankets roughly a tenth of all the land on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess_Plateau; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess; grokipedia.com/page/Loess_Plateau.

question: Pale yellow hills of fine silt run nearly 200 miles beside the Missouri River in western Iowa, piled more than 90 feet deep. Only one other place on Earth, China's Loess Plateau, has such silt heaped into free-standing hills. Long before it reached the Loess Hills, where did all that fine yellow silt first come from?
answer: rock that ice-age glaciers ground to flour
choices: rock that ice-age glaciers ground to flour
ash that ancient volcanoes threw skyward
sand that far-off deserts sent drifting
clay that an ancient inland sea left behind
context: Iowa's loess began as glacial 'flour': as ice-age glaciers ground across North America they crushed bedrock into a dust-fine powder, meltwater flooded that silt down the Missouri River Valley, and wind then lifted and heaped it into the Loess Hills — not desert dust, but the leftover grindings of the ice. The hills run about 200 miles along the Missouri River in western Iowa, the wind-piled silt often more than 90 feet deep and cresting over 350 feet above the floodplain at Murray Hill. The only comparable loess on Earth is in Shaanxi, China — the Loess Plateau — and in a few spots Iowa's crests narrow to blade-thin 'razor ridges' under ten feet wide that fall away at near-ninety-degree angles. That same deep, wind-laid silt is a big reason the Corn Belt's soil runs so thick, dark, and rich. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess_Hills; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loess.

question: Keepers at the Tower of London, the ancient fortress on the Thames, watch over at least six black ravens day and night, counting them and worrying if one goes missing. What does an old legend say will happen if the ravens ever desert the Tower for good?
answer: the Tower will crumble and the kingdom will fall
choices: the Tower will crumble and the kingdom will fall
the crown jewels will crumble to dust
the Tower's great clock will stop forever
England will lose its next great war
context: This is a LEGEND, not history. The Tower's own historians think the raven story was invented in Victorian times, and the first written record of ravens at the Tower is only from 1883. Real ravens are still kept there today, with names like Huginn, Muninn, Edgar, and Poppy. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tower_of_London ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravens_of_the_Tower_of_London

question: Fire broke out in the shop of the king's own baker in London in September 1666. A dry east wind fanned the flames, and within days the Great Fire was devouring much of the city. On which narrow London street did that bakery stand?
context: The baker was Thomas Farriner, the king's baker, and the Great Fire burned for about four days. Pudding Lane took its name not from cakes but from the 'puddings' (animal offal) carted down it toward the river. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Great_Fire_of_London ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London

question: About 38,000 curious Londoners squeezed into the gas-lit wooden cars of the Metropolitan Railway on its first day, 10 January 1863. Steam engines huffed along through brick-lined tunnels dug beneath the crowded streets, and passengers coughed on the smoke and grinned at the novelty. What world first did the Metropolitan Railway set?
context: It ran through brick tunnels dug just below the streets by a method called 'cut-and-cover.' Because electric trains did not exist yet, the steam locomotives carried special 'condensing' gear to swallow their own smoke inside the tunnels. The first line ran 3.75 miles from Paddington to Farringdon. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Metropolitan_Railway ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Railway

question: Every few weeks the Ravenmaster at the Tower of London does one small, deliberate thing to each of his ravens. The birds walk freely about the old royal fortress beside the River Thames, yet that one task quietly keeps the whole flock grounded. What does he do?
answer: trims the lifting feathers on just one of its wings
choices: trims the lifting feathers on just one of its wings
clips a light metal ring around one of its legs
ties a thin leather cord to one of its feet
feeds it a heavy grain so it stays too plump
context: Trimming the flight feathers on only one wing leaves a raven able to hop and glide but too unbalanced to fly far, and comfortable food and shelter do the rest. It is done about once every three weeks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravens_of_the_Tower_of_London

question: For 600 years the Tower of London kept a Royal Menagerie of exotic animals given to English kings: lions, an elephant, and stranger creatures still. One beast, a gift to King Henry III from the King of Norway, was led down to the River Thames on a long rope each day so it could wade in and catch its own fish. What animal was this royal fisher?
context: The white bear arrived around 1252. The Royal Menagerie lasted from 1235 to 1835, when its animals were finally moved out, helping to found London Zoo. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tower_of_London

question: London burned for four days in the Great Fire of 1666. The flames swallowed about 13,200 houses, 87 churches and the old St Paul's Cathedral, and left perhaps 100,000 people homeless. With a whole city ablaze, the death toll might be expected to run huge. How many deaths were officially recorded?
context: Only a handful of deaths were ever verified, often given as around eight, though some historians suspect poorer victims went uncounted. The destruction was enormous, but the fire spread slowly enough that most people could flee. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Great_Fire_of_London

question: Between the glass towers of London's financial district, the square mile still called the City of London, stand chunks of a thick, weathered stone wall. It once ringed the whole town beside the Thames, and its line still roughly traces the boundary of that first walled city. Which ancient people founded London and built that wall?
context: The Romans founded Londinium about AD 47 to 50, soon after invading Britain, and around AD 200 they ringed it with the great London Wall. Its stones still surface between the modern City's glass towers and roughly trace the old walled boundary. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Londinium ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Tower_of_London

question: In the City of London rises the Monument, a tall stone column that Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke built close to where the Great Fire of 1666 first broke out. The column stands exactly 202 feet tall, and that number was chosen on purpose. What else does 202 feet measure?
answer: the distance from the column to the spot where the fire began
choices: the distance from the column to the spot where the fire began
the length of the burning street from one end to the other
the height that the flames were said to have reached
the width of the widest gap the fire leapt across
context: So the Monument's height equals its distance from the fire's starting point on Pudding Lane, a hidden piece of geometry by Wren and Hooke, who also used the hollow column for astronomy experiments. A spiral stair of 311 steps climbs to the top. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Great_Fire_of_London

question: A visitor who climbs 259 steps inside the dome of St Paul's Cathedral, the great church Christopher Wren built after the Great Fire, reaches a narrow walkway. If she murmurs a few words at one spot, a friend more than 100 feet away on the far side hears them clearly. How does the whisper travel so far?
answer: the whisper clings to the curved wall and creeps around it
choices: the whisper clings to the curved wall and creeps around it
the whisper echoes straight across the open dome
the whisper rises up and the dome funnels it back down
the whisper travels through hidden speaking-tubes in the wall
context: This is the Whispering Gallery. The sound does not cross the open space; it hugs the smooth, curved inner wall of the dome and travels along it, so a whisper can run right around and be heard clearly on the opposite side. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul%27s_Cathedral

question: Boudica, the rebel queen of the Iceni, swept down on young London around AD 60, only about ten years after the town was founded, and razed it to the ground. Archaeologists who dig deep enough beneath the modern City of London still meet that day face to face, in one unmistakable band running through the soil. What is that band?
answer: a layer of bright red burnt ash
choices: a layer of bright red burnt ash
a layer of shattered grey pottery
a band of pale river clay
a seam of rusted iron nails
context: Boudica's army burned Londinium so fiercely that the heat baked the earth red. Archaeologists call this scorched stratum the 'Boudican destruction horizon,' and it turns up wherever they dig deep enough beneath the old City. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Londinium

question: A storm surge charging down the North Sea can grow higher and higher as the narrowing Thames Estuary squeezes it toward London, enough to drown the low heart of the city, as a killer flood warned in 1953. Ten huge steel gates now lie along the riverbed at Woolwich, and ships sail over them until a surge threatens. How do the gates rise to wall off the sea?
answer: they rotate upward on pivots to stand upright across the river
choices: they rotate upward on pivots to stand upright across the river
they inflate with air and swell up to the water's surface
they are winched straight up out of slots in the riverbed
they telescope upward, stacking section on section
context: This is the Thames Barrier, working since 1982. Its four big central gates each stand 20.1 m (66 ft) high and weigh about 3,700 tonnes; normally they rest curved-side-down on the riverbed, then rotate up to block the tide. It has been closed against dangerous surges more than 200 times. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Barrier

question: At dawn in Luang Prabang, barefoot monks in orange robes walk the streets in a silent line, holding out their bowls. Townspeople kneel to drop a handful of sticky rice into each. It happens every morning of the year. What is this daily alms-giving called?
context: Tak Bat (also called Sai Bat) is a living daily practice, not a display for tourists. The rice is soaked overnight and cooked before dawn; the monks eat only what they collect, sharing it for breakfast and a single midday meal, then take no more food for the rest of the day. Source: tourismluangprabang.org; rainforestcruises.com.

question: An old royal town in northern Laos, once the capital of a Buddhist kingdom, was called Muang Sua and then Xieng Thong; today it is Luang Prabang. What is the town named after?
answer: a sacred gold statue of the Buddha
choices: a sacred gold statue of the Buddha
the two rivers that meet at its tip
the warrior king who founded the realm
a white elephant of the royal court
context: 'Luang' means royal or great; 'Prabang' (Phra Bang) is the sacred gold Buddha image the town guards. In 1359 the Khmer king of Angkor gave the statue to his son-in-law Fa Ngum, founder of the Lan Xang ('Million Elephants') kingdom, and the capital, once Muang Sua and then Xieng Thong, was renamed in its honour. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luang_Prabang.

question: In the very center of Luang Prabang rises a forested hill about 100 meters high. Pilgrims climb its long stone staircase of more than 300 steps, passing shrines, to a gilded stupa at the summit — and from the top the two rivers curl around the town's temple roofs at sunset. What is this hill in the middle of town called?
context: Mount Phousi (about 100 m) is the sacred hill at the heart of the peninsula; the main route climbs roughly 328 steps to That Chomsi, the gilded stupa on top, the classic place to watch sunset over the Mekong–Nam Khan confluence. The other choices are other famous stair-climbed sacred peaks: Mount Popa (Myanmar), Doi Suthep (Thailand), and Adam's Peak (Sri Lanka). Source: bestpricetravel.com; thecommonwanderer.com.

question: Black Flag raiders stormed Luang Prabang in 1887 and burned much of the town, but they left one temple untouched on purpose: Wat Xieng Thong, the golden royal temple King Setthathirath raised in 1559, with its famous low, sweeping roofs. Why, as the story goes, did they spare it?
answer: one of their leaders had studied there as a monk
choices: one of their leaders had studied there as a monk
the townspeople had walled up its entrance
the raiders feared the temple was cursed
it sat too far out on the river point to reach
context: Wat Xieng Thong (built 1559–1560) is the masterpiece of the 'Luang Prabang style,' its tiered roofs sweeping almost to the ground. Tradition holds that when Haw 'Black Flag' fighters raided the town in 1887, one of their commanders had trained there as a young monk and ordered it left alone — which is why the 16th-century temple survives today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Xieng_Thong.

question: On the red-painted rear wall of Wat Xieng Thong, Luang Prabang's magnificent golden royal temple, thousands of tiny glass tiles form one of the most beloved images in all of Laos. They shimmer against the deep crimson background. What does this famous glass mosaic depict?
context: The back wall of Wat Xieng Thong's main hall carries a 'Tree of Life' rendered in colored mirror-glass mosaic against a deep red ground — one of the most photographed images in Laos. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Xieng_Thong.

question: Kuang Si Falls, about 30 km south of Luang Prabang, pours down pale rock terraces into a staircase of pools that glow an unreal aquamarine, and neither dye nor algae is to blame. The blue-green comes straight from the bedrock under the stream. What does the stream run over that tints Kuang Si's pools?
context: Kuang Si's color is a real earth process, not dye. Flowing water dissolves calcium carbonate out of the limestone bedrock; the fine mineral particles it carries scatter blue light, tinting the pools aquamarine. The same dissolved mineral re-hardens along the rims as travertine, slowly building the terraces higher — which is why Kuang Si is called a travertine waterfall. Source: geologyscience.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuang_Si_Falls.

question: A steep sugarloaf peak towers behind Machu Picchu's ruins in the famous photographs, climbed by a frightening stairway cut into the rock. Many visitors take it for the mountain the city is named after, but that name belongs to another summit. Which peak towers behind the ruins?
context: That sugarloaf is Huayna Picchu, the sharp sister summit; Machu Picchu's ruins sit on the saddle between it and the peak the city is named for. Climbers reach its top by a near-vertical stair carved into the granite, nicknamed the 'Stairs of Death.' The whole site lies at 2,430 m (7,970 ft), so often lost in cloud it's called the 'cloud city.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: Sheer cliffs drop about 450 metres on three sides of the stone saddle where Machu Picchu perches. Far below, one river swings in a tight hairpin almost all the way around the ridge, a natural moat. Which river makes that great loop?
context: The Urubamba River swings around the ridge on three sides in a tight hairpin, roughly 450 m of vertical cliff below the citadel, so that nature very nearly moats the whole site. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: The Inca raised Machu Picchu around 1450, and people lived there for only about 80 years before it was abandoned. Romantic stories long cast it as the ancient city of some lost race, but its real purpose was simpler. What was Machu Picchu built to be?
context: Machu Picchu was a royal estate, a country retreat built around 1450 for the Inca emperor Pachacuti and lived in for only about 80 years (c. 1420-1530), not the work of any vanished ancient race. When the Inca left, the cloud forest simply grew over it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: Hiram Bingham, an American explorer, was guided up to Machu Picchu by a local farmer in 1911, and then told the world he had discovered a lost city hidden by the jungle. His own team's notes gave the famous find away. What did Bingham actually find at the ruins?
choices: fresh offerings laid at a mountain shrine
context: Machu Picchu was never 'lost' to the people of the valley. When Melchor Arteaga guided Bingham up on 24 July 1911, the Richarte and Alvarez families were already farming the old terraces, and Richarte's young son led Bingham the final stretch to the ruins. A local, Agustin Lizarraga, had even carved his name at the site in 1902, nine years before Bingham arrived. Bingham's label 'the Lost City of the Incas' made the ruins world-famous, and quietly erased the families already living there. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu'; salkantaytrekking.com.

question: When the Spanish conquistadors overran the Inca empire, they looted Cusco's temples and tore Inca stonework apart to raise churches on the ruins. Almost every great Inca site met that fate, yet Machu Picchu's walls still stand nearly whole today. Why did this one site come through intact?
choices: the Inca defended it to the last
its granite was too hard to break
an Inca treaty placed it off-limits
context: Machu Picchu sits hidden on a remote cloud-forest ridge, and the Spanish conquistadors simply never located it, so unlike Cusco it was never sacked, never quarried for a cathedral, never burned. That is the real reason its dry-stone walls survived almost untouched for four centuries. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: Hikers on the ancient Inca Trail don't scramble up to Machu Picchu from the valley floor; they arrive the way the Inca did, cresting a high point on the old royal road where the whole city suddenly bursts into view, framed between its two peaks. Inca Trail walkers know this spot by its Quechua name. What is it called?
context: It's the Inti Punku, the 'Sun Gate,' a stone doorway on the Qhapaq Nan, the great Inca road that once knit the empire together. It was the main Inca approach to the estate, and Inca Trail hikers still crest it to catch that first framed view of Machu Picchu cradled between its peaks. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: The wide green terraces cascading down Machu Picchu's slopes look like nothing but farmland. They are flat shelves for growing maize and potatoes on a mountainside. But engineers studying the site found the terraces quietly do a second job just as vital as feeding the estate. What is that hidden second job?
choices: collecting water for the dry months
hiding the city from the valley below
context: Machu Picchu's roughly 5 hectares of terraces (andenes) grew the estate's food, but their deeper genius is structural: packed layers of stone, gravel, and soil behind stout retaining walls turn each terrace into a buttress, anchoring the steep, rain-soaked slope against landslides. The city farms its own mountain into staying put. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu'; waterhistory.org.

question: Machu Picchu was built on ground that shakes, so the Inca engineered even its doorways to ride out earthquakes without cracking apart. Every door, window, and wall-niche at the site is cut to the same distinctive, quake-resistant shape rather than a plain upright opening. What shape are they?
context: Every opening at Machu Picchu is a trapezoid, noticeably wider at the base than the top and tilted slightly inward. That shape lowers the wall's center of gravity so the opening flexes instead of cracking, which is why the doorways still stand square after five centuries of Andean tremors. Source: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu.'

question: At the highest ceremonial point of Machu Picchu, the Inca carved a single squat pillar straight out of the living granite bedrock. Its angled faces align with the sun's yearly path, and Inca priests believed the stone could 'tie' the sun in place at the solstice so it would never wander off. What is this carved solar pillar called?
