context: It's the Intihuatana, Quechua for the 'hitching post of the sun' (inti = sun). Carved from a single piece of bedrock, its faces track the solstices, and Inca priests held that it tethered the sun to its yearly course. Similar stones elsewhere in the empire were later destroyed, making Machu Picchu's a rare survivor. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Machu Picchu'; salkantaytrekking.com.  (Legend.)

question: Visitors to Machu Picchu marvel at the stone temples, plazas, and terraces on the surface. But civil engineer Kenneth Wright calculated that the visible city is only a fraction of the actual work. Well over half of the entire building effort went into structures no tourist ever sees. Where did the majority of the Inca's labor actually go?
choices: into a hidden network of tunnels
context: Kenneth Wright found that roughly 60% of the building effort at Machu Picchu lies underground: deep stone foundations and a hidden bed of crushed rock that drains the region's torrential rain straight through the site instead of letting it wash the terraces off the ridge. As Wright put it, 'Without good drainage, there would be no Machu Picchu existing today.' The most impressive thing about the wonder is the part you cannot see. Sources: Kenneth Wright engineering studies (machupicchu.org; PBS NOVA).

question: On a dirt road near Morondava on Madagascar's west coast, a row of huge trees nearly 30 meters tall rises straight out of flat, bare fields. It is one of the most photographed sights on the whole island. Which trees give this famous 'Avenue' its name?
context: These are Grandidier's baobabs (Adansonia grandidieri), the biggest and tallest of Madagascar's baobabs. Six of the world's nine baobab species grow only on Madagascar, making the island the true home of the baobab. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_of_the_Baobabs

question: The giant bottle-shaped trees near Morondava, on Madagascar's west coast, live through the island's long dry season on water they store up. Each soaks up the rains into its soft, spongy wood, a hidden tank, so one thing about the tree slowly grows and shrinks between the wet and dry seasons. Which one?
context: A Grandidier's baobab trunk can be up to about 3 m across, and it visibly fattens after the rains and shrinks through the drought as the stored water is used up. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adansonia_grandidieri

question: About twenty bottle-shaped giants up to 30 metres tall line a dirt road near Morondava, on Madagascar's west coast. They stand alone in flat, open farmland with no other tall trees anywhere near, and nobody ever planted them in a neat row. Why do these lonely giants stand by themselves in bare fields?
answer: They are the last survivors of a forest that was cleared around them
choices: They are the last survivors of a forest that was cleared around them
They poisoned the soil so no other tree could grow beside them
They were carried there as seedlings by an ancient flood
They only sprout where lightning has burned the older trees
context: The Avenue was once dense tropical forest. As people cleared the land for rice and pasture, they left the massive baobabs standing. Malagasy tradition calls the baobab 'renala' -- 'mother of the forest.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_of_the_Baobabs

question: Biologists who tally Madagascar's wildlife find that more than nine of every ten of its plants and animals live naturally nowhere else on Earth. Few lands have so much life all their own. What long-ago event set the stage for so much unique life to develop only here?
answer: The island broke away and drifted alone for tens of millions of years
choices: The island broke away and drifted alone for tens of millions of years
A ring of active volcanoes walled the island off from the mainland
Repeated ice ages killed off every species that could not adapt
A great desert down the middle trapped species along the coasts
context: Cut off by open ocean, Madagascar's plants and animals evolved on their own for millions of years, producing whole groups of living things unique to the island. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar

question: In western Madagascar rises a forest made not of trees but of stone: thousands of gray limestone blades, packed side by side and sharp enough to slice through boots and skin. The Malagasy name for it warns that this is a place 'where one cannot walk barefoot.' What is this needle-sharp stone forest called?
context: The Tsingy de Bemaraha, above the Manambolo River gorge, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1990. Its razor peaks are so dangerous that almost no one crosses them on foot. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsingy_de_Bemaraha_Strict_Nature_Reserve

question: Blade-sharp grey limestone pinnacles crowd Madagascar's western stone forest, yet no one chiselled or blasted them from the ground. Over millions of years one patient natural force crept into every crack of a level limestone plateau and eroded the rock from the inside, until only thin needles of stone were left. What carved this stone forest?
context: Rainwater is faintly acidic and slowly dissolves limestone. This process -- which also carves caves and sinkholes -- creates the landscape geographers call karst. The Tsingy de Bemaraha is one of the most extreme karst formations on Earth. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsingy_de_Bemaraha_Strict_Nature_Reserve

question: A strange spiny forest grows in Madagascar's parched south, a crowd of tall, leafless, thorn-studded stems of the plant family Didiereaceae. They look so exactly like the cacti of the American deserts that a gardener can graft a piece of one onto a living cactus, and the two will fuse and keep growing as one. What does that successful graft reveal about the two plants?
answer: They are true cousins of the American cacti
choices: They are true cousins of the American cacti
They just evolved to look alike, but are unrelated
They were carried from America by early sailors
They interbred with American cacti long ago
context: This is the surprise: the Didiereaceae are not unrelated cactus look-alikes but genuine relatives of the New World cacti -- close kin, close enough that a piece of one will graft onto a cactus and fuse into a single growing plant, even though the two families live an ocean apart on different continents. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didiereaceae

question: Madagascar tore loose from the rest of the world in two separate steps, tens of millions of years apart, as the ancient southern supercontinent Gondwana broke into pieces. Geologists can trace both breaks. From which two landmasses did the island split, first one and then the other?
answer: First from Africa, then from India
choices: First from Africa, then from India
First from Africa, then from Australia
First from Africa, then from Antarctica
First from Africa, then from Arabia
context: Madagascar rifted from Africa in the Early Jurassic, about 180 million years ago, and only later split from the Indian subcontinent about 88-90 million years ago. Adrift ever since, it carried an ancient cargo of life. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar

question: Whole families of plants grow wild on Madagascar and on no other land in the world. Its life is so unlike anywhere else that ecologists gave the island a grand nickname, one that treats it as a world unto itself. What do they call Madagascar?
context: Ecologists nickname Madagascar the 'eighth continent' because, like a continent, it holds entire plant families (such as Sarcolaenaceae and Sphaerosepalaceae) found nowhere else; over 80% of its plant species are endemic. https://vanilla.symrise.com/the-eighth-continent

question: Astronauts on the International Space Station can recognize Madagascar by an alarming sight: its rivers empty into the sea in enormous plumes the color of blood, spreading red stains far out across the blue water. One astronaut said the island looks as if it is 'bleeding to death.' What turns the rivers of Madagascar blood-red?
answer: Iron-rich red soil washing off the stripped land
choices: Iron-rich red soil washing off the stripped land
A vast bloom of blood-red coastal algae
Red ash drifting from inland volcanoes
Red dust blown in from the African mainland
context: Farmers clearing land by slash-and-burn, along with overgrazing and fires, have stripped much of Madagascar's forest since the 1950s. Bare highland soil -- heavy with red iron oxide -- erodes into the rivers (up to 400 tons per hectare a year) and pours out to sea; the Betsiboka River's red plume is famously visible from orbit. https://www.amusingplanet.com/2018/12/betsiboka-madagascars-red-river.html

question: Between the Scottish islands of Jura and Scarba, the Gulf of Corryvreckan roars loud enough to be heard miles off. A small boat's engine died there in August 1947, and its passengers were swept toward the whirlpool and stranded on a bare rock until lobstermen rescued them. One was a writer living on Jura to finish a novel that became one of the century's most famous. Which book was it?
context: The writer was George Orwell, then living on the Scottish island of Jura to finish Nineteen Eighty-Four. In August 1947 his boat's engine failed in the Gulf of Corryvreckan — between Jura and Scarba, caused by the flood tide racing over a basalt pinnacle — and lobstermen rescued his stranded party. He finished his first draft about three months later. (Animal Farm was already published, in 1945.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Corryvreckan

question: Just below Manaus, in the Brazilian Amazon, the sandy-tan Solimões and the coffee-dark Rio Negro keep apart for about 6 kilometres, two stripes of colour in one channel, before they finally blend. What do Brazilians call this striped spot where the rivers join?
context: Brazilians call it the 'Encontro das Águas' — the Meeting of the Waters. The coffee-black Río Negro and sandy-tan Río Solimões run in two unblended stripes for about 6 km just below Manaus before joining to form the lower Amazon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters

question: No magic keeps the sandy-tan Solimões and the coffee-black Rio Negro apart for about 6 kilometres below Manaus, where they flow on together without blending. Three physical differences between the two waters hold them in their own lanes until they mix downstream. Which three?
context: The warm (~28°C), slow Río Negro and the cold (~22°C), fast Río Solimões — the latter heavy with Andean silt — differ so much in temperature, speed, and sediment (and thus density) that they resist blending. The two-stripe boundary runs ~6 km, but the waters take roughly 60 more km to fully mix into one Amazon. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters

question: Traffic fills the streets of Manaus, a city of high-rises and more than two million people, set deep in the Amazon rainforest about 1,600 km from the Atlantic. For a city of its size, the way almost everyone and everything arrives is startling. How do people and goods reach Manaus?
context: Manaus (~2.3 million people) is one of only two cities inside the Amazon rainforest with over a million residents, yet no paved road reliably links it to the rest of Brazil. About 1,600 km from the Atlantic, it is reached mostly by riverboat or aircraft — just as the rubber traders once were. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manaus

question: Rubber made the barons of Manaus so fabulously rich in the 1890s that they raised something absurd and magnificent in the middle of the Amazon jungle, hauling marble, chandeliers and iron all the way from Europe to build it. What did they build?
context: The Teatro Amazonas (Amazon Theatre) opened on 31 December 1896; its first opera — Ponchielli's 'La Gioconda' — was staged in January 1897. Its grand stage curtain, painted in Paris by Brazilian artist Crispim do Amaral, depicts the Meeting of the Waters itself — the two rivers that paid for the house. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Theatre

question: A soaring dome, visible across Manaus, crowns the landmark the city's rubber barons built in 1896 deep in the Brazilian rainforest. It is covered in 36,000 painted ceramic tiles laid out in three bold colours, and the scheme was no accident. What does the dome's pattern deliberately reproduce?
answer: the colors of the Brazilian flag
choices: the colors of the Brazilian flag
the colors of the Portuguese flag
the colors of the Amazonas state flag
the colors of the Brazilian imperial standard
context: The dome's 36,000 decorated tiles echo the green, yellow, and blue of the Brazilian flag. Much of the theatre was shipped in from Europe: roof tiles from Alsace, steel from Glasgow, Carrara marble from Italy, and 198 chandeliers, 32 of them Murano glass. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Theatre

question: Visitors still cross a bridge over a moat to reach the oldest part of Manila, for over 300 years the heart of Spain's colonial rule in Asia. Inside lies a whole Spanish town begun in 1571, its churches and plazas sealed behind thick walls. What is this walled quarter called?
context: Intramuros is Latin for 'within the walls.' Miguel Lopez de Legazpi established it on June 24, 1571, and for three centuries it was the seat of Spanish power in the islands. Malate, Quiapo, and Ermita are other historic Manila districts, but only Intramuros was the fortified city sealed behind ramparts and a moat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intramuros

question: Spanish governors, officials and friars lived inside the ramparts of old Manila's walled quarter, while the Spanish kept the islands' own people outside. Chinese merchants built their own crowded trading district, pressed against the wall just beyond the gates. What was this Chinese quarter called?
context: The Parian was the Chinese merchants' quarter huddled against the walls of Intramuros; to live 'extramuros' — outside the walls — was the lot of the colony's Filipino and Chinese majority, shut out of the Spanish core. The walled city shows both faces of colonial Manila plainly: Spain's ramparts fenced the islands' own people out, and the same rulers left behind the churches, plazas, and streets that still give the city its face. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intramuros

question: Guarding the mouth of the Pasig River where it pours into Manila Bay stands Fort Santiago, the stone citadel begun in 1571. Carved above its grand gate, finished in 1714, are the Spanish royal arms and an image of the soldier-saint the fortress is named to honor. Which saint?
context: 'Santiago' is the Spanish name for Saint James, patron of Spain and of its soldiers, whom Spanish troops cried out to in battle. Legazpi raised the fort on the very ground where Rajah Matanda's palisaded native fort, armed with bronze cannon, had guarded the river mouth before him. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Santiago

question: The month-long Battle of Manila ground old Manila's walled quarter to rubble in February and March 1945, killing more than a hundred thousand civilians and leaving barely a structure whole. Of the seven great stone churches within the walls, just one still stood when the guns fell silent. Which church survived?
context: San Agustin Church, completed in 1607, is the oldest stone church in the Philippines, and in 1945 it was the lone survivor of Intramuros' seven churches, though the fighting blew out its ancient doors and pocked its walls. The others were destroyed and, in time, rebuilt. In 1993 San Agustin was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, one of the four Baroque Churches of the Philippines. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Agustin_Church_(Manila)

question: The Baluarte de San Diego juts from the ramparts of old Manila's walled Spanish quarter. Raised in 1587 to guard the harbour against pirates and rival fleets, it is the oldest of the walled city's seven bastions, and its defenders likened its stone outline to one particular playing card. Which card?
context: The Baluarte de San Diego (1587) was the oldest of Intramuros' seven bastions; its defensive works were described as shaped 'like an ace of spades' — a great stone playing-card jutting from the walls toward the moat. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intramuros  (Legend.)

question: Manileños love Manila Bay, the vast, sheltered sweep of shallow water, some 2,000 square kilometres across, where the Pasig River empties beside their city. Asked why, most point not to its size but to the one thing it is world-famous for. What is Manila Bay most celebrated for?
context: Manila Bay's sunsets are counted among the most beautiful on Earth, blazing gold and crimson over roughly 2,000 square kilometers of calm, shallow water where the Pasig River meets the sea. Source: https://anchorland.com.ph/golden-hour-top-ways-to-experience-manila-bays-world-famous-sunsets/

question: A mariachi band strikes up in a Mexican plaza, violins singing, trumpets blasting and guitars strumming the beat, the players in short embroidered jackets and wide sombreros. The style grew up on the ranches of one western Mexican state in the 1800s. In which state was mariachi born?
context: Mariachi is the musical emblem of Jalisco, in western Mexico; its big-city home is the Jalisco capital, Guadalajara. From there the serenading bands spread across Mexico and around the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariachi

question: A small town in western Mexico greets visitors with a bold boast on its welcome sign: 'World Cradle of Mariachi.' Here, the town claims, the folk style at the heart of the music first took shape before it spread outward. Which town calls itself the birthplace of mariachi?
context: Cocula proudly styles itself the 'Cuna Mundial del Mariachi' — the World Cradle of Mariachi — as the place where the son jalisciense folk style took shape. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariachi ; https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/mariachi-music

question: A mariachi steps into a plaza in western Mexico dressed as an old-time Mexican horseman: a wide sombrero, a short jacket stitched with embroidery, and tight trousers lined down each leg with shiny silver buttons. The outfit takes its Spanish name from the horseman himself. What is it called?
context: The mariachi's suit is the traje de charro, the outfit of the charro or Mexican horseman, adapted into the band's stage costume. UNESCO's heritage listing notes the 'regional costumes adapted from the charro costume.' Source: https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/mariachi-string-music-song-and-trumpet-00575 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariachi

question: Two mariachi players keep the band's rhythm and bass on round-backed guitars that are seldom met outside Mexico. One strums a small, high-pitched guitar fast for the beat; the other hugs a huge, deep-bellied bass like a barrel to thump out the low notes. What are these two guitars called?
choices: the requinto and the bajo sexto
context: The little five-string vihuela drives the rhythm while the big-bellied guitarrón booms the bass — a rounded-back pair unique to the mariachi sound. Source: https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/mariachi-music ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariachi

question: The bright, blaring trumpet cuts through every mariachi tune today, so central that it seems always to have been there. Through most of mariachi's past, though, the bands had no trumpet at all. It took its place only in the twentieth century, pressed onto bands across Mexico by one booming new industry. Which force added the trumpet to mariachi?
context: The trumpet everyone assumes is ancient joined mariachi only in the twentieth century; accounts date it anywhere from the 1910s to the 1930s. The Handbook of Texas credits commercial radio, which wanted a more penetrating sound for broadcast, and Wikipedia ties it to the rise of Mexico's national radio networks and the fashion for jazz and Cuban music. Source: https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/mariachi-music ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariachi

question: Tour guides love to say the word mariachi comes from the French mariage, marriage, coined when French troops in 1860s Mexico hired local bands to play their weddings. Historians reject that charming tale outright. What is their evidence against it?
answer: the word is on record in Mexico years before the French came
choices: the word is on record in Mexico years before the French came
the French troops never reached the mariachi heartland
the French word mariage never meant a wedding party
the bands of that era played only at church feasts
context: The French-'mariage' story is a myth: the word is on record before the French intervention of the 1860s. About a hundred baptism, marriage and burial records from 1832 into the 1840s name a 'Mariachi' ranch near the Santiago River in Nayarit, and in 1852 the priest Cosme Santa Anna of Rosamorada wrote to the bishop of Guadalajara complaining about the noise and drinking of the mariachis. (French troops did reach the region: Bazaine occupied Guadalajara in January 1864.) Where the word really comes from is still argued; many scholars favour a native root in western Mexico, perhaps the lost Coca language of the Cocula district. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariachi ; Jáuregui, INAH (revistas.inah.gob.mx/index.php/antropologia/article/view/17607) ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Mariachi ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_French_intervention_in_Mexico  (Legend.)

question: At sunset the whole of Marrakech seems to catch fire, its towering ramparts, gates and packed houses all glowing one warm shade of red; that is why people call it the Red City. The colour is not paint. It comes straight from what the buildings are made of. What is that material?
answer: sun-dried red earth rammed into walls
choices: sun-dried red earth rammed into walls
red sandstone cut from mountain quarries
red bricks fired hard in kilns
context: Marrakech's walls, gates and houses are built of pise -- rammed earth packed from the local, iron-oxide-rich red clay, and that iron is what tints the whole city its warm reddish-ochre. The great ramparts were raised around 1122-1123 by the sultan Ali ibn Yusuf. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrakesh; nomads-travel-guide.com/places/walls-of-marrakesh/

question: On calm days the great pool of the Menara, west of Marrakech, turns into a perfect mirror. Dug in the 12th century to hold water, it lies inside an old walled garden, and across it floats the reflection of a snow-capped range on the horizon. Which mountains show up in the water?
context: Marrakech sits on a hot plain right at the foot of the High Atlas. The Menara basin (about 200 m by 150 m, dug in the 12th century to collect Atlas snowmelt) with its later pavilion mirroring the peaks in still water is one of the city's most iconic views. Source: slowmorocco.com/stories/the-basin-and-the-mountains; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrakesh

question: Each night, one legendary open square at the heart of Marrakech becomes a living open-air theatre. Snake charmers pipe, Gnaoua musicians drum, acrobats tumble, and rows of food stalls line the pavement with smoke. Storytellers draw rings of listeners who lean in to hear old tales kept alive by voice alone. What is this world-famous square called?
context: Jemaa el-Fnaa, Marrakech's great square, fills every evening with the halaiqi (storytellers), snake charmers, Gnaoua musicians, acrobats and food stalls -- a living open-air theatre. In 2001 UNESCO proclaimed it a 'Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity,' an honor for its LIVING oral tradition (the storytellers), not its stones; the writer Juan Goytisolo helped lead the campaign. The other three are also famous squares -- Naqsh-e Jahan in Isfahan, the Registan in Samarkand, Sultanahmet in Istanbul. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jemaa_el-Fnaa

question: Above the rooftops of Marrakech's old medina soars the 77-metre minaret of the Koutoubia Mosque, the city's greatest landmark. Its very name, from the Arabic kutubiyyin, remembers the busy trade whose stalls once crowded the streets at the tower's foot. What did those long-vanished merchants sell?
context: 'Koutoubia' comes from kutubiyyin, 'the booksellers': a market of book and manuscript sellers once packed the streets around the mosque. The Almohads founded the mosque in 1147 and finished the minaret about 1195, and it became the model for its two sister towers, the Giralda of Seville and the Hassan Tower of Rabat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutubiyya_Mosque

question: A band of Sanhaja Berbers, desert nomads who had ridden up out of the Sahara, founded a new city on the dusty plain below the mountains around 1070. From this caravan capital they would soon rule an empire reaching from West Africa all the way to Muslim Spain. Which dynasty founded Marrakech?
context: The Almoravids -- Sanhaja Berber nomads of the Sahara, led by Abu Bakr ibn Umar -- founded Marrakech around 1070 as a caravan capital between the desert and the mountains; at its height their empire stretched from West Africa to al-Andalus (Muslim Spain). The later Almohads, Saadians and Marinids each ruled Morocco in turn. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almoravid_dynasty; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrakesh

question: No river crosses the hot, dry plain around Marrakech, yet for nine centuries its gardens bloomed on water from khettaras, long tunnels dug far beneath the plain toward the foothills of a distant snowy range. What moves the water along a khettara to the city?
context: The khettara -- the North African form of the Persian qanat -- is a gently graded tunnel dug back under the plain to the water table near the Atlas foothills, so groundwater and snowmelt flow to the city by gravity alone, with no wheel or pump. Kept in shade the whole way, almost none of the water evaporates on the long journey. Hundreds were hand-dug over nine centuries to keep Marrakech and its gardens green. Source: watermuseums.net/heritage/valuing-ancient-water-cultures/moroccan-khettaras/; waterhistory.org/histories/morocco/morocco.pdf

question: Mecca, the holiest city of Islam, rose in dry western Arabia with no river and no lake for miles around, though most great holy cities, like Varanasi on its Ganges, grew up beside water. What kind of dry landform is the old city tucked inside?
context: Mecca sits in a narrow valley about 277 m (909 ft) above sea level, roughly 70 km inland from the Red Sea port of Jeddah. Ringed by the peaks of the Sarawat range, it earned the nickname 'the Hollow of Mecca' — a great city cupped in dry mountains rather than born on a river or a coast. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca

question: Worshippers in a mosque in Tokyo and in one in Cairo face very different compass directions, yet both aim at the same distant target, the Kaaba in Mecca. Every mosque on Earth is built to face it, so hundreds of millions of daily prayers point to one building. What is this shared prayer direction called?
context: The qibla is the direction of prayer. Every mosque marks it with a niche in one wall (the mihrab), so worshippers everywhere align on the Kaaba — a geography of orientation, with countless sight-lines meeting at one building. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla

question: Workers gather at the Kaaba in Mecca once a year, during the Hajj, to strip the shrine of its old covering and drape a new one in its place: an enormous cloth of black silk, big enough to blanket a small building, stitched with lines of gold Arabic script. What is this yearly covering called?
context: The kiswa is a black silk cloth embroidered with gold Quranic inscriptions, replaced with a fresh one each year during the Hajj. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba

question: In the heart of Mecca, the open courtyards of the largest mosque on Earth spread out in wide rings around the Kaaba. When the Hajj fills them, some 3 million worshippers can pray there at once. What is this great mosque called?
context: The Masjid al-Haram, the 'Sacred Mosque', surrounds the Kaaba and is the largest mosque in the world: it covers about 356,000 m² (88 acres) and can hold on the order of 2.5-3 million worshippers at once. The Masjid an-Nabawi (the Prophet's Mosque) and the Masjid al-Qiblatayn stand in Medina, and the Masjid al-Aqsa in Jerusalem. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Mecca

question: Set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba is the Black Stone (al-Hajar al-Aswad), a dark rock worn glassy-smooth by the touch of millions of pilgrims over the centuries. It is very often said to be a meteorite that fell to Earth in ancient times. What is the real scientific standing of that famous claim?
answer: Untested — it has never been scientifically examined
choices: Untested — it has never been scientifically examined
Confirmed — lab analysis proved it is meteoric
Disproven — tests showed it is ordinary lava
Confirmed — its fall from the sky was recorded
context: The Black Stone has never been scientifically analyzed. London's Natural History Museum has suggested it may be a 'pseudometeorite' (an ordinary earthly rock), and geologists call the meteorite idea doubtful. The tradition that it fell from heaven is exactly that — tradition, not confirmed fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone  (Legend.)

question: Muslims in Islam's first years prayed not toward Mecca at all but toward another sacred city far to the north. Around 623 CE, mid-prayer, Muhammad's community turned south to face the Kaaba. Which city was the first focus of Muslim prayer?
context: The qibla first pointed toward Jerusalem; around 623 CE Muhammad's community turned to face Mecca in the middle of a prayer. The Medina mosque where this happened is still called Masjid al-Qiblatayn — the 'Mosque of the Two Qiblas.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla

question: Pilgrims on the Hajj pass through several sites around Mecca, but the single most essential moment comes on a wide, barren plain about 20 km to the east. There, on one afternoon each year, the whole multitude stands together from noon until sunset. On which plain does this great standing take place?
context: The 'standing' (wuquf) on the Plain of Arafat — from noon to sunset on the 9th day of the month of Dhu al-Hijja — is the climax of the Hajj. The gathering is among the largest recurring assemblies on Earth; the 2012 pilgrimage peaked at about 3.16 million people. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj

question: Visitors from northern Europe or the eastern United States are caught off guard by the weather around the Mediterranean, in Greece, Italy, Spain and southern France. Rain and long dry spells each come in the seasons they least expect. Which way does the year run there?
context: Most of the world gets its heaviest rain in the warm season, when hot air lifts and storms build. The Mediterranean does the reverse: hot, cloudless, rainless summers and mild, showery winters. Greece, Italy, and Spain live by this rhythm -- the olive tree and the grapevine are built to ride out the long summer drought. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_climate

question: Each autumn hot winds sweep down from the desert onto the dry hills around Los Angeles, and whole slopes of oily, knee-high evergreen scrub can go up like a torch. The tangle is one of only five patches of its kind scattered across the world. What is California's fire-prone shrubland called?
context: Chaparral takes its name from the Spanish chaparro, 'scrub oak.' Its signature plants -- chamise, manzanita, and scrub oak -- are packed with flammable oils, and fire sweeps through every few decades as part of the natural cycle. It is one of only five Mediterranean-climate shrublands on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaparral

question: Silvery scrub cloaks the hills of central Chile, pressed between the Andes and the cold Pacific, the one slice of South America that shares California's weather. It is South America's answer to the fire hills far to the north. What is this Chilean shrubland called?
context: Chile's matorral is walled off from the rest of the world -- the bone-dry Atacama Desert to the north, the Andes to the east, the Pacific to the west. That isolation makes about 95% of its plants grow nowhere else, including the towering Chilean wine palm, Jubaea chilensis. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_matorral

question: The oily evergreen shrubs on the hills around Los Angeles burn down to black stubble in the hot autumn wildfires. Within a few weeks, fresh green shoots are already pushing up through the blackened ground. How do these shrubs come storming back so fast after the flames pass?
answer: they resprout from a fire-proof underground burl
choices: they resprout from a fire-proof underground burl
they regrow new leaves along their scorched stems
their seeds sprout quickly in the fresh warm ash
new plants blow in on the wind from unburned slopes
context: Many chaparral shrubs -- like chamise and toyon -- store energy in a woody, fire-resistant swelling at the root crown called a burl (or lignotuber). The branches burn away, but the burl survives underground and sends up new sprouts within days. Fire here is not the end of a plant's life; it is a reset. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaparral

question: A geographer who marks the five Mediterranean-climate regions on a globe sees a hidden pattern in California, central Chile, the South African Cape, southwest Australia and the Mediterranean Basin. All five sit near the same latitude, and each hugs the matching side of its continent. Where on their continents do all five lie?
answer: the west coast, in the mid-latitudes
choices: the west coast, in the mid-latitudes
the east coast, in the mid-latitudes
the west coast, deep in the tropics
the east coast, close to the poles
context: Each region hugs the western edge of its continent between about 30 and 40 degrees from the equator. There, cold ocean currents chill the coast and a belt of high pressure -- the subtropical ridge -- drifts poleward each summer, shoving the rain-bearing storms away. Only in winter, when the high slips back toward the equator, do the fronts break through. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_climate

question: A low, sandy heath in the far southwest of Australia bursts each spring into one of the greatest wildflower shows on Earth. The region holds more than 8,000 native plant species, half of them found nowhere else in the world. What is this southwest Australian heath called?
context: Kwongan is the sand-plain heath of Southwest Australia, holding about 70% of the region's 8,000-plus plant species -- half of them endemic. Alongside the Cape's fynbos, it is one of the planet's supreme wildflower hotspots, ablaze with banksias, kangaroo paws, and orchids each spring. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwongan

question: A wildfire can strip a whole hillside in any of the world's five Mediterranean shrublands down to bare black earth, yet the same plants come roaring back thicker than before. Many of them keep their seeds locked inside hard, woody pods for years, sometimes decades. What finally cracks those pods open to reseed the burnt ground?
answer: the intense heat of the wildfire itself
choices: the intense heat of the wildfire itself
the first heavy rains of winter
years of slow rot and decay
context: This fire-triggered seed release is called serotiny (or pyriscence). Resin seals the woody pods shut until a fire's heat melts it, dropping seeds onto freshly cleared, nutrient-rich ash with no competitors. In Australia's Banksia, a tiny winged 'separator' inside each pod then doles the seeds out gradually over the wet and dry spells that follow. Fire, here, is not a disaster -- it is the trigger the whole shrubland waits for. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serotiny

question: From the hills of California to the Cape of South Africa, shrubs and wildflowers cover five small scraps of land that share one climate. Together these Mediterranean-climate regions take up only about 2% of all the land on Earth. For such a tiny sliver of the planet, how large is their share of the world's known plant species?
answer: nearly a fifth of all known plant species
choices: nearly a fifth of all known plant species
about one plant species in every fifty
roughly half of all known plant species
barely one plant species in a thousand
context: Just five small regions -- about 2% of the land surface -- hold close to 20% of all known plant species, an astonishingly outsized share of the planet's flora. Biologists link this explosion of diversity to the long summer drought and the regular fires, which together carve the land into countless micro-habitats where new species split off and specialize. Source: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6038726/

question: Far out in the western Pacific, at one end of the Mariana Trench, the seafloor drops into the Challenger Deep, the deepest known spot in any ocean and the lowest point on the solid face of Earth. About how far below the waves is its floor?
context: The Challenger Deep bottoms out at about 10,935 m (35,876 ft) -- nearly 11 km straight down, the lowest point on the planet's solid surface. It is named for HMS Challenger, whose 1875 voyage first sounded these depths. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Deep

question: At the Mariana Trench, out in the western Pacific, an enormous slab of the Pacific seafloor bends and dives beneath another plate, down into the hot rock of the mantle. The Mariana is deeper than any other trench, and the reason lies in what kind of crust that plunging slab is made of. What is unusual about this slab of ocean crust?
answer: it is some of the oldest, coldest, densest crust on Earth
choices: it is some of the oldest, coldest, densest crust on Earth
it is some of the newest, warmest, lightest crust on Earth
it is some of the thickest, most buoyant crust on Earth
it is some of the softest, most crumbly crust on Earth
context: The Pacific plate diving here is up to about 170 million years old -- ancient for ocean floor. Old crust is cold and dense, so it sinks steeply and drags the trench down with it: the older and colder the slab, the deeper the trench. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench

question: From Chile to Alaska to Japan, every earthquake of magnitude 9 or higher measured since 1900 has struck the same kind of place: a megathrust, the vast sloping fault where two of Earth's great plates meet. Nowhere else on Earth do quakes get that big. Why do these faults make the largest earthquakes?
answer: the plates jam together, strain builds for centuries, then the fault suddenly lurches
choices: the plates jam together, strain builds for centuries, then the fault suddenly lurches
the plates slide past each other smoothly, so strain leaks away little by little
hot magma rises through the crust, then bursts out in one enormous blast
the crust slowly stretches and thins, until at last it rips itself apart
context: At a locked subduction boundary, friction pins the plates while they keep converging, storing centuries of strain. When the fault finally gives, it slips all at once over hundreds of kilometres -- a megathrust rupture. Every magnitude-9 quake on record has been one. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megathrust_earthquake

question: Alaska's Good Friday quake of 1964 struck the Aleutian megathrust, where the Pacific plate dives beneath North America, and did more than shake the ground. At Montague Island, the seafloor was thrust permanently upward and out of the sea, exposing the ocean bottom to the sky. By roughly how much did it rise?
context: At Montague Island the ground was lifted 13-15 m (43-49 ft) relative to the sea, stranding beaches in the air, while other stretches of coast sank by up to about 2.4 m. The rupture tore roughly 600 miles of fault; at about magnitude 9.2 it was the second-strongest quake ever recorded. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Alaska_earthquake

question: Off the northeast coast of Japan in March 2011, the Pacific plate suddenly slipped many metres beneath the plate that carries Japan. The Tohoku quake shoved Honshu, Japan's main island, about 2.4 metres eastward, sent a giant tsunami up the coast, and even nudged the whole planet's spin very slightly. What did it do to the length of a day?
answer: it shortened the day by about 1.8 microseconds
choices: it shortened the day by about 1.8 microseconds
it lengthened the day by about 1.8 microseconds
it shortened the day by a full second
it lengthened the day by a full minute
context: Redistributing that much mass tightened Earth's spin, like a skater pulling in her arms. The quake shortened the day by about 1.8 microseconds and tipped Earth's axis by an estimated 10-25 cm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami

question: A huge megathrust quake ripped along the Sunda fault off Sumatra on 26 December 2004, where one plate dives beneath another. It tore open the longest earthquake rupture ever observed and unleashed a catastrophic tsunami across the Indian Ocean. About how long was the tear in the seafloor?
context: The rupture ran about 1,300 km -- roughly the distance from London to Rome -- and faulting lasted nearly ten minutes. The quake was so vast it set the whole planet ringing, flexing the Earth by as much as 10 mm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake_and_tsunami

question: The Cascadia fault, off the coast of Washington and Oregon in the Pacific Northwest, last ruptured in a great earthquake around the year 1700 — long before any European or American settler was on that coast to write it down. And yet modern scientists have pinned the date of that ancient quake down almost to the very day. How did they do it?
answer: from Japanese records of a tsunami that struck with no local earthquake
choices: from Japanese records of a tsunami that struck with no local earthquake
from Spanish sailors' logs of a storm far out in the Pacific
from Russian fur-traders' diaries kept along the Alaskan coast
from Chinese court reports of strange tides in the South China Sea
context: Japanese villages logged a mysterious tsunami on 27-28 January 1700 -- big waves with no earthquake to explain them. Tracing this 'orphan tsunami' back across the Pacific, scientists matched it to a Cascadia rupture the evening before, about 9 p.m. on 26 January 1700. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1700_Cascadia_earthquake

question: Along the coast of Washington state, in the Pacific Northwest of the United States, stand eerie 'ghost forests' — groves of grey, long-dead red cedar trees. They were killed off in a single night around the year 1700, when the great Cascadia megathrust earthquake ruptured just offshore. What did the quake do to wipe out an entire coastal forest all at once?
answer: it dropped the coastline, so the sea flooded in and drowned the trees
choices: it dropped the coastline, so the sea flooded in and drowned the trees
it buried the trees under a thick blanket of volcanic ash
it shook so hard the trees were torn out by their roots
it set the forest ablaze with sparks from the grinding rock
context: When the fault slipped, the coast suddenly dropped and salt water poured over the forest, killing the cedars where they stood. Their outermost tree rings all date to 1699 -- the last summer they grew before the flood -- independent proof that fixes the quake to the winter of 1700. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1700_Cascadia_earthquake

question: Augustus the Strong of Saxony opened Europe's first true porcelain works at Meissen on the Elbe in 1710. To guard the newly cracked recipe from rivals, he housed it in a tall Gothic castle on a rocky bluff above the river. Which Meissen castle was it?
context: Production of Europe's first true hard-paste porcelain began in 1710 inside the Albrechtsburg, a 15th-century castle in Meissen — its walled hilltop rooms perfect for hiding a jealously guarded secret. The royal manufactory had been founded that same year by Augustus the Strong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain

question: A dark-red stoneware went on sale at Meissen in 1710, made by Johann Friedrich Böttger before the works produced anything white, and Saxony's princely courts prized it. How were the finest pieces of Böttger's red stoneware worked and decorated?
answer: cut and polished like a gemstone
choices: cut and polished like a gemstone
gilded all over with gold leaf
finished with a thick salt glaze
context: Before Meissen ever produced anything white, Böttger perfected this hard, dark-red stoneware — later called 'Böttger ware' — so dense and tough it could be cut, faceted, and polished like a gemstone. It went on sale in 1710, the first true product of Europe's first porcelain works. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Friedrich_Böttger

question: Johann Böttger hunted for years, a favourite Meissen legend says, for the pure white clay that makes true porcelain, and it lay close at hand the whole time. That white earth was dug near Aue in the Saxon hills and sold for pennies. In what everyday item had his porcelain clay been hiding?
answer: the powder in his old wig
choices: the powder in his old wig
the flour in the castle kitchen
the chalk in his writing box
context: By a much-loved (if unprovable) Meissen legend, Böttger traced the porcelain clay to the powder in his own wig — 'Schnorr's white earth,' dug near Aue by the ironmaster Johann Schnorr and sold cheap to whiten wigs. Böttger noticed the wig powder felt oddly heavy, had it tested, and found the perfect white clay. Source: ceramicstoday.glazy.org/articles/schnorr.html

question: Kings and queens across Europe locked their porcelain away in guarded cabinets like chests of jewels, for in Böttger's day so few places on Earth could make it that one fine cup could cost a small fortune. Under what glittering two-word nickname did porcelain become known in Europe?
context: Porcelain was so precious it was nicknamed 'white gold' (weißes Gold). The breakthrough came around 1708, when Böttger, working with the scientist Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus, finally cracked the recipe that had eluded Europe for centuries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Friedrich_Böttger

question: Böttger and the scientist Ehrenfried Tschirnhaus knew the Chinese blended a special white earth into their porcelain, but for years they hunted in vain for the right one. The secret that finally gave Meissen its porcelain was a soft, snow-white clay from the Saxon hills. What is this porcelain clay called?
context: Kaolin — white 'china clay' — was the missing key. Fired past 1,300°C it turned white, glassy, and translucent, and rang like a bell when struck. Meissen guarded it fiercely, moving the clay in sealed barrels under sworn secrecy; even so the 'arcanum' leaked, and rival factories sprang up in Vienna, then at Sèvres and in England. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Friedrich_Böttger; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain

question: Meissen's painters began adding a small blue emblem under the glaze around 1720, to prove a piece was genuine and fight off the copycats. The design was borrowed from the coat of arms of Saxony, and it has been used almost without a break ever since, one of the oldest trademarks in the world. What is the famous Meissen mark?
context: The blue crossed swords, adapted from the arms of the Electorate of Saxony and introduced in 1720, are reportedly one of the oldest trademarks still in continuous use anywhere in the world. Two artists then made Meissen famous beyond its chemistry: painter Johann Gregor Höroldt brought brilliant enamel colours in the early 1720s, and sculptor Johann Joachim Kändler modelled the rococo figurines that rival factories scrambled to copy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain

question: Melbourne hides its coolest life in the skinny alleys between its grand streets. Once used for deliveries, they now hold tiny bars, cafes, and murals. The art is painted over so often that no two visits look the same. What does the city call these hidden passages?
context: Melbourne's laneways began as narrow service alleys behind its grand Victorian streets and are now the city's signature -- lined with tiny bars, cafes, and constantly repainted murals. Hosier Lane, opened as an official street-art gallery in 1998, is repainted so often (much of it overnight) that no two visits look the same. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hosier_Lane

question: Green-and-gold trams still roll through Melbourne's streets, on a network the city kept while other cities around the world ripped up their tracks for buses and cars. Today it runs over hundreds of kilometres of track. What distinction does Melbourne's tram network hold?
context: Melbourne kept its trams when almost every other city tore its tramlines out -- spared by wide streets, union backing, and the cost of ripping up track. Today the network runs about 250 km of double track, roughly 24 routes and some 500 trams, and carried about 154.8 million passengers in 2023-24: the largest urban tram network in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trams_in_Melbourne

question: A driver turning right at certain tram-crossed junctions in central Melbourne first pulls into the far-left lane, then waits in the middle of the junction until the road clears, so that cars never block the trams. Australians drive on the left, so a right turn normally starts from the right. What is this manoeuvre called?
context: Australia drives on the left, so a right turn normally begins from the right-hand lane. Melbourne's 'hook turn' inverts that: at tram-crossed intersections, drivers turn right from the far-left lane and wait mid-junction until the way clears, so turning cars never block the trams. Written into Victoria's road rules by 1939, it is the only such rule that exists purely for the trams' sake. Source: https://www.racv.com.au/royalauto/transport/vic-road-rule-guides/what-are-hook-turns-how-to-do-one.html

question: At the peak of the 1850s boom, about two tonnes of gold a week poured into Melbourne's Treasury from fields just inland, wealth that paved the grand boulevards of what admirers dubbed 'Marvellous Melbourne.' Which two towns were the great goldfields feeding the boom?
context: Gold was struck in Victoria in 1851, and strikes at Ballarat and Bendigo made it one of the world's great goldfields. In 1856 alone Victoria yielded over 3 million troy ounces (about 95 tonnes) of gold. The wealth built 'Marvellous Melbourne' -- a nickname coined by British journalist George Augustus Sala in 1885 -- whose population had leapt from about 29,000 in 1851 to 123,000 by 1854. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_gold_rush

question: Melbourne sits on a weather knife-edge, where cold fronts sweeping off the Southern Ocean slam into hot air from Australia's baking interior. On a summer afternoon the temperature can crash about 15C in under an hour, then climb again -- sometimes more than once in a day. What do locals call that abrupt southerly blast that ends a hot spell?
context: Melbourne's famous 'four seasons in one day' comes from its position on the boundary where cold fronts off the Southern Ocean collide with hot air from inland Australia. A 'cool change' -- the sudden arrival of that colder southerly air -- can drop the temperature by around 15C in under an hour before it swings back to sun, sometimes several times a day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Melbourne

question: Dark basalt plains dotted with the cones and craters of a geologically young volcanic field spread around Melbourne, though Australia is often called the most geologically stable continent. A big southern city there might be expected to have almost no volcanoes near it. How many separate eruption points dot the region around Melbourne?
context: Melbourne sits on flat basalt plains at the head of Port Phillip Bay, where the Yarra River meets the sea. The plains to its west and north are Quaternary (geologically young) basalt from the Newer Volcanics Province -- with over 400 eruption centres, one of the world's largest young volcanic fields. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Geography_of_Melbourne

question: The Ancestral Puebloans made their home on Mesa Verde, a high, flat plateau above deep, steep-walled canyons in southwest Colorado, from about 550 to 1300 AD. Yet they did not put their stone villages up on its flat green top. Where did they build them?
answer: Inside rock alcoves in the cliff faces
choices: Inside rock alcoves in the cliff faces
Up in the branches of tall trees
Down along the flat riverbanks below
context: The Ancestral Puebloans built their villages inside natural sandstone alcoves worn into the canyon walls, sheltered under the cliff overhangs -- which is why they are known as 'cliff dwellings.' The name 'Mesa Verde' is Spanish for 'green table,' for the tree-covered plateau above. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa_Verde_National_Park

question: At Mesa Verde the Ancestral Puebloans gathered for their ceremonies in round rooms sunk into the ground. No door led in: a worshipper climbed down a ladder through a hole in the roof, past a central firepit. What are such rooms called?
context: These round, sunken ceremonial rooms are called kivas -- reached by a ladder down through a hole in the roof, with a central firepit and a roof once carried on stone pillars. (A cenote is a Maya sinkhole, a kachina a Pueblo spirit being, a hogan a Navajo home.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa_Verde_National_Park

question: The builders of Mesa Verde's stone villages left around 1300 CE, and a popular myth says they mysteriously vanished. They did nothing of the kind: they moved away, and their direct descendants still farm the same corner of the country today. Who are those living descendants?
choices: The Navajo of the high desert
The Apache of the southern mountains
The Comanche of the open plains
context: The builders did not vanish -- their direct descendants are today's Pueblo peoples, including the Hopi, the Zuni, and the Rio Grande pueblos such as Acoma and Taos; some 26 tribes and pueblos trace their ancestry to Mesa Verde. The old name 'Anasazi' is a Navajo word meaning roughly 'ancient enemies,' which is why scholars now say 'Ancestral Puebloans.' Source: https://www.nps.gov/subjects/swscience/ancestral-puebloan.htm

question: Nearly every stone village the Ancestral Puebloans built at Mesa Verde around 1200 AD faces south or southwest, out toward the sun. The builders chose that direction on purpose, watching how the sun's angle changes across the year. What did facing that way do for the people living inside?
answer: Let winter sun warm the rooms and summer shade cool them
choices: Let winter sun warm the rooms and summer shade cool them
Hid the homes and made them hard for raiders to storm
Drained the rains away and kept the rooms from flooding
Kept the river close and the daily climb short
context: The alcoves were chosen for what we now call passive-solar design: facing south and southwest, they let the low winter sun reach in and warm the stone, while the overhang shaded the rooms from the high summer sun and kept them cool. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa_Verde_National_Park

question: Mesa Verde stood empty after about 1300 CE, when the Ancestral Puebloans left it and migrated south. For six centuries no one knew what had driven them out, until scientists studied the tree rings preserved in the builders' own cut roof-beams, each ring marking a single year. Ring by ring, the beams recorded a slow calamity that had gripped the region for a generation. What was it?
answer: A long drought that emptied the streams
choices: A long drought that emptied the streams
A long freeze that killed the crops
A long chill that shortened the summers
A long wet spell that rotted the harvests
context: Reading dates from tree-rings is called dendrochronology. The beams record a 24-year 'Great Drought' from 1276 to 1299 -- among the driest stretches in 2,000 years -- the leading explanation for why the people left, though other pressures likely added to it. Astronomer A.E. Douglass published the first Mesa Verde tree-ring dates in 1929. Source: https://www.nps.gov/archeology/sites/npsites/mevetreerings.htm

question: The god Huitzilopochtli told the wandering Aztecs, as legend has it, to build where they saw a great eagle on a spiny cactus; there they founded Tenochtitlan, which grew into Mexico City. That eagle still sits in the middle of Mexico's flag. What is the eagle doing?
context: In Aztec legend the god Huitzilopochtli told his wandering people to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus devouring a snake; they spotted it on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan there in 1325. The omen is legend, but that eagle-and-snake still sits at the very center of Mexico's flag today. Source: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/tenochtitlan/

question: Hernán Cortés marched into the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, in 1519 and found some 200,000 people living on its islands in a lake in central Mexico. He wrote home to King Charles that it matched the grandest cities of Spain. That same year, how did the Aztec capital compare with Henry VIII's London?
context: With roughly 200,000 people Tenochtitlan was about five times the size of Henry VIII's London; Cortes compared it to Seville and Cordoba, and only Paris, Venice, and Constantinople might have rivaled it. This was no primitive village but one of the largest and most engineered cities on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan

question: Spanish forces and their native allies razed Tenochtitlan in 1521 and built their capital on its ruins, a city that flooded again and again. Over the next centuries Spanish engineers did something drastic to the lake around it, and parts of Mexico City now drop nearly half a metre every year. What did they do?
context: The fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521 was both a real razing (Cortés and his allies besieged the island for over 90 days, cutting its aqueduct) and a real epidemic collapse, as smallpox swept the city beforehand. To end the floods afterward, Spanish authorities began draining Lake Texcoco in the 1600s, and over the centuries it shrank by more than 95%. The city now rests on the old lakebed's waterlogged clay, which is collapsing as wells over-pump the groundwater beneath, so Mexico City sinks, as much as 9 metres over the last century. The Angel of Independence shows it: unveiled in 1910 with nine steps, it has since had fourteen more added as the ground fell away. Source: Grokipedia, 'Lake Texcoco'; Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City

question: Aztec kings once escaped to Chapultepec, a rocky wooded hill in what is now Mexico City, and a castle crowns it today. The park around it covers nearly 700 hectares, one of the biggest city parks in the Americas. Which famous U.S. park is about half its size?
context: Chapultepec covers about 686 hectares — more than double New York's Central Park — and its Nahuatl name means 'grasshopper hill.' The Aztec kings prized the wooded hill both as a retreat and as the source of the fresh spring water piped into Tenochtitlan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapultepec

question: Builders began the Metropolitan Cathedral on Mexico City's main plaza in 1573, and it grew into one of the grandest churches in the Americas. By the 1990s one corner had sunk far below the rest as the soft ground gave way. Working deep below the floor, engineers saved it. What did they do to keep it from toppling?
answer: reshaped the soil beneath it to level it
choices: reshaped the soil beneath it to level it
drove deep steel piles under one side
encased the whole church in a steel frame
rebuilt it on higher, firmer land
context: Engineers drilled shafts and carefully removed soil from under the higher side so the cathedral would settle back toward level — a technique called underexcavation. The uneven tilt comes from the same soft, drained lakebed that troubles the whole city. Source: https://www.cnn.com/2026/05/05/climate/mexico-city-sinking-nasa-aquifer-water

question: For 500 years, every ruler of the Valley of Mexico has fought the same problem. After heavy rain, water floods the basin and will not drain away by itself. In most big cities a river carries flood water off to the sea. Why does the water have nowhere to go in the Valley of Mexico?
answer: no river flows out of the mountain-ringed basin
choices: no river flows out of the mountain-ringed basin
the ground stays frozen most of the year
the surrounding desert swallows every drop
the sea sits higher than the valley floor
context: The Valley of Mexico is endorheic — a closed basin with no natural river to the sea, cupped by mountains at 2,240 m (7,350 ft). Water can leave only by evaporation or by the drains people dig, which is why floods and drainage have shaped the city's entire history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City

question: Two snow-capped giants stand side by side on the horizon from the higher parts of Mexico City on a clear day. Aztec legend tells of a warrior who came home from war to find his princess dead and knelt beside her until both turned to stone beneath the snow. The romance is legend, but the two white peaks are real. What are these two landmarks?
choices: the peaks of Orizaba and La Malinche
context: Popocatepetl (5,426 m, Nahuatl for 'the smoking mountain') is an active volcano that still puffs ash; its neighbor Iztaccihuatl ('the white woman,' 5,230 m) is dormant, its snowy ridge said to look like a sleeping woman — the princess of the legend. Both loom over the Valley of Mexico. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popocat%C3%A9petl

question: Buildings fell across Mexico City in the great quakes of 1985 and 2017, though both epicentres lay hundreds of kilometres away and towns much closer to where the earth first broke barely rattled. Seismologists blame one feature of the ground the modern city was built upon. What is Mexico City sitting on that makes far-off earthquakes so deadly there?
answer: a soft bed of old lake-clay
choices: a soft bed of old lake-clay
a deep nest of active faults
a hollow maze of lava tubes
a vast pocket of underground gas
context: The soft, water-logged lakebed clay traps earthquake waves and amplifies them 5 to 50 times, making the ground roll like jelly for long seconds while firm rock at the valley's edge barely moves. That is why the far-off 1985 and 2017 quakes struck the old lake-center so violently. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Mexico_City_earthquake

question: Crews hacked out the first great drainage channel of the flood-prone Valley of Mexico, the Tajo de Nochistongo, by hand in 1607, and their successors were still at it four centuries later. In 2019 they finished a colossal bored tunnel over 60 kilometres long and as deep as 200 metres, among the longest drainage tunnels on Earth. What is this giant modern tunnel called?
context: The Tunel Emisor Oriente, 62.5 km long and up to 200 m deep, was completed in 2019 to carry stormwater and sewage out of the sinking basin — the newest move in a 400-year campaign the cosmographer Enrico Martinez began with the 1607 Nochistongo cut. As the city keeps sinking, moving water OUT only grows harder. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emisor_Oriente_Tunnel

question: Off Miyajima island in Japan, a giant vermilion gate stands in the sea on two thick wooden pillars, with a curved beam across the top, and it seems to float free on the water. What is this kind of gate called?
context: A 'torii' is the traditional Shinto gateway that marks the boundary between the everyday world and sacred ground; Miyajima's vermilion O-torii is one of the most iconic images of Japan. The island's popular name Miyajima means 'shrine island' (its formal name is Itsukushima), and it has been revered as an island of the gods since ancient times. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itsukushima_Shrine; gltjp.com/en/article/item/20233/

question: Calm water rises around the wooden posts of the huge red gate in the bay off Miyajima, near Hiroshima, and mirrors it from below, so the gate seems to float. Hours later visitors walk out across bare sand to its pillars. What natural change raises the water around its base?
context: The 'floating' is a tidal illusion, not the gate moving. At low tide the sea drains away and the same gate that seemed to float now stands on walkable sand; to see it truly float, the tide must rise to about 250 cm to cover its base, so guides publish daily Miyajima tide tables. The O-torii stands about 16.5 m (50 ft) tall, roughly 160 m out in the bay. Source: japan-guide.com/e/e3450.html; japanactivity.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itsukushima_Shrine

question: At Miyajima island in western Japan, even the main halls of the Itsukushima Shrine do not sit on the island's solid ground. They are built on tall wooden posts driven into the shallow flats, so the whole shrine can look as if it is floating out over the water. Why did the ancient Shinto builders refuse to set the shrine down on the island itself?
answer: so no one would tread on the sacred island's soil
choices: so no one would tread on the sacred island's soil
so the sea gods could bless passing ships
so the halls would ride out the region's tsunamis
so pilgrim boats could dock beneath the shrine
context: The island itself was held so sacred that ordinary people were forbidden to set foot on its soil, so Itsukushima Shrine and its gate were built on wooden piers out over the tidal zone, technically never touching the holy ground; pilgrims once approached only by boat, passing through the torii from the sea. Ancient taboos even forbade births, deaths, and burials on Miyajima to guard its ritual purity, and there is no cemetery on the island. The chancellor Taira no Kiyomori had the shrine rebuilt into its grand present form in 1168, dedicating it to three sea goddesses. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itsukushima_Shrine; travel.gaijinpot.com/itsukushima-shrine/; quiltripping.com

question: Mohenjo-daro rose on the Indus River around 2500 BCE and may have held 40,000 people. Seen from the air today, its ruins show one feature that almost no other Bronze Age city shares: the street plan. How were Mohenjo-daro's streets laid out?
answer: In a deliberate grid of right angles
choices: In a deliberate grid of right angles
In rings around a central palace
In a maze of winding lanes
context: Mohenjo-daro's grid -- laid out around 2500 BCE, more than two millennia before Greece or Rome -- covered roughly 300 hectares and may have housed about 40,000 people: a fully planned city on a scale the world would not match again for ages. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro)

question: Brickmakers at Mohenjo-daro, beside the Indus in Pakistan, baked every brick to one fixed shape, its sides in a 1-to-2-to-4 ratio. Exactly that brick shows up in other Indus cities hundreds of miles away. What does that brick reveal the Indus cities all shared?
answer: They shared a single system of measurement
choices: They shared a single system of measurement
They were built by one traveling workforce
They were all governed by one king
context: The 1:2:4 brick (thickness:width:length) turns up in Indus cities hundreds of miles apart -- proof the whole civilization shared a system of measurement and planning, not merely a building fashion. (world-archaeology.com/great-discoveries/mohenjo-daro)

question: In a Mohenjo-daro house from 2500 BCE, a paved bath floor drained through a chute in the wall. The water ran out to a covered sewer under the street. Most of the ancient world saved bathrooms like this for kings. How common were private bathrooms across the city?
choices: About half of all houses had one
Roughly one house in three had one
Only the grandest houses had one
context: Almost every Mohenjo-daro house -- not just the wealthy ones -- had its own bathing floor and latrine, wastewater running out through chutes in the walls. Private indoor bathrooms were essentially unknown elsewhere for thousands of years. (thearchaeologist.org/blog/sanitation-of-the-indus-valley-civilisation)

question: At the very heart of Mohenjo-daro sits the Great Bath -- a sunken brick basin about 12 metres long and 2.4 metres deep, its floor sealed watertight with a thick layer of natural tar and reached by a staircase at each end. Among all the structures of the ancient world, what distinction does the Great Bath hold?
answer: The world's oldest known public water tank
choices: The world's oldest known public water tank
The world's oldest known irrigation tank
The world's oldest known swimming pool
context: Sealed with bitumen over finely fitted bricks and gypsum plaster, the Great Bath (about 12 m by 7 m, 2.4 m deep) is the oldest known public water tank on Earth -- and many believe it may also be the world's oldest ritual bathing pool, though what ceremonies happened there is unknown. (worldatlas.com/articles/interesting-facts-about-the-great-bath-mohenjo-daro)

question: John Marshall lifted a bronze figure out of the Mohenjo-daro ruins in 1926, just 10 centimetres tall, one hand resting on its hip and bangles running up one arm. It had been cast about 4,000 years earlier by the lost-wax method. What nickname does this famous little bronze go by today?
context: 'Dancing Girl' is only a modern nickname -- nothing proves she danced. Cast around 2000 BCE by the lost-wax method and found by John Marshall in 1926, the 10.5 cm bronze still astonishes people with how lifelike a 4,000-year-old figure can look. (smarthistory.org/dancing-girl-mohenjodaro)

question: Local people gave the ruined city its modern Sindhi name, Mohenjo-daro, Mound of the Dead Men, long after it lay dead. The people who built it four and a half thousand years ago never called it that. What is known about the name the city's own people used?
answer: Its true ancient name is unknown
choices: Its true ancient name is unknown
Its name is carved on the Great Bath
Its name meant 'City of the River'
context: 'Mohenjo-daro' -- 'Mound of the Dead Men' -- is a modern Sindhi name for the ruins. Because the Indus script has never been read, the name the city's own people used for their home is lost completely. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro)

question: Egypt and Sumer shouted the power of their rulers in stone -- pharaohs' pyramids, kings' palaces, gilded tombs. At Mohenjo-daro, archaeologists have found none of these: no royal tomb, no clear palace, no ruler's monument anywhere in the city. What do many scholars cautiously conclude from this absence?
answer: It may have been a strikingly equal society
choices: It may have been a strikingly equal society
A hidden priesthood may have ruled it
Merchant families may have held the wealth
Its kings may have shunned all display
context: Sir John Marshall first noted Mohenjo-daro's missing kings, and a 2026 University of York study found its houses actually grew more equal in size over time -- so many read it as an unusually egalitarian city, though whether it hid rulers is still debated. (york.ac.uk/news-and-events/news/2026/research/world-first-city-prospered-wealth-gap-shrank)  (Legend.)

question: At Lothal, a sister-city of the Indus world built near the sea, archaeologist S.R. Rao uncovered an enormous brick basin about 37 metres long, linked by channels to a tidal river. Marine fossils and crusts of salt prove that seawater once filled it. What is this great basin widely believed to have been?
choices: The world's oldest known public bath
context: Excavated by S.R. Rao between 1955 and 1960, the Lothal basin (about 37 by 22 m) is widely identified as the world's oldest known dockyard, where boats could load and unload on the tide -- though some scholars argue it was instead a giant water tank. Salt crusts and marine microfossils confirm seawater once filled it. (lothal.org/lothal-dockyard-history)  (Legend.)

question: The great cities of the Indus, Mohenjo-daro among them, fell silent around 1900 BCE as their people drifted away, and no single cause is written plainly in the ruins. Researchers have argued over several explanations. Which do most of them today consider the leading theory?
answer: A drying of the region's climate
choices: A drying of the region's climate
context: The leading modern theory ties the Indus decline (around 1900 BCE) to a weakening monsoon -- perhaps a 20-30% drop -- and the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra / Sarasvati rivers during the global '4.2-kiloyear' drought. It remains the leading theory, not settled fact; the old idea of a violent conquest has largely been abandoned. (nature.com/articles/s43247-023-00763-z)  (Legend.)

question: Orthodox monks built monasteries on top of stone pillars some 400 metres tall in central Greece from the 1300s, at Meteora, a name meaning suspended in the air. For centuries no stairs were cut into the rock. How did a monk or a visitor reach the top?
answer: hoisted up in a rope net raised behind them
choices: hoisted up in a rope net raised behind them
carried up a stone stair cut into the pillar
led up a narrow ledge spiralling the rock
walked across a bridge from the cliffs behind
context: The nets stayed the main way up until stone staircases were finally cut in the 1920s. Asked how often they replaced the fraying ropes, the monks famously answered, 'When the Lord lets them break.' Of two dozen monasteries once built on these rocks, six are still lived in today. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteora)

question: A climber who looks closely at the towers of Meteora, in central Greece, sees that they are made of small round pebbles glued together into stone, and only rolling in moving water rounds a pebble. About 60 million years ago this highland was no highland at all. What kind of place laid the rock down?
answer: the delta of an ancient river
choices: the delta of an ancient river
the beach of a vanished sea
the bed of a mountain torrent
the outwash of a melting glacier
context: Geologists read the rounded river gravel like a fingerprint: about 60 million years ago a great river dumped its load of pebbles here, building a delta that later hardened into rock. Uplift and erosion then carved that rock into the towers the monks would one day climb -- the landform came first, and without it there could be no monasteries. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteora)

question: Bhutan's Paro Taktsang monastery clings to a sheer cliff, 900 metres above the valley floor. The 8th-century master Guru Padmasambhava reached it, the story says, on the back of a magic creature, and meditated in its cave to tame the local demons. What creature does the legend name?
context: The monastery's name, Paro Taktsang, means 'Tiger's Nest,' straight from this legend. The cave where Guru Padmasambhava is said to have meditated became sacred, and in 1692 a monastery was built around it, clinging to the granite 'like a gecko.' (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paro_Taktsang)

question: The monks of Mount Athos, a self-governing peninsula in northern Greece, have kept an old rule called the avaton for about a thousand years, and both Orthodox tradition and Greek law still enforce it. Under this rule, who is banned from setting foot on the peninsula?
context: The monks regard the whole mountain as the garden of the Virgin Mary, kept for her alone; by tradition not even most female animals may be brought onto it. Male pilgrims may visit, but only a limited number each day. Mount Athos has governed itself for over a thousand years and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Athos)

question: Boats from the town of Ouranoupoli are the only way onto Mount Athos, a peninsula of twenty monasteries that juts 50 kilometres out into the Aegean Sea, with no road from the mainland. A boat ticket alone will not do. What else must every visitor get before being allowed to land?
answer: a special written permit to enter
choices: a special written permit to enter
a blessing from the mainland bishop
a promise to fast during the stay
a letter from a home parish priest
context: The document is called the diamonitirion, checked when the boat lands. From Ouranoupoli the vessel carries pilgrims down a coast lined with monasteries founded over a thousand years ago -- the oldest, the Great Lavra, back in the year 963. There is still no road: the sea is the only door. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Athos)

question: St Catherine's Monastery stands alone in the desert at the foot of Mount Sinai in Egypt. Through centuries of wars that swept the region, no army ever destroyed it -- and the monks credit a document they still guard, said to carry the personal pledge of a great leader that his people would forever protect them. Whose promise is that charter said to bear?
context: The charter is the Ashtiname, said to bear the handprint of the Prophet Muhammad himself and to grant the monks his protection. Whether or not the original was truly his, ruler after ruler honoured it, and the monastery survived unbroken where countless others fell. It is also built around what tradition holds is the biblical Burning Bush. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Catherine's_Monastery)  (Legend.)

question: Byzantine emperors ordered religious images smashed and burned across the empire in the 700s and 800s, a campaign called iconoclasm. St Catherine's Monastery, alone in the Sinai desert, lay far beyond the image-breakers' reach, and its old icons came through untouched. Which world-famous image is among the treasures it saved?
answer: the earliest known icon of Christ Pantocrator
choices: the earliest known icon of Christ Pantocrator
the earliest known icon of Archangel Michael
the earliest known icon of Apostle Paul
the earliest known icon of Prophet Elijah
context: Because St Catherine's lay in the Sinai desert, beyond the reach of the emperors' image-breakers, it kept its ancient icons when almost every early example elsewhere in the empire was destroyed -- among them the earliest known icon of Christ Pantocrator, Christ shown as 'ruler of all,' which survived the very iconoclasm that wiped out such images everywhere else. Never sacked and never rebuilt, the monastery also still holds the oldest wooden roof-truss in the world, from Justinian's original 6th-century church. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Catherine's_Monastery)

question: Constantin von Tischendorf, a scholar, took pages away from St Catherine's Monastery in the Egyptian desert in 1844, and again in 1859. They came from a Bible copied by hand in the 4th century, one of the oldest nearly complete Bibles on Earth, kept in a library second only to the Vatican's. What name does that ancient book go by today?
context: The manuscript is the Codex Sinaiticus, written in Greek in the 4th century -- one of the two oldest near-complete Bibles in existence. Its pages are now shared among four institutions, including the British Library, but it first came to light in this remote desert monastery, kept safe by the dry air for 1,500 years. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Catherine's_Monastery)

question: The Zapotec began building their capital, Monte Albán, around 500 BC on a ridge about 400 metres above Mexico's Valley of Oaxaca. Before they laid a single wall, they reshaped the mountain itself to give the new city a fit platform. What did they do to the mountaintop?
