context: Archaeologists call this the artificial levelling of the mountaintop. On the flattened ridge -- about 1,940 m above sea level -- the Zapotec laid out a Main Plaza roughly 300 by 150 m and coated it in white plaster: a giant artificial platform in the sky, home to some 17,200 people at the city's height. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('created through artificial levelling of the mountaintop'; ridge rises 'some 400 m from the valley floor'; '~1,940 m above sea level'; population '~17,200').

question: Travellers in the 1800s named the carved figures on one early wall at Monte Albán los Danzantes, the dancers: more than 300 stone slabs, each a naked man twisted into an odd pose. Archaeologists today say the name is wrong. What do they think the figures really are?
context: The twisted poses once suggested dancing, but the figures show wounds and mutilation, some are labelled by name, and they are now read as tortured, sacrificed war prisoners, displayed in stacked rows like a public gallery of the defeated. Carved early in the city's life (c. 500-200 BC), they are among Monte Alban's oldest monuments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('19th-century notion... now discredited'; 'tortured, sacrificed war prisoners, some identified by name'); corroborated famsi.org/reports/93003/93003Orr01.pdf.

question: Alfonso Caso dug into Tomb 7 at Monte Albán in 1932 and struck the richest single treasure ever found in ancient Mesoamerica: more than 300 objects, among them some 121 pieces of worked gold. One find is famous above all the rest. What was it?
answer: a human skull covered in turquoise mosaic
choices: a human skull covered in turquoise mosaic
a jade mask inlaid with obsidian eyes
a gold breastplate shaped like the sun
a headdress of green quetzal feathers
context: Caso opened Tomb 7 on 9 January 1932. The turquoise-mosaic skull, its eye-sockets set with polished seashell disks, lay among about 121 gold items weighing some 3,598 g. The hoard was actually a later Mixtec burial that re-used the centuries-old Zapotec tomb -- not the work of Monte Alban's original builders. Source: eluniversal.com.mx (Caso, 9 Jan 1932; ~300 Mixtec objects; 121 gold items ~3,598 g; turquoise-mosaic skull); montealbanoaxaca.com/wiki/tomb-7/.

question: Every building on the great central plaza of Monte Albán lines up neatly with the plaza's grid except one. The Zapotec shaped Building J like an arrowhead and turned it on purpose to a different angle, its stone point aimed away from every other wall. What did they build it to line up with?
answer: the rising of the star Capella
choices: the rising of the star Capella
the fixed point of the North Star
context: Building J's steps align with the heliacal rising of Capella -- the first dawn each year the star reappears -- which in that era fell within a day of the Sun passing directly overhead (the zenith) at Monte Alban's latitude. Its arrowhead footprint, set askew to everything else, still marks it out on the site. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('unusual arrow-like shape'; 'steps... aligned... to the rising of the star of Capella... within a day of the Sun passing directly overhead over Monte Alban').

question: More than 40 carved slabs line the walls of Building J at Monte Albán, each showing a place-name sign beneath an upside-down human head. Archaeologists read the whole gallery as a single claim that Monte Albán's rulers made about dozens of other towns. What did they claim?
context: The place-signs sit beneath inverted heads -- a Mesoamerican sign for a defeated, sacrificed enemy. The slabs list towns Monte Alban's elite claimed to have conquered, and for at least one, the Canada de Cuicatlan region, archaeology confirms the conquest really happened. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('more than 40 large, carved slabs... place-names... upside-down heads... places which the Monte Alban elites claimed to have conquered... confirmation in the Canada de Cuicatlan region').

question: Zapotec builders founded Monte Albán around 500 BC, and they made more than a mountaintop capital there. They are credited with one of the earliest examples, anywhere in ancient Mesoamerica, of a skill that would spread across the region in the centuries that followed. Which skill did they help pioneer here?
context: Cut into the Danzantes and conquest slabs are dot-and-bar dates and hieroglyphic signs -- among the earliest writing and calendar notation known from Mesoamerica, and an early step toward true written language in the Americas. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Alban ('the Zapotecs had writing and calendrical notation... among Mesoamerica's earliest writing traditions'); corroborated people.wku.edu (bars, dots, and hieroglyphs on the slabs).

question: Underwater forests as tall as a 15-story building rise from the rocky floor of California's Monterey Bay, and divers swim up through them toward the sunlit surface. Yet these forests hold no trees at all. What are they made of?
context: Giant kelp (Macrocystis pyrifera) is the largest of all marine algae -- normally about 100 ft (30 m) tall and up to 175 ft (53 m) in ideal conditions, forming the tallest underwater forests on Earth. Source: Monterey Bay Aquarium, 'Giant kelp.'

question: A kelp forest off California's Monterey Bay grows in layers like a rainforest, its fronds climbing from the rocky floor to a canopy spread across the surface. Each frond is held up toward the light by a row of its own tiny gas-filled floats. What are these floats called?
context: Each giant-kelp frond is buoyed toward the sunlit canopy by its own gas-filled float called a pneumatocyst -- a tiny balloon at the base of every blade, filled with a mix of oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide. (The kelp grips bare rock not with roots but with a claw-like holdfast, and its stemlike stipes carry the leaflike blades.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Pneumatocyst'; Wikipedia, 'Macrocystis pyrifera.'

question: Spiny sea urchins in California's Monterey Bay would chew its kelp forests down to bare rock if one animal did not keep eating them, and biologists call that animal the classic keystone species. Which animal keeps the kelp forest alive?
context: The Monterey kelp forest stays standing only because sea otters -- the classic 'keystone species' -- eat the sea urchins that would otherwise mow the kelp down to bare rock. When otters vanish, urchins multiply and strip the seabed into an 'urchin barren'; since 2014 much of California's coast has flipped to barrens, with otters now guarding only the surviving kelp patches. Source: UC Santa Cruz News, 'Sea otters maintain remnants of healthy kelp forest amid sea urchin barrens' (2021).

question: Archaeologists digging in the caves and along the shores of South Africa's Cape coast keep turning up beads, stone tools and painted art. Just offshore sways the Great African Sea Forest, a golden wilderness of giant bamboo kelp running for about 1,000 km. For how long do the finds suggest people have lived beside it?
context: South Africa's Great African Sea Forest is the only forest of giant bamboo kelp (Ecklonia maxima) on Earth, running about 1,000 km along the Cape coast -- and the caves beside it hold art and tools suggesting people have lived alongside it for nearly 100,000 years. Source: Sea Change Project, 'Great African Seaforest'; Discover Wildlife, 'Great African Sea Forest.'

question: Divers off Monterey Bay, Chile, South Africa and Tasmania swim through kelp forests. Yet in the warm, sunny tropics, where the sea's greatest forests might be expected to grow, there are almost none. What do all these kelp coasts share that the tropics lack?
context: Giant kelp thrives only where the sea stays below about 21 C (70 F) and cold currents well up nutrients from the deep -- which is why kelp forests ring cool coasts like California, Chile, South Africa's Great African Sea Forest and Tasmania, but almost never the warm tropics. Source: Wikipedia, 'Macrocystis pyrifera.'

question: Jacques Cartier climbed the one green hill in the middle of what is now Montreal in 1535, led by guides from the nearby Iroquoian village of Hochelaga. That same hill still rises over the city today. What is it called?
context: Cartier named it 'Mont Real,' the royal mountain, in honour of King Francis I of France, and the city's name 'Montreal' grew straight out of the hill's. Mount Royal's wooded slopes still tower over the downtown core. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Royal

question: Frederick Law Olmsted, the father of American park design, laid out the great park on the slopes of Montreal's Mount Royal in the 1870s. He was best known for helping to design another city's most famous park. Which park was it?
context: Olmsted and Calvert Vaux designed New York's Central Park in 1858; Olmsted then shaped Mount Royal Park, inaugurated on May 24, 1876, across about 280 hectares (692 acres). He believed a wild green mountain inside the city could rest a weary mind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Royal

question: Seen from across Montreal, Mount Royal has the smooth, rounded profile of an old volcano. But geologists studying its hard grey rock, formed about 125 million years ago, found a stranger story. What is Mount Royal really the remains of?
answer: a mass of magma that hardened underground and never erupted
choices: a mass of magma that hardened underground and never erupted
the collapsed rim of a volcano that blew its own top off
a slope of lava that froze solid partway down a mountain
a mound of rubble left behind by a meteorite strike
context: Around 125 million years ago molten magma pushed up into soft sedimentary rock and cooled hard while still trapped underground - a magma intrusion. The softer rock around it slowly eroded away, leaving the tough igneous core standing as the hill. Mount Royal is one of the Monteregian Hills, a whole line of these bared intrusions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Royal

question: Montrealers beat their brutal winters by going underground. The RESO, from réseau, the French word for network, joins malls, ten metro stations, offices, universities and hotels through about 32 kilometres of warm tunnels, and nearly half a million people a day walk and shop in it without stepping outside. What record does the RESO hold?
answer: the largest underground pedestrian network in the world
choices: the largest underground pedestrian network in the world
the world's first fully underground shopping city
the longest indoor walkway in North America
context: The RESO - from reseau, French for 'network' - grew out of the 1962 Place Ville Marie tower into roughly 32 km of passages, the largest underground pedestrian network on Earth. Montrealers can cross downtown in shirtsleeves while the streets above sit far below freezing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_City,_Montreal

question: René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle was certain a river shortcut across the continent would lead him to the silk and spice riches of Asia. He left his estate just above Montreal and returned years later with nothing. Mocking the broken dream, his neighbours gave his land and the wild rapids beside it a name that has stuck for over 350 years. What was it?
context: La Salle's seigneury and the impassable rapids beside it have been called Lachine ('La Chine,' China) ever since, and his men were teased as 'les Chinois,' the Chinese. Those same Lachine Rapids, too violent for boats to run, forced every fur trader to stop and portage here - which is exactly what made Montreal the great hinge of the North American fur trade. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lachine,_Quebec  (Legend.)

question: The great ice sheet of the last ice age halted along the shores of New York and southern New England, and as it melted it left its rubble there in a line: Long Island, Block Island, Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket and Cape Cod. What do geographers call these five glacier-built places together?
context: The Outer Lands are a chain of terminal moraine strung along the Laurentide Ice Sheet's farthest edge across southern New England and New York. The other choices are all real but not glacier-dump islands: the Outer Banks are barrier islands off North Carolina, the Sea Islands lie off Georgia and South Carolina, and the Thousand Islands dot the St. Lawrence River. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_moraine

question: High on the wall of an alpine valley, hundreds of feet above the floor, runs a long ridge of shattered rock. Frost cracked it off the cliffs and dropped it onto the edge of the glacier that once filled the valley. When the ice melted down, the ridge stayed perched up high like a bathtub ring at the old ice level, and some such ridges run 3 km long and 140 m tall. What is a ridge like this called?
context: A lateral moraine lines the flank of a glacier's valley with frost-shattered debris fallen off the walls; when the ice shrinks, the ridge is left perched high and dry, its steep inner face — the side that once leaned against the ice — reaching slopes near 80 degrees. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraine

question: Two dark stripes run straight down the middle of a great Swiss glacier like racing lines painted on the ice. These medial moraines start at Konkordiaplatz, where its feeder ice streams merge, and run on to its toe 23 km below. This river of ice is the largest glacier in the Alps. What is it called?
context: A medial moraine forms when two ice streams merge and their two inner side-ridges join into one dark band carried down the glacier's center. The Aletsch's two stripes even have names — the Kranzbergmoräne (west) and the Trugbergmoräne (east). At about 23 km long and 82 km², the Aletsch is the largest glacier in the Alps. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aletsch_Glacier

question: A giant valley glacier slid south in the last Ice Age, grinding deeper the long trough at the southern foot of the Alps that now holds Lake Garda, Italy's largest lake. When the ice finally melted, it left a curved line of low hills right across the valley's open end, a natural dam that pens the lake in to this day. What kind of dam is it?
answer: a ridge of rubble a glacier dumped
choices: a ridge of rubble a glacier dumped
a flow of lava a volcano hardened
a heap of rock a landslide dropped
a slab of crust a fault dropped
context: The Garda glacier heaped concentric rings of rubble across the valley's mouth over successive ice ages, building the great horseshoe geologists call the Anfiteatro morenico del Garda — the 'morainic amphitheatre.' That arc of moraine dams Italy's largest lake (~370 km²). Lava flows, landslides, and fault movements dam other lakes, but Garda's dam is glacial rubble. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Garda

question: Geologists walking up a glacier-carved valley cross a dozen low ridges of till, the glacier's jumbled rubble, one behind the next like the rungs of a ladder. Taken in order, the row lets them rebuild the valley's ice-age history. What does each single ridge in the row record?
answer: a pause in the ice sheet's slow retreat
choices: a pause in the ice sheet's slow retreat
a separate, far older ice age's advance
a single hard winter's deep snowfall
an ancient meltwater river's buried channel
context: These are recessional moraines: each transverse ridge marks a spot where the melting glacier's front briefly stalled before shrinking further, so a single valley can hold ten or more — and some form on a yearly cycle (annual moraines). Read in order, they map the ice sheet's retreat like bookmarks in the melt. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/recessional-moraine

question: Red Square opens beside the red-brick walls of Moscow's Kremlin, yet its Russian name, Krasnaya Ploshchad, owes nothing to communism or to the bricks. It comes from an old word whose meaning has since shifted. When the square was first named, what did the word mean?
context: Krasnaya Ploshchad really means 'Beautiful Square'. In old Russian 'krasnaya' meant beautiful; over time it came to mean 'red', while a new word, 'krasivaya', took over 'beautiful' -- both growing from the same ancient Slavic root. So the name has nothing to do with communism or red bricks; it was simply 'the beautiful place'. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Square

question: Seventy-six bronze figures crouch along the platform of Moscow's Ploshchad Revolyutsii metro station. One is a border guard kneeling beside his dog, and riders rub one spot on the dog for luck, above all before exams, until it shines like gold. Which part of the dog do they rub?
context: The station is Ploshchad Revolyutsii ('Revolution Square'), opened in 1938, lined with 76 life-size bronze figures by Matvey Manizer -- sailors, soldiers, students and farmers. Generations of hopeful passengers, students most of all, have rubbed the border dog's nose before exams, wearing the bronze to a bright polished gold. Source: https://www.rbth.com/multimedia/pictures/2016/11/22/metro-close-up_649969

question: Ivan the Terrible had St Basil's Cathedral built on Red Square after he stormed the city of Kazan in the 1550s. From the square it looks like one wildly chaotic building of swirling domes, but visitors who step inside find it put together another way. What is St Basil's, really?
answer: nine separate chapels fused into one
choices: nine separate chapels fused into one
one great hall beneath the tallest dome
a monastery of many linked cloisters
a fortress-church ringed by high walls
context: Ivan the Terrible had it built in 1555-1561 to celebrate taking Kazan (and Astrakhan). It is really eight smaller churches arranged around a taller ninth central chapel dedicated to the Intercession -- nine chapels fused into a single wildly beautiful whole. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil%27s_Cathedral

question: Master-builders brought in from Italy raised the Moscow Kremlin's red-brick walls in the 1480s and 1490s, more than 2 km around with 20 towers, and crowned them with battlements in the style of northern Italy's fortresses. What shape are those battlements?
answer: notched in two horns, like a swallow's tail
choices: notched in two horns, like a swallow's tail
pointed upward, like a row of spearheads
rounded off, like a row of onion domes
squared off, like a row of chess rooks
context: The Kremlin, a triangular fortress of red-brick walls about 2,235 m around and 5 to 19 m high with 20 towers, was raised by Italian master-builders in 1485-1495, among them Pietro Antonio Solari and Marco Ruffo. Its battlements are swallowtail merlons, double-horned notched 'teeth' in the style of northern Italian castles; the walls are often compared with Milan's Sforza Castle. It still houses Russia's government today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Kremlin_Wall

question: The onion domes of St Basil's Cathedral on Moscow's Red Square swirl in candy-bright colours, no two of them alike. Yet for its first century the cathedral looked nothing like that, because the swirls were only painted on much later. What did it look like when Ivan the Terrible first saw it finished?
context: When first finished under Ivan the Terrible, St Basil's was mostly plain red brick and white stone. The famous swirled rainbow was only added between the 17th and early 18th centuries -- so the candy-coloured domes everyone photographs are a later flourish, not the original look. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil%27s_Cathedral

question: Muscovites came to call the great cathedral on Red Square 'St Basil's', though Ivan the Terrible built it to trumpet his conquest of Kazan. The name honours a man buried in a small chapel added in 1588. Who was this Basil that the cathedral took its everyday name from?
answer: the barefoot holy fool who wandered Moscow
choices: the barefoot holy fool who wandered Moscow
the tsar's warrior brother who died in war
the pilgrim monk who walked from Kiev
the architect who raised the great domes
context: The cathedral's formal name is the Cathedral of the Intercession, but its popular name comes from a chapel added in 1588 over the grave of Basil the Blessed -- a 'holy fool' who wandered Moscow barefoot and was deeply revered. So the church built to glorify a fearsome tsar is remembered by the name of a penniless beggar-saint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil%27s_Cathedral

question: In a Moscow legend, Ivan the Terrible had the architect of St Basil's Cathedral blinded so that he could never again build anything so lovely. Historians call the tale a myth. What do the records suggest really happened to the builder, Postnik Yakovlev?
answer: he went on to build other cathedrals
choices: he went on to build other cathedrals
he was rewarded with a great estate
he died before the work was done
context: This is a popular tale, not history. Records show the builder, Postnik Yakovlev, went on to work on other cathedrals after St Basil's was finished -- so he plainly was not blinded. Historians treat the blinding story as a myth that grew up around Ivan the Terrible's dark reputation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Basil%27s_Cathedral  (Legend.)

question: Moscow's Komsomolskaya station is no bare subway stop: a golden baroque ceiling rides on 68 white-marble columns, dripping with chandeliers, while eight great mosaics by the artist Pavel Korin blaze overhead. Korin filled that ceiling with a single, proud theme from Russia's past. What do his eight mosaics show?
choices: the saints of the Orthodox church
context: Komsomolskaya (opened 1952) crowns its golden ceiling with eight mosaics by Pavel Korin of Russia's great military figures -- Alexander Nevsky, Dmitry Donskoy, Suvorov, Kutuzov, and Soviet soldiers raising the flag over the Reichstag. The station won the Grand Prix at the 1958 Brussels World's Fair. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komsomolskaya_(Koltsevaya_line)

question: The whole east side of Red Square, directly facing the Kremlin wall, is filled by one enormous building from the 1890s. Its stone front stretches 242 metres, and a soaring roof of iron and glass shelters long indoor streets below. Muscovites have poured through it for well over a century; today it is called the Glavny Universalny Magazin, or GUM. What kind of place is it?
context: GUM (today short for Glavny Universalny Magazin, the 'Main Universal Store'; in Soviet times the State Department Store) is a vast shopping arcade, built in 1890-1893 with a light iron-and-glass roof engineered by Vladimir Shukhov. Its 242-metre front runs the entire east side of Red Square, and it once held around 1,200 shops along its glass-roofed indoor streets. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GUM_(department_store)

question: Riders descend some 740 escalator steps to reach Moscow's Park Pobedy, or Victory Park, station, about 84 metres underground and the deepest in the whole metro. On the platform, two vast mosaics by Zurab Tsereteli face each other, each showing a war in which Russia hurled back a foreign invader. Which two invasions do they depict?
choices: Sweden's Charles XII and Nazi Germany
the Mongol horde and Napoleon's France
the Teutonic Knights and the Ottoman Turks
context: Park Pobedy ('Victory Park', opened 2003) averages about 84 m underground -- Moscow's deepest station and the fifth-deepest in the world -- reached by a 126 m escalator of 740 steps that takes about three minutes. Facing each other at the bottom are two vast mosaics by Zurab Tsereteli: one depicts Russia's defeat of Napoleon's 1812 invasion, the other the crushing of Nazi Germany in World War II -- the two 'Patriotic Wars' the park commemorates. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Pobedy_(Moscow_Metro)

question: Soviet planners dug many stations of the Moscow Metro far deeper underground than a train line alone would ever need. It was no accident of engineering: they had a grim wartime use in mind if the city ever came under attack. Why were so many stations buried so deep?
choices: to house an underground command bunker
to hide the army's tanks and guns
to keep the government's gold safe
context: Many Moscow stations were dug deep precisely so they could double as bomb shelters. In World War II the metro became an underground city: trains ran by day, and by night the platforms filled with cots, toilets and water fountains where thousands of Muscovites slept safe from air raids. Mayakovskaya station even served as a wartime command post. Source: https://www.gw2ru.com/history/248213-how-the-moscow-metro-became-a-true-underground-city-in-1941-photos

question: Climbers who reach the top of Mount Everest, the highest point on Earth, stand on grey rock full of fossil trilobites, armoured little sea creatures that died out long before the first dinosaurs. Where did this rock first form, about 450 million years ago?
answer: On the floor of a shallow sea
choices: On the floor of a shallow sea
Inside the crater of a volcano
At the foot of a great glacier
context: Everest's summit cap is Ordovician marine limestone -- geologists call it the Qomolangma Formation -- laid down on the floor of a warm, shallow tropical sea about 450 million years ago. It is studded with the fossils of trilobites, crinoids (sea lilies) and brachiopods; samples have been chipped from barely six metres below the highest point on Earth. Seashells on the roof of the world. Sources: iugs-geoheritage.org (Ordovician rocks of Mount Everest); spacedaily.com.

question: Tibetans living in the shadow of Mount Everest honoured the mountain long before outsiders renamed it, and they still call it by its own name of deep respect, Chomolungma. What does Chomolungma mean?
context: In Tibetan, Chomolungma (Qomolangma) means 'Goddess Mother of the World.' In Nepal the mountain is Sagarmatha -- 'Brow of the Sky,' or Goddess of the Sky. Both peoples honoured the summit as a living deity long before it was renamed for a British surveyor. Sources: montana.edu/everest (Naming); Wikipedia, 'Mount Everest.'

question: Near the top of Mount Everest, above about 8,000 metres, the air is so starved of oxygen that climbers can linger only briefly, never resting or sleeping there for long, before they must head back down. Mountaineers gave this highest band of the mountain a blunt two-word name. What is it?
context: Above roughly 8,000 metres -- the 'death zone' -- so little oxygen reaches the blood that even bottled oxygen only slows the decline. The body cannot acclimatise and steadily deteriorates, so climbers try to spend as few hours as possible up there before descending. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Effects of high altitude on humans'; namasadventure.com.

question: Sir George Everest served as Surveyor General of India in the 1800s, running the great survey that measured the heights of the Himalayas. After he retired, his successors named the tallest peak of all after him, and the name stuck though he objected. What was the irony in naming that peak for that man?
answer: He had never once seen the mountain
choices: He had never once seen the mountain
He had never traveled outside Britain
He had died decades before it was found
He had already been honoured elsewhere
context: British surveyors first catalogued the peak as plain 'Peak XV.' In 1852 the Indian mathematician Radhanath Sikdar calculated it was the highest mountain on Earth, and in 1856 it was named Mount Everest for Surveyor General Sir George Everest -- over his own objection. He never laid eyes on the mountain that carries his name. Sources: Wikipedia, 'George Everest'; allthatsinteresting.com.

question: Just below the summit of Mount Everest, the standard route once met its last great barrier: a near-vertical wall of rock about 12 metres high, the final test before the top. An earthquake in Nepal in 2015 seems to have toppled it into a mere snow slope. What was this famous rock band called?
context: The Hillary Step -- named for Sir Edmund Hillary, who with Tenzing Norgay made the first confirmed ascent on 29 May 1953 -- was the last major obstacle before Everest's summit. Climbers confirmed in 2017 that it had collapsed, most likely in Nepal's 2015 earthquake, and is now an easier snow slope. Sources: BBC News (2017); Wikipedia, 'Hillary Step.'

question: Not far above Everest Base Camp, the standard route crosses the most feared stretch of the climb: glacier ice grinding downhill about a metre a day, so the ladders and ropes fixed across it must be re-rigged again and again. Crevasses split it more than 100 metres deep, and one avalanche here in 2014 killed 16 Nepali guides. Teams hurry across before dawn, while the night cold holds it firmest. Which named section of the climb is this?
context: The Khumbu Icefall, between Base Camp and Camp I on the South Col route, is a slow-motion avalanche of glacier ice creeping about a metre a day. Its danger is not thin air but sudden collapse: seracs and crevasse walls give way without warning. A single 2014 avalanche killed 16 Nepali guides, and roughly 47 people died in the icefall between 1953 and 2023. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Khumbu Icefall'; peregrinetreks.com.

question: Nirmal Purja took a photograph near the summit of Mount Everest on 22 May 2019 that went viral around the world and set off a fierce argument about what climbing Everest has become. Eleven climbers died on the mountain that spring. What did his photograph show?
answer: A single-file line of hundreds of climbers
choices: A single-file line of hundreds of climbers
A single climber alone on a vast empty ridge
An avalanche pouring down the mountainside
A storm cloud swallowing the whole summit
context: Nirmal Purja's image showed roughly 300 climbers backed up single-file along the exposed summit ridge, deep in the death zone. It sparked a fierce debate about overcrowding on Everest: eleven people died during the 2019 season, several from exhaustion or from running out of bottled oxygen while stuck waiting in line for their turn at the top. Sources: CNN (2019); snopes.com.

question: Far out in the Pacific, the foot of a Hawaiian volcano sits so deep on the sea floor that far more of it lies hidden below the waves than rises above them. Mount Everest reaches highest above sea level, but measured from base to summit, this volcano is the tallest mountain on Earth. Which volcano is it?
context: Everest is the highest point above sea level (8,848.86 m), but Hawaii's Mauna Kea -- rising from a base on the Pacific sea floor -- stands more than 10,200 m from bottom to top, over a kilometre 'taller' than Everest, though most of it is submerged. 'Highest above sea level' and 'tallest base-to-summit' are simply different measurements. Sources: sciencefocus.com; spacedaily.com.

question: The jet stream, a river of wind that circles the whole planet, batters the summit of Mount Everest at over 300 km/h for most of the year, far too fierce to climb through. Only when one great seasonal wind system sweeps across South Asia does it shift north off the peak, opening a brief calm window for the climbers. Which wind system opens that window?
context: For most of the year the jet stream scours Everest's summit with winds over 200 mph (320 km/h). As the South Asian summer monsoon advances in late May, it shoves the jet stream northward off the peak, granting a short, relatively calm window -- often only a few days -- when most summit attempts are made. Sources: everestweather.com; wunderground.com (weather history).

question: The Arun river, near Mount Everest, was captured by another river network about 89,000 years ago and gouged out a deep gorge, stripping billions of tonnes of rock off the land around it. A 2024 study found that this gave Everest, still rising roughly 2 millimetres a year, a surprising extra boost. How could losing all that rock push the mountain higher?
answer: The lightened crust springs upward, floating higher
choices: The lightened crust springs upward, floating higher
The freezing river water shoves the peak up
The empty gorge fills with rising molten lava
The wind heaps the eroded rock onto the summit
context: This is isostatic rebound: Earth's crust floats on the denser, slowly-flowing mantle below, so when erosion strips away weight, the crust rises like a lightened boat. A 2024 Nature Geoscience study by UCL and the China University of Geosciences estimated that the Arun-Kosi river's gorge-carving has added roughly 15-50 m of extra height to Everest, on top of the plate-collision uplift of about 2 mm a year. Sources: UCL News (2024); phys.org.  (Legend.)

question: Snow caps the cone of Mount Fuji, rising 3,776 metres over Japan and almost perfectly even on both sides, the very picture of a volcano. Big cone-shaped peaks like Fuji, built up by many eruptions, all share one name. What kind of volcano is Fuji?
context: A stratovolcano (also called a composite volcano) is built up in steep layers of hardened lava and ash from many eruptions, which is why it forms the tall, symmetrical cone the whole world pictures — and Fuji, at 3,776 m, is the textbook example. Shield volcanoes like Hawaii's Mauna Loa are broad and gently sloped, cinder cones are small and stubby, and lava domes are bulging plugs of thick lava. Source: worldhistory.org/Mount_Fuji (3,776 m / 12,389 ft, 'classically symmetrical snow-capped cone'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji.

question: Ash from Mount Fuji fell like grey snow for weeks on the shogun's crowded capital after the volcano's last eruption began in December 1707. The eruption poured out no lava at all, yet it hurled about 800 million cubic metres of ash aloft, and winds carried it nearly 100 km to the city, darkening its midday sky. Which city did Fuji's ash bury?
context: The city was Edo — present-day Tokyo — about 100 km from the mountain. The Hoei eruption began on 16 December 1707 and, with no lava, rained roughly 800 million cubic metres of ash that reached Edo by the next day and darkened the capital's midday sky for weeks. Fuji is dormant, not extinct; 1707 was its last confirmed eruption. Sources: fujisan-kouhai.metro.tokyo.lg.jp (~800 million m3 ash, reached Edo ~100 km); education.nationalgeographic.org (last eruption 16 Dec 1707, ash on Edo by Dec 17).

question: The top of Mount Fuji is not a sharp point but a gaping crater, about 780 metres across and 240 metres deep. For centuries the pilgrims who struggled all the way up did not just peer in and head back down; they kept a special summit custom called ohachi-meguri. What did they do at the crater?
answer: Walk a full loop around its rim
choices: Walk a full loop around its rim
Bathe in a hot spring inside it
Light a bonfire on its edge
context: The circuit is called ohachi-meguri — roughly 'going around the bowl' — a walk along the rim of Fuji's summit crater, which is about 780 m across and 240 m deep. Pilgrims traditionally completed the loop after the long climb to the top. Sources: worldatlas.com/mountains/mount-fuji.html (crater 780 m diameter, 240 m deep; ohachi-meguri rim walk); worldhistory.org/Mount_Fuji.

question: Mount Fuji's flawless cone looks like one simple mountain, but that smooth shape is only about 10,000 years old. The cone that climbers scale today is called New Fuji, the youngest volcano to rise on this exact spot, and it grew right on top of whatever was already there. What does New Fuji actually sit upon?
context: Beneath New Fuji, which took its present shape only about 10,000 years ago, lie two older volcanoes: 'Old Fuji' (Ko-Fuji), built up around 100,000 years ago, and, buried deepest of all, the ancient Komitake. So the single graceful cone is really three volcanoes stacked over time. Source: britannica.com/place/Mount-Fuji (Komitake, surmounted by Old Fuji ~100,000 years ago, then New Fuji).

question: Katsushika Hokusai made a print of a huge claw of water curling over tiny fishing boats, about to crash down, as one of a series all about Mount Fuji. Fuji is in it too, a small calm cone far in the distance, almost lost behind the churning sea. What is this print, the most famous piece of Japanese art in the world, called?
context: It is 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa,' from Katsushika Hokusai's woodblock series 'Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji,' first published for the New Year of 1831 — often called the most recognizable work of Japanese art on Earth. The other choices are real prints too: 'South Wind, Clear Sky' (Red Fuji) comes from the same Fuji series, while the other two are famous works by Hiroshige. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty-six_Views_of_Mount_Fuji; asia-archive.si.edu (Great Wave most recognizable Japanese art).

question: The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization added Mount Fuji to the World Heritage List in June 2013, after years of work. Fuji is both a striking volcano and a peak woven into Japanese life for over a thousand years, so it could have made the list in more than one way. Which category did the organization pick for Fuji?
answer: As a cultural site, for inspiring art and faith
choices: As a cultural site, for inspiring art and faith
As a natural site, for its volcanic landscape
As a mixed site, for its rocks and forests
As an endangered site, for the crowds it draws
context: UNESCO added Fuji to the World Heritage List on 22 June 2013 as a CULTURAL site — 'Fujisan, sacred place and source of artistic inspiration' — honouring the centuries of pilgrims and artists it inspired, not its geology. Sources: worldatlas.com/mountains/mount-fuji.html (UNESCO Cultural Site, 22 June 2013); whc.unesco.org.

question: White-robed pilgrims have climbed Mount Fuji for more than a thousand years, and shrines to the mountain's spirit ring its summit and its base. Yet in all those centuries one whole group of people was forbidden the sacred summit, a ban Japan did not lift until 1872. Who had been barred from the top of Fuji?
context: The barred group was women, kept off the summit as ritually impure (kegare) until authorities lifted the ban in 1872 — a striking irony, since Fuji's own deity is a goddess, Konohanasakuya-hime, the 'Flower-Blossom Princess.' Her head shrine, Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha, dates to 806, and over 1,300 branch Sengen shrines were built across Japan to calm the volcano. Sources: japanupmagazine.com (women banned until 1872); worldhistory.org/Mount_Fuji (Konohanasakuya-hime; Sengen shrines).

question: Geologists asking why so huge a volcano grew on this exact spot in Japan point deep beneath Mount Fuji, to an arrangement of Earth's tectonic plates so unusual that few places on the planet share it. What lies beneath Fuji that makes the mountain possible?
answer: A meeting point of three plates
choices: A meeting point of three plates
A tear along two spreading plates
A crack within one solid plate
A slab of ocean floor sinking alone
context: Fuji rises at a rare TRIPLE JUNCTION where three tectonic plates meet: the Amurian (part of the Eurasian plate), the Okhotsk (part of the North American plate), and the Philippine Sea plate. That collision is why a volcano can grow here. Note: the Pacific plate is NOT one of the three — it subducts deeper to the east, beneath the Philippine Sea plate. Sources: worldatlas.com/mountains/mount-fuji.html (triple junction: Amurian, Okhotsk, Philippine Sea); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji.

question: Every climbing season, teams reach the tops of peaks in the Himalayas far taller than Mount Kailash, a 6,638 m pyramid in far western Tibet. Yet Kailash holds one mark that none of the taller peaks can claim. What is it?
answer: No human has ever stood on its summit.
choices: No human has ever stood on its summit.
Its slopes have never held permanent snow.
It sits at the exact center of the Himalayas.
Pilgrims are forbidden even to look at it.
context: Climbing Mount Kailash is forbidden — China bars any ascent out of respect for the faithful who hold the peak sacred — so while lesser mountains all around it are summited routinely, Kailash has never been climbed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash

question: Tibetans trekking the cold pilgrim path around Mount Kailash, a lone white pyramid of snow in western Tibet, do not call the mountain Kailash. They whisper another name as they walk, Gang Rinpoche. What does Gang Rinpoche mean?
context: Gang Rinpoche translates as 'Precious Jewel of Snow'; the mountain's Chinese name, Kangrinboqe (岗仁波齊), echoes the same Tibetan words. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash

question: On the pilgrim path around Mount Kailash, some walkers circle clockwise and others anticlockwise, because the peak is holy to more than one faith at once. Hindus honour it as the home of a god, and other faiths, each with its own story of the mountain, hold the same summit sacred. How many separate religions honour Kailash?
context: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Tibet's ancient pre-Buddhist Bon religion all hold Mount Kailash sacred — four faiths, one mountain; the Bon even circle it counter-clockwise while the others walk clockwise. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash

question: Pilgrims come to Mount Kailash not to conquer it but to honour it, so they never head for the summit. Instead they walk a circuit of roughly 52 km all the way around the mountain's base, over three hard days. What is this sacred circling of the peak called?
context: The circuit is the kora in Tibetan, or parikrama in Sanskrit — a circumambulation, walking around a holy place rather than climbing it. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash

question: Many Buddhists and Hindus who walk around Mount Kailash see in it far more than a peak of rock: they identify it with the world-mountain at the heart of creation, the axis the whole universe spins around. By what name do they know this cosmic mountain?
context: In Buddhist cosmology Kailash is identified with Mount Meru, the cosmic axis at the center of the universe; the mountain's real, walkable form gives that vast idea a physical home. This is a religious belief. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash  (Legend.)

question: The three-day walk around Mount Kailash climbs to one brutal high point: a wind-scoured pass at 5,650 metres, higher than the summit of any mountain in the lower 48 states of the United States. There, pilgrims string prayer flags and leave a lock of hair behind them. What is this famous high pass called?
context: The Drölma La (Dolma Pass), at 5,650 m, is the highest point of the Kailash kora; 'La' is the Tibetan word for a mountain pass. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash

question: Buddhist pilgrims say that a single walk around Mount Kailash washes away the sins of a whole lifetime. Some keep walking for months, seeking the greater reward said to await anyone who completes a sacred number of circuits: freedom from the cycle of rebirth. How many circuits are said to bring that freedom?
context: 108 is a sacred number across the dharmic faiths (a mala prayer-string has 108 beads); completing 108 koras of Kailash is said to bring nirvana. This is a religious belief. https://himalayanexpeditions.com/wp/trips/mt-kailash-erase-the-sins-of-a-lifetime/  (Legend.)

question: Within about 60 km of Mount Kailash, giants among Asia's rivers begin their long journeys: the Indus, the Sutlej, the Brahmaputra and one more, making the land around the peak one of Earth's greatest watersheds. That last river is a major feeder of which other sacred river?
context: The fourth is the Karnali (Ghaghara), a major tributary of the Ganges — so the region around one mountain feeds the Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra, and the Ganges. The rivers rise nearby, not from the summit itself. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash

question: Hindus who look up at the snow-capped pyramid of Mount Kailash, in far western Tibet, see no ordinary mountain but the home of one of their greatest gods. They picture him seated in eternal meditation on its icy summit, with his divine wife at his side. Which Hindu god is said to dwell atop Kailash?
context: Hindus revere Kailash as the abode of Shiva, who dwells there with his consort Parvati — a belief held sacred by the faithful. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash  (Legend.)

question: Reinhold Messner, the first mountaineer to climb all fourteen of the 8,000-metre peaks, was offered a permit to climb Mount Kailash in the 1980s and turned it down. Standing on that summit, he warned, would destroy something far greater than any climbing record. What did Messner say conquering Kailash would conquer?
choices: The last secret of the Himalayas
The pride of the Tibetan people
His own will to climb again
context: Messner reportedly explained: 'If we conquer this mountain, then we conquer something in people's souls' — leaving Kailash the great peak deliberately left unclimbed out of respect. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kailash

question: Two large lakes lie side by side at the foot of Mount Kailash, and pilgrims marvel at how unlike they are. One is Manasarovar, round and holy, its fresh water lying about 4,590 metres up. Its next-door neighbour is distinctly salty and avoided as an unlucky place, even though fresh Manasarovar spills over into it. What is the salty neighbour called?
context: Rakshastal ('lake of the demon') sits right beside sweet, sacred Manasarovar, which even overflows into it through a natural channel, the Ganga Chhu — a freshwater lake and a salt lake as next-door neighbors. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailash_Mansarovar

question: A long vertical gash runs down the south face of Mount Kailash, and Tibetan Buddhists explain it with a legend. The great yogi Milarepa and a priest of the older Bön faith held a contest of miracles, racing to reach the summit at dawn. Milarepa won by riding the rays of the rising sun, and his startled rival fell, carving the scar. What did the Bön priest tumble from?
context: In the legend the Bon priest Naro Bönchung fell from his flying drum, which gouged the mark still visible on Kailash's south face today. This is a traditional legend, not history. https://thehikinglife.com/2020/04/mount-kailash-kora-trekking-around-tibets-sacred-mountain/

question: Mount Roraima rises straight up out of the South American rainforest, flat on top and walled by steep cliffs on every side, standing alone like an island above the trees. The Pemon people gave such table-mountains a name. What is a mountain like Roraima called?
context: 'Tepui' is the Pemon word for these flat-topped table mountains; it means roughly 'house of the gods.' A tepui's walls rise so sheer that the summit is cut off from the world below, like an island in the sky. Source: Grokipedia 'Mount Roraima'; geologyscience.com 'Mount Roraima or Roraima Tepui.'

question: Hikers on the broad rock plateau atop Mount Roraima, in the Guiana Highlands of northern South America, can cross international borders without ever leaving the summit. How many countries share Roraima's cliff-walled top?
context: Venezuela holds about 85% of the summit, Guyana about 10%, and Brazil about 5% — three nations meeting on one cloud-wrapped tabletop 2,810 m up, which is also the highest point in all of Guyana. Source: Grokipedia 'Mount Roraima'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Roraima.

question: Mount Roraima has loomed over the Pemon people of the Guiana Highlands for centuries, yet almost nobody could see its top, and early travellers rarely glimpsed the summit at all. Something covers it day after day. What almost always hides the top of Roraima?
context: Roraima's summit sits high enough to stay wrapped in cloud and mist almost every day — cool at around 10 C by day and near freezing at night, while the jungle far below swelters at 24-26 C. It is a cold, hidden island floating above the tropics. Source: Grokipedia 'Mount Roraima' (Climate and Hydrology); beautifulworld.com 'Mount Roraima.'

question: Geologists have dated the pale sandstone of Mount Roraima's cliffs to nearly two billion years old, laid down in the geological era known as the Precambrian. It stands among the most ancient exposed rocks found anywhere on Earth. What was true of the world back when this rock was first forming?
answer: no animals or plants existed anywhere yet
choices: no animals or plants existed anywhere yet
the dinosaurs were at their peak
early humans were spreading across the land
the continents already held their modern shapes
context: The Roraima Supergroup sandstone formed roughly 1.7-2 billion years ago, long before complex life. Dinosaurs came less than 250 million years ago and humans less than a million; two billion years ago, Earth's land was bare rock under a young sky. Source: Grokipedia 'Mount Roraima' (Origin and Composition; U-Pb zircon max age 1883 Ma); geologyscience.com 'Mount Roraima.'

question: Mount Roraima's summit has stood marooned on its cliffs for millions of years, its plants and creatures sealed off from the jungle far below. Cut off so completely, life on the plateau has gone its own way, as it does on a lonely island. What is remarkable about many of the living things up there?
answer: they exist nowhere else on Earth
choices: they exist nowhere else on Earth
they grow far larger than their lowland kin
they change colour with the seasons
they were carried up by early climbers
context: Isolation on a 'sky island' breeds endemism — species found in one place only. Roraima's tiny black pebble toad, for instance, lives on this tepui and one neighbour and nowhere else in the world, a vivid proof that each cut-off summit grows its own life. Source: Grokipedia 'Mount Roraima' (biodiversity / sky islands); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oreophrynella_quelchii.

question: Rain drenches Mount Roraima's flat summit almost daily, gathers into clear streams, and then spills straight over the cliff rim in long silver ribbons. Those summit-born streams run off to join the Orinoco, the Essequibo, and the Amazon, among the mightiest rivers on the continent. Local people gave Roraima a fond nickname for sending its rain out to so many distant lands. What do they call it?
context: Streams born on Roraima's summit — the Arabopo, the Waruma, the Cotingo — flow into the Orinoco, Essequibo, and Amazon systems, so Roraima is fondly called the 'mother of waters.' (Note: the giant Angel Falls is NOT here — it drops from a different tepui, Auyan-tepui, to the west.) Source: Grokipedia 'Mount Roraima' (Hydrology).

question: Trekkers who reach the summit of Mount Roraima describe stepping into an alien world — towers of black rock, shallow sandy gorges, deep sinkholes, and pools scoured out by the endless rain. In one broad hollow the ground itself sparkles and glints underfoot, so dazzling in the light that hikers gave the place its own nickname. What lies scattered thickly across the ground there?
answer: a scatter of clear quartz crystals
choices: a scatter of clear quartz crystals
context: Trekkers call it the 'Crystal Valley' — one of the summit's wonders, where clear quartz crystals lie strewn across the sandstone, weathered out of the ancient rock over ages. The plateau also holds crystal-clear pools nicknamed the 'jacuzzis.' Source: Grokipedia 'Mount Roraima' (Unique Geological Features); beautifulworld.com 'Mount Roraima.'

question: Mount Roraima's cliff-walled plateau is sealed off on every side, and rumour said its unreachable top might hide almost anything. The idea fired the mind of Arthur Conan Doyle. His famous adventure novel of 1912 is set on a South American table mountain just like it, where explorers led by the fierce Professor Challenger find dinosaurs still roaming. What is the novel called?
choices: Journey to the Center of the Earth
context: Doyle's 1912 novel 'The Lost World' drew on real accounts of Roraima's inaccessible summit — an 'island in the sky' that explorers imagined might still hide prehistoric life. The book helped make tepuis famous around the world. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lost_World_(Conan_Doyle_novel); Grokipedia 'Mount Roraima.'  (Legend.)

question: A snowy cone of a volcano stood quiet for years above the forests of Washington State. Then, on 18 May 1980, it blew up in the deadliest volcanic blast in United States history. Which Cascade volcano was it?
context: Mount St. Helens stands in Washington's Cascade Range, a chain of volcanoes running down the Pacific Northwest. Its eruption on 18 May 1980 remains the deadliest and most destructive in United States history. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: Magma shoved its way into Mount St. Helens in the spring of 1980, and the mountain's north face swelled outward. Geologists simply nicknamed it 'the bulge', and it crept out so relentlessly that surveyors could measure its advance from one day to the next. About how far did the bulge push out each day?
context: As magma pushed in, the bulge grew about 5 to 6 feet (1.5-1.8 m) per day, shoving the north face more than 400 feet outward by mid-May — a mountainside visibly moving from one day to the next. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: Mount St. Helens' north face had bulged outward for weeks until the whole slope was dangerously oversteepened. Then, at 8:32 on the morning of 18 May 1980, one sudden natural event let the unstable slope break loose and begin to slide. What set the collapse off that morning?
context: The trigger was a magnitude 5.1 earthquake centered about a mile beneath the north slope. It shook the oversteepened bulge loose at 8:32 a.m. and set the whole collapse in motion. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: Forests for miles around Mount St. Helens lay flattened after the morning of 18 May 1980, when the mountain's whole north face let go and the volcano tore itself apart. That morning also set a world record that still stands, though people often misremember which one. Which record does the 1980 event hold?
answer: The largest landslide in recorded history
choices: The largest landslide in recorded history
The largest volcanic eruption in recorded history
The deadliest volcanic eruption in recorded history
The tallest eruption column ever recorded
context: About 0.67 cubic miles (2.8 km3) of mountain slid away at 70-150 mph — the largest landslide (debris avalanche) in recorded history. Bigger eruptions and deadlier ones have occurred; St. Helens' true record was this colossal collapse. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: Geologists studying the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens were stunned above all by one detail: the direction its opening blast travelled, which the eruption is still remembered for. Which way did that first great blast explode from the mountain?
answer: Sideways, tearing out across the land
choices: Sideways, tearing out across the land
context: With the north face stripped away, the pressurized magma was uncorked and blasted sideways — a lateral blast that tore outward at over 300 mph (briefly supersonic) at up to 660 degrees F (350 C), flattening about 230 square miles (600 sq km) of forest as far as 17 miles away. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: David Johnston, a 30-year-old geologist with the United States Geological Survey, was manning a lonely monitoring post about 6 miles north of Mount St. Helens on the morning of 18 May 1980. The instant the eruption began, he keyed his two-way radio and shouted a warning to his team, and seconds later the blast swept over the ridge; his body was never found. What did he shout?
context: Johnston was at the Coldwater II post about 6 miles (10 km) north, radioing the USGS office in Vancouver, Washington. His body was never found, and the ridge where he died was renamed Johnston Ridge in his honor. Of the 57 people killed, most died from inhaling hot ash. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_A._Johnston

question: Harry Truman, 83, had run the lodge at Spirit Lake beneath Mount St. Helens for 52 years, and when officials ordered everyone off the mountain in 1980, he flatly refused — 'You couldn't pull me out with a mule team,' he said. When the eruption buried his lodge under 150 feet of debris, the old innkeeper went down with a houseful of animals he would not abandon. What were they?
context: Harry R. Truman had run the Mount St. Helens Lodge at Spirit Lake for 52 years. His defiance made him a national folk hero, with over 100 songs written about him; he was buried with his 16 cats under about 150 feet of avalanche debris. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_R._Truman

question: Ash from Mount St. Helens punched about 80,000 feet into the sky within minutes of the 1980 eruption, and fast high-altitude winds seized the cloud and carried it eastward across the continent. Then it kept going, all the way around the planet. About how long did that trip around the whole Earth take?
context: The ash column rose about 80,000 feet (24 km) in under 15 minutes. Ash fell like snow across the Northwest, turned midday to darkness in Spokane, reached Denver by the next day, and circled the entire Earth in about 15 days. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: Mount St. Helens lost about 1,300 feet of its summit in a few minutes on 18 May 1980, its peak dropping from 9,677 feet to 8,363. Where a symmetrical snow-capped cone had once towered, the eruption left a gaping crater a mile wide, with one very distinctive shape. What shape was the new crater?
context: The summit fell from 9,677 feet (2,950 m) to 8,363 feet (2,549 m) — about 1,314 feet (401 m) lost in minutes — leaving a mile-wide horseshoe-shaped crater open to the north. A new lava dome has slowly rebuilt inside it ever since. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: When Mount St. Helens' avalanche roared into Spirit Lake at the mountain's foot, it shoved the whole lake's surface nearly 200 feet higher and churned it into chaos. More than 40 years later, one eerie remnant of that morning still drifts back and forth across Spirit Lake, shifting with the wind. What still floats on the lake today?
answer: A vast raft of floating logs
choices: A vast raft of floating logs
context: The debris avalanche raised Spirit Lake's surface by about 197 feet and swept thousands of blasted-down trees into it. The huge raft of shattered logs still floats on the lake, drifting with the wind more than 40 years later. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: Venice's rulers did something drastic in 1291: they banished every glassmaker's furnace from the city to the island of Murano, across the water. Venice loved its glass, yet one danger from the furnaces kept happening. What was it?
answer: The furnaces kept setting the city on fire.
choices: The furnaces kept setting the city on fire.
The furnaces kept blackening the churches with smoke.
The furnaces kept fouling the canals with waste.
The furnaces kept sickening the people with fumes.
context: Venice was a crowded city built largely of wood, and the glassmakers' roaring furnaces set off fire after fire. The decree of 8 November 1291 moved every furnace to Murano, a cluster of islands less than two kilometers north in the same lagoon — close enough to control, far enough to contain both the flames and, later, the trade's secrets. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murano_glass.

question: Murano's glassmakers grew famous for a dazzling glass shot through with tiny repeating patterns, each a little burst of color. They called it 'millefiori.' Word for word from Italian, what does that name mean?
context: 'Mille' means thousand and 'fiori' means flowers — 'a thousand flowers.' The name fits: the glass is packed with countless tiny flower patterns hidden inside it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murrine.

question: The Venetian Republic guarded a Murano glass master almost like a prisoner, since his rare skill was a state treasure, and he could not leave Venice without permission. If a master slipped abroad and taught the craft to a rival city, what did the law threaten?
context: Betraying the glass secret could cost a master his life — or the confiscation of everything he owned. The artisans became, in effect, prisoners of their own skill. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murano_glass.

question: A Murano glasshouse of the early 1600s discovered a glittering brown glass flecked with thousands of tiny copper sparks, as if the night sky were caught inside it. Its makers called it aventurine, after the Italian phrase 'a ventura'. What does that phrase mean?
context: 'A ventura' means 'by chance' — the glass, also called goldstone, was reportedly discovered partly by accident, first documented in 1626. The English word 'adventure' shares the same root, which makes 'by adventure' a tempting trap. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murano_glass.

question: Now and then a Murano master defied the law that kept him in Venice and fled abroad, carrying the glass secret in his head. Unable to reach the runaway, the Republic turned its pressure on those he had left behind on the island. Whom did Venice imprison to force him home?
context: Venice would jail a fugitive glassmaker's family to force his return. According to accounts, if he still refused, the Republic could send an assassin to kill him abroad — so the secret would die with him. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murano_glass.  (Legend.)

question: Venice honored Murano's glass masters as it honored few craftsmen anywhere, and a decree of 1376 gave their daughters a rare privilege no other craftsman's daughter in the city could dream of. Into which class could a glass master's daughter marry without losing rank?
context: By the decree of 22 December 1376, a glass master's daughter who married a Venetian nobleman lost no rank — and her children were still counted as nobles, unheard-of for an artisan family. Glass masters were also allowed to carry swords and enjoyed a measure of immunity from prosecution. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murano_glass.

question: Ordinary medieval glass carried an ugly greenish tint from iron in the sand until Angelo Barovier of Murano beat it in the 1400s. He purified his materials into 'cristallo', a glass so clear it looked like pure spring water, by adding one mineral that canceled the color out. What did he add?
context: Barovier added manganese dioxide — nicknamed 'glassmaker's soap' — which cancels the green-brown iron tint. Cristallo (from 'rocca di cristallo,' rock crystal) was first documented on 24 May 1453; Barovier's family had worked Murano glass since at least 1331, and he died in 1460. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murano_glass.

question: Angelo Barovier of Murano invented 'lattimo,' an opaque milk-white glass that seemed to glow. He made it for one clever reason: to imitate a rare and costly luxury that rich Europeans were importing from the East. What white treasure was lattimo made to copy?
context: Lattimo (from 'latte,' milk) was Barovier's milk-white glass, made to imitate the porcelain of China that Europe's rich prized above almost anything. He also created 'calcedonio,' a marbled glass swirled to look like veined chalcedony stone. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murano_glass.

question: Murano's most magical trick hides a tiny, perfect flower deep inside solid glass. The maker bundles many colored glass rods into a flower picture, fuses them into one thick rod, then heats it and pulls it out long and thin — shrinking the picture without smearing it. What must the maker do next to reveal the flower?
choices: blow it into a hollow bubble
grind it down to a powder
hammer it into a flat sheet
context: The maker slices the long rod crosswise, and every thin slice reveals the very same flower hidden inside — exactly like cutting through a stick of seaside rock. The colored rods are called 'canes,' and the sliced pieces 'murrine.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murrine.

question: Marietta Barovier, daughter of the Murano master Angelo, ran the family glass workshop herself, in a trade that passed from father to son and was closed to women. In 1487 the Republic granted her a working privilege almost unheard-of for a woman of her time. What did she win?
answer: a glass furnace of her own
choices: a glass furnace of her own
a seat on the guild council
context: In 1487 Marietta Barovier won permission for her own kiln to make her 'beautiful, unusual and not blown' works — and she is credited with inventing the striped 'rosetta' or chevron bead around 1480, later traded across the world for centuries. A rare woman master in a father-to-son trade. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marietta_Barovier.

question: The road into the rocky citadel of Mycenae, in Greece, passes through a gate cut in its massive fortress wall. Above the doorway, two great stone creatures rear up on their hind legs, facing each other across a central column. What beasts stand guard over the gate?
context: This is the Lion Gate, built around 1250 BC and the oldest monumental sculpture in Europe still standing where it was first set. The two lionesses' heads were carved from separate blocks (probably steatite) and were lost long ago, so today the beasts face each other headless. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion_Gate

question: Greeks of later ages looked at the walls of Mycenae, built from limestone blocks so huge that some weigh close to 100 tonnes, and refused to believe ordinary men had ever moved them. They said a race of giants must have piled the stones. What is this style of huge-block work still called?
context: The giants the Greeks blamed were the Cyclopes, the one-eyed monsters of legend -- so we call the huge-block style 'cyclopean' masonry to this day. Of the similar walls at nearby Tiryns, the ancient writer Pausanias marveled that 'a pair of mules could not move the smallest stone from its place to the slightest degree.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclopean_masonry

question: Hidden inside the fortress wall of Mycenae, a narrow secret stairway of about 99 steps plunges some 15 meters straight down through solid rock. It ends far below the citadel floor. What did the Mycenaeans build at the bottom of that deep hidden stair?
choices: An escape tunnel to the plain
context: The stair led down to an underground cistern fed by a spring piped in from outside the walls, so the citadel never ran dry -- its people could keep drinking fresh water even while an enemy army camped at the gates. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenae

question: Heinrich Schliemann lifted a golden death mask from a grave shaft deep inside Mycenae in 1876 and announced that he had gazed upon the face of Agamemnon, the legendary king of the Trojan War. The mask is real and gorgeous, but archaeologists are certain it never covered Agamemnon's face. What is wrong with the famous name?
answer: The mask is far older than Agamemnon could ever have been
choices: The mask is far older than Agamemnon could ever have been
The mask clearly shows a woman's face, not a king's
Schliemann's own workmen hammered it out overnight
A Victorian restorer added the beard much later
context: The Mask of Agamemnon is real Bronze-Age gold, but it dates to about 1550-1500 BC -- roughly three centuries before the traditional time of the Trojan War, so it cannot be Agamemnon's. It is a genuine treasure attached to the wrong name. (Schliemann's dramatic 'gazed upon the face of Agamemnon' line may itself be a later invention.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon  (Legend.)

question: Just outside the gates of Mycenae stands the Treasury of Atreus, a beehive-shaped tomb roofed by a smooth stone dome about 14.5 metres across -- each ring of blocks laid a little further inward than the ring below, with no mortar at all. For more than a thousand years, no builder anywhere on Earth roofed a wider space. Which later dome finally beat its record?
context: The corbelled dome of the Treasury of Atreus (a 'tholos' or beehive tomb, built around 1300-1250 BC) held the record for the widest dome in the world until the Romans raised the Pantheon around 126 AD, whose span of about 43 metres finally surpassed it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasury_of_Atreus

question: At Mycenae, the builders of the citadel's great gate laid a single flat block, the lintel, across the two upright doorposts. Directly above it they deliberately left a hollow triangular gap in the wall. Why did the Mycenaean builders leave that triangular gap over the lintel?
answer: To channel the wall's weight around the lintel
choices: To channel the wall's weight around the lintel
To vent the gatehouse chamber's smoke and heat
To frame a narrow lookout slot over the road
To cradle a bronze lamp above the great doorway
context: Directly above the lintel the builders left a hollow triangular gap -- a 'relieving triangle' -- that channels the crushing weight of the wall outward to the sides, so the lintel below never has to bear it and cannot snap. The celebrated slab of two lionesses is simply the light decorative filler plugging that structural hole. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion_Gate ; https://www.thearchaeologist.org/blog/the-mycenaean-lion-gate-the-architecture-of-power

question: Bronze Age builders laid a single lintel slab across the great stone doorway of the Treasury of Atreus, the grandest of the beehive tombs outside Mycenae. Of all the blocks Greek builders ever shaped for a structure, this one holds a record no other Greek stone can match. What record does it hold?
answer: It is the heaviest stone the Greeks ever raised
choices: It is the heaviest stone the Greeks ever raised
It is the oldest carved stone still standing in Greece
It is the most tightly fitted stone in any Greek wall
It is the only stone at the tomb hauled from overseas
context: That single lintel block weighs about 120 tonnes -- roughly 8 metres long, 5 metres wide, and 1.2 metres thick -- the heaviest stone known from all of Greek architecture. How Bronze-Age crews lifted it into place above the door is still debated. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasury_of_Atreus

question: Between the two rearing stone beasts over the gate at Mycenae stands a carved column with a strange shape. Every later Greek column tapered toward the top, but this one grows wider at the top than at the base. The upside-down pillar was a sacred symbol the mainland Mycenaeans borrowed from an older, more refined civilization they deeply admired. Which people did they copy it from?
context: The tapering-upward pillar is a Minoan column, the reverse of a normal Greek one -- a religious emblem the Mycenaeans of the mainland adopted from the earlier Minoan civilization on the island of Crete, whose art and palaces they deeply admired. Source: https://www.greecehighdefinition.com/blog/2017/9/7/the-lion-gate-of-mycenae-1300-1250-bce

question: Visitors to the ruined city of Nan Madol, off the Pacific island of Pohnpei, cross the tidal channels between its 92 or so stone islets by canoe. Early travellers thought it looked like a famous canal city of Europe and nicknamed it 'the ___ of the Pacific'. Which city fills the blank?
context: Nan Madol's roughly 92 stone islets, off Temwen Island in Pohnpei, Micronesia, are threaded by saltwater tidal canals that visitors cross by canoe, so it became known as the 'Venice of the Pacific.' Source: Ancient Origins (ancient-origins.net); Grokipedia/Wikipedia (Nan Madol).

question: The builders of Nan Madol raised their whole city out in the shallow sea off Pohnpei, stacking stone on the natural shelf just beneath the tide, where most ancient builders sought bedrock or dry high ground. Nan Madol is the only ancient city built on top of what?
context: UNESCO made Nan Madol a World Heritage Site in 2016 — the first in the Federated States of Micronesia — billing it as the only ancient city ever built atop a coral reef. Source: smithsonianmag.com; whc.unesco.org (2016 inscription).

question: On the reef of Pohnpei, a small Pacific island in Micronesia, an ancient people raised a whole stone city on the water: nearly a hundred artificial islets laced together by narrow canals. In the Pohnpeian language the city's name carries a quietly poetic meaning. What does the name Nan Madol mean?
context: 'Nan Madol' means the space between — a nod to the tidal canals weaving among its islets; its older traditional name was Soun Nan-leng, 'Reef of Heaven.' Source: Ancient Origins; Khan Academy/Smarthistory; Gene Ashby, 'Pohnpei, An Island Argosy.'

question: Double walls of dry-stacked basalt, rising some 25 feet with no mortar at all, still ring Nandauwas, the grandest islet of Nan Madol, the Saudeleur lords' city on the reef beside Pohnpei. What did these great walls guard at their heart?
answer: the tomb of the first Saudeleur king
choices: the tomb of the first Saudeleur king
a shrine to the thunder god Nahn Sapwe
the dynasty's hoard of sacred treasure
the great feasting hall of the priests
context: Nandauwas, the grandest islet, is the royal tomb compound in the sacred sector; its double-tiered, dry-stacked basalt walls rise up to about 7.6 m (25 ft), guarding the tomb of the first Saudeleur ruler. Source: labrujulaverde.com; thearchaeologist.org ('over 25 feet high').

question: Pohnpei's builders cut every dark basalt column of Nan Madol from a single volcanic plug on the island, then somehow moved each one out to the reef and stacked it into the walls. Where on Pohnpei did they cut all that stone?
choices: on the same shore as the reef city
in a river valley just inland
context: The columnar basalt came from a volcanic plug on the far side of Pohnpei (some accounts place it near Sokehs, roughly 25 miles away) and was moved clear across the island and out over the water to the reef. Source: heritagedaily.com (2020); clickpetroleoegas summary.

question: Scholars have added up every basalt column and every basket of coral fill stacked onto the reef at Nan Madol, a load its builders shifted with no wheels, no pulleys and no metal tools at all. By their rough estimate, how much stone did the builders haul out into the sea?
context: Scholars estimate roughly 750,000 tonnes of basalt and coral were stacked here (a scholarly estimate, not a measured figure) — averaging about 1,850 tonnes a year across four centuries of building, all with no metal, wheels, or pulleys. Source: clickpetroleoegas floating-city article; WebSearch corroboration on the 750,000-tonne estimate.

question: Basalt columns weighing 5 tonnes, some of them as much as 50, travelled from the quarry on Pohnpei out to the reef at Nan Madol, though the builders had no wheels and no draft animals. No one has ever proved how, but archaeologists have one leading idea, still unproven. What is their best guess?
answer: they floated the columns on log rafts at high tide
choices: they floated the columns on log rafts at high tide
they rolled the columns overland on palm-trunk rollers
they dragged the columns across the reef on ropes
they ferried the columns inside large sailing canoes
context: How the multi-tonne columns were moved is still unsolved; the leading idea is that they were floated around the coast on palm- or bamboo-log rafts riding the tides — but there is no definitive proof, and dragging or a mix of methods remain possible. Source: clickpetroleoegas summary; vocal.media/history (Nan Madol basalt transport).

question: The Saudeleur lords began raising Nan Madol on a reef beside Pohnpei around the year 1200: nearly a hundred small artificial islets of stacked basalt logs. They are remembered for a first as remarkable as their stonework, one no earlier chief on Pohnpei had ever managed. What was it?
answer: uniting all of Pohnpei under one rule
choices: uniting all of Pohnpei under one rule
inventing a written script for the island
sailing on to settle distant Hawaii
carving the Pacific's first stone money
context: The Saudeleur were priest-kings — the first dynasty to unite Pohnpei's roughly 25,000 people under a single rule — and they governed from Nan Madol's islets until about 1628, when oral tradition says the warrior Isokelekel overthrew the last Saudeleur. Source: heritagedaily.com (2020); Grokipedia/Wikipedia (Nan Madol).

question: Two named precincts divide the roughly 92 islets of Nan Madol, on the reef of Pohnpei: Madol Powe and Madol Pah, each set aside for a different half of Saudeleur life. Along what line did the Saudeleurs divide their city?
answer: one half for the sacred dead, the other for the living rulers
choices: one half for the sacred dead, the other for the living rulers
one half for the noble-born, the other for the commoners
one half for the farmers, the other for the fishing clans
one half for the warriors, the other for the merchants
context: Nan Madol split in two: Madol Powe, the sacred upper sector (about 58 islets) where priests lived and the dead were entombed, and Madol Pah, the lower royal-administrative sector for the living. Source: Grokipedia/Wikipedia (Nan Madol); smarthistory.org/nan-madol.

question: Pliny the Younger, then 17, watched Mount Vesuvius erupt from Misenum, across the Bay of Naples, in AD 79, and wrote the only eyewitness account that survives. To capture the towering ash cloud, he compared its shape to a tree that grows all over Italy. Which tree did he name?
context: Pliny wrote that the cloud rose on a long trunk that then 'spread out into a number of branches' -- the exact silhouette of the Italian stone pine, or umbrella pine, whose flat, spreading canopy still crowns Italian hillsides. His letters to the historian Tacitus are why we can still picture that day. Source: cmuntz.hosted.uark.edu (Pliny the Younger, letters); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Younger.

question: Allied forces were camped all around the Bay of Naples in March 1944, in the middle of World War II, when Mount Vesuvius erupted again. Its falling ash and hot cinders rained down on a nearby base and wrecked about 80 war machines parked there. What did the eruption destroy?
context: The eruption buried the village of San Sebastiano and destroyed or badly damaged roughly 80 American B-25 Mitchell bombers parked at a nearby airfield -- a volcano stealing planes out from under an air force. It was Vesuvius's last eruption to date; the mountain has been ominously quiet ever since. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Vesuvius.

question: West of Naples lies the Campi Flegrei, the 'burning fields', where the ground itself runs hot and gases hiss up through cracks. At its Solfatara crater, visitors can walk right up and stand beside more than 150 of one bubbling, blistering feature. What bubbles away at Solfatara?
context: Solfatara is a shallow crater inside the Campi Flegrei that has steamed for thousands of years -- the Romans imagined it an entrance to the underworld. Its fumaroles hiss out sulphur gases, and more than 150 mud pools plop and bubble at boiling heat: a small, safe window onto the giant volcanic system sleeping below. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campi_Flegrei.

question: The Campi Flegrei, the supervolcano west of Naples, unleashed the Campanian Ignimbrite about 39,000 years ago, hurling out roughly 200 cubic kilometres of magma and dwarfing anything Vesuvius has done. Geologists still dig up its grey ash layer, which settled far from the volcano. How far from Naples did the ash carry?
