context: The Campanian Ignimbrite spread its ash as far as Eastern Europe -- one of the biggest eruptions the Mediterranean has ever seen, and far larger than the AD 79 blast that buried Pompeii. Its ash has also turned up in a cave in Libya. It is a reminder that the gentle holiday coast of the Bay of Naples sits directly atop one of the most powerful volcanic systems on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campi_Flegrei; eprints.soton.ac.uk/378140 (Barton et al. 2015).

question: The ground near Pozzuoli, inside the restless Campi Flegrei, split open in 1538 and erupted for eight days straight. When it finally stopped, the terrified locals found the landscape changed for good: a new feature had appeared where there had been none a week earlier. What had the eruption created?
context: The new hill was named Monte Nuovo -- 'New Mountain' -- and at nearly 500 years old it is still one of the youngest mountains in Europe, built in a single week by the Campi Flegrei. It is a vivid reminder that this sleeping supervolcano can reshape the map almost overnight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campi_Flegrei.

question: Pozzuoli, a port inside the Campi Flegrei west of Naples, lives with bradyseism, its name Greek for 'slow earthquake'. Over months and years the whole town swells upward by metres, then settles back, and in the 1980s the rise left its harbour useless. What drives this slow heaving of the ground?
answer: magma and gas pushing up from far below
choices: magma and gas pushing up from far below
the ground warming and cooling with the seasons
the tides of the bay rocking the coastline
the African plate slowly flexing the crust
context: Bradyseism is driven by heat and pressure from magma and gases deep under the Campi Flegrei: they push the ground up, then let it settle, moving whole neighbourhoods vertically by metres over years. In the 1980s Pozzuoli rose so much that its harbour became unusable and part of the old town had to be evacuated. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macellum_of_Pozzuoli; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campi_Flegrei.

question: The three marble columns still standing in the ruined Roman market at Pozzuoli each carry a neat band of small round holes, several metres up the shaft -- always in the same narrow band, never higher or lower. What made those holes in the hard marble?
context: The holes were drilled by Lithophaga, marine 'date mussels' that bore into rock -- and they can only have done so while the columns stood underwater in the sea. Because the columns never fell, that band of borings, up to about 5.8 m (19 ft) high, proves the whole market slowly sank beneath the waves and later rose back up. The geologist Charles Lyell put these columns on the frontispiece of his 'Principles of Geology' (1830). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macellum_of_Pozzuoli.

question: Beneath the streets of Naples runs a vast labyrinth cut into soft volcanic tuff. The Greeks first dug it 2,500 years ago for building stone; the Romans turned the shafts into aqueducts and water cisterns. Then, in the 1940s, as World War II reached Naples, the people of the city put the ancient caverns to a dramatic new use. What did Neapolitans use the old tunnels for during the war?
context: The caverns were enlarged with stairways and packed with tens of thousands of people sheltering from Allied bombing raids -- all cut into the same soft tuff the local volcanoes had laid down, quarried by Greeks, plumbed by Romans, and finally hiding Neapolitans from the bombs. Tuff is easy to carve yet hardens in air, which is why a single rock made Naples both buildable above and hollow below. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naples_underground_geothermal_zone.

question: Over a thousand sika deer wander the parks and stroll the streets of Nara, the old capital in central Japan. Visitors buy small brown biscuits called shika senbei, and the deer swarm anyone holding one. Many have picked up a funny little trick to beg for a treat. What is it?
answer: Dip their heads in a bow
choices: Dip their heads in a bow
Nudge bags open with their noses
context: Nara's roughly 1,200 free-roaming sika deer are a designated natural treasure, and their head-dip 'bow' -- a learned trick used to beg for shika senbei rice crackers -- is the city's signature sight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nara_Park; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nara,_Nara.

question: The deer of Nara, an old capital in central Japan, have walked its streets freely among people for more than a thousand years. For most of that time, killing one of the deer was punished by death, and the last person executed for it died in 1637. What made these deer so fiercely protected?
answer: They were revered as sacred messengers of a Shinto god
choices: They were revered as sacred messengers of a Shinto god
They were believed to carry the souls of the dead
They were royal game reserved for the emperor's hunts
They were kept as living charms to ward off fire
context: The deer of Nara were revered as sacred messengers of the god of Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Shrine). By legend the tie began when the thunder god Takemikazuchi rode to Nara's Mount Mikasa on a white deer to guard the new capital. Harming a deer stayed a capital offense until 1637, the last recorded execution for it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nara_Park; worldhistory.org/Kasuga_Taisha.

question: A huge wooden pillar inside the hall of the Daibutsu, Nara's giant bronze Buddha cast more than 1,200 years ago, has a hole cut through its base said to be the size of one of the statue's nostrils. Temple lore tells what happens to children who squeeze all the way through. What happens to them?
answer: They are granted good fortune or enlightenment
choices: They are granted good fortune or enlightenment
They must leave an offering at the altar
They may ring the temple's great bell once
They earn a blessing written by the monks
context: The pillar hole in Todai-ji's Great Buddha Hall (Daibutsuden) is said to match the size of the Daibutsu's nostril; crawling through it is a popular custom said to bring good luck or enlightenment, and a queue forms for it. The hole and the tradition are real; the reward is folklore. Source: travel/reference accounts incl. muza-chan.net 'Sightseeing Nara, the Hole in the Pillar.'  (Legend.)

question: Researchers at Nara Women's University argued that the deer of Nara learn their famous bow rather than doing it by instinct, since deer at other parks, such as Miyajima, never bow at all. One unusual stretch of time bore them out, when the deer suddenly bowed far less. What had changed?
answer: The COVID lockdown had emptied the park of tourists
choices: The COVID lockdown had emptied the park of tourists
A harsh winter had thinned the herd's numbers
The temple had banned the sale of deer-crackers
The oldest, tamest deer had died off that year
context: Nara Women's University found the deer bow specifically to beg shika senbei from people -- and when COVID-19 travel limits emptied the park, bows fell from about 10.2 to 6.4 per session, evidence the bow is learned from tourists, not instinct. Deer at Miyajima never learned it. Source: sj.jst.go.jp/stories/2023/s0712-01p.html.

question: Ten thousand monks and 4,000 dancers gathered in Nara in 752 to bless the giant bronze Buddha, newly finished. A priest from India named Bodhisena led the last and most important act of the ceremony. What did he do to finish the statue?
choices: Lit a flame in its open palm
Rang a bronze bell nine times
context: The 752 'eye-opening' (kaigen) ceremony marked the Daibutsu's completion at Todai-ji. The Indian monk Bodhisena painted in the pupils before 10,000 monks and 4,000 dancers -- a sign of how far Buddhism's networks reached, carrying a priest from India to eighth-century Japan. The seated bronze Vairocana stands about 15 m tall. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Ddai-ji.

question: When the temple in Nara rebuilt the Daibutsuden, the vast hall over the Great Buddha, in 1709, it ran short of money and cut the hall from 11 bays wide to 7, only about two-thirds the width of the first. Even so, this smaller hall held a world record right up until 1998. What record was it?
answer: The largest wooden building on Earth
choices: The largest wooden building on Earth
The widest stone hall in the world
The heaviest tiled roof ever raised
The tallest timber hall ever built
context: Todai-ji's Daibutsuden was the world's largest wooden building until 1998. Completed in 1709 (about 57 m long, 50 m wide, 49 m high), it is roughly 30% smaller than its predecessor, cut from 11 bays wide to 7 for lack of funds -- so even the shrunken version held the record. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C5%8Ddai-ji.

question: Empress Genmei founded a fixed capital at Nara in 710 and ended a costly habit: until then, Japan had moved its whole capital to a new site after nearly every emperor's death. Why had the capital kept moving when an emperor died?
answer: A place where someone had died was believed spiritually polluted
choices: A place where someone had died was believed spiritually polluted
Each dead emperor's ghost was believed to haunt his old palace
The gods were believed to abandon a city once its ruler died
Priests declared a used palace unlucky for the coming harvest
context: Heijo-kyo, founded in 710 under Empress Genmei, was Japan's first permanent capital. Earlier the capital had moved after nearly every emperor's death, because a place of death was believed spiritually polluted; the Taiho Code of 701 helped centralize the state and end the practice. Nara was laid out on a vast grid modeled on Chang'an, the Tang capital of China (today's Xi'an). Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Nara_period; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heij%C5%8D-ky%C5%8D.

question: The old Nazca people scraped huge pictures into a desert in Peru, with some lines running for miles. Up close, each one just looks like a scratch in the dirt. The big shapes come into view from only one place. Where must a viewer look from?
context: Most Nazca figures reveal themselves best from about 500 m up, which is why the giant shapes went almost unnoticed for so long. A huge design drawn on the ground like this — by the Nazca here, or in the chalk-cut horses of England — is called a geoglyph. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (best seen ~500 m up; 'geoglyph'); worldhistory.org/article/665/nazca-lines.

question: Dark reddish pebbles, stained by rust, carpet the floor of the Nazca desert in Peru. The Nazca people used no paint and dug no deep ditches, yet their pale lines and giant animal shapes stand out plainly on that dark ground. How did they make them?
answer: they scraped away the dark pebbles to bare the pale ground
choices: they scraped away the dark pebbles to bare the pale ground
they poured pale river clay along each outline
they scorched the surface stones white with rows of fire
they laid down long lines of bleached seashells
context: Each line is a shallow trough only 10-15 cm deep. The Nazca simply lifted away the dark, iron-oxide-coated pebbles that carpet the surface, baring the paler subsoil beneath — a faint colour contrast that reads clearly from above. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (reddish iron-oxide surface pebbles removed to reveal pale subsoil; lines 10-15 cm deep).

question: The long straight lines and huge animal shapes of the Nazca plain in southern Peru are only 10 to 15 cm deep, scratched into loose desert dirt. Wind should have wiped them out in a few lifetimes, yet they have lasted about 2,000 years. What feature of the land explains why the shallow marks are still there?
answer: it lies in one of the driest deserts on Earth
choices: it lies in one of the driest deserts on Earth
it is sealed under a hard crust of salt
it stays buried under drifting sand
it is floored with the hardest rock on Earth
context: The Nazca pampa, on Peru's bone-dry southern coast, is one of the driest places on Earth. With almost no rain to wash them away, the shallow lines have barely eroded in some 2,000 years — the very aridity of this coastal desert is what made the drawings, and their survival, possible. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (one of the driest places on Earth; near-total lack of rain preserves the lines).

question: Nazca artists scratched more than 70 huge animal shapes into a dry plain of southern Peru about 2,000 years ago. One of them, about 93 metres across, has become the symbol of the whole site and the most common picture on Peruvian postcards and stamps. Which animal is it?
context: The Nazca hummingbird, about 93 m long with a needle beak and outstretched wings, is the best known of the figures. The pampa holds more than 70 animals in all, among them a monkey with a tightly spiralled tail, a condor stretching some 134 m, and a spider about 47 m across. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (hummingbird ~93 m; >70 zoomorphic figures; condor ~134 m, spider ~47 m); machutravelperu.com/blog/nazca-lines-hummingbird.

question: Workers building a new tourist lookout on a dusty hillside above the Nazca plains spotted a faded shape on the ground in 2020: a lazy, long-tailed animal about 37 metres across. It dates from about 200 BCE, older than the other famous Nazca drawings. Which animal is it?
context: The 'Nazca cat,' about 37 m across, dates to roughly 200-100 BCE (the Late Paracas period) — older than the hummingbird and the other classic figures, and one of the oldest geoglyphs on the pampa. Fading and nearly lost to erosion, it was spotted only in 2020 during work on a hillside viewpoint. Source: Peru Ministry of Culture, Oct 2020, via smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/2000-year-old-cat-etching-found-peru; cnn.com/style/article/nazca-lines-peru-cat.

question: A figure about 35 metres tall, one hand raised, stands on a hillside above the Nazca desert, so strange-looking that an early pilot nicknamed it 'the Astronaut'. In the 1960s, writers who claimed the desert lines were runways for alien spacecraft pointed to it as a visiting spaceman. Archaeologists, giving the Nazca full credit for their own art, read it as a figure from Nazca belief. What do they think it depicts?
context: The 'ancient astronaut' idea came from Swiss writer Erich von Daniken, whose 1968 bestseller Chariots of the Gods? branded the desert's long trapezoids alien runways and this hillside figure a spaceman. Investigator Joe Nickell later laid out a giant Nazca figure using only wooden stakes and cord, showing a small team needed no help from the stars. Archaeologists read the round-headed figure as an owl-man or shaman. Source: allthatsinteresting.com/nazca-lines; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines (von Daniken 1968; Nickell's period-tool recreation).

question: Researchers combing the Nazca desert on foot turned up new figures only slowly, one at a time, for decades. Then in 2024 the known count almost doubled in a single six-month stretch, with more than 300 new figures at once. What made this sudden burst of discovery possible?
answer: an AI trained to spot faint figures in old aerial photos
choices: an AI trained to spot faint figures in old aerial photos
a rare rainstorm that darkened the pale lines
a swarm of tourists' camera drones, by chance
a rediscovered box of century-old survey maps
context: In 2024 a survey by Japan's Yamagata University with IBM used AI to comb aerial imagery and turned up 303 new figurative geoglyphs in just six months — nearly doubling the known total and speeding discovery roughly 16-fold. Many are small 'relief-type' figures of people and llamas set beside ancient walking trails. Source: yamagata-u.ac.jp/en/information/info/20240924; france24.com/en/live-news/20240924-ai-research-uncovers-300-ancient-etchings.

question: Maria Reiche, a German mathematician, lived beside the Nazca desert for four decades, measuring every line and sweeping the sand off them with a broom; locals half-joked that she was a witch. The lines' real purpose is still debated, but she spent her life defending one big idea about what they were. Which idea was it?
answer: a giant calendar of the sun and stars
choices: a giant calendar of the sun and stars
a giant map of the Nazca homeland
a giant plan for irrigation canals
context: Maria Reiche (1903-1998) mapped the lines for four decades and championed the idea that they formed a giant astronomical calendar marking solstices and star-risings. The theory traces to 22 June 1941, when historian Paul Kosok watched the midwinter sun set exactly along one line and called the desert 'the largest astronomy book in the world.' Today many scholars lean instead toward water and fertility ritual — and, because each animal is one unbroken line, toward ceremonial paths meant to be walked — so the calendar remains just one contested theory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Reiche; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kosok; worldhistory.org/article/665/nazca-lines.  (Legend.)

question: Earthen levees taller than a house hold the Mississippi back at New Orleans. A walker who climbs one out in Lakeview, a neighbourhood built on drained swamp below sea level, can look out at the passing river and then turn to look back at the town. What does the walker see?
answer: The river runs higher than the streets.
choices: The river runs higher than the streets.
The river flows straight through the streets.
The river drops over a waterfall downtown.
The river splits the town into islands.
context: New Orleans really does sit lower than the river beside it. About 65% of the city lies at or below mean sea level, while the Mississippi at its yearly high-water mark rises to roughly 14 feet above sea level, so behind the levees the river runs higher than the streets, and only those earthen walls and the pumps hold it out. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Orleans.'

question: Hurricane Katrina put whole neighbourhoods of New Orleans under water in 2005, but the French Quarter, the oldest part of town, stayed mostly dry. It stands where the first settlers built in 1718. On land this flat, where was the highest, safest ground?
answer: Right along the river, on its natural high banks.
choices: Right along the river, on its natural high banks.
On the shore of Lake Pontchartrain, to the north.
Far out on a sandy island in midstream.
Up on a low hill set a mile inland.
context: In a flat delta the highest ground is the strip of land right beside the river. Every flood, the Mississippi dropped its heaviest silt first at its own edge, building a 'natural levee' ridge 10-20 feet above sea level. Bienville's settlers laid the French Quarter (the Vieux Carre) on that ridge in 1718, which is why it stayed mostly dry in Hurricane Katrina while lower, drained-swamp neighborhoods flooded. Sources: Wikipedia, 'New Orleans'; SERC/Carleton coastlines module.

question: Locals in New Orleans, a city built on soggy ground below sea level, say a hard rain once lifted buried coffins out of their graves to float down the street. That tale, together with an old French and Spanish habit brought by the early settlers, led the city to bury its dead in one very unusual way. What is it?
answer: Above-ground stone tombs, in rows like little streets.
choices: Above-ground stone tombs, in rows like little streets.
Deep graves sealed under heavy concrete slabs.
Graveyards set far off on high, dry ridges.
Cremation, the ashes kept inside the cathedral.
context: New Orleans buries much of its dead above ground in stone tombs, whole 'Cities of the Dead' laid out like little streets. St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, opened in 1789 on Basin Street, is the oldest: a single square block holding thousands, including the voodoo priestess Marie Laveau, believed to lie in the Glapion family crypt. The high-water-table 'floating coffins' story is the reason locals give; the French-Spanish Catholic custom of wall vaults also shaped the tradition. Sources: experienceneworleans.com; Wikipedia, 'St. Louis Cemetery.'  (Legend.)

question: The Mississippi does one dramatic thing, plain to see from the levee, as it flows past the Vieux Carré, the old French Quarter of New Orleans. What does the river do as it passes the old quarter?
answer: It curls around the old city in a great bend.
choices: It curls around the old city in a great bend.
It splits into two channels around a midstream island.
It tumbles over a line of rapids downtown.
It runs dead straight for miles past the docks.
context: The Mississippi curls around the old French Quarter in a huge sweeping bend, and it is from that great crescent-shaped curve that New Orleans takes its nickname, 'the Crescent City.' Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville founded the city in 1718 for the French Mississippi Company, naming it La Nouvelle-Orleans for Philippe II, Duke of Orleans. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Orleans.'

question: A. Baldwin Wood, a New Orleans engineer, built the most powerful water pumps on Earth in 1913, giant spinning screws that sucked the swamps dry so the city could raise whole new neighbourhoods like Lakeview on the drained land. Yet draining the swamp is the very reason New Orleans keeps sinking today. How does pulling the water out make the land itself drop?
answer: The drained soil dries, rots, and packs down.
choices: The drained soil dries, rots, and packs down.
The pumps crack the bedrock, which slumps down.
Lake water seeps in and hollows the earth.
The weight of new buildings presses the mud down.
context: Wood's 1913 screw pump was 12 feet across, the largest and most powerful in the world; his 1927 version could move a million gallons every five minutes, and some 1913 pumps still ran through Hurricane Katrina. But draining the swamp let the spongy organic soil dry out, decay, and compact, so the ground itself dropped: more than half the city is now below sea level. Geographer Richard Campanella said of the pump builders, 'Their intentions were good... Instead, they created a new and bigger one.' Wood's drainage designs were copied worldwide, even helping drain the Netherlands' Zuiderzee. Source: Historic New Orleans Collection, 'The Pumps That Built (and Sank) the City.'

question: The Mississippi has wandered across its delta for thousands of years, switching course again and again, and today it is straining to do so once more: to forsake its long, sluggish channel past Baton Rouge and New Orleans for a shorter, steeper run to the Gulf. Since 1963 a single giant floodgate complex, the Old River Control Structure, has fought to hold it in place. Where is the river trying to go instead?
context: The Old River Control Structure, completed in 1963, holds roughly a 70/30 split, letting about 30% of the flow go to the Atchafalaya while the rest stays in the channel past Baton Rouge and New Orleans. In the great flood of 1973 the river nearly tore the structure out and almost captured the Atchafalaya for good, which would have left both cities stranded on a stagnant backwater while the Mississippi built a whole new delta near Morgan City. The close call forced the Army Corps of Engineers to add an auxiliary structure. Source: Wikipedia, 'Old River Control Structure.'

question: The Statue of Liberty went up on her small island in New York Harbor in 1886, her outer skin the shiny reddish-brown of a new penny. Over the decades she slowly turned the pale mint-green she wears today. What turned her green?
choices: Workers repainted her a protective green
Her bronze surface tarnished like an old coin
Salt spray bleached the dark metal pale
context: The statue's skin is copper only about 2.4 mm thick -- roughly two pennies stacked. Air, water, and pollution weathered it to a green layer of verdigris (copper patina) that now actually protects the metal underneath; the green is corrosion, not paint or bronze. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty

question: Central Park stretches across the middle of Manhattan, a huge green rectangle of 843 acres. Its rolling meadows, quiet lakes and rocky woods look like a piece of wilderness the city simply grew up around. What is the truth about that natural-looking scenery?
answer: Almost every hill, pond, and tree was placed on purpose
choices: Almost every hill, pond, and tree was placed on purpose
It is the last untouched wilderness left on the island
It was once a royal hunting forest from colonial days
It formed in a glacier-carved valley long ago
context: Central Park only looks natural. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux's winning 'Greensward Plan' (chosen April 1858) landscaped the whole park from scratch in the 1850s-60s -- the 'natural' park is the most man-made thing in the city. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park

question: The day it opened in 1883, one New York bridge held the record as the longest suspension bridge in the world. Its main span stretched almost 1,600 feet across the East River and joined the island of Manhattan to Brooklyn for the very first time. Which bridge was it?
context: The Brooklyn Bridge opened May 24, 1883; its 1,595.5-foot main span made it the world's longest suspension bridge, and it was among the first strung from bundled steel wire -- each of its four main cables holds 5,282 galvanized steel wires. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge

question: A commuter crossing the main hall of Grand Central Terminal in 1913, two months after New York's great station opened, looked up at its painted ceiling of gold zodiac stars on a blue-green sky. He told the newspapers the star map was wrong. What was the mistake?
answer: The whole sky is reversed, east swapped with west
choices: The whole sky is reversed, east swapped with west
Two of the twelve zodiac signs are missing
The stars glow in the wrong seasonal colors
A thirteenth constellation was invented and added
context: A commuter spotted the reversed zodiac within two months of the 1913 opening. Officials floated a 'God's-eye view from outside the heavens' explanation; astronomer Harold Jacoby's leading theory is that the painter laid the flat sky-chart on the floor and projected it upward, flipping the image. https://www.untappedcities.com/the-hidden-history-of-grand-central-terminals-celestial-ceiling/

question: Restorers scrubbed the painted sky of Grand Central Terminal in New York in the 1990s, until decades of grime were gone and its gold stars glowed on turquoise again. Near the star sign Cancer, though, they left one small dark patch untouched on purpose. Why keep that one grimy patch?
answer: To show how much indoor tobacco smoke had blackened it
choices: To show how much indoor tobacco smoke had blackened it
To hide an old water stain they could not remove
To preserve the original artist's faded signature
To mark the center point of the painted sky
context: During the 1990s restoration, one dark rectangle near Cancer was deliberately left uncleaned -- a preserved patch showing how much tar and nicotine from decades of indoor tobacco smoking had blackened the whole ceiling. https://www.untappedcities.com/the-hidden-history-of-grand-central-terminals-celestial-ceiling/

question: Workers clearing the rocky site of Central Park in the 1850s, in the middle of Manhattan, set off enormous gunpowder charges day after day to break up its ridges and swampy hollows. Today's peaceful meadows and duck ponds give no hint of it. How much gunpowder did the blasting take?
answer: More than was fired at the Battle of Gettysburg
choices: More than was fired at the Battle of Gettysburg
More than was fired at the Battle of Bunker Hill
More than was fired at the Battle of Yorktown
More than was fired at the siege of the Alamo
context: Building Central Park meant hauling out about 5 million cubic feet of soil and rock and trucking in over 18,500 cubic yards of topsoil from Long Island and New Jersey -- and blasting the rocky site used more gunpowder than was fired at the Battle of Gettysburg. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park

question: The men who sank the stone towers of New York's great bridge over the East River dug inside giant air-pressurized chambers called caissons, deep under the riverbed. Many came up racked with pain, some paralysed and some killed, by an illness the doctors of the 1870s could not explain. What is that illness called today?
context: Surfacing too fast from the pressurized caissons caused decompression sickness -- 'caisson disease,' the bends. Chief engineer John A. Roebling died of tetanus before construction began; his son Washington, left paralyzed by the bends, directed the work by telescope from his bedroom while Emily Warren Roebling ran the site for years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Bridge

question: Manhattan's streets were laid out in 1811 as a rigid grid of square blocks, yet one road older than the grid cuts slantwise across the island from end to end. Wherever it crosses the blocks it opens a famous triangle of space: Times Square, Herald Square, Madison Square. Which road is it?
context: Broadway is the one great diagonal breaking Manhattan's grid -- an older route following the island's natural lay of the land. It slices across the right-angle streets and carves out the triangular 'squares.' The rigid grid itself was set by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioners%27_Plan_of_1811

question: Twice a day the current of New York's Hudson River stops beside Manhattan and runs backward, as the ocean tide pushes some 150 miles upstream to Troy. Its old Native American name means a river that flows two ways. Because of this, the lower Hudson is not really a river. What is the lower Hudson, then?
context: The Hudson beside Manhattan is a tidal estuary -- an arm of the sea whose current reverses with the ocean tides all the way up to the Federal Dam at Troy, about 150 miles inland, though the salt water itself usually reaches only to about Newburgh. The Mohican name Muh-he-kun-ne-tuk means 'the river that flows two ways'; the Lenape called it Muhheakantuck. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River

question: New York's tallest skyscrapers crowd together in just two districts, Midtown and the Financial District. In those two places very hard, ancient bedrock comes near the surface, firm enough to bear such enormous towers. What is this tough base rock called?
context: Manhattan's skyscrapers stand on hard metamorphic bedrock -- chiefly Manhattan schist -- well suited to carrying enormous towers. Where that rock lies near the surface, in Midtown and the Financial District, is where the tallest clusters rise. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan

question: When the Empire State Building opened in New York City in 1931, it was the tallest tower on Earth, its 102 stories soaring above Manhattan. The slender metal spire crowning the very top was not mere decoration — it was built for a strange, futuristic job that never once worked in practice. What was the spire originally meant to do?
answer: Let zeppelins dock and drop off passengers
choices: Let zeppelins dock and drop off passengers
Broadcast the world's first television signal
Serve as a giant lightning rod for the city
Hold a rotating searchlight for ships at sea
context: The Empire State Building's spire was designed as a mooring mast where zeppelins would dock and let passengers off -- but the plan was abandoned once it was clear the high winds swirling around the tower made airship docking impossible. Built in about 410 days during the Great Depression, the tower stayed the world's tallest for roughly 40 years. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building

question: Over a billion gallons of water flow into New York City every day through long tunnels from mountain reservoirs in the Catskills and the Delaware watershed, as far as 125 miles to the north. What is remarkable about the way nearly all of it reaches the city's taps?
answer: It runs the whole way downhill by gravity, with no pumps
choices: It runs the whole way downhill by gravity, with no pumps
It is filtered clean through the bedrock as it travels
It is pulled from the Atlantic and then desalinated
It is chilled inside mountain tunnels to stay fresh
context: About 95% of New York City's drinking water -- over a billion gallons a day -- arrives by gravity alone, no pumps, flowing downhill through aqueducts from Catskill and Delaware watershed reservoirs up to about 125 miles north. Part of it runs through the Delaware Aqueduct, at about 85 miles the world's longest continuous tunnel, carrying roughly half the city's water beneath the Hudson River without a single pump. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_water_supply_system

question: New Zealand's two mountainous islands look alone in the South Pacific. Charts of the sea floor show they are only the high ground of a vast slab of continental crust, nearly all of it drowned. What did geologists name this sunken continent?
context: About 94% of Zealandia lies underwater; only New Zealand, New Caledonia and a few smaller islands rise above the sea. Because it is genuine, continuous continental crust -- not scattered ocean islands -- geologists formally argued in 2017 that it counts as a true continent. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealandia

question: Far to the north of New Zealand, a group of tropical islands rises from the drowned continent New Zealand stands on, about 94 per cent of which lies under the southwest Pacific. They and New Zealand are its only large lands above the waves. Which land is that northern partner?
context: New Caledonia and New Zealand are the only large pieces of the continent Zealandia to break the surface -- New Caledonia near its northern end, New Zealand toward the south. Everything between is drowned continental shelf. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealandia

question: Snow and ice cap the highest point of a whole drowned continent, a peak in the Southern Alps of New Zealand's South Island. The continent beneath it lies almost entirely under the Pacific, yet this summit rises 3,724 metres into the clouds. Which mountain is it?
context: Officially Aoraki / Mount Cook, keeping its Maori name Aoraki. At 3,724 m it is the highest point not only of New Zealand but of the whole continent of Zealandia -- nearly all of which lies drowned beneath the Pacific. Source: geosociety.org/gsa-today/march-april-2017/zealandia-earths-hidden-continent

question: New Zealand broke away about 80 million years ago, then sailed off on its own for so long that one whole group of land animals never got there. Only two tiny kinds ever crossed the sea, so birds took over the empty places, and with no hunters on the ground, some gave up flight for good. Which group is New Zealand almost entirely missing?
context: New Zealand's only native land mammals are two tiny bat species. With no cats, rats, deer or monkeys to hunt them or compete with them, birds and insects evolved to fill the empty roles -- several birds even lost the power of flight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna_of_New_Zealand

question: A nearly ruler-straight crack runs about 600 km down the length of New Zealand's South Island, where the Pacific and Australian plates grind past each other. Along it a young mountain range is still being shoved skyward, and it last broke in a great earthquake around 1717. What is this plate-boundary fault called?
context: The Alpine Fault runs about 600 km up the spine of the South Island, where the Pacific and Australian plates slide past each other and heave up the Southern Alps. It ruptures in huge earthquakes roughly every few centuries; the last great one struck around 1717 AD. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_Fault

question: Ice Age glaciers cut a maze of steep valleys into the wild southwest of New Zealand's South Island, and the sea later flooded them into long, dark, cliff-walled arms. The most famous, Milford Sound, gets over 6 metres of rain a year, and Rudyard Kipling ranked it as the world's eighth wonder. What is this whole region called?
context: The region is named for its fiords -- sea-drowned glacier valleys such as Milford Sound. Though early sailors called them 'sounds' (a word for river-carved inlets), they are technically fiords, gouged by ice and later flooded by the sea. Milford is one of the wettest inhabited places on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milford_Sound

question: Lake Taupō, in the middle of New Zealand's North Island, looks like a calm holiday lake, but its broad basin is the crater of a supervolcano. About 25,600 years ago the volcano hurled out some 1,170 cubic km of rock and ash, one of only a few super-eruptions known on Earth. Among them all, what is the Taupō blast?
context: The Oruanui eruption about 25,600 years ago was Earth's most recent VEI-8 event -- the very top of the volcanic explosivity scale, and no volcano anywhere has erupted on that scale since. Lake Taupo sits in the Taupo Volcanic Zone, fed by the Pacific plate diving beneath the North Island, the same engine behind Rotorua's geysers and boiling mud. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taup%C5%8D_Volcanic_Zone

question: Neolithic farmers with neither writing nor metal tools raised Newgrange, a grass-topped stone mound over a burial chamber in Ireland's Boyne Valley, around 3200 BC. It is about 500 years older than two of the most famous ancient landmarks on Earth. Which two?
answer: Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza
choices: Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza
Petra and the Great Wall of China
context: Newgrange went up around 3200 BC -- roughly five centuries before either Stonehenge's great stone circle or Egypt's Great Pyramid of Giza. Its Neolithic builders had no metal tools and no writing. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newgrange ; https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: A curved wall of bright white stone, studded with dark round cobbles, gleams across the front of Newgrange, the great grass-topped tomb in eastern Ireland. Its Stone Age builders hauled that white rock about 80 km from the Wicklow Mountains, with no wheels and no metal tools. What is the white stone?
context: The bright facade is white quartz carried from the Wicklow Mountains, set with dark granite cobbles from the Mourne Mountains to the north -- stone moved dozens of kilometres by people with no carts. (The gleaming wall is a modern reconstruction from quartz found scattered at the mound's foot.) Source: https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: A dome of stone and earth about 85 metres across rises over the Boyne Valley at Newgrange, in eastern Ireland. Its Stone Age builders, with no metal tools and no wheels, gathered every rock and basketful of earth by hand and stacked it by muscle alone. Roughly how much did they pile up?
context: The mound is about 85 metres wide, 12-13 metres high, and covers roughly an acre -- an estimated 200,000 tonnes of stone and earth, all gathered and stacked by hand in the Stone Age. Source: https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: The builders of Newgrange aimed their whole tomb at a single sunrise each year. Above the doorway they left a small stone opening, so that at dawn on that one morning a blade of sunlight shoots 19 metres straight down the passage and floods the pitch-dark inner chamber -- even with the great stone door shut. Which sunrise did they build it to catch?
context: For a few mornings around the winter solstice -- the shortest days of the year -- the rising sun threads the passage and lights the inner chamber for about 17 minutes before fading, a light show engineered over 5,000 years ago. Sources: https://www.newgrange.com/winter-solstice-newgrange.htm ; https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: At the door of Newgrange sits a huge 5-tonne slab. It is carved with Ireland's most famous ancient symbol: a bold pattern of coils winding in and out of each other. It was cut 5,000 years ago with only flint, since Ireland then had no metal at all. What is this coiled symbol called?
context: The great entrance stone (Kerbstone K1) carries a bold triple spiral -- a 'triskele' -- about 3 metres long, cut with nothing but stone and flint tools. Another famous triskele hides deep inside the chamber. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newgrange ; https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: Flat stones climb nearly 6 metres over the inner chamber of Newgrange, each jutting a little farther inward than the one below it, with no mortar anywhere. After more than 5,000 years, the chamber beneath that roof is still bone-dry. What did the builders do to keep the rain out?
answer: they cut grooves in the stones to run rainwater off
choices: they cut grooves in the stones to run rainwater off
they sealed the joints with sticky river clay
they smeared the stones with black pine tar
they dug hidden drains beneath the chamber floor
context: The mortar-free corbelled vault has kept the chamber watertight for over 5,000 years -- partly because the builders cut grooves into the roof-stones to channel rainwater outward, away from the room below. Source: https://www.knowth.com/newgrange.htm

question: One dawn in 1967, the archaeologist Michael J. O'Kelly stood alone in the black inner chamber of Newgrange and watched the ancient sunbeam creep down the long passage and light the tomb, the first person in modern times to see it. He studied the small stone slot above the entrance that lets the beam in, and gave it the plain English name it still carries. What did he call it?
context: On 21 December 1967, Michael J. O'Kelly watched the solstice beam creep in, 'lighting up everything as it came' -- the first recorded modern witness -- and coined the term 'roof-box' for the opening that channels the light. Source: https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2025/1220/1549633-newgrange-winter-solstice-light-show-sunrise-discovery-michael-j-okelly/

question: Newgrange rises within Brú na Bóinne, a loop of Ireland's River Boyne where Stone Age people raised a whole ritual landscape of tombs, at least 90 monuments in all. Two other giant passage-tombs share the ground, each a grass-topped mound with carved stones and a dark chamber of its own. What are these two sister-tombs called?
context: Newgrange, Knowth, and Dowth are the three great passage-tombs of Bru na Boinne -- a Neolithic ritual landscape of at least 90 monuments in a loop of the River Boyne, older than the pharaohs and named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. Knowth alone holds more than a third of all the megalithic art in Western Europe. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%BA_na_B%C3%B3inne ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowth

question: Niagara Falls thunders on the border between New York and Ontario as three waterfalls side by side. The Horseshoe Falls curves along the Canadian side, and two smaller falls pour down the American side. How much of the river goes over the Horseshoe alone?
context: Niagara is really three waterfalls side by side: the giant Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side, the wide American Falls, and the slender Bridal Veil Falls beside it. The Horseshoe crest curves about 670 m (2,200 ft) across, and its water drops an average of 57 m (188 ft) into a plunge pool roughly 35 m deep. Almost the whole river — close to nine-tenths of the flow — thunders over the Horseshoe alone, leaving only about a tenth for the American and Bridal Veil falls combined. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls

question: A big wooded island, Goat Island, stands in midstream right at the brink of Niagara Falls, exactly where the river tips over the edge into its gorge on the border of the United States and Canada. What does Goat Island do to the great waterfall?
answer: Splits it into two separate falls
choices: Splits it into two separate falls
Splits it into three separate falls
Separates the small Bridal Veil Falls off
Bends the flow into the Horseshoe's curve
context: Goat Island parts the river into the Canadian Horseshoe Falls and the American Falls. A second, much smaller scrap of rock — Luna Island — then splits the slender Bridal Veil Falls off from the American Falls, which is how Niagara ends up as three falls in all. Both big falls were already there when Europeans first described the site before 1678. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls

question: Geologists have proved that Niagara's falls only look fixed in place. Over the roughly 12,000 years since the Ice Age, the falls have shifted about 11 km from the cliff where they first began to thunder. What are they slowly doing?
choices: Sinking down into a deepening pit
Growing taller as fallen rock piles up
Drifting sideways toward the Canadian shore
context: A waterfall that walks: Niagara gnaws its way upstream, toward Lake Erie, leaving the long gorge behind it as its trail. It once retreated fast — up to about a metre a year — but since engineers diverted much of the flow, today's regulated erosion has slowed to roughly 0.3 m a year or less (some estimates near 0.1 m). Source: ijc.org/en/niagara-falls-moving

question: Townsfolk climbed down onto the bare bed of the Niagara River in late March 1848, when the water over the crest of the falls had slowed to a trickle and the rock lay drying in the sun. By many accounts, what long-buried things did they pry out of the mud?
answer: Old muskets, bayonets and iron tomahawks
choices: Old muskets, bayonets and iron tomahawks
Spanish gold coins and jeweled crosses
Dinosaur bones and ancient fossil shells
Ship timbers and heavy iron anchors
context: With the falls stilled, people reportedly walked far out on the dry bed — some all the way to Goat Island, a few even driving buggies — and a cavalry troop is said to have paraded on the exposed rock. Treasure-hunters dug up weapons from the War of 1812, which had been fought along this very river. These colourful accounts are widely retold but not all independently verified. Source: smithsonianmag.com/travel/when-niagara-falls-ran-dry-180972198  (Legend.)

question: People living beside Niagara Falls woke to an eerie silence on 29 March 1848. The falls that thundered day and night had all but stopped, and children walked out on rocks no one had ever seen. Something far upstream, out on Lake Erie, had choked off almost the whole flow of the river. What had blocked it?
answer: A huge jam of lake ice had dammed it
choices: A huge jam of lake ice had dammed it
A sudden earthquake had shifted its channel
A landslide had buried the gorge in rock
A long drought had emptied Lake Erie
context: A warm spell cracked the winter ice on Lake Erie; then easterly winds shoved the floes into the mouth of the Niagara River, where they piled into a natural ice dam between Buffalo and Fort Erie. For roughly 30 to 40 hours barely a trickle went over the crest — the only near-total stoppage ever recorded. When the dam gave way, the river roared back to life. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls

question: A few kilometres below Niagara Falls, the gorge swings around a sharp bend and the whole river spins in a deep basin, the Niagara Whirlpool. About 5,500 years ago, when the falls stood at this bend, they broke into something hidden underground. What did they cut into?
answer: An old river gorge, long buried under debris
choices: An old river gorge, long buried under debris
A soft pocket of ash from an old volcano
A deep cavern carved by underground streams
A crack left open by a long-ago earthquake
context: The falls sliced into the St. David's Gorge, an ancient valley that an earlier river had carved and glaciers had then packed with loose debris, lying crosswise to Niagara's path. The whirlpool basin is about 518 m long, 365 m wide and up to 38 m deep, and it can even run backward — at full flow the water spins counter-clockwise, but the churning sometimes reverses and forces incoming water to dive beneath itself to reach the outlet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Whirlpool

question: Engineers of the U.S. Army Corps did something startling at Niagara in June 1969: they switched the American Falls off. They dumped tens of thousands of tons of rock across the river, a dam that shoved the whole flow over the Horseshoe Falls and left the American Falls bone dry for months. Why did they shut the falls down?
answer: To let geologists examine the crumbling rock face
choices: To let geologists examine the crumbling rock face
To hunt the dry riverbed for sunken treasure
To film a blockbuster movie on the bare cliff
To lay the footings for a new stone bridge
context: Starting June 9, 1969, the Army Corps built a 600-foot cofferdam out of more than 28,000 tons of rock, steering the river toward the Horseshoe Falls and leaving the American Falls dry for about five months so scientists could study its unstable, crumbling face. Source: history.com/articles/niagara-falls-dewatering-1969

question: A huge heap of fallen boulders lay at the foot of the American Falls when engineers dammed the river at Niagara and left the cliff dry in 1969. Past rockfalls had dumped it there, and everyone assumed it ought to be hauled away so the falls would look grand again. The experts found a surprise. What were the boulders doing?
answer: Bracing the cliff and holding it up
choices: Bracing the cliff and holding it up
Cementing into a solid new stone ledge
Making the cliff collapse even faster
Washing slowly downstream in the current
context: The talus — rubble from rockfalls in 1931 and 1954 — was actually propping up the fragile cliff. Clearing it away would only trigger MORE collapse, so in 1975 the International Joint Commission decided to leave the boulders in place and simply pin the rock face with bolts and cement. Source: history.com/articles/niagara-falls-dewatering-1969

question: Ice 2 to 3 km thick still buried southern Ontario at the close of the last Ice Age, and Niagara Falls did not yet exist. Then, about 12,500 years ago, the glaciers melted back. What did that great melt do to give birth to the falls?
answer: It filled the Great Lakes, which spilled over a long ridge
choices: It filled the Great Lakes, which spilled over a long ridge
It cracked open a fault that split the land apart
It let the sea rush inland and flood a deep valley
It uncovered a volcano that blasted out a gorge
context: As the ice sheets melted about 12,500 years ago, the newly filled Great Lakes had to drain toward the sea — and their overflow began pouring over the edge of a long cliff-like ridge called the Niagara Escarpment, near Queenston. That first plunge was the birth of the falls, which have been marching upstream ever since. Source: niagaraparks.com/visit-niagara-parks/plan-your-visit/niagara-falls-geology-facts-figures

question: A Viking who wanted to record a name or a boast had no paper, no pen and no ink, for none of them had reached Scandinavia. His whole alphabet was built from short, straight lines. How did he make the letters?
answer: Cut them into wood or stone with a knife
choices: Cut them into wood or stone with a knife
Pressed them into wet clay with a reed
Brushed them onto bark with berry dye
Wove them into cloth with coloured thread
context: Runes are an alphabet made to be knifed into wood and stone -- no paper or ink required. Being cut by hand is why they are all short, sharp strokes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runes

question: The row of runes carved across Viking Scandinavia is named by the same trick that made the word alphabet from the Greek alpha and beta: its first six letters run together into one word. What is the rune-row called?
context: The runic alphabet is the FUTHARK, named f-u-th-a-r-k after its first six runes -- the same naming trick behind 'alphabet' (alpha + beta). An 'aett' is a group of runes within the row; ogham is a separate Irish script, and a kenning is a figure of Norse poetry, not a script at all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runes

question: At Jelling in Denmark stands a great royal runestone, raised around 965 CE by King Harald Bluetooth. Its runes spell out a boast: that Harald had 'won for himself all Denmark and Norway' -- and then done one more thing that changed his people forever. What else does the stone boast that Harald did?
context: The inscription calls him 'the Harald who won for himself all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian.' Because it records the kingdom's conversion, the stone is nicknamed 'Denmark's baptismal certificate' -- though it is a king's own boast in stone, not neutral history. Source: en.natmus.dk/historical-knowledge/denmark/prehistoric-period-until-1050-ad/the-viking-age/the-monuments-at-jelling/the-jelling-stone/  (Legend.)

question: One face of the great Jelling stone in Denmark shows Christ with his arms flung wide -- but he isn't nailed to a wooden cross. Instead his body is wrapped and tangled in ribbon-like branches, as though held fast in a living tree. This carving, made around 965 CE, holds a famous record. What record is it?
answer: The oldest image of Christ in Scandinavia
choices: The oldest image of Christ in Scandinavia
The oldest human figure carved in the North
The only image of Christ on any runestone
The first Christian carving in Scandinavia
context: It is the oldest known image of Christ found in Scandinavia. Scholars think the carver posed Christ 'hanging in a tree' on purpose, to echo Odin, who in Norse myth hung nine nights on the world-tree Yggdrasil -- the old gods giving way to the new faith, frozen in stone. Source: en.natmus.dk/historical-knowledge/denmark/prehistoric-period-until-1050-ad/the-viking-age/the-monuments-at-jelling/the-jelling-stone/

question: The great runestone at Jelling in Denmark stands today as bare grey granite, rough and weathered. Researchers studying tiny traces caught deep in its carved grooves realised it looked utterly different on the day King Harald first raised it. How did the Jelling stone look at first?
context: The bare grey stone was once painted in vivid colour. Denmark's National Museum used surviving specks of pigment to reconstruct the original hues -- a reminder that Viking monuments, like ancient Greek temples, once blazed with colour rather than standing plain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelling_stones

question: Engineers picked the name Bluetooth for a new wireless technology in 1997, after King Harald Bluetooth of Denmark, who had united quarrelling Danish tribes much as the technology links gadgets together. A popular story holds that the little logo hides a secret about the king himself. What is the Bluetooth logo said to be?
answer: His two initials, joined into one rune
choices: His two initials, joined into one rune
A tiny map of his united kingdom
The shape of his blackened tooth
context: The Bluetooth NAME really was inspired by Harald Bluetooth -- proposed by Intel's Jim Kardach in 1997 because Harald united Denmark as the tech unites devices. The logo being his bind-rune (the runes Hagall/H and Bjarkan/B merged) is the popular, widely-repeated story rather than a documented fact. His own nickname likely came from a dark, dead tooth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluetooth  (Legend.)

question: A father named Varinn raised the tall grey Rök stone in Sweden around 800, in memory of his dead son Vamod. Of the many thousands of runestones known across Scandinavia, it holds one celebrated record. What record does it hold?
answer: The longest runic inscription ever found
choices: The longest runic inscription ever found
The tallest runestone in all Sweden
context: The Rok stone carries about 760 runes -- the longest known runic inscription -- carved across all five faces of the slab. It is also a puzzle-box of cipher runes and riddles, and it even name-drops the Gothic king Theodoric the Great on his horse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%B6k_runestone

question: Rune-carvers in Viking Scandinavia built every letter from diagonal and upright strokes and almost never cut a flat horizontal line across one. It was no matter of style; it came straight from the way each rune was made. Why did the carvers avoid horizontal strokes?
answer: It runs along the grain and splits the plank
choices: It runs along the grain and splits the plank
It was the hardest stroke to cut cleanly
It took twice as long to carve
It needed a much longer knife to cut
context: Runes are angular on purpose. Cut by knife into wood, a horizontal stroke runs along the grain -- blurring the letter and threatening to split the plank -- so carvers used clean diagonal and upright cuts. Curves were dropped for the same reason: they are hard to slice cleanly. Runes also had no fixed direction, running left-to-right, right-to-left, or alternating line by line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runes

question: Golden seaweed gathers in the Sargasso Sea, in the calm centre of a slow wheel of currents as wide as the North Atlantic. Winds and the spinning Earth turn five such wheels across the oceans. What are they called?
context: Each of the five subtropical gyres turns clockwise north of the equator and counterclockwise to the south; the Sargasso Sea sits inside the North Atlantic Gyre, walled by its currents. Eddies are much smaller swirls, a maelstrom is one violent whirlpool, and vortices can be any size -- only 'gyre' names an ocean-wide loop. Source: oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/gyre.html

question: Charles Moore, a yacht captain, sailed by accident in 1997 into a swirl of floating plastic in the calm heart of one of the ocean's great wheels of current. It was the first such swirl ever found, and it covers about twice the area of Texas. Which of the ocean's trash swirls is it?
context: It drifts in the calm heart of the North Pacific Gyre, halfway between California and Hawaii. Yacht captain Charles Moore sailed into it by accident in 1997, and oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer coined the name 'garbage patch.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pacific_garbage_patch

question: A single drop of water riding the biggest of the ocean's five great wheels of current takes about four and a half years to go once around. Four mighty currents wall in its turning sea of about 20 million square kilometres. Which of the five is this giant?
context: The North Pacific Gyre spans roughly 20 million square kilometers, walled by the North Equatorial, Kuroshio, North Pacific, and California currents. A drop of water takes about 54 months to finish one loop. Source: grokipedia.com/page/North_Pacific_Gyre

question: Halfway between Hawaii and California, in the calm heart of the North Pacific, a swirl of floating plastic trash spreads across an enormous stretch of open sea. Yet no satellite has ever photographed it, and no camera in orbit can see it at all. Why is something so enormous invisible from space?
answer: It's really a thin haze of fingernail-size microplastics, not a solid raft
choices: It's really a thin haze of fingernail-size microplastics, not a solid raft
It sinks far too deep below the ocean surface for any camera to spot
It stays hidden beneath a permanent, thick bank of ocean storm clouds
It drifts far too fast for any orbiting satellite to lock onto it
context: About 94% of the patch's estimated 1.8 trillion pieces are microplastics smaller than a fingernail — so diffuse the 'patch' is more a peppery soup than an island you could ever walk on. Source: nature.com/articles/s41598-018-22939-w

question: The Ocean Cleanup's ships hauled up and weighed the plastic drifting in the vast swirl of trash in the North Pacific, out between Hawaii and California. One kind of debris outweighed every other, nearly half of the total mass. Which kind makes up almost half the swirl's weight?
context: The 2018 Ocean Cleanup study put the patch's plastic near 79,000 tonnes, and roughly 46% of that mass was discarded or lost fishing gear — 'ghost' nets that keep snaring sea life for years. Source: nature.com/articles/s41598-018-22939-w

question: Christopher Columbus's ships pushed west into the Sargasso Sea in 1492 and found the water matted, mile after mile, with thick golden weed. His sailors grew frightened, not of storms or monsters, but of the seaweed itself. What did they fear the weed would do?
answer: snag the ships and hold them trapped forever
choices: snag the ships and hold them trapped forever
clog the hulls until the timbers rotted away
hide sea serpents coiled within the weed
grow thick enough to walk across to land
context: Columbus's 1492 crossing left the first written account of the Sargasso Sea. His crew's dread of being caught fast in the weed seeded centuries of legends about ships trapped forever in the Sargassum — though the weed never actually stops a vessel. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea

question: Around 30° north, the belt of ocean surrounding the Sargasso Sea can go so windless that old sailing ships sat becalmed for weeks, their sails hanging dead, unable to move. Spanish crews gave this dead-calm zone a grim nickname: the 'horse latitudes.' Where did that strange name come from?
answer: Crews threw dying horses overboard to save their drinking water
choices: Crews threw dying horses overboard to save their drinking water
The glassy calm water mirrored the shape of a horse's head
Wild horses once swam across these waters between continents
The first ship to chart the zone was named the Sea Horse
context: Becalmed for weeks with drinking water running low, crews reportedly threw dead and dying horses overboard to save what water remained — the grim story behind the name 'horse latitudes.' Source: oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/horse-latitudes.html  (Legend.)

question: More than 6,000 slim tower houses stand packed together inside the walled Old City of Sanaa, in the mountains of Yemen. Many climb five to nine storeys, iced with white trim like frosted gingerbread, early skyscrapers of the Arabian Peninsula. What are these towers mostly built from?
context: Sanaa's tower houses are built of packed (rammed) earth and burnt mud brick, with only the lowest floor in stone -- yet they climb five to nine stories and have stood for centuries, earning old Sanaa its nickname as a city of ancient skyscrapers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a; UNESCO WHS 'Old City of Sana'a' (whc.unesco.org/en/list/385/).

question: Sanaa, beneath Mount Nuqum in the mountains of Yemen, has been home to people for some 2,500 years with no break at all. Yemeni legend reaches back further, to the family of Noah after the Flood, and names the man who first laid out the city at the mountain's foot. Who was he?
context: In Islamic and biblical tradition, Shem (Sam) is a son of Noah, and Yemeni legend credits him with founding Sanaa below Jabal Nuqum, the mountain that overlooks the old city. Historians cannot confirm any founder, but the unbroken 2,500-year habitation is well established. This is legend, not verified history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a.

question: The afternoon sun pours into the top rooms of a Sanaa tower house through half-round fans of red, blue and green glass. Set above each window in lacy carved white gypsum, they splash the walls with coloured light. What are these fanlights called?
context: These are QAMARIYA windows -- the name comes from qamar, Arabic for 'moon,' for their crescent-fan shape. Panes of colored glass are set into fretted gypsum plaster. By contrast, a mashrabiya is a projecting latticed wooden window-screen, not a stained-glass fanlight. Qamariya windows are a hallmark of old Sanaa's tower houses. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/385/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a.

question: From a distance, Sanaa's brown mud towers look iced like gingerbread -- every floor outlined and swirled with bright white patterns. But the builders didn't paint those white gypsum friezes only to look beautiful. On a house made of mud brick, what practical job does the white gypsum coating do?
answer: it sheds rain that would wash the mud away
choices: it sheds rain that would wash the mud away
it reflects the sun to keep the rooms cool
it seals cracks against burrowing insects
it lets the family mark out their own house
context: Old Sanaa gets real rain, and unprotected mud brick would erode. The white gypsum (juss) friezes and copings act like a waterproof skin, channeling rainwater off the vulnerable earthen walls -- so Sanaa's famous 'gingerbread' decoration is also its raincoat. Source: whc.unesco.org/en/list/385/.

question: Traders, pilgrims and travellers crowd through a tall fortified gate in the high clay walls of Sanaa's Old City, in the mountains of Arabia's southwest corner. For centuries it has been the great way into the walled city. What is this gate called?
context: This is BAB AL-YEMEN, the 'Gate of the Yemen' -- the main gate in old Sanaa's fortified walls of packed clay, on the southern edge of the Old City. It is often called a thousand years old, though the geographer Carl Rathjens dated its present look to the 17th century. The other choices are famous gates of other Islamic cities: Bab al-Nasr and Bab Zuweila in Cairo, Bab Boujeloud in Fez. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bab_al-Yaman; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a.

question: Workers repairing the roof of the Great Mosque of Sanaa, among the oldest mosques on earth, pulled sacks of ancient parchment out of its attic in 1972. Under ultraviolet light, one page showed a faint second layer of writing beneath the visible text: long ago, someone had scraped the page clean and written over it. What did scholars find in that erased under-layer?
answer: an even older copy of the Quran
choices: an even older copy of the Quran
a merchant's tally of spice prices
a map of the caravan roads to Mecca
a Christian gospel in old Syriac
context: This is the SANAA PALIMPSEST (part of the 'Sanaa manuscript'). A palimpsest is a page whose original writing was scraped off and overwritten; here, ultraviolet imaging recovered a lower Quranic text older than the upper one. Radiocarbon dating placed the parchment at roughly 578-669 CE, ranking it among the very oldest Qur'anic manuscripts known -- a rare window into how the earliest copies were written. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a_manuscript.

question: Palenque's grandest building rises out of the jungle of Chiapas, in southern Mexico: a steep stepped pyramid crowned by a small temple, with a hidden stairway dropping deep into its heart. What is this Maya pyramid-temple called today?
choices: the Temple of the Foliated Cross
context: The pyramid takes its name from three stone tablets in its summit temple carved with 617 Maya glyphs, one of the longest hieroglyphic texts in the ancient Americas, recording the life of the king buried within. In 1948 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier spotted the trapdoor-like floor slab that hid the stairway. Source: Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: Alberto Ruz Lhuillier noticed lifting holes in a floor slab of Palenque's summit temple in 1948. Beneath it ran a rubble-packed stairway, and his crew spent four seasons clearing it. Some 25 metres down, in 1952, they broke through a walled-up doorway. What lay beyond?
context: It was the first tomb ever found inside a Maya pyramid, overturning the old belief that these pyramids were only solid platforms for temples. In the anteroom lay the skeletons of six young attendants, apparently sacrificed to accompany their king. The king within was K'inich Janaab' Pakal. Source: mayan.org, Pakal's Tomb; Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: Inside the tomb of the Maya king Pakal at Palenque, the royal skeleton lay wearing a mask built from some 200 small fitted pieces of a single precious stone, its eyes made of shell and gleaming obsidian. The Maya prized this green stone above gold itself. Of what stone was Pakal's death mask made?
context: Jade, carved and polished and set in mosaics, was the most treasured material of the Maya world, a symbol of breath, water, and life. Pakal's mosaic mask, about 200 pieces of jadeite with eyes of shell and obsidian, now rests in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City. Source: mayan.org, Pakal's Tomb; Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: Pakal's coffin lid at Palenque is a slab of carved limestone weighing about five tons, and on it the king leans back at the instant of death. Erich von Däniken claimed in 1968 that it showed Pakal at the controls of a rocket. Maya scholars reject that: the king is falling along a sacred image at the very centre of the Maya universe. What is that image?
context: That sacred image is the Maya World Tree, a great cross-shaped ceiba whose roots reach the underworld and whose branches hold up the sky; von Daniken mistook its branching, cruciform form for a rocket. Pakal is carved at the instant of death, falling down the trunk into the underworld, as the scholar Linda Schele put it, 'down the Milky Way.' The ancient-astronaut reading ignores the Maya writing and symbols carved all around the figure, which name the scene plainly. Source: Wikipedia, K'inich Janaab' Pakal.  (Legend.)

question: A hollow, serpent-shaped stone tube runs beside the hidden stairway inside Palenque's great pyramid, all the way from Pakal's sealed tomb to the temple floor 25 metres above. Alberto Ruz found it as he cleared the steps, and archaeologists puzzled over why the Maya would run a narrow duct out of a sealed tomb. What is it thought they built it to carry?
context: Alberto Ruz Lhuillier named this hollow stone tube the 'psychoduct.' Shaped like a serpent, it runs from Pakal's sarcophagus up the hidden stairway to the temple floor above, and the Maya are thought to have built it as a road for the dead king's soul to pass between his tomb and the living world. It is one of the eeriest features of any Maya pyramid. Source: Wikipedia, Temple of the Inscriptions.

question: Rising from the middle of Palenque's rambling royal palace is a structure found at no other Maya city in the world. From its upper rooms, whose walls carry carved glyphs of the planet Venus, Maya priests seem to have watched the jungle horizon and tracked the movements of the sky. What is this famous Palenque structure?
context: Palenque's four-storey palace tower is unique in the Maya world, its inner walls carved with glyphs of Venus, whose cycles the Maya followed closely. One striking claim: at sunset on the winter solstice, seen from the tower, the sun appears to drop straight into the Temple of the Inscriptions, the pyramid holding Pakal's tomb. Source: World History Encyclopedia; Wikipedia, Palenque.

question: Beneath the plaza of Palenque, the Maya vaulted the Otulum stream inside a stone channel running nearly 300 metres. In one stretch, known as the Piedras Bolas aqueduct, they engineered a first for the entire ancient Americas, a feat of water control no other New World people is known to have managed. What did Palenque's builders achieve here?
context: By vaulting the stream and then sharply narrowing part of the channel, Palenque's engineers forced the water under pressure, able to spurt upward, perhaps to feed a fountain or basin. Penn State researchers call the Piedras Bolas aqueduct the earliest known pressurized water feature in the New World, centuries before the Spanish arrived. Source: Penn State News, 'Maya plumbing'; Wikipedia, Palenque.

question: Palmyra grew rich two thousand years ago as a caravan stop in the Syrian desert, between Rome and Persia. Down the heart of its golden-stone ruins runs a street over a kilometre long, once lined by hundreds of tall pillars. What is it called?
context: The Great Colonnade is Palmyra's spine -- a ceremonial street about 1.1 km long lined with columns roughly 9.5 m high, mostly raised in the 2nd century AD, and you can still walk between the standing pillars today. Palmyra's beauty earned it the nickname the 'Bride of the Desert.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Twenty kinds of date palm once ringed Palmyra, deep in the empty Syrian desert and far from any river. Every caravan on that long crossing had to stop at the one natural source of fresh water that made the city possible, the only reliable water for days. What is it called?
context: The Efqa spring was Palmyra's whole reason for being -- an oasis in a sea of sand, the one dependable water on the desert crossing, so every caravan crossing the wilderness HAD to stop there. That is exactly why a great city could rise in such an unlikely spot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Caravans hauling silk and spices between the Mediterranean and Persia were funnelled through Palmyra, a desert city in Syria that grew into one of the richest of the Roman East. How did Palmyra turn all those caravans into a fortune?
answer: charged a toll on their goods
choices: charged a toll on their goods
context: Palmyra worked like a desert toll-booth on the Silk Road. It even carved its customs law onto a great stone slab -- the Palmyrene Tariff -- spelling out the tax on every kind of good passing through, and those profits paid for the city's grand monuments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Outside Palmyra, in a bleak desert gully now called the Valley of the Tombs, more than fifty grand monuments to the dead still stand. Some held whole families across a hundred years or more. Palmyra's grandest tombs took a shape rarely seen anywhere else in the old world. What shape did these family tombs take?
context: Palmyra's tower tombs rose as high as four storeys -- stone apartment blocks for the dead, with family members sealed in shelf-niches floor above floor. The most recent one dates to about AD 128. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra

question: Queen Zenobia of Palmyra broke away from Rome and ruled a desert empire of her own for a few years. Around 272 the emperor Aurelian marched on her city, crushed the revolt and took her prisoner. By many accounts, what fate did his captive queen then meet?
answer: paraded through Rome in golden chains
choices: paraded through Rome in golden chains
beheaded on the spot in the desert
ransomed back to the Persian court
died of fever on the road to Rome
context: By many accounts Aurelian spared his royal captive. After leading Zenobia through Rome in golden chains in his triumph of AD 274, he is said to have let her live out her days in a comfortable villa at Tibur (modern Tivoli). The ancient sources disagree about her end, so Zenobia's final fate is really legend as much as settled history. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenobia

question: Militants of ISIS (the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria) dynamited Palmyra's greatest monuments on purpose in 2015, among them the Temple of Bel and the Arch of Triumph. Yet archaeologists are sure the ruins can be rebuilt, stone by stone. What made that possible?
choices: carved fragments buried in the sand
context: Detailed 3-D scans and photographs had been made before the war, so the 'New Palmyra' project (2015) -- built on work by the Syrian coder Bassel Khartabil -- created digital models to guide the rebuilding, and reconstruction of the Arch of Triumph began in October 2022. The scans mattered all the more because of what ISIS had done in August 2015: days before it began dynamiting the city's ancient temples, it publicly beheaded Palmyra's 83-year-old antiquities chief, Khaled al-Asaad, who had guarded the ruins for about half a century, for refusing to reveal where the city's treasures were hidden. He had said, 'I am from Palmyra, and I will stay here even if they kill me.' Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khaled_al-Asaad

question: A hillside in southwestern Turkey gleams white, stepped with hundreds of pools, as if a waterfall of snow had frozen in mid-tumble. Hot mineral springs built it out of soft chalky rock, and locals named the place Pamukkale. What does that Turkish name mean?
context: The soft, piled-up look of the white rock reminded people of mounds of cotton: pamuk means 'cotton' and kale means 'castle.' Pamukkale sits in Denizli Province in southwestern Turkey, in the valley of the Menderes -- the river the ancient Greeks called the Meander. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamukkale

question: Pamukkale's blinding-white cliff in southwestern Turkey is travertine, stone laid down by hot spring water heavy with dissolved lime. Exactly the same mineral recipe, working slowly in the dark, builds a famous feature of limestone caves. Which feature?
context: Travertine forms as hot spring water cools at the surface: the dissolved lime (calcium carbonate) it carries hardens out in another paper-thin layer. Stalactites grow by the very same recipe, drip by drip in the dark of a cave, while at Pamukkale it builds terraces in open sunlight. Gypsum, salt and ice are other substances altogether. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamukkale

question: Mineral-rich water bubbles up from hot springs at Pamukkale, in southwestern Turkey, and spills down a huge white cliff stepped with hundreds of pools. The cliff is no dead fossil left from long ago. As long as the springs keep flowing over its ledges, what is happening to the stone, year after year?
choices: the old stone is dissolving away
the terraces are turning to marble
the whole cliff is sliding downhill
context: The terraces are alive: as long as the seventeen hot springs flow, fresh travertine is laid down and the whole white formation -- already about 2,700 m long and 160 m high -- keeps growing. When pools grey with algae and grime, keepers rotate and re-flood clean water across them to keep the white bright; a hotel-driven greying in the late 20th century was reversed by closing the terraces to bathers and traffic. Source: https://www.naturalworldheritagesites.org/sites/hierapolis-pamukkale/

question: Marble ruins still crown the top of Pamukkale's vast white cliff, stepped with hot-spring pools, in southwestern Turkey. Two thousand years ago its healing springs drew visitors from across the ancient world. What did they build up on the clifftop?
context: The city is Hierapolis, the 'holy city' -- a Greco-Roman spa resort with a theatre seating around 15,000, colonnaded streets, temples, and one of the ancient world's largest necropolises (a sprawling city of tombs) for pilgrims who came to 'take the waters.' In 1988 UNESCO listed Hierapolis-Pamukkale as a single World Heritage Site, honoured for BOTH its natural white terraces and its ancient ruins. Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/485

question: Long ago an earthquake shook down the ancient town on top of Pamukkale's white cliffs in southwestern Turkey, and a portico's marble columns tumbled straight into a hot spring below. That pool, nicknamed for the Egyptian queen Cleopatra, stays a swimmable 36 degrees Celsius all year. What can bathers do there that they can do almost nowhere else on Earth?
answer: swim in among the sunken ancient columns
choices: swim in among the sunken ancient columns
drink the spring said to cure blindness
walk a glass floor above the ruins
float over a mosaic of the sea-god
context: The bath is nicknamed Cleopatra's Pool (the Antique Pool); legend even says Cleopatra herself once swam here -- a charming story, not history. Long ago an earthquake toppled the pool's marble portico straight into the thermal spring, and its fluted columns and carved blocks still rest across the bottom -- so bathers float in the roughly 36 degrees C mineral water directly above the fallen ancient stone. Source: https://visitingturkey.com/destinations/pamukkale/cleopatra-pool

question: At Hierapolis, above Pamukkale's white cliffs, priests drove bulls and birds up to the opening of one cave, and within moments the beasts fell dead. The Greeks and Romans built a shrine over that killing cave and gave it a dreadful name. What did they call it?
