context: They called it the Ploutonion -- 'Pluto's Gate' -- a doorway to the underworld of Pluto, god of the dead. The geographer Strabo wrote of it: 'I threw in sparrows and they immediately breathed their last and fell.' Long dismissed as a myth, the walled-up cave was rediscovered in 2013 by archaeologist Francesco D'Andria, together with an inscription to Pluto and Kore and a statue tied to Hades and the three-headed dog Cerberus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ploutonion_at_Hierapolis  (Legend.)

question: For centuries the priests of Hierapolis, on Pamukkale's cliffs, seemed to carry divine protection. They could stride right up to the mouth of a cave where any animal dropped dead, and walk back out alive every single time. What simple, natural reason kept the priests alive?
answer: the deadly gas lay in a low invisible layer
choices: the deadly gas lay in a low invisible layer
the priests had slowly grown immune to it
the priests quietly held their breath inside
the gas only turned deadly after nightfall
context: The carbon dioxide seeping from the cave is heavier than air, so it collects in an invisible 'lake' along the ground -- lethal to a low animal (or one held down into it) but harmless to a tall priest whose head stayed up in the breathable air above. It looked like a miracle; it was simple physics. A 2018 study led by biologist Hardy Pfanz measured CO2 up to 91% deep in the grotto, with the gas layer about 40 cm deep and deadliest at dawn after building up overnight -- and researchers still found freshly killed birds, mice, and dozens of beetles at the site. Source: https://www.science.org/content/article/roman-gate-hell-killed-its-victims-cloud-deadly-carbon-dioxide

question: Ground stations planted in North America and in Europe, across the Atlantic from each other, creep apart by about 2.5 cm a year as the plates beneath them drift. One space-age tool clocks that split in real time, down to the millimetre. Which tool?
context: GPS was built to tell you where your car is, but it is precise enough to watch continents move -- fixed ground stations on either side of the Atlantic creep apart on the readouts by roughly 2.5 cm a year. It turned Wegener's century-old idea into something we now measure directly. Source: https://earthhow.com/continental-drift-plate-tectonics/.

question: Abraham Ortelius, a map-maker, pointed out in 1596 that two facing coasts across one ocean look like torn halves of a single shape, the outward bulge of one sliding into the inward curve of the other, long before anyone could explain it. Which two coastlines fit together like puzzle pieces?
answer: West Africa and eastern South America
choices: West Africa and eastern South America
eastern North America and northwest Europe
context: The resemblance is striking enough that people noticed it for centuries -- Abraham Ortelius pointed it out in 1596 -- yet it took until the 1900s and Alfred Wegener to argue the coasts really had been torn apart, not just coincidentally shaped alike. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_drift.

question: Geologists dug up the same small fossil reptile, Mesosaurus, in the rocks of Brazil and of South Africa, on facing shores of the South Atlantic. It was a freshwater creature that could never have swum across a salt ocean. Which idea did the fossils support?
answer: the two coasts were once a single joined land
choices: the two coasts were once a single joined land
an ancient land bridge later sank beneath the sea
the same species arose on each coast separately
river floods rafted the fossils across the ocean
context: Wegener stacked up more of these twin-continent clues: the Glossopteris fern turns up across South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica -- one flora scattered over five now-separate lands. The tidiest explanation was that the lands had once been joined. Yet geologists still resisted for decades, because Wegener could not name a force strong enough to move a continent. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_drift (Glossopteris: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Wegener).

question: The drilling ship Glomar Challenger hauled up long cores of rock from deep beneath the floor of the Mediterranean Sea in 1970. Studying the layers, Kenneth Hsü and William Ryan found a record of about 5.5 million years ago and reached a startling conclusion about the whole sea. What had once happened to it?
answer: it had dried up into vast salt flats
choices: it had dried up into vast salt flats
it had frozen over into a thick ice shelf
it had drained away through the seafloor
it had boiled off in a volcanic upheaval
context: Cut off from the Atlantic when the Strait of Gibraltar sealed, the Mediterranean -- itself the shrinking remnant of the ancient Tethys Ocean -- evaporated almost completely, dropping kilometers below sea level and leaving buried salt over 2 km thick. Around 5.33 million years ago the Atlantic burst back through Gibraltar and refilled it in the Zanclean flood, one of the largest floods Earth has ever seen. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messinian_salinity_crisis.

question: J. Tuzo Wilson, a geologist, showed that oceans open wide and then slam shut again in the same belts of the globe, over and over. Right where the Atlantic now lies, an earlier ocean had already opened and closed hundreds of millions of years before it. What is that vanished ocean called?
context: This open-and-shut rhythm is called the Wilson cycle, after J. Tuzo Wilson, who described it in 1966. It runs on a slow conveyor of rock: fresh crust is shoved out at mid-ocean ridges while old, cold, heavy crust is dragged back down at deep trenches. Because of it the map never stops rearranging -- roughly 250 million years from now the Atlantic is expected to close and today's continents to crowd into a brand-new supercontinent. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_cycle ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea_Proxima.

question: Deep under the streets of Paris, mile after mile of tunnel is lined with human bones. Skulls and thigh-bones are stacked into neat walls and archways. They are the remains of about six million people. What is this underground maze of bones called?
context: The bones were carted here in the 1780s from Paris's overflowing graveyards and later stacked into deliberate walls and archways; the famous count of about six million is only an estimate. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs_of_Paris  (Legend.)

question: For hundreds of years Paris buried its dead in packed churchyards like the Cimetière des Innocents. The ground itself rose into a mound taller than a man. In the spring of 1780, the crowding finally caused a disaster that forced the city to act. What happened?
answer: Gas from the decaying dead burst through a cellar wall.
choices: The flooding Seine washed loose bones into the streets.
A fire tore through the cemetery's wooden crosses.
Gas from the decaying dead burst through a cellar wall.
Grave-robbers tunnelled into the burial vaults.
context: In spring 1780 the pressure of the rotting dead burst a wall into a neighbouring cellar. The city closed the Cimetière des Innocents and, from 1785, moved the bones by torchlight into the empty tunnels beneath the city — so the Catacombs' dead were relocated there, not buried where they now lie. Source: history.com/articles/paris-catacombs-origins

question: Long before a single skeleton went down into them, workers spent centuries hollowing out the tunnels that now hold the bones of Paris, leaving the ground beneath the city honeycombed with passages. They had not been digging tombs. Why had the tunnels been dug at first?
answer: To quarry the stone that Paris was built from.
choices: To quarry the stone that Paris was built from.
To carry the city's sewage down to the river.
To move soldiers secretly during sieges.
To store and cool the city's wine.
context: Paris was largely built from limestone dug out from directly beneath itself, honeycombing the ground with tunnels. When the mines emptied, those same galleries later became the perfect place to store the dead. Source: history.com/articles/paris-catacombs-origins

question: Both the Arc de Triomphe and the Louvre in Paris were built of the same pale, creamy stone. It was laid down on the bed of a warm, shallow sea about 45 million years ago. Geologists gave this famous 'Paris stone' its own name. What is it called?
context: It is Lutetian limestone, named after Lutetia — the Roman name for Paris — and about 48–40 million years old. The Louvre, Les Invalides, Place de la Concorde and the Arc de Triomphe are all built from it. Portland, Bath and Caen stone are all real building limestones too, but from England and Normandy, not Paris. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutetian_Limestone

question: Skulls and thighbones stacked into endless neat walls line the tunnels beneath Paris, carried down from the city's overflowing cemeteries in the 1780s. A stone slab over the doorway leading in gives every visitor a stark warning in French. What does it say?
answer: Stop! This is the empire of Death.
choices: Stop! This is the empire of Death.
Remember, traveller, that you too must die.
Abandon all hope, you who enter here.
Here sleep the forgotten children of Paris.
context: The carved warning reads 'Arrête! C'est ici l'empire de la Mort.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacombs_of_Paris

question: French police on a training run in the off-limits tunnels under Paris stumbled on a strange hidden room in August 2004. It covered about 3,000 square feet, ran on stolen electricity, and held a bar, stone benches and a recording of barking dogs set up to scare people off. What had the secret tunnel explorers built down there?
context: The builders were 'cataphiles' — illegal explorers of the tunnels. Police reportedly found a bar and benches carved from the rock, plus a recording of barking dogs to frighten off intruders. The full network of quarry galleries beneath Paris runs up to about 300 km, most of it off-limits. Source: faroutmagazine.co.uk/the-mysterious-cinema-discovered-in-the-tunnels-of-the-paris-catacombs  (Legend.)

question: Light pours into the upper room of a small royal chapel in the heart of old Paris through fifteen stained-glass windows, each 15 metres tall, that show over a thousand Bible scenes. The room has almost no solid wall and glows like the inside of a jewel. What is this chapel called?
context: The Sainte-Chapelle's fifteen windows hold 1,113 separate scenes across about 670 sq m of stained glass; it was consecrated on 26 April 1248. Nearly two-thirds of that glass is still the original 13th-century glass. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Chapelle

question: King Louis IX raised a glass-walled royal chapel on an island in the Seine at the heart of Paris in the 1240s, not as an ordinary church but as one gigantic gilded reliquary. It was a container for a single sacred treasure he had bought at enormous cost. What holy relic was the chapel built to house?
context: King Louis IX (Saint Louis) built the Sainte-Chapelle in the 1240s to house the Crown of Thorns and other relics of Christ's Passion. The upper chapel, where the relics were kept, was reserved for the royal family; the lower chapel was for servants and soldiers. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Chapelle

question: The whole glass-walled royal chapel that King Louis IX built in Paris, gilded spire and all, cost him about 40,000 livres. He also had to pay for the sacred relic the chapel was made to hold. How did the price of the relic compare with the cost of the whole building?
answer: The relic cost more than three times the whole chapel.
choices: The relic cost about the same as the chapel.
The relic cost more than three times the whole chapel.
The relic cost roughly a tenth of the chapel.
The relic was a gift and cost nothing at all.
context: Louis IX paid about 135,000 livres for the Crown of Thorns — more than three times the roughly 40,000 livres it cost to build the entire Sainte-Chapelle around it. The container cost far less than the treasure inside. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Chapelle

question: When the Paris Metro opened in 1900, the architect Hector Guimard shaped its street entrances from green cast iron. They curl and branch like plant stems and hold up orange lamps like flower buds. These famous entrances became the symbol of which art movement?
context: Art Nouveau means 'new art.' Guimard painted his railings green to imitate weathered brass, and his style became known as the 'style Métro.' He built 141 entrances (the last in 1913), and about 86 survive today as protected historical monuments. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Métro_entrances_by_Hector_Guimard

question: On a hot, sunny summer day the sun beats hard on one side of the Eiffel Tower, 300 metres of bare wrought iron standing over Paris, while the other side stays in shade. Because of the way metal responds to heat, what does the tower do?
answer: Its sunlit side lengthens, tipping the top away from the sun.
choices: Its sunlit side lengthens, tipping the top away from the sun.
Its shaded side lengthens, tipping the top toward the sun.
It sinks a few centimetres deeper into its foundations.
It slowly twists around on its four feet.
context: The sun-warmed iron on the lit side expands and lengthens, so the top can shift by up to about 15 cm, leaning away from the sun — on a hot day the tower even stands a little taller, like a giant thermometer in wrought iron. It is 300 m tall, built for the 1889 World's Fair. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower  (Legend.)

question: Gustave Eiffel's iron tower was only ever meant to be temporary — built for the 1889 World's Fair and licensed to stand for just 20 years before being torn down for scrap. Yet it still stands today. What surprising new use convinced the authorities to keep it?
answer: It made a superb radio and telegraph antenna.
choices: It became the world's tallest tourist restaurant.
It served as a giant lightning rod for the city.
It anchored the cables of a planned river bridge.
It made a superb radio and telegraph antenna.
context: Permitted for only 20 years, the tower was saved because its great height made a superb antenna for wireless telegraph and radio. It was assembled from 18,038 iron pieces held by 2.5 million rivets, designed by engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower

question: Crowds wait on the walkways facing Perito Moreno Glacier in Argentine Patagonia, listening for a boom like a cannon. It comes when a tower of ice splits from the glacier's front wall and crashes into the lake. What do scientists call this event?
context: Calving is the sudden breaking-away of ice from the front of a glacier. Perito Moreno's ice wall runs about 5 km wide and rises roughly 74 m (240 ft) — as tall as a 20-story building — straight out of Lago Argentino, and blocks tumble off it throughout the day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier.

question: Boats on Lago Argentino float right up to the towering face of Perito Moreno Glacier, whose old ice has been packed so tight for so long that it swallows nearly every colour of sunlight and returns only one. What colour does it glow?
context: The oldest, most tightly compressed glacier ice has had nearly all its air squeezed out, so it absorbs the longer red wavelengths of sunlight and reflects the blue — giving the exposed ice face its startling deep-blue glow. Sources: blogpatagonia.australis.com; quasarex.com/patagonia/perito-moreno-glacier.

question: Perito Moreno, a giant tongue of blue-white ice in Argentine Patagonia, drew scientists and tourists for decades, in years when most of the world's glaciers were slowly melting back. It could claim something almost no other big glacier of that time could. What was it famous for in those years?
answer: staying in balance instead of shrinking
choices: staying in balance instead of shrinking
having the deepest crevasses in the Andes
being the tallest ice cliff ever measured
flowing faster than any glacier on Earth
context: As glaciers worldwide retreated, Perito Moreno crept forward about 2 m a day, its advance almost exactly replacing the ice that calved off its front — so it stayed in near-perfect balance, earning the nickname the 'balanced glacier.' Honest update: that era has ended. A 2025 study found its front thinning jumped more than sixteenfold (from 0.34 m/yr in 2000-2019 to about 5.5 m/yr in 2019-2024), and it has retreated over 800 m since 2019 as it detaches from a ridge that once anchored it. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier; nature.com/articles/s43247-025-02515-7.

question: Every few years Perito Moreno Glacier creeps forward until its ice wall touches the far shore of Lago Argentino and dams off one arm of the lake, the Brazo Rico. The trapped meltwater has no outlet, so it climbs and climbs before pressure breaks a way through. How much higher than the main lake can it rise?
context: Perito Moreno is one of the only places on Earth where visitors can watch a glacier dam a lake. Pressed against the Península de Magallanes, the ice seals the Brazo Rico so completely that the trapped water can rise as much as 30 m (about 100 ft) — a 10-story wall of extra water — above the level of the main lake. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier; quasarex.com/blog/the-perito-moreno-rupture-phenomenon.

question: Every few years Perito Moreno Glacier pushes across Lago Argentino until it dams the Brazo Rico, an arm of the lake, and the trapped water stands far above the main lake. Crowds then wait, sometimes for days, for the famous rupture. How does the water finally break free?
answer: it bores a tunnel under the ice until the arch falls
choices: it bores a tunnel under the ice until the arch falls
it rises until it pours over the top of the ice
it melts a notch down through the sunlit ice face
it lifts the whole ice wall up off the far shore
context: The pent-up water bores a tunnel through the base of the ice dam, hollowing out a soaring arch that thins until it collapses -- the celebrated rupture of Perito Moreno. It keeps no fixed schedule: on average about every 4 to 5 years, but sometimes twice in a year and sometimes not for a decade. Recorded ruptures include 1917 (the first documented), 1940, 1988, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2012, 2013 (twice), 2016, 2018, and 2019. Sources: quasarex.com/blog/the-perito-moreno-rupture-phenomenon; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier.

question: About 48 glaciers, Perito Moreno among them, spill off the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, a plateau of ice stretching some 350 km along the southern Andes between Argentina and Chile. This ice field is commonly called the third-largest reserve of fresh water on Earth; only two frozen places hold more. Which two?
context: Honest nuance on the superlative: some sources call the Southern Patagonian Ice Field the world's third-largest freshwater reserve (after the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets), while others describe it more precisely as the second-largest continuous ice field outside the poles, after Alaska's. Either way it is immense — its glaciers include Pío XI (Brüggen), the largest glacier in the Southern Hemisphere outside Antarctica, plus Viedma and Upsala. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perito_Moreno_Glacier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Patagonian_Ice_Field.  (Legend.)

question: A reindeer herder by Siberia's Yuribei River found Lyuba, a baby woolly mammoth, in 2007. After more than 40,000 years her skin and organs were whole, and her last meal was still in her stomach. What had kept her soft body so perfect?
choices: A thick coat of tree resin
context: Siberia's permafrost is a natural deep-freeze for the deep past. Lyuba, found near the Yuribei River in 2007, had been frozen for more than 40,000 years, yet the ground preserved her skin, her internal organs, even her last meal still inside her stomach. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/magazine/article/mammoths

question: Builders in Yakutsk, which may be the coldest city on Earth, work over permafrost that runs hundreds of metres deep in Russia's Sakha Republic. A heated building is a hazard there, since its own warmth would thaw the frozen soil beneath it until the ground gave way. How do the city's apartment blocks keep from melting the ground that holds them up?
answer: They stand on stilts driven into the ground
choices: They stand on stilts driven into the ground
They float on thick rafts of gravel
They pump cold brine through their foundations
They are jacked back level every spring
context: Yakutsk and Norilsk are the only two large cities in the world built on continuous permafrost. Their buildings stand on stilts driven into the frozen ground, lifting the heated floors clear of the soil so the permafrost stays frozen and the foundations don't sink and buckle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permafrost

question: Round craters some 60 to 80 metres across lie punched into the flat tundra of Russia's remote Yamal Peninsula, each ringed by a rampart of soil and ice hurled outward, and herders keep stumbling on them. The first appeared in 2014 and stunned scientists. What kind of crater is a Yamal crater?
context: Yamal's craters are gas-blowout craters: as the permafrost thaws, methane builds up underground until the ground bursts, flinging out a rampart of soil and ice. Instruments have measured methane inside them up to 50,000 times normal levels. They are NOT meteorite impacts or collapse sinkholes. The first was spotted near the Bovanenkovo gas field in 2014. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamal_crater

question: Sergey and Nikita Zimov send horses, bison and muskoxen across the winter tundra of Pleistocene Park, beside Siberia's Kolyma River, to trample the deep snow into a thin, packed crust. Left alone, that snow would lie over the frozen ground all winter as a thick, loose, fluffy layer. What does such fluffy snow do to the soil beneath it?
answer: It traps the ground's heat like a blanket
choices: It traps the ground's heat like a blanket
It draws out heat and freezes it harder
It reflects sunlight and keeps the ground cool
It has no real effect on the ground
context: Fluffy, un-trampled snow works like a blanket, trapping the ground's warmth and letting the permafrost thaw. At Pleistocene Park on the Kolyma River (founded 1996, about 160 square km), Sergey and Nikita Zimov's grazing herds pack that snow down so the deep cold reaches the soil - trampling cut winter ground temperatures by about 7 C. Their larger goal is to rebuild the ice-age 'mammoth steppe.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene_Park

question: A double staircase of 111 shallow steps climbs to the great terrace of Persepolis, in southern Iran, each step only about 10 centimetres high. Tradition says the builders made the steps so low and broad for one memorable reason. What could visitors do on them?
answer: ride their horses straight up onto the terrace
choices: ride their horses straight up onto the terrace
roll the tribute-carts up to the halls
march ten soldiers up side by side
carry the king's throne on their shoulders
context: The 111 steps are only about 10 cm high and the flights nearly 7 m wide. A popular tradition says they were kept so shallow that riders could trot their horses straight onto the terrace; modern scholars dispute this, arguing the low risers were meant for a slow, dignified ceremonial ascent on foot. Source: surfiran.com/mag/persepolis; madainproject.com/persepolis; Lonely Planet (Grand Stairway).  (Legend.)

question: The Apadana of Persepolis, the hall where the Persian King of Kings received the world, once held up its cedar roof on 72 columns. A Greek visitor, used to the sturdy pillars of the temples back home, would have stared. How were the Persian columns so different?
answer: they soared far taller and more slender
choices: they soared far taller and more slender
they were half-sunk into the walls
context: Each Apadana column rose about 20 m -- the height of a six-story building -- yet was far thinner than any Greek column, like a stone reed. Of the original 72, only about 14 still stand today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persepolis; WebSearch on the Apadana columns.

question: At the head of every column in the Apadana, the main hall of the palace-city Darius the Great raised at Persepolis in southern Iran, Persian sculptors carved a striking shape just below the cedar roof-beams. What did they carve there?
answer: the front halves of two beasts, set back-to-back
choices: the front halves of two beasts, set back-to-back
a ring of curling acanthus leaves
a pair of scroll-like spiral volutes
context: Each capital showed the front halves of two animals set back-to-back -- twin bulls, twin lions, or twin eagle-headed griffins -- kneeling so their backs cradled the roof-beams. The paired royal beasts stood for the king's power and cosmic order. Source: WebSearch on Persian column capitals; metmuseum.org Achaemenid bull's-head capital.

question: A stone parade, once painted in bright colours, runs the whole length of the great Apadana staircase at Persepolis, the ceremonial capital Darius the Great began in southern Iran around 515 BC. Figure after figure marches in twenty-three groups toward the Persian king on his throne. Who are these twenty-three groups?
answer: subject peoples bearing tribute, each in native dress
choices: subject peoples bearing tribute, each in native dress
the royal bodyguard regiment called the Immortals
a long march of gods and winged spirits
the noble families of Persia and of Media
context: Twenty-three delegations of subject nations advance toward the king, each led by the hand by a Persian or Median usher, each dressed in its own national fashion, each carrying the special goods of its homeland -- a frozen stone photograph of the whole empire. Source: WebSearch (cabinet.ox.ac.uk apadana-tribute-reliefs; smarthistory.org).

question: On the carved stairway of the Apadana at Persepolis, in southern Iran, a band of figures from hot lowland Elam, near the city of Susa, climbs toward the King of Kings. It brings one of the most startling gifts on the whole stairway. What do the Elamites bring?
answer: a lioness padding along with her two cubs
choices: a lioness padding along with her two cubs
a two-humped camel loaded with bundles
an elephant tusk and a bundle of ivory
a chest of gold dust and silver rings
context: On the Apadana reliefs the Susians (Elamites) bring a lioness with her two cubs; other delegations bring the two-humped Bactrian camel, an elephant tusk from Nubia, and gold from India -- each gift a clue to its land. Source: thecollector.com/fascinating-facts-from-the-bas-reliefs-of-persepolis.

question: Two colossal stone guardians loom on either side of the Gate of All Nations at Persepolis, set there to ward off any evil approaching the King of Kings. These winged creatures were carved to overpower anyone who came before him. What were they?
answer: winged bulls with the heads of bearded men
choices: winged bulls with the heads of bearded men
winged lions with the heads of eagles
winged lions with the heads of women
winged bulls with the heads of rams
context: These guardians are lamassu -- winged bulls with human heads, believed to ward off evil. Persepolis's lamassu were given their natural four legs, unlike the older Assyrian winged bulls, which were carved with five so they looked complete from both front and side. Source: worldhistory.org Gate of All Nations; royalacademy.org.uk lamassu from the Gate of Xerxes.

question: The cedar roofs and painted halls of Persepolis roared up in flame soon after Alexander the Great took it in 330 BC, and the palace-city never rose again. The ancient writers who described the fire could not agree on why he did it, and historians still argue over it. What two rival explanations do the ancient writers hand down?
answer: planned revenge for Persia's burning of Athens, or a drunken feast
choices: planned revenge for Persia's burning of Athens, or a drunken feast
an accidental cooking-fire, or a lightning strike in a storm
a signal to his troops, or an offering to the Greek gods
to deny it to rebels, or to smother a plague in the city
context: The historian Arrian says Alexander burned Persepolis in cold, deliberate revenge for the Persian king Xerxes' burning of Athens in 480 BC. Diodorus, Plutarch, and Curtius tell a wilder tale: at a drunken victory feast the Athenian courtesan Thais urged it on and, after the king himself, hurled the first blazing torch into the palace. The ancient sources never agreed, and neither can we. Source: livius.org/sources/content/diodorus; worldhistory.org; brewminate.com.  (Legend.)

question: Alexander's fire left the palace of Persepolis in ashes. Scattered through the ruined record-rooms lay tens of thousands of soft clay tablets covered in cuneiform -- the working paperwork of the empire, listing workers' wages, food rations, and travel passes. What did the flames do to the tablets?
answer: baked them rock-hard, so they survive to be read
choices: baked them rock-hard, so they survive to be read
melted them into shapeless, unreadable lumps
cracked them into worthless, powdery dust
burned the writing clean off their faces
context: The fire that destroyed Persepolis paradoxically saved its greatest treasure: it baked the soft clay tablets as hard as pottery. More than 30,000 survived -- the Persepolis Fortification Archive -- written mostly in Elamite and recording the everyday accounts of the empire. Chicago's Oriental Institute unearthed them in the 1930s, letting us read the empire's daily records 2,500 years later. Source: iranicaonline.org/articles/persepolis-elamite-tablets; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persepolis_Administrative_Archives.

question: About 26 million knots, more than 300 to every square inch, fill the Ardabil Carpet, woven in Iran in the 1500s. Each knot wraps a wool tuft around a loom thread; the trimmed tops make the soft pile. How were the knots made?
answer: Each one tied by hand, one at a time
choices: Each one tied by hand, one at a time
Stamped out in rows by a knotting machine
Pressed into the wool with a heated iron
Glued to the backing with boiled tree resin
context: The Ardabil Carpet holds roughly 26 million knots - about 300 to 350 in every square inch - and every one was looped and trimmed by a weaver's own fingers. No machine tied a single knot. A knotted carpet has no woven picture on top: its whole soft surface, the 'pile,' is nothing but the trimmed ends of millions of tiny wool knots, each looped by hand around the stretched threads of the loom.

question: Worked small into one corner of the Ardabil Carpet, among the flowers, is the name Maqsud of Kashan. The great carpet was woven in Iran in the 1500s for a shrine and is now kept in London's Victoria and Albert Museum, and almost no other old carpet carries a name at all. Who was Maqsud?
answer: The weaver who made the carpet
choices: The weaver who made the carpet
The Shah who ordered the carpet
The poet whose verse it carries
The merchant who later sold it
context: Maqsud of Kashan signed the Ardabil Carpet as 'a servant of the court.' It was finished in 946 of the Islamic calendar (1539-40 CE) under Shah Tahmasp, and above his name he wove a couplet by the poet Hafez. It hangs today in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardabil_Carpet

question: A garden carpet from Iran, spread on the floor, shows a walled garden seen from above, laid out on the ancient plan called the chahar bagh, Persian for 'four gardens'. Four equal quarters fill it with painted flowers and fruit trees. What runs between the quarters and divides them?
context: This fourfold plan - chahar bagh, 'four gardens' - splits a walled garden into four beds with cross-shaped water channels, so a garden carpet is a whole paradise garden seen from directly above. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_carpet

question: Turkish weavers loop each carpet knot evenly over two threads; Persian weavers in Iran wrap theirs around just one. That single difference lets a Persian rug show one kind of design that a Turkish rug can draw only clumsily. Which kind?
choices: Large blocks of a single color
context: The asymmetric 'Persian' or Senneh knot wraps a single warp thread, so a design can bend into fine spiraling flowers and vines. The symmetric 'Turkish' or Ghiordes knot, looped over two threads, makes blockier, more geometric shapes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_carpet

question: The Ardabil Carpet, more than ten metres long and woven in Iran in the 1500s for the shrine at Ardabil, has been the pride of London's Victoria and Albert Museum since 1893. Yet it hides a secret about how it began. What is the truth about it?
answer: It was woven as one of an identical pair
choices: It was woven as one of an identical pair
It was cut down from a far larger carpet
It was left unfinished by its weaver
It was stitched together from many small rugs
context: The Ardabil was woven as one of two matching carpets, a pair made for the shrine at Ardabil. The larger went to London's V&A in 1893 (the designer William Morris urged its purchase for GBP 2,000); the second, smaller carpet now lives at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardabil_Carpet

question: Xenophon, a Greek soldier who served in Persia, carried home the Persians' word for the walled gardens that Persian garden carpets copy. Its old Iranian form, pairidaeza, joins pairi, 'around', and daeza, 'wall': a walled-around place. From Greek it moved through the Bible into English. What everyday English word grew from it?
context: Xenophon, a Greek who served in Persia, wrote the word down as 'paradeisos' for the walled royal parks; it passed through Greek and the Bible into English as 'paradise.' pairi = 'around,' daeza = 'wall.' The form pairi-daeza is Avestan, an old Iranian language; Old Persian had paridaida. Sources: etymonline.com/word/paradise; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradise

question: King Khosrow I of Persia spread the most fabulous carpet ever made across his palace floor around 550, a whole spring garden knotted so that he could stroll among blossoms even in deep winter. It was called the Spring of Khosrow, and its paths, streams and flowers were not made of ordinary thread. What were they made of?
answer: Gold paths, silver streams, and jewelled flowers
choices: Gold paths, silver streams, and jewelled flowers
Silver paths, crystal streams, and pearl flowers
Bronze paths, glass streams, and coral flowers
Ivory paths, amber streams, and enamel flowers
context: The 'Spring of Khosrow' (Baharestan) carpet covered the palace floor at Ctesiphon around 550 CE, its garden knotted in silk with paths of gold, streams of silver, and flowers of real jewels, so King Khosrow I could 'walk in the garden' even in winter. We know it only from later descriptions. Source: britannica.com/topic/Spring-of-Khosrow-Carpet  (Legend.)

question: A master weaver in Iran can spend years knotting one Persian carpet. A charming story is often told about such work: every Persian carpet hides one small mistake, woven in on purpose. In this old tradition, why would a master weaver spoil a perfect carpet with a flaw?
answer: Because only God is perfect, never human work
choices: Because only God is perfect, never human work
To leave a hidden mark only the weaver could find
To let bad luck escape the finished rug
To make each carpet unlike every other
context: This is folklore, not a rule of the craft. Weavers sometimes spoke of the idea, but myth-debunkers note there is no real evidence carpets were made with a deliberate flaw - it is a charming tradition, not an actual weaving practice. Source: historymyths.wordpress.com  (Legend.)

question: When Arab armies stormed the Persian capital Ctesiphon in 637 CE, they carried off Khosrow's priceless silk garden carpet as war-loot. The Caliph Umar himself decided the fate of the greatest carpet ever woven. What did he order done with it?
answer: Cut into pieces and shared out among the soldiers
choices: Cut into pieces and shared out among the soldiers
Burned in the square as a pagan idol
Sent whole to hang in the mosque at Mecca
Locked away in the treasury at Damascus
context: When Arab armies captured Ctesiphon in 637 CE, the Caliph Umar had the Spring of Khosrow cut into pieces and shared among the soldiers as loot. Not a single fragment survives; we know the carpet only from the historian al-Tabari's account. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baharestan_Carpet  (Legend.)

question: Earth's oldest knotted carpet lay for some 2,500 years in a Scythian chieftain's burial mound high in Siberia's Altai Mountains, though wool should crumble to dust within a few centuries. The Pazyryk carpet survived only because of a freak accident inside the tomb. What saved it?
answer: Water seeped in and froze it solid in ice
choices: Water seeped in and froze it solid in ice
Dry desert air slowly mummified it
A deep peat bog sealed it from all air
Falling volcanic ash buried it hard
context: Water flooded the Scythian tomb in the Altai Mountains and froze, sealing the Pazyryk carpet in ice until it was dug out in 1949. About 2,500 years old (5th century BC), it shows a row of horsemen and grazing deer and now lives in the Hermitage in St Petersburg. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazyryk_carpet

question: In Iran's carpet trade a dealer can often name a rug's home city at a single glance. Rugs from one great weaving city are famous for the 'Mahi,' or 'fish,' design - a field of small curved leaves swimming around a central medallion. Which city is the home of the fish-pattern carpet?
context: Iran's weaving cities each have a signature look: Tabriz its bold medallions and the 'Mahi' fish pattern, Isfahan its flowing 'Shah Abbas' florals, Kashan its dense fine-wool flower fields, and Kerman its bright pictorial gardens. Source: catalinarug.com

question: Al-Khazneh, the Treasury, rises nearly 40 metres up a cliff of red sandstone at Petra in southern Jordan, its columns and statues glowing pink in the desert sun. How did Petra's builders make this huge front?
answer: They carved it downward straight out of the solid rock cliff.
choices: They stacked and mortared cut sandstone blocks.
They carved it downward straight out of the solid rock cliff.
They cast it from concrete over a timber frame.
They assembled marble columns shipped from Greece.
context: Al-Khazneh was sculpted from the top down straight into the living sandstone cliff -- carved out, not built up from blocks. Petra's people cut whole temples, tombs, and a theatre this way. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khazneh

question: Petra's cliffs, in the desert of southern Jordan, glow in bands of pink, red and orange, richest in the low sun of morning and evening. It is known as the Rose City. What gives its sandstone that colour?
answer: Iron in the sandstone stains it red and orange.
choices: The glow of low, slanting sunlight.
Red paint the Nabataeans brushed on.
Iron in the sandstone stains it red and orange.
A crust of windblown desert dust.
context: The pink, red, and orange bands are iron oxides in the sandstone itself, so Petra is rose-coloured all the way through -- which is why it is called 'the Rose City.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra

question: Temples, tombs and an open-air theatre are cut into the walls of a hidden desert valley at Petra, in southern Jordan. Over two thousand years ago this was no ruin but a busy capital. Which people built Petra as their capital?
context: The Nabataeans were a wealthy Arab trading people who turned a dry gorge into a caravan city of tens of thousands -- master engineers and stone-carvers, not simple desert nomads. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra

question: Travellers bound for Petra's Treasury walk for more than a kilometre through the Siq, a shadowy slot barely 3 metres wide between cliffs 150 metres high. It was never chiselled out by hand. What created it?
answer: A crack where the rock was split apart by the earth.
choices: A river that carved the slot over the ages.
Wind slowly scouring away the soft sandstone.
A crack where the rock was split apart by the earth.
A meteor that gouged the passage on impact.
context: The Siq is a natural fault -- a crack where earth movements split the rock apart, later smoothed by water running down from Wadi Musa. It was never carved by hand or by a river. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siq

question: Petra's most famous facade, Al-Khazneh, in southern Jordan, goes by the nickname the Treasury. Archaeologists who studied the rooms inside found no vault and no riches, only bare carved chambers. What was Al-Khazneh built to be?
context: Al-Khazneh was almost certainly a mausoleum, most likely built for the Nabataean king Aretas IV. The 'Treasury' name came much later, from local legend. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khazneh

question: Local marksmen fired again and again, for generations, at a giant stone urn high on the front of Al-Khazneh at Petra, in southern Jordan, sure they could break it open. The urn is pocked with their bullet marks. What did they believe was inside it?
answer: Gold sealed inside by an ancient pharaoh.
choices: An evil spirit trapped long ago.
Gold sealed inside by an ancient pharaoh.
A sacred spring waiting to burst out.
The bones of a Nabataean king.
context: The urn is solid sandstone and never held anything. Bedouin tradition said a pharaoh had hidden gold inside, so marksmen shot at it hoping to crack it open -- which is how Al-Khazneh got its nickname 'the Treasury.' (Legend.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khazneh

question: The Bedouin of Petra's valley, in southern Jordan, let no stranger near, and the city lay forgotten by the outside world for centuries. Johann Burckhardt, a Swiss explorer, finally slipped inside in 1812 by a clever trick. What was his ruse?
answer: He posed as a pilgrim seeking to sacrifice at Aaron's tomb.
choices: He bribed a guide with a purse of silver coins.
He posed as a pilgrim seeking to sacrifice at Aaron's tomb.
He claimed to be a healer sent to a sick sheikh.
He traded a fine stallion for safe passage.
context: Burckhardt, disguised as a Muslim pilgrim, claimed he had vowed to sacrifice a goat at the tomb of Aaron above the valley -- a pretext that got a guide to lead him through the Siq. He was the first European to see Petra in centuries. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra

question: Long camel caravans trekked up from southern Arabia to Petra, in southern Jordan, and the city, which made almost nothing of its own, grew rich by taxing them. They were loaded with two precious substances worth their weight in gold. What did they carry?
context: The Nabataeans controlled the incense road, taxing caravans of frankincense and myrrh -- fragrant resins burned in temples across the ancient world. A single caravan could stretch for miles with up to 2,500 camels. Source: https://calvin.edu/news-stories/who-were-nabataeans-3

question: Some twenty thousand people lived for centuries in Petra's bone-dry gorge in southern Jordan, a place with almost no rain and no river. How did the city's builders keep a desert city that big supplied with fresh water all year long?
answer: They caught flash floods in dams and hidden cisterns.
choices: They dug deep wells down to a buried aquifer.
They caught flash floods in dams and hidden cisterns.
They hauled it in by camel from the distant coast.
They melted mountain snow piped across the desert.
context: The Nabataeans built dams, rock-cut channels, and hundreds of underground cisterns that captured every flash flood and stored the water out of the sun. They caught so much that they even sold the surplus. Source: https://nabataea.net/explore/petra/petra-water-works/

question: Caravan tolls and a clever water system kept Petra, in southern Jordan, thriving for centuries, until in AD 363 a single catastrophe shattered its buildings and broke the waterworks the city relied on. Petra never truly recovered. What struck the city?
context: The earthquake of AD 363 wrecked much of Petra and crippled the water network that made desert life possible, hastening the city's long, slow abandonment. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra

question: A climb of some 800 rock-cut steps above the valley floor at Petra leads to its biggest monument, a facade about 47 metres tall carved high into the mountainside, larger even than the famous Treasury. What is this giant facade called?
context: Ad-Deir, 'the Monastery,' is Petra's largest carved facade -- about 47 m tall and 48 m wide. It was originally a Nabataean monument; its name comes from Christian crosses cut inside during the Byzantine era. The 800-step climb keeps it far quieter than the Treasury. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed-Deir,_Petra

question: Spring water ran for miles into Petra through clay pipelines laid by the city's builders. They shaped each section of pipe with one clever detail that controlled the water's speed and cut down turbulence, a refinement modern engineers rediscovered only in the last couple of centuries. What was it?
choices: A lead lining sealing every joint.
A spiral groove cut inside each pipe.
Small valves that opened on their own.
context: Each clay pipe had tapered ends that slotted into the next to reduce turbulence and control the flow, with settling basins to clean the water -- plumbing centuries ahead of its time, feeding a city in the desert. Source: https://interestingengineering.com/culture/amazing-engineering-feats-lost-city-of-petra

question: In the Zambales Mountains on Luzon in the Philippines, a jungle-covered peak had slept for about 500 years. It was so quiet that few of the farmers on its slopes knew it was a volcano at all. In June 1991 it woke in one of the century's biggest eruptions. Which mountain is this?
context: Mount Pinatubo rises in the Zambales Mountains of Central Luzon. Before 1991 it had been dormant for roughly 500 years and was so overgrown with jungle that hardly anyone recognized it as a volcano. Source: Wikipedia, '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo'; USGS Fact Sheet 113-97.

question: Mount Pinatubo, on the island of Luzon in the Philippines, blew up on 15 June 1991 and shot an ash column about 40 kilometres into the sky. Its blast was one of the biggest volcanic eruptions of the whole 20th century, and only one eruption that century was bigger. Which one?
context: Only Novarupta, in Alaska, outdid Pinatubo — its 1912 eruption was the largest of the 20th century. Pinatubo itself rated VEI 6, a 'colossal' blast on the Volcanic Explosivity Index. Source: Wikipedia, '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo'; USGS Fact Sheet 113-97.

question: When Mount Pinatubo, in the Philippines, erupted in 1991, it blasted about 17 million tonnes of one gas high into the stratosphere, far above the weather. Instruments have never measured more of that gas from any eruption. Which gas did the volcano send up?
context: Pinatubo injected about 17-20 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere — the largest sulfur injection ever recorded by instruments. High above the weather, that gas would slowly turn into a haze of fine sulfate droplets. Source: USGS Fact Sheet 113-97; Wikipedia, '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo'.

question: For about two years after Mount Pinatubo erupted, the whole Earth ran a slight fever in reverse: average global temperatures fell by roughly half a degree Celsius — one mountain chilling an entire planet. High in the stratosphere, the volcano's veil of tiny droplets spread right around the globe. How did that veil cool the world below?
answer: It reflected sunlight back into space before it reached the ground
choices: It reflected sunlight back into space before it reached the ground
It choked the sky with dark ash that shaded the ground for years
It tore a hole in the ozone layer that let the surface heat escape
It chilled the oceans by burying them under cold volcanic dust
context: The sulfate haze acted like a planet-sized mirror, bouncing part of the incoming sunlight back to space and dimming the light reaching the surface by around 10%. The global chill peaked about 18 months later, around December 1992. Source: USGS, 'Volcanoes Can Affect Climate'; USGS, Self et al., 'The Atmospheric Impact of the 1991 Mount Pinatubo Eruption'.

question: Volcano scientists of the Philippines, working with the U.S. Geological Survey, read the swarming earthquakes, the rising gas and the swelling lava dome of Mount Pinatubo, and forecast its climactic blast about two days ahead. What did that forecast let officials do in the little time they had?
answer: Evacuate tens of thousands of people from the slopes
choices: Evacuate tens of thousands of people from the slopes
Reinforce the roofs across the towns downwind
Clear the ash from the roads and airfields
Steer the coming mudflows away from the villages
context: The PHIVOLCS-USGS forecast set evacuations in motion roughly 48 hours before the 15 June climax; about 60,000 people left the danger zones (some 100,000 were relocated in all). USGS credits the warning with saving 5,000 to 20,000 lives and averting at least $250 million in losses. Source: USGS, 'Remembering Mount Pinatubo 25 Years Ago'; USGS Fact Sheet 113-97.

question: Worshippers at the 16th-century San Guillermo Church in Bacolor, near Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines, step inside through what were once its upper windows, for grey volcanic mud fills it to half its 12-metre height. The flow that buried the town struck in 1995, four years after the eruption. What do volcano scientists call such a flow?
context: For years after 1991, monsoon rains kept remobilizing Pinatubo's loose ash into lahars — churning rivers of volcanic mud (not lava) that buried whole towns downstream. On 3 September 1995 a lahar filled San Guillermo Church in Bacolor, Pampanga; parishioners still worship inside, entering near the old upper windows. Source: Wikipedia, '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo' and 'San Guillermo Parish Church (Bacolor)'; VERA Files.

question: Some 20,000 people still live among the grey courtyard shops and narrow lanes of Pingyao, a small town in the northern Chinese province of Shanxi. Unlike almost every other old Chinese city, Pingyao never tore down one great thing. What did it keep?
context: Pingyao's wall was rebuilt in gray brick over rammed earth in 1370, the third year of the Ming Hongwu Emperor — about 6,163 m (6.2 km) around and roughly 12 m high. While nearly every other old Chinese city eventually tore its walls down, Pingyao kept its entire Ming wall intact. Today around 20,000 people still live inside, and visitors can walk the full unbroken loop atop it; UNESCO named the town a World Heritage Site in 1997. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pingyao

question: Seen from above, Pingyao shows the plan its Ming builders laid out: the south gate is a head, two wells just outside it are eyes, the north gate is a tail, and the side gates stick out like legs. They shaped the town on one long-lived creature, hoping it would live as long. Which creature?
context: Seen from above, Pingyao is laid out as a tortoise: the south gate is the head, two wells just outside it are the eyes, the north gate is the tail, the four east–west gates are the four legs, and the zigzag streets form the pattern of the shell. The tortoise, a Chinese symbol of long life, was chosen so the town would 'live' as long as a turtle. Source: https://www.china-tour.cn/Pingyao/Ancient-City-Walls-Gates.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pingyao

question: Rishengchang opened on Pingyao's West Street in 1823 and is known as China's first bank of its kind. It spared traders a deadly job, hauling chests of silver along roads where bandits waited. A trader could now hand his silver in at one branch and collect the same sum at another a thousand kilometres away. What did he carry on the road instead of coins?
context: Rishengchang ('Sunrise Prosperity') opened on West Street in 1823 and is widely regarded as China's first 'draft bank' (piaohao) — the first modern-style remittance bank, not literally the first exchange of value. A merchant deposited silver at one branch and drew it out with a paper note at a distant branch, avoiding bandits; the bank grew to 50-plus branches, reaching Russia, Mongolia and Japan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishengchang

question: Pingyao's Ming wall has watchtowers along its top and battlements notched all around it. By old tradition the builders did not pick the numbers at random. They matched them to the sage Confucius: one watchtower for each of his gifted disciples, and one battlement for each of his students. How many did they build?
context: Pingyao's wall carries 72 watchtowers and more than 3,000 battlements, a count traditionally said to honor Confucius's 72 wisest disciples and his 3,000 students. Four larger towers stand at the corners, and a moat about 4 m wide and 4 m deep runs outside. This honoring is traditional lore rather than documented fact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pingyao ; https://www.ancient-origins.net/ancient-places-asia/pingyao-021363  (Legend.)

question: Far from any big city or seaport, the small Shanxi town of Pingyao was home by the 1800s to about 22 banks that moved much of the Qing empire's silver across thirty-plus cities. That was more than half of all such banks in China. What nickname did the little town earn?
answer: the Wall Street of old China
choices: the Wall Street of old China
the Fort Knox of old China
context: Because its draft banks handled so much of the empire's money, Pingyao was called the 'Wall Street of old China.' At its peak the small town held around 22 piaohao — among them Rishengchang and Weitaihou — more than half of all such banks in the country, doing business in 30-plus cities. Rishengchang controlled nearly half of China's silver trade before going bankrupt around 1914 and closing in 1932. Source: http://www.goshanxi.com.cn/pingyao/2023-11/20/c_940390.htm ; https://www.travelchinaguide.com/attraction/shanxi/pingyao/street.htm

question: Workers had built only about three storeys of the marble bell tower beside Pisa's cathedral, in central Italy, when it began to tilt around 1178, long before it was finished. The lean was never a design choice. What made the tower start to tilt so early?
answer: The soft, waterlogged ground gave way unevenly
choices: The soft, waterlogged ground gave way unevenly
An earthquake jolted the foundation loose
The marble blocks were set off-level
Coastal winds pushed hard on one side
context: The tower rests on a shallow foundation only about 3 metres deep, sitting on weak, waterlogged subsoil — layers of clay, fine sand and silt studded with old marine shells. That soft ground compresses unevenly, so one side settled more and the whole tower tipped. It was a foundation problem from the very start, not a flaw in the design. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa

question: Builders worked on Pisa's leaning tower for nearly two centuries, and when they raised the upper floors they made the columns on the sinking side taller, hoping to straighten the climb. The fix left the tower with a strange, subtle shape that can still be seen today. What shape is the Leaning Tower built in?
context: Work on the 8-story tower stretched from 1173 to about 1372 — nearly 200 years, with a century-long pause during Pisa's wars with Genoa, Lucca and Florence. When building resumed around 1272 under Giovanni di Simone, masons made the columns and floors on the sinking side taller to fight the tilt. Because each phase leaned a little differently, the tower ended up subtly curved — banana-shaped — rather than straight. Source: https://www.ice.org.uk/what-is-civil-engineering/infrastructure-projects/stabilising-the-leaning-tower-of-pisa

question: Engineers closed Pisa's tower in 1990, when it leaned a dangerous 5.5 degrees and was edging toward collapse, and searched for a way to save it. Their solution sounds backward: to ease the tower back toward upright, they slowly scooped small amounts of soil out from under its foundation. Where did they dig?
answer: Under the high side, which had sunk least
choices: Under the high side, which had sunk least
Under the low side, which had sunk most
Under the south side, by the cathedral
Evenly under all four sides at once
context: The rescue was led by an international committee including engineer John Burland, using a method called 'underexcavation.' By drilling in and removing small amounts of soil from beneath the high north side — the side that had sunk less — engineers let that side settle so the tower eased back toward vertical. It pulled the top back about 44 cm, easing the lean to roughly 3.97 degrees. The tower reopened on 15 December 2001 and should stay stable for another 200-300 years. Source: https://www.building.co.uk/focus/the-man-who-saved-the-leaning-tower-of-pisa/1455.article

question: Polynesian families sailed thousands of miles across the open Pacific with no compass and no chart, carrying water and food to settle new islands. What kind of boat carried them across that huge ocean?
context: Polynesians settled the largest ocean on Earth in double-hulled voyaging canoes — two long hulls lashed side by side with a deck between for people, water and food — sailing thousands of miles with no compass, chart or instrument, navigating purely by 'wayfinding' (the stars, sun, swells and signs of nature). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation ; https://hokulea.com/polynesian-wayfinding/

question: Three far-flung islands mark the corners of a vast patch of ocean: Hawaii in the north, Easter Island in the southeast and New Zealand in the southwest. The Pacific between them is wider than any country on Earth. What is this region called?
context: The Polynesian Triangle spans more than 10 million square miles — about 5% of Earth's surface, wider than any nation on the planet — with Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa (New Zealand) and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) at its three corners. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_Triangle ; https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/what-is-the-polynesian-triangle.html

question: On a moonless night halfway from Hawaii to Tahiti, a Polynesian navigator holds his course by memory alone. He knows the 32 named houses that ring the horizon, and which house each guiding star climbs out of and drops back into. What did navigators call that whole ring?
context: The star compass divided the horizon into 32 'houses' (each 11.25° of arc); a navigator memorised exactly which house each guiding star rose out of in the east (hikina) and set into in the west (komohana), holding course by that ring of star-houses all night. Some Pacific navigators carried bearings for as many as 150 stars. Source: https://worldwidevoyage.hokulea.com/education-at-sea/polynesian-navigation/the-star-compass/

question: Several canoes work their way toward the low Tuamotu atolls, and each crew chases a different sign of sea and sky, sure it points to a hidden island just past the horizon. Only one crew has truly read the ocean and is heading for land. Which crew is steering right?
answer: the crew following white terns at dusk
choices: the crew following white terns at dusk
the crew following white terns at dawn
the crew steering into the running swell
the crew chasing a frigatebird overhead
context: Terns and noddies roost on land but fly far out to sea at dawn to hunt fish, returning at dusk — so a navigator sails against the flock in the morning and with it in the evening, and the birds lead him home to the island. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: A master navigator bound for the Tuamotus does something that looks like sleeping: he lies flat in the bottom of the canoe, eyes shut, letting the hull's every motion pass through his body. From this alone he knows an island lies ahead, still hours away and far below the horizon. What is he feeling?
answer: swells that wrap around the island and cross beneath him
choices: swells that wrap around the island and cross beneath him
a current that keeps dragging the canoe off course
a chop that steepens over a rising seabed
a wind that bends around the land and shifts
context: Long ocean swells run in steady straight lines, and their pattern bends and wraps around an island; a navigator lying in the hull can feel an unseen island over the horizon by the way the crossing swells make the canoe pitch and roll. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation ; https://hokulea.com/polynesian-wayfinding/

question: Tupaia, a navigator from Raiatea, joined Captain Cook's ship in 1769 and drew the crew a sailing chart of some 2,000 miles of the Pacific, naming 74 islands with their bearings and sailing times. The map covered nearly a quarter of the whole ocean. Where had every scrap of it come from?
choices: old charts kept by Tahitian priests
a Spanish map traded years before
Cook's own running survey of the coast
context: In 1769 the Raʻiatean priest-navigator Tupaia drew Captain Cook a chart from memory naming 74 islands (he knew about 130), covering the ocean within roughly 2,000 miles of Raʻiatea — a single man carrying a map of a quarter of the Pacific in his head. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: Sailing from Tahiti toward the Tuamotu atolls, a navigator watches the sky, not the sea. The atolls are rings of coral so low that they stay hidden below the horizon until a canoe is almost upon them. The wide, shallow lagoon inside each hidden atoll leaves a telltale mark on the cloud piled above it. What does the lagoon cast up onto that cloud?
context: A lagoon's shallow water throws a faint green tint onto the underside of the cloud piled above it; navigators sailing from Tahiti toward the low Tuamotu atolls watched the clouds for that green glow to reveal a hidden atoll like Anaa long before its land showed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_navigation

question: Each spring the long-tailed cuckoo vanished from Rarotonga and other tropical islands, flying off into the empty southwest horizon. Māori tradition says the ancestors read a message in that yearly flight and launched their canoes into the open ocean to follow it. What had the cuckoo's flight told them?
answer: undiscovered land lay to the southwest
choices: undiscovered land lay to the southwest
rich fishing grounds lay to the southwest
a warm ocean current ran to the southwest
a belt of storms guarded the southwest
context: The long-tailed cuckoo (koekoeā) breeds only in New Zealand yet winters scattered across the tropical Pacific, migrating each spring; settlers bound for Aotearoa are thought to have reasoned that land lay to the southwest and followed the cuckoo — a roughly 1,700-nautical-mile (3,000 km) run from Rarotonga to New Zealand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_long-tailed_cuckoo ; https://teara.govt.nz/en/canoe-navigation/page-3  (Legend.)

question: The island of Raiatea in the Society group is remembered across the Pacific as 'Hawaiki,' the ancestral homeland the voyagers set out from. On it stands the grandest temple in Polynesia. It is a vast open-air platform of stone where navigators gathered before a voyage and chiefs sailed in from far-off islands to worship. It is now a World Heritage site. What is this great marae called?
context: Raʻiatea's ancient name was Havaiʻi — the 'Hawaiki' named in Māori, Tahitian, Sāmoan and Hawaiian memory as the ancestral homeland. Its temple, the marae of Taputapuātea, was the religious heart of Eastern Polynesia and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taputapuātea_marae ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiki

question: Sceptics long insisted that Polynesians never truly navigated, but merely drifted onto their islands by luck. In 1976 a new canoe, Hōkūleʻa, set out to answer them, sailing from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti, roughly 2,500 miles, steering only by stars, swells and birds. A month later she glided into Papeʻete harbour. What was waiting on the shore?
choices: three French gunboats ordering her away
a dozen officials and little else
an empty shore, her arrival unannounced
context: Hōkūleʻa left Maui on 1 May 1976 and reached Papeʻete on 4 June — about 2,500 miles guided only by traditional wayfinding, no instruments — where some 17,000 Tahitians crowded the shore to greet her, proving the ancient methods truly worked and answering the 'accidental drift' theory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hōkūleʻa ; https://www.robertshawaii.com/blog/hokulea-a-tradition-of-hawaiian-voyaging

question: To guide the canoe Hōkūleʻa across the open ocean to Tahiti, her crew had to seek out Mau Piailug, one of the last masters of instrument-free wayfinding, and persuade him to teach it back to them. The art had long since died out in Hawaiʻi itself. Where had it survived?
answer: on Satawal, a tiny island in Micronesia
choices: on Satawal, a tiny island in Micronesia
on Rapa Nui, at the far southeast corner
on Tahiti, in the Society Islands
context: Mau Piailug (1932–2010) of Satawal in Micronesia was a 'palu' master navigator of the Weriyeng school who had kept the vanishing knowledge alive and agreed to teach it back to the Hawaiians who had lost it; he guided Hōkūleʻa in 1976 and in 2007 led the first pwo master-navigator initiation on Satawal in 56 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Piailug

question: Metres of ash from Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii in AD 79, and for about 1,700 years it lay lost. Even after digging began there in 1748, years passed before the diggers knew which town they had found. What finally told them?
answer: a stone carved with its name
choices: a stone carved with its name
a coin stamped with its name
a map painted on a villa wall
a sailor's chart of the coast
context: Digging at the site began in 1748, but the town was not identified until 20 August 1763, when the diggers uncovered an inscription naming the 'Rei Publicae Pompeianorum', the commonwealth of the Pompeians. Vesuvius had buried Pompeii in AD 79 under about 4-6 metres (13-20 ft) of ash and pumice, and it had lain lost for roughly 1,700 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeii

question: The entrance hall of Pompeii's House of the Tragic Poet still holds a floor mosaic and two blocky Latin words, preserved in tile since Vesuvius buried the town in AD 79. Countless visitors have grinned once they learned the message. What does the Latin cave canem warn?
context: The mosaic sits in the entrance of the House of the Tragic Poet, built from tiny stone tiles called tesserae, showing a dog above the words CAVE CANEM -- 'Beware of the Dog.' It is essentially a Roman 'Beware of Dog' sign, 2,000 years old. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_the_Tragic_Poet

question: Pompeii's ash hardened into rock around the eruption's victims. The bodies inside slowly rotted away. They left hollow, person-shaped holes in the stone. In 1863 the dig's director, Giuseppe Fiorelli, came up with a famous trick that used these holes. What was his method?
answer: Pour liquid plaster in to cast the victims
choices: Pour liquid plaster in to cast the victims
Fill them with cement to steady the ruins
Lower wax models in for the museum
Press paper inside to take rubbings
context: The bodies had decayed inside the hardened ash, leaving voids. Fiorelli poured in liquid plaster, let it set, then chipped away the rock -- casting the victims in their exact final poses. Modern teams now use clear resin. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeii

question: A guard dog was chained by its collar at Pompeii's House of Orpheus when Vesuvius erupted in AD 79. The shape its body left in the hardened ash is now one of the most famous sights of the buried town. How was the dog caught in its final moment?
answer: On its back with all four legs in the air
choices: On its back with all four legs in the air
Crouched flat beneath a stone bench
context: The dog was chained at the House of Orpheus and caught on its back, all four legs thrust up, frozen mid-writhe as the ash rose. Its plaster cast is among Pompeii's most haunting. Source: https://seepompeii.com/en/pompeii-casts-where-they-are-found-and-what-they-are/

question: More than 1,500 painted campaign slogans still cover the walls of Pompeii, real Roman election posters, and some are nasty attack ads. One so-called endorsement was really an insult, claiming a candidate was backed by a certain shady crowd. Who supposedly supported him?
context: Among 1,500+ preserved election notices, some used negative campaigning: one 'endorsement' claims all the late drinkers back a candidate, and another that a rival is supported by petty thieves. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/pompeiis-graffiti-captures-every-joke-boast-and-argument-of-an-ancient-roman-city-frozen-in-time-180987831/

question: The searing heat at Herculaneum saved things that almost never survive from ancient times, among them a round loaf of bread dug up in 1930, blackened and rock-hard but completely whole. What everyday detail is still baked into the 2,000-year-old loaf?
answer: Deep cuts splitting it into eight wedges
choices: Deep cuts splitting it into eight wedges
A crust studded with poppy seeds
A market ribbon knotted around it
context: The Herculaneum loaf survived scored into 8 wedges (a panis quadratus) and stamped with its baker's mark, naming the maker as a slave of Quintus Granius Verus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculaneum_loaf

question: Vesuvius's ash preserved thousands of messages that Pompeians had scratched around their town -- love notes, election jabs, and jokes that read like ancient social media. Tour guides today quote one of them more than any other, because its joke still lands 2,000 years later. Which real Pompeii scrawl is that famous line?
answer: A wall marveling it hasn't collapsed under so many scribbles
choices: A wall marveling it hasn't collapsed under so many scribbles
Successus the weaver's boast that he loves the barmaid Iris
Severus's taunt that Iris does not love his lovesick rival
A campaign smear that only petty thieves back a candidate
context: The full graffito, found scratched on several Pompeii walls, reads: 'I am amazed, O wall, that you have not collapsed, having to carry the tedious scribblings of so many writers.' It is an ancient complaint about graffiti -- written as graffiti. Other walls carry real scrawls just as lively: the weaver Successus and his rival Severus dueled over a barmaid named Iris ('you love Iris, but she does not love you'), and election notices claimed a rival was backed by the town's petty thieves. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/pompeiis-graffiti-captures-every-joke-boast-and-argument-of-an-ancient-roman-city-frozen-in-time-180987831/

question: About 300 people fled to the stone boat sheds on Herculaneum's ancient shoreline as Vesuvius erupted, crowding together in the hope of rescue by sea. Archaeologists found them nearly two thousand years later, still huddled side by side. What killed this crowd?
context: About 300 skeletons were found in Herculaneum's shoreline boat-house vaults, killed almost instantly by heat shock as they waited for rescue. One, the 'Ring Lady,' still wore rings on her finger bones and reached a 1984 National Geographic cover. Source: https://bomv.commons.gc.cuny.edu/the-ringed-lady/

question: One grand seaside mansion at Herculaneum is now called the Villa of the Papyri. It is thought to have belonged to Julius Caesar's father-in-law. It held about 1,800 papyrus scrolls that Vesuvius charred black. Why do scholars prize this find above nearly every other Roman one?
answer: The only library to survive intact from antiquity
choices: The only library to survive intact from antiquity
The oldest scrolls ever unearthed anywhere on Earth
The largest scroll collection in any museum today
The only ancient scrolls written in gold ink
context: The Villa of the Papyri, linked to Lucius Calpurnius Piso (Julius Caesar's father-in-law), held about 1,800 carbonized scrolls -- the only library to survive intact from the entire ancient world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculaneum

question: Those who first tried to open the Villa of the Papyri's blackened scrolls destroyed many of them, and for 250 years no one could read the ones still rolled shut. Beginning in 2023, the Vesuvius Challenge cracked the problem by studying scrolls that stayed tightly rolled. Which technology let the team see and read the hidden writing?
answer: High-energy X-ray scans read by AI
choices: High-energy X-ray scans read by AI
Infrared cameras aimed at the ink
Strong magnets pulling the ink out
context: The Vesuvius Challenge (launched March 2023 by Nat Friedman, Daniel Gross, and scientist Brent Seales) scanned the scrolls inside a particle accelerator at resolutions as fine as 4 micrometers, then trained AI to read them virtually -- never opening them. The carbon-based Roman ink was invisible on X-ray, so models learned to spot a faint 'crackle' texture it left, an idea sparked by contestant Casey Handmer. Source: https://scrollprize.org/grandprize

question: Charred black and rolled tight, the papyrus scrolls of Herculaneum's buried library are too fragile to open without crumbling to dust. In October 2023 Luke Farritor, a 21-year-old American computer-science student, read a single word sealed inside one of those unopened scrolls, the first ever recovered. What was that word?
context: Farritor, also a SpaceX intern, won the $40,000 First Word prize for reading 'porphyras' (Greek for 'purple') inside an unopened scroll. In February 2024 he and teammates Youssef Nader and Julian Schilliger won the $700,000 Grand Prize for recovering about 5% of a scroll -- a lost treatise on pleasure by the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus. Source: https://scrollprize.org/firstletters

question: More than 130,000 people crowded into the icy air of Potosí, high in the Bolivian Andes, around 1600, making it one of the biggest cities on Earth. The only reason anyone lived there was what miners dug from the cone-shaped mountain above. What was it?
context: Silver. The mountain was Cerro Rico ('Rich Hill'), and its silver made Potosi improbably huge: an account of 1603 counts at least 120,000 native Andeans, about 6,000 Spaniards and other Europeans and 5,000 Africans, making it one of the largest cities in the world at the time and one of the highest anywhere, at about 4,067 m (13,343 ft). Tradition credits a Quechua herder, Diego de Huallpa, with first finding the silver in 1545. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi.

question: Spanish speakers still use the name of a cold Bolivian mining city in a common saying, 'vale un Potosí', and Cervantes named the city in Don Quixote. When a Spanish speaker says a thing 'vale un Potosí', what does he mean?
choices: that it's not worth the bother
that it's worth the long wait
context: 'Worth a fortune.' So much silver poured out of Cerro Rico that Potosi's name became shorthand for staggering wealth across the Spanish-speaking world. In Don Quixote, Cervantes has a character say that even 'the mines of Potosi would be too little to pay you.' Source: historia.nationalgeographic.com.es (de donde viene la expresion 'valer un Potosi').

question: The mint of Potosí, the Casa de la Moneda, struck coins that circled the whole globe. Spanish treasure fleets carried them east across the Atlantic to Europe, and Manila galleons carried them west across the Pacific to Asia, until they were the closest thing the 1600s had to one world money. What nickname are these coins still known by?
context: 'Pieces of eight' -- the Spanish eight-real silver coin (real de a ocho), minted by the millions at Potosi and carried worldwide by the treasure fleets and the Manila Galleons until it was the era's global money. It survives as the famous cry of Long John Silver's parrot in Treasure Island. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potosi.

question: Spain's colonial rulers drove Andean highland communities into the mita, a forced labour draft, from 1574: each had to send about one in seven of its grown men down into Cerro Rico above Potosí. So many never came back up that the mountain earned a grim name. What did people call it?
choices: the mountain that buries the brave
the mountain that takes the young
context: 'The mountain that eats men' (el cerro que come hombres). After 1565 the ore was refined with mercury (the patio process), which slowly poisoned the workers underground. The colonial death toll was never recorded and is fiercely disputed -- estimates range from hundreds of thousands up to about 8 million, though that largest figure is sometimes applied to the whole Viceroyalty of Peru rather than Potosi alone. Sources: npr.org (Bolivia's Cerro Rico, 'the mountain that eats men'); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico.  (Legend.)

question: Miners have honeycombed Cerro Rico, the cone-shaped peak above Potosí, with more than 100 km of tunnels over five centuries. Surveyors who measure the mountain year after year report a startling change to its famous silhouette. What is happening to Cerro Rico itself?
answer: it is slowly losing height and wearing down
choices: it is slowly losing height and wearing down
it is tilting steadily toward one side
it is cracking apart into two peaks
it is spreading outward across its base
context: It is shrinking. So much rock has been pulled out that the summit keeps subsiding several centimeters a year, and estimates of total height lost run from about 250 m (leaving it near 4,753 m in 2025) to as much as 400 m -- one mining engineer predicts it may end up a flat-topped 'truncated cone.' The danger was formal enough that in 2014 UNESCO placed Potosi and Cerro Rico on its List of World Heritage in Danger. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico; news.mongabay.com (2025).

question: For some two hundred years miners hauled the metal that was Potosí's whole reason for being out of Cerro Rico, the peak above the city in the Bolivian Andes. Geologists can read the mountain's own stone to reconstruct how that metal first gathered there. How did it come to be sealed inside Cerro Rico?
answer: hot fluids rose through the cracks, cooled, and left the metal behind
choices: hot fluids rose through the cracks, cooled, and left the metal behind
ancient rivers washed metal grains down and buried them deep
a shallow sea dried away and left the metal in flat beds
a great meteorite struck and scattered metal through the rock
context: Hot, mineral-rich fluids. Cerro Rico is a polymetallic deposit of volcanic origin: superheated, mineral-laden water -- geologists call it hydrothermal, meaning 'hot-water-driven' -- circulated through fractures in the rock and, as it cooled over millions of years, crystallized out the silver, tin, lead and zinc. Those metal-filled cracks are what miners chase as 'ore veins.' The whole mineralized mass rises straight off the high Altiplano plateau. Source: metalorix.com (geology of Cerro Rico, Potosi).
