question: A crowd gathers on Prague's Old Town Square as the Astronomical Clock strikes the hour. A carved skeleton beside the dial rings his bell and tips his hourglass. Then a pair of windows swings open, and carved figures glide past in procession. Who are they?
context: The clockwork 'Walk of the Apostles' has drawn crowds on the hour for centuries. The skeleton is Death, who rings his bell and turns his hourglass to show time running out, while the two little windows reveal the Twelve Apostles gliding past two at a time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: The carved figures on Prague's Astronomical Clock finish their hourly round, and a gilded bird above the windows flaps its wings and gives a cry to end the show. It was added when the clock was repaired in the 1860s. What bird is it?
context: The gilded cockerel was added in an 1860s restoration; its cry closes the 'Walk of the Apostles' each hour, after which the crowd drifts away. A rooster announcing the hour echoes the bird's ancient role as herald of the dawn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: Each hour a carved skeleton, Death himself, rings his bell on Prague's Astronomical Clock. Three figures stand with him: Vanity with a mirror, a miser clutching his gold, and a turbaned figure for earthly pleasure. The three answer him with one gesture, as if not yet ready to follow. What do they do?
context: The four are the Orloj's carved vices: Vanity with his mirror, Greed the miser with his gold, Death the skeleton, and a turbaned Turk standing for earthly pleasure. When Death rings his bell and turns his glass, the other three shake their heads, as if refusing to follow him for one more hour. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: The clockmaker Mikuláš of Kadaň and the astronomer Jan Šindel made the Orloj, the Astronomical Clock on Prague's Old Town Square, and records first mention it in 1410. More than 600 years on, it holds one claim to fame among Europe's astronomical clocks. What is that claim?
answer: the oldest astronomical clock still running today
choices: the oldest astronomical clock still running today
the first astronomical clock ever built
the largest astronomical clock in the world
the most accurate astronomical clock ever made
context: The Orloj was built in 1410 by the clockmaker Mikulas of Kadan with Jan Sindel, an astronomy professor at Charles University. Older astronomical clocks were built before it, but all of them have stopped -- making Prague's the third-oldest ever constructed, yet the oldest one still keeping time. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: Inside the walls of Prague Castle runs a lane of tiny, candy-colored cottages with doorways so low a grown-up must stoop. They were built into the castle wall in the late 1500s for Emperor Rudolf II's guards. Later, craftsmen moved in, and their delicate trade gave the lane its name. Who were they?
context: Golden Lane (Zlata ulicka) began as cramped quarters for Rudolf II's castle guards in the late 1500s; goldsmiths later took over the cottages and gave the street its name. Centuries afterward the writer Franz Kafka spent about a year writing in cottage No. 22. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lane

question: Thirty blackened baroque statues of saints line Charles Bridge as it crosses the Vltava on sixteen stone arches. Tourists file past most of them but crowd around a single bronze plaque at the foot of one statue, rubbing it smooth. Local tradition promises all who touch that plaque one particular reward. What does the tradition promise?
answer: that they will return to Prague someday
choices: that they will find their true love
that they will return to Prague someday
that they will be safe from drowning
that they will never go hungry
context: The statue is St John of Nepomuk, and rubbing the bronze relief below it is said to ensure the visitor's return to Prague (some say it also grants a wish). His statue, placed in 1683, is the oldest of the thirty on Charles Bridge. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bridge  (Legend.)

question: Whole Bohemian villages sent cartloads of one surprising kitchen item to Prague, a legend says, while Charles Bridge rose across the Vltava in the 1300s. The master builders, the story goes, mixed it into their mortar to harden it. What was it?
context: The legend is rich with detail: the town of Velvary is said to have boiled its eggs so they wouldn't smash on the road, and one village reportedly sent a wagon of cheese by mistake. Is it true? A 2008 Czech chemistry-institute test of the old mortar found protein traces that fit the tale, but a 2010 Charles University study found no organic additive -- so the egg legend is one that lab evidence only partly backs. Source: https://prague-now.com/history/charles-bridge-built-with-a-curve-and-with-egg/

question: Master Hanuš, as one of Prague's most famous legends tells it, built the Astronomical Clock on the Old Town Square, and the town councillors feared he would build an even finer one for a rival city. So, the story goes, they made sure he never could. Historians say it never happened. What does the legend say they did to him?
choices: they threw him in the river
context: The blinding of Master Hanus is Prague's most beloved clock legend: the tale says the councillors blinded him so he could never repeat his masterpiece, and that the ruined clockmaker climbed the tower and thrust his hand into the gears to stop the clock forever. In truth the Orloj was built in 1410 by Mikulas of Kadan with the scholar Jan Sindel; Hanus was a real later clockmaker who came to no such harm. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_astronomical_clock

question: King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia had the priest John of Nepomuk bound and hurled from Charles Bridge into the Vltava in 1393, legend says because John refused to reveal what the queen had told him in confession. He drowned and was later made a saint. In art, one halo sets St John of Nepomuk apart from every other saint. What does his halo contain?
context: The five stars recall the legend that five lights appeared on the Vltava where John of Nepomuk drowned in 1393, on the order of King Wenceslaus IV. His 1683 bronze is the oldest statue on Charles Bridge, and touching the plaque beneath it is said to bring a visitor back to Prague. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Nepomuk

question: Behind one door in St Vitus Cathedral, inside Prague Castle, lie the Crown Jewels of Bohemia, the golden crown of St Wenceslas among them. The cathedral also holds the tombs of the Bohemian kings, but it guards the jewels far more closely: the door was built so that no single official, not even a king acting alone, could ever open it. What secures it?
answer: seven locks, their seven keys split among seven guardians
choices: seven locks, their seven keys split among seven guardians
two locks, one key held by the king and one by the archbishop
three locks, opened only when the three chief lords of Bohemia agree
five locks, their keys shared among the cathedral's canons
context: The Crown Jewels of Bohemia -- including the crown of St Wenceslas, made in 1347 -- rest in a chamber inside St Vitus Cathedral behind a door with seven separate locks. Seven keys are held by seven different people (among them the president, the prime minister, and the Archbishop of Prague), and all seven must gather in person before the door can be opened. The cathedral, begun in 1344 under Charles IV and not consecrated until 1929, also glows with an Art Nouveau stained-glass window designed by the Czech painter Alfons Mucha. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vitus_Cathedral

question: Bohemian kings, Holy Roman emperors and, to this day, the Czech president have made their seat at Prague Castle, its palaces, gardens and cathedral towers crowning the hill above the Vltava. Guinness World Records credits the castle with one worldwide record. What record does it hold?
answer: the largest ancient castle complex in the world
choices: the largest ancient castle complex in the world
the oldest stone castle in the world
the tallest castle towers in the world
the most-visited castle in the world
context: Prague Castle sprawls over roughly 70,000 square metres -- about 570 metres long and 130 wide -- which earns it a place in Guinness World Records as the largest ancient castle complex in the world. Founded around 880, it is still the official residence of the Czech president. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Castle

question: A crowd of furious Bohemian Protestants stormed into Prague Castle on 23 May 1618, seized two Catholic royal officials and their secretary, and threw all three out of a high window, a drop of some 21 metres. Not one of them died. Catholics cried that angels had caught them, but the Protestants scoffed that something far humbler had broken their fall. What did the Protestants say saved them?
context: The 1618 Defenestration of Prague hurled two imperial regents -- Jaroslav Borita of Martinice and Vilem Slavata of Chlum -- and their secretary Philip Fabricius from a Prague Castle window; all three survived the ~21 m fall by landing in the refuse heaped in the moat below. The quarrel helped ignite the Thirty Years' War, and the lucky secretary was later ennobled as 'Baron von Hohenfall' -- Baron of Highfall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defenestrations_of_Prague  (Legend.)

question: Prambanan's tall Hindu towers rise from a plain in central Java. Less than an hour's drive across the same plain stands their great Buddhist neighbour: no spire, but a vast, low, terraced mound crowned with rings of bell-shaped stupas. What is it called?
context: The two masterpieces are near-contemporaries on the same plain: Borobudur, the broad Buddhist mandala, and Prambanan, whose central Hindu tower stabs 47 metres (about 154 ft) straight up -- the tallest Hindu temple in Indonesia. Prambanan was built around 850 CE and dedicated in 856 CE under King Rakai Pikatan, and the two colossal temples rose within about a century of each other on the same fertile volcanic plain. Prambanan is the largest Hindu temple site in the country and the second-largest in all Southeast Asia, after Angkor Wat in Cambodia. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan

question: Prince Bandung Bondowoso could wed Princess Roro Jonggrang, a Javanese legend says, only if he raised a thousand temples at Prambanan in a single night. His ghost-workers had finished 999 when the unwilling princess tricked them into fleeing before dawn. What did the furious prince do to her?
context: The tale of Roro Jonggrang ('slender virgin') is folklore, not history. In the legend, the prince Bandung Bondowoso -- having killed her father, King Boko -- was told he could marry the princess only by building a thousand temples in one night; with summoned spirits he raised 999, but Roro Jonggrang lit fires and had her maids pound rice in the east to counterfeit the dawn. The roosters crowed, the spirits fled, and the enraged prince cursed her into stone as the missing final statue. Tradition still points to the statue of Durga slaying the buffalo demon, in the Shiva temple's north chamber, and calls it Rara Jonggrang -- the very princess turned to stone. The tale grew up to explain Prambanan's many small shrines and that famous image. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rara_Jonggrang

question: Prambanan's three tallest towers stand in a row, and the middle spire soars above the two beside it. It is dedicated to the Hindu god of destruction and rebirth, the cosmic dancer whose steps whirl the universe into being and out again. Which god does that great middle tower belong to?
context: The three tall central temples honor the Hindu Trimurti: the 47-metre central tower belongs to Shiva the destroyer, flanked by shorter temples for Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver, each about 33 metres tall. The whole compound was raised around 850 CE by the Hindu Mataram (Sanjaya) dynasty, begun by Rakai Pikatan and dedicated to Shiva -- its original Sanskrit name was Shivagrha, 'House of Shiva,' recorded in the Shivagrha inscription of 856 CE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan

question: Along the inner walls of Prambanan's main temple, the carved stone unfolds panel by panel into one of Hinduism's greatest stories: a virtuous prince whose bride is snatched away by a ten-headed demon-king. Then comes the long war to win her back, fought beside an army of monkeys and their leaping, flying general. Which tale is it?
context: Panel after panel along the inner balustrades follows the Ramayana: Princess Sita, carried off by the demon-king Ravana, and her rescue by Prince Rama with the help of Hanuman and his monkey army. The epic still comes alive at Prambanan today -- performed as an open-air ballet on full-moon nights beneath the towers. Prambanan was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan

question: Walkers stroll around Quebec City's old town on top of its stone ramparts, about 4.6 km of them, passing great gates, with the St. Lawrence far below. Among all the towns north of Mexico, what record do those walls give Quebec?
answer: the only town still ringed by walls
choices: the only town still ringed by walls
the oldest walled town on the continent
the first town Europeans fortified here
the biggest town the French ever built
context: Old Quebec is the only intact fortified colonial town in North America north of Mexico — about 4.6 km of ramparts that visitors can walk atop, pierced by old gates. Most walled cities elsewhere pulled their walls down for traffic; Quebec's survived, and in 1985 UNESCO named the old town a World Heritage Site. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ramparts of Quebec City' / 'Old Quebec.'

question: Long before any French fort stood on the cliff above the St. Lawrence, Algonquin people had a word for that exact spot on the great river: kebec. Quebec City still carries the name. What does kebec mean?
choices: where the cliff meets the water
context: 'Kebec' is Algonquin for 'where the river narrows.' Just below the city the wide St. Lawrence squeezes tight against the cliffs — so whoever held the high rock commanded the water gateway to the whole interior of the continent. Champlain planted his 1608 settlement on exactly that chokepoint. Source: Wikipedia, 'Quebec'; Musee de la civilisation, Trousse Premiers Peuples.

question: Jacques Cartier scrambled up the great cliff above the St. Lawrence, spotted stones glittering in the rock and was sure he had struck it rich. He named the cliff Cap Diamant, or Cape Diamond, and the name stuck. When the glittering diamonds were examined, what did they turn out to be?
context: Cartier's 'diamonds' were only quartz — the blunder gave French the old phrase 'faux comme un diamant du Canada' ('false as a Canadian diamond'). But the name held: Cap Diamant, the cliff rising about 100 m straight out of the St. Lawrence, still crowns Quebec City, a natural fortress that decided where the town would stand. Source: Britannica, 'Cape Diamond'; Wikipedia, 'Cap Diamant.'

question: Soldiers still man the Citadelle on the cliff above Quebec City, and a cannon booms from its walls each noon. It is a star fort: its ramparts jut out into sharp angled points called bastions instead of running in plain straight walls. What did those angled points let defenders do to anyone attacking a wall?
answer: catch them in crossfire from two sides
choices: catch them in crossfire from two sides
pour boiling oil straight down on them
keep the cannon hidden from their view
flood the ditch below with river water
context: The Citadelle is the largest British-built fortress in North America — four bastions and three straight curtain walls set at angles so every stretch of wall could be swept by fire from the bastions on either side, leaving attackers no blind approach. It is still an active army base, home of the Royal 22e Regiment (the 'Van Doos') since 1920, and a cannon still booms from it every day at noon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Citadelle of Quebec.'

question: One building rears over Quebec City's old town like a medieval castle — turrets, steep copper roofs, perched on the cliff edge above the river. Yet the Chateau Frontenac has always been a hotel, opened to its first guests in 1893. Who built this fairy-tale castle?
context: The Chateau Frontenac was raised by the Canadian Pacific Railway, which opened it in 1893 to lure travelers onto its trains — a 'castle' built to sell railway tickets. It holds a Guinness World Record as the most photographed hotel on Earth, and takes its name from Louis de Buade, Count of Frontenac, the governor who defended New France against British and Iroquois attacks in the 1690s. Source: Britannica, 'Chateau Frontenac'; WorldAtlas.

question: The British soldiers marched out of Quebec City in the 1870s, and many townsfolk wanted the old stone walls and gates gone: they choked the traffic and seemed a useless relic. The ramparts were nearly torn down for good. Why do they still stand?
answer: the Governor General intervened to save them
choices: the Governor General intervened to save them
a sudden war made the walls needed again
the demolition crews hit bedrock and gave up
the walls proved too costly to tear down
context: The walls standing today are the masonry ramparts an engineer, Gaspard-Joseph Chaussegros de Lery, raised in 1745. When the British garrison left in 1871, Quebec began demolishing them for road traffic, until Lord Dufferin, Governor General from 1872, intervened, even having grand new gates built in the late 1870s, so the fortifications would survive. That rescue is why Old Quebec is a walled city at all. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ramparts of Quebec City'; ville.quebec.qc.ca (history 1867-1945).

question: Westerly winds off the Pacific pour rain on southern Chile, then crash into the tall Andes. On the far side of the mountains almost no rain falls, and a desert spreads out even close to the sea. What is this South American desert called?
context: Argentine Patagonia is a COLD winter desert -- average temperatures near 3 C with frequent frost -- and the largest desert in Argentina (about 673,000 sq km, roughly the 8th-largest on Earth). The Andes block the westerly Pacific winds so completely that much of it stays arid within about 200 miles of the sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patagonian_Desert

question: Wet Pacific wind blows east across Washington State until it slams into the Cascade Range, which forces it up the western slope. By the time the air spills down the far side, almost all its water is gone. What happens to that water on the climb?
answer: it cools as it rises, condenses, and falls as rain there
choices: it cools as it rises, condenses, and falls as rain there
the warm air sinking down the far side dries it back out
the peaks block the clouds and scrape them off the wind
the thin summit air simply lets the water escape upward
context: This is the heart of every rain shadow: moist air forced up the windward slope expands and cools, its vapour condenses, and it falls as rain on that side -- so the air clears the crest already 'wrung dry,' leaving desert behind the mountains. Western Washington soaks under Pacific rain on the Cascades' windward flank, while the Columbia Basin just east lies in their dry shadow. The common misconception is that the far side is dry because the sinking air warms; the real cause is that the rain already fell on the way up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow

question: Trade-wind rain soaks Mount Waialeale on Kauai, in Hawaii, almost every day, and its 11,000 mm a year make it one of the wettest spots on Earth. Yet a sunny town just 15 miles off, on the dry side of the mountain, gets only 20 inches a year. Which town is it?
context: Mount Waialeale's summit sees rain on about 289 days a year and averages roughly 11,430 mm (450 in) -- a record 666 inches fell in 1982. Yet leeward Waimea, only about 15 miles away on the same island, averages just ~20 inches. The wettest and driest places on Kauai almost touch. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Wai%CA%BBale%CA%BBale

question: New Zealand's Southern Alps stand broadside to the roaring westerlies off the Tasman Sea. On the West Coast the rain pours down, up to 15 metres a year near the mountain spine, feeding dense temperate rainforest. Barely 30 km east of the crest, on the sheltered side, the yearly rain collapses about fifteen-fold to a single metre. Which region there is the driest, brownest land in the country?
context: The Southern Alps meet the prevailing westerlies head-on. The West Coast drinks up to ~15,000 mm of rain a year near the Main Divide (coastal towns ~3,000 mm), but only about 30 km east of the crest rainfall collapses to roughly 1,000 mm -- a near fifteen-fold drop -- making Central Otago the driest land in New Zealand. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Alps

question: Winter rain off the Mediterranean turns the hills around Jerusalem green, about 600 mm a year on the ridge where the city sits. A few miles east, down the ridge's dry lee side, the total falls to barely 100 mm, and the green vanishes into bare, folded land plunging toward the Dead Sea. Which desert lies there?
context: The Judaean Desert lies in the rain shadow of the hills of Jerusalem, immediately east of the city. Rainfall drops from about 600 mm on the western, Mediterranean-facing side to roughly 100 mm in the east, where the land falls steeply to the Dead Sea -- a full desert only a few miles from the green coast. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaean_Desert

question: A Kingston DJ in the 1950s would haul big speaker stacks into a dirt yard and throw an all-night dance. By the mid-1950s the best of them drew bigger crowds than any live band. What did Jamaicans call the whole rig, speakers and crew?
context: The Jamaican 'sound system' — a mobile DJ outfit of huge speaker stacks and a generator — was the engine of the island's whole music culture, and the men who ran the biggest ones became stars. The first great commercial system belonged to Chinese-Jamaican businessman Tom Wong ('Tom the Great Sebastian'); rivals like Duke Reid and Coxsone Dodd battled for the loudest bass and the rarest records. Every genre that followed — ska, rocksteady, reggae, dub — was built to be played on these speakers. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sound system (Jamaican).'

question: Kingston bands sped up American rhythm-and-blues records and flipped the guitar onto the off-beat, a springy up-stroke, as Jamaica was winning its independence around 1962. Ernest Ranglin, a guitarist, said that American rhythm and blues goes "chink-ka," but the Kingston sound goes "ka-chink." What was this bouncy new style called?
context: Ska was Jamaica's first homegrown pop genre — jumpy and brass-driven, born of American R&B sped up and flipped onto the off-beat. Its greatest band, the Skatalites, cut hard instrumental hits like 'Guns of Navarone,' while independence-year anthems such as Derrick Morgan's 'Forward March' (1962) caught the mood of a nation just cutting free from Britain. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ska.'

question: Kingston sweltered through a heat wave in the summer of 1966, and ska, the island's fast, brassy dance music, felt too jumpy to bear. Bands in Kingston's tiny studios slowed the tempo into a cool, easy sway, and at that lazy pace the electric bass stepped out front. What was the slower new sound called?
context: Rocksteady took its name from Alton Ellis's 1966 hit 'Rock Steady,' and bandleader Lynn Taitt summed it up: 'Rocksteady is really slow ska.' It lasted barely two years, but by slowing everything down it handed the spotlight to the bass — the deep, rolling foundation that reggae would soon build its entire sound upon. Source: Wikipedia, 'Rocksteady.'

question: One poor Kingston neighborhood, its houses built from scrap wood and rubble, turned out a lineup of music stars in the 1960s. Bob Marley, Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer of the Wailers all grew up there, and from its cramped housing yards reggae went out to the world. What is this Kingston district called?
context: Trench Town, a poor Kingston neighborhood built of timber-and-rubble 'knog' housing, was the cradle of reggae — home also to Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, and Toots. Bob Marley immortalized it in 'No Woman No Cry' (1974), singing of sitting 'in the government yard in Trenchtown,' the real public-housing yard on First Street where he grew up. In 2018, UNESCO honored the reggae music of Jamaica as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, praising its voice on 'injustice, resistance, love and humanity.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Trench Town'; UNESCO (2018).

question: Clement Dodd, known to everyone in Kingston as Coxsone, ran a hit factory on Brentford Road that fans called the Motown of Jamaica. It launched Bob Marley and the Wailers, Toots and the Maytals, Burning Spear and the Skatalites. What was Coxsone Dodd's music house called?
context: Studio One was the beating heart of Jamaican recording — its house band and back catalogue shaped ska, rocksteady, and reggae, and its old rhythms are still sampled around the world. Coxsone Dodd's chief rivals each had a legendary room of their own, among them Lee 'Scratch' Perry's backyard Black Ark studio, built in 1973. Source: Wikipedia, 'Studio One (record label).'

question: In his small Kingston studio, a radio fixer named Osbourne Ruddock, known as King Tubby, took finished reggae records and wiped the vocals off them. Then he rebuilt the bare bass and drums into spacey, echo-soaked tracks, the far ancestors of every modern remix. What Jamaican style did King Tubby help invent?
context: Dub — Jamaica's gift to the age of the remix — reportedly began by accident in 1968, when engineer Byron Smith left the vocals off a pressing of the Paragons' 'On the Beach' and the dance crowd went wild for the bare instrumental. King Tubby made dub an art, 'playing' his 12-channel mixing desk like an instrument in his tiny Waterhouse studio, riding echo and faders live. He was shot dead outside his Kingston home in 1989. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dub music' and 'King Tubby.'  (Legend.)

question: At Kingston's sound-system dances, the DJs stopped just spinning discs: they grabbed the microphone and rode the beat with their voices, trading rhymes live over the bare track. Singles of the late 1960s carried that track on the flip side, an instrumental version with only the riddim left. Count Machuki and U-Roy made it an art many historians call an ancestor of rap. What was this vocal style called?
context: Toasting — the Jamaican DJ chanting rhythmically over an instrumental 'version' — is widely seen as one ancestor of rap. Its pioneers, Count Machuki and U-Roy, grabbed the mic at sound-system dances and 'chatted' over the bare riddims, turning the DJ from a record-spinner into a star performer in his own right. Source: Wikipedia, 'Toasting (Jamaican music).'

question: Wayne Smith, a Kingston teenager, and Noel Davey, a keyboardist, hit the rock preset on a cheap Casio keyboard in 1985. King Jammy, the producer, polished it into the Sleng Teng riddim, the first Jamaican beat made wholly by machine, and its robotic bassline turned up on about 500 records. What all-electronic era of Jamaican music did it open?
context: Here is the twist: the 'Sleng Teng' bassline that reshaped Jamaican music wasn't written in Kingston at all. It was a factory preset built in 1980 by a young Casio engineer in Japan, Hiroko Okuda, who had studied reggae for her thesis. She only learned years later that her little demo tune had sparked a whole genre — and was amazed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sleng Teng.'

question: Ships sailing into Reykjavik's harbour on Iceland's southwest coast see snowy mountains just behind the town. The city stands at roughly 64 degrees north latitude, a short hop south of the Arctic Circle. Among the world's capitals, what record does that far-north spot earn Reykjavik?
answer: the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign country
choices: the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign country
the coldest capital of any country on Earth
the world's only capital inside the Arctic Circle
the world's northernmost city of any kind
context: Reykjavik sits at 64 degrees 08' north. Nuuk, the capital of Greenland, actually lies a touch farther north at 64 degrees 10' N -- but Greenland is a self-governing territory of Denmark, not a sovereign state, so Reykjavik keeps the title of northernmost capital of a fully independent country. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: Nearly every home in Reykjavik, on the volcanic island of Iceland, stays warm and snug through the long, dark winter, yet the city burns almost no oil or coal, and its winter air stays clean and clear. What heats the city instead?
answer: naturally hot water piped up from volcanic rock
choices: naturally hot water piped up from volcanic rock
rooftop solar panels across the city
heat pumps drawing warmth from the sea
context: Naturally hot water is pumped from volcanic rock and run through a district-heating network that warms nearly all of Reykjavik's buildings; about 90% of Iceland's homes are heated this way. Because the city burns almost no fuel for heat, greenhouse-gas emissions from space heating in the Reykjavik area fell from around 270,000 tonnes a year in 1960 to roughly 12,000 tonnes today. Iceland's first geothermal district-heating system opened in 1930, warming a school, a hospital, a pool and about 60 homes. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geothermal_power_in_Iceland ; https://web.mit.edu/nature/archive/student_projects/2009/bjorn627/TheGeothermalCity/Reykjavik.html

question: Norse settlers rowed into a bay on Iceland's southwest coast around the year 874 and saw pale plumes rising from the ground, steam venting from hot springs. They named the place for what they took the plumes to be, joined to their word for a bay. What does the name Reykjavik mean?
context: In Old Norse, reykr means 'smoke' and vik means 'bay,' so Reykjavik is 'Smoky Bay.' The settlers took the steam drifting off the hot springs for smoke and named their new home for it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: Gudjon Samuelsson designed Hallgrimskirkja, the tall pale church rising above Reykjavik's low houses, in the 20th century. He shaped it to echo one of Iceland's most famous natural rock forms, born of the island's fiery volcanic past. Which form did he copy?
choices: jagged fields of black volcanic ash
context: Basalt is the dark volcanic rock that covers much of Iceland; when a thick lava flow cools slowly it cracks into tall, many-sided (often hexagonal) columns, like those seen behind the Svartifoss waterfall. Gudjon Samuelsson drew Hallgrimskirkja's stepped, upward-sweeping shape from those columns. Designed in 1937 and built from 1945 to 1986, the church stands 74.5 m (244 ft) tall -- the tallest in Iceland. Source: https://guidetoiceland.is/travel-iceland/drive/hallgrimskirkja

question: Winter comes to Reykjavik, close to the Arctic Circle at the top of the world, yet the city seldom gets colder than minus 15 C and is sometimes milder than cities hundreds of miles farther south. What keeps this far-north capital so mild?
answer: the warm Atlantic Ocean current along its coast
choices: the warm Atlantic Ocean current along its coast
heat rising from Iceland's volcanoes and lava fields
tall mountains that block the cold Arctic winds
warm winds blowing up from mainland Europe
context: The warm water of the North Atlantic (an arm of the Gulf Stream system) washes Iceland's coast and keeps Reykjavik's winters mild -- rarely below minus 15 degrees C, sometimes milder than places far to its south. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk

question: A Portuguese fleet sailed into a bay on Brazil's coast on 1 January 1502, the traditional story goes, and named the place Rio de Janeiro, River of January. No river flows there. By that old story, why did they call it a river?
answer: Explorers mistook the wide bay for a river mouth
choices: Explorers mistook the wide bay for a river mouth
Mapmakers copied a mislabelled older chart
Settlers named it for a river back in Portugal
context: By the traditional account, a Portuguese fleet -- usually credited to Gaspar de Lemos and Goncalo Coelho -- sailed into the huge bay on 1 January 1502 and took its narrow, cliff-flanked entrance for the mouth of a great river, naming the spot 'River of January' for the month. There is no river: Rio in fact curls around a bay, Guanabara Bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro  (Legend.)

question: Arms flung open 28 metres wide, a 30-metre figure of pale soapstone has watched over Rio since 1931 from the 700-metre granite peak of Corcovado. In a worldwide vote in 2007 it was named one of the New Seven Wonders. Which monument is this?
context: Christ the Redeemer (Cristo Redentor) is 30 m tall with arms 28 m wide on an 8 m pedestal, built of reinforced concrete faced in pale soapstone atop the 700 m peak of Corcovado, and inaugurated on 12 October 1931 after nine years' work. On 7 July 2007 it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_the_Redeemer_(statue)

question: The bare granite peak at the mouth of Rio's bay reminded Portuguese traders of something from their sugar trade: sugar cooked down and poured into moulds to harden as blocks of one shape. So they named the peak Pao de Acucar, Sugarloaf. What shape was the block?
context: Refined sugar in that era was boiled down and molded into a tall cone -- a 'sugarloaf' -- for storage and shipping. Portuguese traders thought the bare 396 m granite dome at the bay's mouth looked just like one, so they named it Pao de Acucar; in English, Sugarloaf Mountain. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarloaf_Mountain

question: Coffee plantations stripped the slopes of Rio's inner mountains bare in the 1800s, and the springs feeding the city were drying up. Today the Tijuca Forest, one of the largest forests inside any city on Earth, covers those slopes and looks like untouched jungle. From 1861, on the orders of Emperor Pedro II, the rainforest was brought back. How was it restored?
answer: it was replanted by hand, tree by tree
choices: it was replanted by hand, tree by tree
it grew back on its own once farming stopped
it was seeded from aircraft after a fire
it was transplanted whole from the Amazon
context: The Tijuca Forest (~3,958 hectares) is one of the world's largest urban forests -- and hand-made. After coffee plantations stripped the slopes and choked the streams supplying Rio, Emperor Pedro II placed the land under federal control in 1861 and ordered it replanted, overseen by Major Manuel Gomes Archer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tijuca_Forest

question: Workers set more than 100,000 trees into the slopes of Rio's Tijuca Forest between 1861 and 1887, slopes that coffee plantations had scraped down to bare dirt. So big a planting sounds like a job for an army of foresters, yet records credit most of that quarter-century of work to a startlingly small crew. How many of them did the bulk of it?
context: Records credit most of that quarter-century of planting to just six enslaved workers -- Eleuterio, Constantino, Manuel, Mateus, Leopoldo, and Maria -- who set out more than 100,000 trees between 1861 and 1887, growing back an entire forest tree by tree under Major Manuel Gomes Archer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tijuca_Forest

question: A great statue stands with its arms flung wide on an exposed 700-metre peak above Rio, and the city's fierce summer storms batter it. In February 2008 its head, eyebrows and fingers were chipped, and in 2014 a fingertip broke clean off. Which storm hazard keeps scarring it?
context: Because it crowns an exposed ~700 m peak with its arms flung wide, Christ the Redeemer is struck by lightning often. A February 2008 strike chipped the head, eyebrows, and fingers; a 2014 strike broke off a fingertip. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_the_Redeemer_(statue)

question: Many of Rio's favelas cling to steep granite slopes, and in a heavy summer downpour their thin soil soaks through until whole hillsides give way. In the mountains north of Rio, landslides killed more than 900 people in 2011, a year after another disaster, and the city then rolled out a safeguard across its most exposed hillside favelas. What did it install?
context: In January 2011, extreme rain in the mountains north of Rio set off thousands of landslides that killed well over 900 people -- among the deadliest natural disasters in Brazil's history; an April 2010 downpour of 288 mm in 24 hours had already triggered some 300 slides. Rio responded by installing 'Sirenes Cariocas' -- sirens that sound in hillside favelas when rainfall reaches dangerous levels. Source: rioonwatch.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_2010_Rio_de_Janeiro_floods_and_mudslides

question: The Nile met the Mediterranean through seven mouths in the age of the pharaohs, and Greek writers named them one by one: the Pelusiac branch in the east, the Canopic in the west and five more. Over the last two thousand years, river silt and modern flood-control dams have sealed the small branches off. How many of the seven still carry the Nile to the sea today?
context: Only two flowing branches survive: the Rosetta and the Damietta, which give the delta its two great arms. The others — the Pelusiac, the Canopic, the Sebennytic and more — silted up or were closed by flood management. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile_Delta

question: Long sandbars and islands slice the mouth of the Ganges and the Brahmaputra into a branching maze. A delta's shape is decided by a three-way tug-of-war: when the river's mud wins it pokes out long fingers like the Mississippi's, and when the sea's waves win they smooth a curved fan like the Nile's. Which third force carves this maze?
context: Geographers sort deltas by which of three forces wins: river (fluvial), wave, or tidal. Tide-dominated deltas like the Ganges-Brahmaputra get combed into long, finger-like sandbars aligned with the rise and fall of the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_delta

question: The Ganges and the Brahmaputra, two of Asia's biggest rivers, join and dump so much Himalayan mud and rock into the sea that they build the largest river delta on the planet. More than 250 million people live on this green lowland. What is this delta called?
context: The Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna together build the Bengal (or Ganges-Brahmaputra) delta — over 105,000 km² across Bangladesh and India's West Bengal, the largest and most populous delta on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganges_Delta  (Legend.)

question: In the far north of Siberia, the Lena River ends a 2,700-mile journey from the mountains of the south by fanning out over the frozen tundra of Yakutia into the icy Laptev Sea. Its many mouths build the greatest delta in the Arctic, a low, marshy fan nearly 250 miles wide, where winter and summer are two different worlds. What happens to this delta over a single year?
answer: It lies frozen as hard tundra through the long winter, then thaws into a lush green wetland each summer.
choices: It lies frozen as hard tundra through the long winter, then thaws into a lush green wetland each summer.
It stays locked beneath solid ice all year, never thawing even at the height of summer.
Its channels dry to cracked mud through the rainless season, then refill when the snowmelt returns.
It vanishes under deep snowdrifts each winter, then reappears as bare gravel flats in the short summer.
context: The Lena builds the largest delta in the Arctic, fanning about 400 km (250 mi) wide into the Laptev Sea off Siberia's north coast. It lies frozen as tundra for roughly seven months a year, then bursts into a lush wetland for a few short summer months when the thaw floods across its islands. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_Delta

question: Upstream dams have cut the Mississippi's load of fresh mud nearly in half, and levees wall the river off from its own marshes, so its starved delta is sinking and drowning, handing coastal Louisiana back to the Gulf of Mexico. A delta only grows while its river keeps feeding it. At its worst, the coast was vanishing at a rate people described as losing how much?
context: USGS measured coastal Louisiana shrinking by about 2,006 square miles (5,197 km²) between 1932 and 2016. At its worst that was a football field of wetland lost every 34 minutes; even at slower recent rates it is roughly one every 100 minutes. Source: https://www.usgs.gov/news/national-news-release/usgs-louisianas-rate-coastal-wetland-loss-continues-slow  (Legend.)

question: About 50,000 fans poured into Rome's Colosseum through 80 arched entrances in its outer wall. Above every arch the Romans carved the same kind of marking. What did they carve above each one?
context: Each of the 80 entrances was carved with a number (I to LXXX); spectators' tickets sent them to the right numbered arch and straight to their seats — crowd control that works exactly like a modern stadium. Capacity estimates range from about 50,000 to 80,000. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum

question: The official Appius Claudius Caecus began the Via Appia in 312 BC, the first of Rome's great paved highways, running dead straight south out of the city on tightly fitted blocks of volcanic stone that walkers still tread today. So prized was the road that the Romans gave it a grand royal nickname. What did they call the Via Appia?
context: Its Latin nickname was regina viarum, 'the queen of roads.' Its polygonal lava paving stones can still be walked about 2,300 years later. The road first ran ~212 km from Rome to Capua and was later extended to the port of Brundisium (modern Brindisi). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian_Way  (Legend.)

question: Roman harbours and sea walls have stood in salt water for 2,000 years, and modern scientists traced that strength to one special ingredient the Romans dug from the ground near Pozzuoli, on the Bay of Naples. Mixed with lime and water it forms a mineral glue so tough it even sets hard underwater. What was this key ingredient?
context: The ash is called pozzolana, after Pozzuoli near Naples; blended with lime it makes a hydraulic cement that hardens even underwater, which is why Roman marine concrete has lasted 2,000 years in the sea. Source: https://www.sciencealert.com/we-finally-know-why-ancient-roman-concrete-lasts-thousands-of-years

question: Admir Masic, leading a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2023, traced the 2,000-year endurance of Roman concrete to tiny white flecks of lime scattered through the ancient mix. Those flecks give it one remarkable ability that modern concrete lacks. What can it do?
context: The lime flecks (lime clasts) form when the Romans 'hot-mixed' the concrete with reactive quicklime. When water seeps into a crack, the flecks dissolve and re-crystallize as calcium carbonate, gluing the crack shut before it can spread. In the MIT test (led by Prof. Admir Masic), cracked hot-mixed concrete sealed itself within two weeks, while concrete made without quicklime did not heal. Source: https://news.mit.edu/2023/roman-concrete-durability-lime-casts-0106  (Legend.)

question: Rome's aqueducts carried water for tens of miles into the city with no pumps — just a channel sloping gently downhill the whole way, so gently that too little tilt would leave the water stalled and stagnant. The Roman writer Vitruvius even set a rule for the least slope a channel could have. Over each kilometre of its long run, how far did a typical aqueduct actually drop?
context: The channels ran gently downhill the entire way, often dropping just a few centimetres over a whole kilometre. The Roman engineer Vitruvius advised a minimum tilt of about 1 in 4,800 (roughly 20 cm per kilometre). With no pumps anywhere on the route, that barely-there slope still moved water for tens of miles across arches and through tunnels into Rome. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Roman_aqueduct

question: Tarquinius Priscus, an Etruscan king of early Rome, ordered a great stone drain in the 6th century BC to carry a swampy hollow's water into the Tiber, long before Rome had an empire. The hollow later became the Forum. The drain is the Cloaca Maxima, the Greatest Sewer. What is most remarkable about it?
answer: it is still in use today
choices: it is still in use today
it was rebuilt three times over
it now carries a subway line
context: Begun under the Etruscan king Tarquinius Priscus in the 6th century BC, the Cloaca Maxima still carries rainwater down to the Tiber roughly 2,500 years later — one of the world's oldest sewers still in use. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloaca_Maxima  (Legend.)

question: The Rapa Nui people of Easter Island, a speck of land with 2,000 miles of ocean on every side, set up the giant stone moai and carved rows of tiny signs, rongorongo, onto wooden tablets. What is rongorongo's place in the whole story of writing?
answer: The only script ever invented anywhere in the Pacific
choices: The only script ever invented anywhere in the Pacific
The oldest writing system in the world
The largest writing system, with thousands of signs
The fastest writing ever to spread worldwide
context: Across the thousands of islands of Oceania, only Rapa Nui developed a glyph-script of its own -- which is why rongorongo is so often called the only writing ever invented anywhere in the Pacific. Scholars still debate whether it is true writing or a proto-writing 'memory aid' for chants, so its exact status is unsettled. Roughly 600 distinct signs are known: stylized people, plants, and seabirds like the frigatebird, most carved into Pacific rosewood. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo.  (Legend.)

question: A reader of rongorongo, the tiny glyph-script of Easter Island, begins at the bottom-left corner of a wooden tablet and reads one line straight across. Scholars call the style reverse boustrophedon. To read the very next line, what must he do?
answer: Flip the whole tablet upside down
choices: Flip the whole tablet upside down
Read the next line from right to left
Turn it over to read the back face
Rotate it a quarter-turn and read down
context: In reverse boustrophedon, every other line is carved upside down, so a reader flips the tablet a full 180 degrees at the end of each line and reads on. The glyphs stand only about a centimetre tall. The longest surviving text, the 'Santiago Staff,' carries roughly 2,920 of them; the Mamari tablet seems to hold a lunar calendar -- one of the very few passages scholars have even tentatively identified. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo.

question: Peruvian slave raiders carried off Easter Island's trained tablet-chanters in 1862, and an islander told Bishop Jaussen afterwards that nobody remained who could read the rongorongo signs. Scholars learned to read Egyptian hieroglyphs and the Maya script again after both fell silent. Where does rongorongo stand today?
answer: It is one of the world's last completely undeciphered scripts
choices: It is one of the world's last completely undeciphered scripts
A bilingual tablet unlocked it, like the Rosetta Stone
It proved not to be real writing, just carved decoration
Computer analysis of its glyphs finally cracked the code
context: One islander later told Bishop Jaussen that 'there was nobody left on the island who knew how to read the characters, since the Peruvians had brought about the deaths of all the wise men.' Only about two dozen inscribed objects survive worldwide, and rongorongo remains completely undeciphered; scholars still argue over whether it was ever true writing at all. Egyptian hieroglyphs were also unreadable for centuries before the Rosetta Stone cracked them -- but rongorongo has no such key. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo; history.com/articles/easter-island-people-rapanui.

question: A whiff of rotten eggs hangs over the whole of Rotorua, in New Zealand, and locals call it Sulphur City. Hot rock deep underground keeps leaking one particular gas up through the soil. Which gas is it?
context: It is hydrogen sulphide (H2S) -- the very gas that gives rotten eggs their stink -- seeping up from Rotorua's geothermal ground. Locals wear the 'Sulphur City' nickname (and the joke name 'Rotten-rua') with a grin. Carbon dioxide and methane are odourless, and sulphur dioxide smells sharp and acrid rather than eggy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotorua

question: The ground steams and hisses in the Whakarewarewa valley at Rotorua, in New Zealand, and one geyser outshines all the rest. Up to twenty times a day it roars to life and blasts boiling water as high as 30 metres, the Southern Hemisphere's biggest active geyser. What do local Maori guides call it?
context: Pohutu -- Maori for 'big splash' -- is the largest active geyser in the Southern Hemisphere (not the whole world; the tallest active geyser is Yellowstone's Steamboat). Old Faithful also erupts in Yellowstone, Strokkur in Iceland, and Lady Knox is a real geyser at nearby Wai-O-Tapu. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pohutu_Geyser

question: Te Arawa Maori families at Whakarewarewa village, in Rotorua, still cook the way their grandparents did, with no fire and no stove at all, on ground that steams and bubbles from the heat below. How do they cook a basket of corn, seafood and greens?
answer: they lower it into a naturally boiling hot spring
choices: they lower it into a naturally boiling hot spring
they bake it on hot stones in an earth oven
they smoke it slowly over a driftwood fire
they dry it for days in the summer sun
context: The Te Arawa and Tuhourangi people lower flax baskets of food on cords into the boiling Parekohuru hot spring, and build wooden steam boxes over natural vents -- cooking corn, seafood and vegetables with the ground's own heat, no fire needed. (Hot stones in an earth oven is the hangi, the more familiar Maori method used where there is no geothermal spring.) Source: whakarewarewa.com / en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whakarewarewa

question: At the Whakarewarewa valley in Rotorua, one smaller geyser can be trusted to play first. It sprays up 7 to 9 meters a few minutes before the big geyser roars to life. Guides watch it as a natural signal that the great eruption is about to begin. What is this smaller signal geyser called?
answer: the Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser
choices: the Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser
context: The Prince of Wales Feathers Geyser got its name during a 1901 royal visit, because its triple plume resembled the three feathers of the Prince of Wales crest; it reliably plays just before Pohutu, so it earns the nickname 'the Indicator.' Kereru is another Whakarewarewa geyser, Lady Knox is at Wai-O-Tapu, and Waimangu was a famous New Zealand geyser (now dormant). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whakarewarewa

question: Steam curls off the Champagne Pool at Wai-O-Tapu, near Rotorua, a blue pool 65 metres wide, fizzing with bubbles. Around it runs a bright orange shelf where minerals crust out of the scalding water. Which two elements paint that vivid rim?
context: The orange rim is a crust of arsenic and antimony minerals -- orpiment and stibnite -- settling out of water that also carries faint traces of gold and silver. The pool fizzes like a glass of champagne because carbon dioxide bubbles rise through it. It is about 65 m across and 62 m deep; its surface sits near 74 C, while the water feeding it from below reaches roughly 260 C. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne_Pool

question: Rotorua's geysers roar, its mud pools boil and its ground steams at the northern end of one vast volcanic system that runs down the middle of New Zealand's North Island as far as the Tongariro volcanoes. What is this whole volcanic belt called?
context: The Taupo Volcanic Zone stretches across the central North Island, where the crust is being slowly pulled apart and thinned, letting magma rise close to the surface and boil the groundwater. Rotorua sits at its northern end. The Auckland, Coromandel and Northland volcanic regions are all real, but they are separate systems. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taupo_Volcanic_Zone

question: Beneath Rotorua's hot pools lies a volcanic zone that has poured out more than 3,900 cubic km of lava from over 300 eruptions in the last 350,000 years. That output makes it the world's most productive source of which volcanic rock?
context: Rhyolite is a pale, silica-rich lava that tends to erupt explosively rather than flow quietly. The Taupo Volcanic Zone is the most productive rhyolitic volcanic region on Earth, which is why the whole area -- Rotorua's geysers included -- sits over such shallow, restless heat. Basalt, andesite and obsidian are other real volcanic rocks, but the zone's record is for rhyolite. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taupo_Volcanic_Zone

question: Monks at the Ryoan-ji temple in Kyoto tend a famous dry garden made of almost nothing: a low earthen wall, a bed of raked white gravel and fifteen plain stones. Only one green, living plant grows among those stones. Which plant is it?
context: The only green at Ryoan-ji is a thin skirt of moss ringing the base of each stone — everything else is gravel and rock. Karesansui means 'dry landscape': a garden of stone and sand with no pond, no stream, and almost no plant life, built to be looked at rather than lived in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryōan-ji.

question: Waterbirds came every winter to a large, peaceful pond in the grounds of Ryoan-ji, in Kyoto, a pond older than the temple's famous bone-dry rock garden. For centuries people called it by an affectionate name borrowed from those winter visitors. By what name was the pond long known?
context: Ryoan-ji is known everywhere for its waterless garden, yet the temple grounds hold a large old pond, Kyoyochi, dug long before the rock garden. People long called it the Oshidori-ike — the 'Mandarin Duck Pond' — for the mandarin ducks that came to winter there, a reminder that water and life surround the one bone-dry courtyard the temple is famous for. Source: discoverkyoto.com/places-go/ryoan-ji/.

question: Every morning at Ryoan-ji, a monk rakes the white gravel into long straight lines and curved sweeps around each of the fifteen stones. In a dry Zen garden like this, the raked gravel is meant to stand for one natural element. What does the raked gravel represent?
context: The classic reading of a karesansui: the raked gravel is water and the standing stones are islands or mountain peaks rising from it — an entire seascape conjured in a bone-dry courtyard. The furrows are recombed by hand every day. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryōan-ji; studiomatrx.org/architecture-canon/ryoan-ji-rock-garden.

question: A visitor sitting on the wooden veranda at Ryoan-ji counts the stones in the garden and finds fourteen at most. There are fifteen, set in five groups so that from anywhere on the veranda at least one hides behind another. An old temple story names one thing that lets a person see all fifteen at once. What does the story say it takes?
answer: reaching a state of inner enlightenment
choices: reaching a state of inner enlightenment
rowing a boat across the temple pond
waiting for the light of a full moon
climbing up to the abbot's private room
context: From every spot on Ryoan-ji's veranda at least one of the fifteen stones stays hidden behind another, so a visitor can only ever count fourteen. Temple tradition offers a single exception: it is said that only a person who has reached inner enlightenment could ever behold all fifteen at once. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryōan-ji; sacred-japan.net/guides/ryoanji/.  (Legend.)

question: Behind the fifteen stones runs a low wall, and part of Ryoan-ji's quiet beauty is the soft brown, cloud-like blotches that stain it. The monks did not paint those patterns, and no artist designed them. What slowly created the stains over the centuries?
answer: oil seeping out of the clay
choices: oil seeping out of the clay
rain washing rust from the tiles
context: When the wall was built, its clay was boiled together with rapeseed oil. Over the following centuries the oil slowly wept back out through the surface, leaving the soft brown, cloud-shaped stains prized today. The Japanese have a word for this kind of beauty found in age, weathering, and imperfection: wabi-sabi. Source: muza-chan.net/japan/index.php/blog/ryoanji-earthen-wall; najga.org/using-earthen-walls-for-japanese-gardens.

question: Near Ryoan-ji's stone garden in Kyoto sits a low stone water basin ringed by four Japanese characters. Read on their own, the four make no sense — each is only half a character. The empty center of the basin is itself meant to be read as a fifth character, one that all four share to become complete. Which character is the empty center?
context: The empty center reads as 口 (kuchi), the character for 'mouth' — a simple box shape that completes each of the four surrounding characters. Joined together they read 'ware tada taru wo shiru': 'I know only contentment,' a Zen teaching about needing no more than you already have. The basin is said to have been donated by Tokugawa Mitsukuni, a lord of the Tokugawa family. Source: traditionalkyoto.com/gardens/ryoan-ji/; discoverkyoto.com/places-go/ryoan-ji/.

question: A blinding white plain runs perfectly flat to the horizon in every direction on the Altiplano, the high treeless plateau of Bolivia's Andes, nearly two miles above the sea. No hill, rock, plant or bird breaks it. What world record does this Bolivian plain hold?
context: The Salar de Uyuni sprawls across 10,582 km2 of the Bolivian Altiplano -- roughly 100 times the size of the USA's Bonneville Salt Flats -- making it the largest salt flat on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: After a few centimeters of rain, the Salar de Uyuni turns into a thin sheet of still water. For a few weeks it stretches about 129 kilometers across before it dries. What title does this flooded plain earn?
context: After the rare rains, a thin sheet of dead-still water turns the Salar into a flawless reflector about 129 km (80 miles) across -- the world's largest natural mirror, where sky and salt blur into a single white void. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: Small hotels stand on the Salar de Uyuni, a treeless plain high in the Bolivian Andes, hundreds of kilometres from the nearest forest or quarry. With no wood or stone to build with, their builders cut walls, beds and tables from the one thing the plain offers without limit. What is that material?
context: With no rock or timber for hundreds of kilometres, hotels here -- the Palacio de Sal, Luna Salada, and Playa Blanca -- are built almost entirely of cut salt blocks: walls, beds, tables, and floors. Source: https://www.forbes.com/sites/jimdobson/2018/01/05/escape-to-the-last-jedi-battleground-in-bolivia-and-stay-in-a-hotel-made-entirely-out-of-salt/

question: The ground rises and falls by less than a single metre across all 10,582 km2 of the Salar de Uyuni, the flattest large surface on Earth. Space agencies prize this glass-smooth, dazzling-bright plain for one particular job. What do they use it for?
choices: to track the planet's slow wobble
context: Because the Salar is so flat and bright, satellites are calibrated against it about 5 times better than against the ocean surface; NASA's ICESat used it to verify its altitude measurements to within about 2 cm. Source: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20050071074 ; https://icesat.gsfc.nasa.gov/icesat/publications/GRL/fricker-2.pdf

question: Under the dry salt crust of the Salar de Uyuni lies a hidden lake of buried brine, and dissolved in it sits roughly a fifth of the world's known supply of one soft, silvery metal. It is the metal at the heart of nearly every phone and electric-car battery. Which metal is trapped in the brine below?
context: The brine beneath the crust holds a huge share of the world's lithium RESOURCES -- Bolivia has roughly 22% of the known global total (about 23 of ~105 million tonnes). That figure is the store in the ground, not the amount actually mined. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: Some 10 billion tonnes of salt lie spread across the Salar de Uyuni, more than two miles up in Bolivia's Andes and far from any ocean, a white plain so vast it can be seen from space. Where did such a mountain of salt come from?
answer: the dried-up bed of an ancient Ice-Age lake
choices: the dried-up bed of an ancient Ice-Age lake
a cut-off ancient arm of the Pacific Ocean
mineral ash blasted out by nearby volcanoes
salt dust blown up from the Atacama Desert
context: The whole flat is the dried bed of Lake Tauca, an Ice-Age lake that filled the basin during the Pleistocene and then evaporated away roughly 12,000-13,000 years ago, leaving the salt behind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salar_de_Uyuni

question: A rocky hill breaks the blinding-white emptiness near the middle of the Salar de Uyuni: Incahuasi, an island marooned in a sea of salt. Thousands of one strange plant bristle on its slopes, the tallest topping 12 metres and some older than a thousand years. What covers Incahuasi Island?
context: Incahuasi Island's giant cacti (Trichocereus/Echinopsis) reach up to 12 m and grow only about 1 cm a year, so the tallest are over a thousand years old. The 'island' itself is fossilized coral and stromatolites -- a petrified reef stranded at about 3,650 m, proof this white desert was once underwater. Source: https://www.machupicchu.org/isla-incahuasi-2026-the-cactus-island-in-the-uyuni-salt-flats.htm

question: Traders once filled a vast paved square at the heart of Samarkand, in Uzbekistan, its old marketplace and the stage for the great ceremonies of Timur's empire. Three towering Islamic colleges frame it, and its Persian name means sandy place. What is this square called?
context: The Registan ('sandy place' in Persian) was Samarkand's medieval marketplace and the ceremonial heart of Timur's empire, framed by three great madrasas: the Ulugh Beg (1417-1420), the Sher-Dor (1619-1636), and the Tilya-Kori (1646-1660). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registan

question: The builders of the Sher-Dor college, raised on Samarkand's great square in the 1600s, broke a rule Islamic sacred art almost always keeps, that it shows no living creatures: across its grand doorway they set a startling scene of animals. What does the Sher-Dor doorway show?
answer: two tiger-lions chasing does under sun-faces
choices: two tiger-lions chasing does under sun-faces
a phoenix and a dragon around a flowering tree
peacocks flanking a cypress under a crescent moon
context: 'Sher-Dor' means 'Lion-Bearing.' Two striped tiger-lions chase white does across the portal while sun-discs with human faces rise from the cats' backs — an echo of pre-Islamic Zoroastrian sun-symbolism. Such figural images are rare in Islamic sacred art, which is what makes the 1619-1636 mosaic so startling. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher-Dor_Madrasa

question: A huge bright-blue dome, deeply ribbed and bulging outward, crowns the Gur-e-Amir in Samarkand, where the conqueror Timur, known also as Tamerlane, lies buried. The dome is fondly nicknamed for an everyday object it resembles. What is the dome most often compared to?
context: The melon-shaped, ribbed azure dome of the Gur-e-Amir (built 1403-1404) is about 15 metres across and 12.5 metres high, its bright-blue tiles set with deep rosettes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gur-e-Amir

question: In a Samarkand legend, enemies behead Kusam ibn Abbas, a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, as he prays. The Shah-i-Zinda, a hillside lane of more than 20 blue-tiled tombs, is named for him: the Living King. What does Kusam do next, in the legend?
answer: carries his severed head down a deep well
choices: carries his severed head down a deep well
rises into the sky on a shaft of light
sleeps in a cave until the last day
steps from his tomb each night to pray
context: The Shah-i-Zinda ('The Living King') is an avenue of more than twenty blue-tiled mausoleums, among the finest tilework in Central Asia. By legend Kusam ibn Abbas, beheaded at prayer, took up his own head and descended a well where he lives to this day — an oral tradition, not history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah-i-Zinda

question: Timur ordered the Bibi-Khanym mosque in Samarkand to be the biggest in all Islam. Its outer walls were longer than a football field, its main dome some 40 meters high. It was finished in 1404, but it had been thrown up at reckless speed. What happened to the great Bibi-Khanym soon after it was finished?
answer: bricks began falling from its great dome
choices: bricks began falling from its great dome
cracks split its huge entrance arch
its minarets leaned and had to be propped
its foundations sank into the soft ground
context: Raised in just 1399-1404 with the plunder of Timur's Indian campaign, the Bibi-Khanym mosque (outer walls 167x109 m, main dome ~40 m) was among the largest ever attempted — and so over-ambitious that masonry began dropping from its dome within a few years. Later earthquakes ruined it further; it was rebuilt in the 20th century. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibi-Khanym_Mosque

question: Worshippers stepping into the prayer hall of the Tilya-Kori, a college on Samarkand's great square that was also its chief Friday mosque, find one of the most dazzling rooms in Central Asia. Its walls and domed ceiling are worked in one precious material that also gives the building its name. What covers the inside of the Tilya-Kori?
context: 'Tilya-Kori' means 'Gilded.' Built 1646-1660, it served as both a madrasa and Samarkand's main Friday mosque; its prayer hall is lavishly covered in gold leaf worked over intricate patterns — the source of its name. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registan

question: Uzbekistan won its independence from the Soviet Union in 1991 and took as a proud national symbol the famous mosaic over the great arch of Samarkand's Sher-Dor college, one of the rare pictures of living creatures on a Muslim building. Where does that design turn up in everyday Uzbek life?
context: The Sher-Dor's tiger-lion-and-sun mosaic, echoing ancient Zoroastrian sun-symbolism, became a symbol of Uzbek identity and is printed on the country's 200-som banknote. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher-Dor_Madrasa

question: Over Timur's grave in Samarkand's Gur-e-Amir lies a dark-green slab, the largest single block of jade on Earth, brought there by his grandson Ulugh Beg. Before it ever reached Samarkand, the great green stone had lived two lives far to the east. It first graced a Chinese emperor's palace. Then a khan of Genghis Khan's line had the block cut down. What did he make of it?
context: Over Timur lies the world's largest block of dark-green nephrite jade, brought from the east by Ulugh Beg. It had earlier been a worship-object in a Chinese emperor's palace and then the throne of a Chagatai khan — a descendant of Genghis Khan. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gur-e-Amir

question: Ulugh Beg, Timur's grandson, ruled Samarkand more as a scientist than a king. Around 1428 he raised a great observatory there, whose main instrument was so vast it had to be partly sunk into a trench cut in the hill: a curved arc of stone some 40 metres in radius, used to fix the positions of the sun and stars. What kind of instrument was this giant buried arc?
context: The Fakhri sextant was a stone meridian arc with a radius of about 40 metres, partly sunk in a hillside trench — the largest astronomical instrument in the world in its day. Ulugh Beg's observatory dated to about 1428. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulugh_Beg_Observatory

question: The master builder of Samarkand's giant Bibi-Khanym mosque fell in love with Timur's wife as he worked, a famous legend tells, and swore he would finish the mosque only if she granted him one thing first. In the tale, what did he demand?
context: By this Samarkand legend the kiss burned a mark onto the queen's cheek, and the enraged Timur then decreed that women should veil their faces so as not to tempt other men — a folk origin-tale, not documented history. Source: https://www.advantour.com/uzbekistan/legends/bibi-khanym.htm

question: Samarkand's astronomer-king, Ulugh Beg, timed the length of the year in the 1430s with naked-eye instruments alone, no telescope and no accurate clock. His figure was closer to the truth than the one Copernicus reached a century later. How far off was Ulugh Beg's measurement?
choices: by a quarter of an hour
context: Ulugh Beg measured the year as 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes, 15 seconds — wrong by under a minute, and more accurate than Copernicus a century later. His trigonometric tables were correct to eight decimal places. Source: https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Ulugh_Beg/

question: Mikhail Gerasimov, a Soviet scientist, opened Timur's tomb in Samarkand in mid-June 1941 to study the conqueror's bones. Word later spread of an inscription warning that whoever disturbed the grave would 'unleash an invader more terrible than I.' Barely two days later came an event that seemed to answer it, though historians call it coincidence. What happened on 22 June 1941?
answer: Germany stormed into the Soviet Union
choices: Germany stormed into the Soviet Union
the siege of Leningrad was lifted
context: This is a famous legend, and historians call it coincidence — people close to Gerasimov say the curse tale was invented. He opened the grave on 19-20 June 1941; on 22 June Hitler launched Operation Barbarossa, the invasion of the USSR. Timur was reburied with full Islamic rites in December 1942, weeks before the Soviet victory at Stalingrad. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_of_Timur

question: Bahian women who had moved to a dockside district of Rio de Janeiro nicknamed Little Africa threw house parties in the early 1900s. At those parties African drumming, dance and the rites of Candomblé blended into a brand-new city music. What was it called?
context: Tia Ciata's home in the Pequena África (Little Africa) district near the port was the legendary incubator: the Bahian 'tias baianas' (aunties) mixed Candomblé, cooking, and drumming into the new urban samba. The other choices are real genres born elsewhere — tango in Buenos Aires, rumba in Cuba, calypso in Trinidad. Source: Wikipedia 'Samba' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba).

question: For years Rio de Janeiro's Carnival parade wound through regular downtown streets. Then in 1984 the city opened a permanent parade arena, built for nothing but the parade. Oscar Niemeyer designed it, and its grandstands seat about 90,000. What is this stadium called?
context: The Sambódromo Marquês de Sapucaí opened in 1984; its roughly 700 m avenue ends at Niemeyer's giant tri-legged 'Apotheosis' arch. The other choices are all real Rio landmarks — the Maracanã football stadium, the Copacabana Palace hotel, and the Teatro Municipal opera house. Source: Wikipedia 'Sambadrome Marquês de Sapucaí' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sambadrome_Marqu%C3%AAs_de_Sapuca%C3%AD).

question: Rio de Janeiro's police often harassed Black street drummers in the 1920s for playing. Musicians from the Estácio neighbourhood struck back around 1929, forming the first organised Carnival group and naming it Deixa Falar, Let Them Talk. The idea spread, and rival groups still parade for the Carnival crown. What are these groups called?
context: 'Deixa Falar' (c. 1929, Estácio) pioneered the escola de samba model, and marching as one organized group also helped shield players from the police. The other choices are real Carnival groups from other places — New Orleans has krewes, Cuba and Argentina have comparsas, Uruguay has murgas. Source: Wikipedia 'Samba' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba).

question: In a Rio Carnival parade, drummers march together in a giant drum band called the bateria, and one drum sets the master tempo that every other drummer and dancer locks onto. Its deep, booming pulse has been nicknamed the 'heartbeat' of the whole ensemble. Which drum anchors the group?
context: The biggest, the surdo de primeira (up to about 26 inches across), pounds out the marcação beat that anchors the entire bateria. The other choices are its real bandmates — the tiny high cuíca, the small tamborim, and the two-toned agogô bell. Source: Go Samba 'The Mighty Surdo' (https://gosamba.net/blogs/news/the-mighty-surdo); Wikipedia 'Surdo' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surdo).

question: One drum in the bateria, the great drum band of a Rio Carnival parade, wails a high, laughing squeak that can slide up into a chattering, monkey-like cry. Brazilians named it after a screeching opossum famous for making the same eerie sound. Which drum makes this laughing sound?
context: The cuíca is a friction drum: a stick fixed inside the drumhead is rubbed with a wet cloth, and pressing a finger on the outside of the head slides the pitch up into a monkey-chatter or down into a moan. It is named after a screeching Brazilian opossum. Source: Wikipedia 'Cuíca' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cu%C3%ADca).

question: João Gilberto, a guitarist in Rio's South Zone, worked out in the late 1950s how to fold an entire samba band's rhythm into one classical guitar. He sang over it in a soft, almost whispered voice, a cool, hushed break from the brassy Brazilian singers before him. What was this new style called?
context: Around 1957–59 in Rio's South Zone, João Gilberto's gentle 'batida' guitar and whispered voice became bossa nova — literally 'new trend' or 'new wave.' The 1959 record 'Chega de Saudade' is often called its birth. The other choices are real Brazilian styles: the ballad-like samba-canção, the older instrumental choro, and the later tropicália. Source: Wikipedia 'Bossa nova' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bossa_nova).

question: The musician Donga registered a song late in 1916, and it set Rio's 1917 Carnival ablaze. It is usually credited as the first samba ever put on record, though scholars still argue whether a slightly earlier tune deserves that crown. What was the song called?
context: 'Pelo Telefone' means 'By Telephone' — a surprisingly modern title for 1917. Donga registered it in late 1916; it was released January 19, 1917. Scholars debate whether a slightly earlier tune was truly first, so the honor is contested. The other choices are other real Brazilian songs from later decades. Source: Wikipedia 'Samba' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba).  (Legend.)

question: A 17-year-old named Heloísa strolled past the Veloso bar in Rio de Janeiro every day in the winter of 1962, on her way to the beach. Two regulars, the composer Tom Jobim and the poet Vinícius de Moraes, wrote a soft, hushed song about her, and it grew into one of history's most-recorded pop songs. Which beach neighbourhood, which also gave the song its title, was she walking to?
context: The song is 'The Girl from Ipanema' (Garota de Ipanema, 1962), music by Tom Jobim and Portuguese lyrics by Vinícius de Moraes — often cited as the second-most-recorded pop song ever, behind only the Beatles' 'Yesterday.' The real 'girl,' Helô Pinheiro, walked past the Veloso bar, later renamed 'Garota de Ipanema' in the song's honor. The other choices are neighboring Rio beach districts. Source: Wikipedia 'The Girl from Ipanema' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Girl_from_Ipanema); The Rio Times.

question: The United States Navy wanted San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge striped black and yellow so ships could spot it in fog. The architect Irving Morrow refused and chose one bold colour that pierces the mist yet suits the hills and water. What is it called?
context: Morrow liked the reddish primer the steel arrived coated in and fought to keep it; 'International Orange' became the bridge's identity and is repainted continuously to keep it glowing against the fog. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate_Bridge  (Legend.)

question: John C. Frémont, the explorer, coined the name Golden Gate in 1846, more than ninety years before the famous bridge opened. In his day it named a real feature on the water around San Francisco. What did Golden Gate first name?
answer: the ocean strait into the bay
choices: the ocean strait into the bay
the island in the middle of the bay
the long beach along the ocean shore
the calm harbor deep inside the bay
context: Fremont likened the strait to Byzantium's 'Golden Horn,' picturing a golden gateway to Pacific trade -- and he named it in 1846, roughly eighteen months before gold was even found at Sutter's Mill. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate  (Legend.)

question: An operator on one of San Francisco's little hill cars hauls back on a tall lever with his whole body, and the car climbs slopes far too steep for ordinary streetcars. No other city still runs a hand-worked system like it. What is that lever doing to move the car?
answer: clamping onto a moving cable that runs endlessly beneath the street
choices: clamping onto a moving cable that runs endlessly beneath the street
meshing a toothed wheel into a notched rail up the middle of the track
swinging a pole up to a live electric wire strung overhead
letting a sinking counterweight on a parallel track pull it up
context: Andrew Hallidie opened the first line, the Clay Street Hill Railroad, on September 1, 1873; a constantly moving underground cable does the pulling, and the operator's grip is the only link between car and cable. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_car_(railway)  (Legend.)

question: Spanish ships sailed up and down the California coast for some two hundred years and slipped past the Golden Gate without ever noticing the vast bay hidden behind it. When that great harbour was finally found in 1769, how did it happen?
answer: a party exploring overland spotted it from a high ridge
choices: a party exploring overland spotted it from a high ridge
a storm drove a Spanish galleon in through the narrow gap
a Russian fur-trading fleet charted it from the open sea
a native guide led coastal missionaries to it on foot
context: On November 4, 1769, Gaspar de Portola's overland expedition sighted San Francisco Bay from Sweeney Ridge, near today's Pacifica; the first ship to actually sail in through the Golden Gate, Juan de Ayala's San Carlos, did not arrive until 1775. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay  (Legend.)

question: On a summer afternoon, San Francisco can shiver under gray fog while valleys inland bake past 100 F, and that inland heat pulls in ocean air. As the sea air is cooled below its dew point, it turns into a low advection fog that then pours through the Golden Gate like a slow gray river. What chills the incoming ocean air enough to fog it up?
answer: the cold California Current running down the coast
choices: the cold California Current running down the coast
a cold undersea canyon lurking just off the coast
meltwater from the distant Sierra Nevada snowpack
icy air sliding down off the high inland desert
