context: The California Current pulls cold, deep water up along the shore (upwelling), chilling the marine air into the low 50s F just offshore; dragged inland by the summer heat, that cold air is why San Francisco summers are famously foggy and cool. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_fog

question: Wardens at Alcatraz, the federal prison on a bare rock about a mile and a quarter off the San Francisco waterfront, boasted that no one could break out and survive, and not because of the cell walls. What made escape from the Rock nearly impossible?
answer: the deadly cold and ripping currents of the surrounding bay
choices: the deadly cold and ripping currents of the surrounding bay
sheer sea-cliffs dropping straight down into deep water
a pack of guard dogs loosed across the island each night
a triple ring of electrified razor-wire fencing
context: The bay hovers near 50-55 F with currents strong enough to sweep a swimmer out the Golden Gate; the island sits about 1.25 miles from shore. In the famous June 1962 escape, Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers rafted off on prison-made floats and were never seen again. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcatraz_Island  (Legend.)

question: Joseph Strauss, chief engineer of San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge, hung a giant movable safety net beneath the deck, the first ever used on a job that size. It caught nineteen workers who slipped and fell hundreds of feet toward the water. What grimly cheerful nickname did those men give their group?
answer: the Half Way to Hell Club
choices: the Half Way to Hell Club
the Bottom of the Bay Club
context: Strauss's movable net saved nineteen men, but the bridge still cost eleven lives -- ten of them on February 17, 1937, when a work platform tore loose and ripped through the net into the strait. The bridge opened three months later, on May 27, 1937. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate_Bridge  (Legend.)

question: The San Andreas Fault ruptured just off San Francisco as dawn broke on 18 April 1906, and the ground heaved violently. Yet when the ruin was tallied, some 25,000 buildings gone across 490 blocks, investigators found the shaking itself had not done the worst of it. What levelled most of the city after the ground stopped moving?
answer: fires that raged unchecked through the broken city
choices: fires that raged unchecked through the broken city
a towering tsunami surging in through the Golden Gate
a second, far larger aftershock the following night
floodwater pouring from the city's shattered reservoirs
context: The quake snapped both the gas mains that fed the fires and the water mains needed to fight them; an estimated 80-95% of the destruction came from three days of flame, and over 3,000 people died. The San Andreas marks where the Pacific and North American plates grind past each other. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906_San_Francisco_earthquake  (Legend.)

question: When the Loma Prieta earthquake struck during the 1989 World Series, most of San Francisco rode it out -- but the Marina District shook hardest, and its buildings sank and burned. There the ground briefly lost all firmness and flowed like a liquid, an effect geologists call 'liquefaction.' Why did the Marina turn to jelly while bedrock neighborhoods held firm?
answer: it stands on loose rubble and sand dumped in as landfill
choices: it stands on loose rubble and sand dumped in as landfill
it was built over a buried, still-flowing underground creek
it lay on thin sand spread straight over hard bedrock
it rested on deep clay dried and cracked by long drought
context: The Marina sits on rubble and bay mud dumped as fill for the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition; violently shaken, the water-logged fill lost its strength and behaved like a fluid, so buildings there tilted, sank, and caught fire while homes on bedrock nearby stood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Loma_Prieta_earthquake

question: San Francisco's Lombard Street runs down a hill so steep, about a 27% grade, more than four times a steep highway, that a car pointed straight down its one block would be nearly impossible to control. Rather than close it, the city rebuilt that block in 1922 into the spectacle tourists now creep down at 5 mph. What did engineers build into the block to tame the plunge?
answer: a set of tight switchbacks that zigzag cars down
choices: a set of tight switchbacks that zigzag cars down
a run of shallow terraced ramps stepping down
a single hairpin curve sweeping around the block
a rough cobbled surface to grip the tires
context: The natural block plunges at about a 27% grade -- roughly a 27-foot drop over 100 feet, more than four times a steep highway -- so in 1922 the city rebuilt that one block into eight tight switchbacks with a 5 mph limit, making a slope too steep to drive straight down into something cars can zigzag safely. (It is a 27% grade, not '27 degrees' -- a common mix-up between two very different steepnesses.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombard_Street_(San_Francisco)

question: Rain and Sierra Nevada snowmelt from about 40% of California funnel toward the sea through the Golden Gate. Two great rivers gather that runoff from the north and the south, meet in a wide inland delta and let San Francisco Bay flush it out to the Pacific. Which two rivers drain California's heartland through the Golden Gate?
answer: the Sacramento and the San Joaquin
choices: the Sacramento and the San Joaquin
context: The Sacramento (draining the north) and the San Joaquin (draining the south) join in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, then empty through San Francisco Bay and out the Golden Gate -- the single outlet for runoff from roughly 40% of the state. (It is a huge estuary, though the Salish Sea to the north is larger.) Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay

question: Ferries crossing Santorini's drowned volcanic bay pass two small islands of bare black lava at its centre. The younger one has been rising from the seabed since the great eruption and is still growing, proof the volcano is only asleep. What is this young lava island called?
context: Nea Kameni ('New Burnt Island') is a lava dome about 114 m high that has grown inside the flooded crater in eruptions since the ancient collapse; its older twin is Palea Kameni ('Old Burnt Island'). Thirasia and Aspronisi are surviving pieces of the original caldera rim across the bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nea_Kameni

question: The volcano Thera, today's Santorini, tore itself apart around 1600 BC in one of the mightiest explosions in human history, shooting a column of ash and pumice roughly 35 km, about 20 miles, straight up. Which layer of Earth's atmosphere did the ash punch into?
context: At about 35 km the plume drove well into the stratosphere (roughly 10-50 km up), where the ozone layer sits and airliners never fly. Ash and gas flung that high can dim sunlight around the world for years. The eruption blasted out an estimated 28-41 cubic km of rock. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_eruption

question: Spyridon Marinatos, the archaeologist who uncovered Akrotiri, believed the memory of Thera's catastrophe lived on for centuries and found its way into one of Plato's tales, of a brilliant Bronze Age world wrecked in a single disaster. Most scholars reject the link, since the dates and geography do not fit. Which legendary land did Marinatos tie to Santorini?
context: Marinatos (and later Angelos Galanopoulos) proposed Thera as the origin of Atlantis, the island Plato described in his dialogues Timaeus and Critias as vanishing 'in a single day and night... into the depths of the sea.' It is a popular idea but is not accepted by current scholarship. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_eruption  (Legend.)

question: Guards in silk robes change the watch twice a day beneath the painted gate of a royal palace in the heart of Seoul. The Joseon kings held court there from 1395, and its name means roughly palace of shining blessings. What is this palace called?
context: Gyeongbokgung was founded in 1395 by King Taejo, the founder of Joseon; its name was drawn from a line in the ancient Chinese Book of Odes wishing the new dynasty long, bright happiness. It stayed the dynasty's main palace, and the changing-of-the-royal-guard ceremony is re-enacted today at its main gate, Gwanghwamun ('gate of light and harmony'). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongbokgung

question: Rows of old homes with heavy grey tile roofs, their eaves curving upward, still wrap around walled courtyards in Seoul's Bukchon quarter, just uphill from the royal palace and among the city's glass office towers. What are these traditional houses called?
context: A hanok is the traditional Korean house, built with a tiled or thatched roof and warm floors. Bukchon ('north village,' for its site north of the old Cheonggyecheon stream) was historically the residential quarter of the yangban -- Joseon's high officials and nobility. Machiya and minka are Japanese houses; a siheyuan is a Chinese courtyard house. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukchon_Hanok_Village

question: A family in a traditional Seoul home sits, eats and sleeps on the floor, because the floor is the heater: heat and smoke from the kitchen fire run through stone flues beneath it, warming the room from below. Elders and honoured guests get the warmest spot, nearest the fire. What is this heating system called?
context: Ondol heats a room from below: the agungi (firebox) in the kitchen sends heat through gudeul (stone flues) under the floor before smoke escapes up an outdoor chimney -- so Koreans traditionally live at floor level on the warm stone. A hypocaust is the Roman version, a kang is a Chinese heated sleeping platform, and an irori is a Japanese sunken hearth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ondol

question: About 50 km north of Seoul's palaces, the Korean peninsula is slashed clean across by a strip of land, roughly 250 km long and only 4 km wide. Fences, watchtowers, and mines have kept the two Koreas apart since the guns fell silent in 1953. What is this fortified dividing strip called?
context: The DMZ was created by the armistice signed on 27 July 1953, which halted the Korean War without a peace treaty. It runs about 4 km wide (2 km on each side of the central Military Demarcation Line) near the 38th parallel. Despite the name 'demilitarized,' it is one of the most heavily fortified borders on Earth. Sources: https://grokipedia.com/page/Korean_Demilitarized_Zone ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Demilitarized_Zone

question: Hikers climb bald granite domes and wooded trails at the northern edge of Seoul, a city of some ten million people split by the broad Han River. That wild mountain was made a national park in 1983, and very few big cities on Earth hold a mountain park like it inside their limits. Which mountain is it?
context: Bukhansan means 'mountain north of the Han.' Made a national park in 1983 (Korea's 15th), its bare granite domes draw millions of hikers a year and are world-famous for rock climbing. Hallasan is the volcano on Jeju Island, Seoraksan lies on the east coast, and Namsan is the small hill in central Seoul crowned by N Seoul Tower. Sources: https://grokipedia.com/page/Bukhansan_National_Park ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukhansan

question: Japanese invaders burned the Joseon kings' chief palace in Seoul to the ground in the Imjin War of 1592. A king might have been expected to rebuild his main palace within a few years, but the blackened site at the heart of the capital met a stranger fate. What became of the ruined palace?
answer: it was left in ruins for nearly 270 years
choices: it was left in ruins for nearly 270 years
it was left in ruins for only about 20 years
it was rebuilt even grander within a decade
it was replaced by a brand-new capital city
context: The 1592 invasion is remembered as the Imjin War. Gyeongbokgung was not rebuilt until the 1860s, when the regent Heungseon Daewongun -- ruling for the boy-king Gojong -- finally raised it again after roughly 270 years of abandonment. So the palace tourists walk through today is largely a 19th-century reconstruction of the 1395 original. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongbokgung

question: No farmer has ploughed and no bulldozer has broken ground since the armistice of 1953 in the mine-laced strip that cuts the Korean peninsula in two, the no-man's-land between two armies that never signed a peace treaty. Sealed off from people for so long, that guarded frontier quietly became something no general ever planned. What did the abandoned strip turn into?
choices: a buried maze of secret tunnels
context: With people locked out since 1953, nature reclaimed the DMZ's abandoned rice paddies as wetlands and forest, making it one of the best-preserved strips of temperate habitat in the world. Endangered red-crowned cranes and vulnerable white-naped cranes now winter in the mined no-man's-land -- rare wild things thriving on the ground where thousands of soldiers once died. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/travel/wildlife-thrives-dmz-korea-risk-location-180967842/

question: A wild granite mountain at Seoul's northern edge and the royal palace at its heart look like different worlds, yet Joseon's founders treated them as one. Following pungsu, Korean geomancy, they studied the line of the mountain's ridge in the 1390s to settle one decision about the palace. What did the mountain help decide?
choices: which way its throne would face
how high its main hall could rise
how many gates it would have
context: In Korean geomancy a 'guardian mountain' at one's back marks an auspicious site, and Bukhansan served as the guardian mountain to the north of the Joseon capital. Its granite ridge helped fix exactly where Gyeongbokgung was placed in the 1390s -- so the mountain at the city's edge and the palace at its heart are geographically linked. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Bukhansan_National_Park

question: A Cherokee silversmith from the mountains of what is now Tennessee could not read a single word of any language. Yet Sequoyah did something almost no one in recorded history has done alone. What did he create?
answer: a complete writing system for his people's language
choices: a complete writing system for his people's language
a spoken war code later used by the U.S. Army
a system of knotted cords for keeping records
a hand-sign language shared among many tribes
context: Sequoyah was born around 1770 in Tuskegee, in what is now Tennessee, deep in the Cherokee country of the southern Appalachians. He is one of the very few people in recorded history known to have invented a writing system from scratch -- and the only one known to have managed it while completely unable to read any language. Source: education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/sequoyah-and-creation-cherokee-syllabary/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoyah

question: In Cherokee country, Sequoyah gave every spoken syllable of Cherokee, sounds like ga, no and hi, a single symbol of its own, about 85 in all. Learning to read English can take a child years. Once a Cherokee speaker had learned those symbols, how fast could he read his own language?
answer: in a few days to a few weeks
choices: in a few days to a few weeks
in a single afternoon of practice
in a couple of months of lessons
in about a year of steady study
context: Because each symbol stands for a whole syllable rather than a single sound, Sequoyah's invention is a SYLLABARY, not an alphabet -- about 85 symbols (originally 86, later streamlined). The Cherokee National Council officially adopted it in 1825. The linguist Albert Gallatin marveled that a Cherokee could become literate almost the moment the symbols were learned. Source: education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/sequoyah-and-creation-cherokee-syllabary/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_syllabary

question: In the Cherokee towns of the southern Appalachians, his neighbours feared the paper marks Sequoyah had worked out for the Cherokee language in the early 1820s, one symbol for each syllable. They took the scribbles for witchcraft, and he was put on trial as a sorcerer. To show that the marks held real speech, what test did he use?
answer: he had his daughter read back words he wrote in a separate, closed room
choices: he had his daughter read back words he wrote in a separate, closed room
he wrote down a bystander's words and read the same page aloud himself
he matched his symbols one by one against the settlers' printed book
he had elders memorize a message and repeat it after seeing the marks
context: His daughter Ayoka was only about six. Father and daughter were shut in different rooms; each wrote down messages, the papers were carried between them, and Ayoka read aloud words her father had written and could not possibly have overheard -- proving the marks truly carried speech. Even Sequoyah's own wife had at first feared the writing as sorcery. Source: smithsonianmag.com/innovation/man-created-written-language-cherokee-did-efficiently-elegantly-peers-thought-magic-180988850/; education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/sequoyah-and-creation-cherokee-syllabary/

question: The Cherokee Nation's printers at New Echota, their capital in Georgia, began in 1828 to turn out something no Native people had made before: a newspaper in two columns, one in Sequoyah's script and one in English. What was this first Native American newspaper called?
context: The first issue of the Cherokee Phoenix appeared on February 21, 1828, printed in both the syllabary and English at New Echota, the Cherokee capital in Georgia. Its first editor was Elias Boudinot, whose Cherokee name was Galagina, 'Buck' Oowatie. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_Phoenix

question: In the Cherokee country of the southern mountains, Sequoyah liked the look of the letters he saw in a settler's spelling book, so he borrowed some of their shapes for his own syllabary. A symbol shaped like the English letters D or R turns up in his script. But what did Sequoyah do about the sounds those borrowed shapes originally made?
answer: he gave the borrowed shapes entirely new Cherokee sounds
choices: he gave the borrowed shapes entirely new Cherokee sounds
he kept each shape's original English sound to help learners
he flipped every borrowed shape to signal a different sound
he placed the borrowed shapes in English alphabetical order
context: Some Cherokee symbols also resemble Latin, Greek, and Cyrillic letters, but not one of them shares the sound of the letter it looks like. Sequoyah, who could not read English, chose the shapes purely because he liked them, with no idea what sounds they carried -- so a Cherokee character shaped like 'D' or 'R' sounds nothing like ours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_syllabary

question: Stephan Endlicher, an Austrian botanist, gave California's giant sequoias, the most massive living things on Earth, their genus name in 1847 and never wrote down why. A popular story says he named them in Sequoyah's honour, but some scholars doubt it entirely. What origin do these skeptics propose instead?
answer: the Latin sequi, 'to follow,' because its seed count fell in sequence after related trees
choices: the Latin sequi, 'to follow,' because its seed count fell in sequence after related trees
a Latin word meaning 'gigantic,' because the trees dwarf every other kind around them
a Sierra Nevada valley, because the earliest known specimen was measured there
an early surveyor's surname, because he was the first to map the great groves
context: This is the popular tribute, not a proven fact. The Austrian botanist Stephan Endlicher coined the genus name 'Sequoia' in 1847 but never recorded why; the story that it honors Sequoyah only spread in the 1850s and 1860s. Some scholars argue Endlicher drew the name from the Latin sequi, 'to follow,' because the number of seeds per cone fell in sequence after related trees. Either way, the giant sequoia and coast redwoods are among the largest and tallest living things on Earth. Source: landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu/discovery-and-naming-sequoiadendron-giganteum-sierra-redwood; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoiadendron_giganteum  (Legend.)

question: The Cherokee carried Sequoyah's syllabary with them on the Trail of Tears, when they were forced west in 1838, and today it fills daily life around Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the Cherokee Nation's capital, on street signs, in immersion classrooms and even on phones. How does a script invented in 1821 now appear on smartphones and laptops?
answer: it joined Unicode, the code behind all on-screen text
choices: it joined Unicode, the code behind all on-screen text
Apple and Google each ship their own Cherokee font
it borrows the Unicode block reserved for Latin letters
each device first needs a downloadable Cherokee keyboard app
context: The syllabary was added to the Unicode standard (blocks U+13A0-13FF and U+AB70-ABBF), so it types on any computer or phone; Cherokee immersion schools teach it with syllabary keyboards. Road and street signs carry it in Tahlequah, Oklahoma and in Cherokee, North Carolina, and the Cherokee Phoenix is still published from Tahlequah today -- the script having survived the Trail of Tears of 1838. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_syllabary; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee_Phoenix; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoyah

question: Someone at the Serabit el-Khadim turquoise mine, in Egypt's Sinai desert, scratched a few dozen signs into the rock around 1800 BC. Those signs became the parent of nearly every alphabet in use today, from Greek and Latin to Arabic and Hebrew. Who made them?
context: The signs are called the Proto-Sinaitic script, from about 1900-1800 BCE, and they are the oldest known ancestor of the alphabet -- the line runs from these scratches to Phoenician, then Greek and Latin, and on to our own letters. The astonishing part is who made them: Semitic-speaking laborers from Southwest Asia and the Nile Delta who worked the turquoise mines, not scribes or royalty. Scholars still debate the exact century -- an early date around 1850 BCE (the alphabet born inside Egypt) versus a late date around 1550 BCE (developed later in Canaan). Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sinaitic_script; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serabit_el-Khadim; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_alphabet.

question: The first alphabet-writers at Serabit el-Khadim, in the Sinai, borrowed Egyptian hieroglyphs and used each picture for the first sound of its name, so an eye stood for one sound and a head for another. The letter B began the same way, as a picture of one everyday object. What did that first B show?
context: The trick is called acrophony -- 'first-sound' writing. The miners took a handful of Egyptian hieroglyphs but used each picture only for the first sound of its Semitic name: the house, bayt, gave 'b' (our B); the ox-head, alp, gave the throat-catch that opens 'ox' (our A); the water-squiggle, mem, gave 'm' (our M). A whole alphabet grew from a few pictures used for their opening sounds. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_alphabet; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sinaitic_script.

question: Alan Gardiner, an Egyptologist, looked in 1916 at the scratches of Serabit el-Khadim, long taken for meaningless doodles, and noticed one short group of signs repeating again and again. Reading each sign by its first sound, he found they spelled a real word he recognised, and that one word cracked the whole code. What did the repeated word turn out to be?
context: The repeating signs spelled l-b-'-l-t -- 'to Baalat', meaning 'to the Lady'. Baalat was the Canaanite miners' name for Hathor, the Egyptian goddess worshipped at Serabit as 'Mistress of Turquoise'. Because those few signs spelled a name by first-sounds, Alan Gardiner's 1916 reading proved the marks really were an alphabet -- and that ordinary desert miners, not a royal court, had taken the first step toward the ABCs. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serabit_el-Khadim_proto-Sinaitic_inscriptions; library.biblicalarchaeology.org (Gardiner 1916).

question: The Almohads raised the brick shaft of Seville's Giralda between 1184 and 1198, and centuries later a Renaissance bell room was stacked on top, lifting the tower to about 96 metres. What was the original 12th-century tower built to be?
answer: the minaret of the city's great mosque
choices: the minaret of the city's great mosque
the watchtower over the river approach
the lighthouse for ships reaching port
the keep of the Almohad royal castle
context: The Giralda's lower ~50 m is the original Almohad minaret, begun in 1184 and finished in 1198. Rather than tear it down, Christian Seville stacked a Renaissance belfry on top in 1558-1568 — a Muslim prayer-tower reborn as a cathedral bell tower, minaret re-used, not erased. Source: Wikipedia (Giralda), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giralda; Grokipedia (Giralda) checked first.

question: A climber inside the Giralda, the tall bell tower of Seville Cathedral, finds not a single stair. Instead 35 broad, gently sloping brick ramps spiral up around its solid core, and the builders made them wide and easy on purpose. What could someone do all the way to the top of the Giralda?
answer: ride a horse all the way to the top
choices: ride a horse all the way to the top
roll the great bells up to hang them
wheel carts of building stone upward
carry pilgrims up in sedan chairs
context: The Giralda's 35 ramps let a rider climb to the summit on horseback — by tradition the muezzin rode up to call the faithful to prayer. The gentle grade replaces stairs entirely, spiralling around the tower's solid brick core. Source: Wikipedia (Giralda), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giralda.

question: Christian builders laboured from 1401 to 1506 on an immense new church beside Seville's Giralda, a church so vast that its own canons reportedly said onlookers would 'take us for mad.' What claim to fame does the finished Seville Cathedral hold?
answer: the largest Gothic church in the world
choices: the largest Gothic church in the world
the tallest cathedral in the world
the largest brick-built church in the world
the widest nave of any church in Europe
context: Seville Cathedral (built 1401-1506 on the demolished mosque's footprint) is about 126 m long and 76 m wide — the largest Gothic church on Earth. When finished it even took the 'largest cathedral' title from Constantinople's Hagia Sophia, which had held it for roughly a thousand years. The canons' reported vow: a church so grand 'those who see it finished will take us for mad.' Source: Wikipedia (Seville Cathedral), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville_Cathedral.

question: Seville crowned its Giralda bell tower, high above the city, in 1568 with a striking new feature, something that never stops moving. The Giralda is named for it, after the Spanish verb girar, meaning to turn. What is this moving feature?
answer: a bronze statue on top that pivots to face the wind
choices: a bronze statue on top that pivots to face the wind
a spiral ramp that turns as it climbs the tower
a ring of bells that swivel as they toll the hours
a beacon that once revolved to guide river ships
context: The turning feature is El Giraldillo — a ~4 m, ~1,500 kg bronze statue of Faith set on the summit in 1568 that swings to face the wind like a weathervane. The whole tower took its name, 'the Giralda' (from girar, 'to turn'), from this giant pivoting figure. Source: Wikipedia (Giralda), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giralda.

question: The tomb of Christopher Columbus, the Genoese explorer who sailed for the Spanish crown to the New World in 1492, lies in Seville's great cathedral, yet his coffin has never been lowered into the ground. It breaks the usual rule for what a grave should look like. How is the coffin displayed instead?
answer: lifted aloft on the shoulders of four bronze bearers
choices: lifted aloft on the shoulders of four bronze bearers
suspended over the altar from four iron chains
raised high on a single tall porphyry column
set upright inside a huge bronze cathedral door
context: Four crowned bronze bearers — representing the medieval kingdoms of Castile, León, Aragón and Navarre — hold Columbus's coffin aloft, so he seems carried in endless procession rather than buried; sculptor Arturo Mélida installed it in 1899. Spain and the Dominican Republic long both claimed his real bones, until 2024 DNA testing led by José Antonio Lorente of the University of Granada confirmed the Seville remains are truly Columbus's. Source: Wikipedia (Tomb of Christopher Columbus), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_Christopher_Columbus.

question: Treasure fleets from the Americas, hulls heavy with New World gold and silver, all had to sail to one port in the 1500s and 1600s to be counted and taxed by the Spanish crown: Seville, in southern Spain. Yet Seville makes an odd choice for a great sea port, because of one strange fact about where it sits. What is that fact?
answer: it lies far inland, reached only up a winding river
choices: it lies far inland, reached only up a winding river
it sits on an exposed island out in the Atlantic
it hides behind a long sandbar blocking the coast
it lies below sea level, ringed by earthen dikes
context: Seville sits about 90 km inland, up the winding Guadalquivir, which meets the Atlantic at Sanlúcar de Barrameda — yet from 1503 its Casa de Contratación (House of Trade) held a royal monopoly on all trade with the Americas: every ship to and from the Indies had to register in this river-city, until the monopoly moved to Cádiz in 1717. Sources: Wikipedia (Casa de Contratación) and Port of Seville, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_de_Contratación; Grokipedia (Casa de Contratación) checked first.

question: A long row of grand European stone banks and hotels lines the west bank of the Huangpu River in Shanghai, its old towers like a slice of old London dropped into China. What is this famous waterfront called?
context: The Bund's roughly 52 historic buildings — Gothic, Baroque, Neoclassical, Art Deco and Beaux-Arts — went up after China's defeats opened the treaty ports; by the 1863 International Settlement, British, French, American and Japanese banks and trading houses stood shoulder to shoulder facing the river, staring across at what is now Pudong. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bund

question: At night a wall of glass supertowers blazes across the Huangpu River from Shanghai's grand old waterfront, on China's east coast. As recently as 1990 that shore held rice paddies, farmland and warehouses, until it was thrown open to builders almost overnight. What is this district called?
context: China opened Pudong for development on April 18, 1990 — the district's 'birthday.' In one generation its Lujiazui riverfront became the first place on Earth where three supertall skyscrapers rose within a few blocks, staring back across the Huangpu at the century-old Bund like the future facing the past. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pudong

question: Pan Yunduan, a Ming-dynasty official, spent nearly twenty years building the Yu Garden in Shanghai's old town, folding pavilions, ponds and rock piles into barely two hectares. He built it not for himself. Whom was this peaceful retreat for?
context: Pan Yunduan built the Yu Garden between 1559 and 1577, folding pavilions, ponds and rockeries into barely two hectares; its name evokes peace and comfort in old age. Its prized Exquisite Jade Rock is a porous, 5-ton, 3.3-m boulder said to come from an emperor's collection. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu_Garden

question: One supertower over the Huangpu River corkscrews as it climbs 632 metres, its glass skin spiralling through 120 degrees from base to crown. The spiral is no mere style: it spills the wind, cutting the building's wind load by nearly a quarter. Which tower is it?
context: The Shanghai Tower reaches 632 m (2,073 ft) across 128 floors — China's tallest building, and the world's 2nd or 3rd tallest, not the tallest overall. Designed by the American firm Gensler, its spiral form uses about 25% less structural steel and saved roughly US$58 million. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Tower

question: A train with no wheels glides just above its guideway on magnets, then streaks along at 431 km/h (268 mph) — for seventeen years the fastest passenger train in regular service anywhere on Earth. This Shanghai maglev was built to whisk travellers to a single destination. Where does it race?
context: Opened in 2004, the Shanghai maglev was the world's first commercial high-speed maglev line, covering the ~30 km from Longyang Road to Pudong Airport in under 8 minutes and holding the regular-service speed record from 2004 to 2021. On a non-commercial test run on November 12, 2003, it hit 501 km/h (311 mph) — faster than many small planes cruise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_maglev_train

question: Two bronze lions, rubbed shiny by generations of passing hands, guard the door of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation's building of 1923 on Shanghai's old waterfront. When it opened, its owners boasted that it was the most luxurious building anywhere between two far-flung landmarks. Which two did they name?
answer: the Suez Canal and the Bering Strait
choices: the Suez Canal and the Bering Strait
the Cape of Good Hope and Cape Horn
the Panama Canal and the Strait of Malacca
the Strait of Gibraltar and the Sea of Japan
context: The 1923 HSBC Building, guarded by two bronze lions, was boasted to be 'the most luxurious building between the Suez Canal and the Bering Strait' — a stretch spanning much of the globe. Next door, the 1927 Custom House carries a clock tower built to imitate London's Big Ben, nicknamed 'Big Ching.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bund

question: In Shanghai's old town, the Nine-Turn Bridge crosses a lotus pond toward the Huxinting Teahouse not in a straight line but in a series of sharp, deliberate zigzags. According to local folklore, why did the builders bend it into nine crooked turns?
answer: To block evil spirits, who move only in straight lines
choices: To block evil spirits, who move only in straight lines
To slow visitors so they savor the garden views
To keep the wooden walkway clear of the flood line
To trace the nine bends of a nearby sacred river
context: The spirit-blocking story is folklore: tradition holds that evil spirits can travel only in straight lines, so the crooked turns supposedly bar them. The zigzag bridge leads to the Huxinting Teahouse, built in 1784 in the middle of the pond — Shanghai's oldest surviving teahouse — and the nine turns also carry numerology, since nine, the highest single-digit odd number, symbolizes completeness and is linked to heaven and the emperor. Source: foresyteapp.com/yu-garden-nine-turn-bridge-shang (corroborated by trip.com and theculturetrip.com)  (Legend.)

question: Freya Stark, the British explorer, crossed Yemen's Wadi Hadhramaut in the 1930s and made a nickname stick for Shibam: the Manhattan of the desert. About 500 tower houses stand jammed inside its single wall, from five to eleven storeys tall. What are these tall desert houses built from?
context: Freya Stark, the British explorer who crossed the Hadhramaut in the 1930s, made 'the Manhattan of the desert' stick — but unlike Manhattan's steel and glass, every one of Shibam's roughly 500 towers is raised from sun-dried mud brick, packed inside a single defensive wall and rising five to eleven stories. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shibam; National Geographic, 'This Ancient Mud Skyscraper City is the Manhattan of the Desert.')

question: Shibam's tower houses rise as high as eleven storeys in Yemen's Wadi Hadhramaut, and by rights the desert gales should tear such tall buildings apart. Yet they have ridden out the wind for centuries. What hidden reinforcement inside the walls lets each tower take it?
choices: a cage of woven palm ribs
context: Shibam's builders laced an internal matrix of wooden beams through the mud walls, tying each tower together so it can resist the lateral push of the wind — the hidden reinforcement that keeps an all-earth high-rise standing, with nothing on the outside to give it away. (Source: archup.net, 'Shibam / Hadramout,' on the internal timber matrix.)

question: The tallest towers of Shibam climb more than 30 metres above the Yemeni desert, and their soft, heavy walls ought to slump and crack under their own weight. Yet they have stood for centuries. What is the builders' main trick for keeping them upright?
answer: the walls taper, thick at the base and thin at the top
choices: the walls taper, thick at the base and thin at the top
a deep stone foundation reaches down to bedrock
the towers lean inward and brace on one another
iron rods are threaded through every floor
context: Shibam's tower walls are about 1.2 m thick at the base and taper to roughly 0.4 m at the top, with smaller bricks laid on the upper floors. Widening the base and lightening the crown spreads the load so sun-dried mud brick can safely rise more than 30 m. (Sources: archup.net and clickpetroleoegas.com.br, 'Shibam / Hadramout.')

question: Pilgrims climbing to the Shwedagon Pagoda, Myanmar's holiest shrine on its hill above Yangon, press something small onto the base of the great stupa with their fingertips. What do they press onto it?
context: The Shwedagon is a literal mountain of gold: its bell-shaped stupa rises about 99 m (367 ft counting its crown) and is sheathed in over 20,000 solid gold plates - 8,688 on the lower stupa and 13,153 above. Ordinary pilgrims keep it alive by buying thin squares of gold leaf and pressing them onto the lower stupa by hand, so the shrine is re-gilded by the faithful themselves. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda; sacred-destinations.com; factsanddetails.com.

question: Four covered stairways climb Singuttara Hill to the Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon, and at each gateway stands a pair of huge guardian beasts like lions, with white bodies and golden heads. What are these temple guards called in Myanmar?
context: The four covered stairways climb the hill from the cardinal directions, each gate guarded by a pair of chinthe - Burmese leogryphs with white bodies and golden heads. The chinthe is so iconic that it appears on Myanmar's national currency. Source: sacred-destinations.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda (leogryph guardians at the four entrances).

question: A small golden orb sits at the very tip of the Shwedagon's stupa, studded with thousands of diamonds and crowned by a single great one. From the right place on the terrace at sunrise or sunset, a watcher sees that top gem do something the old craftsmen planned. What does the gem appear to do?
answer: It flashes red, then green, then white
choices: It flashes red, then green, then white
It beams a single ray straight upward
It appears to float above the spire
It seems to slowly spin in place
context: The tip holds the 'sein bu,' a hollow golden orb set with 4,351 diamonds (about 1,800 carats), and resting on its point a single huge diamond of about 72 carats (sources say 72-76). Ancient artisans aimed the gem so that from the right spot on the terrace at dawn or dusk it flashes color - sources variously describe red, green, and white, or red, orange, and purple. Source: renown-travel.com; seasia.co; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda.

question: By tradition, four Buddhas of this present age each gave a relic to the Shwedagon in Yangon, among them a staff, a water filter and a scrap of robe. The holiest, and the reason worshippers walk clockwise and barefoot around the stupa, came from the Buddha Gautama. What is it said to be?
context: By tradition the shrine enshrines relics of the four Buddhas of this age - the staff of Kakusandha, the water filter of Konagamana, a piece of Kassapa's robe, and eight hairs from the head of Gautama. Because the sacred hairs are believed to lie inside, worshippers circle the stupa clockwise and barefoot, removing their shoes at the very foot of the covered stairways. This is religious tradition, not a physical claim. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda.  (Legend.)

question: British troops who seized Yangon, in Myanmar, hauled the Shwedagon's great Singu Min bell off as loot, 23 tons of bronze cast in 1779, but it slid from their barge into the Yangon River and sank, and their engineers gave up trying to raise it. How did the Burmese get their bell back?
answer: They floated it up on rafts of bamboo
choices: They floated it up on rafts of bamboo
They dragged it out with teams of elephants
They waited for the dry season and dug it free
They raised it with chains and pulleys
context: The recovered Singu Min (Maha Ganda) bell hangs in its pavilion to this day; the Burmese refloated the 23-ton bronze by lashing bamboo beneath it until it rose. Nearby hangs the even larger 42-ton Tharrawaddy Min bell of 1841. An earlier giant - the roughly 300-ton Great Bell of Dhammazedi (1485) - was carried off by the Portuguese mercenary Filipe de Brito in 1608 and lost in the Bago River, never recovered. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shwedagon_Pagoda; renown-travel.com.

question: Worshippers at the Shwedagon pour cups of water over one of eight planetary posts around its base, the one for the day of the week they were born. The Burmese week runs to eight days because Wednesday splits at 6 p.m., its evening half becoming the day of the shadow-planet Rahu. Each post bears an animal. Which animal marks the post for Rahu's half of Wednesday?
context: The Burmese week runs to eight days because Wednesday splits: until 6 p.m. it is Wednesday, and from 6 p.m. to midnight it becomes the day of Rahu, the shadow-planet. Each of the eight posts carries an animal emblem - garuda for Sunday, tiger for Monday, lion for Tuesday, a tusked elephant for Wednesday morning, and a tuskless elephant for Rahu's evening half, then a mouse for Thursday, a guinea pig for Friday, and the naga (dragon-serpent) for Saturday. Worshippers find the post for the day they were born and pour cups of water over its Buddha image for luck. Source: myanmar2day.com; tourhq.com.

question: Shin Sawbu, a famous 15th-century queen of Bago, reportedly made a great gift of gold to gild the Shwedagon's stupa, and tradition says she set the pattern for every donor who followed in the centuries after her. What did she reportedly give?
choices: A solid gold statue of herself
A thousand bars of pure gold
A golden bell for each shrine
context: Queen Shin Sawbu, the 15th-century ruler of Bago, is said to have donated her own body weight in gold to gild the stupa, beginning the custom of pilgrims from across Buddhist Asia giving gold to maintain it ever since. This is tradition rather than documented fact. Source: renown-travel.com; sacred-destinations.com.  (Legend.)

question: A sheer column of granite, Sigiriya, juts about 180 metres straight up out of the flat jungle of central Sri Lanka. A king made it his royal capital in the 5th century. Where on the rock did he build the palace itself?
choices: On an island in the moat
context: Sigiriya is an inselberg -- the hardened granite magma plug of a long-dead volcano -- rising about 180 m above the plain (349 m above sea level). King Kashyapa set his palace on the roughly flat summit, a royal court in the sky. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya.

question: The only path to Sigiriya's summit narrowed near the top. Every climber was forced up a staircase leading into the open mouth of a colossal brick beast crouching against the rock. Passing through its jaws was the last gate to the palace above. What animal was this great gatehouse built as?
context: The gate gave the rock its name: Sinhagiri, 'Lion Rock,' which wore down to 'Sigiriya.' You climbed a staircase set between the lion's enormous paws and into its mouth. The head collapsed centuries ago, so today only the two carved paws survive -- each about 3 m long -- flanking the roughly 1,200-step climb. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; nationalgeographic.com.

question: Halfway up the sheer face of Sigiriya, a shallow overhang has sheltered a row of life-sized figures from sun and monsoon rain for about 1,500 years. Around two dozen survive from a painted band that once ran 140 metres along the cliff. What do these figures show?
context: These are the famous 'cloud maidens' -- bare-shouldered celestial women (apsaras), among the oldest surviving frescoes in Sri Lanka (Anuradhapura period). Only about 21-22 remain of a band that may once have held some 500 ladies, 140 m long and 40 m high. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; nationalgeographic.com.

question: Just below Sigiriya's cliff frescoes runs a long wall of brick, coated by the ancient builders in a hard, pale lime plaster. Sinhalese tradition holds that King Kashyapa prized this wall for one startling reason as he walked beside it. What did tradition say he could do at its surface?
context: This is the Mirror Wall: the lime plaster was polished so glassy that, tradition says, King Kashyapa could see his own reflection as he passed. Brick masonry lies beneath the mirror-bright coating, which still shines in places today. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; ccf.gov.lk.  (Legend.)

question: Long after King Kashyapa's time, ordinary travellers kept climbing Sigiriya to see its famous cliff paintings. Below the paintings ran a long plastered wall. Generation after generation added something to it. Over 1,500 survive from the 700s to the 900s, left by everyone from governors to housewives. What did these visitors leave behind?
context: The Mirror Wall is covered in over 1,500 short poems -- ancient graffiti admiring the painted maidens. One marvels at 'the rock that captivates the mind'; another, some 1,200 years old, reads: 'The caress of the gentle breeze was delicate upon their bodies, illuminated by the light of the moon's rays.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; nationalgeographic.com.

question: King Kashyapa raised the whole Sigiriya fortress partly out of fear: he had seized Sri Lanka's throne by murdering his own father, and he dreaded the vengeance of his half-brother Moggallana, who had fled overseas to raise an army. In 495 CE that army finally returned. Where did Kashyapa meet his end?
answer: On the battlefield below the rock
choices: On the battlefield below the rock
In his palace on the summit
context: As Moggallana advanced, Kashyapa's troops turned aside to skirt a swamp; believing himself abandoned, the king took his own life on the battlefield at the foot of his own rock. Afterward Sigiriya was given over to Buddhist monks. (The death is known from the Sinhalese chronicles.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; nationalgeographic.com.  (Legend.)

question: At the foot of Sigiriya spread symmetrical royal water gardens, fed through underground clay pipes and pressure chambers built by King Kashyapa's engineers around 1,500 years ago. Set flush into the garden paths are round fountains cut from limestone plates. What still surprises visitors about these ancient fountains?
answer: They still jet water when it rains
choices: They still jet water when it rains
They mark the four compass points
They doubled as the palace sundials
context: Fed by the monsoon, the limestone-plate fountains still spurt water after some 1,500 years -- among the oldest surviving landscaped, hydraulic gardens on Earth. The grounds stack three garden kinds up the slope: the symmetrical water gardens on the flat approach, wilder boulder gardens with carved stone seats, and terraced gardens climbing to the cliff. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya; ccf.gov.lk.

question: In Henan province, in central China, archaeologists digging out a Stone Age village of the Yangshao culture uncovered a scrap of woven silk. It dates to about 3630 BC, making it the oldest piece of silk cloth ever discovered on Earth. What had this most ancient silk been used for?
choices: binding a bundle of ritual millet
context: The woven silk from about 3630 BC — over five thousand years old — was found at a Yangshao site in Henan wrapped around the body of a child, a sign that silk was treasured as something precious and sacred from the very dawn of the craft. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_silk

question: The shoreline of Singapore keeps creeping out to sea. Since the 1960s the crowded island city has grown by about a quarter, and it holds the world record as Earth's fastest-growing country. Which process gave it all this extra ground?
context: Land reclamation grew Singapore from about 582 km² in the 1960s to roughly 723 km² today — a ~24% gain and the fastest of any nation (a Guinness World Record). Volcanic eruptions, river sedimentation (delta-building), and coral reef growth all add land in nature, but only reclamation — piling imported sand into the shallow sea — builds Singapore's new coast on purpose. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation_in_Singapore; guinnessworldrecords.com

question: Warm downpours drench Singapore, in Southeast Asia, nearly every day of the year, and the island city knows no summer and no winter. It lies only about 85 miles from a famous imaginary line drawn on the globe. Which line lies so close?
context: Lying just ~137 km (85 miles) north of the equator, where the sun stays nearly overhead all year, Singapore has no summer or winter — only warm, wet weather. The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn and the Prime Meridian all cross the globe elsewhere. Source: britannica.com/place/Singapore; distancefromequator.com

question: Eighteen steel towers up to 50 metres tall stand at Gardens by the Bay, on Singapore's Marina waterfront, each wrapped in living ferns and vines. The tallest also bear solar panels and catch rain, and every night the towers glow in a light show. What are these plant-covered towers called?
context: Gardens by the Bay's 18 Supertrees, 25–50 m tall, are vertical gardens on steel frames; the tallest carry solar cells and rainwater collectors, and they light up nightly in the 'Garden Rhapsody' sound-and-light show. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardens_by_the_Bay

question: Rain that falls on the great glass dome of Jewel Changi Airport, in Singapore, pours down through a round opening in its roof, and terraced gardens of ferns and palms ring the falling water. The cascade is called the Rain Vortex. Which world record does it hold?
choices: the world's one and only indoor waterfall
the world's most powerful indoor waterfall
context: Jewel Changi Airport's Rain Vortex, opened in 2019, drops 40 m and can flow at up to about 37,850 litres a minute. Guinness lists it as the world's tallest indoor waterfall. Outdoor giants like Venezuela's Angel Falls (about 980 m) fall far farther, but no indoor cascade drops farther than the Rain Vortex. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewel_Changi_Airport

question: Lee Kuan Yew, Singapore's first prime minister, set out in 1967 to turn his young island nation into a lush, tree-filled city. For decades he planted a young tree himself almost every year, while government crews lined every road and public square with greenery. What nickname did Singapore take to match?
context: Lee Kuan Yew, nicknamed the nation's 'Chief Gardener,' made greenery state policy from 1967, and Singapore embraced the 'Garden City' name; today it has over 100 hectares of rooftop gardens and green walls. 'Lion City' (from Singapura) is its older name, 'Green City' is a generic label used for many eco-cities, and 'Pearl of the Orient' belongs to other Asian ports. Source: cnbc.com; nas.gov.sg/archivesonline/gardencity

question: The water of Marina Bay laps at the heart of downtown Singapore, an island with almost no room for rivers or lakes. Singapore completed the Marina Barrage there in 2008, a dam sealing the bay off from the sea, and rainwater slowly washed the salt away. What does the bay now mainly supply?
context: Sealed from the tides and refreshed by rain, Marina Bay became Singapore's 15th reservoir — a freshwater drinking supply in the middle of downtown that also eases floods in low-lying Chinatown and hosts kayakers and dragonboats. The Marina Barrage opened 31 October 2008. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marina_Barrage

question: Olive trees, baobabs and desert succulents grow in cool, dry air inside the Flower Dome at Gardens by the Bay, in Singapore, a hall of plants about 1.2 hectares across under one great curve of steel and glass. Which world record did it set in 2015?
context: The Flower Dome, opened 2012, spans about 1.2 hectares under a column-free steel-and-glass shell — the world's largest columnless glasshouse (Guinness, 2015) — kept cool and dry to grow olive trees, baobabs, and desert succulents. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardens_by_the_Bay

question: Sand ran short in Singapore when its neighbours stopped selling it, yet the crowded island still needed more ground. In 2016 it borrowed a centuries-old method from the Netherlands: rather than pile sand into the shallows, engineers enclose a patch of sea and pump it dry, using far less sand. What is land made this Dutch way called?
context: A polder is land reclaimed the Dutch way — ringed by a dike and pumped dry — and Singapore adopted the method in November 2016 to build new land using far less sand than piling it into the sea. A cofferdam also walls off water and pumps it dry, but only temporarily, to work in the dry on a bridge pier or dam foundation; a breakwater is an offshore wall that calms the waves; a caisson is a watertight box sunk to build underwater foundations. Singapore turned to polders because its neighbours had cut off its sand: Malaysia banned exports in 1997, Indonesia (once over 90% of the supply) in 2007, and Vietnam in 2009. Only about 10% of the country was reclaimed by 1991, and it plans to add roughly another 7–8% by 2030. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation_in_Singapore

question: West of the city, Singapore fused seven small offshore islets into a single artificial island, completed in 2009 and covering over 3,500 hectares. Though the country pumps no crude oil of its own, this made-from-scratch island refines about 1.5 million barrels a day. What is it called?
context: Jurong Island, completed in 2009, was formed by reclaiming and merging seven islets (from ~991 to over 3,500 hectares). With no crude of its own, Singapore refines about 1.5 million barrels a day here, ranking among the world's top three refining centres. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurong_Island

question: Singapore grew up beside a narrow sea-gate between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, the shortest sea route between the Indian and Pacific oceans. At its tightest, near the city, this passage pinches to just 2.8 km wide. What is this waterway called?
context: The Strait of Malacca is the shortest sea route between the Indian and Pacific oceans; near Singapore, the Phillips Channel narrows to about 2.8 km. The Straits of Hormuz, Gibraltar, and Dover are famous sea-gates elsewhere — joining the Persian Gulf, the Mediterranean, and the North Sea to their neighbouring waters — but only Malacca threads its narrows past Singapore between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strait_of_Malacca

question: A winter storm in 1850 stripped the grass and sand from a low mound above the Bay of Skaill, in Scotland's Orkney islands. Underneath lay the stone walls of a village buried for about 5,000 years. What is this Stone Age village called?
context: A wild storm in the winter of 1850 tore the turf from a mound above the Bay of Skaill, exposing the stone houses. Excavation eventually revealed a complete Neolithic (Stone Age) village -- the best-preserved in all of Western Europe. Source: Historic Environment Scotland, historicenvironment.scot/visit-a-place/places/skara-brae/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.

question: People lived in the stone village of Skara Brae, on Orkney, for some six centuries, between about 3200 and 2500 BC, before sand hid it for thousands of years. Egypt's Great Pyramid of Giza strikes many as the very dawn of history. How does Skara Brae's age compare with the pyramid's?
answer: older than the Great Pyramid by centuries
choices: older than the Great Pyramid by centuries
the same age as the Great Pyramid
younger than the Great Pyramid by a thousand years
younger than the Great Pyramid by two thousand years
context: Skara Brae was a thriving village around 3200-2500 BC, lived in for roughly 600 years -- older than Stonehenge and older than the Egyptian pyramids. Historic Environment Scotland puts it plainly: 'Long before Stonehenge or even the Egyptian pyramids were built, Skara Brae was a thriving village.' (The Great Pyramid of Giza dates to about 2560 BC.) Source: historicenvironment.scot/visit-a-place/places/skara-brae/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.

question: Drifting sand buried Skara Brae so gently and so fully, with its beds, dressers and tools, that it sealed a normal day of Stone Age life just as the villagers had left it. The little Orkney village earned a nickname from a famous buried city in Italy. What nickname did Skara Brae earn?
context: The nickname is only a comparison about preservation -- no volcano was involved. Wind-blown sand, not volcanic ash, gradually buried Skara Brae and sealed its furniture and tools, freezing a moment of Stone Age daily life much as Vesuvius's ash froze Roman Pompeii in AD 79. Source: thearchaeologist.org (Neolithic Skara Brae: the Scottish Pompeii); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.

question: Beds, seats and dressers still stand inside the houses of Skara Brae, on Orkney, after 5,000 years, while at most ancient sites the wooden furniture rotted away within a few centuries. Why did this one village's furniture last when almost all other prehistoric furniture has crumbled?
answer: the villagers built it from stone, not wood
choices: the villagers built it from stone, not wood
the cold peat bog tanned and preserved the wood
it lay sealed airtight inside a rock-cut tomb
it was carved from rot-proof bog-oak
context: Windswept Orkney had almost no trees for timber, so the villagers made their furniture from flat slabs of local stone -- stone beds, stone seats and stone dressers -- which is why it has survived 5,000 years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae; historicenvironment.scot/visit-a-place/places/skara-brae/.

question: Atlantic gales drive wind, rain and salt spray across Orkney, and the builders of Skara Brae set their houses close together against them. They joined each house to the next, so the villagers could pass from home to home without ever stepping into the storm. How were the houses of Skara Brae linked?
answer: by low passages roofed over with stone slabs
choices: by low passages roofed over with stone slabs
by a single roofed hall all the doors opened onto
by tunnels bored down through the solid bedrock
by covered walkways around an enclosed courtyard
context: Skara Brae's houses were joined by low passages, roofed over with stone and only about a metre high, so people could move from home to home sheltered from the weather. The walls were further insulated by 'midden' -- composted ash, bone and shell -- packed between double stone skins. Source: orkneyology.com/skara-brae.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.

question: Almost every house at Skara Brae, the Stone Age village on Orkney, has a small stone cubicle set into its thick wall, just big enough for one person. Archaeologists think each one served a very familiar everyday purpose. What do they believe these little wall-recesses were?
context: Skara Brae had a drainage system running in stone-lined channels beneath the houses, and each little wall-cubicle was plumbed into it -- one main reason archaeologists read the recess as a toilet. If so, it gave Skara Brae indoor sanitation that most later Orcadians would not have again until the 20th century. (The reading as a toilet is likely but not certain.) Source: orkneyology.com/skara-brae.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skara_Brae.  (Legend.)

question: The Stone Age people of Orkney closed the largest hall at the Ness of Brodgar, a great temple complex near Skara Brae, sometime between about 2400 and 2200 BC. Rather than quietly walking away, they marked the closing with one enormous ceremony and left the evidence heaped in the ruins. What did archaeologists find there?
answer: the shin-bones of some 400 slaughtered cattle
choices: the shin-bones of some 400 slaughtered cattle
the shards of thousands of smashed clay pots
a ring of carved stone balls set into the floor
the ashes of a huge timber roof burnt to the ground
context: The Ness of Brodgar, between the Ring of Brodgar and the Stones of Stenness, held 'Structure Ten,' one of the largest Neolithic buildings in northern Britain. Around 2400-2200 BC it was ceremonially closed with a vast feast: excavators found roughly 400 cattle tibias (shin-bones), the remains of hundreds of slaughtered animals. Skara Brae, Brodgar and Stenness together make up the UNESCO 'Heart of Neolithic Orkney.' (A closing feast is the leading interpretation of the bone deposit.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ness_of_Brodgar.  (Legend.)

question: Crowds stroll the embankments of St Petersburg past midnight for a few weeks around midsummer, when the city never really goes dark. The sun barely dips below the horizon, and the sky still glows bright enough to read outdoors. What are these luminous nights called?
context: Near the solstice St Petersburg gets about 18 hours 50 minutes of daylight, and even the rest of the night stays in bright twilight, light enough to read outdoors. This isn't the true 'midnight sun' (where the sun never sets at all): here it slips just below the horizon, so the sky glows rather than shines. The season fills the embankments and bridges with crowds past midnight. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_sun; russiable.com/white-nights-st-petersburg/

question: More than 60 rivers and canals thread between the islands of St Petersburg, in the low delta where the Neva meets the Baltic. Over 300 bridges tie the city together, and the maze earned it a nickname from a famous European water-city. What is the nickname?
context: Land reclamation trimmed the delta's original ~101 islands to about 42, and the city is crossed by 342 bridges over its rivers and canals, with some tallies running past 500. All that water threading between the islands is why St Petersburg is called the Venice of the North. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bridges_in_Saint_Petersburg; introducingsaintpetersburg.com/bridges

question: Peter the Great ordered a brand-new capital built in 1703 on a cold, misty marsh at the mouth of the Neva. Forced peasants and Swedish war prisoners drove countless wooden piles into the swamp, and tens of thousands died in the mud. What grim folk nickname did St Petersburg earn?
choices: the city of a thousand sorrows
context: The founding date, 27 May 1703, is still marked as the city's birthday. Peter the Great forced his capital onto ground everyone called unbuildable; conscripted peasants and Swedish prisoners of war drained the swamp and drove countless wooden piles, and tens of thousands of forced laborers died, the real human cost behind the grim folk name. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg

question: A special staff has hunted rats and mice in the cellars of St Petersburg's Hermitage museum for nearly 300 years. Empress Elizabeth first brought them in during the 1740s to guard the Winter Palace and its treasures, and each of them still receives a name and a passport. What are these guardians?
context: A resident population of cats has protected the Hermitage's cellars and courtyards from rats for centuries, a tradition dating back to imperial times: Empress Elizabeth first had cats brought in to guard the palace. They still work the basements today, though they are kept out of the galleries. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitage_Museum

question: Tiny Hare Island, in the Neva delta, holds the very first structure of St Petersburg, which Peter the Great began on 27 May 1703; the whole imperial capital spread outward from it. Which landmark is it?
context: The Peter and Paul Fortress was laid down on 27 May 1703 on tiny Zayachy (Hare) Island in the Neva delta. The citadel came first, and the imperial capital grew outward from it across the marsh; it is the founding kernel of the whole city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg

question: Catherine the Great started the collection of St Petersburg's Hermitage in 1764 by buying a batch of about 225 paintings. Today, behind the Winter Palace's facade, it holds some three million works of art and objects. Where does that place the Hermitage among the world's museums?
context: The single largest is the Louvre in Paris; the Hermitage ranks second by the size of its collection. It grew from Catherine the Great's 1764 purchase of about 225 paintings from the Berlin merchant Johann Ernst Gotzkowsky, the batch that founded the imperial collection, now spread through the Winter Palace and its neighboring buildings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermitage_Museum

question: A walker who lingers on the far bank of the Neva in St Petersburg after about 1 a.m., on any night from spring to autumn, can find himself stranded there until nearly dawn. What do the river's great bridges do in those hours?
answer: rise open to let ocean ships pass
choices: rise open to let ocean ships pass
lift to let spring ice floes through
close off for their nightly maintenance
swing shut against Gulf storm surges
context: St Petersburg is a working seaport, and ocean-going cargo ships can only move along the Neva when the bridges lift. In navigation season (roughly late April to November) the drawbridges open on a nightly schedule; the famous Palace Bridge splits open around 1:10 a.m. and lowers again near 4:55 a.m., so anyone caught on the wrong bank waits for dawn. Source: russiable.com/drawbridges-st-petersburg-schedules/; travelallrussia.com/blog/drawing-bridges

question: St Petersburg's Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood glitters inside with more than 7,500 square metres of mosaic, more than any other church on Earth. But its grim name comes from the very ground it covers: the exact spot where, in 1881, someone was killed. Who died there?
answer: a tsar, killed by a bomb blast
choices: a tsar, killed by a bomb blast
a grand duchess, lost in a fire
an army general, shot by an assassin
context: The victim was Tsar Alexander II, struck down by a bomb on this spot in 1881, the killing that gave the church its name, 'Savior on Spilled Blood.' Inside, over 7,500 square metres of mosaic cover the walls and vaults, more than in any other church in the world. Source: historyhit.com/locations/church-of-the-saviour-on-spilled-blood/

question: At Peter the Great's palace of Peterhof outside St Petersburg, more than 100 fountains have played every summer since 1721. The giant Grand Cascade shoots water skyward without using any machinery whatsoever. What lifts the water into those towering jets?
answer: gravity, from springs on higher ground
choices: gravity, from springs on higher ground
the daily rise and fall of Baltic tides
steady wind off the Gulf of Finland
context: The secret is elevation: water is gathered from natural springs in the Ropsha Heights about 22-24 km away and some 90 m higher, then channeled downhill. Arriving under its own weight, it has enough pressure to shoot skyward, no pumps needed. Engineered by Vasily Tuvolkov, the system has run this way since 1721, and the Grand Cascade alone feeds 64 fountains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peterhof_Palace; unesco.ru/en/news/55-peterhof/

question: The golden centerpiece of Peterhof, its tallest fountain, fires a single jet some 20 metres straight up and celebrates Russia's crushing victory over Sweden. At its heart, a gilded strongman is locked in combat with a great beast. Which hero and beast does the statue show?
answer: Samson tearing open a lion's jaws
choices: Samson tearing open a lion's jaws
context: The Samson Fountain marks Russia's victory over Sweden: a lion is Sweden's heraldic emblem, and Samson, standing for Russia, rips its jaws apart. Its single vertical jet reaches about 20 metres (66 ft), the tallest of all Peterhof's fountains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peterhof_Palace

question: Four hundred men spent months hauling a lone slab of granite weighing about 1,500 tonnes overland to St Petersburg, rolling it over a track of bronze balls without animals or machines. On it now rears the Bronze Horseman, Peter the Great on his horse. What is the rock called?
context: The Thunder Stone is a single granite boulder of roughly 1,500 tonnes (about 1,250 after carving), among the largest stones ever moved by people. Workers hauled it overland on a metal sled sliding over a track of bronze balls, 400 men over about nine months, with no animals or machines, then floated it the rest of the way by barge. The statue was sculpted by the Frenchman Etienne Maurice Falconet for Catherine the Great and unveiled in 1782; Alexander Pushkin's 1833 poem gave it the enduring name 'The Bronze Horseman.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Horseman

question: The Neva freezes solid for months every winter in St Petersburg, yet around midsummer the sky over the same city never fully darkens and people linger outdoors at midnight. One fact about the city's position causes both extremes. Which fact is that?
choices: how low it sits above the sea
how far it lies inland from the sea
how mountainous the land around it is
context: At about 60 degrees north (59 degrees 57 minutes N), St Petersburg sits on the polar edge, far enough from the equator that the swing between summer and winter light is extreme. Near midsummer the sun barely dips below the horizon, giving the glowing White Nights; in deep winter it scarcely rises and the Neva locks in ice. Latitude alone sets the whole rhythm of the city's year. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg; russiable.com/white-nights-st-petersburg/

question: Lake Mälaren spills its fresh water into the salty Baltic at Stockholm, and the old city does not hug one bank of the channel as most cities would. It spreads itself right out across the water. How is historic Stockholm laid out?
choices: A city raised on 14 wooden piers
A city split by 14 river channels
context: Stockholm sits on 14 islands at the outlet of Lake Mälaren into the Baltic, historically nicknamed 'the city between the bridges' (Staden mellan broarna) for the bridges stitching its islands together — Wikipedia counts about thirty bridges in the central city. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Stockholm

question: The streets of Gamla Stan, Stockholm's medieval old town on one small island, twist and narrow between tall ochre-gold houses. Tightest of all is a stepped alley, Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, the narrowest street in the city. How wide is it at its tightest squeeze?
answer: About 90 centimeters — barely a shoulder's width
choices: About 90 centimeters — barely a shoulder's width
About 3 meters — a single cart's width
About 6 meters — two carts side by side
context: Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, a stepped alley in Gamla Stan, is the narrowest street in Stockholm — about 90 cm at its tightest squeeze. Gamla Stan ('the Old Town'), crowded onto the island of Stadsholmen, dates to the 13th century and is one of the largest and best-preserved medieval city cores in Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamla_stan

question: A sailor heading east from Stockholm watches the Swedish coast break up into countless little islands, skerries and bare rocks reaching far out into the Baltic. Counts vary from source to source. About how many islands make up the Stockholm Archipelago?
context: The Stockholm Archipelago scatters some 30,000 islands, islets, and skerries into the Baltic — a skerry being a small rocky islet too barren to build on. The exact total is genuinely uncertain: counts range from about 24,000 to over 30,000 depending on the source, so 'roughly 30,000' is the honest figure. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_Archipelago  (Legend.)

question: Riders stepping off a train in the Stockholm Metro find no ordinary station: most of its roughly 100 stops open into caverns of raw bedrock painted with colour, and at T-Centralen huge blue vines climb the bare stone. What nickname has the metro earned around the world?
context: The Stockholm Metro is called 'the world's longest art gallery': more than 90 of its ~100 stations are painted, sculpted, or blasted straight into the bare bedrock and decorated by over 150 artists along 105.7 km of track. At T-Centralen, the central hub, Per Olof Ultvedt painted cave-like blue vines and leaves across the raw rock. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_metro  (Legend.)

question: Crowds packed Stockholm's harbour in August 1628 to cheer the Vasa, the pride of the Swedish navy: the tallest, most heavily armed warship the kingdom had ever built, glittering with hundreds of gilded carvings. For all that glory, what humiliating fact is the Vasa remembered for?
answer: She capsized and sank in the harbor on her very first voyage
choices: She capsized and sank in the harbor on her very first voyage
She rotted at her moorings, never once putting to sea
She was captured by the Danish fleet within a year
She was lost with all hands in a storm off Poland
context: On 10 August 1628, the Vasa capsized and sank on her maiden voyage after sailing barely 1,300 m — going down only about 120 m from shore, as roughly 30 people drowned, in full view of the watching crowd. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)

question: The Vasa's builders crowded two full decks of heavy bronze cannon high in her hull to make her a terror at sea, but left too little ballast in her belly to steady all that weight. A light breeze in Stockholm's harbour pushed on her sails and heeled her far over. Why was that single lean enough to sink her?
answer: Her open lower gunports let the sea pour in
choices: Her open lower gunports let the sea pour in
Her tall masts snapped and dragged her under
Her powder store caught fire deep in the hull
Her loose cannon smashed out through the deck
context: The Vasa's center of gravity sat too high over two gundecks of cannon, with too little ballast below; a light gust heeled her, and water flooded in through the open lower gunports until she went down. She carried 64 guns, mostly 48 heavy 24-pounder bronze cannon — the very weight, mounted high, that doomed her. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)

question: The warship Vasa came up from the bottom of Stockholm's harbour in 1961, after 333 years under the Baltic. Shipworms devour oak hulls in most seas within decades, but the Baltic is too cold and too fresh for them, and they never touched her. How much of her original oak was still intact?
context: Because the cold, brackish (low-salt) Baltic water excludes the wood-eating shipworm Teredo navalis, about 98% of the Vasa was still original oak when she was raised in 1961 after 333 years on the bottom. She is the only almost-fully-intact 17th-century ship ever salvaged, now displayed whole in the Vasa Museum (opened 1990). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)

question: New skerries of bare rock break the surface of the Baltic in the Stockholm Archipelago, and the islands already there stand a few millimetres higher above the water every year. Old shorelines creep inland as the land climbs out of the sea. What keeps lifting these islands, year after year?
choices: A slow fall in the sea level
Silt piling up from the rivers
context: As the kilometer-thick ice sheets of the last Ice Age melted, the enormous weight lifted off the crust, which is still slowly springing back — post-glacial (isostatic) rebound — raising the Stockholm region about 3 mm a year and lifting the archipelago's 'joint valley landscape' up out of the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_Archipelago

question: In Stone Town on Zanzibar, families traditionally built one part of the house before the walls went up. Hundreds still stand along the narrow alleys. Each is a heavy slab carved with symbols that showed the owner's trade, faith, and wealth. What is it?
context: Stone Town is famous for more than 500 hand-carved wooden doors. The door went up first when a house was built, and its carvings advertised the owner -- Qur'anic verses for the devout, a fish for a fisherman, lotus flowers and chains for prosperity. (Source: Wikipedia 'Stone Town'; TingaTinga Art 'The Zanzibar Door'; Preservation Journey 'The Doors of Zanzibar')

question: Merchants in Zanzibar's Stone Town cut a local rock into blocks, bound them with lime mortar and raised tall houses of several storeys, while the coastal villages around them rose in mud and thatch. That stone gave the town its name. What stone is it?
context: The stone is coralline ragstone -- fossil coral quarried from the reef -- laced with mangrove-pole timber. Fusing Swahili, Arab, Indian and European styles, the old town became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. (Source: UNESCO WHC 'Stone Town of Zanzibar'; Wikipedia 'Stone Town')

question: Rows of fat brass spikes bristle from the oldest doors of Stone Town, on Zanzibar, though the island never faced a siege. The design came from India, where such studs on fort gates blunted an attack that could otherwise batter a gate off its hinges. What were the studs first meant to stop?
context: Indian fort gates were studded to keep war elephants from battering them down. Zanzibar never fought such a war, so on the island the brass spikes became pure decoration -- a badge of a merchant's wealth during the spice-trade boom. (Source: TingaTinga Art 'The Zanzibar Door'; Atlas Obscura 'The Doors of Stone Town'; Preservation Journey 'The Doors of Zanzibar')  (Legend.)

question: Plantations spread across Zanzibar, off the coast of East Africa, under its Omani rulers until, by the mid-1800s, the small island grew more of one aromatic spice than anywhere else on Earth, and traders took to calling it the Spice Island. Which spice was it?
context: The Omani ruler pushed clove plantations across the island, and by the mid-1800s Zanzibar dominated the world clove trade -- the source of the 'Spice Island' name. (Source: Britannica 'Said ibn Sultan'; Capable Africa Tours 'History of Zanzibar'; BlackPast 'Sultanate of Zanzibar')

question: One of the twentieth century's most famous rock singers began life in 1946 in an ordinary house in Stone Town's alleys -- born Farrokh Bulsara to Parsi parents, before his family left the island for England when he was 17. His birthplace is now a small museum on the visitor trail. Which rock star was born there?
context: He was born Farrokh Bulsara in Stone Town in 1946; the family later moved to England, where he became Freddie Mercury, frontman of the band Queen. The house where he lived is now a small museum. (Source: Machu Picchu 'Stone Town Zanzibar Guide 2026'; Wikipedia 'Stone Town')

question: Said bin Sultan, Oman's ruler, did something startling around 1840: he moved his capital from Muscat, in Arabia, across the ocean to Stone Town, on the African island of Zanzibar that his family ruled. A ruler almost never leaves his ancestral seat. What made the island worth more to him than Oman?
choices: its fort on a sea strait
