context: The wealth pouring out of his East African clove and trade empire had grown larger than Oman's own revenue, so Said bin Sultan moved his capital from Muscat to Stone Town around 1840. (Source: Britannica 'Said ibn Sultan'; Gulf News 'Zanzibar: A slice of Oman'; BlackPast 'Seyyid Said')

question: Traders in Stone Town once bought and sold captives carried from deep in the African interior, at East Africa's largest slave market. Once Britain had forced the market shut, workers raised the Anglican Christ Church Cathedral on that ground from 1873 and set its altar on the very spot where one grim fixture of the market had stood. What was it?
context: The Anglican Christ Church Cathedral was begun on Christmas Day 1873 and opened in 1879 on the old slave-market site; its altar stands where the market's whipping post once stood. Below, the cramped underground cells where captives were packed to await sale are still preserved. (Source: Wikipedia 'Christ Church, Zanzibar'; Pongwe 'Christ Church Cathedral & the Old Slave Market')

question: Sultan Barghash bin Said built a vast ceremonial palace on the Stone Town seafront in 1883, with marble floors and tall pillared verandas rising over the old town's alleys. People called it the House of Wonders, Beit-al-Ajaib, for two marvels: one no other building in East Africa had, the other new to Zanzibar. What made the palace so wondrous?
answer: it had electric light and an elevator
choices: it had electric light and an elevator
it had a rooftop garden and a zoo
it had gold walls and an ivory throne
it had a moat and a working drawbridge
context: The House of Wonders (Beit-al-Ajaib), built by Sultan Barghash in 1883, was the first building in East Africa to have an elevator and the first in Zanzibar with electric light, running water and marble floors -- hence its name. A corner of it collapsed during a restoration in 2020, and Oman offered to help rebuild it. (Source: The National 'What is the House of Wonders?'; Wikipedia 'Stone Town'; Anadolu Agency)

question: Flat stone beams ride in a ring on top of the standing stones of Stonehenge, and they do not simply balance there. About 4,500 years ago the builders locked each one in place with a joint borrowed from woodworking. What is this joint called?
context: A tenon -- a carved knob on top of each upright -- was dropped into a mortise, a hollow cut into the underside of the lintel, reproducing a woodworking joint in solid stone around 2500 BC. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge

question: The rising sun at Stonehenge, on one special morning each year, climbs over a lone outlying stone and pours straight down the monument's main line into the ring. To which sunrise is this 5,000-year-old alignment set?
context: At midsummer the sun rises over the Heel Stone and runs along Stonehenge's axis, so the monument works as a roughly 5,000-year-old solar calendar marking the year's turning points. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Solstice_at_Stonehenge

question: Stonehenge's builders shaped the curved beams of its top ring to lock end to end, each joined to the next with a carpenter's joint, so the whole ring holds together as one unbroken hoop. Nothing like it is known at any other prehistoric stone circle. Which joint links the beams?
context: A tongue carved on one lintel's end slotted into a groove in the next, so Stonehenge's sarsen lintels interlocked all the way around the ring like fitted timber -- unique among the world's ancient stone circles. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge

question: The Devil, an old English folk tale says, boasted that no one could ever count the stones of Stonehenge, then caught a friar quietly tallying them and hurled a huge block at him. According to the tale, what happened when the stone reached the friar?
answer: it bounced off the friar's heel
choices: it bounced off the friar's heel
it crushed him where he stood
it split in two as it fell
it sank deep into the soft ground
context: In the folk tale the stone struck the friar's heel so hard it dented the stone -- which is why the outlying block is nicknamed the 'Friar's Heel' or Heel Stone. This is legend, not history. Source: https://blog.stonehenge-stone-circle.co.uk/2011/03/16/stonehenge-folklore/

question: Stone Age builders hauled the smaller bluestones of Stonehenge, just 2 to 4 tons each, some 230 km to Salisbury Plain, one of the longest stone-hauls of the ancient world, while its giant outer sarsens came from close at hand. Where did the bluestones come from?
context: The bluestones were quarried in the Preseli Hills of west Wales and moved roughly 230 km to Stonehenge -- among the longest-distance transports of monument stone known anywhere in the ancient world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge

question: Visitors once strolled right over a long, flat slab at the very centre of Stonehenge without a second look: the Altar Stone, about five metres of stone lying flat instead of standing. Much of it is hidden from view today. What keeps so much of it out of sight?
answer: a huge toppled sarsen lying across it
choices: a huge toppled sarsen lying across it
deep soil that drifted over and buried it
a thick mat of turf grown across it
a heap of chalk rubble piled over it
context: The Altar Stone (Stone 80) lies flat near Stonehenge's centre, partly pinned beneath a toppled sarsen, Stone 55, that fell across it -- which is why much of the slab stays hidden and it is so easily missed today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar_Stone_(Stonehenge)

question: David Nash, a geographer, led a team in 2020 that read the chemical fingerprint of the giant sarsens in Stonehenge's outer ring, 25-ton stones whose source had been a mystery for centuries. The fingerprint pointed to one particular place. Where did the great sarsens come from?
context: A 2020 study led by geographer David Nash traced 50 of the 52 surviving sarsens to West Woods near Marlborough, only about 25 km north of Stonehenge, using portable X-ray fluorescence. Source: https://theconversation.com/stonehenge-how-we-revealed-the-original-source-of-the-biggest-stones-143564

question: Archaeologists digging at the Welsh quarry that gave Stonehenge its bluestones turned up a puzzle. The stones were cut there around 3400 BC, but they were not standing at Stonehenge until roughly 2900 BC, which is centuries later. What do many archaeologists now suspect happened in between?
answer: the bluestones first stood in an older Welsh monument
choices: the bluestones first stood in an older Welsh monument
the Welsh quarry kept cutting stone for other circles
the quarry dates were measured wrongly
the stones lay abandoned at the quarry for ages
context: The centuries-long gap hints the Preseli bluestones may have been raised in a stone circle in Wales first, then dismantled and carried to Salisbury Plain -- though this remains a hypothesis. Source: https://phys.org/news/2019-02-quarrying-stonehenge-bluestones-dated-bc.html

question: The flat Altar Stone at the centre of Stonehenge long passed for just another bluestone, from the same hills as the rest. Then laboratory tests in 2024 delivered a shock: the six-tonne slab had come from somewhere hundreds of kilometres away that no one had suspected. Where did it come from?
context: In 2024 researchers traced the Altar Stone to the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland -- over 700 km away and the longest journey known for any stone in any Neolithic monument. Source: https://theconversation.com/stonehenges-giant-altar-stone-came-all-the-way-from-north-east-scotland-heres-how-we-worked-out-this-astonishing-new-finding-236630

question: Researchers who traced the Altar Stone of Stonehenge to a source hundreds of miles from Salisbury Plain then faced a second puzzle: how a six-ton slab made that journey, long before the wheel is thought to have reached Britain. How do they think it got there?
answer: shipped by sea along the coast
choices: shipped by sea along the coast
floated down a chain of rivers
context: Because a 700 km overland haul of a six-tonne slab would have been extraordinary long before the wheel reached Britain, researchers think the Altar Stone most likely reached Salisbury Plain by sea, carried along Britain's coasts from northeast Scotland. Source: https://theconversation.com/stonehenges-giant-altar-stone-came-all-the-way-from-north-east-scotland-heres-how-we-worked-out-this-astonishing-new-finding-236630

question: Two of Stonehenge's giant sarsens, stones 26 and 160, stubbornly refused to match when scientists fingerprinted the great stones in 2020, though 50 of the 52 that survive traced to one single source. What does that tell archaeologists about those two?
answer: they came from a different, still-unknown source
choices: they came from a different, still-unknown source
they are natural boulders, never quarried at all
they were added by Victorian restorers
they are the oldest stones on the whole site
context: Stones 26 and 160 did not share West Woods' chemical signature, meaning at least two of Stonehenge's giant sarsens were hauled from a second source that has still not been identified. Source: https://blogs.bournemouth.ac.uk/research/2020/07/30/conversation-article-stonehenge-how-we-revealed-the-original-source-of-the-biggest-stones/

question: Gangkhar Puensum rises 7,570 metres where Bhutan meets Tibet, and Bhutan's government honours its high peaks as the sacred homes of the gods. Among all the world's great mountains, it holds one unusual record of its own. Which record is it?
choices: The most remote of all great peaks
The last great peak to be mapped
context: Gangkhar Puensum (7,570 m / 24,836 ft) on the Bhutan-Tibet border is the highest mountain on Earth that has never been climbed; its Dzongkha name means 'White Peak of the Three Spiritual Brothers.' Four expeditions failed in 1985-86, Bhutan banned peaks over 6,000 m in 1994 and all mountaineering in 2003 out of respect for the peaks as homes of gods, and a 1998 Japanese permit was later revoked. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangkhar_Puensum

question: A British team led by Jimmy Roberts set out up Machapuchare, the sacred Fish Tail of the Nepalese Himalayas, in 1957, the only attempt in its history. About 50 metres below the top, they turned around and came down. Why did they stop so close to the summit?
answer: They had promised the king to leave the top untouched
choices: They had promised the king to leave the top untouched
A sudden storm drove them back down the ridge
Their food and oxygen supplies had run out
A wall of unstable ice blocked the final climb
context: Machapuchare ('Fish Tail,' 6,993 m / 22,943 ft) in Nepal's Annapurna region was attempted only once, in 1957, by a British team under Jimmy Roberts; Wilfrid Noyce and A.D.M. Cox reached about 50 m below the top and stopped because King Mahendra had granted permission on one condition: no one set foot on the summit. The team kept the promise, no permit has been issued since, and the peak is sacred to the Gurung people as a home of Shiva. A rumored 1980s ascent by Bill Denz is unconfirmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machapuchare

question: Joe Brown and George Band made the first ascent of Kangchenjunga in 1955. At 8,586 metres it is the third-highest mountain on Earth, on the border of Nepal and Sikkim, and they had promised Tashi Namgyal, the Chogyal, or ruler, of Sikkim, to honour its sacredness. What did that promise lead them to do at the end of the climb?
answer: Stop a few steps below the true summit
choices: Stop a few steps below the true summit
Bury an offering at the true summit
Climb the last stretch only by night
context: Kangchenjunga (8,586 m / 28,169 ft), the world's third-highest mountain on the Nepal-Sikkim border, saw its first ascent in 1955 by Joe Brown and George Band, who stopped a few steps below the true summit to keep a promise to Tashi Namgyal, the Chogyal of Sikkim, that the very top stay inviolate; Norman Hardie and Tony Streather did the same two days later, and many climbers still honor the custom. The name means 'the Five Treasures of the High Snow' - salt, gold, turquoise, sacred scriptures, and invincible armour - said to reveal themselves to the devout in times of peril. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangchenjunga

question: The Tibetans who live beneath Kawagarbo, the highest mountain in China's Yunnan province, believe that anyone standing on its summit would bring disaster on them all. No one ever has, and the local government outlawed every climb in 2001. What do they believe would happen?
answer: Their guardian warrior god would abandon them
choices: Their guardian warrior god would abandon them
The mountain's glaciers would flood the valleys
The winter snows would never melt again
The spirits of the dead would lose their way
context: Kawagarbo / Kawa Karpo (Meili Snow Mountain, 6,740 m / 22,113 ft), the highest peak in China's Yunnan province, has never been summited; Tibetans believe their guardian warrior god would abandon them if any human stood on top. On 3 January 1991 a nighttime avalanche killed all 17 members of a Sino-Japanese expedition, one of the deadliest mountaineering disasters in history, and in 2001 the local government permanently banned all climbing on religious grounds. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawagarbo

question: Shinto shrines crown the summit of Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain at 3,776 metres and an active volcano, sacred in Shinto belief to the goddess Konohanasakuya-hime. Every summer, from July to early September, the mountain keeps one tradition tied to that sacred peak. What is that tradition?
answer: Pilgrims climb by the thousands to worship at the top
choices: Pilgrims climb by the thousands to worship at the top
Its summit shrines are sealed against all visitors
Only the mountain's priests may ascend above the clouds
Fires are lit around its base but never its peak
context: Mount Fuji (3,776 m / 12,389 ft), Japan's highest peak and an active volcano, is sacred in Shinto to the goddess Konohanasakuya-hime, with shrines at its summit. Rather than forbidding the top, it invites pilgrims up: an official season runs July to early September, and about 300,000 people climb each year as an act of devotion. Some sacred mountains must never be touched; others are climbed in worship. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji

question: High on a frozen mountain in Arctic Norway, a lone door in the snow opens into a vault. Inside are backup copies of the world's food crops. They came from over 80 countries so farming could restart after a global disaster. What is this famous 'doomsday' backup called?
context: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, near Longyearbyen in Norway's high-Arctic Svalbard islands, opened in 2008 as a free backup for the world's roughly 1,700 other seed banks, holding duplicate samples from gene banks in over 80 countries — the Arctic World Archive, also on Svalbard, stores data rather than seeds. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Svalbard_Global_Seed_Vault

question: Engineers drilled the Svalbard Global Seed Vault 130 metres into a mountainside whose rock has stayed frozen solid, all year round, for thousands of years. Even if the power failed, the mountain itself would keep the seeds cold. What is this kind of frozen ground called?
context: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen year-round for years on end. Deep in the mountain the permafrost would keep the seeds frozen even without power, while machines chill them further to −18°C; engineers estimate a total freezer failure would still take roughly 200 years to warm the chambers to 0°C. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svalbard_Global_Seed_Vault

question: Anyone walking out of Longyearbyen, the small town near the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, passes the last houses and steps straight into true Arctic wilderness, at about 78 degrees north. By long custom, residents of the world's northernmost town of more than a thousand people are urged to carry one thing whenever they leave. What are they urged to carry?
context: By long-standing Svalbard practice, people carry a rifle outside the settlements because of polar bears. Longyearbyen, at about 78° N, is the world's northernmost town with a permanent population over 1,000; nearby Ny-Ålesund lies even further north but is a research station, not a town. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longyearbyen

question: One hundred and twenty-eight crates of wheat, barley, lentil and chickpea seeds came out of the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in 2015 to be regrown elsewhere, the first withdrawal it had ever made. Most people had thought the vault would stay sealed until some far-off global disaster. What disaster forced that first withdrawal?
context: The seeds belonged to the ICARDA gene bank in Aleppo, Syria, whose researchers had to abandon the city during the civil war. The vault's first-ever withdrawal — about 38,000 samples in 128 crates — was regrown at safe stations in Lebanon and Morocco, then re-deposited. The 'doomsday' vault had done its job for real. Source: https://www.seedvault.no/2019/09/11/withdrawal-of-icarda-aleppo-seeds-accomplished/

question: Meltwater from a warm winter came seeping into the entrance tunnel of the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in 2017, and news reports soon announced that the vault had flooded. Millions of irreplaceable seeds lay deep inside. What actually became of them?
answer: the water froze in the tunnel before reaching them
choices: the water froze in the tunnel before reaching them
about a third of the samples thawed and spoiled
a batch of the oldest wheat seeds was ruined
they were flown to the mainland as a precaution
context: The meltwater reached only about 15 m into the entrance tunnel and froze, touching some electrical gear but never getting near the seeds, which sit behind a second sealed door deeper in the mountain. No seeds were harmed. Norway later rebuilt the tunnel to be waterproof, at a cost of about $13 million. Source: https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/doomsday-seed-vault-flooded/

question: Longyearbyen's little cemetery, on Arctic Svalbard, has taken no new burials since around 1950; the town's dead are flown south to mainland Norway instead. The reason lay underground, in an unsettling discovery the townsfolk had made about anyone laid to rest in the frozen soil. What was it?
answer: the frozen ground had preserved the bodies, which never decayed
choices: the frozen ground had preserved the bodies, which never decayed
the shifting soil kept pushing the coffins back up to the surface
meltwater had flooded and collapsed the older graves
there was never soil soft enough to dig a proper grave
context: Burials stopped around 1950 after bodies of townsfolk who died in the 1918 flu pandemic were found still preserved in the permafrost, undecayed decades later — researchers later exhumed some hoping to study the 1918 virus. It isn't literally 'illegal to die' there; there are simply no burial options, so the dead are flown to mainland Norway. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longyearbyen

question: Great white curved shells lean together like sails swelling in the wind on a narrow spit of land in Sydney's harbour, in Australia. The building beneath them opened in 1973 as one of the world's most famous concert halls. Which building is it?
context: The Sydney Opera House opened in 1973 on Bennelong Point, its white 'shells' reading as sails over the water. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most recognized buildings on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

question: A vast steel arch leaps clear over Sydney Harbour, in Australia: the Sydney Harbour Bridge, opened in 1932, among the widest steel arches in the world. To Sydneysiders its shape looked just like a common household object, and they nicknamed the bridge after it. Which object?
context: The Sydney Harbour Bridge, opened in 1932, is one of the world's widest long-span steel-arch bridges. Sydneysiders looked at its great curved silhouette and dubbed it 'the Coathanger,' and the name stuck. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge

question: Engineers spent years stumped by the swooping white roof shells that Jørn Utzon, a Danish architect, had designed for a concert hall on Sydney's harbour, each of which seemed impossible to cast in concrete. Then in 1961 Utzon cracked the puzzle: every shell could be cut from the surface of the same simple imaginary shape. Which shape?
context: Utzon's 1961 'spherical solution' let every shell be cut from the surface of one imaginary sphere (about 75 m radius), so all shared a single curve and could be mass-cast from common moulds -- the breakthrough that finally made the roof buildable. Source: sydneyoperahouse.com/our-story/the-spherical-solution

question: From across the harbour in Sydney, the great curved roof shells of Jørn Utzon's concert hall gleam a smooth, even white. Up close they never look flat or plain, and in changing light they seem to shimmer and shift. What actually covers the shells?
answer: a million glazed tiles in two shades of white
choices: a million glazed tiles in two shades of white
thousands of polished white marble slabs
hundreds of enameled white steel panels
many coats of specially mixed white paint
context: The shells wear about 1,056,006 tiles made in Sweden by Hoganas, in two finishes -- glossy white and matte cream -- laid in a chevron pattern so the roof shimmers and never looks flat. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

question: A narrow tongue of land jutting into Sydney Harbour once held an old stone battery, Fort Macquarie, and later a busy tram depot, both cleared away to make room for Jørn Utzon's shell-roofed concert hall. What is this famous point of land called?
context: Bennelong Point honors Bennelong, an Aboriginal man who lived alongside the first British governor, Arthur Phillip. A fort and then a tram depot (Fort Macquarie) stood there before both were demolished for the Opera House. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House

question: Visitors in grey jumpsuits, clipped to a safety line, do something on the Sydney Harbour Bridge that almost no other great bridge in the world lets tourists do. Its single vast steel arch springs high above the harbour. What do they do on it?
answer: climb the arch on foot to its very summit
choices: climb the arch on foot to its very summit
walk a glass floor hung beneath the road deck
ride a lift up a stone pylon to a lookout
abseil down a steel cable to the water below
context: On 'BridgeClimb,' visitors roped to a safety line ascend the steel arch to its summit -- 134 metres, more than 400 feet, above the harbor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge

question: Ships sailing into Port Jackson, Sydney's great harbour, pass the rocky Heads at its mouth, and the water beyond fans out into a maze of deep coves branching inland for miles. What do geographers call this kind of coastal feature?
context: A ria is a river valley drowned by rising seas -- here, Port Jackson's ancient valleys flooded as Ice Age ice melted, giving Sydney a shoreline that branches for miles and runs deep enough for the greatest ships. (A fjord, by contrast, is a drowned GLACIER-carved valley.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Jackson

question: Governor Arthur Phillip steered the First Fleet into Sydney's harbour in 1788 and was stunned by its size and shelter. He wrote that here was 'the finest harbour in the world,' with room for a fleet so vast he fixed it in a single ringing phrase. What did he say could ride there in perfect safety?
answer: a thousand ships of the line
choices: a thousand ships of the line
a hundred ships of the line
every ship in the Southern seas
context: Arriving in Port Jackson in 1788, Phillip called it 'the finest Harbour in the World, in which a thousand Sail of the line may ride in the most perfect security.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Jackson

question: Huge crowds at the opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge in 1932 waited for Premier Jack Lang to cut the ceremonial ribbon. Before Lang could act, a man in military uniform, Francis de Groot, spurred his horse forward and did something that stole the moment and got him arrested. What did de Groot do?
answer: slashed the ribbon with his cavalry sword
choices: slashed the ribbon with his cavalry sword
seized the scissors and hurled them into the harbor
chained his horse across the empty roadway
tore down the official banner overhead
context: Before Premier Lang could cut the ribbon, de Groot galloped up and slashed it with his cavalry sword, declaring the bridge open 'in the name of the people.' He was arrested and the ribbon retied for the official ceremony. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge

question: Jørn Utzon, the Danish architect who dreamed up the soaring roof shells over Sydney's harbour, resigned in 1966, worn down by bitter fights over money and control, and left Australia; a local team finished the building without him. Honoured at last with the Pritzker Prize in 2003, Utzon died in 2008 with one quiet sorrow shadowing his triumph. What was it?
answer: he had never once returned to Australia to see it
choices: he had never once returned to Australia to see it
he had asked to have his name struck from it
he had spent his last years suing the government
he had never designed another major building
context: Utzon resigned in 1966 amid disputes over money and control; an Australian team finished the building. He won the Pritzker Prize in 2003 but died in 2008 having never returned to Australia to see his masterpiece complete. Source: classical-music.com (Sydney Opera House history)

question: French conservators restored temple after temple across Angkor in the early 1900s. At Ta Prohm, where huge roots had poured over the walls, swallowed the doorways and cracked the roofs apart, they made a famous decision. What did they do with the temple?
answer: They braced it against collapse and left it wrapped in the jungle.
choices: They braced it against collapse and left it wrapped in the jungle.
They felled the trees and rebuilt the galleries stone by stone.
They dismantled the temple and moved it to safer ground.
They cleared the roots and laid a formal garden around it.
context: When the Ecole francaise d'Extreme-Orient restored Angkor in the early 1900s, they deliberately left Ta Prohm tangled in forest 'as a concession to the general taste for the picturesque.' The conservator Maurice Glaize said it was chosen because it had 'best merged with the jungle, but not yet to the point of becoming a part of it' -- wild enough to be spectacular, sound enough not to collapse. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: Locals at Angkor point tourists toward Ta Prohm by a nickname borrowed from Hollywood. An adventure blockbuster of 2001 filmed its star sprinting through the temple's root-choked galleries, and the place has carried the movie's name ever since. Which film was it?
context: The 2001 film Lara Croft: Tomb Raider, starring Angelina Jolie, was shot among Ta Prohm's roots -- Lara picks a jasmine flower and falls through the earth into the ruins -- and the site has been the 'Tomb Raider temple' ever since, the world's most famous 'lost temple.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: Enormous pale roots pour over the stone walls of Ta Prohm, deep in the Cambodian jungle at Angkor, and pry the ancient carved blocks apart. Most of them belong to a single giant species of tree that towers high above the ruins. Which tree holds Ta Prohm in its grip?
context: The dominant giant is the silk-cotton tree (Tetrameles nudiflora, locally called 'spung'), joined by smaller strangler figs (Ficus gibbosa). The trees never grew up from the ground: birds dropped their seeds onto the temple's gallery roofs, the seedlings took hold high up, and their roots crept DOWN through the walls, splitting the stonework as they descended. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm

question: King Jayavarman VII built Ta Prohm as a Buddhist monastery, consecrated in 1186, and its founding stone still stands at the site, boasting of the people it took to run the place: hundreds of dancers, dozens of high priests, thousands living inside the walls and many more in the villages that fed them. How many people did the inscription say served Ta Prohm?
context: The figure comes from Ta Prohm's foundation stele (inscription K.273), which records that nearly 80,000 people were needed to maintain and serve the monastery -- including 615 dancers, 18 high priests, and 12,640 people living inside the temple walls. Its real name was Rajavihara, the 'Royal Monastery,' built by the Khmer king Jayavarman VII and consecrated in 1186; scholars suspect the stele's numbers were inflated to glorify the king. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm  (Legend.)

question: Shah Jahan, the Mughal emperor, mourned one death in 1631 so deeply that for two years he gave up music and fine clothes, and over the grave he raised the Taj Mahal at Agra, a vast white marble tomb. For whom did he build it?
context: Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 giving birth to her fourteenth child. Shah Jahan's grief became a building project that ran for roughly two decades, turning a personal loss into the most beautiful tomb on earth. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: The Taj Mahal's tomb gleams white because its brick core is entirely sheathed in one prized stone, quarried more than 300 km from Agra and dragged there by oxen and elephants. Masons chose it for a whiteness no nearer rock could match. Which stone sheaths the Taj Mahal?
context: The white marble came from the Makrana quarries in Rajasthan, still worked today, while the red sandstone of the surrounding complex came from Fatehpur Sikri. The other choices are famous white marbles too -- Carrara from Italy, Pentelic from Greece, Proconnesian from Turkey. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: Visitors to the Taj Mahal swear the tomb wears a different color at every hour -- blush pink at dawn, dazzling white at midday, and soft gold beneath a full moon. Photographers return year after year to catch each fresh shade. Why does the tomb seem to change color through the day?
choices: the dome is sheathed in gold leaf
colored glass fills the arched windows
river mist tints the stone at dawn
context: Nothing is ever painted or coated. The fine Makrana marble is faintly translucent and simply reflects whatever light falls on it, so the tomb glows pink at sunrise, white at noon, and gold under the moon. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: Two beautifully carved marble tombs sit at the center of the Taj Mahal's great domed hall, ringed by an inlaid screen, and thousands of visitors file past them each day believing they stand over the dead. Yet neither tomb holds a body. Where do the bodies actually lie?
answer: in a plain vault one floor below
choices: in a plain vault one floor below
inside the hollow of the great dome
under the mosque beside the tomb
context: The ornate tombs on display are false cenotaphs. The real graves sit in a plain, undecorated lower chamber, laid north-south with the faces turned toward Mecca -- a Mughal convention that kept the actual resting place simple and hidden. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: The four slender minarets at the corners of the Taj Mahal's platform were not built standing straight up: each leans about two degrees outward, away from the great dome. Study of the tomb has shown this tilt was deliberate, worked in by its Mughal builders. What were they planning for?
context: The outward lean is an earthquake-safety trick centuries ahead of its time: if a quake ever toppled the towers, their built-in tilt would carry them falling away from the tomb rather than crashing down onto the dome. Source: tajwithguide.com (25 fascinating facts about the Taj Mahal).

question: Flowers, vines and leaves so finely shaded that visitors take them for paintings scatter across the white marble of the Taj Mahal. They are not paint at all, and a single blossom can hold as many as 64 separate pieces. What are the Taj's flowers made of?
answer: cut gemstones set into the marble
choices: cut gemstones set into the marble
colored enamel fired onto the surface
context: The craft is pietra dura, called parchin kari here: chips of agate, jasper, carnelian, and lapis cut and polished flush into the marble so a whole garden of flowers glows in stone. A single cenotaph blossom can hold 64 inlaid pieces. Source: tajwithguide.com (25 fascinating facts about the Taj Mahal).

question: The grieving Shah Jahan, a famous legend says, meant to raise a second Taj Mahal in black marble on the far bank of the Yamuna, a dark twin for his own tomb joined to the white one by a bridge. Ruins of dark stone across the river seemed to prove it. What did archaeologists find when they excavated those ruins in the 1990s?
answer: white marble blocks blackened by age
choices: white marble blocks blackened by age
the foundations of an unfinished black tomb
a buried cache of black marble slabs
a bridge footing pointing across the river
context: The 'Black Taj' is a legend. The 1990s excavation showed the dark ruins across the river were ordinary white marble stones darkened by centuries of weathering -- there was never a black twin. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Taj_Mahal.

question: Narrow cobbled lanes wind under red-tiled roofs and church spires in Tallinn's Old Town, in Estonia, all ringed by a towered stone wall. Most medieval town centres like it are long gone, bombed flat or turned into museums. What is remarkable about Tallinn's?
answer: it is still a lived-in, working town
choices: it is still a lived-in, working town
it was rebuilt from rubble after the war
it is an open-air museum of moved houses
it is a modern replica built for tourists
context: Tallinn's Old Town is a rarity: a still-lived-in medieval city of cobbled lanes and red-tiled roofs, not a ruin or a museum but a working town. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 1997 for its 'exceptionally intact 13th-century city plan' -- one of Europe's best-preserved medieval towns. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tallinn Old Town' (UNESCO 1997).

question: A great stone wall ringed medieval Tallinn, on Estonia's Baltic coast, bristling with 46 towers along a rampart up to 16 metres high. Most of Europe's medieval town walls have long since crumbled away. How many of Tallinn's towers still stand guard today?
answer: about half of them -- some two dozen towers
choices: about half of them -- some two dozen towers
all forty-six, every one still intact
just one lone surviving gate tower
none at all, only their foundations
context: In its 16th-century prime Tallinn's wall ran about 2.4 km, stood 14-16 m high and up to 3 m thick, and carried 46 towers -- one of the most fortified towns in northern Europe. About half survives today: nearly 2 km of wall and around two dozen towers still stand, one of the best-preserved medieval city walls in northern Europe. Source: inyourpocket.com 'Town Fortifications'; historyhit.com 'Tallinn City Walls'.

question: Merchants filled Tallinn's lower town by the harbour, but the town's rulers sat above them on Toompea, the hilltop upper town, held in turn by Danes, German knights, Swedes and Russians. What has its home at the top of Toompea today?
context: Toompea, the upper town on the hill, was held in turn by Danes, the Livonian Order, Swedes and Russians; Estonia's parliament, the Riigikogu, meets in Toompea Castle today. The merchants' lower town spread below, and the two stayed separate towns until they were administratively united in 1878. Source: Wikipedia, 'Toompea'.

question: Tallinn spent the Middle Ages as a rich merchant town on the Baltic, its harbour crowded with cargo ships and its guildhalls and spired churches raised on trading profits. Tallinn owed that wealth to membership in one great medieval alliance of northern European trading towns. Which league was it?
context: The Hanseatic League was the great medieval merchant network of the Baltic and North Seas. Tallinn's guildhalls and spired churches survive so nearly intact that UNESCO listed the whole Old Town in 1997 as a preserved town of 'medieval and Hanseatic origin'. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tallinn Old Town'.

question: Lightning has hit St Olaf's Church in Tallinn at least eight times, and the church has burned to the ground three times and been rebuilt again and again. Sailors far out in the Gulf of Finland still use it as a landmark. By old tradition, what world record did St Olaf's hold before a great fire in 1625?
choices: the tallest lighthouse in the Baltic
the largest church in northern Europe
the northernmost cathedral in the world
context: By tradition St Olaf's spire soared to about 159 m and was the tallest building in the world from 1549 until lightning burned it in 1625 -- though historians reckon the true medieval height was more like 115-125 m, so the record is a claim, not a certainty. The steeple has been struck by lightning at least eight times and the church has burned down three times; it still stands about 124 m tall, a landmark visible far out at sea. Legend/claim flagged. Source: Wikipedia, 'St. Olaf's Church, Tallinn'; visitestonia.com.

question: Tallinn's upper town, Toompea, stands on the tip of the Baltic Klint, a pale limestone cliff-line that runs for hundreds of kilometres along Estonia's coast and drops 20 to 30 metres to the lower town. Long before any stone wall went up, what did that drop give the rulers on the hill?
answer: A natural wall of rock around the hilltop
choices: A natural wall of rock around the hilltop
A harbour deep enough for warships
A spring of fresh water inside the town
Soil rich enough to farm on the hill
context: Toompea's hill is part of the North Estonian Klint, a subsection of the Baltic Klint -- a pale limestone escarpment that runs for hundreds of km along the coast. 'Klint' is the local name for this kind of long cliff-line; geographers call it an escarpment (a long steep face where higher ground drops to lower). Rising 20-30 m above the lower town, it gave the upper town a natural rampart before a single wall was built. Source: Wikipedia, 'Toompea'.

question: Mount Tambora blew apart on an Indonesian island in April 1815, and the roar carried some 2,600 km to Sumatra. Soldiers stationed there took it for heavy gunfire and were sure a battle had begun nearby. What did they do?
answer: Marched out to defend a nearby post they believed was under attack
choices: Marched out to defend a nearby post they believed was under attack
Fired their own cannons in reply to the distant booming
Rushed to load ships and evacuate the governor to safety
Fled far inland, certain that warships were shelling the coast
context: The eyewitness detail comes from Sir Stamford Raffles's memoir, which records that the noise was 'almost universally attributed to distant cannon.' Tambora's 1815 blast was the largest eruption in recorded human history, and its roar carried roughly 2,600 km (1,600 mi) to Sumatra. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora  (Legend.)

question: About 71,000 people died when Mount Tambora erupted on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa in April 1815. Only around 11,000 died in the eruption itself, from the choking ash, the fiery flows and the tsunamis that swept the coasts. What killed the far larger number in the weeks and months afterwards?
answer: Starvation, after the ashfall smothered the islands' crops
choices: Starvation, after the ashfall smothered the islands' crops
Floods, as rivers dammed by falling debris burst downstream
Wildfires that spread from the still-glowing ash
Fresh eruptions from the crater the following spring
context: About 71,000 people died in all -- some 10,000-12,000 in the eruption itself (ash, pyroclastic flows, and 4-metre tsunamis), and tens of thousands more from the starvation and disease that followed once the ash smothered the fields of Sumbawa and nearby islands. It remains the deadliest eruption in recorded history. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora

question: Tambora's 1815 eruption threw so much dust and haze around the globe that the following year, 1816, brought freakish cold to lands half a world away. In New England, snow fell in June and killing frosts returned in July and August; across Europe and North America the grain harvests failed. By what haunting name did people come to remember 1816?
context: Snow lay about 46 cm (18 in) deep at Cabot, Vermont on June 8, 1816, and Americans nicknamed the disaster 'Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death.' The freakish cold was traced back to the dust and haze from Tambora's eruption the year before. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer  (Legend.)

question: Storms kept a group of English writers indoors for days at Lord Byron's villa beside Lake Geneva in 1816, a summer whose skies Tambora's distant haze had dimmed. Byron challenged each of them to write a ghost story, and eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley took up the dare. What novel did she begin that gloomy summer?
context: The gathering was at Byron's rented Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva. The same ghost-story contest produced John Polidori's 'The Vampyre' (an ancestor of Dracula), and Byron wrote his apocalyptic poem 'Darkness,' imagining a world where the sun goes out. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer  (Legend.)

question: Karl Drais, a German inventor, built a wooden 'running machine' and showed it off in 1817, looking for a way to travel without a horse: Tambora's haze had wrecked the harvests of 1816, sending oat prices soaring and making horses too costly to feed across Europe. Of which everyday machine is it the direct ancestor?
context: With oats scarce and expensive, Karl Drais's pedal-less 'running machine,' or draisine, of 1817 is widely remembered as the direct ancestor of the bicycle -- a chain running from a volcano in Indonesia to the machine kids ride today. The famine is the commonly cited spur for his invention. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer  (Legend.)

question: Millions of tonnes of sulphur gas shot from Tambora into the stratosphere in 1815 and turned into a fine haze of sulphate droplets that circled the globe for over a year, dimming the sun and cooling the planet by about half a degree. What did the haze do to the sunlight passing through it?
answer: Reflected much of it straight back out into space
choices: Reflected much of it straight back out into space
Absorbed it up high, warming the haze but not the ground
Bent it away from the equator and toward the poles
Scattered it into a red glow that carried no heat
context: Tambora lofted an estimated 60 megatons of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it formed sulfate aerosols that reflected sunlight and cooled the globe by roughly 0.4-0.7 C for over a year. The eruption column reached about 43 km (27 mi) up; the resulting 'dry fog' dimmed the sun enough that people could see sunspots with the naked eye, and it tinted the lurid skies in J.M.W. Turner's paintings. Sources: https://grokipedia.com/page/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora

question: Haraldur Sigurdsson, a volcanologist, dug down through about 3 metres of ash on Sumbawa in 2004 and found a house of the small kingdom that Tambora's 1815 eruption wiped out, people, language and all. Bronze bowls and iron tools lay beside two of its inhabitants, right where the blast caught them. What nickname did the lost kingdom earn?
context: In a 2004 dig, volcanologist Haraldur Sigurdsson uncovered the buried house under about 3 m of ash. The Tambora people's language, thought to be related to the Mon-Khmer tongues of mainland Southeast Asia, was wiped out with them. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambora_culture ; https://today.uri.edu/news/uri-volcanologist-discovers-lost-kingdom-of-tambora/  (Legend.)

question: A Highland clansman caught on the open hills on a cold night needed no blanket: tradition pictures him unbelting the long tartan he had worn wrapped around him all day and rolling himself up in its folds to sleep. Which garment was it?
context: The feileadh mor, or 'great kilt' (belted plaid), really was a single four-to-six-yard length of tartan belted at the waist with the top draped over the shoulder. The image of a Highlander unbelting it to sleep rolled up inside like a blanket is the traditional picture of how handy the one-piece garment was. The tailored knee-length 'small kilt' came later. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_kilt  (Legend.)

question: Someone jammed a scrap of checked wool into the mouth of a clay pot as a stopper and buried the pot in Scotland. That scrap, the Falkirk tartan, woven around the 3rd century AD, is the oldest tartan-like cloth ever found there. What was the little rag keeping sealed inside?
answer: a hoard of Roman silver coins
choices: a hoard of Roman silver coins
the ashes of a cremated chief
context: The 'Falkirk tartan,' from about the 3rd century AD, is the oldest tartan-like cloth found in Scotland. The checked scrap of undyed wool had been used to plug a pot holding almost 2,000 Roman coins — a humble rag stopping up a small fortune. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartan

question: The British government in London turned its anger on the everyday clothing of the Scottish Highlands once the Jacobite Rising of 1745 had been crushed at Culloden in April 1746. That year it passed the Dress Act, aimed at the kilt and tartan worn by Highland men. What did the law do to Highland dress?
choices: required a licence to wear it
context: The Dress Act of 1746, part of the Act of Proscription after the Jacobite defeat at Culloden, outlawed the plaid, the little kilt, and tartan for men and boys across the Highlands — one of the rare times a government has banned a pattern of cloth outright. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_Act_1746

question: Jail for six months awaited any Highlander caught in the kilt or a tartan plaid for the first time under the Dress Act of 1746, passed after the Jacobite defeat at Culloden. A second offence brought a far harsher sentence, the same one Scottish courts handed out to thieves, forgers and other serious criminals. What was done to a repeat offender?
choices: branded on the cheek with hot iron
context: A first offence under the Dress Act meant six months in prison; a second meant being 'transported to any of His Majesty's plantations beyond the seas' for seven years — exile for the crime of wearing Highland dress. The ban ran 36 years before its repeal in 1782. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_Act_1746

question: Sir Walter Scott, the novelist, coaxed the Highland clan chiefs into parading in matching patterns at one great event, and the rule that each clan owns one fixed tartan took hold there. Many families now treat their clan tartan as an ancient badge. At which event did this tradition take hold?
answer: King George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh
choices: King George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh
the Jacobite defeat at Culloden in 1746
the lifting of the tartan ban in 1782
Queen Victoria's move to Balmoral in the 1850s
context: When King George IV visited Edinburgh in 1822, Sir Walter Scott choreographed a tartan pageant so lavish it fixed the 'one clan, one tartan' image in the public mind — largely a romantic invention, not ancient law. The stout king even wore a Royal Stuart kilt cut so short he added pink tights to cover his knees. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visit_of_George_IV_to_Scotland

question: Two Welsh-born brothers named Allen published the Vestiarium Scoticum in 1842, a book that claimed to copy a lost ancient manuscript listing each clan's true tartan, and many of Scotland's 'official' clan tartans still trace back to it. Scholars proved it a fake. To prop up the hoax, what did the brothers claim to be?
choices: heirs of the executed Lord Lovat
context: The Vestiarium Scoticum (1842) claimed to reproduce a lost ancient manuscript giving each clan's true sett, and many 'official' clan tartans still trace to it — but it was exposed as a forgery. Its authors, the Welsh-born Allen brothers, styled themselves the 'Sobieski Stuarts' and falsely claimed to be grandsons of Bonnie Prince Charlie, dressing fake ancient tartans in fake royal glamour. Rob Roy MacGregor, Simon Fraser (Lord Lovat, beheaded after Culloden), and Flora MacDonald were all real Jacobite-era Highlanders, but the brothers claimed no descent from them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestiarium_Scoticum

question: Moss and lichen hang heavy from every trunk in Washington's Hoh Rain Forest, soaked by about 140 inches of rain a year, yet the forest grows in a cool northern climate, far from the tropics. What is a rainforest like this, drenched but cool, called?
context: A cool, drenched, moss-hung forest like the Hoh is a TEMPERATE rainforest -- rainforest without the tropics. The North American rule of thumb: cool (mean temperature about 4-12 degC) and soaked with more than 140 cm (55 in) of rain a year, so a rainforest does not have to be hot. The Hoh's giants are Sitka spruce and western hemlock, draped in 'lettuce lichen.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoh_Rainforest and /wiki/Temperate_rainforest.

question: Chris Atkins and Michael Taylor, two climbers, came upon the tallest known living thing on Earth in 2006, in the cool, foggy forests near the coast of northern California: a tree over 116 metres high, higher than a 35-storey building. They named it Hyperion. What kind of tree is it?
context: Hyperion is a coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens), measured at 116.22 m (381.3 ft) -- the tallest known living tree on Earth. Chris Atkins and Michael Taylor found it in Redwood National Park on 25 August 2006. In 2022 the National Park Service closed the area (fines up to $5,000) after visitors trampled the ferns at its base, and its exact spot is kept secret. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperion_(tree).

question: Young hemlocks and spruces in Washington's Hoh Rain Forest sometimes stand in one straight, evenly spaced line beneath the mossy giants, as if someone had set them out with a ruler. What lined the seedlings up so neatly?
answer: they sprouted along a fallen tree trunk that has since rotted away
choices: they sprouted along a fallen tree trunk that has since rotted away
park rangers replanted that strip in rows after a wildfire
their seeds washed into a dead-straight crack in the bedrock
they followed the line of an old logging road through the grove
context: The rotting trunk was a 'nurse log' -- as it decays, moss, needles and soil fill it and seedlings take root along its length. When the log finally crumbles away, the young trees are left standing in a dead-straight 'colonnade' that traces exactly where the old giant fell. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nurse_log.

question: A cool, dripping forest clings to a narrow strip of southern Chile, pinned between the open Pacific and the wall of the Andes and drenched by up to 6,000 mm of rain a year. It is the mirror twin of the forests of the Pacific Northwest, and only they are bigger. What is this Chilean rainforest called?
context: It is the Valdivian rainforest, named for the Chilean city of Valdivia -- a cool, dripping forest getting 1,000 to over 6,000 mm of rain a year, the second-largest temperate rainforest on Earth after the Pacific Northwest. Its signature tree, the alerce (Fitzroya), is a cypress relative; one giant, the Gran Abuelo, was ring-counted at 3,622 years in 1993. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdivian_temperate_rainforest and /wiki/Fitzroya.

question: Australian scientists weighed the carbon held in cool, wet rainforests, the mossy giants of places like Tasmania, against the carbon in tropical forests like the Amazon, which most people name first as the planet's great carbon stores. Acre for acre, how does such a cool rainforest's carbon store compare?
answer: it locks away even more carbon than a tropical rainforest
choices: it locks away even more carbon than a tropical rainforest
it holds only a small fraction of a tropical rainforest's carbon
it holds almost exactly as much as a tropical rainforest
its stored carbon leaks back out faster than a tropical rainforest's
context: Acre for acre, temperate rainforest can out-store the tropics. An Australian National University study (Keith, Mackey & Lindenmayer, PNAS 2009) measured 377 tons of carbon per hectare above ground in temperate moist forest versus 171 tons in tropical rainforest; Australia's Mountain Ash forests reached up to 2,844 tons per hectare including roots. Being cool, they rot slowly, so the wood piles up -- among the densest carbon stores on land. Source: news.mongabay.com/2009/07/temperate-forests-store-more-carbon-than-tropical-forests-finds-study/.

question: Water ringed the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, on every side when it rose in the 1300s on an island in a shallow mountain lake in central Mexico, with no farmland of its own. On which large lake did the Aztecs build it?
context: Tenochtitlan was founded on islands in shallow, salty Lake Texcoco, traditionally dated to about 1325. Lake Pátzcuaro and Lake Chapala are real lakes elsewhere in Mexico; Titicaca lies far to the south, high in the Andes. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec god, promised his wandering people a homeland, so the legend goes, and told them to settle where they saw a certain sign on a nopal cactus in the marsh. When they spotted it, they founded Tenochtitlan there. What did they see on the cactus?
context: The eagle-on-a-cactus omen is the Mexica founding legend — and that exact image sits at the centre of Mexico's flag and coat of arms today. (The modern flag adds a serpent in the eagle's beak; the oldest Aztec pictures show just the eagle on the cactus.) Source: Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan' and 'Coat of arms of Mexico'.

question: The Aztecs of island-bound Tenochtitlan had no fields of their own, so they built farm plots out into the shallows, piling up lake-bottom mud and rotting plants and lashing the beds down with willow roots. The plots were so rich they cropped up to seven times a year. What were these lake gardens called?
context: Chinampas were artificial garden-plots raised from the lakebed and anchored by the roots of ahuejote willows — so productive they helped feed a city of 200,000. They are often called 'floating gardens,' though they were rooted to the lakebed, not floating. Andenes are Inca terraces, waru waru are Andean raised fields, and a milpa is a maize-bean-squash plot. Source: Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'; https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/412/

question: Canoes glided between the houses of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital of some 200,000 people, along a grid of canals that split its garden plots. The Spanish conquistadors who arrived in 1519 were stunned. After which European water-city did they nickname it?
context: The Spanish called Tenochtitlan 'the Venice of the New World.' Amsterdam, Bruges, and Stockholm are all famously threaded with canals too. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinampa'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Three broad raised roads carried travelers across the water to island Tenochtitlan. One ran north to Tepeyac, one south to Iztapalapa, and one west to Tlacopan, each wide enough for ten horsemen abreast. The Aztecs gave these causeways a defense that could seal the city off from an attacking army. What was it?
context: The raised roads across the water are called causeways; gaps in them were spanned by wooden bridges the Mexica could pull up, cutting the island off. Cortés had to fight past exactly this defence in 1521. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Aztec builders ran a stone aqueduct from the springs of Chapultepec, a wooded hill to the west, into the heart of island Tenochtitlan, because the lake around the city was too salty to drink. They built it as two matching channels side by side, not one big one. Why two channels instead of one bigger one?
answer: so one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
choices: so one could be cleaned while the other kept flowing
so one carried water and the other carried off sewage
so the second doubled the flow in the dry season
so priests could bless one and use the other
context: Aztec rulers began the twin aqueduct around 1418; one channel carried water while the other was scrubbed clean, so the city never ran dry. It was maintenance engineering as shrewd as any in Europe at the time. Moctezuma reportedly bathed every day thanks to the fresh Chapultepec water. Source: Grokipedia, 'Chapultepec aqueduct'; Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapultepec_aqueduct

question: Boatmen still push flat-bottomed boats down the canals of one district in southern Mexico City, past old garden plots that farmers still work, where Aztec Tenochtitlan's way of farming the lake bed outlived the empire. Visitors come from all over the world to ride them. What is this floating-garden district called?
context: Xochimilco, in southern Mexico City, still keeps working chinampas and canals — a living remnant of Tenochtitlan's farming, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinampa'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Priests climbed every day to two shrines side by side atop a great stepped pyramid at the sacred heart of Tenochtitlan, to offer sacrifice. One shrine honoured Huitzilopochtli, Aztec god of war and the sun; the other, Tlaloc, god of rain and lightning. By what name is this twin-shrined pyramid known today?
context: The Templo Mayor was the sacred centre of the Mexica world; its twin shrines honoured war and rain, the two forces the city lived by. The Pyramid of the Sun stands at Teotihuacan; El Castillo and the Caracol at Chichén Itzá. Source: Grokipedia, 'Templo Mayor'; Wikipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Just north of Tenochtitlan lay a huge market. Cortes claimed sixty thousand people came to trade there every single day: gold, obsidian blades, turkeys, healing herbs, and cotton cloth, all under one roar of haggling voices. In which neighboring sister-city was this great market held?
context: The market of Tlatelolco, Tenochtitlan's twin city, astonished the Spanish; friar Sahagún and soldier Bernal Díaz put the daily crowd at 20,000–40,000, Cortés at 60,000. Texcoco and Tlacopan were Tenochtitlan's partners in the Triple Alliance; Azcapotzalco was an older rival city. Source: mexicolore.co.uk, 'The great market of Tlatelolco'; Grokipedia, 'Tenochtitlan'.

question: Workers digging a trench beneath downtown Mexico City on 21 February 1978 struck the edge of a carved stone disc more than three metres across and weighing 8.5 tons, buried under the streets for 450 years. It led archaeologists straight to buried Tenochtitlan's holiest temple. Whose dismembered body is carved across the disc?
context: The Coyolxauhqui Stone, over three metres wide, shows the Aztec moon goddess dismembered by her brother Huitzilopochtli in myth. Struck by chance on 21 February 1978, it lay at the foot of the Templo Mayor, the twin-shrined great pyramid at the heart of Tenochtitlan, and triggered one of the largest urban digs in history, led by the archaeologist Eduardo Matos Moctezuma. Source: smarthistory.org, 'Templo Mayor: the Coyolxauhqui Stone'; Wikipedia, 'Coyolxauhqui Stone'; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Templo_Mayor

question: Parts of Mexico City, built where the Aztecs' island capital of Tenochtitlan once rose from its lake, sink by as much as 50 centimetres a year, and the great Metropolitan Cathedral visibly leans. Geologists call this slow sinking subsidence. What mainly drives it?
answer: wells pumping water out of the clay
choices: wells pumping water out of the clay
a buried volcano slowly caving in
hot springs dissolving the deep rock
context: Mexico City stands on the heavily saturated clay of the old bed of Lake Texcoco. Pumping groundwater out faster than rain refills it makes the clay compact, so the ground sinks: some areas have dropped as much as nine metres since the early 1900s, and parts of the city still sink almost 50 centimetres a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City

question: A road straight as an arrow, about 40 metres wide, runs through the ruined city of Teotihuacan between flat platforms. The Aztecs, who found the city empty centuries after its fall, took them for the tombs of old lords and named the road to match. What did they call it?
context: The Aztecs came upon Teotihuacan centuries after its fall and, certain the platforms flanking the great road were royal tombs, named it Miccaotli -- the Avenue of the Dead. They were wrong: the platforms are temple bases, not graves. The road runs about 40 m wide and some 4 km long. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'  (Legend.)

question: Beside the great avenue of Teotihuacan, north of Mexico City, a flat-topped mountain of stone and rubble rises about 65 metres on a square base nearly 230 metres to a side, among the largest pyramids anywhere on Earth. Which of Teotihuacan's pyramids is this?
choices: the Temple of the Feathered Serpent
context: The Pyramid of the Sun stands about 65.5 m (215 ft) high on a base roughly 230 m square -- the largest building at Teotihuacan and one of the biggest in ancient Mesoamerica. Its name, like the city's, was given by the much later Aztecs. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pyramid of the Sun.'

question: Well over 100,000 people lived in Teotihuacan, in the Valley of Mexico, around 500 CE, in one of the largest cities on Earth, a place of stone pyramids and apartment compounds. Archaeologists have studied its ruins for over a century, yet one basic fact about its people has never been recovered. Which fact is still unknown?
context: Teotihuacan's own people left no readable record of what they called themselves or their city; 'Teotihuacan' is a name the Aztecs coined centuries later, so scholars simply call them 'the Teotihuacanos.' Population estimates for its peak run from 100,000 to well above. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: Painted murals once blazed on the inner walls of the stone apartment blocks where most families of Teotihuacan lived. The most famous, at a compound called Tepantitla, shows a great mountain pouring out streams of water, with dozens of tiny people scattered across the land below. What kind of place do scholars think it shows?
answer: a watery paradise of the afterlife
choices: a watery paradise of the afterlife
a great flood that drowned the valley
a map of the city's canals
the mountain where its stone was quarried
context: The Tepantitla mural, often called the Paradise of Tlaloc (Tlalocan), is usually read as a blissful, watery afterlife tied to the rain god -- the mountain gushes water while people swim, sing and gather flowers below. Teotihuacan's apartment walls were covered in such vivid paintings. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan'; Tepantitla murals.

question: The Aztecs came upon the empty ruins of Teotihuacan, in the Valley of Mexico, centuries after the city fell. Grander than anything they knew, the ruins earned a lofty name in the Aztecs' own Nahuatl language. What is 'Teotihuacan' usually taken to mean?
context: Awed by the abandoned city, the Aztecs named it Teotihuacan in their Nahuatl language -- usually glossed as 'birthplace of the gods' or 'the place where the gods were born.' It was to them a sacred site of creation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: Teotihuacan's workshops knapped obsidian, a volcanic glass, into razor-sharp blades and traded them far across Mesoamerica, and the city controlled a rare kind from the Sierra de Pachuca hills. Most obsidian is plain black. What made Teotihuacan's easy to spot?
context: The Sierra de Pachuca yielded a rare golden-green obsidian found almost nowhere else in Mesoamerica. Teotihuacan controlled its supply, working it into blades, mirrors and ornaments that traveled hundreds of miles in trade -- a signature of the city's reach. Source: Ponomarenko 2004; Tulane University research on Pachuca green obsidian.

question: Pits beneath and around Teotihuacan's Temple of the Feathered Serpent hold the mass offering its builders made when they dedicated it, around 150 to 200 CE, and diggers have since opened them. What did the builders bury there to consecrate the temple?
context: More than 200 people -- many with their hands bound, apparently war captives and soldiers -- were sacrificed and buried in pits beneath and around the Temple of the Feathered Serpent when it was dedicated about 150-200 CE, along with jade, obsidian and animal offerings. Source: Wikipedia, 'Temple of the Feathered Serpent, Teotihuacan.'

question: Diggers in Tlailotlacan, a neighbourhood of Teotihuacan, found tombs, burial urns and carvings in a foreign style: a whole quarter where migrants from far away kept the customs of their old homeland. The great city drew people from all over Mesoamerica. Which people made this quarter their home?
context: Teotihuacan was a genuine melting pot. Its Tlailotlacan barrio housed Zapotec migrants from the Oaxaca Valley, who kept their homeland's tomb styles and hieroglyphs; other quarters held Gulf-coast and Maya traders. Bone-isotope tests confirm many residents grew up hundreds of miles away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: Sergio Gómez, an archaeologist, finished excavating a tunnel under Teotihuacan's Temple of the Feathered Serpent in 2015, a passage sealed for about 1,800 years. Among jade statues, carved shells and shiny pyrite spheres, his lamps also picked out pools of a strange liquid on the tunnel floor. What was it?
context: Sergio Gomez of Mexico's INAH found pools of liquid mercury in the sealed chamber, along with jade statues, carved shells and pyrite spheres. He suspects the shimmering metal stood for an underworld river or lake -- and may mark the way to the first royal tomb ever found at Teotihuacan. Source: Archaeology Magazine, 27 April 2015.

question: At the north end of Teotihuacan's great avenue, the Pyramid of the Moon rises about 43 m, with the sacred mountain Cerro Gordo looming directly behind it. This was no accident: the builders deliberately tied the pyramid to the mountain at its back. In what way?
answer: its outline mirrors the mountain's silhouette
choices: its outline mirrors the mountain's silhouette
its stairway aims straight at the summit
it sits on the mountain's center line
its shadow reaches the peak at dawn
context: The 43 m Pyramid of the Moon was built to mimic the contours of Cerro Gordo, the mountain directly behind it, so that from the avenue the pyramid and peak read as one continuous silhouette -- binding the city's sacred architecture to the living landscape. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pyramid of the Moon.'

question: Teotihuacan's builders set their whole city about 15.5 degrees off true north, its long avenue, its pyramids and its thousands of buildings all laid on one giant grid. Astronomers found that the tilt is no mistake: it lines the city up with something in the sky. What did the builders orient their city to?
answer: sunrise and sunset on certain dates
choices: sunrise and sunset on certain dates
context: Teotihuacan's grid is turned about 15.5° east of north, and the Pyramid of the Sun's orientation records sunrise on 11 February and 29 October and sunset on 30 April and 13 August -- dates that likely anchored the ritual calendar. The whole city was squared to the sky, not the compass. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: Someone set fire to the main buildings of Teotihuacan around 550 CE, and the city that had been the greatest power in Mesoamerica for centuries fell. Archaeologists still argue about the cause. What is the leading answer today for what brought Teotihuacan down?
answer: a revolt from within the city
choices: a revolt from within the city
a war with a rival city
context: Because the burning around 550 CE targeted the elite civic buildings along the Avenue of the Dead rather than ordinary homes, most archaeologists now blame an internal uprising -- likely sharpened by drought and failed harvests -- instead of a foreign invasion. Source: Wikipedia, 'Teotihuacan.'

question: Over the old Ethiopian city of Aksum, once capital of a powerful ancient kingdom, towers a stone pillar 24 metres tall and about 160 tonnes: the Obelisk of Axum. Its size is not what amazes builders and archaeologists. How was the whole pillar made?
answer: carved from a single block of stone
choices: carved from a single block of stone
context: One solid piece of nepheline syenite, a hard granite-like rock, standing 24 m (79 ft) tall and weighing roughly 160 tonnes. Unlike Great Zimbabwe's mortarless dry-stacked walls or the stacked basalt logs of Nan Madol, the Obelisk of Axum is a single carved monolith. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: Fake window frames climb all 24 metres of the Obelisk of Axum, and at its foot the carvers cut a fake doorway. Into that stone door they added one clever detail so that it would look like the entrance of a real home. What did they carve into the door?
context: The whole monolith imitates a nine-storey Aksumite tower-house laid out flat and stood upright, false windows and beams carved storey above storey. At the base its two false doors even carry carved false locks, as if the dead king's monument were a lived-in house. Source: https://www.ancient-origins.net/artifacts-other-artifacts/obelisk-axum-0011516

question: A smooth, rounded crown shaped like a half moon tops the Obelisk of Axum, where an Egyptian obelisk would end in a sharp point. Old fixings show the crown once wore a cover, stripped away long ago. What is thought to have capped it?
context: The moon-shaped crown was once fitted with metal frames or plates, thought to be bronze, so the grey stone skyscraper was capped in shining metal. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: A field of huge carved standing stones, the stelae, rises at the edge of Aksum, high in the mountains of northern Ethiopia. The tallest and most finely carved of them were each raised as a marker over something hidden in the rock below. What did the greatest stones of Aksum stand over?
answer: the tomb of a king or noble
choices: the tomb of a king or noble
a temple to the sun god
a spring feeding the city's wells
context: Rock-cut burial chambers and vaults run beneath the stelae field; the giant carved stones were grave-markers, the biggest and most decorated standing over the tombs of Aksum's kings and nobles. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksum

question: Soldiers of an invading army cut the great Obelisk of Axum, a 24-metre carved stone from the ancient Ethiopian city of Aksum, into three pieces in 1937. The pieces were hauled by truck to the coast and shipped overseas, and the conqueror raised the obelisk again in its own capital as a war prize. Which foreign power seized it, and in which city did it set it up?
context: Mussolini's Italy, having invaded Ethiopia, looted the obelisk in 1937, cut it into three sections, trucked it to the Red Sea port of Massawa, shipped it to Italy, and raised it in Rome near the Circus Maximus on 28 October 1937. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: The looted Obelisk of Axum, all 24 metres and 160 tonnes of it, finally went home to Ethiopia in 2005 after 68 years far away. Its three colossal stone sections made the journey back to Aksum by the most dramatic means the modern age could manage. How did the obelisk travel home?
answer: flown aboard a giant cargo plane
choices: flown aboard a giant cargo plane
hauled home by a convoy of trucks
context: The pieces were flown home in April 2005 aboard an Antonov An-124, one of the world's largest cargo aircraft and among the heaviest airfreight loads ever carried. The operation cost Italy about $7.7 million; the obelisk was re-erected at Aksum and unveiled on 4 September 2008, home after 68 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: Lightning struck the looted Obelisk of Axum in 2002, while it still stood abroad, and cracked the old stone. Builders blamed three steel bars driven through it in 1937, which had turned the pillar into a huge lightning rod. When Ethiopia later raised the obelisk again, what strong modern material bound its pieces?
context: Italy's three steel bars had acted as a lightning rod, so when the obelisk was rebuilt at Aksum the steel was replaced with eight bars of Kevlar, the aramid fibre used in bulletproof vests, so it would no longer attract lightning. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum

question: The Great Stele of Aksum lies in huge broken chunks across the stele field, 33 metres from end to end and more than 500 tonnes. It may be the biggest stone anyone ever cut to stand on end as a monument, yet it does not tower over the field. What most likely brought this giant down?
answer: it fell while being raised and never once stood
choices: it fell while being raised and never once stood
an earthquake toppled it a thousand years later
invaders pulled it down and smashed it apart
its own weight cracked it after centuries upright
context: The Great Stele probably collapsed during the very attempt to stand it up and never successfully stood; as it toppled it crushed a stone chamber beneath it called Nefas Mawcha, and it lies where it fell to this day. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksum

question: Aksum's giant stelae had to be dragged about four kilometres from the quarry at Gobo Dura, a hill west of the city, with no river to float them and no wheels to help. Local Aksumite tradition still names a powerful helper that, it is said, hauled the blocks into place. According to that tradition, what moved the megaliths?
context: The quarry at Gobo Dura (Gobedra) and the roughly 4 km drag are established fact; the elephant-haulers are local tradition, presented as such. Unlike Egypt's obelisks, cut at distant Aswan and floated down the Nile, Aksum's stones were quarried close to home and moved by organized manpower. Source: https://www.africanhistoryextra.com/p/megalithic-landscapes-of-ethiopia  (Legend.)

question: Mani, a Persian prophet of the 3rd century AD, wrote of only four truly great kingdoms on all the Earth and said none surpassed them. One of them was Aksum, the Red Sea empire that raised the stelae of northern Ethiopia. Which three empires did Mani name alongside it?
context: In his Kephalaia, Mani listed four great kingdoms: Babylon and Persia, Rome, the kingdom of the Aksumites, and Silis (China), 'there is none that surpasses them.' Tiny Aksum was ranked beside Rome, Persia and China. Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-137-11786-1_2

question: One white dome of ice and rock rises above every other peak of the Alps, high on the border where France, Italy and Switzerland meet. At 4,808 metres it is the highest point in Western Europe. Which peak is this rooftop of the West?
context: Mont Blanc — French for 'White Mountain' — rises 4,808 m on the French-Italian border, the highest summit in the Alps and Western Europe. Monte Rosa (4,634 m), the Matterhorn (4,478 m), and the Eiger (3,967 m) all fall short. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps

question: Michel-Gabriel Paccard, a doctor, and Jacques Balmat, a crystal hunter, both of Chamonix, clawed their way to the summit of Western Europe's highest peak on 8 August 1786, the first people ever to stand there. Their climb is remembered as the birth of a whole new sport. What is the sport called?
context: Dr. Michel-Gabriel Paccard and Jacques Balmat, both of Chamonix, made the first ascent of Mont Blanc on 8 August 1786 — a climb now seen as the birth of alpinism, the high-mountain sport that took its very name from the Alps. Bouldering (climbing low rocks), spelunking (cave exploring), and orienteering (cross-country navigation) are other outdoor pursuits. Source: 1786.travel

question: Climbers high on the Alps sometimes find fossil seashells in the rock beneath their boots, stone that once formed on an ocean floor and now stands kilometres up in the sky. The Alps rose when the African plate ground north into Europe and slammed shut the sea that had lain between them. What was that vanished ocean called?
context: As Africa drove into Eurasia, it closed the ancient Tethys Ocean and thrust its former sea floor skyward — which is why marine fossils and old seabed rock now sit atop Alpine peaks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_the_Alps

question: Snow and glaciers high in the Alps melt into rivers that run off in every direction to four different seas, the North Sea, the Mediterranean, the Adriatic and the Black Sea, and geographers call the range Europe's water tower. Which great European river is born there?
context: The Rhine, the Rhône, the Po, and the Inn (a Danube tributary) all rise in the Alps, which supply up to about 90% of some lowland regions' water. The Rhine begins as Alpine meltwater in eastern Switzerland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps

question: Ötzi melted out of an Alpine glacier still carrying a fine axe with a shiny metal blade, and the metal rewrote history: it proved metalworking had come to the Alps far earlier than scholars had thought. What was the blade made of?
context: Ötzi's axe blade was nearly pure copper, showing metalworking had reached the Alps by about 3,300 BC — earlier than scholars thought — even though he still carried flint tools and a bow. Source: britannica.com/topic/Otzi

question: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure of Geneva chased the summit of Western Europe's highest peak for years and even offered a cash prize, back in 1760, for the first person to reach it. In 1787, once the prize had been claimed, Saussure made the climb himself, with porters hauling a heavy load up the ice. What did they haul to the summit?
choices: chests of gold and silver coins
a carved altar of white marble
context: Saussure left Chamonix on 1 August 1787 and reached the summit of Mont Blanc on 3 August, with porters carrying barometers, hygrometers and other instruments, and spent hours taking scientific measurements on top. Decades earlier, in 1760, he had funded the cash prize whose lure helped spur the first ascent in 1786. Source: lindahall.org (Scientist of the Day, Horace-Benedict de Saussure); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace-Benedict_de_Saussure

question: Hikers crossing a high pass on the Italian-Austrian border in September 1991 spotted a brown, shrivelled body half-melted out of the ice and assumed a climber had died there not long before. Then scientists dated the corpse, soon nicknamed Ötzi, and got a shock. Roughly how long ago had he died?
context: Hikers Erika and Helmut Simon found the body in the Ötztal Alps; dating showed 'Ötzi' died about 5,300 years ago — Europe's oldest known natural human mummy, kept in the ice since the Copper Age. He is now displayed in Bolzano, Italy. Source: iceman.it; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%96tzi

question: Africa drove into Europe so hard that whole slabs of Alpine rock were shoved tens of kilometres from where they formed, stacking older layers on top of younger ones, the reverse of nature's usual order. What do geologists call these displaced masses of rock?
