context: A 'nappe' (French for 'tablecloth') is a large sheet of rock folded over and thrust far from where it formed; the Alps are the classic example, with older rock shoved atop younger. Synclines are downward folds, while horsts and grabens are up- and down-dropped fault blocks — all real tectonic structures, but not the far-traveled thrust sheets that define Alpine geology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_the_Alps

question: One enormous river rolls through the rainforests of South America carrying about a fifth of all the fresh water the world's rivers pour into the oceans, more than the next seven biggest rivers on Earth put together. Which river is it?
context: The Amazon's average discharge is about 215,000–230,000 cubic metres per second — enough to make it the largest river on Earth by volume, though not the longest. (The Congo is a distant second by discharge.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).

question: Two teams measure the same broad stretch of the Amazon, in the rainforests of South America. One records the river as about 11 km wide. The other, standing on the same bank, cannot even see the far side, yet neither team is wrong. What accounts for the huge difference?
answer: One was taken in the dry season, the other at the flood's peak.
choices: One was taken in the dry season, the other at the flood's peak.
One counted the river's mid-stream islands, the other left them out.
One measured the deep central channel, the other the full surface.
One was recorded at high tide, the other at low tide.
context: In the dry season a broad stretch of the Amazon runs about 11 km across; at the height of the annual flood the same stretch can swell to over 48 km (about 30 miles) wide — more than four times as far — so a boat in the middle is out of sight of either bank, and at its mouth the estuary spans hundreds of kilometres. It is a river that changes size with the seasons. Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).

question: Riverboats on the Amazon pass big river cities like Iquitos and Manaus on the long run through the rainforests of Peru and Brazil. Along that whole vast run from the Andes to the Atlantic, how many bridges cross the main river?
choices: a dozen or so, across Brazil
dozens, up and down its length
context: Not one bridge crosses the Amazon's main stem. The only bridge over any part of the system is the Ponte Rio Negro (2011), linking Manaus and Iranduba — and it spans the Rio Negro tributary, not the Amazon's main stem, so 'no bridge over the Amazon' still holds. Source: Live Science, 'Why are there no bridges over the Amazon River?' (https://www.livescience.com/why-no-bridges-over-amazon-river).

question: The pale, sandy-brown Rio Solimões rolls in from the west at Manaus, deep in the Brazilian Amazon, milky with fine sediment washed down from the Andes, and meets the coffee-black Rio Negro coming from the north. No mud darkens the Rio Negro. What stains its water almost black?
answer: tannins leached from rotting leaves and jungle plants
choices: tannins leached from rotting leaves and jungle plants
oils and resins washed from flooded rubber trees
a bloom of dark microscopic algae in the slow water
soot blown in from distant rainforest fires
context: The Rio Negro is a 'blackwater' river: almost sediment-free, its water is stained dark like strong tea by tannins from decaying leaves and plants draining off the forest. The Solimões is a sediment-rich 'whitewater' river carrying Andean silt. Where they meet at Manaus, the two run side by side as the Meeting of the Waters (Encontro das Águas). Source: Wikipedia, 'Meeting of Waters' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters).

question: People on the Amazon's banks near its mouth hear it coming long before they see it: a wall of water up to 4 m high that the rising Atlantic tide drives back upriver, against the current, for hundreds of kilometres. Its local name is usually translated 'great roar.' What is it called?
context: This is the pororoca, a tidal bore: at the spring tides near the equinoxes (September and March) the Atlantic tide funnels into the shallow river mouth and rears up into a wave up to 4 m high that races as far as 800 km inland. The name comes from the indigenous Tupi language and is usually translated 'great roar.' (The mascaret, aegir, and benak are real tidal bores on other rivers.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Pororoca' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca).

question: Picuruta Salazar, a Brazilian surfer, caught the Amazon's tidal bore in 2003 and rode it 12.5 km upriver without once falling off. An ocean surfer is lucky to stay on one wave for twenty seconds before it collapses, but a bore is a single wave that keeps rolling upstream. How long did Salazar's one ride last?
context: Riding the pororoca upstream, Picuruta Salazar stayed on one wave for about 37 minutes and 12.5 km (7.8 miles) in 2003 — a record ride. An annual pororoca surfing championship has been held since 1999 at São Domingos do Capim. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pororoca' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca).

question: Engineers could span the Amazon if they had to, for bridges cross wider water elsewhere in the world. What stands in the way of a bridge over the main river through Peru and Brazil is neither its width nor its strong current but the ground along its banks. What makes the banks so hard to build on?
answer: they are soft, waterlogged, and shift with every flood
choices: they are soft, waterlogged, and shift with every flood
they are steep rock gorges too narrow to anchor a pier
they are honeycombed with deep limestone sinkholes
they are packed with hard clay that cracks in the heat
context: The Amazon's banks are soft, waterlogged wetland that shifts as the river rises and falls up to 10 m a year, so a bridge would need very deep foundations and miles of approach viaducts across the floodplain. There is also little reason to build one: the river runs through sparsely populated rainforest with few roads, and it is cheaper to move Manaus's factory goods to São Paulo by boat than by road. Source: Live Science, 'Why are there no bridges over the Amazon River?' (https://www.livescience.com/why-no-bridges-over-amazon-river).

question: Fish swim between the tree trunks of the central Amazon for months at a time each year, when the river rises about 10 m, the height of a three-storey house, and spills far out into the rainforest. What is this seasonal drowned forest called?
context: This drowned floodplain forest is the várzea, flooded each year by sediment-rich whitewater. The annual 'flood pulse' of roughly 10 m (locally 9–14 m) shapes life along the whole river, and fish move among the tree trunks to feed while the forest is underwater. (The pantanal, cerrado, and caatinga are other Brazilian landscapes.) Source: seasonal flood-pulse research, PMC / US National Library of Medicine (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7612842/).

question: Snowmelt trickling off Nevado Mismi, high in the Peruvian Andes, sets the Amazon on its way. Its westernmost source lies only about 160 km from one ocean, yet the river runs the whole width of South America before it reaches the sea. Which ocean lies so close to the source?
context: The Amazon rises on Nevado Mismi (about 5,597 m) in the Peruvian Andes. Its westernmost source is only about 160 km from the Pacific, yet the water turns east and crosses the whole continent — running downhill through the Apurímac, Ucayali, and Marañón headwaters before it becomes the Amazon — to empty into the Atlantic some 6,400 km away. Source: Wikipedia, 'Amazon River' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River).

question: Sailors and satellites more than 100 km out in the open Atlantic, far past the shoreline where the Amazon finally meets the sea, find the water strangely changed by the river's outflow. What has the river done to the ocean that far from land?
answer: freshened it into a vast low-salt plume
choices: freshened it into a vast low-salt plume
warmed it into a band of unusually hot water
dyed it bright green with drifting algae
stilled its waves into a glassy calm
context: The Amazon's freshwater plume spreads a brownish, low-salinity layer across the open Atlantic — reaching well beyond 100 km from shore and covering nearly a million square kilometres of ocean surface, enough fresh water to measurably lower the sea's saltiness far from any coast. Source: Amazon–Orinoco plume literature review, SALINITY-PIMEP case studies (https://www.salinity-pimep.org/case-studies/river-plumes/amazon_orinoco/literature_review.html).

question: A driver heading inland from the coast of Chile into the central Andes may cover up to 700 km before reaching the mountains' far edge, though most other ranges are crossed in an hour or two. For a range of such colossal length, none on Earth is broader. What gives the Andes this tremendous breadth?
answer: several parallel mountain chains side by side
choices: several parallel mountain chains side by side
a single broad dome of uplifted crust
a wide plain of stacked lava flows
a thick belt of tightly folded rock
context: The Andes are the widest mountain range on Earth for their enormous length, swelling from about 200 km to as much as 700 km across and staying 200-300 km wide along most of their run. That breadth comes not from a single wall of rock but from several parallel cordilleras -- mountain chains marching side by side -- with high basins and plateaus trapped between them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes.

question: More than fifty peaks of the Andes push above 6,000 metres into the thin, freezing air, crowded close together along the western spine of South America. Only one other mountain region on Earth packs in more giants like these. Which region is that?
choices: the Southern Alps of New Zealand
context: Outside the Himalaya-Karakoram belt of Asia -- home to every one of Earth's fourteen peaks above 8,000 m -- no place packs together as many 6,000 m summits as the Andes. The Alps top out near 4,800 m and the Rockies near 4,400 m, so neither comes close. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes; Guinness World Records ('Over fifty of the Andes peaks reach over 6,000 metres').

question: Andean peoples have held the cold, deep-blue water of Lake Titicaca sacred for thousands of years, high on the plateau at 3,812 metres, where Bolivia meets Peru. Across all of South America, what record does the lake hold?
answer: the largest lake on the continent
choices: the largest lake on the continent
the deepest lake on the continent
the saltiest lake on the continent
the youngest lake on the continent
context: By surface area Titicaca is the biggest lake in South America, and it is also widely described as the highest large lake in the world that boats can still navigate, sitting some 3,812 m above the sea. Reed boats and even 19th-century steamships have crossed its waters. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Titicaca; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano ('the largest lake in South America').

question: Wind scours the Altiplano, a bare tableland some 3,750 metres high lying between the eastern and western chains of the Andes and spreading over parts of Bolivia, Peru, Chile and Argentina. Only one plateau on Earth is both bigger and higher than the Altiplano. Which one?
choices: the Colorado Plateau of North America
context: The Altiplano is the most extensive high plateau on Earth outside Tibet, and the world's second-highest. Its wide, flat basins -- floored with salt pans, shallow lakes, and volcanic ash -- formed as crust piled up and downwarped between the two Andean mountain chains. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano ('the most extensive high plateau on Earth outside Tibet').

question: On the lonely, lofty border between Chile and Argentina, the huge cone of Ojos del Salado rises above the desert among the fire-born peaks of the Andes, its slopes nearly bare of snow in the bone-dry air. Among all the volcanoes on the planet, what record does this Andean giant hold?
choices: the most active volcano on Earth
context: At 6,893 m, Ojos del Salado is the tallest volcano anywhere on Earth and the second-highest peak in the Americas, just behind Aconcagua. It is only rarely active. The world's largest volcano by bulk is Hawaii's Mauna Loa, a completely different kind of mountain. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojos_del_Salado; britannica.com 'Mount Ojos del Salado'.

question: Almost exactly on the equator in Ecuador, one Andean peak stands on the outward bulge of the Earth's middle. It is more than 2,500 metres lower than Mount Everest, yet its summit juts farther out into space, the single spot on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre. Which peak is it?
context: Chimborazo's summit stands 6,263 m above sea level -- 2,585 m lower than Everest -- yet because it sits on the equatorial bulge it reaches about 2.1 km (1.3 mi) farther from Earth's centre than Everest's peak does. That makes its summit the closest point on the planet's solid surface to outer space. Cotopaxi, Cayambe, and Antisana are its fellow Ecuadorian volcanoes, but Chimborazo is the tallest of them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimborazo.

question: Just off the Pacific coast of South America, a heavy slab of ocean floor meets the continent and is dragged down into the hot mantle beneath it. The sinking rock melts and rises again to feed the volcanoes of the Andes, and the grinding of the two still sets off earthquakes. Which ocean plate is diving beneath South America?
context: The Andes are built by subduction: the oceanic Nazca plate plunges beneath the South American plate, and the melting slab feeds the Andean Volcanic Belt while the grinding boundary still unleashes major earthquakes and eruptions today. Unlike the Himalayas (two continents in head-on collision), the Andes rise where ocean floor dives under a continent. The Cocos plate subducts off Central America, the Scotia plate lies to the far south, and the Caribbean plate to the north. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes.

question: From the air, the Appalachians are mile after mile of low, rounded, tree-covered ridges, with none of the bare rock spires or snow-capped horns of the Alps or the Rockies. What does such a soft, rounded shape usually reveal about a range?
answer: It is very old, worn down over immense time.
choices: It is very old, worn down over immense time.
It rose recently and is still growing taller.
It sits far from any tectonic plate boundary.
It was built by a single volcanic eruption.
context: Old ranges erode into smooth, low ridges; young ranges like the Himalaya and Rockies stay jagged because uplift still outpaces erosion. The Appalachians have been wearing down for over 240 million years — you are looking at the worn-down nubs of what were once towering peaks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains

question: One forested peak, 6,684 feet tall, stands higher than any other land east of the Mississippi River in North America. Its windy top is far colder than that modest height suggests. Which Appalachian peak is it?
context: Mount Mitchell (6,684 ft / 2,037 m), in North Carolina's Black Mountains, is the highest point in North America east of the Mississippi. Clingmans Dome (6,643 ft, in the Great Smoky Mountains) is a close second, and Mount Washington is the Northeast's highest. The whole range runs about 2,050 miles, from Alabama up into Canada. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains

question: The Appalachians first rose in eastern North America about 480 million years ago, when the continents wore very different shapes and life on land was just beginning. One thing now thought of as a timeless part of nature had not yet appeared, and would not for another 100 million years. What was missing?
context: The first true trees — like Archaeopteris, the earliest forest-builder — appeared around 385 million years ago, roughly 100 million years AFTER the Appalachians first rose. Rivers, rain, and sand are all far older. So these forested mountains are, quite literally, older than forests themselves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/385-million-year-old-fossils-reveal-worlds-oldest-forest-had-modern-tree-roots-180973810/

question: Sascha Kempf led a study in 2023 that used dust measured by a NASA space probe to date one of the grandest sights in the solar system. It may be only 100 to 400 million years old, a figure still debated, but younger even so than the Appalachian Mountains, which first rose about 480 million years ago. Which planet's showpiece is it?
context: A 2023 study led by Sascha Kempf (University of Colorado Boulder), using dust measurements from NASA's Cassini probe, set an upper limit of about 400 million years on Saturn's rings — possibly as young as 100 million. The ring age is still debated, but even the oldest estimate is younger than the Appalachians: a range of hills on Earth predates a feature of another planet. Source: https://www.colorado.edu/today/2023/05/12/how-old-are-saturns-rings-far-younger-once-thought-according-new-study ; https://science.nasa.gov/missions/cassini/nasas-cassini-data-show-saturns-rings-relatively-new/  (Legend.)

question: Africa rammed into North America some 300 million years ago and heaved the young Appalachians up into a wall of towering, snow-capped peaks. Today's soft green ridges are the ground-down stumps of that giant. Geologists estimate that at their height the Appalachians stood as tall as one of today's mightiest ranges. Which one?
context: The final and greatest uplift — the Alleghanian orogeny (~325-260 Mya) — pushed the Appalachians to an estimated 15,000 feet or more, rivaling today's Himalayas. Every gentle ridge you see now is the eroded stump of that lost, colossal range. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alleghanian_orogeny ; https://vividmaps.com/central-pangean-mountains/

question: A collision of continents heaved up the Appalachians some 300 million years ago, when North America and Africa slammed together. That same crash pressed most of Earth's land into one vast supercontinent, with the young range running down its centre like a great spine. Which famous supercontinent did the collision help assemble?
context: As Laurussia and Gondwana crushed together (~300 Mya), the Appalachians formed the central spine of the enormous Central Pangean Mountains, and the collision helped weld the supercontinent Pangaea. Gondwana and Laurasia would later become its southern and northern halves; Rodinia was a far older supercontinent that had assembled and broken up long before. Source: https://vividmaps.com/central-pangean-mountains/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Pangean_Mountains

question: The Appalachians once ran on past North America's coast as part of one unbroken mountain chain, long before the Atlantic existed. When the ocean began to open, about 200 million years ago, it tore through the chain and rafted the pieces off on separate continents. Which two ranges are the Appalachians' long-lost other halves?
context: When Pangaea rifted and the Atlantic opened (~200-180 Mya, in the Jurassic), it split one ancient mountain belt across three continents. Geologists match the Appalachians' rocks to Scotland's Highlands (raised in the Caledonian orogeny) and Morocco's Anti-Atlas — once a single continuous chain. In a poetic twist, Scottish Highlanders who emigrated in the 1700s settled the Appalachians, unknowingly returning to a broken-off piece of their own homeland's mountains. Source: https://vividmaps.com/central-pangean-mountains/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains

question: Salt and sand now spread across the dry bed of the Aral Sea, on the border of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, which within living memory ranked as the world's fourth-largest lake before more than 90% of its water drained away. Maps call this desert the Aralkum. What title do geographers give it?
context: Most of the old seabed is now the Aralkum -- a salt-and-sand desert that geographers call the newest desert on Earth, formed within a single human lifetime. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea; geographyrealm.com/aralkum-desert-worlds-newest-desert/

question: The Aral Sea once spread wide between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and the old Turkic word it is named for fit the place perfectly. Now that most of the water is gone, the name has turned painfully ironic. What is 'Aral' usually translated as?
context: 'Aral' is usually translated as 'Sea of Islands,' a nod to the more than 1,000 islands that once dotted its waters. Now that most of the sea is dry land, the old name reads like a sad joke. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea

question: Soviet planners deliberately diverted the Aral Sea's two great feeder rivers into vast irrigation canals, beginning in the 1960s, all to raise one thirsty crop across the desert. Starved of its inflow, the sea evaporated. Which crop did the planners choose to grow?
context: Cotton -- nicknamed 'white gold' -- was the priority. The rivers that had filled the Aral for millennia were bled into the cotton fields, and by 1988 Uzbekistan was the world's largest cotton exporter, even as the sea behind it collapsed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea

question: The shrinking Aral Sea pulled back in July 2001 from a patch of Kazakh seabed that had lain about 20 metres under water, and on that fresh dry ground archaeologists made a big find, now called the Kerderi site. What had the retreating water laid bare?
context: The retreating Aral uncovered Kerderi -- a lost medieval town called Aral-Asar and a domed mausoleum, inhabited around the 14th century and found in July 2001 after lying about 20 metres underwater. It proved the Aral had grown and shrunk before: people once lived and were buried on ground that later became sea floor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerderi; advantour.com/uzbekistan/aralsea/history.htm

question: Wind tears an estimated 80 to 100 million tons of dust off the dry bed of the Aral Sea every year and hurls it across Central Asia, and it is no clean sand: decades of irrigated farming left the old seabed caked with salt, pesticides and fertilizer. Where have scientists traced this poisoned dust settling, far from the Aral?
context: Aral dust has been traced onto distant glaciers, including Greenland's, and it settles on the snowpack that feeds Central Asia's rivers -- carrying the disaster far beyond the old shoreline. Source: geographyrealm.com/aralkum-desert-worlds-newest-desert/; eurekalert.org/news-releases/1041605

question: Vozrozhdeniya, or Rebirth Island, sat in the Aral Sea for decades, left off Soviet maps and ringed by water that kept everyone away. As the sea shrank it joined the mainland, and the world grew alarmed at what the Soviets had left buried there. What had the island secretly been?
context: Vozrozhdeniya was a secret Soviet site where anthrax and plague agents were trialled. Isolated by water for years, it became reachable on foot around 2001-2008 as the sea receded, raising fears the buried pathogens could be reached. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea

question: Kazakhstan finished the Kokaral Dam in 2005, a long dyke that sealed off the Aral Sea's smaller northern lobe and trapped the water of the Syr Darya inside instead of letting it drain south. The water climbed more than 12 metres, and then something that had vanished from these waters came back, years ahead of every scientific forecast. What was it?
context: Behind the Kokaral Dam the North Aral rose over 12 metres by 2008 and its saltiness fell from about 30 back toward 8 grams per litre -- fresh enough for the native fish to breed again. The comeback outran every forecast: Kazakh fish were being exported as far as Ukraine by 2006. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dike_Kokaral; eros.usgs.gov/earthshots/kok-aral-dam

question: At the top of the world lies an ocean so nearly locked in by North America, Europe and Asia that a traveller could almost walk around it. It is the smallest and shallowest of Earth's five oceans. Which ocean is it?
context: The Arctic Ocean covers only about 14 million km² with an average depth near 1,038 m — smaller and shallower than the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, or Southern Ocean. Eurasia and North America wrap almost all the way around it, so it is nearly landlocked, the one ocean a traveller could very nearly circle on foot. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean

question: A traveller who reaches the exact North Pole sees flat white ice running to the horizon in every direction under a low sun. He looks down at his boots and wonders what lies directly beneath that spot. What is really there?
answer: drifting sea ice floating on deep ocean
choices: drifting sea ice floating on deep ocean
a mile-thick ice cap resting on bedrock
a small rocky island hidden by snow and ice
ground frozen solid for many kilometres down
context: This is the load-bearing surprise of the far north: the geographic North Pole is not land at all, but a raft of sea ice only a few metres thick drifting over about 4 km of water (measured at 4,261 m in 2007). The South Pole is its opposite — solid Antarctic rock under a deep ice cap. Nothing permanent can be built at the North Pole, because the ice beneath it is always moving. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pole

question: A ship heading out of the Arctic toward the Pacific has just one door to pass through: a channel only 82 kilometres wide, between Siberia and Alaska. What is this lone Pacific gateway called?
context: The Bering Strait is the Arctic Ocean's only doorway to the Pacific — about 82 km wide and just 40–50 m deep, between Siberia and Alaska. Every other connection the Arctic has runs to the Atlantic. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia

question: Off the coast of Greenland, towering icebergs drift out into the open ocean, some as tall as buildings. They look like sea ice, the frozen crust of the ocean itself, but they reached the sea another way. How is one of these Greenland icebergs born?
answer: a chunk breaks off the end of a glacier and floats out to sea
choices: a chunk breaks off the end of a glacier and floats out to sea
a mountain snowbank slides downhill and freezes onto the waves
a frozen waterfall snaps off a coastal cliff and topples in
a river freezes solid and a slab floats free when spring arrives
context: Sea ice is frozen seawater — as the ocean freezes, most of its salt is squeezed out, so sea ice is far less salty than the water it came from. An iceberg is completely different: it is freshwater ice that calved (broke off) from a glacier or ice shelf that formed on land, like the glaciers that ring Greenland. Same-looking ice, opposite origins. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_ice

question: The sun at the geographic North Pole climbs above the horizon in spring and then stays up, never once setting; when at last it sinks, it does not rise again for one long, unbroken night. About how long does each last, the endless day and the endless night?
context: At the North Pole the sun essentially rises and sets just once a year: it climbs above the horizon around the March equinox and stays up for about six months (the midnight sun), then sinks around the September equinox for about six months of continuous polar night. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pole

question: Far beneath the drifting Arctic ice, sonar has traced a hidden mountain range running about 1,800 kilometres across the deep basin, from the New Siberian Islands to Ellesmere Island. It rises over 3,000 metres above the seabed and splits the deep Arctic in two. Russia, Canada and Denmark all claim it, because owning it could redraw the seabed borders. What is this undersea range called?
context: The Lomonosov Ridge is a submarine mountain range about 1,800 km long, running from the New Siberian Islands to Ellesmere Island and rising 3,300–3,700 m above the roughly 4,200 m deep basin floor. It splits the deep Arctic into the Eurasian and Amerasian basins, and Russia, Canada, and Denmark all argue over it because it could decide where the seabed border runs. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lomonosov_Ridge

question: Norway's Fridtjof Nansen locked his ship, the Fram, into the sea ice off Siberia in 1893, meaning to ride it. About three years later the ship came out near Svalbard, right where he had predicted. Whatever freezes into the ice off Siberia drifts the same way, past the Pole and out of the Arctic by the Fram Strait. What great current of drifting ice carries it?
context: The Transpolar Drift is a current of moving ice that sweeps from the Siberian coast, past the North Pole, and out through the Fram Strait into the Atlantic over roughly two to four years. In 1893 Fridtjof Nansen let his ship Fram freeze into the ice to ride it; the Fram drifted for about three years and emerged near Svalbard, right where he had predicted, proving the current was real. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transpolar_Drift_Stream  (Legend.)

question: Weather stations in a desert of northern Chile have run for years, sometimes over a decade straight, without recording a single measurable drop of rain. Its soil is more like moon dust than dirt. Which desert is this, the driest on Earth outside the poles?
context: The Atacama, in northern Chile, is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth; at some stations, instruments have never recorded measurable rain. Antarctica is technically drier, but as a polar desert it stands in a class of its own. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert'.

question: NASA engineers drove a test rover across the ground near Yungay, in Chile's Atacama Desert, for four field seasons. The soil there is so dry and dead that scientists call it Earth's closest stand-in for another world. Which world was the rover practising for?
context: NASA's ARADS project (Atacama Rover Astrobiology Drilling Studies) ran four field seasons near Yungay because the core Atacama's soil holds so few microbes that it fools life-detection hardware the same way Mars would. Source: NASA, 'ARADS'.

question: Families in some villages on the Atacama's Chilean coast fill their jugs with fresh drinking water every single morning, though no river runs past, almost no rain falls and the groundwater is far too salty to drink. How do they do it?
answer: they string mesh nets to catch fog
choices: they string mesh nets to catch fog
they truck it in from the Andes
they seed the clouds for rain
context: Atacama villagers hang Raschel-mesh 'fog collectors' on the hills to catch the camanchaca; one roughly 40 m² net yields about 200 litres a day, and in the 1980s the village of Chungungo was supplied by around 100 of them. Source: Mongabay, 'Can fog harvesting help solve water scarcity in Chile's Atacama Desert?'

question: High on Cerro Paranal, a 2,635-metre peak rising straight out of the Atacama, sit four 8.2-metre telescopes that can be linked to work as a single eye — built here because this desert has some of the clearest, most cloudless night skies on Earth. Which observatory scans the southern sky from that ridge?
context: On Cerro Paranal (2,635 m) in the Atacama sits the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope: four 8.2-metre telescopes that can be combined into a single giant instrument, the largest optical/infrared observatory in the Southern Hemisphere, built here for the desert's exceptionally clear, cloudless night skies. Source: Wikipedia, 'Paranal Observatory'.

question: Sixty-six giant dish antennas stand together in the cold on the Chajnantor plateau, more than 5,000 metres up in the thin, dry air of Chile's Atacama Desert. They move as one to catch faint radio hums from galaxies being born and from the chilly clouds of gas and dust where stars and planets form. Which observatory is it?
context: ALMA — the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array — has 66 antennas on the 5,059 m Chajnantor plateau; the thin, bone-dry air barely absorbs the millimetre-wave signals it hunts. Nearby on Cerro Paranal, ESO's Very Large Telescope enjoys some of Earth's clearest night skies. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Large Millimeter Array'; 'Paranal Observatory'.

question: Long before anyone there learned to embalm the dead, Chile's Atacama Desert was turning bodies into mummies by itself. Along its coast some human remains have survived for as long as 9,000 years, skin and all, with no resin and no wrappings. Besides the rainless air, what feature of the ground preserves flesh so perfectly here?
context: The Atacama's rainless air plus salty, nitrate-rich soil mummifies flesh naturally; one naturally preserved body on this coast dates to about 7020 BC. The same chemistry preserved the region's later, deliberately made mummies. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinchorro mummies'.

question: A people of the Atacama's northern coast, near Arica in Chile, took their dead apart, dried them and rebuilt them around frames of sticks and reeds. They began around 5050 BC, roughly 2,000 years before the Egyptians mummified a single pharaoh, and left the oldest deliberately made mummies on Earth. What are these mummies called?
context: The Chinchorro of the Atacama coast practised artificial mummification from about 5050 BC — some 2,000 years before Egypt. They mummified everyone, even infants; 'black mummies' were taken apart, cleaned and reassembled, later 'red mummies' painted with ochre. UNESCO named the sites a World Heritage Site in 2021. Source: Wikipedia, 'Chinchorro mummies'.

question: A cold fog climbs the coastal cliffs of Chile's Atacama Desert at dawn, drifts inland off the chilly Pacific, and burns away as the sun rises. Lichens and cacti drink straight from it in a land of almost no rain. What do Chileans call it?
context: The camanchaca rolls in off the cold Humboldt Current that runs up this coast, and the Atacama is the largest fog desert on Earth. It is why the Atacama is called the 'driest' desert, not a desert with no water at all — the fog keeps hardy plants alive. (The cassimbo is its Angolan cousin, tule fog shrouds California's Central Valley, and sea fret is the cold sea-fog of Britain's North Sea coast.) Sources: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert.

question: The world's wealthiest nations have hauled heavy equipment up onto the high plateaus of Chile's Atacama Desert, hundreds of kilometres of bare rock where almost no one lives. They have spent billions of dollars building there, in the middle of nowhere. What did they come to this desert to build?
context: The air above the Atacama is the clearest and driest of almost anywhere on Earth — over 200 cloudless nights a year, high up and far from any city's glow. With so little cloud or moisture to blur the view, the European Southern Observatory and others put their giant telescopes here rather than anywhere else on Earth. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert' (ESO).

question: Scientists studying the driest heart of Chile's Atacama Desert found signs of an almost unimaginable stretch with no real rain at all. Elsewhere, deserts go a few weeks, or sometimes a year or two, between rains. Roughly how long did the Atacama's dry spell last?
context: The evidence points to roughly 1570 to 1971 — about four centuries — with no significant rain in that spot. It is an estimate from soil and climate clues, not a rain gauge, so scientists give it carefully. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert.'  (Legend.)

question: Workers on the Atacama's Chajnantor plateau carry bottled oxygen in the thin air, 5,000 metres up. There, 66 dish antennas link together as a single telescope. Sitting on the ground, it should be no match for the Hubble Space Telescope up in orbit, yet it sees the sky more sharply than Hubble does. About how much sharper?
context: At 5,000 m, ALMA is the highest major observatory on Earth. Its 66 linked antennas cost about US$1.4 billion — the most expensive ground-based astronomy project ever built. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Large Millimeter Array.'

question: Night falls over the Valle de la Luna, the 'Valley of the Moon', a maze of wind-carved salt ridges near the oasis town of San Pedro de Atacama. In the deep silence, as the fierce heat of day gives way to a freezing night, the salt-crusted ground makes a startling sound. What do people hear?
context: The salt crust crackles and pops as it expands and shrinks with the desert's huge day-to-night temperature swings. A neighbouring basin is grimly named Valle de la Muerte — 'Death Valley.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Valle de la Luna (Chile).'

question: Pink flamingos wade in the bright turquoise lagoons of the Salar de Atacama, a vast salt flat in Chile's Atacama Desert. Beneath its crust lies a briny soup of dissolved metals, and one of them is packed in more richly than in any other brine on Earth: about a quarter of all the world's known reserves sit right here. Which metal is the Salar's great prize?
context: The Salar de Atacama holds the highest lithium concentration of any brine on Earth — roughly a quarter of the world's known reserves. Source: Wikipedia, 'Salar de Atacama.'

question: The sand of Chile's Atacama stays bare and brown most years, until a rare, freak rain soaks it and wakes seeds that have lain asleep underground for years. For a few weeks between September and November, some 200 kinds of wildflower then carpet the desert from horizon to horizon, a bloom so prized that Chile made a national park to protect it. What is this rare bloom called?
context: 'Desierto florido' means 'flowering desert.' The blooms include the pink añañuca and the mallow, sprung from seeds that can wait years underground for a single soaking rain. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Desert.'

question: Desert people outlined the Atacama Giant on a lonely hillside of Cerro Unita, in northern Chile, between about 1000 and 1400 CE. At about 86 metres, it is the largest ancient figure of a human drawn on the land anywhere. Its true purpose is still debated, but one popular idea is that the giant worked as a practical tool. What might it have been used as?
answer: a calendar to track the seasons
choices: a calendar to track the seasons
a burial tomb for a chieftain
context: By one leading theory, lines running from the giant's head line up with the moon to mark the seasons and predict when the rains would come. Its meaning is still disputed, and some sources put its height as high as 119 m. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atacama Giant.'  (Legend.)

question: Suetonius wrote of a Roman emperor who loved to perform in public and swore he would appear on a reed pipe fed by a bag squeezed under his arm. Rome knew the bagpipe long before Scotland made it famous. Which emperor made that vow?
context: Long before the Highland pipes, the bag-and-pipe was already at home in the ancient Mediterranean. The Roman historian Suetonius wrote that the emperor Nero — a compulsive public performer — vowed to appear on stage as a 'tibia utricularis' player, a reed pipe fed from a bladder or bag squeezed under the arm, exactly like a bagpipe's air-bag. Every bagpipe works this way: a squeezed bag of air feeds a fingered melody pipe (the chanter) and one or more pipes that drone a single steady note beneath the tune. So although Scotland treats the Great Highland Bagpipe as its national symbol, the instrument itself has no single birthplace. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagpipes ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Highland_bagpipe  (Legend.)

question: Writers in ancient Greece, long before Scotland had its pipers, described a pipe fitted into a puffed-up bag of animal skin, squeezed under the player's arm to sound one steady droning note. What did the Greeks call this instrument?
context: The bagpipe's roots reach deep into the ancient Mediterranean. Greek writers describe a bag-and-reed pipe they called the askaulos — a name built from askos ('wineskin') and aulos ('reed pipe'), so the word means, almost literally, 'wineskin-pipe.' Roman writers, too, tell of an emperor performing on a bladder-fed pipe. Long before any piper skirled in the Highlands, the bag-and-pipe was already at home around the Mediterranean and across Europe — which is why Scotland, though it made the Great Highland Bagpipe its national symbol, cannot claim to have invented the pipes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagpipes  (Legend.)

question: In the green, rainy northwest of Spain, among the stone villages of Galicia and Asturias, people prize their own bagpipe as a badge of the region, loved as the Highland pipes are loved in Scotland. What is this Spanish bagpipe called?
context: Galicia and Asturias, on Spain's rainy Atlantic northwest, wear their gaita as proudly as Scotland wears its pipes. Bagpipes were never only Celtic: cousins ring across Europe — Brittany's mouth-blown one-drone biniou, and Bulgaria and the Balkans' single-drone gaida, a near-cognate of the Spanish gaita. In modern times Pakistan even became the world's largest bagpipe manufacturer. Source: https://worldinstruments.org/instruments/gaita/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagpipes

question: Scotland's Great Highland pipes are blown hard by the mouth and skirl loud enough for a battlefield. Ireland's own bagpipe is the gentle opposite — soft and sweet, played sitting down indoors, and never blown by the mouth at all: the seated piper feeds the bag dry air from a small bellows instead. Its Irish name, 'uilleann,' refers to which body part?
context: The uilleann ('elbow') pipes took shape in Ireland in the early 1700s. A bellows strapped to the waist and arm, pumped by the elbow, feeds the bag dry air — so unlike mouth-blown pipes the reeds stay dry and the tone stays sweet. Played seated, they reach a full two-octave range, and a full set adds keyed 'regulators' the piper's wrist can tap to sound chords. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uilleann_pipes

question: Boats at Burntcoat Head, in eastern Canada, lie on bare mud one hour and float the next. Twice a day the sea there rises and falls about 16 metres, as high as a four-storey house: the greatest tides on Earth. Where do these tides rise?
context: The Bay of Fundy sits between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Its mean spring tides average about 14.5 m, with an extreme range near 16.3 m recorded at Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia — the figure Guinness recognized in 1975 as the greatest tides on Earth, measured by a Canadian Hydrographic Service tide gauge. (Wikipedia, 'Bay of Fundy' and 'Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia')

question: On the Bay of Fundy's New Brunswick shore, the falling tide bares sandstone pillars 12 to 21 metres tall, many wider at the top than the base and crowned with shrubs. Visitors walk the seabed around them at low tide; hours later a kayak floats over the same spot. What are these 'flowerpots' called?
context: The Hopewell Rocks stand on the New Brunswick shore of the Bay of Fundy. The tide carves them by eating the softer base away faster than the top, leaving the wide-crowned 'flowerpot' shape — some 12 to 21 m tall, with shrubs and small trees rooted on their crowns. Visitors walk the exposed sea floor at low tide, and hours later the same ground lies deep enough to paddle over. (Wikipedia, 'Hopewell Rocks')

question: Twice a day the tide pours into Canada's Bay of Fundy, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, carrying some 100 billion tonnes of salt water, and a few hours later it drags the whole load back out. How does one tide's flow measure up?
answer: More than every river on Earth combined
choices: More than every river on Earth combined
About as much as the Amazon carries
Roughly the water in the five Great Lakes
More than all the rain that falls on Earth in a week
context: About 100 billion tonnes of water flood in and out of the Bay of Fundy with each tide — roughly twice the combined flow of all the freshwater rivers on Earth. Much of it squeezes through the narrow Minas Passage in the bay's upper reaches. (Wikipedia, 'Bay of Fundy'; bayoffundy.com)

question: An ocean wave usually carries a surfer for less than a minute before it breaks. In July 2013 surfers caught the tidal bore that the Bay of Fundy's returning tide drives up New Brunswick's Petitcodiac River, and rode it the whole way to Moncton. About how far did that one wave carry them?
context: A tidal bore is a wave that runs upstream when a strong incoming tide overpowers a river's outflow. On the Petitcodiac the bore has topped 2 m; in July 2013 surfers rode a bore about 29 km upstream from Belliveau Village to Moncton, a North American continuous-surfing record. Rafters ride the Shubenacadie River bore in Nova Scotia. (Wikipedia, 'Tidal bore')

question: At Cape Split, a long finger of cliff reaching into the Bay of Fundy, the incoming tide races through the narrows at about 8 knots. The churning water grows so loud that a deep, hollow roar rises up and fills the forest on the clifftops — a sound local people have long called by one haunting name. What is it?
context: Cape Split reaches into the Bay of Fundy near the Minas Channel, where the tidal current can hit about 8 knots (15 km/h). Locals say the turbulence sends a deep hollow roar up into the clifftop forest, which they call the 'Voice of the Moon' — fitting, since the moon's pull drives the tides. (fundydiscovery.ca, 'Fundy Fun Facts')

question: The Saint John River, at the city of Saint John in New Brunswick, pours over a set of hidden rock ledges as a churning rapid just before it empties into the Bay of Fundy. Twice a day the giant Fundy tide comes surging in and overpowers the river completely. What happens to the rapids then?
answer: The rapids reverse and churn upstream, uphill
choices: The rapids reverse and churn upstream, uphill
The rapids freeze into a standing sheet of ice
The river splits and pours down two channels
The fresh water turns salty in a matter of seconds
context: This is the Reversing Falls (or Reversing Rapids) at Saint John, New Brunswick. When the Fundy tide surges in, it overpowers the Saint John River and forces its rapids to churn backward, upstream over submerged ledges. At slack tide the flow pauses for a few minutes — the only safe window for boats to pass — before it turns and runs seaward again. (Wikipedia, 'Reversing Falls')

question: The sea at Burntcoat Head, on the Bay of Fundy, rose to roughly 21.6 metres, the highest water ever measured there, on one October night in 1869, bursting the Minas Basin dykes. Almost a year before, a Royal Navy instructor had warned that extreme tides would strike that very day, and was laughed at until that night proved him right. By what name is that night remembered?
context: The Saxby Gale of October 4–5, 1869 drove Fundy's highest water on record, about 21.6 m (71 ft) at Burntcoat Head, when a hurricane's surge landed atop a perigean spring tide and burst the Minas Basin and Tantramar dykes. It is named for Lt. Stephen Saxby, a Royal Navy instructor who had warned nearly a year earlier that three lunar events falling within hours would drive extreme tides that day — he was mocked as an astrologer until the storm proved him right. (Wikipedia, 'Saxby Gale')  (Legend.)

question: Between Siberia and Alaska, at the height of the ice ages, the sea floor lay bare as dry land, joining Asia to North America for thousands of years until rising seas drowned it again some 11,000 years ago. Eric Hultén, a Swedish botanist, named this lost country in 1937. What did he call it?
context: The lost land is BERINGIA, named in 1937 by the Swedish botanist Eric Hultén after Vitus Bering, the Danish-born explorer who sailed into the strait in 1728 (which is why the strait bears his name too). During the ice ages, enough of the planet's water was locked in ice sheets to drop the sea more than 50 metres — plenty to expose Beringia's floor — and up to about 120 metres at the peak of the Last Glacial Maximum. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia

question: Across the Bering Strait, Siberia and Alaska face each other only 82 kilometres apart, at the gap where Asia and North America almost touch. A water gap between two great continents sounds as if it ought to be a deep ocean trench, a real barrier. On average, how deep is the strait's floor?
context: Only about 40–50 m (130–160 ft) deep on average, the Bering Strait's floor is so shallow that a fairly modest fall in sea level is enough to turn the whole strait into dry land — which is exactly what the ice ages did. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia ; https://hakaimagazine.com/features/sunken-bridge-size-continent/

question: Ice Age Beringia, the land bridge between Siberia and Alaska, lay far in the north at the height of the cold, while vast ice sheets buried much of North America. Fierce, dust-laden winds swept across it. What covered most of its ground?
answer: a cold, dry sea of grass
choices: a cold, dry sea of grass
a thick sheet of glacier ice
a dark forest of spruce trees
a soggy maze of moss bogs
context: Beringia was the 'mammoth steppe' — a cold, dry grassland of grasses and herbs rather than forest, named for the great Ice-Age beasts that grazed it. It was no narrow footpath either: at its greatest extent the land bridge stretched up to about 1,000 km (620 mi) from north to south — a whole grassy country between two continents. Source: https://home.nps.gov/subjects/beringia/nature.htm ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia

question: When the world's seas stood at their lowest, at the peak of the last Ice Age, Beringia spread out between Siberia and Alaska as one vast, open plain: no mere sliver of shore bared by a falling tide, but a whole country between two continents. At its greatest, roughly how large was this drowned land?
answer: as large as British Columbia and Alberta combined
choices: as large as British Columbia and Alberta combined
as large as Alaska and Yukon combined
as large as Texas and California combined
as large as France and Germany combined
context: At its greatest extent Beringia covered roughly 1.6 million square kilometres — an area comparable to the Canadian provinces of British Columbia and Alberta combined. This was no bridge to be scurried across in a day but a broad, grassy world in its own right; the first peoples out of Asia crossed it on foot during the Ice Age, before the rising seas drowned it again around 11,000 years ago. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia

question: As the ice melted and the seas climbed once more, Beringia's plain flooded and split the two continents apart again. Almost the whole land bridge now lies drowned — but a handful of small islands still break the surface, the last high points of that lost country. Which islands are these surviving remnants of Beringia?
context: They are the Diomede Islands. Big Diomede (Russia) and Little Diomede (Alaska, USA) sit just 3.8 km (2.4 mi) apart — yet both the U.S.–Russia border and the International Date Line run between them, so Big Diomede is nicknamed 'Tomorrow Island' and Little Diomede 'Yesterday Island,' nearly a full day apart in time. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Diomede-Islands ; https://polarjournal.net/diomede-islands-only-3-8-kilometers-separate-the-usa-and-russia/

question: Stone Age hunters once fished the rivers and marshes of a plain that now lies under the North Sea. The same worldwide fall in sea level that bared Beringia had laid that floor dry, joining Britain to mainland Europe, until the returning sea drowned it for good. What is this lost North Sea land called?
context: This drowned plain is Doggerland, now under the North Sea. Its end was violent as well as slow: around 6150 BC a giant undersea landslide off Norway, the Storegga Slide, sent a tsunami sweeping across the North Sea. The same worldwide sea-drop had also joined Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania into one continent, Sahul — New Guinea split off about 8,000 years ago and Tasmania about 6,000 years ago. So Beringia was just one door among several the ice ages briefly opened. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doggerland ; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/tiny-islands-survived-tsunami-almost-separated-britain-europe-study-finds-180976430/ ; https://www.britannica.com/place/Sahul

question: In the Mississippi Delta, the flat cotton country where the blues was born about a century ago, bluesmen made their guitar strings wail and cry like a grieving human voice. What classic Delta trick made them cry that way?
context: The tool is a 'slide' or 'bottleneck' - a smooth glass or metal tube (originally the broken-off neck of a real bottle, or even a pocketknife) worn on one finger and glided along the strings so the notes bend and 'cry' like a voice. Slide playing is the hallmark of Delta blues. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_blues

question: Long before anyone in the Mississippi Delta picked up a guitar, the sound of singing carried across the flat Delta country. One voice would call out a line, and a whole crowd would answer straight back, over and over. The blues grew directly out of this older Black music. What were these songs called?
context: The blues grew straight out of the field hollers and call-and-response work songs of Black laborers in the Delta's cotton fields - one voice cries a line and the others answer it back. That answering pattern carried right into the blues, where the guitar 'answers' the singer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_blues

question: B.B. King once stood on a giant cotton plantation near Cleveland, Mississippi, and said that the blues all started right there. Around 1900 Charley Patton and a cluster of the first blues musicians lived, worked and played on its land. What is this plantation, often called the cradle of the blues?
context: Dockery Farms, a huge cotton plantation near Cleveland, Mississippi, is often called the birthplace of the blues; Charley Patton and other founders lived and played there. B.B. King said, standing on the grounds, that 'it all started right here.' Source: https://msbluestrail.org/blues-trail-markers/birthplace-of-the-blues

question: Charley Patton, called the Father of the Delta Blues, worked the crowds of the Mississippi Delta as a wild showman, and his rough voice was said to carry 500 yards with no microphone. Long before rock stars made the same trick famous, what did Patton do with his guitar to please a crowd?
context: Patton - about five foot five - played guitar behind his head, down between his knees, and behind his back, clowning that showmen like Jimi Hendrix would echo decades later. His gravelly voice was said to carry 500 yards with no amplification. Source: https://mississippiencyclopedia.org/entries/charley-patton/

question: Thousands of songs from the cotton country of the Mississippi Delta, each with its own story, ride on one shared frame, the twelve-bar blues, simple enough that any player can jump in. How many chords does that whole frame use?
context: The '12-bar blues' runs twelve measures on just three chords (the I, IV, and V of the key) and usually carries an AAB lyric - the singer states a line, repeats it, then answers with a rhyming third line ('I woke up this morning...' twice, then the payoff). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-bar_blues

question: Outside Clarksdale, Mississippi, two country highways cross at a lonely spot. Blues fans still gather there for the Delta's most famous tale. The guitar player Robert Johnson was a clumsy beginner who vanished for a season and came back strangely brilliant. Legend says he went to this crossroads alone at midnight. What does the legend claim happened there?
answer: he sold his soul to the devil
choices: he sold his soul to the devil
he was cursed by a hoodoo woman
he was blessed by a river spirit
he stole a rival's magic guitar
context: This is folklore, not fact. The crossroads sits where Highways 61 and 49 meet in Clarksdale, Mississippi; the legend of a midnight deal for supernatural talent lies behind Johnson songs like 'Cross Road Blues' and 'Hellhound on My Trail.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Johnson

question: Son House, an older bluesman, remembered Robert Johnson leaving the Mississippi Delta a fumbling beginner and coming back a master. Researchers later traced the change to long nights of practice with Ike Zimmerman, his mentor, who knew a quiet local spot where no one would bother them after dark. Where did the two practise at night?
context: Son House said Johnson simply vanished and returned brilliant. Modern research credits long night practice with mentor Ike Zimmerman in graveyards - quiet, with no one to disturb them. The soul-selling tale was actually first told about a different bluesman, Tommy Johnson. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Johnson

question: Bluesmen heading north out of the Mississippi cotton country followed one U.S. highway, which starts in New Orleans, threads through the heart of the Delta and climbs on to Memphis. Bob Dylan later borrowed its name for a landmark 1965 album. Which road is nicknamed 'The Blues Highway'?
context: U.S. Highway 61, 'The Blues Highway,' runs from New Orleans up through the Delta to Memphis and on north, carrying Delta bluesmen out of Mississippi during the Great Migration. Bob Dylan named his 1965 album 'Highway 61 Revisited.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_blues

question: W.C. Handy, a bandleader, sat stranded for nine hours at the tiny depot in Tutwiler, Mississippi, in 1903, his train running late. A lean, ragged man beside him made his guitar moan, pressing something hard against the strings and sliding it as he sang a strange refrain about two railroads crossing. Handy called it 'the weirdest music I ever heard.' What was the man pressing against his strings?
context: Handy's nine-hour wait at Tutwiler gave him the first blues he ever heard - a knife pressed to the strings, 'the weirdest music,' he wrote. He noted the trick was done 'in a manner popularized by Hawaiian guitarists who used steel bars.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._C._Handy

question: Near Moorhead, in the Mississippi Delta, two railroads cross: the Southern and a smaller line, the Yazoo and Mississippi Valley, which local people knew by a colourful nickname. W.C. Handy, who had chased down a haunting line sung about that crossing, wove the nickname into a song of 1914. What was the little railroad nicknamed?
context: The Yazoo & Mississippi Valley Railroad was nicknamed the 'Yellow Dog' for its mustard-yellow cars painted with the initials 'YD.' At Moorhead it crossed the Southern Railroad - the spot behind the line 'Goin' where the Southern cross the Dog' - and Handy spun it into his 1914 'Yellow Dog Blues.' Source: https://msbluestrail.org/blues-trail-markers/w-c-handy

question: Elmore James, like many a future bluesman in the cotton country of the Mississippi Delta, first taught himself the blues on a homemade instrument that any poor child could throw together from a scrap of wood and wire, years before he could hold a real guitar. What was this homemade instrument called?
context: The one-string 'diddley bow' - wire nailed to a porch or wall, plucked while a glass bottle slides along it to bend the pitch - taught many bluesmen (Elmore James among them) their first notes and shaped the slide sound. It traces back to single-string instruments of West Africa's Sahel. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diddley_bow

question: Pilgrims setting out on the Camino Francés from Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, a village in France, face a hard first day: a climb over the high wall of mountains that divides France from Spain, then down to Roncesvalles. Which mountain range do they cross?
context: The Pyrenees form the natural wall between France and Spain. The popular 'Route Napoleon' over them tops out at the Lepoeder pass (about 1,430 m) before dropping through beech forest to Roncesvalles at 945 m -- where, in AD 778, Charlemagne's rearguard was ambushed and wiped out, the real battle behind the medieval epic 'The Song of Roland.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camino_de_Santiago; pilgrim.es french-way stage 1; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_of_Roland.

question: Almost every walker on the Camino de Santiago, the pilgrim road across northern Spain walked since the Middle Ages, still wears the road's ancient emblem clipped to a pack: one kind of seashell. Which shell is the old badge of the Camino?
context: Pilgrims have worn the scallop -- the vieira -- since the Middle Ages. Look closely and its grooves all fan out and meet at a single point: a picture of the many pilgrim roads across Europe all converging on the one tomb at Santiago. Source: caminoways.com/camino-markings; caminoways.com/the-scallop-shell-and-the-camino-de-santiago.

question: About a third of the way to Santiago, the Camino leaves the green mountains behind and strikes out across the burning heart of Castile. Walkers cross this high, flat, treeless tableland for a week with no hill in sight, and many pilgrims dread this part most. What is this vast central tableland called?
context: The Meseta Central makes up much of interior Spain. On the Camino it runs roughly 220 km almost dead straight between the great cathedral cities of Burgos and Leon; the punishing leg out of Carrion de los Condes crosses about 17 km with no village, no shade, and no water in between. Source: caminoadventures.com/blog/meseta-camino-de-santiago; followthecamino.com/en/blog/the-meseta-on-the-camino-de-santiago.

question: A hermit in the 800s, the legend says, was drawn night after night to one spot in the woods of Galicia, where he uncovered the lost tomb of St James the Great, the apostle. The cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, the goal of the Camino, rises over it today. What drew him there?
answer: a light in the night sky
choices: a light in the night sky
context: From this legend the place is read as Campus Stellae -- 'field of stars' -- the likely root of the name 'Compostela.' The cathedral was raised over the shrine of St James and became the end of every pilgrim road in Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_de_Compostela_Cathedral.

question: Elías Valiña, the parish priest of the mountain village of O Cebreiro, set out in 1984 to mark the whole Camino Francés from Roncesvalles to Santiago himself. Most of the marks that guide pilgrims along its 800 kilometres are his work. With what unlikely kit did he do it?
answer: a bucket of leftover yellow road paint and his old Citroen 2CV
choices: a bucket of leftover yellow road paint and his old Citroen 2CV
a cart of carved granite waymark stones and a pack mule
a can of whitewash and a tall wooden painter's ladder
a surveyor's theodolite and a stack of printed maps
context: The colour stuck: those humble marks became the famous yellow arrows that now guide pilgrims not just along the Camino Frances but across the whole of Spain. Valina made the run from Roncesvalles to Santiago in that battered 2CV, dabbing an arrow at every turn from a bucket of leftover yellow road paint, and he did it in a single push in 1984. Source: vivecamino.com/en/elias-valina-and-the-yellow-arrows-of-the-camino-de-santiago-no-190; caminoways.com/camino-markings.

question: High on the last mountain before the road drops into green Galicia sits O Cebreiro, a tiny stone village wrapped in mist at 1,296 m. Among its lanes stand round houses with thick stone walls and steep straw roofs and no chimney -- a design lived in here since Celtic times and found almost nowhere else. What are these ancient round dwellings called?
context: Pallozas kept out the mountain cold with drystone walls and a thick thatch of rye straw, sheltering families and their animals under one roof; some were lived in at O Cebreiro into the 20th century. O Cebreiro is the gateway where the Camino climbs into Galicia, the last region before Santiago. Source: caminoways.com/o-cebreiro; vivecamino.com/en/o-cebreiro.

question: Beyond the cathedral of Santiago, many pilgrims keep walking, about 90 kilometres more, to a wild headland on the Atlantic that the Romans named the end of the earth. There they watch the last sun of the day drop into the sea. What is this cape, the true finish of the walk for so many?
context: The Romans named it Finis Terrae -- 'the end of the earth.' It is not truly Iberia's westernmost point, though: Cabo da Roca in Portugal reaches about 16.5 km farther west, and even nearby Cabo Tourinan sticks out a little more. Pilgrims here watch the last sun of the day and, by old custom, burn a boot. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Finisterre.

question: A ship sailing the Caspian Sea, between Europe and Asia, crosses some 371,000 square kilometres of water, more than Germany's whole area, yet finds no channel out to any ocean. People call it a sea because of its size, but geographers give it a different title. What is the Caspian, really?
context: By both surface area (about 371,000 km2) and volume, the Caspian is the largest lake on Earth -- bigger than Germany, ringed by five nations (Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran, and Turkmenistan), and holding roughly 40% of all the lake water on the planet. It is called a 'Sea' only for its size and its salt; with no link to the ocean, it is truly a lake. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea.

question: Several great rivers pour into the Caspian Sea from Russia and Central Asia. Yet the Caspian is strange among the world's waters: not one river flows out of it toward the ocean. With water always rushing in and no outlet, how does the Caspian keep from spilling over?
answer: it evaporates away into the air under the sun
choices: it evaporates away into the air under the sun
it drains through a hidden channel to the Black Sea
it spills over into the desert each spring
it flows back up the rivers each season
context: A lake fed by rivers but with no outlet to the sea is called ENDORHEIC -- a 'closed basin.' The Caspian loses water only to evaporation under the sun, so its size is a balance between the rivers pouring in and the sunshine drying it out. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea; geographyrealm.com.

question: The Caspian Sea has climbed and dropped by whole metres within a single lifetime, its level riding on the rivers that feed it. One river alone brings some 80 per cent of all the water flowing in, so its flow largely decides whether the sea rises or falls. Which river holds this power?
context: The Volga, the longest river in Europe, provides roughly 80% of the Caspian's inflow. Because the Caspian is a closed basin, its level then swings by whole metres over the decades -- it fell about 3 m from 1929 to 1977, then rose about 3 m by 1995 -- marching the shoreline at Baku in and out. The Ural also reaches the Caspian; the Danube flows to the Black Sea, and the Amu Darya once fed the Aral. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea.

question: On the Absheron Peninsula near Baku, on the Caspian shore, a curtain of flame some 15 metres wide dances straight out of the bare hillside, fed by natural gas seeping up through the sandstone. Neither rain nor snow can smother it. What is this ever-burning hillside called?
context: Yanar Dag means the 'Burning Mountain.' By one local account a shepherd set it alight by accident in the 1950s; others hold that it has burned far longer. Ground-fires like it gave Azerbaijan its nickname Odlar Yurdu, the 'Land of Fire,' and long ago drew Zoroastrians, who revered fire as sacred; Marco Polo wrote of such eternal flames near Baku centuries before anyone drilled for oil. The other three are real eternal-flame sites too -- Baba Gurgur burns in Iraq, Mount Chimaera in Turkey, and Darvaza is Turkmenistan's fiery gas crater, the 'Door to Hell.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yanar_Dagh; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Land_of_Fire.

question: A swimmer off the Caspian shore who swallows a mouthful tastes the sea in it: not fresh like a mountain lake, yet only about a third as salty as the open ocean. The lake carries salt because it is the shrunken remnant of a real ancient sea, walled off from the world ocean millions of years ago as the land slowly rose. What was that vanished sea called?
context: The Paratethys was a vast sea across ancient Eurasia; tectonic uplift and falling sea level cut it off from the world ocean in the Late Miocene, about 5.5 million years ago. The Caspian, Black, and Aral seas are its surviving remnants -- which is why a landlocked lake is still brackish, about 1.2% salt. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea.

question: Along the Caspian's eastern shore, in Turkmenistan, a wide shallow gulf bakes under the desert sun so fiercely that it dries out faster than any river could fill it. To make up the loss, Caspian water is pulled in through a narrow strait and bakes away, leaving blinding flats of salt, while the water that remains grows nearly as salty as the Dead Sea. What is this gulf called?
context: Kara-Bogaz-Gol reaches about 35% salinity -- as briny as the Dead Sea, far saltier than the Caspian's own 1.2%. In 1980 the Soviets dammed its strait to stop it draining the Caspian; the lagoon dried out by 1984 and wind blew poisonous salt dust across the land, until Turkmenistan removed the barrier in 1992 and Caspian water flowed back in. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garabogazkol.

question: Near Baku on the Caspian shore stands the Ateshgah, a five-sided stone temple built over natural gas vents, where the altar flame burned on its own for centuries and drew Zoroastrian, Hindu and Sikh pilgrims. Then, after years of gas being drawn from the ground nearby, the flame went out in 1969. How is the altar kept burning for visitors today?
answer: gas piped in from outside keeps it lit
choices: gas piped in from outside keeps it lit
a keeper relights it fresh each dawn
a newly found vent under the altar feeds it
oil drawn from the temple's own well fuels it
context: The Ateshgah drew Zoroastrian, Hindu, and Sikh pilgrims to its self-kindling altar. Decades of nearby gas extraction finally starved the natural vents, and the eternal flame went out in 1969; today the altar is kept alight with piped gas for visitors. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ateshgah_of_Baku.

question: A crowd of some 50,000 Romans could empty out of the packed Colosseum in a few minutes, streaming down wide passages in the stands and out through the 80 arches of its outer wall. What were these fast exit passages called?
context: 'Vomitoria' comes from the Latin for 'to spew forth' -- the passages let the stands disgorge a huge crowd fast, exactly like the numbered gates and concourses of a modern stadium. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum  (Legend.)

question: The great arena in the heart of Rome had a proper name of its own, but by around the year 1000 the people of the city were calling it the Colosseum. Where did that popular name come from?
answer: a giant bronze statue that stood beside it
choices: a giant bronze statue that stood beside it
a steep hill of Rome that rose behind it
a Latin word for a ring of stone seats
the family of emperors who had built it
context: The statue was the Colossus of Nero, a bronze giant some 30 metres tall that stood beside the arena. Vespasian later crowned it with sun rays and renamed it for the sun god Sol, but it was still called the Colossus, and by about the year 1000 'Colosseum', the place by the Colossus, had become the arena's everyday name. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Colosseum ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colossus_of_Nero  (Legend.)

question: The emperor Vespasian began a great arena in the heart of Rome, and Titus, his son, opened it around AD 80 for gladiator fights before crowds of some 50,000. They named it not for its huge size but for their own family dynasty. What was the arena's proper name?
context: Vespasian, Titus, and Titus's brother Domitian were the three Flavian emperors: Vespasian began the arena around AD 70-72, Titus dedicated it in AD 80, and Domitian later added the underground level. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum

question: When the afternoon sun beat down on the Colosseum, a huge canvas awning called the velarium was hauled out over the seats to shade the crowd. Rigging that much heavy canvas on ropes and masts took a rare skill, and only one kind of crew had it. What was their usual trade?
context: The awning was worked by sailors brought from the Roman navy's base at Misenum on the Bay of Naples -- only crews used to a ship's rigging could manage the ropes, masts, and vast canvas overhead. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velarium  (Legend.)

question: The ground under the Colosseum was once the heart of Nero's private estate around his Golden House. When Vespasian took power, he turned it into a public arena for the people, but first he had to tear out the showy feature Nero had built there. What did Vespasian clear away?
context: Nero had flooded an ornamental lake, the stagnum, into the middle of Rome for his Golden House (Domus Aurea). Vespasian drained it and built the public Colosseum on the lakebed -- turning an emperor's private playground into a gift to the people. Source: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Golden-House-of-Nero  (Legend.)

question: Beneath the Colosseum's sand-covered wooden floor, the emperor Domitian fitted out the hypogeum with lifts, pulleys and trap doors. To the thrilled crowd above, all that hidden gear worked one big effect during the games. What did the hypogeum make suddenly appear in the arena?
context: Caged beasts and painted scenery rode the hidden lifts up their shafts; when a trap door in the floor sprang open, a lion or bear seemed to erupt out of nowhere. The sand on the floor was there partly to soak up blood. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum  (Legend.)

question: Caged animals rose from the hypogeum under the Colosseum to the arena floor with no engine at all, each cage wound some 7 metres up its shaft by a capstan, a simple winch pushed round by hand. It sounds like work for a few strong men, yet running every lift at once took a small army hidden below the sand. About how many men did it take?
context: The hypogeum held roughly 24-28 lifts, each capstan cranked by as many as eight men -- so running them all at once took over 200 workers coordinating below the floor like a stage crew. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/travel/how-ancient-romans-got-wild-animals-colosseum-180955580/

question: A team of engineers rebuilt one of the Colosseum's long-vanished animal lifts in 2014, using only the materials and hand tools the Romans had, and tested it in the arena itself. For the first time in more than 1,500 years, a live wild animal rode a Roman lift up onto the Colosseum floor. What animal was it?
context: The reconstruction was built for the PBS/NOVA documentary 'Colosseum: Roman Death Trap.' The wolf reached the arena floor calmly and was rewarded with a biscuit rather than a fight. Source: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/travel/how-ancient-romans-got-wild-animals-colosseum-180955580/

question: Ancient writers Cassius Dio and Martial claimed the Colosseum's very first games included a naumachia -- the whole arena flooded so boats could stage a mock sea-battle on the water. Historians are skeptical it ever really happened there, and they point to one later change to the building that would have made flooding flat-out impossible. What change ruled it out?
answer: a two-level maze of tunnels was dug out under the floor
choices: a two-level maze of tunnels was dug out under the floor
the sand floor was resurfaced with waterproof concrete
a deep drainage cistern was sunk at the arena's center
the foundations were driven far deeper into bedrock
context: Once Domitian excavated the stone hypogeum beneath the arena, there was no watertight basin left to fill. No physical proof of the early sea-battles survives, and skeptics add that a shallow one-metre pool couldn't float real warships -- so scholars still debate whether, or how, it was ever done. Source: https://www.througheternity.com/travel-guide/did-sea-battles-take-place-in-the-colosseum-a-history-of-roman-naumachiae  (Legend.)

question: The Colosseum's honey-colored travertine stone is pitted with thousands of small holes, as if a swarm of giant insects had bored into the rock. These pockmarks are not from weather or war but scars from something people dug out of the walls in the Middle Ages, when the ruined arena was mined like a quarry. What were medieval scavengers prying out of the stone?
answer: the iron clamps binding the blocks
choices: the iron clamps binding the blocks
the bronze cramps sealing the joints
the copper ties joining the blocks
the iron dowels pinning the joints
context: The Romans set over 100,000 cubic metres of travertine largely without mortar, pinning the blocks together with roughly 300 tons of iron clamps. Medieval Romans chiselled the metal out to melt down and reuse, leaving the pockmarks that still scar the building. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum  (Legend.)

question: The bed of central Africa's Congo River, near its mouth on the Atlantic, plunges about 220 metres down into blackness, where some of its fish have no eyes at all. What title does the Congo hold among the rivers of Earth?
context: No other river comes close — and this is a river depth, not a lake. Scientists first grasped how deep the Lower Congo runs when fish hauled up from the bottom showed the 'bends,' the same decompression injury that strikes divers who rise too fast, proving the channel plunges far deeper than anyone had guessed. Sources: worldatlas.com, 'The Congo River — World's Deepest River'; livescience.com, 'Congo River.'

question: The Congo sends nearly the same huge flood to the sea every month of the year as it drains the huge rainforests of central Africa, while most of the world's rivers run high in the rainy months and low in the dry ones. What keeps the Congo's flow so steady?
answer: it crosses the equator twice, so rain always falls somewhere in its basin
choices: it crosses the equator twice, so rain always falls somewhere in its basin
it is fed by high glaciers, so meltwater trickles in every season
it is dammed in stages, so stored water flows through the dry months
it sits in the monsoon belt, so heavy rain soaks it each month
context: The Congo is the only major river to cross the equator twice. Because its huge basin sits both north and south of the line, one part is always in a rainy season while the other is dry — so the river is fed all year and never fails. Source: livescience.com, 'Congo River.'

question: Below Kinshasa, near the end of its run, the whole Congo funnels into a narrow gorge and crashes down a staircase of about 32 giant rapids, called cataracts, dropping some 270 metres on its way to the sea. What is this thundering staircase of whitewater called?
context: Livingstone Falls, named for the explorer David Livingstone, is a staircase of cataracts some 350 km long; if its rapids are counted as a waterfall, it carries more water than any other waterfall on Earth. One stretch, the Inga rapids, drops 96 m and holds around 40 gigawatts of hydropower potential — one of the largest untapped power sites on the planet. Source: Wikipedia, 'Livingstone Falls.'
