It opens where the moving ice tears away from ice frozen fast to the headwall; the meltwater that seeps in, freezes, and plucks blocks loose is the freeze-and-pry 'quarrying' that keeps a cirque's back wall so steep — the very wall that now rises above Red Tarn on Helvellyn. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirque

question: The young Charles Darwin scrambled through the Welsh valley of Cwm Idwal in 1831 and walked straight past its story. Returning in 1842, after a bold new theory had taught naturalists to read scratches, mounds and stranded boulders, he wrote that 'a house burnt down by fire did not tell its story more plainly than did this valley.' What had Darwin learned to see in Cwm Idwal's rocks?
answer: that glaciers had once carved the valley
choices: that glaciers had once carved the valley
that floods had once drowned the valley
that seas had once covered the valley
that earthquakes had once shattered the valley
context: By 1842 a bold new idea — that great sheets of ice had once buried much of Britain — had taught naturalists to recognise the scratches, mounds, and out-of-place boulders that glaciers leave behind. Reading them at last in Cwm Idwal, Charles Darwin wrote that 'a house burnt down by fire did not tell its story more plainly than did this valley' — perhaps the clearest description ever written of reading a glacier's fingerprint in the land. Source: https://www.geolsoc.org.uk/science-and-policy/100-great-geosites/fire-and-ice/cwm-idwal-darwins-boulders/  (Legend.)

question: Swimmers wading into the surf on Peru's coast, near the equator, expect warm water and gasp. The Humboldt Current drags cold water north from the sub-Antarctic seas along South America's Pacific shore, chilling the sea right through the tropics. How cold can the water get?
context: That chill comes from the Humboldt Current, which drags cold sub-Antarctic water thousands of kilometres north along the shores of Chile and Peru — so a coast that sits deep in the tropics feels almost temperate. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current)

question: Off Peru, coastal winds push the warm surface water out to sea, and cold water rich in food rises from below to take its place, growing masses of plankton. Peru's fishery became the richest on Earth, and in 1970 it landed over 12 million tonnes. About what share of the world's fish catch was that?
context: One nation's tiny anchovies, off one cold coast, made up a fifth of everything humans pulled from the sea. Just a handful of upwelling zones — a sliver of the ocean — supply about a quarter of the world's fish. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current)

question: For thousands of years vast flocks of seabirds nested on three small islands off Peru, in a climate so rainless that their droppings never washed away. Layer by layer the droppings hardened into cliffs up to 60 m (200 ft) thick, and in the 1800s miners hacked out this 'guano' by the shipload. Which islands were these?
context: On the Chincha Islands the guano lay deeper than a twenty-story building is tall — preserved only because rain almost never falls there. The word 'guano' comes from the Quechua 'wanu.' (Source: audubon.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guano)

question: Ships crossed whole oceans to Peru in the 1840s to load a cargo worth more to the nation than its gold or silver: hardened seabird droppings mined off its coast. The trade became Peru's biggest source of money, and rival powers even fought over the deposits. What made this 'white gold' so priceless?
answer: It was the world's finest fertilizer
choices: It was the world's finest fertilizer
It burned as a clean lamp fuel
It was pressed into cheap bricks
It was ground into a rare medicine
context: Guano's nitrogen and phosphorus revived exhausted European and American farm soil. The craze ran so hot the U.S. passed the 1856 Guano Islands Act, letting citizens claim any unclaimed guano island — and Spain's seizure of Peru's richest guano islands sparked the Chincha Islands War of 1864–66. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guano)

question: The coastal wind off Peru blows roughly parallel to the shore, but it shoves the surface water off at a right angle, out to sea, and deeper water must rise from below to replace it. What bends the moving water about 90 degrees away from the wind that drives it?
answer: The Coriolis force of Earth's spin
choices: The Coriolis force of Earth's spin
The gravitational pull of the Moon
The drag of the deep seafloor
context: This right-angle twist of wind-driven water is called Ekman transport. Because Earth's rotation deflects the moving surface layer, the wind ends up shoving it offshore — and cold, food-rich water wells up to fill the gap. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upwelling)

question: Near the town of Lüderitz, off the desert coast of Namibia, a cold current drives the most intense upwelling on Earth, turning a barren shore into another vast fishing ground. It is a cousin of the Humboldt, one of the cold, fish-rich currents scattered around the globe. What is it called?
context: The Benguela's upwelling cell off Lüderitz is the most powerful on the planet. Like the Humboldt, it turns a cold current and a barren desert shore into one of the world's great fishing grounds. (Source: namibian.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upwelling)

question: A geographer who marks the world's four great cold-current fisheries on a map, off Peru, California, Namibia and Morocco, sees a pattern at once: every one hugs the same kind of coastline, which is exactly why the upwelling that feeds them happens where it does. Where do all four sit?
answer: Along the western coasts of continents
choices: Along the western coasts of continents
Along the eastern coasts of continents
context: On the western edges of continents the prevailing winds blow toward the equator and, bent by the Coriolis force, shove the surface water offshore — so cold, food-rich water wells up all along these shores. That is why the world's biggest fisheries cluster on cold, west-facing coasts. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upwelling)

question: A herd of painted bison crowds the low ceiling of Altamira cave, in northern Spain, so lifelike that the animals seem to swell right out of the rock. Its beauty earned the ceiling a nickname borrowed from a famous Italian ceiling. What is it called?
answer: the Sistine Chapel of prehistoric art
choices: the Sistine Chapel of prehistoric art
the Mona Lisa of prehistoric Spain
the Last Supper of the Ice Age
the School of Athens of the Stone Age
context: Altamira's low ceiling writhes with a whole herd of bison; the Ice-Age painters used the natural bulges of the rock as the animals' humped shoulders and bellies, so the bison seem to stand out in three dimensions. Its beauty earned the nickname 'the Sistine Chapel of Paleolithic art.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_Altamira

question: Four French teenagers near Montignac squeezed into a hole left by a fallen tree in September 1940, after an animal had darted down it, and dropped into Lascaux cave, its walls blazing with Ice Age paintings. What animal led them there?
context: The dog was named Robot, and his owner Marcel Ravidat came back with three friends -- Jacques Marsal, Georges Agnel, and Simon Coencas -- and slid down the shaft on 12 September 1940 because they hoped it was a secret tunnel to a nearby manor. Instead they had found Lascaux. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascaux  (Legend.)

question: Tourists poured into Lascaux cave, in France, after it opened in 1948, but the warm, damp breath of the crowds soon bred mould across paintings that had survived 17,000 years, and France sealed the real cave in 1963. What do the thousands who visit Lascaux today walk through?
answer: an exact, full-size replica of the cave
choices: an exact, full-size replica of the cave
a glass tunnel built over the paintings
context: Up to 1,200 visitors a day breathed out carbon dioxide and moisture, feeding the mold, algae, and lichen, so France closed the real cave in 1963. Today tourists walk through exact copies -- Lascaux II (opened 1983) and the full-scale Lascaux IV (opened 2016) -- not the original. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascaux

question: Experts who first saw the horses and lions of France's Chauvet Cave, found in 1994, guessed from their skill that the art was fairly recent. Then radiocarbon dating delivered a shock: Chauvet's paintings are among the oldest ever found anywhere on Earth. About how old are they?
context: Radiocarbon dating put Chauvet's horses, lions, and woolly rhinos at roughly 36,000 years old (about 37,000-33,500 years ago) -- among the oldest known cave paintings anywhere. Discovered on 18 December 1994, Chauvet was sealed from the start so it would not be ruined like Lascaux, and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chauvet_Cave

question: Deep inside France's Chauvet Cave, past the painted lions and rhinos, explorers came upon a strange, deliberate arrangement. A single object had been set squarely on top of a flat, fallen block of stone, like an offering placed on an altar. What had Ice-Age people set there?
context: More cave-bear skulls lay scattered on the floor around the block. Many scholars read this careful arrangement as a sign that Chauvet was a sacred, ritual place, not merely an art gallery -- one of the eeriest hints of Ice-Age belief. Sources: https://www.worldhistory.org/Chauvet_Cave/ ; https://archive.archaeology.org/1103/features/werner_herzog_chauvet_cave_primer.html

question: Eight-year-old Maria de Sautuola wandered into Altamira cave in Spain in 1879, looked up and, as the story is told, cried 'Look, Papa, oxen!' at the great bison herd painted across the ceiling. When her father showed the find to Europe's leading scholars, how did they treat it?
answer: They dismissed the paintings as a forgery.
choices: They dismissed the paintings as a forgery.
They hailed him as Spain's greatest scholar.
They rushed to dig for more caves.
They shipped the ceiling off to a museum.
context: Europe's experts insisted that Ice-Age people could not possibly have painted so beautifully, and Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola died in 1888 still branded a fraud. Only after more painted caves turned up in France did the leading skeptic, Emile Cartailhac, publicly apologize in his 1902 article 'Mea culpa d'un sceptique' ('the apology of a skeptic'). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_Altamira ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelino_Sanz_de_Sautuola  (Legend.)

question: Painters in Ice Age caves across Europe, from Lascaux to Altamira, left what scientists call some of the oldest signatures on Earth. An artist pressed part of the body against the rock and blew powdered pigment all around it. Lifting it away left a pale stencil that has lasted 30,000 years. Which part of the body did the artists stencil, again and again?
context: An artist pressed a hand flat to the wall and blew a mouthful of powdered pigment all around it -- sometimes through a hollow bone tube -- then lifted the hand away, leaving a pale outline. Found in caves across Europe, these handprints are among the oldest 'signatures' humans have left anywhere. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lascaux ; https://www.worldhistory.org/Chauvet_Cave/

question: Archaeologists in 2021 dated a life-size painting of a wild pig, deep in a limestone cave on a tropical island far from Europe, to at least 45,500 years ago, older than any of Europe's famous painted caves, Chauvet, Lascaux and Altamira among them. On which island is the world's oldest known animal painting?
context: The painting, in the Leang Tedongnge cave, shows a Sulawesi warty pig and is dated to at least 45,500 years old -- far older than France's Chauvet Cave. It is a reminder that Europe's caves are the most famous Ice-Age art, but not the first. Sources: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/45500-year-old-pig-painting-worlds-oldest-animal-art ; https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.abd4648

question: On a bitter, clear morning over the frozen plains of North Dakota, the low Sun can appear flanked by two smaller bright suns — one burning to its left, one to its right, at the very same height. Farmers and old sailors had a homely name for this pair of false suns. What did they call them?
context: 'Parhelion' comes from Greek — para + helios, 'beside the sun.' The homely folk name 'sun dog' comes from the way the two false suns seem to follow the real Sun across the sky, the way a dog trails its master. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_dog; sciencenotes.org/what-is-a-sun-dog)

question: A farmer on the Canadian prairies looks up on a deep-winter day at a faint ring around the Sun, two false suns perched on it. The ring always sits 22 degrees out from the Sun, and she can check that distance without any instrument. What spans the gap from the Sun to the ring?
answer: an outstretched hand at arm's length
choices: one finger held up at arm's length
an outstretched hand at arm's length
both arms flung out to the sides
the full Moon's bright round disk
context: This is the 22-degree halo, the most common of all ice-crystal halos. A hand held out at arm's length spans roughly 20 degrees — almost exactly the halo's radius, so the ring seems to fit just inside a spread hand. Inside the ring the sky looks darker, because ice prisms bend no sunlight to angles smaller than 22 degrees. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/22-degree_halo)

question: Miles above the Rocky Mountains, in the highest, thinnest cirrus clouds, sunlight can bend into a pale 22-degree halo that shimmers with a faint hint of color, almost like a washed-out rainbow. Far overhead, millions of tiny prisms are bending that sunlight to make the ring. What are those prisms made of?
context: A rainbow is made by round droplets of liquid water; a halo is made by six-sided (hexagonal) ICE crystals high in cold cirrus — the same sunlight, split by different sky-stuff. The magic 22 degrees is simply the smallest angle a hexagonal ice prism can bend light: about 21.84 degrees. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/22-degree_halo; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_dog)

question: Around Fairbanks, Alaska, false suns and halos sometimes hang in a sky with no clouds anywhere. On the coldest mornings, the freezing air right at street level fills with countless tiny drifting specks of ice, enough to bend the sunlight and paint a halo without a single cloud. What do northerners call this ground-level haze?
context: Diamond dust is a ground-level haze of tiny ice crystals that forms in very cold, moist air — proof that sun dogs and halos need no high cirrus. It's famous around Fairbanks and across the far north, where halos can hang right down at street level. (Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_dog; carpenternaturecenter.org/sun-dogs-halos-and-diamond-dust)

question: A glowing shaft of light rises straight up above a bright streetlamp in Montreal on a still, bitterly cold night. This light pillar is built by tiny column-shaped crystals hovering with their flat faces held level in the freezing air. What does the pillar look like?
answer: a single glow the same color as the lamp
choices: a single glow the same color as the lamp
a soft silver-white glow, whatever the lamp's color
a glow that flickers between light and dark
a full spread of rainbow colors, like a halo's
context: Unlike a 22-degree halo or a sun dog, which split sunlight into a faint rainbow, a light pillar is made by REFLECTION — light bouncing off the level faces of column-shaped ice crystals like millions of tiny mirrors — not by refraction (prism-splitting). Because reflection doesn't separate colors, a pillar simply glows in the color of whatever light it reflects: orange above a sodium street lamp, white above a low winter Sun. Pillars can even stretch below the light as well as above it. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_pillar)

question: Over the winter skies of Finland, the loveliest of all the ice-optics sometimes appears when the Sun sits low: the circumzenithal arc, a short bright band curving like a smile — an 'upside-down rainbow' whose colors glow even purer than a true rainbow's. Scientists insist it isn't rare at all, yet hardly anyone ever spots one. Why is it so easily missed?
answer: it hangs directly overhead, where almost nobody thinks to look up
choices: it hangs directly overhead, where almost nobody thinks to look up
it needs the Sun sitting almost exactly 22 degrees high, a narrow window
it forms only in a small patch low near the horizon
it lasts only a few seconds before the crystals drift apart
context: The circumzenithal arc forms when horizontal plate crystals let sunlight enter through their flat TOP face and leave by a SIDE face — the reverse of the path that makes a halo. Its colors are purer than a rainbow's because they overlap far less: blue-violet on top, red toward the Sun. It appears only when the Sun is below 32.2 degrees and glows brightest when the Sun is 22 degrees up — yet it's missed so often simply because it rides high overhead, where almost nobody thinks to look. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumzenithal_arc)

question: False suns and glowing rings filled the sky over Stockholm for two hours on the morning of 20 April 1535, and the reformer Olaus Petri took them for a warning from God to King Gustav Vasa. A painting of that sky, the Vädersolstavlan, is the oldest known image of false suns, and a copy hangs in Stockholm's cathedral today. What second 'oldest' record does it hold?
answer: the oldest color view of Stockholm
choices: the oldest color view of Stockholm
the oldest royal portrait in Stockholm
the oldest color map of Stockholm
the oldest church mural in Stockholm
context: The Vadersolstavlan ('weather-sun painting') is the oldest surviving color depiction of Stockholm as well as the oldest known image of sun dogs. The reformer Olaus Petri read the eerie sky as a warning from God against King Gustav Vasa; the king took it as a jab at his rule and dismissed it. The version that hangs today in Storkyrkan cathedral is a 1636 copy by Jacob Heinrich Elbfas. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vadersolstavlan)  (Legend.)

question: From Cusco, high in the Peruvian Andes, the Inca governed about ten million people in the 1400s. Their officials collected tribute, filled storehouses and even counted the whole population, yet the Inca had no written language. How did officials keep the empire's accounts?
context: The Inca called these knotted-string records quipu (also spelled khipu). From Cusco they governed millions across the Andes with cords instead of writing -- the accounting of a whole empire hung on colored strings. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: Two identical knots sit on one Inca quipu cord, yet one stands for a single unit and the other for a full hundred. A reader in the Andes took in the number with his fingers as much as his eyes. What decides whether a knot counts as one, ten or a hundred?
answer: how high up the cord it is tied
choices: how high up the cord it is tied
what color the cord was dyed
how tightly the knot was pulled
which way the cord was twisted
context: The quipu is a base-10 place-value machine: knots low on a hanging cord count ones, higher up tens, higher still hundreds and thousands. A reader took in the number by a knot's position -- with the fingers as much as the eyes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: On a single quipu cord, an Inca knot-keeper in the Andes has to record 308: three hundreds, no tens and eight ones. He ties knots for the hundreds and the ones, but the tens place holds zero. How does the quipu show that zero?
answer: that spot is left bare, with no knot at all
choices: that spot is left bare, with no knot at all
a special 'nothing' knot is tied there
that stretch of cord is dyed solid black
the cord is cut short just below there
context: Most striking of all: a bare gap with no knot is the Inca zero. They kept a place-holder for zero centuries before the idea reached much of Europe. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: A trained Inca knot-keeper held an entire province's accounts in his cords and in his memory. He tracked the tribute owed, the llama herds, and the grain stored in every Andean storehouse. The Sapa Inca demanded these figures be flawless. By some colonial accounts, what could happen to a knot-keeper who got the imperial accounts wrong?
answer: he could be put to death
choices: he could be put to death
he could be fined a herd of llamas
he could be sent to the fields
he could be made to retie it
context: The role of khipukamayuq was hereditary and demanded a prodigious memory -- a single error in a knot's color, shape, or position could change the record. The death penalty comes from colonial-era testimony, so it is reported as claim, not certainty. Sources: worldhistory.org/Quipu; machutravelperu.com/blog/quipu  (Legend.)

question: Scholars holding an Inca quipu from the Andes today can read its numbers clearly: herd counts, tribute totals, storehouse tallies. But the same cords carry colours, cord orders and knot patterns that may hide names, words, even whole stories. How far have scholars got with that non-number content?
choices: it was proved to hold only numbers
context: Scholars can fully read the quipu's numbers, but its possible 'language' -- part ledger, part story -- is still unread. In 2005 Gary Urton and Carrie Brezine argued that three figure-eight knots on one cord spell the place-name Puruchuco, perhaps the first word ever read off a quipu. Sources: theconversation.com; artsandculture.google.com (the Puruchuco khipus)

question: Spanish churchmen in conquered Peru branded the Inca knot-records 'idols of the devil,' obstacles to winning the Andean people for Christianity. In 1583 the Third Council of Lima ordered the quipus destroyed. What became of thousands of the knotted cords?
context: Thousands of quipu were burned as idolatrous, and only about 1,400 pre-Columbian quipu survive today, mostly in museums -- the conquered people's own records largely erased by the men who conquered them. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu

question: Archaeologists digging at Mohenjo-daro, an ancient brick city in what is now Pakistan, found small stone seals carved with rows of little signs left by the Indus Valley people. What is still true of that Indus script today?
answer: It cannot be read by anyone alive.
choices: It cannot be read by anyone alive.
It is still used to write Sindhi today.
It gave rise to the Arabic alphabet.
It was fully deciphered a century ago.
context: First unearthed at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, the Indus Valley script has resisted every reader since: no scholar can say what a single seal says. Its people mastered covered drains and grid streets, yet left a writing that no one can yet open. (grokipedia.com/page/Indus_script; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro)

question: Indus carvers at Mohenjo-daro cut tiny stamp seals from polished stone, each about the size of a coin, and set one animal above a short row of signs on every one. One creature appears far more often than the rest. Which animal turns up most on the Indus seals?
context: Scholars nickname it the 'unicorn,' but it is almost certainly a bull drawn side-on, the near horn simply hiding the far one. This one-horned figure stands above the signs on more Indus seals than any other creature. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script)  (Legend.)

question: The Indus Valley people of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa left thousands of tiny inscriptions on seals and pottery about 4,500 years ago, while other ancient peoples carved long texts on temple walls and clay tablets. How long is the longest Indus text ever found, carved on a copper plate from Mohenjo-daro?
context: The record-holder carries just 26 signs, on a copper plate from Mohenjo-daro. There is no long text anywhere in the Indus world — no story, no law, no letter — leaving codebreakers with no paragraph to get a grip on. (grokipedia.com/page/Indus_script)

question: Iravatham Mahadevan, a linguist, catalogued 417 different signs of the Indus script in 1977, gathered from seals found at Mohenjo-daro and the other brick cities of the Indus Valley. Half a century later, scholars still cannot agree on one basic point about those signs. What have they never settled?
answer: Whether its signs are truly writing at all
choices: Whether its signs are truly writing at all
Whether its signs are over 4,000 years old
Whether its signs turn up outside the Indus Valley
Whether its signs were cut into stone seals
context: Mahadevan's 1977 concordance counted 417 signs — too many for a 20-to-30-letter alphabet, yet far too few for a one-sign-per-word system that would need thousands. That maddening in-between has fueled a real scholarly fight over whether the Indus marks are true writing at all, or symbols that never recorded language. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script)

question: Merchants of Ur, in Mesopotamia, knew the distant Indus land as Meluhha, and Indus seals have turned up in their city. On one Mesopotamian cylinder seal, a man named Shu-ilishu is labelled by his trade, a reminder of how closely Ur and the Indus cities were once bound by sea. What was Shu-ilishu's trade?
choices: Scribe in the temple of Ur
context: The Akkadian cylinder seal names him 'Shu-ilishu, interpreter of the Meluhhan language' — proof that people once spoke and translated the Indus tongue. Yet even a named ancient interpreter cannot unlock them: the seals stay silent. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus-Mesopotamia_relations)

question: Codebreakers read Egyptian hieroglyphs with the help of the Rosetta Stone, and they cracked Greek's lost Linear B too. Scholars fear the Indus script of Mohenjo-daro may never join them, blocked by a wall those scripts never faced. What is the deepest reason it still resists every codebreaker?
choices: Its clay tablets have all crumbled away
Its signs were deliberately kept secret
Too few seals have ever been dug up
context: Egyptian hieroglyphs were cracked with the Rosetta Stone, and Greek's Linear B was eventually read too, because scholars could tie the signs to a language they already knew. The Indus script has no such bilingual key, and no one knows what language its people spoke — so it may stay silent forever. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script)

question: Seven miles up over the North Atlantic, a narrow band of wind screams from west to east. A jet from New York to London rides it and lands more than an hour early, while the flight home against it drags. What is this fast, high-altitude river of wind?
context: The jet stream flows near the tropopause, about 30,000 feet up, always west to east. The classic mix-up is the Gulf Stream — that is a warm WATER current in the ocean, not a wind. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream

question: Wasaburo Oishi, a Japanese weather scientist, ran a lab near Mount Fuji and logged 1,288 upper-air readings between 1923 and 1925. They proved that a fierce, permanent wind blew high over Japan, the first record of the jet stream. What did he use to measure winds seven miles up?
context: Oishi released small hydrogen 'pilot balloons' and followed them with a theodolite — a surveying telescope — reading the wind's speed and direction at each height as the balloon rose. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasaburo_Oishi

question: The world's scientists ignored Wasaburo Oishi's discovery of the jet stream over Japan for decades, and for an odd reason. An idealist, Oishi wrote all 19 of his observatory reports in a made-up international language that almost no scientist could read. Which language was it?
context: Oishi was a devoted Esperantist. His 1926 report and 18 more through 1944 were all in Esperanto, so his jet-stream discovery sat unread until the West rediscovered the winds during World War II. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasaburo_Oishi

question: Japan launched about 9,300 balloon bombs, called fu-go, into the winter jet stream during World War II, to drift some 6,000 miles across the Pacific to North America, the very first intercontinental weapon. What were the balloons made of?
context: Each fu-go was many sheets of washi (mulberry paper) glued with konnyaku, a paste made from konjac potato. About 300 reached North America in 30 to 100 hours. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fu-Go_balloon_bomb

question: The jet stream that steers the storms of Europe and North America rides the polar front, a sloping boundary where cold polar air meets warm subtropical air. It howls in winter and slackens in summer. Why does it blow hardest in winter?
answer: the cold-to-warm contrast across the front is sharpest then
choices: the cold-to-warm contrast across the front is sharpest then
the front rises higher, into thinner air with less drag
the dense winter air slides along the front faster
the low winter Sun heats the high air more strongly
context: The jet forms and speeds up along the polar front, the sloping boundary between cold polar and warm subtropical air. Winter's sharper cold-versus-warm contrast is why the jet stream is strongest then. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_stream

question: A British Airways Boeing 747 crossed from New York to London in just 4 hours 56 minutes in February 2020, riding an unusually strong jet stream at a ground speed of 825 mph, faster than the speed of sound at sea level. Yet no sonic boom ever thundered down. How could a plane race across the ground faster than sound without one?
answer: Its airspeed stayed subsonic while the racing air carried it
choices: Its airspeed stayed subsonic while the racing air carried it
Its swept wings broke up the shock wave before it could form
The thin air seven miles up muffled the boom before it fell to earth
The tailwind blew the shock wave forward, far out of earshot
context: The plane's speed through the air stayed below the sound barrier — the whole river of air was racing east at hundreds of miles per hour and simply carried the jet along, setting a subsonic transatlantic record of 825 mph. A sonic boom depends on speed through the air, not speed over the ground. Source: https://www.flightradar24.com/blog/flight-tracking-news/special-event/british-airways-sets-new-transatlantic-speed-record/

question: Much of Texas lost power in a brutal freeze in February 2021, when Arctic cold spilled far south. Far above the Arctic turns a ring of fierce winds, the polar vortex, which normally pens the planet's coldest air near the pole. What can weaken and split it, setting the cold loose?
answer: a sudden warming high in the stratosphere
choices: a sudden warming high in the stratosphere
a sudden deep chill high in the stratosphere
a burst of solar wind striking the pole
a great volcanic eruption in the far north
context: When the stratospheric polar vortex is strong, it locks cold in the Arctic; a 'sudden stratospheric warming' can weaken and split it, sending the jet stream and Arctic air plunging south into North America and Europe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_vortex

question: Grass and camelthorn trees speckle the red sands of the Kalahari, which sprawl over some 900,000 square km across Botswana, Namibia and South Africa, where hardly any water stands on the ground. Yet geographers say the Kalahari is not a true desert. Why not?
answer: it catches too much rain to be one
choices: it catches too much rain to be one
its sandy soil is too rich to be one
it lies too close to the ocean to be one
its sands are too young to be one
context: Despite its name and its red sand, most of the Kalahari is not a true desert but a semi-arid 'thirstland': it catches from about 110 mm of rain a year in the driest south-west to over 500 mm in the north-east, enough for grass, camelthorn trees and wide grazing after good rains. Yet the rain drains fast into the deep sand, so almost no water lies on the surface. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalahari_Desert ; https://www.britannica.com/place/Kalahari-Desert/Climate

question: In southern Africa the Tswana people named this immense sweep of red sand across Botswana and Namibia after their own word Kgala. Travellers who cross its 900,000 km² of dunes learn very quickly why the name fits. What does the name Kalahari mean?
context: 'Kalahari' comes from the Tswana word Kgala, 'the great thirst' (or Kgalagadi, 'a waterless place'), for a vast land of sand with no permanent surface water, spreading about 900,000 km² across Botswana, Namibia and South Africa. Yet despite the name it is not a true desert but a semi-arid 'thirstland' that catches 110 to over 500 mm of rain a year — enough for grasses and camelthorn trees. Source: Wikipedia 'Kalahari Desert'.

question: The Okavango River comes down from Angola's highlands but never reaches the sea: it fans out into a huge green wetland in the Kalahari, a dead end for water. By what route does almost all of the river's water leave?
answer: it rises into the sky as evaporation and thirsty plants
choices: it rises into the sky as evaporation and thirsty plants
it sinks away to refill hidden underground lakes
it hardens into vast sheets of white surface salt
it is drunk and carried off by huge animal herds
context: The Okavango flows in from the Angolan highlands and dies in the sand: an estimated 96–98% of its water vanishes as evaporation and plant transpiration or soaks away, and almost none escapes. Because it drains inward and never reaches the sea, the Okavango forms a rare inland delta in an 'endorheic' (closed) basin; in the June–August flood it swells to about three times its permanent size, drawing animals from kilometres around. In 2014 it became the 1000th site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Source: Wikipedia 'Okavango Delta'.

question: The blinding-white Makgadikgadi salt pans stretch over some 16,000 square km of the Kalahari, dead flat, the dried bed of a vast ancient lake that vanished around 10,000 years ago. When geologists traced its old shoreline, the size of the lost lake astonished them. How big was it?
choices: as large as the whole Sahara Desert
as vast as the Mediterranean Sea
context: The Makgadikgadi pans are the ghost of Lake Makgadikgadi, an ancient inland sea that covered roughly 80,000–275,000 km² — bigger than Switzerland, rivaling the United Kingdom or New Zealand — with an average depth around 30 m. Fed by the Okavango, Upper Zambezi and Cuando rivers, it existed from about 2 million until roughly 10,000 years ago. Source: Wikipedia 'Lake Makgadikgadi', 'Makgadikgadi Pan'.

question: Lake Makgadikgadi, the great lost lake of the Kalahari, brimmed so full about 20,000 years ago that it overflowed and spilled its waters away to the northeast. Geologists believe that outflow helped carve one of Africa's mightiest waterfalls. Which waterfall did the lost lake help create?
context: Around 20,000 years ago the brimming lake overflowed to the northeast, and that outflow helped cut the gorge of Victoria Falls on the Zambezi. A drying climate plus the Gumare fault lowering the land then let the Okavango spread out and starve the lake, and by about 10,000 years ago it was gone. Source: Wikipedia 'Lake Makgadikgadi'.

question: Kubu Island, a lone crescent of granite, rises barely ten metres above the white Makgadikgadi salt pan in the Kalahari. Marooned there, miles from the nearest water, stands a grove of gnarled trees, some reckoned to be over 2,000 years old, that once shaded the shore of the vanished lake. What kind of trees crown Kubu Island?
context: Kubu Island (Lekhubu) is a crescent of granite over two billion years old, about a kilometre long and 10 m high, crowned with baobabs some estimated at over 2,000 years old that once stood on the vanished lake's shore. A national monument and sacred site — 'Kubu' means hippopotamus in Setswana — it holds stone-age relics including a curving dry-stone wall about 1.25 m high and 344 circular stone cairns left by people who lived at the water's edge. Source: Wikipedia 'Kubu Island'; amusingplanet.com 'Kubu Island: A Desert Island of Baobabs'.

question: The San people, at home in the central Kalahari for many thousands of years, find water where a stranger would perish. In a dry riverbed they scrape down to damp sand, sink a hollow grass stem into it and suck the moisture up. They blow it through a second straw into a container, stopper it and bury it as a hidden canteen. What is that canteen?
context: The San carry the water home in ostrich eggshells, corked and buried as hidden canteens; in the driest months a buried wild tsama melon (a wild watermelon, its seeds about 35% protein) can be the only water for people and animals alike. The central Kalahari is the San's ancestral land, and DNA studies suggest their ancestors began diverging from all other humans roughly 200,000 years ago — among Earth's oldest continuous cultures. Source: Wikipedia 'San people'.

question: Central Asian traders crossing the high Karakoram Pass named it for what they saw at their feet, long before any climber came to the range's deadly 8,000-metre peaks. Europeans later gave the name to the whole range. What does Karakoram mean?
context: 'Kara' means black and 'korum' (koram) means gravel or rubble in Turkic. The name first belonged only to the Karakoram Pass, whose high route is floored with dark, broken scree; European surveyors later stretched it over the entire range of giants. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram

question: One small tangle of Karakoram valleys, on the Pakistan-China border, packs four of Earth's 8,000-metre giants closer together than anywhere else on the planet. Which four peaks crown the Karakoram?
answer: K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I, Gasherbrum II
choices: K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I, Gasherbrum II
context: The Karakoram packs four of Earth's fourteen 8,000-metre peaks -- K2, Broad Peak, Gasherbrum I, and Gasherbrum II -- into one small knot of valleys, more giants per square mile than anywhere else. The Everest region and the rest of the Himalaya hold the other ten. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram

question: Trekkers who climb for days up a wide highway of ice reach Concordia, a frozen crossroads high in the Karakoram, where four of the world's mightiest peaks stand ringed around them at once. Galen Rowell, an American photographer, stood there in 1975 and gave the amphitheatre a name that stuck. What did he call it?
answer: the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods
choices: the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods
the Rooftop Hall of the Snow Kings
the Cathedral of the Frozen Giants
the Great Court of the Sky Gods
context: Galen Rowell coined 'the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods' during the 1975 American K2 expedition and made it the title of his 1977 book. From Concordia (~4,600 m), where the Baltoro and Godwin-Austen glaciers meet, all four of the range's 8,000-metre peaks can be seen at once. Source: Galen Rowell, In the Throne Room of the Mountain Gods (1977); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltoro_Glacier  (Legend.)

question: A single river of ice about 63 km long grinds down the heart of the Karakoram, feeding the Braldu River and, in time, the mighty Indus. Nearly a third of the whole range lies frozen. What is this great glacier called?
context: The Baltoro Glacier runs about 63 km, one of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions, and its meltwater joins the Braldu and then the Indus. Outside the Arctic and Antarctic the Karakoram is the most heavily glaciated place on Earth -- roughly a third under ice, versus about 8-12% of the Himalaya and 2% of the Alps. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltoro_Glacier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram

question: Kenneth Hewitt, a geographer, surveyed the ice of the Karakoram in the early 2000s, while nearly every mountain glacier on Earth was shrinking back, and found dozens of glaciers there behaving strangely. He named the puzzle the Karakoram anomaly. What were those glaciers doing?
context: Geographer Kenneth Hewitt named the 'Karakoram anomaly' in a 2005 paper: between 1997 and 2002, 13 glaciers (10-20 km long) advanced and 9 larger ones thickened by 5-15 m, some rebuilding moraines that had been ice-free for over half a century -- while glaciers almost everywhere else retreated. Source: Kenneth Hewitt, Mountain Research and Development 25 (2005)

question: Nathan Forsythe and Hayley Fowler, with colleagues at Newcastle University, put forward the leading explanation for why many Karakoram glaciers grow while hot summers melt mountain ice elsewhere: each summer a pool of cold, high-altitude air settles over the range, wrapping it in cloud and snow while the Himalaya to the south bakes. Which word follows 'Karakoram' in the name they gave it?
context: The leading explanation is the 'Karakoram vortex,' a swirl of cold air that in summer contracts to sit over the range, keeping its summers cool and snowy while the rest of the Himalaya warms -- so the ice is fed, not starved. Proposed by a Newcastle University team (Nathan Forsythe, Hayley Fowler), it remains an active area of study, not settled fact. Source: sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/08/170807112835.htm; nature.com/articles/s41561-019-0513-5  (Legend.)

question: Three old royal cities, Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, sit close together in Nepal's green Kathmandu Valley. At the heart of each, a wide plaza wraps around the old king's palace, crowded with tiered wooden temples. What is this palace plaza called?
context: Each of the three old capitals — Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur — kept its own royal court, so the valley has three Durbar ('palace') Squares, not one. Around each king's palace, generations of Newar craftsmen raised clusters of tiered, many-roofed temples, making the squares open-air museums of Nepali woodcarving. All three belong to the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site (WHC #121). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu_Valley

question: Bold animals roam in gangs up the long stone stairway of Swayambhunath, a Buddhist shrine on a hill above Kathmandu in Nepal, snatching snacks straight from pilgrims' hands. Because of these noisy locals, English-speaking visitors gave the shrine a nickname. What is that nickname?
context: Troops of rhesus macaques really do rule Swayambhunath's hill and its 365-step eastern stairway, so travelers have long called it the 'Monkey Temple.' A Buddhist legend explains them: the bodhisattva Manjushri, tending the hill, let his hair grow long, and the lice in it are said to have turned into the monkeys. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swayambhunath

question: On a green hill above the Kathmandu Valley rises Swayambhunath, a white, dome-shaped Buddhist shrine capped by a golden spire. On each of the spire's four sides is painted the same huge image, one of the most famous sights in all of Nepal. What is painted there?
context: The great painted 'all-seeing eyes' of the Buddha look out from all four sides of Swayambhunath's spire, symbolizing a wisdom that watches every direction at once. Between them curls a squiggle that looks like a nose; it is really the Nepali numeral 1, standing for unity and the single path to enlightenment. A stupa is a dome-shaped Buddhist monument, often holding relics. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swayambhunath

question: In Kathmandu, a richly carved wooden palace faces the main plaza. Its resident is a little girl chosen after a careful search; then she is kept apart, her feet never touching the open street. She appears at a lattice window so crowds below can bow and be blessed. What is this special child believed to be?
context: She is the Kumari — a young girl worshipped as the living embodiment of the goddess Durga (locally Taleju). Chosen as a small child and revered until adolescence, she lives in the Kumari Ghar in Kathmandu's Durbar Square and appears at its window on festival days; once, even the king came to receive her blessing. The tradition is centuries old and still observed. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu_Durbar_Square

question: Pilgrims walk clockwise all day around a vast whitewashed dome on the valley floor just east of Kathmandu, spinning long rows of prayer wheels as they go. It is one of the largest Buddhist stupas anywhere on Earth. Which great stupa is it?
context: This is Boudhanath, rising about 36 m (118 ft) — among the biggest stupas in the world. Walking clockwise around it while spinning prayer wheels inscribed 'Om mani padme hum' is called doing kora. After the 1959 Tibetan uprising, thousands of Tibetan refugees settled around it and built more than 50 monasteries, making Boudhanath a great living center of Tibetan Buddhism on the old Tibet-to-India trade route. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boudhanath

question: Travellers on the old trade road once sheltered in Kasthamandap, a wide wooden pavilion in the main square of Kathmandu, and the city takes its very name from it. Local legend claims the whole huge pavilion came from one remarkable source. What was it said to be built from?
answer: the timber of a single tree
choices: the timber of a single tree
beams salvaged from a fallen palace
wood from every house in the city
context: The pavilion is Kasthamandap ('kastha' = wood, 'mandap' = pavilion), and the city of Kathmandu takes its very name from it. Tradition holds the whole rest-house was raised from the timber of a single great sal tree. Kasthamandap stood for centuries until it collapsed entirely in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake; it has since been rebuilt. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu_Durbar_Square  (Legend.)

question: Manjushri, the bodhisattva, came to the rim of the Kathmandu Valley when it was still a vast lake with a lotus of light at its heart, as the Buddhist Swayambhu Purana tells it. To reach the light and open the land for people, he struck the rim a single blow, splitting the rock open into the deep Chobar gorge, and the lake drained away. What did he strike it with?
context: In the legend Manjushri cleaves the gorge with his flaming sword of wisdom, and the self-arisen ('Swayambhu') lotus of light comes to rest on the hill where Swayambhunath now stands. Remarkably, geologists agree the valley really was a lake for much of its deep past, slowly drained through the Chobar gorge — so the legend preserves a memory of the land's true history. Source: https://sacredsites.com/asia/nepal/swayambhunath_stupa.html

question: Araniko, a young architect from the Kathmandu Valley, led eighty Nepali craftsmen over the Himalayas in the 1260s to serve Kublai Khan. In Dadu, the Mongol emperor's new capital, he raised a monument some 50 m tall that still stands in Beijing today. What did he build there?
context: The architect was Araniko (Arniko, 1245–1306). When his king hesitated to send so young a man abroad, he answered, 'My body is indeed young, but my mind is not.' In Kublai Khan's capital Dadu (modern Beijing) he built the White Stupa of the Miaoying Temple, about 50.9 m tall, and it still stands. Kublai made him Director of All Artisan Classes, and he was later named Duke of Liang. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Araniko ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Araniko

question: Lapita seafarers set out from near New Guinea around 1500 BCE and sailed east in wooden canoes, landing on island after island of the western Pacific as far as Fiji. They left no writing. Yet archaeologists can pinpoint where they first came ashore on each island, from one calling card found on beach after beach. What is that calling card?
context: That signature is called Lapita ware: reddish-brown clay stamped before firing with rows of tiny toothed ('dentate') geometric patterns, pressed in with a comb-like tool. Wherever a matching shard turns up, the first seafarers had reached that spot -- which is how we know who sailed into the empty Pacific first. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: An archaeologist digging on New Caledonia asked a local man in 1952 what the spot was called, and wrote down the answer as 'Lapita.' A whole ancient seafaring people now carries that name. But the Haveke word he half-heard meant something else. What did it really mean?
context: The Haveke word was 'xapeta'a', meaning something like 'to dig a hole' -- so an entire ancient civilization ended up named, through an archaeologist's mishearing, after a word for digging (fittingly, exactly what archaeologists do). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: Lapita voyagers sailed across the western Pacific about 3,000 years ago, and the trail of what they left behind runs island by island from near New Guinea east to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, over more than 4,000 kilometres of open ocean. What do archaeologists say that trail records?
answer: the greatest ocean migration in prehistory
choices: the greatest ocean migration in prehistory
the widest trade network of the ancient world
the first empire to rule the open Pacific
the oldest island religion ever found
context: That trail maps the peopling of Remote Oceania -- the first humans ever to reach these far-flung islands, crossing thousands of kilometres of empty sea. It is counted as the greatest ocean-going migration in all of prehistory. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: Scientists drew ancient DNA from 3,000-year-old Lapita graves at Teouma, on Vanuatu, and found that those first settlers group with the native peoples of Taiwan and the northern Philippines, far to the northwest. Which people did these Pacific voyagers become the direct ancestors of?
context: These first voyagers were the direct ancestors of the Polynesians -- the eastern leading edge of the great Austronesian expansion that began near Taiwan and the northern Philippines. Ancient DNA from the Teouma graves carries the classic 'Polynesian motif' (haplogroup B4a1a1a) and clusters the earliest settlers with indigenous Taiwanese and Philippine peoples rather than with the nearby Papuans. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: The Lapita set out from the Bismarck Archipelago near New Guinea around 1500 BCE in great ocean-going canoes. They hopped from island to island, ever deeper into a Pacific that no human had sailed before, and they did not simply drift there. To settle each new island, what living cargo did they carry across the open sea?
context: Their canoes were floating farms: pigs, dogs and chickens plus taro, yam, coconut and breadfruit, all carried to seed each new island with food. It was a provisioned, planned colonisation of empty islands -- powerful evidence the Lapita were skilled voyagers who sailed out on purpose, not castaways drifting on the current. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapita_culture

question: Archaeologists at the Teouma cemetery on Efate, in Vanuatu, the oldest burial ground yet found in the Pacific, uncovered many 3,000-year-old Lapita skeletons with no skulls at all. Once a body's flesh had rotted away, the living had carefully lifted its skull out. Where did the diggers find some of the missing skulls?
context: On one old man's chest lay three skulls set side by side, with three more placed between another person's legs; a seventh was tucked inside a decorated Lapita pot -- part of over 100 vessels found at Teouma, the largest single haul of Lapita pottery anywhere. The site was found by chance in 2003 when a bulldozer clearing land for a shrimp farm turned up red pottery shards. Source: https://humanities.org.au/power-of-the-humanities/lapita-cemetery-in-vanutu-thelps-solve-ancient-mystery/

question: On a clear evening off Hawaii, beachgoers watch the Sun's last rim slip into the Pacific. In the second before it vanishes, they sometimes catch it doing something startling, which sailors have told tales of for hundreds of years. What can the Sun's final rim do?
context: The classic 'green flash.' It's best seen over a clean, unobstructed ocean horizon on a clear, still evening — off Hawaii, the California coast, or Key West — and it's over in a blink, about one to two seconds. The Sun doesn't really turn green; only a thin rim of green light shows at its very top edge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_flash.

question: As the Sun touches the sea off California, the thick air near the water bends its light like a weak prism and fans out the colours at its top rim. Blue should show at that edge as well as green, yet beachgoers see only green. On its long, slanting path through the air, what happens to the blue light?
answer: the air scatters it out of the beam
choices: the air scatters it out of the beam
water vapor absorbs it near the sea
it bends down below the horizon first
the red light overpowers and hides it
context: It's the same reason the daytime sky is blue: air molecules scatter short-wavelength blue light out of the beam (Rayleigh scattering). The low air over the horizon also bends and separates the Sun's colors like a weak prism (refraction and dispersion); with the blue scattered away and the red already set, a rim of green is the last light left at the Sun's edge. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_flash.

question: Admiral Byrd's men at Little America, their Antarctic base by the Bay of Whales, watched the Sun barely sink at all in October 1929; it crawled sideways along the icy horizon. A green flash usually lasts a single second, but theirs, a brilliant green spot, kept winking on and off at the edge of the world. How long did it keep flickering?
context: Byrd's own account: 'a tiny but brilliant green spot... no sooner disappeared than it flashed forth again... it remained on the horizon with short interruptions for thirty-five minutes.' Near the poles the Sun moves almost parallel to the horizon, so instead of a one-second blink the flash can wink on and off for many minutes; optics researchers reconstructed the 16 October 1929 event in a 2015 study. (Little America sat near the Bay of Whales at about 78 degrees S — not the geographic South Pole.) Sources: aaas.org/membership/scientia/catching-elusive-green-flash; opg.optica.org/ao/abstract.cfm?uri=ao-54-4-B54.

question: The River Thames in London froze hard enough to walk on in the coldest winters of the Little Ice Age, from about 1300 to 1850. The name sounds as if mile-high ice sheets had crushed the continents. How much colder than today's winters were its coldest winters in Europe and North America?
context: Despite the fearsome name, the Little Ice Age (c.1300-1850) was a modest, patchy REGIONAL cooling — European and North American winters ran up to about 2°C colder than today's — not a true planet-wide glacial ice age with continental ice sheets. You read it not in mile-high ice but in frozen rivers, advancing glaciers, and the winter art people painted. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Ice_Age.

question: Tents, shops and taverns crowded the frozen Thames in London during the coldest winters of the Little Ice Age, at the famous frost fairs. At the very last one, in 1814, Londoners led a single big animal onto the ice below Blackfriars Bridge to show how thick it was. What animal walked across the river?
context: Londoners called these ice carnivals 'frost fairs' (the term dates to the fair of 1608), pitching tents, shops, taverns, and even printing presses on the frozen Thames. The February 1814 fair was the last great one, and the elephant led across the ice below Blackfriars Bridge is its most famous — and most often-retold — image. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames_frost_fairs.  (Legend.)

question: Londoners blamed the cold for freezing the Thames, but the river's own shape did half the work. Before the 1800s it ran broad, shallow and slow, and one crowded medieval bridge pinched its current through narrow arches between nineteen fat stone piers. At low tide drifting ice jammed against it and held back the water like a dam. Which Thames bridge choked the river?
context: Old London Bridge's nineteen piers wore bulky timber 'starling' casings that squeezed the tide into narrow arches, damming the sluggish, shallow river until it froze. It was demolished in 1831 and replaced with wider arches, and through the 1800s the banks were walled with embankments — so the Thames ran narrower, deeper, and faster, and it has never frozen solid in London since. The frost fairs ended partly because the RIVER changed, not only because the climate warmed. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames_frost_fairs.

question: Mont Blanc's glaciers ground forward above Chamonix, in the French Alps, during the Little Ice Age and buried whole hamlets; by 1616 one village had only six houses left standing at the ice front. Around 1645 the frightened villagers summoned the Bishop of Geneva, who climbed to the glacier's snout and performed a solemn church rite on the ice. What rite was it?
context: The advancing ice between about 1600 and 1610 destroyed the hamlets of Le Chatelard (settled since the 1200s), La Bonnenuit, and La Bonneville. The exorcism didn't work — only the end of the Little Ice Age, two centuries later, finally halted the glaciers. Recorded tradition. Sources: chamonix.net history of Chamonix glaciers; academic.emporia.edu Late Holocene climate.  (Legend.)

question: Hendrick Avercamp painted the canals of the Netherlands as the Little Ice Age froze them each winter. Deaf and unable to speak, he was nicknamed 'the mute of Kampen,' and his crowded 1608 canvases show whole towns swarming out onto the ice. What pastime, painted again and again and still a Dutch passion today, fills those scenes?
context: Avercamp's 'Winter Landscape with Ice Skaters' (1608) helped pioneer the Dutch winter-landscape genre — a whole art form born from the Little Ice Age's frozen canals, and a near-photographic record of those winters. Skating on the frozen waterways became a lasting Dutch passion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendrick_Avercamp.

question: Erik the Red led Norse colonists to Greenland around 985, and through the milder centuries that followed they built some 500 farms, home to a few thousand people raising cattle and sheep. Then the Little Ice Age crept in, and by the late 1400s the colony had vanished. Historians still debate the causes, but the climate's main blow was plain. What did the deepening cold do that doomed the farms?
answer: left summers too short to grow winter hay
choices: left summers too short to grow winter hay
buried the farms under advancing glaciers
froze the soil into permanent permafrost
locked the fjords in ice all year round
context: The Western Settlement emptied around 1350 and the Eastern by the late 1400s. Cooling shortened the growing season and disrupted the seal hunt — but the colony had also funded itself by exporting walrus ivory to Europe, and that trade collapsed when African elephant ivory undercut it and the walrus were over-hunted. So climate was one thread among several, not the whole story. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_colonization_of_North_America.

question: A satellite passing over the Dasht-e Lut, a remote desert basin in southeastern Iran, clocked its bare ground at the hottest land-surface temperature ever caught from orbit. No thermometer on the ground took that reading. What temperature did the satellite record?
context: That 80.8 C (177 F) reading, captured by NASA's MODIS satellite instrument in 2018, is the hottest land-SURFACE temperature any satellite has recorded, a peak that Mexico's Sonoran Desert has matched -- an earlier 2005 pass had already clocked 70.7 C. One thing worth remembering: this is the temperature of the GROUND, seen from space, not of the air. The world's hottest reliably-recorded AIR temperature is much lower -- 56.7 C (134 F), set at Furnace Creek in California's Death Valley on 10 July 1913. Sources: NASA Science, 'Iran's Lut Desert'; Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (MODIS surface-temperature study); WMO Death Valley air-temperature record.

question: Sunlight pours onto the bare floor of Iran's Dasht-e Lut, and from orbit its ground has measured as hot as any on Earth. The secret lies in what the desert floor is made of, and its colour. Why does the Lut's ground heat up so fiercely?
answer: Ancient lava blackened it, so it drinks sunlight like a black iron pan
choices: Ancient lava blackened it, so it drinks sunlight like a black iron pan
Dark obsidian gravel sheets it, baking like a tray of broken glass
A red iron crust bakes it, hoarding the day's heat long past sundown
Fine volcanic ash blankets it, dark and soft as fireplace soot
context: More than half the Lut's surface is covered by dark volcanic rock, blackened by ancient lava -- and dark ground drinks in sunlight instead of bouncing it away, exactly like a black cast-iron pan left in the sun. A ring of mountains around the basin then traps that heat, with almost no wind to carry it off, so the surface bakes far past what the sunshine alone could explain. Sources: NASA Science, 'Iran's Lut Desert'; Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (over half the surface covered by volcanic rock).

question: Locals in Iran's Lut Desert call its single hottest patch, a plateau of dark lava, Gandom Beryan: Persian for 'Toasted Wheat.' A local legend explains that curious name. According to the tale, how did the plateau earn it?
answer: A load of wheat left out on it was scorched black by the ground within days
choices: A load of wheat left out on it was scorched black by the ground within days
Traders roasted their wheat there by burying the sacks in the scalding sand
Bread left on the rock came out toasted golden by the heat of the ground alone
A caravan hauling wheat vanished on it, leaving only spilled, blackened grain
context: Gandom Beryan ('Toasted Wheat') is a dark plateau in the northern Lut, long reputed to be the desert's single hottest ground. The story that a stash of wheat, simply left on the surface, blackened within days is folk legend rather than measured fact -- but it fits a place whose bare ground is among the hottest any satellite has measured. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (Gandom Beryan); Adventure Iran, 'Gandom Beryan Lut Desert'.

question: Fierce winds roar in from the northwest across Iran's Lut Desert and hurl sand against its bedrock, grinding the rock into long, parallel ridges that the locals call kaluts and geologists call yardangs. They run for tens of kilometres. Seen from high above, what do the ridges look like?
answer: the streets and towers of an abandoned ghost city
choices: the streets and towers of an abandoned ghost city
a single giant fingerprint pressed into the sand
the curved ribs of some enormous buried beast
a frozen sea of rolling, wind-worn stone waves
context: These corrugated ridges are yardangs -- rock and hard sediment carved by relentless, sand-laden wind. In the Lut, the winds sweep in from the northwest between June and October, sculpting yardangs up to 75 m tall that run for over 150 km. From high above, the endless ranks of ridges and hollows look so much like a ruined metropolis that the region is nicknamed the 'abandoned city of ghosts' -- and the Lut holds some of the finest yardangs found anywhere on Earth. Sources: NASA Science, 'Iran's Lut Desert'; UNESCO World Heritage Convention; Wikipedia, 'Dasht-e Lut' (yardangs to 75 m, over 150 km).

question: Iranians hailed a first in 2016, when the Lut Desert joined the United Nations' list of World Heritage Sites. For decades every one of Iran's listed sites had been a palace, a mosque or an ancient city such as Persepolis or Pasargadae. The Lut was a new type of site altogether. What type was it?
answer: a natural site -- the raw land honoured for its own sake
choices: a natural site -- the raw land honoured for its own sake
an endangered site -- a treasure judged already at risk
a transboundary site -- one wonder split across two nations
a mixed site -- wild desert wrapped around ancient ruins
context: On 17 July 2016, at UNESCO's 40th session in Istanbul, the Lut Desert (World Heritage list no. 1505) became the first NATURAL site anywhere in Iran to earn World Heritage status, inscribed for its yardangs and vast sand seas under criteria vii and viii. Every Iranian site listed before it had honoured human culture; the Lut was the first chosen to protect the land itself. Sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, list no. 1505; IFP News, 'Lut Desert inscribed... Iran's first natural site'.

question: The Maldives scatters about 1,200 tiny coral islands across the Indian Ocean southwest of India. Its land averages only about 1.5 metres above the sea, and even its highest natural ground stands just 2.4 metres or so above it. What world record does the Maldives hold?
context: No nation has a lower high point. The Maldives averages about 1.5 m (4.9 ft) above sea level, and even its natural summit on Addu Atoll is only about 2.4 m (7 ft 10 in). A resort on Villingili markets a 5.1 m landscaped mound as the 'highest peak in the Maldives,' but that is an artificial dune, not natural ground. Source: Wikipedia, 'Geography of the Maldives'; earthsky.org.

question: Maldivians live on about 1,200 tiny islands in the Indian Ocean, set on rings of coral reef that each enclose a turquoise lagoon. English borrowed its word for such a ring, 'atoll,' straight from the language the islanders speak. What is that language called?
context: English 'atoll' comes from the Dhivehi word 'atholhu.' Dhivehi is the language of the Maldives; Sinhala (Sri Lanka), Tamil, and Malayalam are neighboring South Asian languages, but the word 'atoll' came only from Dhivehi. Source: Wiktionary, 'atoll'; Wordnik.

question: Rings of living coral like those of the Maldives puzzled Charles Darwin: each stands alone in the open ocean around a lagoon, with no island in the middle. In 1842 he gave a bold answer. A volcanic island had once stood there, fringed by a coral reef. What became of that island, in Darwin's theory?
answer: it slowly sank beneath the sea
choices: it slowly sank beneath the sea
it slowly eroded away in storms
it was buried under drifting sand
it split off on the moving seafloor
context: Darwin's 'subsidence theory,' published in 1842 in his first book, The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs: the volcano slowly sank while the reef-building coral kept growing upward toward the sunlight it needs, so when the island finally vanished under the sea, a ring of living coral marked where it had stood. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs'; Britannica, 'Darwinian subsidence theory.'

question: On the Keeling atoll in the Indian Ocean in 1836, Charles Darwin was struck that tiny, soft coral animals had built the whole vast reef. In The Voyage of the Beagle he wrote that these 'mountains of stone' dwarfed humanity's grandest ancient ruins, and he named the most famous of them. Which monument did Darwin say the coral dwarfed?
context: Darwin wrote: 'We feel surprise when travellers tell us of the vast dimensions of the Pyramids and other great ruins, but how utterly insignificant are the greatest of these, when compared to these mountains of stone accumulated by the agency of various minute and tender animals!' Source: Darwin, The Voyage of the Beagle, ch. 20; standardebooks.org.

question: Charles Darwin worked out how atolls form before he had ever seen one. Sailing on HMS Beagle in November 1835, he studied the coral reef ringing one lush Pacific island and sketched his whole theory of atolls there. Only months later did the Beagle reach a true atoll, the Keeling Islands, to test it. At which Pacific island did Darwin first dream up his theory?
context: Darwin first sketched the subsidence idea after visiting Tahiti in November 1835, then tested it against a real ring-reef when the Beagle surveyed the Keeling (Cocos) Islands in April 1836 -- six months before the voyage came home. He had the theory before he had the proof. Source: Wikipedia, 'The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs'; darwinproject.ac.uk.

question: Engineers on Enewetak Atoll, in the Pacific, drilled straight down through more than four thousand feet of coral in 1952. Darwin's atoll theory had stayed unproven for over a century, because no drill had ever bored through the whole towering pile. At last the bit reached the floor beneath. What did the drillers find at the very bottom?
context: At Enewetak in 1952, drills bored through roughly 4,200-4,600 ft (about 1,300-1,400 m) of coral and struck volcanic basalt -- the drowned volcano Darwin had predicted in 1842, confirmed more than a century later. Earlier holes fell short: Funafuti in the 1890s reached about 1,114 ft and Bikini in 1947 about 2,556 ft, both still in coral. Source: royalsociety.org; Britannica, 'atoll.'

question: Mohamed Nasheed, president of the Maldives, staged a first for any government in 2009 to make the world's climate summit pay attention. A living coral atoll can grow taller as the sea climbs, but only so fast, and his low islands would be among the first to feel any rise. What did Nasheed do to sound the alarm?
choices: marched his ministers to the North Pole
chained himself to the summit gates
shut every airport in the country
context: In October 2009, President Mohamed Nasheed and his ministers, in scuba gear, held a cabinet meeting about 5 m (16 ft) underwater and signed a document to hand to the Copenhagen climate summit. Nasheed even floated buying higher land abroad (naming Sri Lanka, India, and Australia) as a possible new home for the population; his successor later dropped the idea. The UN's IPCC has warned the low atolls could become uninhabitable this century if seas rise faster than the coral can build. Source: CBC News; commondreams.org.

question: Far out in the western Pacific, the floor of the Mariana Trench drops into the Challenger Deep, almost 11 km down, the deepest spot on Earth. Suppose Mount Everest, the tallest mountain, were dropped in. How far under the sea would its peak still be?
context: Challenger Deep bottoms out around 10,935 m (about 6.8 miles) down — more than 2 km deeper than Everest is tall (8,849 m), so the whole mountain would vanish beneath the surface. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench (2021 depth study; 'more than 2 km farther from sea level than the peak of Mount Everest').

question: Beneath the western Pacific the Mariana Trench plunges to the Challenger Deep, the deepest point on Earth's seafloor. The nearest big island lies only a few hundred kilometres away. Which island is it?
context: Guam, the largest of the Mariana Islands, is the nearest sizeable inhabited land to the Challenger Deep, which lies roughly 300 km to the southwest in the western Pacific. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('about 200 km east of the Mariana Islands near Guam').

question: The Mariana Trench gashes the floor of the western Pacific for about 2,550 km from end to end, yet it is never more than about 70 km wide. Seen straight down from a satellite, what shape does it trace?
context: The Mariana Trench is a crescent-shaped gash about 2,550 km long but only 69 km wide, curving across the western Pacific seafloor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('crescent-shaped... about 2,550 km in length and 69 km in width').

question: A tiny steel sphere slung beneath a float full of fuel sank for nearly five hours into the black over the Challenger Deep on 23 January 1960. Inside it, 85 years after the Deep's discovery, two men became the first ever to touch bottom at the deepest point on Earth. Who were they?
context: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom on 23 January 1960 after a descent of nearly five hours — the first humans ever to reach the deepest point on Earth, and for 52 years the only ones. Sources: geology.com/records/bathyscaphe-trieste.shtml; earthmagazine.org (Benchmarks: 23 January 1960).

question: Deep into the Trieste's 1960 descent toward the Challenger Deep floor, the two-man crew suddenly heard a startling bang echo through the cabin. Something on the craft had cracked under the monstrous pressure — yet they chose to keep sinking. What had cracked?
context: On the way down, the Trieste's outer Plexiglas viewport cracked under about 16,000 psi of pressure with a loud crack; Piccard and Walsh kept descending anyway, but the crack and stirred-up silt limited them to about 20 minutes on the bottom. Source: geology.com/records/bathyscaphe-trieste.shtml.

question: A lone pilot squeezed into the tiny sub Deepsea Challenger in March 2012 and rode it down to the floor of the Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench, on the deepest solo dive ever made. The man crammed inside was famous for directing hit Hollywood films. Who made the dive?
context: James Cameron, director of Titanic and Avatar, dived solo to about 10,908 m in the Deepsea Challenger on 26 March 2012 — the deepest solo dive ever. His descent took 2 hours 37 minutes and he spent about three hours on the bottom. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepsea_Challenger.

question: On the floor of the Challenger Deep, nearly 11 km down in the Mariana Trench, the seawater presses on everything at more than a thousand times sea-level pressure. Pressed onto a single square inch, that force would be like balancing what on it?
context: At the bottom the water presses at about 1,086 bar (15,750 psi) — roughly 1,072 times sea-level pressure, or about 8 tons on every square inch, as if an elephant stood on a postage stamp. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench ('1,086 bar... approximately 1,071.8 times... eight tons per square inch').

question: Animals on the floor of the Challenger Deep live where no ray of sunlight has ever reached, so nothing there can grow by photosynthesis. They feed instead on a constant, faint fall of dead plankton and scraps sinking from the sunlit ocean far above. What poetic name did scientists give this endless food supply?
context: No sunlight reaches the pitch-black trench floor, so life there depends on 'marine snow' — a steady drift of dead plankton and organic scraps sinking from the sunlit ocean far above. Sources: csmonitor.com (What James Cameron saw 6.8 miles deep); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench.

question: At least 19 enormous mounds rise from the seafloor along the edge of the Mariana Trench, among the biggest 'volcanoes' of their kind on Earth. Fluids wrung from the Pacific Plate as it dives beneath the Mariana Plate are forced up through cracks in the crust to build them. What do these giants erupt?
context: At least 19 serpentinite 'mud volcanoes' rise along the Mariana forearc: fluids squeezed from the subducting Pacific Plate turn mantle rock into serpentine mud that oozes up through faults and feeds sunless chemosynthetic microbes at the edge of life. Sources: pnas.org/content/109/8/2831; publications.iodp.org (IODP Expedition 366).

question: The Matterhorn towers 4,478 metres over the Swiss village of Zermatt, a giant rock pyramid with exactly the shape a Toblerone chocolate bar copies. Climbers long ago noticed a neat trick about its four steep faces. What does each face point toward?
context: The four faces point almost exactly north, east, south, and west — three sit on the Swiss side, the south face on the Italian side. The lonely 4,478 m (14,692 ft) pyramid is so iconic it inspired the Toblerone chocolate logo. Source: grokipedia.com/page/Matterhorn; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matterhorn.

question: The Matterhorn, the pyramid peak on the Swiss-Italian border, looks like a stone spike shoved straight up out of the earth. Geologists say the truth is the opposite: it is the hard rocky core left standing after everything around it was slowly stripped away over millions of years. What did the stripping?
choices: a river carving a canyon through it
context: Four glaciers gnawed bowl-shaped hollows (cirques) into four sides of the same peak at once, grinding the rock between them into knife-edge ridges that meet at a point. A summit carved to a spike this way is called a glacial 'horn' — and a four-faced one is textbook enough that geologists call it the 'Matterhorn type.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramidal_peak; britannica.com/science/horn-glacial-landform.

question: A climber on the very summit of the Matterhorn, in Switzerland, stands on rock that is not European at all. The mountain's top slice is a slab of crust that was shoved up and over Europe when another whole continent slammed into it and squeezed an ancient ocean shut. Which continent's rock forms that summit?
context: Only the top ~1,000 m is African: it is gneiss of the Dent Blanche nappe, a slice of the African (Adriatic) plate thrust up and over Europe when the two continents collided and closed the ancient Tethys Ocean. The rest of the mountain sits on European bedrock — so the very summit of a Swiss peak is a piece of Africa. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dent_Blanche_nappe; earthlymission.com.

question: Edward Whymper's party of seven stood on the Matterhorn's summit on 14 July 1865, the first people ever to reach it, on his ninth attempt. Starting down, the least experienced climber, Douglas Hadow, slipped and pulled three companions off the ridge. The rope tying the falling men to the three still above them snapped, and all four plunged nearly 4,000 feet. What was damning about that rope?
answer: it was the oldest, weakest one, kept only as a spare
choices: it was the oldest, weakest one, kept only as a spare
it had frayed on the sharp rocks during the climb
it was the thinnest, lightest cord they carried
it had been nicked by a falling rock earlier
context: The snapped rope was the oldest and weakest the party carried, brought only as a reserve; the four fell about 4,000 ft down the north face. Whymper and the two Taugwalder guides survived. In 'Scrambles Amongst the Alps' (1871) Whymper wrote that he watched them slide 'downwards on their backs... endeavouring to save themselves,' and warned that courage and strength count for nothing without prudence. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Whymper; smithsonianmag.com.

question: High on the Matterhorn's Hörnli ridge in 2003, a block of rock the size of four houses suddenly broke loose without warning, and helicopters had to lift about 90 climbers off the peak to safety. Investigators discovered that the mountain's cracks had, for thousands of years, been held firmly shut by a hidden binder — until it finally gave way. What was that binder?
choices: natural mineral cement between the grains
compacted rubble wedged in its cracks
context: That ice is permafrost — frozen groundwater cementing the rock's cracks. In the 2003 heatwave it thawed and about 1,500 m3 of rock (roughly four houses' worth) broke off the Hörnli ridge, forcing helicopters to evacuate around 90 climbers. The scare launched the PermaSense project, which now monitors the crumbling ice inside the mountain. Source: news.uzh.ch (Matterhorn-Permasense); futurity.org.

question: Sensors bolted to the Matterhorn show that its rocky summit is never still: it sways up to 14 times more than its base. Some of that faint shaking comes from distant earthquakes, but researchers found the peak is also rocked, tremor by tiny tremor, by something hundreds of miles away with no quake involved. What keeps nudging it?
answer: the pounding of far-off ocean waves
choices: the pounding of far-off ocean waves
the roar of faraway mountain winds
the churn of a great distant river
context: The summit resonates like a slow tuning fork, swaying up to ~14 times more than its base.
