Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome ; https://www.pantheonrome.org/en/rome-pantheon/architecture/pantheon-architecture-dome-engineering

question: As the empire fell, popes and princes tore Rome's ancient temples apart, carting off their columns and marble to raise new churches and palaces. Almost every temple vanished, yet the Pantheon still stands nearly whole, the best-preserved building of ancient Rome. What happened to it in AD 609 that spared it?
answer: it was turned into a Christian church
choices: it was turned into a Christian church
an emperor made it his private palace
it was buried in river mud for ages
a law forbade anyone to touch it
context: In AD 609 Pope Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres ('St Mary and the Martyrs') — which is why it was maintained instead of quarried, and survives nearly intact. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: No steel runs through the Pantheon's dome in Rome, and no column holds up its centre, yet it has borne its own weight, as much as hundreds of elephants, for nearly 1,900 years. All that crushing weight has to go somewhere. Where does the dome pour its load?
answer: into its own colossally thick walls
choices: into its own colossally thick walls
into the granite columns of the porch
into a hidden inner shell of brick
into stone buttresses ringing the outside
context: The dome has no steel, no keystone, and no central support — where a keystone would sit, there is only the open oculus. Its half-sphere geometry channels the load straight down into the rotunda's walls, which swell to as much as 6.4 m thick to carry it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

question: Pope Urban VIII, of the Barberini family, had the ancient bronze torn from the porch of the Pantheon in Rome in the 1600s, and Romans jeered, 'What the barbarians didn't do, the Barberini did.' Most of that bronze was melted down and recast. What is the most famous thing it became?
answer: a bronze canopy over St Peter's altar
choices: a bronze canopy over St Peter's altar
the temple's own tall bronze doors
a giant statue of the pope himself
a ring of bells for St Peter's tower
context: The stripped bronze was recast into cannons for Castel Sant'Angelo and, most famously, Bernini's towering baldachin — the great bronze canopy over the high altar of St Peter's Basilica. The Roman quip puns 'Barberini' on 'barbari' (barbarians). Sources: https://www.pantheonrome.org/en/history ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter%27s_Baldachin

question: As the sun drops behind Mont Blanc, above the French village of Chamonix, the valleys fall into cold blue shadow while the topmost snowfields blush pink and orange, lit as if from nowhere. What do climbers call this rosy glow on the summits?
context: German climbers call it Alpengluehen. Because only the very highest summits catch the color while the valleys stay dark, the peaks look like they float, lit from nowhere. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpenglow)

question: A climber on a ridge in the Alps at dusk who turns away from the fiery sunset sees a soft pink band glowing in the sky opposite, about 10 to 20 degrees above the far horizon. What is this pink arch in the anti-sunset sky called?
context: It is named for the cestus, the girdle or breast-band of the Greek goddess Aphrodite, whom the Romans equated with Venus. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belt_of_Venus)

question: Below the pink band that glows opposite the sunset over the Alps at dusk, a darker blue-grey band hugs the horizon. As dusk deepens, it slowly climbs higher into the sky, lifting the pink arch ahead of it. That rising dark band is a shadow. What casts it?
context: Astronomers call it the 'twilight wedge' or Earth's shadow. As the Sun sinks farther below the horizon, the planet's own shadow rises through the atmosphere, and the pink Belt of Venus rides up on top of it. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belt_of_Venus)

question: In the Dolomites the dusk glow has its own Ladin name, enrosadira, 'the turning-rosy,' when the pale crags flush red and then purple. In Ladin legend the peaks are King Laurin's rose garden: the dwarf king, once captured, laid a curse on it so that no human eye should see its roses again. Yet they still blaze at dawn and dusk. Why did Laurin's curse fail then?
answer: his curse forgot the twilight, neither day nor night
choices: his curse forgot the twilight, neither day nor night
the stolen princess frees his garden each dusk
his magic belt sets the flowers alight at night
the roses had already turned to stone by then
context: Germans still call these peaks the Rosengarten ('rose garden'), Italians the Catinaccio. In the tale, Laurin, captured after kidnapping a princess, swore no one should see his roses 'neither by day nor by night', but overlooked the twilight in between, so they still glow for that instant. (Ladin folk legend; suedtirol.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Laurin)

question: Lake Hillier, a bubblegum-pink pool on Middle Island off Western Australia, lies just a sandbar away from the deep-blue Southern Ocean. A glassful scooped from it stays every bit as pink: the colour travels with the water, so it is no reflection of the sky. What actually tints the whole lake pink?
context: Lake Hillier stays pink even in a glass because the color is life, not a mineral or a sky-trick: a community of salt-loving microbes -- the green alga Dunaliella salina plus pink halophilic bacteria and archaea -- tints the whole 600-metre pool, which sits just beyond a thin rim of sand from the blue Southern Ocean. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Hillier

question: A tiny alga, Dunaliella salina, lives in the brine of Lake Hillier, off Western Australia, water eight times saltier than the sea. Battered by salt and sun, it defends itself by flooding its cells with one protective pigment, packed so densely that this alga is the richest natural source of it on Earth. Which pigment is it?
context: The pigment is beta-carotene -- the very same orange pigment that colors carrots. Stressed by extreme salt and sun, Dunaliella salina packs it to about 14% of its dry weight, making the alga Earth's best natural source of beta-carotene, so the pink lake and the orange carrot share one chemical. A 2022 metagenomic study showed pink bacteria such as Salinibacter ruber add even more pigment alongside the alga. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9768965/

question: Up to three thousand workers wade each day into Senegal's rose-pink Lake Retba, the Lac Rose, whose brine is up to ten times saltier than the sea, to harvest its salt by hand for six or seven hours. Before they go in, they coat their skin all over with a local tree fat so the ferocious brine cannot burn them. What do they rub on their skin?
context: The protectant is shea butter, pressed from the nuts of the West African shea tree; its fat shields the harvesters' skin from the searing 40%-salt brine as up to 3,000 workers pull roughly 38,000 tonnes of salt from Lake Retba each year. The rose color comes from the same Dunaliella salina algae as Lake Hillier -- proof the hue is living, not mineral: when heavy flooding once diluted the salt in 2022, Retba briefly turned green. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Retba

question: A shimmering green curtain ripples across the sky over Tromso, in Arctic Norway, on a clear, dark winter night. What lights up this glowing sky?
answer: charged particles streaming from the Sun
choices: charged particles streaming from the Sun
the deep cold of the Arctic air
the glow of the city lights
context: Earth's magnetic field funnels the solar wind - a stream of charged particles blown off the Sun - down toward the poles, where the particles crash into atoms high in the air and make them glow. The lights need no reflection, no cold and no moon at all. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: The northern lights flare on most clear nights over Tromso in Norway, and over Fairbanks in Alaska and Yellowknife in Canada, thousands of kilometres away. Each of the three towns lies beneath the same ring of sky, where the aurora gathers. What is this zone called?
context: The aurora is not scattered at random: it rides a ring about 6 degrees wide in latitude, centered roughly 67 degrees from the geomagnetic pole. Those three towns all sit almost exactly under this auroral oval - which is why they are the world's great aurora-watching towns. An observer standing right at the pole would be inside the ring and see less. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: Over Fairbanks, Alaska, on a winter night, huge curtains of coloured fire ripple across the sky, and most of their light is a soft glowing green about 100 kilometres up. That green pours from one gas in the air, set glowing when incoming particles crash into it. Which gas glows green?
context: The green comes from atomic oxygen glowing at a wavelength of 557.7 nanometres - the single most frequent auroral color. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: Scientists in Fairbanks, in the interior of Alaska, log over 200 possible aurora nights every year, which sounds like a huge number. On a truly clear, dark night in aurora season, how often do the northern lights actually appear overhead?
answer: about four nights out of five
choices: about four nights out of five
on very nearly every clear night
about one night out of five
context: Fairbanks sits almost directly beneath the auroral oval, so on a clear, dark night the lights appear roughly four times out of five - one of the most reliable aurora shows on Earth. Source: explorefairbanks.com/explore-the-area/aurora-season/

question: In Finland the northern lights that ripple over the frozen fells are called revontulet, a name from an old folk tale: a swift animal races across the snowy hills, and its bushy tail flicks bright sparks up into the winter sky. What does 'revontulet' mean in English?
context: The name comes from a legend that an Arctic fox raced across the fells and struck sparks from the snow with its tail. There is even a grain of truth: in the bone-dry Arctic air, a fox's fur really can throw off tiny static-electric sparks. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revontulet

question: Yellowknife, on the shore of Great Slave Lake in Canada's far north, sees the northern lights shine their familiar soft green on most nights. But during an unusually violent solar storm, a rare blue-purple skirt can appear along the aurora's lower edge, beneath the green ribbon. Which gas makes that blue-purple fringe?
context: The blue and purple light comes from molecular nitrogen glowing lower down, and it shows up mainly during intense solar activity - a different gas from the oxygen that makes the green and red above it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: On a truly powerful night over Tromso, a rare deep-red crown glows at the very top of the aurora, high above the green - up beyond 200 km, where the air is almost pure emptiness. Up there a single glowing atom is left so undisturbed that it is strangely slow to release its light. How long can that take?
choices: a few billionths of a second
context: That red crown is also oxygen, but far higher - above 150 to 200 km. The air is so thin an oxygen atom can glow undisturbed, taking anywhere from under a second to nearly two minutes to shed its energy as 630-nm red light. Where the air is denser, collisions snuff the glow before it can appear. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: For hours the aurora over Yellowknife, in Canada, hangs as a calm, quiet green arc. Then, around local midnight, an auroral substorm breaks: the whole sky writhes with twisting curtains that flare and fade over the next hour or two. What sets off the outburst?
answer: energy stored in Earth's magnetic tail, let go at once
choices: energy stored in Earth's magnetic tail, let go at once
a fresh solar flare striking Earth at that moment
the night air cooling and thinning high overhead
the rising Moon tugging on the magnetic field
context: This sudden flare-up near midnight is an auroral substorm: after energy from a solar storm builds up in Earth's magnetic tail, it dumps into the upper air all at once, and the quiet arc explodes into motion for about one to three hours. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: Thick cloud often smothers the whole of Swedish Lapland while a patch of clear sky opens right over Abisko, a tiny village beside the long Lake Torneträsk, and aurora hunters love it for that. Locals call the patch the 'blue hole.' What natural trick keeps that piece of sky clear?
answer: dry air sinking down the sheltered side of the mountains
choices: dry air sinking down the sheltered side of the mountains
warm water breathing heat up off the long lake
the aurora's own glow gently burning the cloud away
sea winds sweeping the clouds off to the east
context: Abisko sits in the rain-shadow of surrounding mountains and the 75-km-long Lake Tornetrask: air rising over the peaks drops its moisture on the way up, then sinks dry on the far side, tearing a roughly 10-20 sq km hole in the clouds. Abisko averages about 65-70% clear winter nights, versus 40-45% for Tromso 250 km west. Source: lightsoverlapland.com

question: People in Boston could read ordinary newspaper print outdoors near 1 a.m. one night in September 1859, when a colossal solar storm drove the aurora far south in a brilliant blaze. Telegraph operators unhooked their batteries and still went on sending messages for two hours. What was carrying the current down their wires?
choices: leftover charge stored in the wires
static from the cold, dry air
current leaking up from the ground
context: This was the Carrington Event, the most powerful geomagnetic storm on record. The same charged particles that lit the sky induced electric currents in the long telegraph lines - enough that some operators worked for about two hours with their batteries switched off, running on auroral current alone, while sparks leapt from the equipment. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: When the northern lights blaze over Norway, a matching curtain called the aurora australis can glow over Tasmania at the very same moment. Sometimes the swirls are identical, like a reflection in a mirror. Why do the far north and far south match so exactly, at the very same instant?
answer: both sit at the two ends of one magnetic field line
choices: both sit at the two ends of one magnetic field line
both reflect off the same layer of high cloud
the Sun fires a single beam straight through the planet
both are lit by the same passing comet
context: These are conjugate auroras. Earth's magnetic field lines arc from the far south to the far north; the same burst of particles slides down both ends of one line at once, painting near-identical displays in both hemispheres. The match is sharpest near the equinoxes. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora

question: Aurora chasers in Alberta, Canada, began photographing a strange mauve ribbon around 2016, arcing clear across the night sky over a green 'picket fence' of vertical bars. They nicknamed it Steve. When scientists studied it, they found that Steve is not truly an aurora at all. What is it really?
answer: a river of superheated gas flowing across the sky
choices: a river of superheated gas flowing across the sky
moonlight bouncing off a sheet of high ice cloud
a night-time rainbow lit by faint starlight
smoke from far-off wildfires glowing pink
context: The Alberta Aurora Chasers named it after the animated film Over the Hedge; scientists later back-formed STEVE into 'Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement.' A 2018 NASA-led study found STEVE is not made by particles raining down like an aurora - it is a ribbon of gas only about 25 km wide but hundreds of km long, near 3,000 C, streaming west-to-east at about 6 km per second. The green 'picket fence' beside it, though, IS aurora-like. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STEVE

question: Sailors have known for centuries that the Red Sea, the narrow sea that parts Africa from Arabia, runs saltier than the open ocean beyond its slim southern strait. The whole sea lies in a belt of hot, nearly rainless desert. What makes its water so much saltier than ordinary seawater?
answer: the sun evaporates it fast while no rivers refill it
choices: the sun evaporates it fast while no rivers refill it
salt domes on the seabed slowly dissolve into it
desert sandstorms keep dumping salt onto it
a narrow strait bottles up ocean salt inside it
context: With average salinity near 40 parts per thousand (up to 41 by the Gulf of Suez) versus about 35 for normal seawater, the Red Sea is one of the saltiest and warmest seas on Earth. Fierce evaporation under a desert sun, plus almost no river inflow to replace the lost water, concentrates the salt. Source: Wikipedia, 'Red Sea' (high evaporation, low precipitation, no significant rivers).

question: Africa and Arabia are drifting apart down the middle of the Red Sea, and new sea floor is still being paved in the gap of a sea less than 45 million years old. One of today's great oceans began this same way, when the supercontinent Pangaea broke apart. Which ocean was it?
context: Geologists nickname the Red Sea a 'baby ocean' -- a young ocean basin that began forming less than about 45 million years ago, one of the few places you can watch continental rifting turn into ocean floor today. Its slow spreading could eventually widen it into a full ocean, the way the Atlantic opened when Pangaea split apart. Source: ScienceDirect, 'Structure and morphology of the Red Sea'; Eos; Wikipedia, 'Red Sea Rift'.

question: The Red Sea usually shines a bright turquoise, which makes its name a puzzle. The leading guess blames a tiny living thing: every so often huge numbers of them drift through the water, and as they die they stain the surface a rusty red-brown. What are these organisms thought to be?
context: This is a leading but unsettled explanation: blooms of a reddish cyanobacterium, Trichodesmium erythraeum, can cloud the usually turquoise water and turn the surface reddish-brown as the bloom dies off. An alternative scholarly theory holds that 'red' simply meant the direction 'south' in some ancient color-for-direction naming. Source: Wikipedia, 'Red Sea'; LiveScience, 'Is the Red Sea Really Red?'.  (Legend.)

question: Two kilometers down in the Red Sea, a submersible's lights sweep across a real beach with lapping waves at the very bottom of the sea. Beyond it stretches a still, mirror-smooth lake whose water is so heavy that it never blends into the surrounding ocean, and any fish that blunders in is killed within seconds. What are these deadly seabed features called?
context: Deep-sea brine pools are lakes of water 3 to 8 times saltier and denser than the sea above; the brine sinks into hollows and lies unmixed, with its own surface, shoreline and slow waves in the dark. The toxic, oxygen-free water kills animals that stray in, so the floors are littered with dead fish and crabs -- yet mussels, microbial mats and tube worms crowd the rim. They are known in only three seas on Earth (the Gulf of Mexico, the Mediterranean, and the Red Sea), with about 25 described in the Red Sea alone. Source: LiveScience, 'New brine pools found in Red Sea'; OceanX.

question: Mining companies dream about the Atlantis II Deep, some 2,000 metres down in the Red Sea, whose water, at about 68 °C, holds no life at all. Its mud holds the richest known hoard of metals anywhere on the ocean floor, packed about a thousand times denser than in seawater. Which three metals is it richest in?
context: The Atlantis II Deep, about 2,000 m down, is roughly 68 C, salt-saturated (~250 parts per thousand) and airless -- and it holds the largest known metal-ore deposit on any seabed, with copper, cobalt and zinc concentrated about 1,000 times more than in ordinary seawater. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atlantis II Deep'.

question: Corals on one reef shrug off water 5 to 7 °C hotter than their summer maximum, and they came through recent record-breaking heatwaves without mass bleaching, while reefs elsewhere bleach when the water runs only a little above its normal summer peak. Which reef is this heat-proof survivor?
answer: the Gulf of Aqaba reef, at the Red Sea's northern tip
choices: the Gulf of Aqaba reef, at the Red Sea's northern tip
the Great Barrier Reef, off eastern Australia
the Belize Barrier Reef, in the Caribbean
the Maldives reefs, in the Indian Ocean
context: The reefs at the Gulf of Aqaba, the Red Sea's northern tip, tolerate water about 5-7 C above their summer maximum -- heat that would bleach and kill reefs elsewhere -- and rode out recent record marine heatwaves without mass bleaching. Scientists think they inherited this because their ancestors re-colonized the sea from the Arabian Sea through the hot southern Red Sea, a natural filter that let only heat-tolerant corals survive, so the ones now living in the cooler north carry built-in heat resistance. Source: ScienceDirect (Gulf of Aqaba thermal refuge); Earth.org; NCBI/PMC coral studies.

question: A giant horseshoe of volcanoes, about 40,000 km long, rings the Pacific Ocean. It climbs the Andes of South America, sweeps up North America's Pacific coast through the Cascades and Alaska, and curls down past Japan and the Philippines to New Zealand. What do geographers call this fiery belt?
context: The Ring of Fire traces the rim of the Pacific for roughly 40,000 km (25,000 mi), from the tip of South America up through North America, across the Bering Strait, and down past Japan to New Zealand. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire ; https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/plate-tectonics-ring-fire/

question: From the Andes and the Cascades to Japan and Indonesia, more than 450 volcanoes stand in one great horseshoe around the Pacific. Of all the active volcanoes on Earth, about what share stand along this belt?
context: National Geographic counts about 452 volcanoes along the belt — roughly three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes — all riding above ocean plates that dive into deep trenches around the Pacific. Source: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/plate-tectonics-ring-fire/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire

question: About 90 percent of the world's earthquakes strike along a single arc, the Ring of Fire, a horseshoe of faults and volcanoes wrapping the Pacific from the Andes up to Alaska and down through the Aleutians and Japan. Most of the biggest quakes ever recorded struck there too. Why does this one rim shake so much harder than the rest of the planet?
answer: ocean plates diving beneath the land
choices: ocean plates diving beneath the land
mantle plumes rising up under the rim
the deepest ocean basin pressing down
the planet's thinnest crust cracking open
context: About 90% of the world's earthquakes, including most of the largest ever recorded, strike along the Ring of Fire, because so many ocean plates are grinding down beneath the land there. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire

question: Near Tokyo, on Japan's main island of Honshu, a nearly perfect snow-capped cone rises 3,776 metres, the highest mountain in the country, close to where the Pacific Plate slides beneath Japan. Pilgrims and painters treat this Ring of Fire volcano as Japan's most sacred peak; it last erupted in 1707 and has been quiet ever since. What is it called?
context: Mount Fuji stands 3,776 m near a junction of the Eurasian, North American, and Philippine Sea plates, close to where the Pacific Plate subducts. Its last eruption was the Hoei eruption of 1707-08. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji

question: High on the border of Chile and Argentina stands Ojos del Salado, a great snow-streaked volcano built by the slow crash of tectonic plates in the Andes. Near its summit, tucked inside one of its craters, sits a small pool of water fed by melting snow — a crater lake. Of all the lakes on Earth, which record does this crater lake hold?
answer: the highest lake in the world
choices: the highest lake in the world
the highest lake where fish live
context: Near the summit of Ojos del Salado, at roughly 6,480-6,500 m, a small crater lake fed by permafrost and snowmelt is the highest lake in the world — higher even than the highest navigable lake, Lake Titicaca. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojos_del_Salado

question: Snow-capped volcanoes line the Cascade Range of the Pacific Northwest, Mount Rainier, Mount Hood and Mount St. Helens among them. They are fed by a small ocean plate lying just off the coast of Washington and Oregon, which is slowly diving beneath North America and melting into fresh magma far below. Which plate is it?
context: The small Juan de Fuca Plate slides under North America along the Cascadia subduction zone, feeding the Cascade arc — Mount St. Helens, Mount Rainier, and Mount Hood among them. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_eruption_of_Mount_St._Helens

question: Mount Tambora, on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, unleashed the most powerful eruption in recorded history in April 1815, with explosions heard 2,600 kilometres away. When the roar at last died away, what had the blast done to the mountain itself?
answer: blasted away about a third of the whole mountain
choices: blasted away about a third of the whole mountain
raised a brand-new cone inside the old crater
split the island of Sumbawa clean in two
sank its entire summit beneath the sea
context: Tambora's April 1815 eruption reached VEI 7 — the most powerful in recorded history — blasting out some 37-45 cubic km of rock and ash and dropping the mountain from about 4,300 m to 2,851 m, leaving a caldera 6-7 km wide. The blasts were heard at least 2,600 km (1,600 mi) away. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora

question: Along the deep Pacific trenches of the Ring of Fire, an ocean plate bends downward and sinks beneath a continent, dragging wet seawater and hydrated minerals down with it. Kilometres below, heat and crushing pressure squeeze that water out into the scorching solid rock of the mantle just above the sinking slab. What does the added water do to that hot mantle rock?
answer: it melts the rock by lowering its melting point
choices: it melts the rock by lowering its melting point
it freezes the rock by raising its melting point
it turns the rock into solid glass
it has no effect on the rock at all
context: Seawater dragged down with the sinking plate lowers the melting point of the rock above it (flux melting). The resulting magma is sticky and silica-rich (andesite) and traps gas until it bursts — which is why subduction builds steep, dangerous stratovolcanoes. Source: https://volcanoes.sdsu.edu/subducvolc_page.html

question: Runny basalt has oozed out of Hawaii's Mauna Loa for at least 700,000 years, piling up into a vast, gentle shield over a mid-ocean hotspot, far from the Ring of Fire. The volcano holds a record that no explosive Ring of Fire cone comes close to. What record does Mauna Loa hold?
answer: the largest active volcano on Earth
choices: the largest active volcano on Earth
the most active volcano on Earth
context: Mauna Loa sits over a mid-ocean hotspot, not a subduction zone, so it isn't part of the Ring of Fire. Its runny, silica-poor basalt oozes out without big explosions, building a broad shield — the largest active volcano on Earth by mass and volume, about 75,000 cubic km. Only two long-extinct giants, almost wholly under the sea, Pūhāhonu and the Tamu Massif, are bigger. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauna_Loa ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire

question: Arab travellers gave one of the world's largest sand seas, in the south of the Arabian Peninsula, a two-word name that the whole world still borrows: the Rub' al Khali. In plain English, what do those two Arabic words mean?
context: Rub' al Khali means 'the Empty Quarter' — the emptiest, least-inhabited region of the Arabian Peninsula, so barren that few people have ever lived across its France-sized expanse. (Britannica, 'Rub-al-Khali'; Wikipedia 'Rub' al Khali')

question: The Rub' al Khali sprawls across parts of Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen and the United Arab Emirates, a sea of dunes about the size of France. It holds a desert record that the Sahara cannot claim. Which world record does the Rub' al Khali hold?
answer: the largest continuous sand desert on Earth
choices: the largest continuous sand desert on Earth
the single hottest place ever on Earth
the very driest desert on Earth
the widest temperature range on Earth
context: The Sahara is far larger overall, but it is broken up by rock, gravel, and mountains. The Rub' al Khali is the largest CONTINUOUS sand sea on Earth — one unbroken expanse of pure sand covering roughly 650,000 km² across four countries. (Guinness World Records, 'Largest continuous sand desert'; NASA Earth Observatory)

question: Arabian legend tells of Ubar, a rich frankincense city that the sands of the Rub' al Khali swallowed whole. In 1992 a team digging at Shisr, a desert well in Oman that some believe marks Ubar, uncovered a ruined fortress. It had been swallowed, though not by sand. What had happened to it?
answer: it had collapsed into a sinkhole in the limestone
choices: it had collapsed into a sinkhole in the limestone
a flash flood had buried it deep in wadi mud
raiders had torn it down and burned the ruins
a landslide off the hills had buried it whole
context: In 1992 a team led by the archaeologist Juris Zarins dug at Shisr, a desert well in Oman's Dhofar, and uncovered the walls and towers of a fortress; much of it had fallen into a sinkhole where the limestone beneath gave way. Whether Shisr was ever Ubar is still disputed: Zarins himself came to think Ubar was a region, not a city. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantis_of_the_Sands ; https://grokipedia.com/page/Iram_of_the_Pillars  (Legend.)

question: Above ground the Rub' al Khali, roughly the size of France, is about as lifeless as a desert gets: almost no plant or animal survives there. Yet the rock of eastern Arabia just to its north holds the very opposite, a buried abundance first found in 1948 by American engineers drilling on behalf of the Saudi king. What lies hidden there?
answer: the largest oil field ever discovered
choices: the largest oil field ever discovered
the largest gold mine ever discovered
the largest diamond deposit ever discovered
the largest gas field ever discovered
context: The field is Ghawar, discovered in 1948 — the largest conventional oil field on Earth, holding roughly 170 billion barrels. In 1981 it peaked at 5.7 million barrels a DAY, the highest sustained output of any single oil field in history. A second giant, Shaybah (found 1968), lies deep in the dunes, where Saudi Aramco built a whole producing complex. (Britannica 'Al-Ghawar'; Wikipedia 'Shaybah oil field')

question: Scientists digging in the cracked, dry lakebeds of the Rub' al Khali keep unearthing teeth of hippopotamus, long-horned cattle bones and even clam shells, buried in one of the driest sand seas on Earth, where today only rare desert bugs survive. Why do the remains of these water-loving creatures lie beneath the Arabian sands?
answer: only a few thousand years ago, monsoon rains turned Arabia green
choices: only a few thousand years ago, monsoon rains turned Arabia green
ancient caravans carried the animals across the sands
floods swept the bones in from the mountains of Yemen
the creatures adapted to live in the desert as it is today
context: The cracked lakebeds prove it: during the Holocene Humid Period (~11,000–5,500 years ago), strengthened monsoons filled the Rub' al Khali with freshwater lakes and rivers — a time scientists call 'Green Arabia.' One ancient lake filled a ~1,100 km² basin about 42 m deep, then burst, carving a 150-km valley still traceable across the sand today. (Nature, Communications Earth & Environment, 2025; Saudi Aramco World, 'Lakes of the Rub' al-Khali')

question: Harry St John Philby, adviser to the Saudi king, drove deep into the Rub' al Khali in 1932 after local Bedouin rumours of Wabar, a lost city said in legend to have been destroyed by God for its wickedness. Philby never found any city, but he stumbled onto something even stranger scattered across the sand. What had he found?
answer: a field of craters blasted by a meteorite strike
choices: a field of craters blasted by a meteorite strike
the fossil skeleton of a giant sea creature
an ancient temple half-swallowed by dunes
a spring of black oil bubbling to the surface
context: Chasing a rumored lost city, St John Philby instead found a cluster of meteorite impact craters (the largest ~116 m wide), littered with black glass 'Wabar Pearls' — droplets fused straight from the desert sand by the heat of the impact. (Wikipedia 'Wabar craters'; Britannica 'Wabar Craters')

question: Nicholas Clapp, a filmmaker, went hunting in the 1980s and 1990s, with Ronald Blom and Charles Elachi of NASA, for Ubar, or Iram, a rich frankincense city that Arabian legend says the dunes of the Rub' al Khali swallowed. How did they search a sand sea for a lost city?
answer: satellite radar traced buried caravan roads across the sand
choices: satellite radar traced buried caravan roads across the sand
sonar mapped the bedrock hidden beneath the dunes
deep core-drilling sampled the sand for buried ruins
infrared cameras hunted for warm stone at night
context: The real hunt was remarkable: filmmaker Nicholas Clapp and NASA-JPL scientists Ronald Blom and Charles Elachi used Space Shuttle radar (1984), Landsat, and SPOT images to trace ancient camel-caravan tracks — packed rock-hard by hundreds of thousands of camels — converging on Shisr, Oman. A 1992 dig there uncovered a fortress that had collapsed into a limestone sinkhole, literally swallowed by the ground. Whether it truly is the legendary Ubar is still disputed. The phrase 'Atlantis of the Sands,' often credited to T.E. Lawrence, was likely coined by Bertram Thomas, first Westerner to cross the sands (1930–31). LEGEND/DISPUTED. (NASA/JPL; Wikipedia 'Atlantis of the Sands')

question: Under a scorching sun, the Sahara sprawls from Africa's Atlantic coast to the Red Sea, through Algeria, Libya and Egypt. Its roughly 9.2 million square kilometres could swallow the continental United States. Where does the Sahara truly rank among the world's deserts?
answer: the largest hot desert on Earth
choices: the largest hot desert on Earth
the largest desert of any kind
context: The Sahara is the largest HOT desert, but not the largest desert overall — the frozen Antarctic and Arctic deserts are both bigger, because a 'desert' just means a place with very little rainfall. At about 9.2 million km2 the Sahara still blankets roughly 31% of Africa. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sahara' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahara

question: At midday on the open Sahara the sand can bake past 80°C, and near Port Sudan a thermometer laid on the sand once read 83.5°C. An old travellers' saying claims the desert sand gets hot enough to do what?
context: Sand-surface temperatures in the Sahara can top 80 C (176 F); the 83.5 C reading near Port Sudan is among the hottest ground temperatures ever recorded. An egg's white sets at about 70 C, so that sand really could fry one — though water still wouldn't boil until 100 C. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sahara' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahara

question: Fossil lakebeds lie beneath the Sahara's sand, with hippo and crocodile bones, the remains of animals that need rivers and lakes. This whole desert was once a green land full of water. How recently was the Sahara still that green?
context: This was the 'African Humid Period' (roughly 14,500-5,000 years ago), when monsoon rains pushed far north and the Sahara held lakes, rivers, hippos, and giraffes. It dried into desert only a few thousand years ago — recently enough that people painted the vanished green world on the rocks before it was gone. Source: Nature Scitable, 'Green Sahara: African Humid Periods' — https://www.nature.com/scitable/knowledge/library/green-sahara-african-humid-periods-paced-by-82884405/

question: Ancient artists covered the cliff walls of the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau, deep in the Sahara in southeastern Algeria, with about 15,000 paintings and carvings, some as old as 12,000 years. The plateau is bare rock and sand now; the artists worked when the land was green with grass, rivers and lakes. What do their most striking scenes show?
answer: people herding great herds of cattle
choices: people herding great herds of cattle
armies marching off to distant war
context: The Tassili paintings capture a wet Sahara: herders driving cattle, plus hippos and crocodiles, where only rock and sand survive today. Camels don't appear in the oldest scenes — they only reached the Sahara thousands of years later, after the land had already dried. UNESCO named Tassili n'Ajjer a World Heritage Site in 1982. Source: UNESCO, 'Tassili n'Ajjer' — https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/179

question: Travellers ride camels out from Merzouga, in Morocco, to camp among the dunes of Erg Chebbi on the Sahara's edge, sand mountains about 150 metres tall. They stay to watch the dunes do one slow, famous thing through the long day. What are the dunes known for doing as the sun crosses the sky?
choices: booming with a deep humming note
swelling and shrinking with the tides
steaming in the cold morning air
context: Erg Chebbi's dunes near Merzouga rise about 150 m and shift from pink to deep apricot as the light changes — the classic postcard Sahara. (Some dunes elsewhere really do 'boom' or sing as sand slides, but Erg Chebbi is famous for its color.) Ironically, such towering sand seas are actually the minority of the desert's terrain. Source: Wikipedia, 'Erg Chebbi' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erg_Chebbi

question: Astronauts on the space station look down on a giant bullseye in the Sahara near Ouadane, in Mauritania: a ring pattern about 40 kilometres wide that they use as a landmark. Despite its perfect target shape, how did this 'Eye of the Sahara' really form?
answer: the slow erosion of a pushed-up rock dome
choices: the slow erosion of a pushed-up rock dome
the impact of a giant crashing meteorite
the ruins of the lost city of Atlantis
the collapse of an ancient volcano's crater
context: The Eye of the Sahara (the Richat Structure), about 40 km across near Ouadane, Mauritania, is NOT a meteor crater and NOT the lost city of Atlantis, despite popular claims. It's a deeply eroded dome: roughly 100 million years ago magma pushed layers of rock upward, and erosion later stripped them into rings. No impact 'shock' minerals were ever found — an early report of them turned out to be a misidentified mineral. Source: Wikipedia, 'Richat Structure' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richat_Structure

question: László Almásy found a rock shelter in 1933 in the Gilf Kebir, a blazing plateau in the far southwest of Egypt where rain almost never falls. Its wall, painted about 8,000 years ago, is covered with tiny human figures, arms and legs bent in the pose that gave the cave its famous name. What do the little figures appear to be doing?
context: Almasy found these ~8,000-year-old paintings in 1933; the site, in Egypt's now-hyperarid Gilf Kebir, became famous through the novel and film 'The English Patient.' The little figures look like swimmers — a startling image in a place with no water for hundreds of kilometers, and a hint of the wetter Green Sahara. (Some scholars debate whether the figures are truly 'swimming.') Source: Wikipedia, 'Cave of Swimmers' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_of_Swimmers  (Legend.)

question: Strong winds lift about 27 million tons of dust off the Sahara every year and carry it high across the Atlantic Ocean. When satellites tracked where it all settles, they found the dry desert quietly fertilizing a green place thousands of kilometres away, on the far side of the sea. What far-off place does the Saharan dust help to feed?
context: NASA's CALIPSO satellite (2007-2013) measured about 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust crossing the Atlantic each year, carrying roughly 22,000 tons of phosphorus — about as much as the Amazon loses to its rains and floods. The dead desert helps keep the living rainforest fertile. Source: NASA Goddard — https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/goddard/nasa-satellite-reveals-how-much-saharan-dust-feeds-amazons-plants/

question: Winds sweep across one small basin in northern Chad, the dried-out floor of an ancient lake in the Sahara, packed with the phosphorus-rich fossils of countless tiny lake creatures. That basin throws more dust into the sky than anywhere else on the planet. What is this dustiest place on Earth called?
context: The Bodele Depression in Chad — the dried bed of a once-huge lake, its floor full of phosphorus-rich fossil plankton (diatoms) — is the single dustiest place on Earth, and the main source of the very dust that fertilizes the Amazon. Source: NASA Earth Observatory, 'Bodele Depression Dust Feeds Amazon' — https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/7279/bodele-depression-dust-feeds-amazon

question: An ancient river called the Tamanrasset hides under the sand of the western Sahara. It once ran roughly 2,600 kilometres from the mountains of Algeria to the Atlantic before drying up thousands of years ago, and nothing of it shows from the ground. How did scientists finally trace its hidden path?
answer: with radar satellites that peer through sand
choices: with radar satellites that peer through sand
by drilling a long grid of test wells
from the maps of ancient Roman surveyors
context: Radar satellites can penetrate dry sand, and in 2015 they revealed the buried Tamanrasset paleoriver — a channel running some 2,600 km from the Algerian highlands to the Atlantic. Its drainage basin would rank about the world's 12th largest today; it last flowed during the green periods, roughly 11,700-5,000 years ago. Source: Nature Communications (2015) — https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms9751

question: Most of the Sahara's great sand seas, the ergs, roll their dunes to the horizon in Algeria and Libya. Yet all the ergs together cover only about a quarter of the desert's 9.2 million square kilometres. What kind of ground makes up most of the rest of the Sahara?
answer: bare rock plateaus and gravel plains
choices: bare rock plateaus and gravel plains
flat white salt pans and playas
fields of dark shattered volcanic rock
deep dry canyons and dusty gorges
context: Sand seas (ergs) cover only about a quarter of the Sahara. Most of it is rocky plateaus called hamada and gravel plains called reg, plus dry riverbeds (wadis), salt flats, and mountains — a far rockier place than the postcard suggests. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sahara' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahara

question: Emi Koussi towers nearly 3 kilometres straight up from the sandstone plains of northern Chad, a colossal mountain in the Tibesti range about 3,400 metres high. It is no dune, yet it is the highest point in the whole Sahara. What kind of mountain is Emi Koussi?
context: Emi Koussi is a giant shield volcano in the Tibesti Mountains of northern Chad, rising about 3,415 m (~11,200 ft) — nearly 3 km above the plains — and capped by nested collapse craters (calderas). It is the highest point in the entire Sahara. Source: Britannica, 'Mount Koussi' — https://www.britannica.com/place/Mount-Koussi

question: Floating brown seaweed and open water stretch in every direction across one sea in the middle of the North Atlantic, a sea with no coast at all: no beach, no cliff, no shore. Every other sea on Earth has one. Which sea is this?
context: Every other sea on Earth is defined by its shores, but the Sargasso Sea is bounded only by open ocean and the currents that circle it. It sits in the middle of the North Atlantic, with the island of Bermuda near its western edge as the closest land of all. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea

question: Rafts of golden seaweed called sargassum drift for miles across the calm water of the Sargasso Sea, in the middle of the North Atlantic, never sinking and never washing ashore. The weed spends its whole life afloat in the open ocean. What keeps the sargassum from sinking?
context: Sargassum stays up thanks to hundreds of tiny gas-filled floats called pneumatocysts — little berry-like bladders dotting its fronds. The two open-ocean species never attach to the seafloor at all; they live, drift, and even reproduce (by simply breaking apart) entirely afloat. Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2023.1250150/full

question: Christopher Columbus's fleet pushed into the golden weed of the Sargasso Sea, far out in the Atlantic, in September 1492, a mat of floating seaweed stretching to the horizon. His crews grew fearful: weed so thick surely meant shallows, and the hulls would soon grind onto hidden rocks. The sailors dropped a weighted line over the side to feel for the bottom. What did the line find?
context: Columbus's men had sailed into the Sargasso Sea, giving the first written account of it in 1492. The weed made them fear shoals, but their soundings touched no bottom — they were in the middle of the deep open Atlantic, hundreds of km from any shore. The golden weed simply drifts on water miles deep. Source: http://www.sargassoseacommission.org/index.php?id=105&option=com_content&view=article  (Legend.)

question: Grown European eels slip down their home rivers to the coast and swim thousands of kilometres across the open Atlantic to the Sargasso Sea, the mid-ocean water where they hatched, to breed and die. The same sea is also where a second kind of eel is born, one whose home rivers lie on a different continent. Whose eels also spawn in the Sargasso?
choices: eels from the coast of West Africa
eels from the rivers of Japan
context: The Sargasso Sea is the one nursery for eels from both sides of the Atlantic. The European eel makes the longest spawning migration of any eel — 5,000 to 10,000 km from Europe's rivers — while the American eel, from the rivers of eastern North America, makes a shorter crossing of up to about 4,000 km. Two species, two continents, one shoreless mid-ocean sea: each fish grows up in a river, then swims back across the ocean to the water where its life began, spawns, and dies. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-19248-8

question: Aristotle cut open eel after eel and never found a young one inside. Eels turned up in ponds and rivers everywhere, yet no one had ever seen an eel egg, a nest or a newborn eel, for their birthplace far out in the Atlantic's Sargasso Sea was unknown. The world believed Aristotle's answer for 2,000 years. What did he decide was the origin of eels?
answer: they grew straight out of the mud
choices: they grew straight out of the mud
they hatched from tiny sea eggs
context: Aristotle's idea was 'spontaneous generation' — that eels arose from mud with no parents at all. Because eels breed far out in the Sargasso Sea and their young drift back as clear, leaf-shaped larvae that look nothing like eels, no one connected the two, and the mystery of where eels come from lasted roughly 2,000 years. Source: https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/fish/eel-reproduction-mystery  (Legend.)

question: Johannes Schmidt gave nearly twenty years to one of science's oldest riddles: where in the world are eels born? Year after year he dragged fine nets through the open Atlantic and measured every tiny eel larva he caught. The larvae ran to different sizes in different parts of the ocean, and the pattern led him to a single hidden nursery, which he named in 1923. Which larvae marked the birthplace?
answer: the tiniest larvae, caught in the Sargasso
choices: the tiniest larvae, caught in the Sargasso
the biggest larvae, caught off Europe
the biggest larvae, caught in the Sargasso
the tiniest larvae, caught off Europe
context: Schmidt reasoned that the smallest larvae must be closest to where they hatched, so he chased ever-tinier young eels across the Atlantic — and the very smallest turned up in the Sargasso Sea, so in 1923 he declared it the eels' birthplace. Direct proof came only in 2022, when satellite tags on 26 eels tracked them all the way to the Sargasso. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Schmidt_(biologist)

question: Evening light falls on Tanzania's Serengeti, where tall dry grass runs to the horizon and wildebeest and zebra graze. Lone flat-topped trees stand dark against the sky, their branches spread like open green umbrellas, the shape in almost every photo of the African plains. Which tree is it?
context: The umbrella-thorn acacia, with its flat, spreading crown, is the signature tree of the Serengeti, whose name is widely said to come from the Maasai word 'seringit,' the endless plains. Baobabs, marulas and mopane grow across African savanna too, but the lone flat-topped acacia is the classic silhouette. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serengeti

question: Lions hunt across Tanzania's Serengeti, open grassland with rain enough each year to grow a closed forest. Each dry season something wipes out the young tree seedlings, while the deep-rooted grass shrugs it off and grows back. What natural force sweeps the plains and keeps them treeless?
context: The Serengeti gets anywhere from about 500 mm of rain in its dry rain-shadow up to 1,200 mm near Lake Victoria -- easily enough for forest. It stays grassland because fire sweeps through each dry season, killing tree seedlings while the grass simply regrows. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serengeti

question: Over a million wildebeest sweep across Tanzania's Serengeti each year, cropping the grass hard, yet the plains turn green again behind the herds while a nibbled young tree can die outright. Grass keeps the living cells that build each new leaf in an unusual place. Where on a grass plant do those cells sit?
answer: at the base of each blade
choices: up at the tip of each blade
at the base of each blade
context: A grass keeps its growing tissue -- the meristem -- right at the base of each blade and at the crown near the soil, not down in the roots or out at the tips. This 'intercalary meristem' keeps churning out new cells even after the top is grazed, burned, or mown away, so the blade simply pushes up fresh and green. A tree, by contrast, carries its buds up in its branches -- right where teeth and flames reach them -- so the same wildebeest that only trim the Serengeti's grass can kill a young tree by stripping it. Source: https://forages.oregonstate.edu/nfgc/eo/onlineforagecurriculum/instructormaterials/availabletopics/management/regrowth

question: Trees with thick, corky bark and roots that plunge deep for water stand across a vast tropical grassland half a world from Africa, covering about a fifth of Brazil. The bark carries them through the flames, and with some 10,000 plant species this is the most plant-rich savanna on Earth. What is this great Brazilian savanna called?
context: The Cerrado covers about 1.91 million km2 -- a fifth of Brazil -- and the WWF calls it the biologically richest savanna in the world, with roughly 10,000 plant species. It is also a 'cradle of waters,' holding the headwaters of the Parana, Araguaia-Tocantins and Sao Francisco river systems above the vast Guarani Aquifer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerrado

question: Aboriginal Australians have lit small, cool fires across the tropical savanna of northern Australia for tens of thousands of years, burning the country in a careful patchwork so that no single blaze can grow into a monster. What is this ancient practice called?
context: Archaeologist Rhys Jones coined the term 'firestick farming' in 1969 for this deliberate cool-burning, which builds a mosaic of freshly burned and older patches. It is no relic: Australia's 2020 Royal Commission and the Darwin Centre for Bushfire Research found that reviving large-scale traditional cool burning sharply reduced the area lost to wildfires. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire-stick_farming

question: Tall earthen towers stud the open plains of the African savanna, some rising over 5 metres, raised grain by grain by vast insect colonies. Clumps of trees and shrubs crowd in rings around the towers, while bare grass stretches between them. Why do trees take root on the mounds and not on the open plain?
answer: the mound soil holds more water and nutrients
choices: the mound soil holds more water and nutrients
the towers shade the seedlings from the sun
the insects carry tree seeds up to the mound
the mound is the only soft ground for roots
context: Termite-mound soil, worked and enriched by the colony, holds more water and nutrients than the surrounding ground, so browse-friendly trees cluster on and around the mounds. In northern Australia, wedge-shaped 'magnetic' mounds are lined up north-south; in Brazil's caatinga, some 200 million mounds -- the oldest at least 3,820 years old -- cover an area the size of Great Britain and are visible from space. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound-building_termites

question: Ecologists mapping tree cover across sub-Saharan Africa long expected rainfall to settle everything: enough rain makes closed forest, too little leaves open savanna. Then they charted a wide band of rainfall, about 1,000 to 2,500 millimetres a year, and the pattern astonished them. What did they find across that whole band?
answer: both forest and savanna at the very same rainfall
choices: both forest and savanna at the very same rainfall
forest up on the hills, savanna on the flats
a steady climb from grassland toward forest
closed forest wherever the rain was heaviest
context: This is what ecologists call 'alternative stable states.' Across a wide rainfall band -- roughly 1,000 to 2,500 mm a year -- the very same climate can settle into either dense forest or open savanna, and rainfall alone cannot tell you which. What tips the balance is how often fire and grazing knock young trees back: grass fuels the fires that kill tree seedlings and hold the land open, so a burned, grazed patch stays savanna while its unburned neighbour, under identical rain, closes into forest. Source: Staver, Archibald & Levin 2011, Ecology 92(5):1063-1072, https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/10-1684.1

question: After dark in Mosquito Bay, on Puerto Rico's island of Vieques, every paddle stroke and splash lights the water bright blue. What in the water makes it glow?
context: The plankton are dinoflagellates — single-celled ocean drifters that flash the instant the water is disturbed, so the whole bay blazes blue behind a moving paddle. The glow is life itself, not a reflection or a mineral. Source: Guinness World Records, 'Brightest bioluminescent bay'; Discover Puerto Rico (Mosquito Bay).

question: Suppose you trail a hand through the dark water of Mosquito Bay, on Vieques Island in Puerto Rico, after sunset. The water flashes bright blue wherever your fingers jostle it. What does the blue glow do while you stir?
answer: It follows your motion, then fades a second later
choices: It follows your motion, then fades a second later
It floods the whole bay with light at once
It drifts slowly toward the distant shore
It pulses on and off for several minutes
context: Each plankton flashes for only about a tenth of a second when jostled, then goes dark — so the light traces your hand exactly and dies right behind it, like a glowing wake. Source: Guinness World Records, 'Brightest bioluminescent bay'.

question: Kayakers crossing Mosquito Bay at night, on the small island of Vieques off Puerto Rico, see the water glow bright blue-green wherever anything touches it. In 2006 Guinness World Records gave the bay a title no other glowing bay on Earth can claim. What record does Mosquito Bay hold?
answer: The brightest bioluminescent bay in the world
choices: The brightest bioluminescent bay in the world
The largest saltwater lagoon in the Caribbean
The oldest tidal bay in the Americas
The only bay that glows all year round
context: Guinness World Records certified Mosquito Bay as the brightest bioluminescent bay on the planet in 2006. After Hurricane Maria struck in 2017 the plankton crashed and the bay went dark for months — but about eight months later the glow returned, brighter than ever. Source: Guinness World Records, 'Brightest bioluminescent bay'; NPR; Scripps/Latz Lab.

question: Visitors may still wade straight into the blue glow at just one of Puerto Rico's bioluminescent bays, the sheltered lagoons that flash blue-green at the stir of a paddle or a hand. No other country has as many of these bays, and swimming is banned in most of them to protect the fragile life that makes the light. Which bay still lets visitors in?
context: Puerto Rico's three bays are Mosquito Bay on Vieques, Laguna Grande at Fajardo, and La Parguera at Lajas — more than any other country. Swimming is banned in the first two to protect the delicate plankton; only La Parguera lets you wade into the glow. Jamaica's Luminous Lagoon at Falmouth is another rare Caribbean glow-water where visitors can swim. Source: Discover Puerto Rico, guide to the three bioluminescent bays; Traverse Jamaica.

question: A fish darting through Mosquito Bay at night, on the island of Vieques near Puerto Rico, leaves a glowing trail like a shooting star. Up to 700,000 glowing dinoflagellates crowd into a single gallon of the bay's water, a density the open coast just outside never comes close to. What feature of Mosquito Bay traps and concentrates them?
answer: Its narrow S-shaped mouth traps them inside
choices: Its narrow S-shaped mouth traps them inside
A deep central trench holds them down
A ring of coral walls off the open tide
A warm current sweeps more in each day
context: The bay's narrow, twisting mouth lets the plankton in but keeps them from washing back out to sea, while the mangroves ringing the shore feed them nutrients — so they pile up to about 700,000 per gallon (roughly 4.5 litres). Its geography, not luck, makes it the brightest. Source: Guinness World Records, 'Brightest bioluminescent bay'.

question: Every breaking wave on Vaadhoo Island, in the Maldives' chain of low coral islands south of India, scatters cold blue light across the wet sand after dark, and each footprint glows for a moment before it fades. Visitors gave this shoreline a nickname that stuck. What do they call it?
context: Tourists call Vaadhoo's glowing shoreline the 'Sea of Stars.' The blue light is cold light: inside the plankton a molecule called luciferin combines with oxygen to make a glow with almost no heat, which is why it is safe to touch and wade through. Source: All That's Interesting, 'Sea of Stars Maldives'; Visit Maldives; Wikipedia, 'Bioluminescence'.

question: Taiwan's Matsu Islands glow with electric-blue 'blue tears' each spring, made by the plankton Noctiluca scintillans. Lovely as the glow is, scientists watch these blooms warily, because when the plankton spike too far the same water can turn deadly. What harm does the bloom bring?
answer: It forms red tides that choke the oxygen from the water
choices: It forms red tides that choke the oxygen from the water
It coats the coral reefs in a smothering slime
It stains the pale beaches a permanent rusty red
It stings the skin of anyone who swims through it
context: When Noctiluca scintillans blooms too heavily it forms 'red tides' that strip the oxygen from the water and create dead zones where fish suffocate, and coastal pollution has been making the blooms bigger — so the same glow that draws tourists is a warning sign for the sea. NASA even traced Matsu's 'blue tears' across almost 1,000 satellite images from 2000 to 2017 to map how the blooms grow and drift. (A different blue glow, in Japan's Toyama Bay, comes from firefly squid — an animal, not plankton.) Source: NASA Earth Observatory, 'Tracking Blue Tear Blooms'; Atlas Obscura.

question: Coyotes, roadrunners and rattlesnakes share the Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico with one cactus that grows wild here and nowhere else on Earth. Its shape stars on postcards, road signs and old cowboy films. Which cactus is it?
context: The saguaro (Carnegiea gigantea) is native exclusively to the Sonoran Desert — its towering, many-armed silhouette exists in the wild nowhere else on Earth, which is why it stands in for the whole American West. Prickly pear, barrel, and cholla cacti all grow across many deserts, but the saguaro belongs to this one alone. Source: Grokipedia 'Saguaro'; NPS 'Saguaro Cactus Facts' — 'grows only in the Sonoran Desert of the U.S. and Mexico.'

question: Saguaros across the Sonoran Desert raise great upward-curving arms like giants, yet a young saguaro has no arms at all. For a long time it stands as a single branchless column. About how old is a saguaro when it finally grows its very first arm?
context: A saguaro grows no arms at all until it is roughly 50-70 years old (up to 100 in the driest country), by which time the trunk stands about 10-16 feet tall. The famous arms are a sign of an old, well-watered plant — a saguaro can then live on to 150-200 years. Source: NPS Saguaro National Park — first arm at '50-70 years (up to 100 in drier regions)'; Grokipedia 'Saguaro.'

question: A saguaro nearly 79 feet tall, higher than a seven-story building, stood in the Sonoran Desert near Cave Creek, Arizona, the tallest ever measured. Saguaros grow slowly and can live for two centuries, and this giant had stood for hundreds of years when it came down in 1986. What toppled it?
context: That record saguaro stood near Cave Creek, Arizona, until a 1986 windstorm brought it down. A healthy saguaro reaches up to about 50 feet and can weigh 6 tons or more when swelled with water — but its shallow roots and top-heavy arms leave even giants vulnerable to a hard blow of wind. Source: Wikipedia 'Saguaro' (tallest ~79 ft, toppled 1986); Grokipedia 'Saguaro.'

question: Javelinas and Gila monsters roam the Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico, a desert famously green and crowded with life. Most deserts on Earth get one short wet season, if any, and stay mostly bare rock and sand. What natural gift makes the Sonoran so much lusher than almost any other desert?
answer: it gets two rainy seasons each year
choices: it gets two rainy seasons each year
cool ocean fog drips over it nightly
context: Unlike almost every other desert, the Sonoran is watered twice a year — gentle Pacific storms from December to March, then violent monsoon thunderstorms from July to September. No other North American desert drinks in both winter and summer, and that double soaking is exactly why the Sonoran teems with life while other deserts stay bare. Source: Grokipedia 'Sonoran Desert'; Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum, 'Desert Storms.'

question: A downpour drenches the Sonoran Desert, and within just a few hours one of its big cacti soaks up hundreds of pounds of water, until roughly 85 to 90 percent of what the cactus weighs is stored water. What feature of its trunk lets it swell up like this and hold so much?
answer: vertical pleats that open like an accordion
choices: vertical pleats that open like an accordion
a thick, spongy pith at its core
an outer skin that stretches like rubber
context: A saguaro's trunk is pleated with 12 to 24 vertical ribs that fan open like an accordion. After a heavy rain the plant swells outward and can hold roughly 3,000 liters of water, so that 85-90% of a saguaro's weight is simply water in storage, carrying it through months of drought. Source: Grokipedia 'Saguaro' (12-24 ribs, up to ~3,000 L, 85-90% water).

question: Along the warm shores of the Gulf of California, in the Sonoran Desert of northwestern Mexico, one giant columnar cactus grows taller than any other kind of cactus on Earth. It can push up nearly 20 metres, thick arms rising against the desert sky — taller than a five-storey building. Which cactus is it?
context: The cardón (Pachycereus pringlei) grows along the shores of the Gulf of California and is the tallest species of cactus on Earth, its columns reaching nearly 63 feet. The record 79-foot saguaro was a single freak giant; measured as a species, though, the cardón grows the tallest of all cacti. Mild, nearly frost-free winters and two rainy seasons also make the Sonoran the most biodiverse desert in the world — home to more than 2,000 kinds of plants, more than any other desert on Earth. Source: Grokipedia 'Sonoran Desert' (cardón, tallest cactus, ~63 ft); Wikipedia 'Sonoran Desert' (2,000+ plant species, most of any desert).

question: Godfrey Sykes, a Tucson botanist, named a weird tree of the Sonoran Desert's Baja California corner in 1922: a slender spiny column up to 50 feet tall, shaped just like an upside-down carrot. What inspired the name he chose for it, 'boojum'?
answer: a monster in a Lewis Carroll poem
choices: a monster in a Lewis Carroll poem
a word for spirit in Tohono O'odham
context: The boojum tree (cirio in Spanish, meaning 'candle') grows mainly in Baja California, a slender spiny column up to about 50 feet tall. The Tucson botanist Godfrey Sykes named it in 1922 after the boojum — the creature that makes people vanish in Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem 'The Hunting of the Snark.' Source: Wikipedia 'Boojum tree'; Britannica 'boojum tree.'

question: On the sandy Magdalena plain of Baja California grows the 'creeping devil,' a cactus that refuses to stay in one place. Over many years the whole plant slowly travels across the open dunes. How does the creeping devil move across the sand?
answer: its front tip grows forward as its old rear dies off
choices: its front tip grows forward as its old rear dies off
strong winds roll the whole plant across the dunes
its seeds sprout a bit farther downwind each year
hidden runners pull the plant slowly forward
context: The creeping devil (Stenocereus eruca) of Baja's Magdalena plain lies flat and grows forward at its tip while the old rear of the stem dies and rots away — so, root by root, the whole plant slowly wanders across the dunes, a cactus that never quite stays put. Source: Grokipedia 'Sonoran Desert' — Magdalena Region, creeping devil spreads vegetatively across dunes.

question: At Trinidad's Carnival, whole orchestras of steelpans ring out. The steelpan is the country's national instrument, and every gleaming pan is hammered and tuned by hand from one kind of thrown-out metal object. What object is a steelpan made from?
context: A steelpan is built from a discarded 55-gallon oil drum: the maker hammers its top into a shallow concave dish, then dents and tunes a grid of note-ovals — larger ovals ring lower, smaller ones higher. A whole Carnival orchestra, born from oil barrels. Source: Wikipedia 'Steelpan'.

question: Colonial rulers in Trinidad outlawed the African skin drums and stick-fighting that drove Carnival's street parades in the 1880s. Trinidadians kept the rhythm alive with a booming, tuned band that filled the decades until the steelpan came along. What were these pre-pan bands called?
context: With their drums silenced, Trinidadians cut tall bamboo stalks to different lengths and stamped them on the ground for a deep, tuned boom — the 'tamboo bamboo' bands (the name blends the French 'tambour', drum, with 'bamboo'), often joined by a bottle beaten with a spoon. These bands bridged the gap to the steelpan. Sources: Wikipedia 'Steelpan' and 'Tamboo bamboo'.

question: Trinidad's street singers packed their sharp, witty ballads with gossip, jokes and the week's news, set to a rolling beat, and these were the songs the first steelpan players arranged for pan. What is this storytelling Trinidadian song style called?
context: Calypso — historically called 'kaiso' — is Trinidad's storytelling street song, and calypsonians like Lord Kitchener wrote tunes the earliest steelpan pioneers arranged for pan. Its faster, dance-floor descendant is soca, the music that now powers Carnival 'fetes'. Source: Wikipedia 'Steelpan' and 'Winston Simon'.

question: Winston 'Spree' Simon played before a crowd that included the British Governor at Trinidad's Carnival of 1946, the first one held since its wartime ban. On the 14-note pan he had made by hand he played not only the island's own street songs but flowing European classical music. Which classical piece did he play?
context: This was the first Carnival since the wartime ban, and Winston 'Spree' Simon's little pan — the 'ping pong' — carried more than a hymn: he also played Lord Kitchener calypsoes and, before the British Governor and his wife, the British national anthem itself, proving a homemade oil-drum instrument could play anything. Pan folklore also credits Simon with first discovering, around 1942, that a dent hammered into a drum makes a note — that origin story is told as legend. Source: Wikipedia 'Winston Simon'.

question: Every Trinidad Carnival, dozens of steelbands, some with up to a hundred pannists each, spend weeks rehearsing a single tune. Then they face off in a thundering, all-night showdown at the Queen's Park Savannah to be crowned champions. What is this steelband contest, the biggest of its kind in the world, called?
context: Panorama, first held in 1963 at the Queen's Park Savannah in Port of Spain, is the world's largest steelband competition; a full orchestra of up to a hundred pannists arranges one tune. The Pan Am North Stars, led by arranger Anthony Williams, took that first 1963 title. Source: Wikipedia 'Panorama (music competition)'; steelband.co.uk.

question: Pannists in 1940s Trinidad beat a harsh, clanging, tin-can sound out of the first steelpans. Ellie Mannette, later honoured as 'the Father of the Modern Steel Drum', found a simple change in 1946 that gave the pan its warm, singing tone, and every pannist has copied it since. What did Mannette do to soften the pan's tone?
answer: Wrapped the playing sticks in rubber
choices: Wrapped the playing sticks in rubber
Lined the pan's underside with felt
Tempered the steel in an oil bath
Fitted a cloth mute over the notes
context: Ellie Mannette (1927–2018), 'the Father of the Modern Steel Drum,' also in 1946 was the first to sink the drum's flat top into a deep concave bowl, making room for many more notes on the sunken face. He is credited with creating seven of the ten instruments used in steelbands today. Source: Percussive Arts Society; Wikipedia 'Ellie Mannette'.

question: The Trinidad All-Steel Percussion Orchestra (TASPO) sailed to Britain in 1951 and became the first all-steel band to perform overseas. Its pannists silenced the critics who had dismissed the pan as mere 'dustbin' noise. Which landmark British event did TASPO play?
context: TASPO played the Festival of Britain — a huge national exhibition on London's South Bank in 1951 — as the first all-oil-drum steelband to perform abroad. Some players, such as Sterling Betancourt, stayed on and planted steelpan in Britain, where it still thrives. Source: Wikipedia 'Steelpan'.

question: Muddy islands and tidal channels tangle into a maze where the Ganges pours into the Bay of Bengal, between India and Bangladesh. This is the Sundarbans, a forest of about ten thousand square kilometres. Guinness World Records lists it under one world title. Which one?
answer: the largest mangrove forest on Earth
choices: the largest mangrove forest on Earth
the largest bamboo forest on Earth
the largest teak forest on Earth
the largest palm forest on Earth
context: Guinness World Records recognizes the Sundarbans, at the mouth of the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta, as the largest mangrove forest on Earth -- about 10,000 sq km of trees rooted in salt water. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundarbans ; guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/507848-largest-mangrove-forest

question: Low tide in the Sundarbans, where the Ganges meets the Bay of Bengal, bares mud so waterlogged that no oxygen reaches down into it. Yet the mangrove trees rooted there must still breathe. How does a mangrove get air to roots buried in that airless mud?
answer: it grows snorkel roots that poke up into the air
choices: it grows snorkel roots that poke up into the air
it stores a bubble of air inside its trunk
it soaks up air dissolved in the seawater
it opens tiny mouths on its bark at night
context: The airless delta mud has almost no oxygen, so mangroves grow 'breathing roots' (pneumatophores) that poke straight up out of the mud. Tiny pores called lenticels on these snorkel-roots let the tree take in air at low tide. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundarbans ; britannica.com/place/Sundarbans

question: Twice a day the Bay of Bengal's tide floods into the Sundarbans, where the Ganges meets the sea between India and Bangladesh, and drains back out through some four hundred tidal rivers and creeks around about a hundred islands. What does that daily tide do to the land itself?
answer: it drowns about a third of the land
choices: it drowns about a third of the land
it pushes the islands out to sea
it carries the topsoil off to the ocean
it slowly turns the fresh water salty
context: The Sundarbans is a patchwork of about 102 islands laced by roughly 400 tidal rivers, creeks and canals. The tide averages about 2 m and can reach 5.7 m, and about one-third of the land vanishes and reappears every single day. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundarbans ; en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Sundarbans,_The

question: A super-cyclone drove a wall of seawater onto India's Odisha coast in 1999 and killed nearly ten thousand people. Researchers later went village by village, asking why some places lost far fewer lives than others, and found that one thing about a village's mangroves mattered most. What was it?
answer: how wide the mangrove belt was
choices: how wide the mangrove belt was
how tall the mangrove trees were
how old the mangrove forest was
how dense the mangrove roots were
context: The tangled root-wall blunts storm surges. In a rigorous study of the 1999 Odisha super-cyclone -- which killed nearly 10,000 people, more than 70% of them drowned by the surge -- the WIDTH of the mangrove belt between a village and the sea best predicted survival: villages behind wider mangroves lost far fewer lives, and researchers estimated 1.72 more deaths per village would have occurred if the mangroves had been stripped to zero (Das & Vincent, PNAS 2009). After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, coasts with mangroves also suffered less damage than bare coasts (Danielsen et al., Science 2005), though the trees could not stop the very worst zones, and the PNAS authors caution their cyclone result may not fully carry over to tsunamis. Sources: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0810440106 ; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16254180/

question: A big cat swims the tidal channels of the Sundarbans from island to island to hunt, and nowhere else on Earth does it prowl a mangrove forest, though mangroves grow on warm shores in Florida, across Indonesia and along West Africa. Which big cat is this?
context: The Sundarbans is the only mangrove forest on Earth where tigers live -- roughly 180-200 Royal Bengal tigers (estimates vary by census) that swim the tidal channels from island to island to hunt. No other tiger population lives in a mangrove; the tiger is the signature of this place. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundarbans ; whc.unesco.org/en/list/798/

question: Snow slides off the pointed crowns of a single unbroken belt of dark conifers that wraps almost all the way around the top of the world, across northern Canada, Sweden, Finland and Russia. It is the biggest land biome anywhere on Earth. What is this huge northern biome called?
context: The taiga, also called the boreal forest, forms one nearly unbroken ring of conifers across northern Canada, Scandinavia and Russia. It is the largest land biome on Earth -- by some reckonings only deserts and dry shrublands cover more ground overall, so the safe claim is 'largest land biome,' not 'largest biome of any kind.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiga.

question: From Alaska to the far side of Russia, the great northern ring of conifers stands through the long winter, each tree growing slowly in the short summers. Most people assume the world's trees crowd the warm tropics, yet a startling share stand here. Roughly what fraction of all Earth's trees grow in this northern forest?
context: The boreal forest holds roughly a third of all the trees on Earth -- about 27-33% of the world's total forest cover -- which makes it the single largest forest belt on the planet, even though each tree grows slowly in the short, cold summers. Sources: onetreeplanted.org; forest-healing.co.uk.

question: Each autumn the forests of Eastern Siberia blaze gold as their cone-bearing trees shed every last needle, then stand bare through winters near -60°C and grow a whole new coat in spring. Nearly every other conifer on Earth stays green right through winter. Which conifer is this?
context: The Eastern Siberian taiga is a vast forest of larch, a rare 'deciduous conifer' -- it bears cones like a pine but drops its needles each autumn, an adaptation that helps it endure winters colder than -60 C. The Dahurian larch is the most cold-hardy tree on Earth. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiga; conifers.org (Larix gmelinii).

question: Peat fills the bogs of the great northern forest across Canada and Russia, and it holds carbon, as do the forest's conifers and its cold soils. The steamy tropical rainforest is the store most people name first as the planet's greatest. Set against the tropical rainforests, how much carbon do this northern forest and its soils lock away?
answer: more than the tropical forests hold
choices: more than the tropical forests hold
the same as the tropical forests hold
half what the tropical forests hold
less than the tropical forests hold
context: It holds more. Because the cold slows rot to a crawl, the boreal forest's trees, soils and peat bogs store nearly twice as much carbon per unit area as tropical rainforests. The northern permafrost zone alone holds an estimated 1,460-1,600 billion tonnes of frozen organic carbon -- roughly twice as much as is in the entire atmosphere. Sources: nrdc.org; onetreeplanted.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiga.

question: Caravans crossed the Taklamakan, a huge desert of shifting dunes in western China, whose name is commonly read as a warning: 'go in, and you don't come out.' They gave it a second, darker nickname. What was it?
context: The name 'Taklamakan' is popularly read as a warning — 'go in and you don't come out' — and its killing dryness and shifting dunes earned it the grim nickname the 'Sea of Death.' (Scholars actually debate the true etymology: it may come from an Arabic phrase for 'abandoned place' or a Turkic one for 'place of ruins' — but the folk meaning is the memorable one.) Sources: Grokipedia 'Taklamakan Desert'; Wikipedia 'Taklamakan Desert.'  (Legend.)

question: Clouds drifting toward the Taklamakan lose their rain on icy peaks first, for tall mountain ranges wall the desert into a giant bowl on nearly every side. That keeps it one of Earth's driest places. Which range rises along the Taklamakan's northern edge?
