context: The Taklamakan lies in a bowl walled by some of the highest ranges on Earth — the Tian Shan ('Celestial Mountains') to the north, the Kunlun to the south, and the Pamir to the west, many peaks topping 5,000 m. Those walls block nearly all rain, trapping the desert in one of the planet's deepest rain shadows. Source: Grokipedia 'Taklamakan Desert.'

question: Along the Taklamakan's edges once stood busy Silk Road oasis towns like Loulan and Niya, full of houses, orchards, and written records. Then, one by one, they vanished from every map. Explorers found their remains only in modern times. What had become of these towns?
choices: A great flood swept them away.
context: The dunes move so relentlessly that whole Silk Road oasis cities were buried and lost. Loulan — the 'Oriental Pompeii' — was abandoned around 330 CE after the Lop Nur lake dried up, then rediscovered by chance in 1900 by Sven Hedin; Niya was uncovered in 1901 by Aurel Stein, who dug out about a hundred wooden tablets in Kharosthi script, left where they fell when the sand took the town. Sources: China Daily 'Exploring the lost land of Loulan'; Silk Road Foundation 'The Most Important Findings of Niya.'

question: Bodies buried nearly 4,000 years ago in the salt-dry sand of the Taklamakan still keep their skin, their reddish-fair hair and their woven wool clothes. The leggings of one, the Chärchän Man, bore a bold woven pattern that amazed archaeologists, for it closely matched the cloth of the ancient Celtic peoples of far-off Europe. What is that Celtic-style weave called?
context: The salty, rainless sand naturally mummified the dead. The 'Tarim mummies' are up to about 4,000 years old (oldest ~1800 BCE) yet keep their skin, blond-to-red hair, and finely woven wool. The 'Chärchän Man' wore a red twill tunic and tartan-plaid leggings whose checked weave strikingly resembles the ancient Celtic Hallstatt cloth of Europe — an eerie echo across thousands of miles (the resemblance is real and observed; what it means for their origins is a separate, debated question). Source: Wikipedia 'Tarim mummies.'  (Legend.)

question: Scientists sequenced the DNA of the oldest Tarim mummies in 2021, fair-haired dead from the sands of the Taklamakan, dressed in cloth that looked almost European. Their looks had set off a long argument: had these people wandered in from some faraway land, or had their ancestors always lived in this desert? What did the genome reveal them to be?
context: The mummies' Western-looking features made their origins one of archaeology's great puzzles. A 2021 genome study found the earliest Tarim people were NOT migrants from the west but a genetically isolated LOCAL population — about 72% Ancient North Eurasian ancestry, a relic of Ice-Age hunter-gatherers — overturning the older 'European wanderers' idea. The preservation and fine cloth are settled fact; deeper questions about their culture and language remain open research. Source: Wikipedia 'Tarim mummies' (2021 Nature genome study).

question: Chinese engineers drove a paved highway straight across hundreds of kilometres of live, shifting dunes to reach oilfields deep in the Taklamakan's heart, the longest road ever built over a moving-sand desert. The restless dunes kept creeping over it, threatening to bury it entirely. How did the engineers hold the sand back?
answer: They planted a living green belt along the road.
choices: They planted a living green belt along the road.
They paved a second road as a backup route.
They raised the road high on concrete stilts.
They lined both sides with tall steel walls.
context: The Tarim Desert Highway runs about 552 km, roughly 446 km of it over live shifting dunes — the world's longest road across a shifting-sand desert, built in 1993-1995 to reach oilfields in the basin's heart. To stop the marching dunes from burying it, engineers lined it with a living green shelterbelt about 436 km long, watered by more than 20,000 km of drip-irrigation pipe fed from salty groundwater and tended from well-houses every 4 km — over 20 million saplings. In 2024 China 'closed the loop,' finishing a roughly 3,050-km green belt that now rings the entire desert. Sources: Wikipedia 'Tarim Desert Highway'; Tianshannet; China Daily.

question: Poor immigrants in the dockside dance halls of two port cities gave the world the tango in the 1880s, and both cities still claim it: Buenos Aires in Argentina and Montevideo in Uruguay. They face each other across one huge river. Which river is it?
context: Both cities grew up on opposite banks of the Río de la Plata — the wide estuary where the Paraná and Uruguay rivers meet the Atlantic. Tango emerged in the poor port neighborhoods on both shores in the 1880s, so Argentina and Uruguay have argued ever since over who 'owns' it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tango' — originated in the 1880s along the Río de la Plata in the impoverished port areas of Argentina and Uruguay.

question: Young toughs called compadritos gathered in the rough dockside neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires in the late 1800s to practise a new dance, the tango. Women were scarce in those back streets. While the compadritos were still learning the hard steps, who did they mostly dance with?
context: The immigrant docklands had far more men than women, so young men practiced tango with each other — the dance almost a stylized mock duel between two rivals before either ever partnered a woman. Source: National Geographic, 'Sensual and scandalous: How tango took the world by storm'; Escuela de Tango de Buenos Aires — a severe shortage of women meant tango was often danced by two men, expressing symbolic combat.

question: German sailors carried a small button-and-bellows instrument to the docks of Buenos Aires and Montevideo around 1870. In the smoky dance halls above those docks, its deep, sobbing voice slowly became the very soul of tango. What is this instrument called?
context: The bandoneón — a square, button-covered relative of the accordion — gives tango its unmistakable mournful cry. German and Italian sailors and immigrants brought it to the Río de la Plata docks around 1870. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bandoneon' — brought to Argentina about 1870 by German and Italian emigrants and sailors.

question: Grey-haired milongueros, men who had danced tango in the smoky halls of Buenos Aires since they were boys, loved to boast that they could size up any partner from one single thing, the moment the music began and their arms first met. What was it?
context: Tango's defining feature is the abrazo, the close embrace danced chest to chest. From that first point of contact, the milongueros claimed to read a dancer's musicality, his respect, his whole character. Source: Tango Voice; Ultimate Tango School — the close-embrace (milonguero) style is danced chest-to-chest, and masters judged dancers by the embrace.

question: Heinrich Band built the first of tango's sobbing, button-covered instruments in Germany in the 1840s, for a humble purpose far from any dance hall. The instrument sounds so achingly Argentine that most people assume it was invented where tango was born. What was it originally made to do?
answer: replace the pipe organ in poor churches
choices: replace the pipe organ in poor churches
play music for village folk dances
teach schoolchildren to sing in tune
context: Heinrich Band, a German instrument dealer, designed and named the bandoneón as a cheap, portable stand-in for the pipe organ or harmonium in small churches that couldn't afford one. Only later did emigrants carry it to the docks, where it became tango's heart. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bandoneon' — created and named by Heinrich Band, designed to replace organs/harmoniums.

question: Carlos Gardel, the golden-voiced singer who turned tango into song, signed papers in 1920 swearing he was born in Tacuarembó, Uruguay, and both Uruguay and Argentina count him as a native son. His birth certificate, proved genuine in 2012, tells another story. Where was Gardel really born?
context: Gardel's true birthplace was a mystery he made himself. His French birth certificate — confirmed genuine in 2012 — records his birth in Toulouse, France, on 11 December 1890. Yet in 1920 he filed papers in Uruguay claiming he had been born in Tacuarembó, most likely to dodge French military registration — which is why Uruguayans and Argentines alike still claim him as their own. Source: Wikipedia, 'Carlos Gardel' — birth certificate confirmed Toulouse, France, 11 Dec 1890 (verified 2012); filed false Uruguayan papers in 1920 claiming Tacuarembó.

question: Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, a 20-year-old student in Montevideo, wrote a tango around 1917 that became the most famous in the world. When Roberto Firpo's band first played it at the Café La Giralda, the crowd made them play it six times in one night. What is this tango called?
context: 'La Cumparsita' premiered on 19 April 1917 at the Café La Giralda in Montevideo, played by Roberto Firpo's orchestra — and it was such a hit it was encored six times that night. Its young composer went on to become an architect. Source: revistapanorama.com, 'One Hundred Years of La Cumparsita'; notihoteles.com (Confitería La Giralda).

question: Dancers at a milonga in Buenos Aires invite partners from clear across the crowded hall without speaking a word: a locked gaze, then a tiny nod. Holding the gaze means yes; looking away is a gentle no, so no one is ever publicly refused. What is this silent custom called?
context: The cabeceo (from cabeza, 'head') uses a shared glance — the mirada — then a small nod to invite a partner, sparing anyone the embarrassment of a public refusal. Source: Wikipedia, 'Milonga (dance event)' — the cabeceo uses mutual eye contact, a mirada then a nod, to invite partners and minimize embarrassment.

question: Ástor Piazzolla began fusing traditional tango with jazz and classical music in the 1950s, into a startling sound all his own. Argentine purists raged, and some threatened his life, swearing his creation was not tango at all. What did Piazzolla name the movement he founded?
context: Ástor Piazzolla called his style 'nuevo tango,' fusing jazz and classical music with the traditional form and outraging purists who swore it wasn't tango at all. His works include 'Libertango' (1974) and 'Adiós Nonino,' which he wrote in under an hour after learning his father had died. In Paris his teacher Nadia Boulanger urged him to stop imitating the Europeans and write tango. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ástor Piazzolla' — created nuevo tango blending jazz and classical, a controversial figure rejected by traditionalists.

question: Buenos Aires and Montevideo argued for more than a century over which city really gave the world tango. In 2009 the United Nations cultural agency (UNESCO) added the dance to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage. How did the honour fall between the rival nations of Argentina and Uruguay?
answer: jointly, as one shared listing for both nations
choices: jointly, as one shared listing for both nations
solely under Argentina, the larger nation
solely under Uruguay, its true birthplace
as two rival entries, one from each nation
context: Argentina and Uruguay submitted tango together, and UNESCO inscribed it in 2009 as a single shared treasure of both nations — a rare joint listing that finally split the honor evenly between Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 'Tango' (ich.unesco.org/en/RL/tango-00258) — inscribed 2009, jointly submitted by Argentina and Uruguay.

question: Farmers led by Yang Zhifa broke by accident into the buried army of the First Emperor near Mount Li, in central China, in the spring of 1974. They were not scientists, and they were busy with an ordinary chore when they hit the first clay soldier. What were they doing?
answer: digging a well for water during a drought
choices: digging a well for water during a drought
plowing a new field for planting
quarrying stone to build a house
fishing along the banks of a river
context: On March 29, 1974, farmers led by Yang Zhifa were digging a well during a drought in Xiyang Village near Mount Li, outside Xi'an, when they hit the head of a terracotta soldier about a meter down and broke into a pit holding thousands more. The archaeologist Zhao Kangmin was called in and painstakingly reassembled the first warriors from fragments, some as small as a fingernail. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army

question: Archaeologists mapping the pits beside the First Emperor's tomb near Xi'an found more than an honour guard: a whole army in battle order, standing rank on rank in the underground rooms. About how many life-size clay warriors are buried there?
context: More than 8,000 life-size warriors stand in the pits, alongside about 130 wooden chariots, 520 chariot horses, and 150 cavalry horses rendered in terracotta -- an entire buried army drawn up for battle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: Qin Shi Huang, China's First Emperor, had life-size clay soldiers buried in battle formation beside his tomb near Mount Li, in Shaanxi province, more than 2,200 years ago: the Terracotta Army. Why would a dead ruler want a whole army sealed in the ground with him?
answer: to guard the emperor forever in the afterlife
choices: to guard the emperor forever in the afterlife
to carry his spirit up to the heavens
to serve as his laborers in the next world
to replace the live soldiers once buried with kings
context: The clay army was built to protect Qin Shi Huang -- who unified the warring states as China's first emperor in 221 BCE -- in the afterlife, an eternal bodyguard meant to keep him safe forever. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army

question: Compared side by side, the life-size clay warriors guarding Qin Shi Huang's tomb near Xi'an showed archaeologists something almost no other ancient army of statues has. What did they find about the warriors' faces?
answer: each one has a different face
choices: each one has a different face
each one wears the same stern face
each one has no face at all
each one has the emperor's face
context: No two warriors share a face. Sculptors began from roughly ten base facial forms and then modified each by hand -- adding hair, ears, mustaches, and expressions -- so the army looks like a crowd of thousands of distinct, real men. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: Scholars studying freshly dug warriors of the Terracotta Army near Xi'an found faint traces that the army once looked very different from the plain grey baked clay visitors see today. How did the warriors first appear when they were placed in the pits?
choices: covered head to toe in gold leaf
polished to a glossy black shine
context: The warriors were once brightly painted, including with a synthetic pigment scientists call 'Chinese purple' (barium copper silicate) that the Qin craftsmen manufactured. Exposed paint on newly dug figures can curl and flake within minutes of hitting the air, so most now look like bare clay. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: The clay soldiers in the pits by the First Emperor's tomb near Xi'an held real bronze weapons, and diggers have recovered over 40,000 arrowheads, spears and swords. Several bronze swords came out of the ground more than 2,000 years after burial. What did the diggers discover about those blades?
answer: they were still sharp enough to cut
choices: they were still sharp enough to cut
they were plated in thin silver
they were etched with battle maps
they were snapped into short pieces
context: Over 40,000 bronze arrowheads, swords, spears, and crossbow triggers have been recovered. Some swords came out still sharp after 2,000 years underground, and several are inscribed with dates between 245 and 228 BCE. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army

question: Sima Qian wrote that the First Emperor's sealed tomb near Mount Li held a model of his whole realm, its hundred rivers and seas recreated in miniature beneath a ceiling of painted stars and constellations. Many scholars long took this for a tall tale. Then, in 2020, scientists measured the air over the tomb mound with a laser. What did they detect there at strangely high levels?
context: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (c. 94 BCE) described rivers of flowing mercury, long dismissed as myth. In a 2020 study, scientists aimed a laser radar (lidar) at the air over the mound and measured mercury up to about 27 ng/m3, several times the local background of 5-10 ng/m3 -- physical corroboration of the 2,000-year-old account. Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-67305-x

question: Sima Qian, the historian who wrote of the First Emperor about a century after his death, said the tomb near Mount Li, in China, was built to defend itself. He recorded a hidden mechanism set inside the burial chamber, ready to strike on its own at any robber who broke in. What did he say lay waiting for intruders?
context: Sima Qian recorded that the tomb was rigged with automatic crossbows set to fire at anyone who broke in -- an ancient booby trap guarding the First Emperor's body. Whether any such mechanism survives is unknown, since no one has entered the chamber to check. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army  (Legend.)

question: Some 700,000 conscripted workers toiled on the First Emperor's mausoleum near Mount Li, in central China, for roughly 38 years, Sima Qian says, in one of the largest building projects of the ancient world. Work began the very year its owner took the throne of the Qin state. How old was the future First Emperor when construction started?
context: Construction began in 246 BCE, when the future emperor was only about 13, and continued for roughly 38 years. Sima Qian recorded around 700,000 conscripted workers on the mausoleum. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army

question: Millions of visitors come to see the warriors of the Terracotta Army near Xi'an, where archaeologists have dug in the pits for fifty years. They treat the burial chamber of the First Emperor himself, under the grassy pyramid mound at the centre, in a very different way. What is the status of that central chamber today?
choices: it was looted in ancient times
it was moved to a museum
context: Archaeologists deliberately leave the chamber sealed -- partly because exposed paint on excavated figures has flaked within minutes of hitting the air, and partly because of the mercury detected in the mound. What lies inside the First Emperor's tomb remains unseen. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/emperor-qin

question: The warriors of Pit 1, near the First Emperor's tomb outside Xi'an, stand in tight battle ranks, every row facing the exact same direction and gazing out toward the horizon. The emperor had them lined up this way on purpose. Which way does his whole army look?
context: The pits sit about 1.5 km east of the tomb mound, and the warriors face east -- toward the rival warring states the First Emperor had conquered and the direction his old enemies had once come from -- set as an eternal vanguard. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Terracotta_Army

question: Lev Termen, a young scientist in Soviet Russia, showed off a new electronic instrument in 1920. A player waved his hands between its two metal antennas without touching it, drawing out a spooky, wavering wail that later haunted horror and flying-saucer films. What was Termen's invention called?
context: Lev Termen — known in the West as Leon Theremin — invented it in Russia in October 1920, the first musical instrument you play without ever touching it. One critic described its voice as 'a cello lost in a dense fog, crying because it does not know how to get home.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin

question: Visitors at Iceland's Thingvellir walk down into the Almannagjá gorge, whose tall western cliff marks the end of the North American plate. The Eurasian plate's edge rises on the far side of the sunken valley floor. What type of plate boundary runs through here?
context: The North American and Eurasian plates drift apart about 2 cm a year in all, and over the 10,000 years since lava flowed at Thingvellir the valley floor between the Almannagjá and Hrafnagjá faults has widened roughly 70 m and sunk some 40 m. This is a DIVERGENT boundary, one of the few places where the seam between two great plates lies open on dry land. Sources: thingvellir.is/en/education/nature/tectonic-movements ; grokipedia.com/page/Þingvellir

question: A deep ocean trench plunges thousands of metres just off South America's Pacific coast, and behind it the snow-capped volcanoes of the Andes run down the continent's spine. Two tectonic plates meet here, one slowly sliding down beneath the other. What type of plate boundary makes a coast like this?
context: Where the Nazca plate dives under the South American plate at the Peru-Chile Trench, melting rock feeds the Andes' volcanoes and lifts its great peaks. One plate diving beneath another is a CONVERGENT (subduction) boundary. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes)

question: Far from Asia, where Earth's ten tallest mountains all rise in the Himalaya and Karakoram, the long spine of the Andes on the border of Argentina and Chile lifts one peak higher than any other outside Asia. It stands 6,961 metres above the sea. What is this South American mountain called?
context: Aconcagua, in Argentina's Andes, reaches 6,961 m -- the highest summit outside Asia, and the tallest in both the Americas and the Southern Hemisphere. The Andes themselves run about 8,900 km, the longest continental mountain range on Earth. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes)

question: Fences, roads and dry creek beds that cross California's San Andreas Fault have been jogged sideways out of line. The fault runs some 750 miles up the state, and every so often the ground along it lurches free in a sudden earthquake. What type of plate boundary is the San Andreas?
context: Along a TRANSFORM boundary the plates neither build new crust nor swallow old -- they just grind sideways. The San Andreas runs about 750 miles through California; a slip on its northern reach caused the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault)

question: Earth's continents and ocean floors ride on a rocky shell broken into some seven or eight great slabs and about fifteen smaller ones. One of them dwarfs the rest, spanning some 103 million square kilometres, larger than any continent. Which is Earth's largest tectonic plate?
context: The Pacific plate covers about 103 million km2, flooring most of the Pacific Ocean -- the biggest of the roughly 7-8 major plates (plus about 15 minor ones) that tile the planet. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Plate)

question: A lifeguard on a California beach watches the Pacific climb slowly up the sand and slide back out twice a day, like the sea taking two long breaths. What does most of the pulling that lifts the tides?
context: The Moon's gravity is the true master of the sea — its tide-raising pull is more than twice the Sun's (the Sun adds only about 46% as much). Twice a day the whole ocean answers the Moon and rises. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Far out in the open ocean the tide lifts the sea only about half a metre, a swell so gentle that a passing ship never feels it. Yet twice a day the same tide rears up about 16 metres inside Canada's Bay of Fundy. What turns that gentle swell into such a giant?
answer: the funnel shape of the bay, stacking the water higher
choices: the funnel shape of the bay, stacking the water higher
the Moon pulling harder directly over Canada
cold northern seawater piling up denser and taller
the great depth of the bay multiplying the pull
context: Tides are born tiny in the open sea — the Moon lifts it only about 54 cm — and grow into giants only where the shape of the coastline funnels and stacks them. Fundy's tapering funnel is the world champion. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: At Mont-Saint-Michel, the island abbey off the coast of Normandy in France, the tide can sweep across the flat sands very fast. An old warning, often credited to Victor Hugo, matches its speed to one alarming thing. What is it?
context: The saying — often credited to Victor Hugo — is that the sea comes in 'as swiftly as a galloping horse.' Treat it as vivid lore, not a measured speed; the real danger at Mont-Saint-Michel (tidal range about 14 m) is fast-rising water and quicksand that can strand walkers on the flats. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mont-Saint-Michel; thegoodlifefrance.com.  (Legend.)

question: The sea comes up to high tide twice a day on the Bay of Fundy, as on most coasts of the world, about twelve hours apart, and the Moon's pull makes that rhythm. What does the Moon raise on Earth to give two high tides each day instead of one?
answer: a bulge of water on both the near and far sides at once
choices: a bulge of water on both the near and far sides at once
a single bulge the spinning Earth sweeps past twice
a bulge that sloshes back and forth across the ocean
a ring of raised water circling the whole equator
context: The Moon pulls hardest on the ocean facing it, raising a near-side bulge, and least on the far-side water, which is 'left behind' as a second bulge. Earth turns through both each day, so most coasts get two high tides. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Tide-watchers on the Bay of Fundy plan around the spring tides, the highest of each month, when the sea climbs farthest up the shore. The name has nothing to do with the season, for they come in December as surely as in May. When in the Moon's cycle do they arrive?
answer: at the new Moon and the full Moon
choices: at the new Moon and the full Moon
at the first and last quarter Moons
when the Moon swings farthest from Earth
when the Moon crosses over the equator
context: Spring tides come twice a month, at the new and full Moon, when the Sun and the Moon fall into a straight line and their pulls add together. 'Spring' means springing up, the tide leaping to its peak, not the season. When the Moon swings farthest from Earth its pull, and with it the tide, is in fact a little weaker. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Burntcoat Head, in Nova Scotia on the Bay of Fundy, saw the sea surge to 21.6 metres in October 1869, far above the bay's everyday tides of about 16 metres, and no tide there has topped it since. What extra force heaped those final metres onto an already-towering tide?
answer: a violent windstorm driving a surge ashore
choices: a violent windstorm driving a surge ashore
a sudden snowmelt flood pouring down the rivers
the wave from an offshore undersea earthquake
a heavy, days-long downpour swelling the bay
context: The record came during the Saxby Gale of October 1869: fierce winds and abnormally low pressure drove a storm surge on top of a tide already running unusually high. Burntcoat Head's routine maximum is about 17 m — the 21.6 m mark was a storm-amplified one-off, not the everyday tide. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burntcoat_Head,_Nova_Scotia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1869_Saxby_Gale.

question: On the estuary of the Rance river, in Brittany on the northwest coast of France, engineers opened a landmark power station in 1966. President Charles de Gaulle himself came to inaugurate it. For the next 45 years no rival of its kind grew any larger anywhere in the world. What was this station the first in the world to do?
answer: turn the ocean's tides into electricity
choices: turn the ocean's tides into electricity
turn the ocean's waves into electricity
turn the ocean's heat into electricity
turn the ocean's currents into electricity
context: It was the Rance Tidal Power Station — the world's first tidal power plant, using 24 bulb turbines to harness the estuary's roughly 8 m (up to 13.5 m) tide. It stayed the largest tidal station on Earth for 45 years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rance_Tidal_Power_Station.

question: Twice a month even Canada's Bay of Fundy runs slack. For a few days its famous tides shrink, and the sea barely creeps up the shore and back again. Tide tables mark these feeble tides as neap tides. What robs the tides of their strength then?
answer: the Sun and Moon pull at right angles
choices: the Sun and Moon pull at right angles
the Sun and Moon pull from opposite sides
the Moon is new and hidden from sight
the Moon passes through Earth's shadow
context: At the first and last quarter Moons, about a week after the spring tides, the Sun pulls at right angles to the Moon, so the two partly cancel and the tides run slack. 'Neap' comes from an old Anglo-Saxon word read as something like 'without the power'. When the Sun and Moon line up instead, on the same side of Earth at new Moon or on opposite sides at full Moon, their pulls add up into the towering spring tides. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide.

question: Canada's Bay of Fundy, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, narrows like a long funnel, and its tides climb some 16 metres, as high as any on the planet. Many other bays are funnels too. What lucky coincidence makes Fundy a champion rather than one more funnel?
answer: its natural sloshing rhythm matches the tide's own beat
choices: its natural sloshing rhythm matches the tide's own beat
it faces straight into the Atlantic's fastest current
its rivers pour in more fresh water than any other bay
it lies at the one latitude where the tides peak
context: This lucky match is called tidal resonance: the water of the bay and the Gulf of Maine naturally sloshes from end to end in roughly 13 hours, close to the tide's own rhythm of about twelve and a half, so each tide pushes at just the right moment, like timing shoves on a swing, building the water ever higher. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy; Garrett (1972), 'Tidal resonance in the Bay of Fundy and Gulf of Maine', Nature.

question: Ship after ship leaving Europe rode one steady wind across the tropical Atlantic for five centuries: a broad belt of warm air blowing out of the northeast, day after day, that pushed them west to the Americas. What are these winds called?
context: In the Northern Hemisphere the trade winds blow from the northeast; in the Southern, from the southeast, both curving toward the equator. This same reliable highway of wind carried immense wealth and the great Columbian exchange of crops, animals, and ideas between continents, and it also carried European colonization of the Americas and the ships of the transatlantic slave trade. The wind was neutral; what sailed on it was not. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trade winds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds).

question: The trade winds carried England's merchant ships across the tropical Atlantic for centuries, so most people assume the name comes from commerce and cargo. But this 'trade' is older than the money meaning: sailors said 'the wind blows trade' long before. What did 'trade' mean to them?
context: 'Trade' here comes from a 14th-century sense meaning a track, course, or direction, from the nautical phrase 'to blow trade' (to blow steadily one way). Only later, because these winds were so vital to England's merchant fleet crossing the Atlantic, did the money-meaning of 'trade' attach itself and stick. An etymology twist: the name is older than the commerce it came to serve. Source: Wikipedia, 'Trade winds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds); Wiktionary, 'trade wind' (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/trade_wind).

question: Columbus let the northeast wind push him due west from the Canary Islands to the Americas in 1492. Sailing home on that wind would only have shoved him farther west, so he climbed north into cooler middle latitudes to catch a belt of wind blowing back toward Europe. What are these homeward winds called?
context: Columbus began his return on 16 January 1493, looping north to ride the westerlies home. The outbound trades and the homebound westerlies together form a great clockwise wheel of wind across the North Atlantic, the gyre that made round-trip sailing possible. Source: Wikipedia, 'Voyages of Christopher Columbus' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus).

question: Right at the equator, the trade winds of the two hemispheres meet head-on, cancel each other out and rise straight up. They leave behind a belt of dead, breathless calm, where a sailing ship, with wind as its only engine, could sit trapped for weeks. What did sailors call this dreaded belt?
context: Scientists call this belt the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ); 18th-century sailors named it the 'doldrums' for its stagnant, spirit-sapping calm. The doldrums sit under the rising branch of the great tropical loop, right where the air is going straight up instead of blowing sideways, so there is almost no surface wind. Do not confuse it with the horse latitudes, the separate calm belts near 30 degrees where ships were also becalmed, or with the 'calms of Capricorn,' a becalmed belt near 30 degrees south. Source: Wikipedia, 'Intertropical Convergence Zone' (18th-century sailors called it the doldrums; ships becalmed for days or weeks). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertropical_Convergence_Zone

question: Spanish treasure ships crossed the whole Pacific for 250 years, from 1565 to 1815, hauling Mexican silver one way and Asian silk and porcelain the other. They rode the trade winds outward and the warm Kuroshio current home, linking a Spanish port in the Philippines to Acapulco on Mexico's coast. What was this great Pacific crossing called?
context: The Manila galleons ran for 250 years (1565-1815), an early engine of globalization pouring American silver into Asia and Asian silk into the Americas and Europe. It was also a lifeline of Spanish colonial trade, and it ended as Mexico moved toward independence. Source: Wikipedia, 'Manila galleon' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_galleon).

question: A Portuguese caravel working back up the west coast of Africa met a maddening trap: the coastal winds and currents ran steadily against it, so a straight run home was hopeless. Its captain's escape was to sail the wrong way first, far out into the open ocean toward Brazil, and only out there swing around for a homeward wind. What did the Portuguese call this looping detour?
context: 'Volta do mar' means 'turn of the sea.' Its Pacific cousin, the tornaviaje, was cracked by the friar Andres de Urdaneta in 1565. Historians hold that Europe's sea empires could not have arisen without this wind-gyre trick; a 13th-century Genoese expedition, the Vivaldi brothers, sailed south past the Canaries and likely perished, unable to beat back upwind for want of it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Volta do mar' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_do_mar).

question: Crossing the North Atlantic toward the Caribbean, the trade winds slant in from the northeast, while their southern twins come from the southeast. Yet air drawn toward the low pressure on the equator ought to blow straight at it. Hadley guessed that Earth's spin bends the wind, but the bending bears the name of the French scientist who found the true rule in 1835. What is it called?
context: The Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, giving equator-bound wind its westward push: it is why the trade winds slant, from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and the southeast in the Southern, and why hurricanes spin. If the Earth ever stopped spinning, the slant would vanish and the winds would blow straight toward the equator. Hadley had the right instinct (Earth's rotation bends the winds) but used conservation of velocity instead of angular momentum; Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis supplied the correct mathematics in 1835. Source: Wikipedia, 'Coriolis force' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriolis_force); 'Trade winds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_winds); 'George Hadley' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Hadley).

question: A traveller on Bali can see across the Lombok Strait, which is barely 35 kilometres wide, to the island of Lombok. Yet on the far shore the wild animals change completely, as if the strait divided two continents. What is this sharp wildlife border called?
context: Cross the Lombok Strait and Asia's tigers and monkeys give way to Australia's marsupials and cockatoos. The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace mapped this frontier in 1859; Thomas Henry Huxley named it 'Wallace's Line' in 1868, and it is also called the Wallace Line. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Line; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombok_Strait

question: The animals of Bali and Lombok never mixed across the narrow strait between them, though in the ice ages the seas fell about 120 metres and dry land linked island to island across the region. Why did that one gap never close into dry land?
answer: its channel is far deeper than the seas ever fell
choices: its channel is far deeper than the seas ever fell
the seas there never dropped as far as elsewhere
a swift current kept sweeping the sand away
its seabed kept sinking as fast as the seas fell
context: The Lombok Strait plunges to at least 250 metres — more than twice the ice-age sea drop — so its floor never surfaced as land. Everywhere else the falling seas welded islands into two giant landmasses; only across deep gaps like this one did the divide hold. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Line; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombok_Strait

question: Shallow sea, rarely deeper than 50 metres, laps around Bali, Java, Sumatra and Borneo, for all four rest on one wide underwater shelf. When the ice-age seas fell, that shelf became dry land and joined the islands into one big peninsula. Which shelf do these western islands sit on?
context: This is the Sunda Shelf, welded to the Asian mainland. At ice-age low sea it formed 'Sundaland,' a peninsula of Asia spanning roughly 1.85 million square kilometres, where water rarely exceeds 50 metres deep. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunda_Shelf

question: A person could once have walked on dry ground from Australia to New Guinea, across a wide, shallow seabed south of the equator that the last ice age laid bare when the seas fell about 120 metres. Which shallow shelf joined Australia and New Guinea into one landmass?
context: This is the Sahul Shelf, the Australian continental shelf. At low sea it formed the landmass 'Sahul,' joined to New Guinea across the Arafura Shelf; ancient drowned shorelines here now lie 100-140 metres below today's sea. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahul_Shelf

question: Deep water rings Sulawesi, Flores, Timor, Lombok and their neighbours on every side, between the shallow shelves of Asia and Australia, so they were never joined to either continent. Their wildlife is a strange half-and-half mix of the two. What do naturalists call this in-between zone?
context: This is Wallacea — about 347,000 square kilometres of islands, Sulawesi the largest — ringed by deep-water straits on every side, so its life is a blend of Asian and Australian types found nowhere else. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallacea

question: Asian and Australian wildlife blend across the islands that lie between Asia's shallow shelf and Australia's, and one boundary was not enough, so mapmakers drew others. One, drawn in 1896, runs along the eastern rim of that blend zone, pressed tight against the Australian shelf. What is this eastern line called?
context: Richard Lydekker drew this line in 1896 along the edge of the Sahul Shelf, marking the eastern rim of Wallacea. Between it and Wallace's Line runs Weber's Line, the balance point where Asian and Australian life meet in equal measure. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydekker%27s_Line; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weber%27s_Line

question: Far north of Bali, a second great gap in the border between Asian and Australian wildlife splits the huge islands of Borneo and Sulawesi. It is vast, 130 to 370 kilometres across, ten times wider than the narrow strait at Bali, and about 2,500 metres deep, yet the wildlife on its two shores differs just as sharply. What is this wide, deep gap called?
context: This is the Makassar Strait, between Borneo and Sulawesi — 130 to 370 km across, far wider than the 35 km Lombok Strait, yet plunging to about 2,500 m in its northern basin. That proves the Wallace Line's real barrier is deep water, not mere distance. Source: britannica.com/place/Makassar-Strait

question: A swirling new couple-dance, the waltz, swept into the grand ballrooms of Vienna in the early 1800s. Newspapers called it a shocking foreign dance and printed page after page of angry complaints. Of all the things critics fussed about, what did they call the real scandal?
answer: The man held the woman close, face-to-face, his hand at her waist
choices: The man held the woman close, face-to-face, his hand at her waist
Unmarried couples danced together with no chaperone between them
The women bared their arms and shoulders in daring ball gowns
Couples broke off to dance as pairs instead of in group sets
context: Earlier ballroom dances kept couples apart in group formations; the waltz's closed hold - man and woman face-to-face, his hand at her waist, turning together - was the shocking part. In July 1816 The Times of London denounced it as an 'indecent foreign dance,' warning of 'the voluptuous intertwining of the limbs.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz

question: Peasants in the farming villages of Austria and Bavaria stomped through a rough folk dance in a lilting three-beat time, and the elegant Viennese waltz grew out of it once it was cleaned up for the city. What was this peasant dance called?
context: The Ländler was a stomping Austrian and Bavarian peasant dance in 3/4 time; sped up and refined, it became the ballroom waltz. (Modern scholars increasingly treat the two as parallel 'sibling' dances rather than strict ancestor and descendant.) Source: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/stories/11-facts-viennese-waltz/

question: Dancers in Austria and southern Germany were already whirling through the waltz when the word first turned up in print, in 1748, in a single official document. The name comes from 'walzen', a German verb meaning to roll or turn. What sort of document gave 'waltz' its written debut?
context: 'Waltz' comes from the German 'walzen,' to roll, turn, or revolve - for the dance's rolling rotation. The word first appears in print in 1748, in the text of a dance ban. Source: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/stories/11-facts-viennese-waltz/

question: Franz Joseph, the Habsburg emperor, put Johann Strauss the Younger, Vienna's famous waltz composer and the writer of more than 500 dance pieces, on his payroll in 1863, with an official salaried post inside the Austrian imperial household. What court title did Strauss hold?
answer: Music Director of the Royal Court Balls
choices: Music Director of the Royal Court Balls
Music Director of the Imperial Court Opera
Music Director of the Court Chapel Choir
Music Director of the Emperor's Chamber
context: Johann Strauss II (1825-1899) wrote over 500 dance pieces, hundreds of them waltzes, and in 1863 was named KK Hofballmusikdirektor - Music Director of the Royal Court Balls. His father, Johann Strauss I, had forbidden a musical career, wanting the boy to become a banker. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Strauss_II

question: Johann Strauss the Younger wrote a waltz in 1866 that became Vienna's unofficial anthem, the tune the city reaches for whenever it wants to feel most itself: 'By the Beautiful Blue ___'. He named it for the broad river that curls through the heart of Vienna. Which river fills the blank?
context: 'By the Beautiful Blue Danube' (An der schönen blauen Donau), composed 1866 and premiered in 1867, became Vienna's unofficial anthem. It began as a choral piece with satirical lyrics and only a mild success; the orchestral version at the 1867 Paris World's Fair made it a triumph. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blue_Danube

question: Europe's monarchs and diplomats gathered at the Congress of Vienna in 1814 and 1815 to redraw the continent's map after Napoleon's fall. Months passed with little settled, and Prince Charles-Joseph de Ligne mocked that the Congress 'does not advance.' What had swallowed up the delegates' time and energy in the host city?
answer: an endless whirl of balls and dancing
choices: an endless whirl of balls and dancing
secret treaties argued in back rooms
long state banquets and royal hunts
context: At the Congress of Vienna (Sept 1814 - June 1815), the balls so filled the diplomacy that Prince Charles-Joseph de Ligne quipped 'Le congrès danse beaucoup, mais il ne marche pas' - 'the Congress dances a lot, but does not advance.' Source: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Congress_of_Vienna

question: Desert covers almost all of Egypt, yet one great river crosses it to the Mediterranean. Each summer, long ago, its flood spread fresh, rich mud over the dry fields and fed the farms of ancient Egypt for thousands of years. Which river is it?
context: The Nile flows about 6,650 km from the highlands of central Africa north to the Mediterranean — long enough to rival the Amazon for the title of the world's longest river. Its yearly summer flood laid down fresh black silt (the Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'the black land'), letting farms flourish in a desert. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile

question: Asia's longest river tumbles down from high in western China and runs about 6,300 km east to the Pacific, slicing a chain of dramatic gorges through steep cliffs on the way. Which river is it?
context: The Yangtze runs about 6,300 km entirely within China — Asia's longest river and the third-longest on Earth. Where it carves the Three Gorges through Mount Wushan, engineers built the Three Gorges Dam, the largest hydro-electric power station in the world. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze

question: One European river winds from Germany's Black Forest all the way to the shores of the Black Sea, flowing through or along the borders of ten countries, more than any other river on Earth. Which river is it?
context: The Danube touches ten countries — Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova, and Ukraine — more than any other river on Earth. Europe's second-longest river (about 2,850 km, after the Volga), it is also the only river to flow past four national capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube

question: Boats on the Yangtze sail east from the old walled town of Baidicheng into a squeeze of cliff walls hundreds of metres tall. For nearly 200 miles the river runs between them, until it opens out at Yichang. What is this famous run of three canyons called?
context: The Three Gorges — Qutang, Wu, and Xiling — run about 193 miles (311 km) down the Yangtze from Baidicheng in Chongqing to Yichang in Hubei. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges

question: Travellers on the Yangtze in central China pass through three famous canyons, and one is loved above the rest: a 45-kilometre stretch of steep cliffs and twelve famous peaks, crowned by a legendary spire called Fairy Peak. Which gorge is this most beautiful one?
context: Of the three gorges, Qutang is the shortest (just 8 km) and Xiling the longest (66 km), but Wu Gorge (45 km) is the most celebrated, famed for its Fairy Peak and its row of twelve peaks. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges

question: Near the city of Yichang in central China, a colossal wall of concrete blocks the Yangtze River. It stands 185 metres tall and stretches more than 2 km wide. Its 32 huge turbines generate more electric power than any other single power station on Earth. What is this record-breaking dam called?
context: Built at Sandouping near Yichang and completed in 2012, the Three Gorges Dam is the largest hydroelectric power station on the planet — 22,500 MW from 32 main 700-MW generators, making over 100 terawatt-hours of electricity a year. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges_Dam

question: Behind the great dam across the Yangtze near Yichang lies a lake 600 kilometres long, 40 billion tonnes of water lifted high above the old riverbed. Benjamin Fong Chao, a NASA geophysicist, calculated in 2005 that it has a tiny but real effect on the whole planet. What has the raised water done to Earth?
answer: slowed its spin, lengthening the day
choices: slowed its spin, lengthening the day
sped up its spin, shortening the day
context: In 2005, NASA geophysicist Benjamin Fong Chao and colleague Richard Gross calculated that raising about 40 billion cubic metres of water so high shifts enough of Earth's mass to lengthen the day by roughly 0.06 microseconds — 60 billionths of a second, far too small to feel. Source: https://www.sciencefocus.com/news/human-structures-slowing-earths-spin

question: Rising water behind the great dam near Yichang drowned whole towns and farmland up and down the Yangtze valley, ancestral homes lost for good beneath the reservoir. Clearing the flood zone in time meant resettling not a village or two but a major city's worth of people. Roughly how many were forced from their homes?
context: Filling the reservoir forced about 1.3 million people from their homes to clear the valley before the water rose. Planning documents projected that 13 cities, 140 towns, and 1,350 villages would be partly or wholly flooded. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges_Dam

question: The great dam across the Yangtze near Yichang lifts 40 billion tonnes of water into a long reservoir high above the old riverbed, and that shifts Earth's spin very slightly. Scientists explain the effect with a spinning figure skater, who can change her speed just by moving her arms. What does the skater do with her arms to slow down?
context: It is the moment of inertia: moving mass farther from the spin axis makes a turning body rotate slower, so the raised reservoir slows Earth just as a skater slows by spreading her arms. For scale, the natural 2004 magnitude-9.0 Indian Ocean earthquake shortened the day about 2.68 microseconds — dozens of times more than the dam. Source: https://www.sciencefocus.com/news/human-structures-slowing-earths-spin

question: Li Bai, the Tang poet, shot downstream through the Yangtze's gorges in a small boat, past cliffs that travellers carved with verse. In one immortal line he caught a sound that followed him, echoing endlessly from both banks as ten thousand mountains flew past. In Li Bai's line, what was making that sound?
context: Li Bai wrote, 'While monkeys keep howling at both sides of the river, the boat has swiftly passed thousands of mountains.' Poets had carved verse into these cliffs since the Northern Wei dynasty, over 1,500 years ago — much of it now drowned beneath the reservoir. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Gorges

question: The Yangtze empties into the sea beside Shanghai, yet some 6,000 kilometres inland its very first trickle is glacier melt seeping from the ice atop Geladaindong Peak, a 6,621-metre summit of the Tanggula Mountains. On which vast highland is the Yangtze born?
context: The Yangtze is born from glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau, the 'roof of the world.' Its traditional source is the ice atop 6,621-metre Geladaindong Peak, which feeds the Tuotuo headwater stream at the start of the river's 6,236-km journey east to the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geladaindong_Peak

question: A mighty river 5,464 kilometres long flows across northern China, its water a strange yellow-brown all the way from the mountains to the sea, and the colour gave the Yellow River its name. What actually turns the water yellow-brown as it flows?
answer: fine mud it carries in the water
choices: fine mud it carries in the water
golden algae blooming on the surface
context: The color comes from fine sediment: as the river cuts through soft, pale highland soil it picks up enormous amounts of suspended silt, and that mud tints the water yellow-brown for nearly its whole length. (Wikipedia, 'Yellow River')

question: The Yellow River saws through a vast upland in its middle course, soft, pale earth piled more than 90 metres deep in places and so loose that summer rains wash it into the water by the ton. What upland is this?
context: That wind-blown dust is called loess — fine grit that winds carried off deserts like the Gobi and piled over roughly 2.6 million years into the Loess Plateau, 50–80 m thick on average and over 90 m in places. More than 90% of the river's silt is stripped from this one region as it slices through. (Britannica, 'Loess Plateau')

question: The Yellow River runs right past the old capital of Kaifeng in Henan, where families have farmed and traded along its banks for 2,000 years. Yet a visitor who climbs the city wall and looks toward the water gets a shock. Why?
answer: the river flows higher than the city's rooftops
choices: the river flows higher than the city's rooftops
the river plunges over a waterfall taller than the wall
the river splits into dozens of braided channels here
the river disappears into a canyon below the city
context: Two thousand years of silt piling up in the channel forced people to wall the Yellow River in with levees built ever higher, until at Kaifeng its bed climbed about 10 m (33 ft) above the streets — some surveys say 13–14 m — held in only by those man-made banks. Geographers call such a channel a 'suspended,' 'above-ground,' or 'hanging' river: it literally flows overhead behind its levees. (Wikipedia, 'Yellow River'; MDPI Sustainability 2019)

question: Farming families along the middle Yellow River, in northern China, lived for many hundreds of years on an upland of soft, pale soil, tens of metres deep and very easy to dig, and built their homes there in a very unusual way. How did they typically make their homes?
answer: by carving cave-rooms straight into the cliffs
choices: by carving cave-rooms straight into the cliffs
by weaving domed huts from reeds and mud
by raising timber houses up on tall stilts
by stacking bricks baked from river clay
context: These carved dwellings are called yaodong — homes dug straight into the soft loess cliffs, made from the very soil the river is busy washing away downstream. (National Geographic Education, 'Loess')

question: The Yellow River has broken its banks and drowned the plains of northern China again and again, its silt-raised bed forever ready to burst free, and its flood of 1931 is often ranked the deadliest in recorded history. For this, the Chinese gave the river a grim two-word name. Which is it?
context: Between about 595 BC and 1946 the Yellow River flooded some 1,500 times and changed its main course 26 times; the 1931 flood's death toll is estimated at 1–4 million and the 1887 flood's at 900,000–2 million — among the worst disasters ever recorded. For its floods the river is called 'China's Sorrow'; for the civilization it fed, it is also called 'China's Pride.' (Wikipedia, 'Yellow River')

question: Farmers on the Yellow River's floodplain tilled a soft, mineral-rich yellow soil spread by the river's silt, loose enough to work with the simplest tools and generous with grain year after year. Chinese tradition honours this yellow-earth valley with one famous title. Which is it?
choices: the granary of the northern plains
the heartland of the Bronze Age
the birthplace of the Silk Road
context: The soft, fertile loess soil was easy to farm, so China's earliest villages clustered along the Yellow River thousands of years ago; the Loess Plateau and this floodplain are together remembered as 'the cradle of Chinese civilization.' (Britannica, 'Loess Plateau')

question: Round, water-filled pits open in the jungle of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, a flat slab of soft limestone with hardly a river on its surface, and the old Maya drank from them. What are these natural wells called?
context: The name comes from the Yucatec Maya word ts'ono'ot (dzonot), meaning a well or place of reachable groundwater, and is often glossed 'sacred well.' An estimated 6,000 to 10,000 cenotes pockmark the peninsula. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: Divers who slip into a Yucatán cenote float in water so glass-clear they seem to hang in midair, the cavern walls sharp far below them. Cenotes are famous the world over for this glassy clarity. Why is the water so clear?
answer: rain seeps down so slowly that its sediment settles out
choices: rain seeps down so slowly that its sediment settles out
sunlight kills the algae that would cloud the water
cold water keeps silt frozen at the bottom
ocean tides flush the sinkhole clean each day
context: Cenote water is rainwater that has filtered for years down through porous limestone, leaving its particles behind, so the pools glow a deep, transparent blue. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenote

question: Geologists mapping cenotes across the northwest of the Yucatán found the thickest of them lined up in one huge curve through the flat jungle, sweeping from the west coast at Celestún to Dzilam. They were stunned by what lies buried under this Ring of Cenotes. What does the ring trace?
answer: the rim of a giant asteroid-impact crater
choices: the rim of a giant asteroid-impact crater
the fault line of an ancient earthquake zone
the shoreline of a long-vanished inland sea
the channel of a collapsed underground river
context: The ring is a belt only about 5 km wide with a radius near 90 km -- roughly 180 km across -- curving from Celestun on the west coast past Homun and Tekit and back north to Dzilam. It marks the buried rim of the Chicxulub crater; the sinkholes are the surface fingerprint of the impact that ended the age of the dinosaurs 66 million years ago. Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5784/

question: Off the Yucatán's Caribbean shore, where the peninsula's underground rivers meet the sea, a living wall of coral runs more than 1,000 kilometres past Mexico, Belize, Guatemala and Honduras: the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef. Among all the barrier reefs on Earth, how does it rank?
answer: second-largest, behind only Australia's Great Barrier Reef
choices: second-largest, behind only Australia's Great Barrier Reef
the largest of all, ahead of Australia's Great Barrier Reef
second-largest, behind only New Caledonia's reef
second-largest, behind only the Red Sea's reef
context: The Mesoamerican Barrier Reef is the second-largest barrier reef on Earth, outstretched only by Australia's Great Barrier Reef. It runs more than 1,000 km along Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, and Honduras -- where the Yucatan's underground rivers finally reach the sea. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_Barrier_Reef_System

question: An asteroid roughly 10 kilometres wide slammed into the Yucatán about 66 million years ago, blasting out the crater now called Chicxulub, 180 kilometres across, and throwing up enough rock and soot to darken the whole sky. What did this single impact bring to an end?
context: The Chicxulub impactor hit near the present town of Chicxulub Puerto with force millions of times greater than a nuclear bomb. The debris and darkness triggered the mass extinction that wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs and about three-quarters of all species -- the leading scientific explanation for the end of the Cretaceous. Source: https://www.britannica.com/place/Chicxulub

question: A trained cave diver can slip into one Yucatán cenote and swim through drowned stone passages to cenotes far across the jungle, for beneath the surface they link up into flooded mazes. This hidden, water-filled network holds a world record. What record do the Yucatán's flooded caves hold?
answer: the longest underwater cave systems on Earth
choices: the longest underwater cave systems on Earth
the deepest underwater cave systems on Earth
the widest underwater cave systems on Earth
the clearest underwater cave systems on Earth
context: Sistema Sac Actun ('White Cave' in Maya) maps about 378 km of submerged passage; in 2018 divers found a channel linking it to the Dos Ojos ('Two Eyes') system. Nearby, Sistema Ox Bel Ha ('Three Paths of Water') has over 435 km mapped -- the two are rival claimants for the longest underwater cave on Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistema_Sac_Actun

question: Cave divers dropped into a pitch-black flooded chamber deep beneath the Yucatán in 2007 and named it Hoyo Negro, the 'Black Hole.' On a ledge far below the surface, among the bones of Ice Age sabre-toothed cats and giant ground sloths, lay the nearly complete skeleton of a teenage girl. Why did this skeleton, later nicknamed Naia, stun scientists?
answer: she is one of the oldest Americans ever found
choices: she is one of the oldest Americans ever found
she had been buried with a hoard of gold
she stood well over seven feet tall
she was a wholly unknown human species
context: Naia was a 15-to-16-year-old girl who fell into the then-dry cave around 12,000 to 13,000 years ago, near the end of the last Ice Age; rising seas later flooded the chamber. She is among the oldest and most complete humans ever found in the Americas, helping trace how the first people reached the continent. Source: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/140515-skeleton-ice-age-mexico-cave-hoyo-negro-archaeology

question: On the open grasslands of Tuva, in Siberia, a lone herder opens his mouth. One voice sounds two notes at once. A low steady drone hums, and a bright pitch floats above it. What is this steppe singing called?
context: Across Tuva and neighboring Mongolia the art is called khöömei, a Turkic word meaning 'throat' or 'larynx.' A single herder, standing alone on the steppe, can sound like two singers at once. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing

question: Herders on the Mongolian steppe, in Mongolia and Russia's Tuva, sing a strange song in which one voice sounds two notes at once. Asked where the sounds come from, the singers all give the same answer: the sounds are not made up but borrowed. Borrowed from what?
answer: the wild sounds of the steppe itself
choices: the wild sounds of the steppe itself
the melodies of old Mongol war songs
the cries of their own herds and dogs
context: Singers liken the deep growl to the howling winds of winter, and the rolling trill called borbangnadyr to a bubbling brook — so one person's song becomes a map of the homeland: wind, water, and open sky. The whole art grows from an animist belief that a place's spirits live in its sound as much as its shape. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing  (Legend.)

question: A herder on the steppe of Tuva, in southern Siberia, can push a single voice into two notes at once, a low humming drone with a bright whistle floating above it, and each style of the art has its own name. The highest is a piercing, flute-like whistle that seems to hover far above the drone, like a thin wind slicing across the steppe. What is that whistling style called?
context: Sygyt, the high whistle, is one of three main styles, alongside the deep growling kargyraa and khöömei used as its own style, said to sound like 'wind swirling among rocks.' Singers point the tongue against the gums to force the piercing tone out clear and bright. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing

question: A two-string fiddle often plays beside the singers of Tuva, on the steppe of southern Siberia, as each holds a low drone and a bright whistle in one voice; its neck rises into a carved horse's head above the pegs. Its low bowing sounds like horses trotting across the grasslands. What is this Tuvan fiddle called?
context: The igil is Tuva's horsehead fiddle; Mongolia bows a larger cousin, the morin khuur. Played low and steady beneath the voice, its rhythm falls like hoofbeats under the singer's drone. Both fiddles are carved with a horse's head — fitting, for music made by a people who live on horseback. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igil

question: One Tuvan singing style rocks to a steady pulse, flicked out by the soft palate opening and closing as the singer drones. Riders recognize the motion at once: the style's name, ezengileer, comes straight from a piece of a horseman's kit, and the song sways in time with it. Which piece gave the style its name?
context: Ezengileer takes its name from ezengi, the Tuvan word for a stirrup, and its bouncing pulse imitates the sway of a rider posting at a trot. It joins a whole gallery of styles — each one, singers say, a different piece of the moving steppe. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuvan_throat_singing

question: A singer in Tuva holds one low droning note and slowly reshapes his mouth and throat, and a bright, separate pitch rings out above the drone. It sounds like sorcery, yet it is not a second voice; it is pure physics. What is that high pitch, really?
answer: a faint overtone already inside the drone, amplified loud
choices: a faint overtone already inside the drone, amplified loud
an echo of the drone bouncing off the hard palate
the drone itself sliding rapidly up to a high note
air forced into a thin whistle between the teeth
context: Acousticians call this biphonation from filtering: one sound source split into two pitches. The singer's mouth focuses a narrow band of overtones — roughly the 6th to 12th harmonics of the drone — into a single sharp peak while hushing the neighbors, so one faint harmonic rings out as a separate note. UNESCO calls it 'a melody of harmonics' riding a continuous drone. Sources: https://elifesciences.org/articles/50476 ; https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/mongolian-traditional-art-of-khoomei-00396

question: Surfers paddle out on England's River Severn to meet the incoming tide, which rears up twice a day into a wall of water about 2 m tall and races up the river the wrong way. What is this upstream wave called?
context: On the Severn the bore rides one of the greatest tidal ranges on Earth — about 13 m between high and low water — which is why surfers can chase a single wave miles inland. A tidal bore forms only where a big flood tide is funneled into a shallow, narrowing river mouth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severn_bore

question: The Amazon's tidal bore tears whole trees from the riverbanks as it charges inland, and its pounding reshapes the coast near the river's mouth. Between 1845 and 1850 it did something to low, flat Caviana Island that few waves ever do to solid land. What did it do to the island?
context: Between 1845 and 1850 the pororoca's erosion split Caviana Island, near the Amazon's mouth, into two parts — a wave rearranging the map. The same bore constantly tears trees and mud from the banks as it charges inland. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca

question: Crowds have lined the banks of China's Qiantang River, near Hangzhou, each autumn for over a thousand years to watch the biggest tidal bore on Earth: a roaring wall of water up to 9 m tall that charges upstream at 40 km/h, three times the height of England's Severn bore. What is it nicknamed?
context: The Qiantang bore, nicknamed the 'Silver Dragon,' is the world's largest. Tide-watching here is over a thousand years old: the Southern Song court set a Tide Watching Festival on the 18th day of the 8th lunar month, and the world's oldest known tide table (AD 1056) was made for this river. In 2013 Typhoon Trami doubled the bore's height and it broke over the barrier into the crowd. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiantang_River  (Legend.)

question: Boats on France's Seine had to reckon for centuries with the mascaret, a tidal bore that surged up from the sea and that locals called 'la barre.' By the 1960s it had vanished, and the lower Seine has had no bore since. What made the mascaret disappear?
choices: the sea's tidal range slowly shrank
the river's course was rerouted inland
context: A tidal bore needs a shallow, narrowing, funneling estuary; deepening the Seine's channel for shipping erased that geometry and 'la barre' was gone — proof a bore can be engineered out of existence. The reverse can happen too: Canada's Petitcodiac bore, choked by a 1968 causeway, came back after the gates were reopened in 2010. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascaret

question: A climber who reaches the top of Temple IV at Tikal, in Guatemala, the city's tallest pyramid at about 70 metres, pops out into open sky. She has risen above the one thing that hides every other ruin for miles. What has she risen above?
context: Temple IV rises about 70 m (roughly 64.6 m from its own platform to the top of the roof-comb) — high enough to look out over an unbroken sea of treetops. Accuracy note: it is NOT the tallest pre-Columbian structure. It is roughly the second-tallest still standing, after the Great Pyramid of Tonina, and Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun may once have topped it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_IV

question: Two stone pyramids face each other across the Great Plaza of Tikal, in Guatemala. The taller, Temple I, a royal tomb, takes its name from a lintel carved with a king seated on the throne of a fierce jungle predator. Which predator is it?
context: Temple I is the 'Temple of the Great Jaguar,' named for a carved lintel showing a king seated on a jaguar throne. Facing it across the plaza is its shorter twin, Temple II, the 'Temple of the Masks.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: A film crew once hauled cameras up Temple IV at Tikal, in Guatemala, to shoot the view from its summit. On screen the scene became an alien world in one of the most famous science-fiction sagas ever made. Which film borrowed Tikal for its alien planet?
context: In Star Wars: A New Hope (1977), the view from Temple IV's summit stands in for the rebel base on the forest moon Yavin 4. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_IV

question: The people of Tikal walked away from their great city around 900 CE, and the rainforest swallowed its plazas and temples for nearly a thousand years. Across the whole Maya lowlands, what do most researchers now blame for this collapse?
context: The leading explanation is decades of severe drought, worsened by the Maya's own deforestation and soil erosion, though the exact trigger is still debated. After the collapse, the jungle reclaimed Tikal for roughly a thousand years. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: The Maya builders of Temple I at Tikal raised it to its summit shrine on nine great stepped terraces, a number they chose on purpose. Scholars widely think the nine echo a sacred nine at the heart of the Maya view of the world. What do the nine terraces stand for?
answer: The nine layers of the underworld
choices: The nine layers of the underworld
The nine tiers of the heavens
context: Temple I's nine stepped terraces are widely thought to represent the nine levels of the Maya underworld. Its roof-comb is built as two parallel stone walls with a hollow vault between them, cutting the weight while giving a huge surface to carve the king's image. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_I  (Legend.)

question: Tikal's kings, deep in the rainforest of Guatemala, faced a fierce enemy in the forest lowlands to the north, a city whose own kings called their dynasty the 'Snake Kingdom' and stamped a snake-head glyph on every monument. Which city was Tikal's great northern rival?
context: Calakmul, in modern Campeche, Mexico, about 35 km north of the Guatemala border, was the seat of the Kaan ('Snake') dynasty — Tikal's great rival across the Classic Maya lowlands. Its emblem glyph was a snake head reading 'Kaan.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calakmul

question: Archaeologists tunnelled deep into Temple I at Tikal in 1962 and broke into the sealed tomb of Jasaw Chan K'awiil I, one of the city's kings. On the burial bench, still resting on the royal skeleton, lay the richest treasure ever found at Tikal. What jewel-work adorned the dead king?
answer: A necklace of heavy jade beads
choices: A necklace of heavy jade beads
context: The necklace held 114 carved jade beads and weighed 3.9 kg (8.6 lb). Burial 116 also held a jade mosaic vessel carved with the king's own portrait, 37 inscribed human bones, jaguar pelts, spondylus shells, and pearls. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal_Temple_I

question: Tikal drank only rainwater, caught off its wide plazas and held in huge lined reservoirs — water that, in a hot jungle, should have turned foul within weeks. A 2020 study showed the Corriental reservoir somehow stayed clean for centuries, making it the oldest known water-purification site in the Americas. How did the Maya keep it drinkable?
context: The Maya filtered the water through imported zeolite and coarse quartz sand — a natural molecular sieve that stripped out microbes and even toxins like mercury. It is the oldest known water-filtration system in the Western Hemisphere, about 2,000 years old, and the minerals were hauled roughly 30 km (18 miles) from ridges near the Bajo de Azucar. Sources: nature.com/articles/s41598-020-75023-7; uc.edu/news/articles/2020/10

question: Enormous stone reservoirs of rain kept Tikal alive in Guatemala's rainforest, yet in the end they may have turned against the city. Sediment laid down in the largest of them as Tikal declined is laced with a poison leached from the brilliant red pigment the Maya painted on their walls and tombs. Which toxic metal fouled Tikal's water?
context: Sediment studies of Tikal's largest reservoirs found them fouled with mercury, leached from cinnabar — the red pigment the Maya prized — along with blooms of toxic blue-green algae (cyanobacteria). Together they would have made the water undrinkable as the city declined. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikal

question: English speakers said 'from here to ___' for hundreds of years to mean the farthest place on earth, yet the blank was a real, dusty city in what is now Mali, where the Sahara meets the grasslands. Which city's name became this saying for the middle of nowhere?
context: 'As far as Timbuktu' and 'from here to Timbuktu' became English shorthand for the ends of the earth — yet Timbuktu is a real, reachable city of about 85,000 people in modern Mali. In the 1800s Europeans imagined it as a place of mythical riches at the world's edge. Source: NPR/WLRN, 'From Here to Timbuktu'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.  (Legend.)

question: Camel trains staggered out of the Sahara into Timbuktu and loaded their cargo onto boats on a great river 20 kilometres to the south, and the town grew rich at that crossing point. Which river carried Timbuktu's trade on into West Africa?
context: Timbuktu sits on the southern edge of the Sahara about 20 km north of the Niger River — the exact point where desert camel caravans met the river boats. That meeting of sand and water is what made it a great trading city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.

question: Camels hauled one cargo south out of the deep Sahara, from Taghaza and Taoudenni, to Timbuktu and the gold-rich lands beyond, which badly needed it. Traders said it was swapped for gold at nearly equal weight. What was it?
context: Slabs of salt cut at the Saharan mines of Taghaza and Taoudenni were hauled south by camel; salt was so scarce in the gold-rich south that it was famously said to trade toward its weight in gold — an exaggeration, but salt worth pennies in the desert could sell for gold at the Sahara's edge. The 'azalai' caravans ran several thousand camels at a time, each carrying four or five 30 kg slabs on the roughly three-week trip from Taoudenni, about 660 km north. Sources: worldhistory.org, 'The Salt Trade of Ancient West Africa'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azalai.  (Legend.)

question: All through Timbuktu stand the domed shrines of Sufi holy men, the marabouts. The town honors them as guardians watching over the city. Many of these saints lie buried inside its walls. What nickname does this give Timbuktu?
choices: the City of a Thousand Saints
context: Timbuktu is nicknamed the 'City of 333 Saints' for the 333 Sufi marabouts buried in shrines across the town, whose tombs the people venerated as protectors of the city. In 2012 militants smashed several of these tombs; local masons later rebuilt them with UNESCO support. Timbuktu has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988. Sources: newageislam.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.

question: Families in Timbuktu, a trading town on the edge of the Sahara, kept as many as 700,000 manuscripts, all written by hand, in libraries in their own homes, by one estimate. Some of the pages cover medicine, law and poetry. Which two subjects are the manuscripts most famous for?
context: European colonizers spread a myth that Africa kept no written records — yet Timbuktu's families had guarded, for centuries, up to an estimated ~700,000 hand-written manuscripts covering astronomy, mathematics, medicine, law and poetry. The city's astronomy manuscripts, with their star charts and planetary tables, are among the most celebrated: hard proof that pre-colonial West Africa had literate, scientific scholarship centuries before European colonies, directly against the false 'Africa had no written history' trope. (The count is an estimate — hence 'up to ~700,000.') Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu_Manuscripts.  (Legend.)

question: Three great mosques, Djingareyber, Sankore and Sidi Yahya, rise from the flat, sunbaked town of Timbuktu in Mali, on the southern edge of the Sahara, each about 700 years old. Their thick tapered towers bristle with wooden beams sticking straight out from the walls. What material are these mosques built from?
context: All three mosques are built of mud and adobe, not stone. Djinguereber, the oldest, was built in 1327 on the order of the emperor Mansa Musa and designed by the Andalusian architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili; Sidi Yahya was founded around 1400 and completed about 1440. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; grokipedia.com/page/Djinguereber_Mosque.

question: Leo Africanus, a traveller, wandered Timbuktu's crowded markets around 1510 and marvelled at its trade. Of everything sold there, he wrote, one good brought its sellers 'more profit than all other merchandise', worth more even than gold. What was it?
context: Leo Africanus wrote of Timbuktu that 'there is more profit made from this commerce than from all other merchandise' — hand-written books were the single most valuable trade good, worth more than a slave, and owning them was how the wealthy showed off their standing. Source: brians.wsu.edu, Leo Africanus, 'Description of Africa' (1526).  (Legend.)

question: Ahmed Baba, Timbuktu's greatest scholar, wrote more than forty books of his own and filled his home with a library of over 1,600 volumes. Then Moroccan troops stormed the city in 1591. What did the conquerors do to Ahmed Baba?
choices: held him for a heavy ransom
put him to death in the square
burned his house to the ground
context: Ahmed Baba (1556–1627) was Timbuktu's greatest scholar and a chancellor of the Sankoré madrasa — the heart of what is remembered as the University of Timbuktu, one of the world's oldest centers of higher learning, said to have taught as many as ~25,000 students at its height (a historical estimate). He wrote more than 40 books and kept a personal library of over 1,600 volumes, which he lost when Moroccan invaders exiled him from the city in 1591.
