Timbuktu's modern manuscript-research institute is named the Ahmed Baba Institute in his honor. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu; muslimheritage.com, 'The University of Sankore, Timbuktu'; face2faceafrica.com.

question: European explorers died for years trying to reach Timbuktu, dreaming of a fabled city roofed in gold. René Caillié, a Frenchman, finally walked in and out alive in 1828 and claimed a 10,000-franc prize. What did he actually find there?
context: René Caillié (1828) was the first European to reach Timbuktu and return alive, collecting a 10,000-franc prize from the Geographical Society of Paris. Expecting gold, he found only 'a mass of ill-looking houses built of earth.' The Briton Alexander Gordon Laing had reached the city first, in August 1826, but was murdered by his escorts just after leaving. Leo Africanus's earlier tale of a single 970-pound gold ingot in the ruler's treasury had helped feed the golden-city legend. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/René_Caillié; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gordon_Laing; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu.

question: Armed fighters seized Timbuktu in 2012 and began destroying anything they judged un-Islamic, and the city's ancient manuscripts were in serious danger. Abdel Kader Haidara, a quiet local librarian, ran a secret rescue that saved about 350,000 of them. How did he and his helpers keep them safe?
answer: smuggling them south in metal trunks
choices: smuggling them south in metal trunks
burying them in jars under the desert
sealing them inside the mosque walls
context: Librarian Abdel Kader Haidara and a network of helpers secretly smuggled roughly 350,000 manuscripts out in metal trunks and footlockers: first by car past militant checkpoints, then, when the roads grew too dangerous, by boat on the Niger, to safety in Bamako in the south. It was a race against real destruction: on 25 January 2013 the retreating militants swept about 4,200 manuscripts off the tables of the Ahmed Baba Institute and set them on fire, only a fraction, because most had already been smuggled out. Sources: smithsonianmag.com, 'The Race to Save Mali's Priceless Artifacts'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu_Manuscripts; nationalgeographic.com, 'The Badass Librarians of Timbuktu'.  (Legend.)

question: The carved gateways, sunken courtyards and giant statues of Tiwanaku lie in ruins high in the Bolivian Andes near Lake Titicaca. People often confuse its builders with the Inca, who also centred their world on that lake. Where does Tiwanaku fit on a timeline of the great American civilizations?
choices: At the same time as the Aztec
context: Tiwanaku flourished roughly AD 500-1000 and had collapsed by about AD 1000 -- centuries before the Inca empire arose in the 1400s. The two are a common mix-up because both centered on the Andes near Lake Titicaca. Source: Grokipedia: Pumapunku; Wikipedia: Tiwanaku.

question: One carved doorway stands apart from all the rest at the ruined Andean city of Tiwanaku, in Bolivia, cut from a single 10-ton block of andesite. Above the opening stands a figure, probably an Andean creator god, raising a staff in either hand beneath a halo of rays. What is this famous gateway called?
context: The Gateway of the Sun is cut from a single 10-ton block. The commanding figure on its lintel -- holding a staff in each hand, its head ringed by rays -- is usually identified as the creator god Viracocha, though some scholars suggest the Aymara weather god Thunupa. Source: Wikipedia: Gateway of the Sun.

question: Beside the ruins of Tiwanaku, a pre-Inca city high in the Bolivian Andes near Lake Titicaca, stands the temple of Pumapunku, whose stone blocks are so evenly matched and sharp-edged that they look machine-made. Many of them were cut to the very same letter shape. What shape were those Pumapunku blocks?
context: Pumapunku's H-blocks lock together like precise puzzle pieces, forming blind miniature gateways. Their machine-like precision has made the site a magnet for 'ancient aliens' claims -- but archaeologists credit skilled Tiwanaku masons. Alexei Vranich points to well-preserved earlier stonework at nearby Pukara and Chiripa as proof the skill grew among the Titicaca-basin peoples themselves, and Franco Rossi has criticized alien theorists for dismissing the Aymara as incapable builders. Source: Grokipedia: Pumapunku; Wikipedia: Pumapunku.

question: The builders of Pumapunku, a temple beside the ruined pre-Inca city of Tiwanaku high in the Bolivian Andes, used no mortar at all, yet the stones fit so tightly a knife won't slip between the joints. Block was locked to block by a trick that still amazes engineers. What held the giant stones together?
answer: molten metal cast into I-shaped cramps
choices: molten metal cast into I-shaped cramps
iron staples hammered across the joints
reed ropes lashed around the blocks
wooden pegs driven into the seams
context: In carved notches at the joints, Tiwanaku metalworkers poured molten metal that hardened in place into I-shaped cramps of a distinctive copper-arsenic-nickel bronze alloy -- casting the clamps directly at the stone to bind block to block without mortar. Source: Wikipedia: Pumapunku.

question: Pumapunku's builders, beside Lake Titicaca in Bolivia, had no wheels, no strong pack animals and no iron. Yet they quarried their hardest blocks on a peninsula about 90 kilometres away and moved them across or around the lake. The largest stone at the site, a red-sandstone slab, ranks among the heaviest worked stones in the ancient Americas. Roughly how much does it weigh?
context: The red-sandstone slab weighs an estimated 131 tonnes -- a calculated estimate, not a measurement -- and came from a quarry about 10 km off. Pumapunku's harder andesite blocks travelled far farther still: quarried on the Copacabana Peninsula about 90 km away, they had to be moved across (or around) Lake Titicaca itself. Source: Wikipedia: Pumapunku; Grokipedia: Pumapunku.

question: Nights freeze hard on the high plain around Tiwanaku, in Bolivia, cold enough to kill the crops. Yet its farmers fed a city of many thousands by building long raised planting beds separated by water-filled channels, and the water kept the frost off their plants through the night. What is this frost-beating raised-field system called?
context: These raised beds -- called waru waru (also suka kollus) -- were typically 4-10 m wide and up to 100 m long, raised about a meter high. By trapping the day's heat in the channel water they kept the soil roughly 1 degree C warmer at night, out-yielding ordinary fields and helping feed a Tiwanaku of an estimated 10,000-20,000 people around AD 800. The system faltered when a long drought gripped the altiplano around AD 1000, coinciding with the city's decline. Source: Wikipedia: Waru Waru; Wikipedia: Tiwanaku.

question: At one busy Tokyo crossing, every light turns red at the same time. Then up to 3,000 people rush across from every side at once, cutting straight through the middle. Which Tokyo district has this 'scramble crossing,' the busiest on Earth?
context: This is the famous Shibuya Scramble (Shibuya Crossing), which opened in 1973. When the lights change, pedestrians surge across from all sides at once -- up to about 3,000 people per green light. Surveys estimate around 260,000 people cross on a weekday and up to 500,000 on the busiest days, making it the most famous pedestrian crossing on Earth. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shibuya_Crossing  (Legend.)

question: Greater Tokyo sprawls along Tokyo Bay and on into Yokohama, tower after glass tower, home to some 37 million people, nearly as many as live in the whole state of California. Where does that rank it among all the cities ever built?
choices: the second most populous on Earth
context: Greater Tokyo (the Tokyo-Yokohama agglomeration) is home to roughly 37 million people -- the largest single urban area in human history, about the population of the whole state of California or the country of Poland. Rankings depend on where you draw the boundary: a narrower UN definition counts about 33 million, and fast-growing Delhi is projected to overtake Tokyo within about a decade. Source: Statista 2025 urban agglomerations; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Tokyo_Area  (Legend.)

question: The young Emperor Meiji left Kyoto in 1868 and moved his court to the city the Tokugawa shoguns had ruled Japan from for over 250 years. He gave it the name Tokyo, the Eastern Capital. What had the city been called until then?
context: For over 250 years the city was called Edo, capital of the Tokugawa shoguns. When the shogunate fell in 1868, the young Emperor Meiji moved his residence there from Kyoto and renamed it Tokyo (東京), meaning 'Eastern Capital' -- the capital to the east of the old one, Kyoto. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo; britannica.com/place/Tokyo

question: A slim white broadcasting spire was finished on Tokyo's east side in 2012, climbing 634 metres into the sky. When it opened, no other tower on Earth stood as tall. What is this tower called?
context: The Tokyo Skytree rises 634 m (2,080 ft) and opened on May 22, 2012 as a broadcasting tower -- the tallest tower in the world, beating China's Canton Tower (600 m). Some buildings are taller (Dubai's Burj Khalifa is 828 m, Kuala Lumpur's Merdeka 118 is 679 m), but a 'tower' has less than half its height as usable floor space, so the Skytree still holds the tower record. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree

question: Round and round the middle of Tokyo runs a train line with no last stop. Its loop links the great hubs of Shinjuku and Ikebukuro and comes back to where it started in about an hour. Which line is it?
context: The Yamanote Line is Tokyo's famous loop line, circling the city center in a continuous ring that connects its biggest hubs -- Tokyo, Shinjuku, Shibuya, Ikebukuro and more. One full loop takes about an hour. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamanote_Line

question: Passengers pour through one Tokyo railway station at about 3.5 million a day, nearly six times the crowd at its closest rival, Paris's Gare du Nord. They leave by well over 200 exits. Which station is the Guinness record-holder for the busiest on Earth?
context: Shinjuku Station holds the Guinness World Record as the busiest railway station on Earth -- about 3.5 million passengers a day before the pandemic, and still 2.7 million in 2022. Its nearest rival, Paris's Gare du Nord, handles only around 600,000. It has well over 200 exits. Source: guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/busiest-station; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinjuku_Station

question: At the exact centre of Tokyo, a wide moat and high stone ramparts wall off a vast island of forest and gardens, on the grounds of an old castle. What fills this green, guarded heart of the city?
context: The Imperial Palace (Kokyo), residence of the Emperor of Japan, sits on the grounds of the former Edo Castle, ringed by wide moats and forest at the exact center of Tokyo -- so a great island of trees and water fills the heart of the world's biggest city. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Imperial_Palace

question: Out in Tokyo Bay lies Odaiba, a district of shopping malls, a giant Ferris wheel, and a life-sized Gundam robot. It began in 1853 as a ring of cannon batteries built to fend off Commodore Perry's American warships. What kind of ground is this whole waterfront district built on?
context: Odaiba is built on reclaimed land -- one of many artificial islands in Tokyo Bay, where about 249 km2 of ground has been created from the sea. It began in 1853 as a ring of gun batteries ('daiba' means 'battery') to defend Edo against Commodore Perry's 'Black Ships,' and was rebuilt into a futuristic waterfront in the 1990s. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odaiba; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Bay

question: The Tokugawa shoguns ruled Japan for two and a half centuries from a great walled fortress at the heart of what is now Tokyo. Among the fortresses of its age, what record did the shoguns' castle once hold?
answer: the largest castle in the world
choices: the largest castle in the world
the tallest castle in the world
the oldest castle in the world
the strongest castle in the world
context: In its heyday Edo Castle was the largest castle in the world: its outer defenses ran about 16 km (10 miles) around and covered roughly 230 hectares -- more than double Osaka Castle's 106. Today's Imperial Palace grounds are only about a third of the original castle. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_Castle; worldhistory.org/Edo_Castle  (Legend.)

question: Tokyo has been shaken to rubble and rebuilt more than once, because the Kanto plain sits in one of the most geologically violent settings on Earth. What is the underground reason the city is so dangerously earthquake-prone?
answer: three tectonic plates collide beneath it
choices: three tectonic plates collide beneath it
a single deep fault line splits it
a volcanic hotspot rises beneath it
its soft soil amplifies far-off quakes
context: The Kanto region sits on a rare triple plate boundary: the continental (North American/Okhotsk) plate is being pushed under by BOTH the Philippine Sea plate and the Pacific plate, which dive beneath it. (Older texts call the continental plate 'Eurasian.') This double subduction makes Tokyo one of the most seismically active cities on the planet. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Great_Kanto_earthquake; agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com (dual subduction under Tokyo)

question: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck Tokyo and Yokohama at two minutes to noon on 1 September 1923. About 105,000 people died, yet remarkably few of them were killed by the shaking or by falling debris. What caused the overwhelming majority of the deaths in the Great Kanto earthquake?
answer: a firestorm that swept the city
choices: a firestorm that swept the city
context: The Great Kanto earthquake struck at 11:58 a.m. -- lunchtime, when thousands of charcoal cooking fires were burning across a city of wooden houses. Whipped by winds from a passing typhoon, the fires merged into firestorms (one 'fire tornado' at a former clothing depot killed tens of thousands alone), causing about 90% of the roughly 105,000 deaths. The quake was driven by the Philippine Sea plate slipping beneath the continental plate along the Sagami Trough. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Great_Kanto_earthquake

question: The great broadcasting spire on Tokyo's east side stands exactly 634 metres tall, and that oddly precise number was no accident: it was chosen as a hidden pun. Read as digits in an old style of Japanese counting, 6-3-4 sounds out a single Japanese word. What word does '634' spell?
context: 634 metres was chosen as a pun: in an old style of Japanese counting, 6-3-4 reads 'mu-sa-shi' -- Musashi, the ancient name of the province and plain that Tokyo was built on. This kind of number-wordplay is called goroawase. The Skytree opened in 2012 as the world's tallest tower. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Skytree; britannica.com/topic/Tokyo-Sky-Tree

question: The sky over the flat plains of Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas and Nebraska can turn green-black on a spring afternoon, and these plains spawn more twisters than anywhere else on Earth. What nickname do weather experts give this strip of land?
context: Tornado Alley isn't an official line on any map but a nickname for the central Great Plains, where cold, dry air off the Rocky Mountains collides with warm Gulf moisture to breed more twisters than anywhere on Earth. The Dust Bowl was the 1930s drought that scoured these same plains; Hail Alley is the High Plains belt battered by the nation's worst hail; Hoosier Alley is a smaller tornado zone around Indiana and the Ohio Valley. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tornado_Alley

question: Two very different air masses come racing at each other over the flat plains of Oklahoma and Kansas every spring, from April through June, and slam together. Their meeting feeds the towering storms that spin up the region's tornadoes. Which clash of air feeds them?
answer: dry air off the Rocky Mountains riding over moist air from the Gulf of Mexico
choices: dry air off the Rocky Mountains riding over moist air from the Gulf of Mexico
cool marine air off the Pacific sliding under hot air from the Mojave Desert
monsoon moisture from the Gulf of California damming against the Sierra Madre
frigid Arctic air from Canada pouring down onto the humid Atlantic Seaboard
context: The setup is a layer cake of instability: dry, cool air spilling east off the Rockies rides up and over warm, wet air streaming north from the Gulf of Mexico. The trapped moist layer bursts upward into towering, rotating thunderstorms called supercells - the parent storms of most violent tornadoes. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tornado_Alley

question: A colossal tornado dropped from a supercell thunderstorm on the evening of 31 May 2013 and tore across the flat farmland near El Reno, Oklahoma. Storm chasers driving portable Doppler radar dishes clocked the winds inside it past 300 miles per hour, and at one point it spread over 2.6 miles from edge to edge. Which world record does the El Reno tornado hold?
context: El Reno's tornado spread 2.6 miles (4.2 km) from edge to edge - the widest ever measured on Earth. Its winds screamed past 300 mph on mobile radar, yet surveyors rated it only EF3: tornado ratings read the damage left on the ground, not the wind itself, and this giant churned mostly over open country. Its record is width, not strength. Eight people died, including veteran storm researcher Tim Samaras, his son Paul, and Carl Young of the TWISTEX team - the first professional tornado researchers ever killed while chasing. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/2013_El_Reno_tornado

question: Ted Fujita, a scientist at the University of Chicago, drew up a scale in 1971 that still ranks the twisters of Oklahoma and Kansas from 0 to 5, in an updated form since 2007. What sets a tornado's rating on his scale?
answer: the damage it leaves on the ground
choices: the damage it leaves on the ground
the top wind speed clocked by radar
the width of its funnel at its base
the length of the track it carves
context: Ted Fujita of the University of Chicago introduced his F scale in 1971; the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale replaced it in the United States on February 1, 2007. Both rate a tornado by the wreckage it leaves: surveyors read the damage on the ground and estimate the winds from it, so a ferociously fast tornado can still earn a middling rating if it stays over open country, as El Reno's did in 2013. An original F5 meant winds of roughly 261 to 318 mph, 'incredible damage.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale

question: A tornado that tears across Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee or Georgia takes far more lives than one out on the Great Plains, though the Plains see many more of them. Allen Pearson, a meteorologist, named this southern belt Dixie Alley in 1971. What makes its tornadoes so much deadlier?
answer: they strike after dark, when families are asleep and cannot see them
choices: they strike after dark, when families are asleep and cannot see them
they pack far stronger winds than any tornado the Plains can muster
they linger on the ground for hours, not the usual few minutes
they hurl grapefruit-sized hail ahead of the funnel
context: Dixie Alley's twisters strike disproportionately at night - about 29% after dark versus 19% on the Plains - and they hide in rain and dense forest, so people never spot the funnel. Night tornadoes kill roughly 2.5 times as many people, catching families asleep. The meteorologist Allen Pearson coined the name 'Dixie Alley' in 1971. Source: https://grokipedia.com/page/Tornado_Alley

question: In southern China, along the Li River near Guilin, hundreds of steep gray hills rise from flat green rice fields. They look like a crowd of stone thumbs, shaped by water over ages. What is this kind of land called?
context: This is 'tower karst' — solid limestone slowly dissolved away by rainwater over millions of years, not pushed up by any volcano or earthquake. The word 'karst' itself comes from the Kras Plateau in Slovenia, the barren limestone country where these dissolving-rock features were first studied. Karst is no rare oddity: it covers roughly a fifth of the continental United States, and karst springs and aquifers supply about a quarter of the world's drinking water. Sources: Grokipedia 'Guilin' and 'Karst'; Wikipedia 'Tower karst' and 'Karst'.

question: A lone fisherman poles a slim bamboo raft past peaks doubled in glassy still water on the back of China's 20-yuan banknote. The note shows the single most famous view on the Li River, which winds through Guangxi province past hundreds of tall, thumb-shaped limestone peaks. Which real bend of the Li River is this?
context: The spot is Yellow Cloth Shoal (Huangbu), just downstream of Xingping. It is named for a big flat beige slab of rock lying on the clear riverbed that looks like a sheet of yellow cloth spread out underwater; seven karst hills of different sizes stand around it, and it is famed for the finest peak-reflections on the whole Li River. Sources: lirivercruises.com (Li River 20-yuan note); topchinatravel.com (Li River).

question: Along China's Li River, some limestone towers stand alone as spires on the flat plain, while others crowd together as cones on one shared base. Chinese geographers call the first fenglin, 'peak forests', and the second fengcong, 'peak clusters', and both took millions of years to form. How did these towers come to stand so high above the flat land?
answer: rain slowly dissolved away the land around them
choices: rain slowly dissolved away the land around them
an ancient volcano pushed them up as plugs
an earthquake fault thrust them up from below
an ice-age glacier carved them from the plain
context: Both fenglin ('peak forest' of separate towers) and fengcong ('peak cluster' of cones on a shared base) are carved DOWN by dissolving water, never pushed UP by any earthquake or volcano — the towers are simply the hard rock left standing after the softer surrounding limestone dissolved away over millions of years. Sources: Waltham, 'Fengcong, fenglin, cone karst and tower karst'; corroborated ScienceDirect (S0169555X13003826).

question: Visitors can wander on foot between the tall grey blades and pinnacles of the Stone Forest, or Shilin, in China's Yunnan province, some of them 50 metres high, where rain dissolved the rock from the top down. Stranger still is where all that stone began. More than 270 million years ago, long before the pinnacles existed, this ground lay somewhere very different. Where did it lie?
context: Shilin's limestone is over 270 million years old: it began as shell-and-seafloor mud when the region lay beneath an ancient sea, then hardened into limestone and was later dissolved from the surface down into these 50-meter blades — karst at ground level instead of towering river hills. The local Sani (Yi) people tell of Ashima, a girl forbidden to marry the man she loved, who turned to stone in the forest and gave it her name. With Guilin and dozens of other sites, Shilin is protected as the 'South China Karst' UNESCO World Heritage Site, one of Earth's largest karst regions at roughly 500,000 square kilometers. Sources: Grokipedia 'Stone Forest'; Wikipedia 'Stone Forest' (Ashima legend; 270-million-year age; Yi/Sani).

question: Thousands of sheer sky-pillars crowd Zhangjiajie in China's Hunan province, the floating peaks that inspired the Hallelujah Mountains of the film Avatar. They look like a giant field of limestone towers, but no acid ever dissolved them and they are not karst at all. What rock are these pillars actually made of?
context: Zhangjiajie's pillars are quartz sandstone, shaped by freeze-thaw ice and running water — not limestone dissolved by acid — so despite looking like giant tower karst, they are not karst at all. Their floating-peak silhouette inspired the Hallelujah Mountains of James Cameron's Avatar. It is the classic trap: not every stone tower is karst — the real test is whether acid slowly dissolving limestone made it. Source: Wikipedia 'Zhangjiajie National Forest Park' (quartz sandstone; 'not the product of chemical dissolution'; Avatar Hallelujah Mountain).

question: For some 1,200 km up California, the Pacific plate slides slowly past the North American plate, side by side. The two neither crash together to build mountains nor pull apart to leak lava. Which famous fault marks the seam between them?
context: The San Andreas Fault is the flagship transform boundary, running roughly 1,200 km (750 miles) up California. Unlike a subduction zone, where one plate dives beneath another, or a spreading ridge, where plates pull apart and new crust wells up, a transform boundary makes no new crust and destroys none — the two plates simply grind sideways past each other. The Alpine (New Zealand), Denali (Alaska), and North Anatolian (Turkey) faults are other real transform faults. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault; USGS.

question: Wallace Creek runs across California's dry Carrizo Plain toward California's great sliding fault, and its lower half turns up 130 m to the northwest, dragged along by the plates. Most of that shift crept up over ages, but 23 feet of it came at once in a great quake of 1857. Which quake was it?
context: Wallace Creek is a textbook 'offset stream': the San Andreas has sliced its channel and dragged the downstream half about 130 m (425 ft) northwest over thousands of years — but roughly 23 ft of that jump happened in a single instant during the 1857 Fort Tejon earthquake, the great quake that ruptured this southern stretch of the fault. On the treeless Carrizo Plain — under 9 inches of rain a year, so nothing overgrows the ground — you can still walk the dog-legged bend today. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrizo_Plain.

question: San Francisco shook in the great earthquake of 1906 as the great fault that splits California tore open in one violent instant along a continuous seam, jogging the roads and fences that crossed it out of line. The whole fault runs about 750 miles. How much of it tore open in that one rupture?
answer: more than a third of it
choices: more than a third of it
context: The 1906 rupture tore along roughly 477 km (296 mi) of the San Andreas at about magnitude 7.9 — more than a third of the fault's entire 750-mile length ripped open in a single instant. Along the way the two sides slid up to about 6 m (20 ft) past each other horizontally, leaving fences and roads with a clean 20-foot jog that became textbook evidence of how the fault moves. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906_San_Francisco_earthquake.

question: Los Angeles sits on the Pacific plate, which grinds slowly northwest along the plate boundary that cuts through California a few centimetres a year. The Bay City to the north sits on the other plate, the North American. If that slide keeps up for about 20 million years, where does it put Los Angeles?
context: Los Angeles rides the Pacific plate; San Francisco sits on the North American plate; the two creep past each other at 1-2 inches a year. Project that steady slide forward about 20 million years and Los Angeles — today some 350 miles south — would draw right up alongside San Francisco. Not a collision, just two cities that end up neighbours. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault; USGS.

question: Parkfield, a tiny town, sits squarely astride California's great fault. Since 1857 a magnitude-6 earthquake has shaken it roughly once every 22 years, almost like clockwork, and the US Geological Survey filled its ground with instruments for a long experiment in forecasting quakes. What does the town call itself?
answer: the Earthquake Capital of the World
choices: the Earthquake Capital of the World
the Earthquake Capital of the West Coast
context: Parkfield, home to only a few dozen people, straddles the San Andreas and has produced a magnitude-6 quake about every 22 years since 1857 — so predictably that the USGS made it the site of a long-running earthquake-prediction experiment, wiring the ground with instruments. Its proud self-given title: 'the Earthquake Capital of the World.' Source: https://www.earthquaketracker.org/faults/san-andreas; USGS Parkfield experiment.

question: A devastating earthquake struck Erzincan in 1939, and ever since, Turkey's North Anatolian Fault, a near twin of California's great sliding fault, has seen its great quakes come in an orderly chain. Each rupture piles stress onto the next section, so the fault tears open piece by piece, like a zipper. Toward which great city has the chain been working its way?
context: The 1939 Erzincan quake (magnitude ~7.9, over 32,000 dead) began a westward-marching sequence: each rupture transferred stress to the neighbouring segment, more than 1,000 km of the fault breaking over the century. The 1999 Izmit quake (magnitude 7.6, over 18,000 killed) struck less than 100 km east of Istanbul, loading the last unbroken 'Marmara gap' right beneath the city — the segment seismologists now watch most closely. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Anatolian_Fault.

question: Between the tip of the Sinai and the mountains of southern Turkey, the Arabian plate has ground about 105 km northward past the African plate along one great sliding fault. Wherever the fault's line steps to one side, the crust caught between the steps has stretched and dropped into a deep pit, and the pits have filled with water. Which three bodies of water lie in them?
answer: the Dead Sea, the Sea of Galilee, and the Gulf of Aqaba
choices: the Dead Sea, the Sea of Galilee, and the Gulf of Aqaba
the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, and Lake Nasser
the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Sea of Azov
the Persian Gulf, the Tigris, and the Euphrates
context: Where a strike-slip fault steps sideways, the crust in between stretches and drops, opening what geologists call a 'pull-apart basin.' The Dead Sea Transform's left-stepping bends dropped the pits now filled by the Sea of Galilee, the Dead Sea, and the Gulf of Aqaba. The Dead Sea's shore, about 430 m below sea level, is the lowest dry land on Earth — a record that exists only because two plates are sliding past each other. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea_Transform.

question: Archaeologists began digging into Hisarlik, a grassy mound near the Aegean coast of northwest Turkey, in the 1870s. Inside they found city built on top of city, Homer's legendary Troy among them, layered over about 3,000 years. How many cities are stacked inside the mound?
context: Labelled Troy I to Troy IX from bottom to top, the nine cities span roughly 3000 BC to 500 AD -- each one raised on the levelled rubble of the last, piling ~15 metres of ruins into a single hill. (worldhistory.org, Discovery of Troy; UNESCO WHS 849)

question: Visitors at Hisarlik, in Turkey, climb the real stone walls and gateway of Troy. Yet the single most famous object from the tale of Troy's fall was never dug up there, and it belongs entirely to legend. Which fabled object is it?
context: Homer's Iliad set the Trojan War at this mound, and the stone walls are genuine -- but no horse was ever excavated. Oddly, the wooden horse isn't even in the Iliad: it turns up only later, in the Odyssey. (Wikipedia: Trojan Horse)  (Legend.)

question: Mud-brick towns rose, crumbled and were built over on the same spot at Hisarlik, in northwest Turkey, for three thousand years, until their rubble stood about 15 metres above the flat plain. Archaeologists across the Near East have one short name for a mound raised like this. What is it?
context: A tell is a mound raised from the layered remains of successive settlements; Hisarlik, Jericho, and Megiddo are famous examples. A barrow and a kurgan are burial mounds, and a midden is an ancient rubbish heap. (worldhistory.org; UNESCO WHS 849)

question: Most of the cities stacked in the mound of Hisarlik were built of mud brick, and their walls slumped into a soft hill. The builders of Troy VI cut their great walls from a much harder stone quarried nearby, and those walls still stand today. What stone did they use?
context: Troy VI's citadel walls -- mortarless cut blocks sloping inward -- still rise 9-10 m in places and stand up to 5 m thick, much of the horseshoe circuit and its gates surviving at Hisarlik today. The humbler mud-brick cities simply crumbled into the mound. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: Heinrich Schliemann dug a gold hoard out of Hisarlik and named it Priam's Treasure, for the king of Troy in Homer's poem. Its showpieces were glittering golden diadems, crowns fit for royalty, and he gave them a romantic name of their own from Homer's tale. What did he call them?
context: 'Priam's Treasure' held gold diadems nicknamed the 'Jewels of Helen,' along with about 8,750 tiny gold rings, gold goblets, silver vases, and copper weapons. Schliemann tied the crowns to Helen of Troy, the runaway queen of Homer's tale whose flight launched the war. The Mask of Agamemnon and the Cup of Nestor came from Mycenae, and the Ring of Minos from Crete. (Wikipedia: Priam's Treasure)

question: A man-made gash about 40 metres wide slices through the mound of Hisarlik clear down to bedrock. An impatient digger tore it out in the 1870s, racing down to Homer's Troy and wrecking priceless layers on the way. What do visitors still call this scar?
context: Heinrich Schliemann's Trench -- about 40 m wide and cut to bedrock -- sliced straight through the Late Bronze Age citadel, the very layer now thought to be Homer's Troy, destroying much of what he was hunting for. Blegen, Korfmann, and Dorpfeld were later, more careful excavators of the mound. (Wikipedia: Schliemann's Trench; worldhistory.org)

question: When archaeologists dated the layer of Hisarlik that held the gold hoard called Priam's Treasure, named for Troy's king in Homer's war, the royal name fell apart. The gold is real. Set against the war-era Troy of King Priam, how far off is the treasure's age?
context: The hoard came from the Troy II layer, roughly 2400-2200 BC, while Priam's war-era city is Troy VI/VIIa, around 1250 BC -- so the gold predates any King Priam by about a thousand years. The treasure is real; the 'Priam' label is wrong. (Wikipedia: Priam's Treasure; worldhistory.org)

question: Manfred Korfmann's team began digging at Hisarlik in the late 1980s and found a whole lower town around the small stone fort on top of the mound, ringed by a wide ditch cut into the bedrock. For a century, everyone had pictured Troy as that fort alone. Once the lower town is counted, how much bigger is the real Troy?
context: Korfmann's lower town covered about 30 hectares, ringed by a defensive ditch cut into the bedrock -- proof that Troy was over sixteen times the size of the citadel-only ruin everyone had pictured. (Wikipedia: Troy)

question: Homer's Iliad tells of a ten-year Greek siege of Troy, and in Homer's tale the city was at last stormed and put to the torch. In the mound of Hisarlik one layer reads like a 3,000-year-old crime scene: sealed under a black burn line, its lanes strewn with sling-stones and Greek-style bronze arrowheads, its dead left unburied where they fell. Which layer do archaeologists call the best match for Homer's sacked Troy?
context: Fire, embedded weapons, and unburied dead mark a violent sack rather than a natural disaster or slow decline, making Troy VIIa (~1300-1180 BC) the best archaeological match for the sacked Troy of Homer's tale. Carl Blegen led its excavation. Troy II was Schliemann's early treasure layer, and the grander Troy VI just below fell instead to a natural disaster. (worldhistory.org; Wikipedia: Troy)

question: A quake off Japan jolts the seafloor, and a huge wave races out across the ocean. It was once called a tidal wave, though the Moon's tides have nothing to do with it; its name now is the Japanese word 'tsunami.' What does 'tsunami' mean?
context: 'Tsunami' (津波) joins tsu, 'harbour,' and nami, 'wave' — named because the swell that seemed slight far out at sea reared up to wreck Japan's harbours. Calling it a 'tidal wave' is wrong: tides are the gentle Moon-and-Sun pull on the whole ocean, while a tsunami is the water column shoved upward when a quake heaves the seafloor. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: Out on the deep Pacific, a tsunami is just a small bump on the surface, and a ship right over it would hardly feel it. Yet the whole ocean beneath is moving at more than 800 km/h. Which of these travels about as fast?
context: A tsunami is not a wind-blown surface wave — an undersea quake sets the entire depth of the ocean moving at once, so it carries immense energy while barely rising above the swell. In deep water it can race at over 800 km/h (about 500 mph), roughly a jet's cruising speed, crossing an entire ocean in hours; a passing ship feels almost nothing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: Tsunamis raced across the whole Indian Ocean on 26 December 2004, raised when the seafloor ruptured off Sumatra in an earthquake of about magnitude 9.1. They killed about 228,000 people in 14 countries, the deadliest tsunami ever recorded. What was the main reason the toll ran so high?
answer: the region had no tsunami warning system
choices: the region had no tsunami warning system
the tremor felt too small to fear
the waves struck in the dead of night
the earthquake had cut every phone line
context: In 2004 the Indian Ocean had no tsunami buoys and no alert network at all, unlike the Pacific — so the coasts got no warning whatsoever. The waves were still noticed ~8,500 km away at Struisbaai, South Africa. Worst hit were Aceh in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Tamil Nadu in India, and Khao Lak in Thailand. The disaster spurred the world to build an Indian Ocean warning system. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake_and_tsunami.

question: The sea frothed and slid far out from Maikhao Beach in Phuket, Thailand, before the tsunami of 26 December 2004 came in. It happens often before a tsunami, though not always. Why does the sea sometimes pull back like that before the wave strikes?
answer: the wave's trough reaches shore before its crest
choices: the wave's trough reaches shore before its crest
the quake drops the seabed and drains the bay
the wave draws the water up into its crest
the falling tide happens to meet the wave
context: The Lisbon quake (~M7.7+) shook for up to six minutes on All Saints' Day; the sea then drew back, luring the curious onto the mud before the tsunami engulfed the harbour ~40 minutes after the shock; a firestorm then burned for days, and ~40,000–50,000 died. The sea withdraws only when the wave's trough leads its crest — so it happens often, not always. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake.

question: Racing across the deep Indian Ocean in December 2004, the tsunami stood only about a metre tall, with some 200 kilometres between one crest and the next. When it reached Banda Aceh in Sumatra, the same wave reared up 15 to 30 metres high. What turned a one-metre swell into such a wall of water?
answer: it slowed in the shallows and the water behind piled into it
choices: it slowed in the shallows and the water behind piled into it
aftershocks from the quake kept shoving it higher and higher
the rising tide lifted it on top of the normal sea level
a strong onshore wind blew it up into a taller wall
context: In deep water a tsunami's crests can be 200 km apart yet only ~1 m tall; nearing shore, 'shoaling' slams on the brakes — speed falls from ~800 to under 80 km/h and the wavelength shrinks, so the trailing water piles the wave up into a towering wall. At Banda Aceh in 2004 it rose 15–30 m, with a maximum around 51 m. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami.

question: On Maikhao Beach in Phuket, Thailand, on 26 December 2004, ten-year-old Tilly Smith watched the sea froth and pull far back. Curious adults wandered out onto the wet sand. But Tilly screamed for everyone to run. She had seen the warning signs before. Where had she learned them just two weeks earlier?
choices: from a survivor of an earlier wave
context: Tilly Smith's teacher, Andrew Kearney at Danes Hill School, had shown the class the warning signs just two weeks earlier — the sea pulling back, the water frothing, waves that go out but don't return — using footage of the 1946 Aleutian Islands tsunami. Recognizing all three at Maikhao, she got the beach and hotel evacuated, and about 100 people were saved. A geography lesson literally saved lives. Source: International Tsunami Information Center (itic.ioc-unesco.org).

question: High above the hamlet of Aneyoshi in Miyako, Japan, a stone slab carved by ancestors generations ago bears a stark command: 'Do not build any homes below this point. Remember the calamity of the great tsunamis.' Then, in 2011, the greatest tsunami in living memory surged up the valley toward the village. What became of every household that had obeyed the ancient stone and built above its line?
context: The Aneyoshi stone reads in full: 'High dwellings are the peace and harmony of our descendants. Remember the calamity of the great tsunamis. Do not build any homes below this point.' In 2011 the wave climbed the valley and halted about 100 m below the stone — and every household that had stayed above it survived. Japan has hundreds of such tsunami stones, some over 600 years old, many placed after an 1896 tsunami killed ~22,000 — ancestral knowledge carved to outlast living memory. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami_stone; nbcnews.com.

question: An earthquake shook 30 million cubic metres of rock off a cliff into the narrow inlet of Lituya Bay, Alaska, on 9 July 1958. The splash surged 524 metres up the far mountainside, higher than the Empire State Building, and tore away the whole forest. It was the tallest wave ever recorded on Earth, yet how many people did it kill?
context: This was a landslide megatsunami, not an ocean-crossing tsunami: the rockfall's splash surged 524 m (1,719 ft) up the far slope — taller than the Empire State Building — the tallest wave ever recorded. Because Lituya Bay is a remote Alaskan inlet, only about five people died, on fishing boats caught in the bay. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1958_Lituya_Bay_earthquake_and_megatsunami.

question: The sea rose up to 40 metres high along Japan's coast on 11 March 2011, after an earthquake of about magnitude 9.0 struck off the Oshika Peninsula. The tsunami pushed 10 km inland at Sendai and overwhelmed one coastal site whose failure turned a natural disaster into a nuclear one. Which site was it?
context: The magnitude ~9.0 quake struck 72 km off the Oshika Peninsula; the tsunami killed about 19,759 people, ran up to 40.5 m at Miyako, and pushed 10 km inland at Sendai, where people had only 8–10 minutes' warning. It flooded the Fukushima Daiichi plant and caused three reactor meltdowns — a natural disaster that became a nuclear one. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Tōhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami.

question: Tulum's stone temples stand on the edge of a low cliff on Mexico's Yucatan coast, looking straight out over open water, while almost every other great Maya city lies hidden inland under the jungle. Which sea breaks on the cliffs below?
context: Tulum stands on a cliff about 12 metres (39 ft) high on the east coast of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula -- the only major Maya city built on the coast, while almost all the others hide inland in the jungle. Below its temples the Caribbean glows famously turquoise. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tulum'.

question: The Maya who built a clifftop city on Mexico's Yucatan coast called it Zama; the name Tulum came much later. Its temples look straight out over the open sea from the edge of a low cliff. What does Zama mean?
context: Zama means 'dawn' or 'sunrise' -- fitting, because the cliff faces due east, so the temples catch the very first light coming up over the Caribbean each morning. The name we use today, 'Tulum', is different and much newer: it comes from the Yucatec Maya word for 'wall', pointing to the great rampart that ringed the city. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tulum'; Ancient Origins.

question: Tulum's traders once beached canoes loaded with obsidian, jade and salt in the cove below El Castillo, the tallest temple on the city's clifftop. Archaeologists think the temple quietly did a second job beyond worship. What do they think it doubled as?
context: This beacon role is an interpretation, not a proven fact. Because El Castillo lines up with the one natural break in the offshore reef, researchers think lights placed in its windows could have been lined up to guide trading canoes safely through that channel into the sheltered cove. Tulum was a busy Postclassic port trading obsidian, jade and salt. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tulum'.  (Legend.)

question: Each summer the tundra of northern Siberia thaws only in a thin top layer, about a metre and a half deep. Below it lies permafrost, ground frozen solid all year round. How far down does it go in parts of Siberia?
context: 'Permafrost' means ground that stays at or below 0 C (32 F) for at least two years straight. Only a thin top 'active layer' — averaging about 1.5 m — thaws each summer; below that the freeze runs deep, reaching roughly 1,493 m down in Siberia's Lena and Yana river basins. About 15% of the Northern Hemisphere's land sits on permafrost. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permafrost

question: In the Siberian village of Oymyakon, drivers keep their engines running around the clock so the fuel won't freeze solid, and school carries on until the air sinks past -55 C. Only about 500 people endure winters like this, year after year. Which record does Oymyakon share with the Siberian town of Verkhoyansk?
answer: the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth
choices: the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth
the coldest air temperature ever recorded on Earth
the northernmost inhabited village on Earth
the snowiest inhabited town on Earth
context: Oymyakon, in Sakha (Yakutia), hit an official -67.7 C (-89.9 F) on 6 February 1933; Verkhoyansk, its twin 'Pole of Cold', logged -67.8 C in February 1892, so the two share the title of coldest permanently inhabited place. (Antarctica's Vostok station is colder still, but no one lives there year-round.) Oymyakon's yearly swing is astonishing: from that -67.7 C low up to +34.6 C one summer, over 100 C apart. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oymyakon

question: Loggers cleared a hillside in Siberia's Sakha Republic in the 1960s, and the bared permafrost began to thaw and cave in. The scar is now the Batagaika crater, about a kilometre long and up to 100 metres deep, its walls crumbling more than 10 metres wider every year. What grim nickname do the locals give it?
context: The Batagaika crater in Sakha is the world's largest permafrost megaslump, still growing as its headwall retreats over 10 m a year. Its collapsing walls slice open an estimated 200,000 to 650,000 years of frozen record, exposing buried ancient forests and the bones of woolly mammoth, musk ox, and Ice-Age Lena horses. 'Gateway to the Underworld' is a local nickname. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batagaika_crater

question: A climber high on Kilimanjaro or one of Ecuador's Andean volcanoes leaves the last forest behind at the treeline and walks on over bare rock, cushion plants and low mosses. This is alpine tundra, treeless for the same cause as the far north: too much cold and too short a season for trees. On mountains farther and farther from the equator, what happens to the height of the treeline?
answer: it sinks lower and lower until it reaches the sea
choices: it sinks lower and lower until it reaches the sea
it climbs higher and higher until it caps the summit
it stays at one fixed height at every latitude
it drops away all at once at the Arctic Circle
context: Alpine tundra sits above the treeline on tall mountains anywhere on Earth — the Andes, the Himalayas, even peaks in the tropics — while ARCTIC tundra lies at high latitude near the poles; both are treeless for the same reason (too cold, too short a growing season). Moving from the equator toward the poles, the alpine treeline drops lower and lower, until near the poles it reaches sea level and the mountain's alpine tundra merges with the polar tundra at the coast. (Chimborazo in Ecuador sits almost on the equator; Kilimanjaro lies about 3 degrees south, in the tropics.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_tundra

question: At the mouth of Yosemite Valley in California stands one huge wall of pale granite, some 100 million years old, its face climbing 3,000 feet with no break in it. Climbers need days to reach the top. What is this giant rock called?
context: El Capitan is often called the largest exposed granite monolith on Earth. Glaciers didn't gouge Yosemite Valley out of nothing — they widened, deepened, and polished a river-cut gorge, leaving sheer walls like El Capitan towering over the flat green floor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Capitan

question: Visitors entering Yosemite Valley, in California's Sierra Nevada, meet one waterfall first: a slim ribbon of water dropping 620 feet down a sheer cliff. Unlike many Sierra falls, it flows every month of the year. What is this welcoming waterfall called?
context: Bridalveil Fall drops 620 ft (188 m) and flows year-round. To the Ahwahneechee people it was 'Pohono,' the Spirit of the Puffing Wind — gusts funnel up the cliff and blow the thin ribbon sideways, sometimes sweeping it away before it reaches the ground. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridalveil_Fall

question: One of Yosemite Valley's waterfalls does not tumble down a slope; it leaps clear off the cliff and free-falls the whole way. It pours from what geologists call a hanging valley, a side valley left stranded high on the main valley's wall. Why was that side valley left so far above the floor?
answer: its smaller side-glacier couldn't grind as deep as the main glacier
choices: its smaller side-glacier couldn't grind as deep as the main glacier
the tributary river later cut its bed far below the side valley
a rockslide buried the lower end of the side valley long ago
an earthquake dropped the main valley floor much lower
context: The main glacier gouged Yosemite's deep U-trough while the tributary's smaller glacier could only scratch a shallow groove — so when the ice melted the side valley was left dangling, and its stream now free-falls off the lip. Bridalveil is the classic American hanging-valley waterfall. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging_valley

question: J.R.R. Tolkien hiked Switzerland's Lauterbrunnen Valley in 1911, while he was still a young man. He found a deep glacial cleft barely a kilometre wide, walled by limestone cliffs nearly 1,000 m high and laced with dozens of free-falling waterfalls. That valley became his picture of which place in Middle-earth?
context: Lauterbrunnen's cliffs and cascades became Tolkien's mental picture of Rivendell, the elven refuge. The valley is a 'true cleft' whose roughly 1,000 m walls hold a local count of some 72 waterfalls. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauterbrunnen

question: Hikers slip on the bare granite of Yosemite's Lembert and Pothole Domes, buffed to a glassy shine by a glacier long since gone. Yet pure ice is far too soft to scratch hard granite. What actually did the polishing?
answer: grit and boulders frozen into the base of the ice
choices: grit and boulders frozen into the base of the ice
the sheer crushing weight of the overlying ice
meltwater streams rushing beneath the glacier
rain and wind wearing the rock after the ice left
context: Grit and rock frozen into a glacier's underside turn the moving ice into a sheet of sandpaper that abrades and polishes the bedrock. You can still see — and slip on — this glacial polish at Yosemite's Pothole and Lembert Domes. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_striation

question: The lakes far below the peaks of Montana's Glacier National Park glow an unreal turquoise. Melting ice keeps pouring glacial flour into them, rock the glacier has ground into a powder finer than any sand. How does that flour give the lakes their colour?
answer: it hangs in the water and scatters sunlight
choices: it hangs in the water and scatters sunlight
it dissolves and tints the water like a dye
it feeds algae that dye the water blue-green
it coats the lakebed in pale, sky-bright stone
context: Glacial flour is rock ground so fine by the ice that it never settles, staying suspended and scattering light into that turquoise glow. The park's namesake ice is fading fast — from about 150 glaciers in 1850 to roughly 25 by 2010. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier_National_Park_(U.S.)

question: Staubbach Falls leaps 297 m off a sheer cliff in Switzerland's Lauterbrunnen Valley, one of the highest free falls in the country, and the wind tears its water into drifting spray long before it reaches the ground. The Swiss named it for what that airborne water looks like. What does 'Staub' mean?
context: Staubbach Falls plunges 297 m (974 ft), one of Switzerland's highest free-falling waterfalls (the nearby Mürrenbach Falls, dropping in stages, fall farther in all), and pours, like Bridalveil, from a hanging valley. It falls so far that the wind scatters the water into drifting spray, so the Swiss named it 'Staubbach,' the 'dust brook.' Its ghostly mist has drawn writers for centuries — Goethe visited in 1779 and wrote 'Gesang der Geister über den Wassern' ('Song of the Spirits over the Waters'). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staubbach_Falls

question: Long, straight grooves score the granite bedrock of California's Yosemite Valley, cut by a glacier that vanished ages ago. Geologists call them striations, and they hunt for them because the grooves reveal one specific thing about the lost glacier. What do they reveal?
answer: the direction the ice once flowed
choices: the direction the ice once flowed
the thickness the ice once reached
the speed at which the ice moved
the year the ice finally melted
context: Because striations run the way the ice moved, geologists read them like arrows to reconstruct the path a vanished glacier took across the land — long after the ice itself is gone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_striation

question: Norway's Sognefjord snakes more than 200 km inland between towering rock walls, its water some 1,300 m deep, yet a shallow bar of bedrock still guards its mouth where it meets the open sea. A fjord like this is a landform the sea has flooded. Which landform is it?
context: A fjord is simply a glacial U-trough the sea has drowned — the same shape, flooded. The shallow bedrock 'sill' at Sognefjord's mouth is the ridge the glacier left behind; even its side valleys still 'hang,' meeting the main channel far above the deep floor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fjord

question: Seen end-on, Yosemite Valley is not the sharp, narrow V of a river-cut canyon but a smooth, rounded U, and that shape is the fingerprint of how it was carved. A river and a glacier wear rock away in different ways. What does a glacier do that rounds a valley into a U?
answer: it grinds along its whole width and base at once
choices: it grinds along its whole width and base at once
it presses down so hard it flattens only the floor
it plucks blocks from the highest walls alone
it dissolves the granite chemically with its meltwater
context: A river erodes at a single point, leaving a sharp V; a glacier plucks and grinds along its entire width and base, shaving the walls into a smooth parabolic U. That U-versus-V is the fingerprint that tells geologists ice, not water, shaped a valley — a transformation that can take 10,000 to 100,000 years. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U-shaped_valley

question: About 25 km west of Uluru, in Australia's red desert, dozens of huge rounded domes crowd together. The Aṇangu call the formation Kata Tjuta; English maps once labelled it the Olgas, but the Aṇangu name captures the sight far better. What does Kata Tjuta mean?
context: Kata Tjuta means 'many heads' in Pitjantjatjara, and it is a perfect name: the formation is a cluster of 36 separate rounded domes, 25 km west of Uluru. Europeans long called it 'the Olgas' after its tallest dome, Mount Olga. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kata_Tjuta

question: Walkers set out on the marked trail that loops the base of Uluru, the single great rock rising 348 metres out of central Australia's flat red desert. It sounds like a short stroll around one stone. About how far is one full lap?
context: The base walk around Uluru runs 9.4 km — nearly six miles just to circle one rock. Walking it gives a real sense of the monolith's bulk: what shows above ground is one continuous, unbroken hump of stone. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: Uluru looks like an enormous boulder set down on the flat desert of central Australia, its red dome rising 348 metres above the plain. Geologists who followed its rock layers on down beneath the sand made a startling discovery about it. What did they find?
answer: most of it is buried, like an iceberg
choices: most of it is buried, like an iceberg
it is hollow, riddled with caves
it was once the core of a volcano
it is slowly sinking into the sand
context: Uluru's layers were folded until they tilted almost vertical (about 85°), and they plunge kilometres straight down into the earth — the exposed rock is estimated to be at least 2,400 m thick, most of it hidden underground like the bulk of an iceberg. The giant we see is only the tip. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: Uluru gets nearly all the postcards, but 25 km to its west stands its neighbour Kata Tjuta, a cluster of 36 steep red domes. Uluru itself rises 348 metres above the desert plain. Measured from that same plain, how tall is Kata Tjuta's highest dome, Mount Olga?
choices: almost exactly as tall as Uluru
about half as tall as Uluru
context: Mount Olga, the tallest of Kata Tjuta's domes, reaches 1,066 m above sea level — about 546 m above the plain, roughly 200 m higher than Uluru's 348 m rise. So the less-famous formation is actually the taller one. The explorer Ernest Giles named the peak in 1872 for Queen Olga of Württemberg. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kata_Tjuta

question: Tucked against the base of Uluru, in central Australia's red desert, lies Mutitjulu, a sacred site of the Aṇangu, whose land this is, and the setting of one of their ancestral stories. What natural feature sits there, right at the foot of the rock?
context: The Mutitjulu waterhole is a permanent water source at Uluru's base — precious in the desert — and a sacred Aṇangu site tied to the ancestral story of Kuniya the python and Liru the venomous snake. Parks Australia asks that the full story be learned at the place itself rather than casually retold. Source: https://uluru.gov.au/discover/culture/stories/kuniya-liru-stories/  (Legend.)

question: Uluru, the great rock of central Australia, was returned to the Aṇangu in 1985, and to them it is deeply sacred. Exactly 34 years later, Parks Australia carried out a decision the Aṇangu themselves had made about how their sacred site should be treated. What had they decided?
answer: climbing the rock would end for good
choices: climbing the rock would end for good
photographing the rock would be banned
the whole park would close to visitors
visitors would need a permit to enter
context: Ownership of Uluru was formally returned to the Aṇangu on 26 October 1985. Exactly 34 years later, on 26 October 2019, the summit climb was permanently closed — at the Aṇangu's request, as their decision, out of respect for the sacred rock. Uluru and Kata Tjuta were jointly listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 for both their natural and their Aboriginal cultural value. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: Uluru's sandstone, in the red heart of Australia, formed around 550 million years ago, so long ago that the continents lay in shapes no map today would recognise. When the rock was forming, which of these was only just appearing on Earth?
context: Uluru's arkose sandstone is roughly 550 to 530 million years old, from the Neoproterozoic into the early Cambrian — older than the dinosaurs by some 300 million years, and older than nearly every animal that ever walked the Earth. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uluru

question: Uluru and Kata Tjuta rise from the same central Australian desert, just 25 km apart, yet weathering wore them into very different shapes: Uluru into one smooth block of fine sandstone, Kata Tjuta into 36 towering domes. What is Kata Tjuta made of, that broke it into so many domes?
context: Kata Tjuta is conglomerate — cobbles and boulders of many rock types cemented in a sandstone paste, like natural concrete. That coarse, uneven rock weathered into 36 separate rounded heads, while Uluru's finer, more uniform arkose sandstone eroded into one smooth block. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kata_Tjuta

question: One huge rock rises 348 metres from the dead-flat desert in the red heart of Australia, with open plain running to the horizon. Geographers call Uluru an inselberg, German for 'island mountain'. How did it come to stand alone on the plain?
answer: the softer land around it wore away
choices: the softer land around it wore away
a volcano pushed it up through the plain
a glacier dropped it there in an ice age
a meteor strike heaved it out of the ground
context: Uluru is the world's most famous inselberg (German for 'island mountain') — a mass of tough rock left standing when the softer land around it slowly wore away. It rises 348 m above the plain, measures 9.4 km around its base, and its summit reaches 863 m above sea level. Source: Wikipedia, 'Uluru'.

question: The Aṇangu, Uluru's Aboriginal keepers, have handed down their sacred Tjukurpa stories, the Dreaming, for tens of thousands of years, and the stories tie ancestral events to the rock's caves and gullies. Besides their sacred meaning, they carry knowledge that keeps people alive in the harsh desert. What life-or-death knowledge do they hold?
answer: where and when to find water and food
choices: where and when to find water and food
how to forecast the coming year's weather
which stars mark each season's turning
how to heal sickness with desert plants
context: Tjukurpa is the foundation of Aṇangu culture — not written down but memorised and passed to the right people across tens of thousands of years. Its stories map ancestral events onto real places, but they also record how to travel and where and when to find water and food — practical survival knowledge woven into sacred law. Source: Parks Australia, uluru.gov.au (Tjukurpa).

question: Uluru seems to catch fire at dawn and dusk, its whole face blazing red and orange across the desert of central Australia before it fades to purple. Yet inside the caves at the rock's foot, the very same stone is plain grey, so the colour is only skin-deep. What has turned the rock's outer surface red?
answer: iron in the rock has rusted
choices: iron in the rock has rusted
red desert sand has stained it
red algae has spread across it
the sun's heat has scorched it
context: Uluru glows red because iron in its outer rock has literally rusted — the red skin is oxidised iron. The fresh arkose underneath is actually grey, and that original grey still shows inside Uluru's caves. Source: Australian Govt DCCEEW + uluru.gov.au (Geology).

question: Mutitjulu, at the base of Uluru, is the one waterhole that holds water the whole year, and for centuries it was the most trusted Aṇangu campsite in the desert. In Aṇangu Tjukurpa, a powerful ancestor watches over Mutitjulu and all that happens there. What kind of creature is this guardian?
context: In Tjukurpa, Mutiṭjulu is the home of Wanampi, an ancestral water snake believed to guard the pool. Mutiṭjulu is the only permanent (year-round) waterhole at Uluru and was for centuries a key Aṇangu campsite. Source: Parks Australia, uluru.gov.au (Water) + Australian Govt DCCEEW.  (Legend.)

question: The Aṇangu closed the climb up Uluru for good on 26 October 2019. Their law, Tjukurpa, did not permit the climb, but the sign they left at its base stressed a second reason, rooted in their duty as custodians. What did that sign say worried them?
answer: the safety of the visitors themselves
choices: the safety of the visitors themselves
litter left behind on the steep trail
disturbance to the local desert wildlife
context: Signs at the base asked visitors 'Please don't climb', and the Aṇangu message there said: 'As custodians, we are responsible for your safety and behaviour,' speaking too of their worry for climbers and their families. Under Tjukurpa the climb was not permitted, and in November 2017 the Aṇangu-majority board voted unanimously to close it; it closed on 26 October 2019, the 34th anniversary of 'Handback', the 1985 return of the land to its traditional owners. Sammy Wilson, then chairman of the board, called it not a loss: 'Closing the climb is not something to feel upset about but a cause for celebration.' Source: Parks Australia, uluru.gov.au/discover/culture/uluru-climb.

question: Uluru's rock began as flat beds of sand laid down more than half a billion years ago. Then a vast mountain-building event, the Alice Springs Orogeny, squeezed and buckled this whole region of Australia. The bands on Uluru today show what that squeezing did to the once-flat layers. How do they lie now?
choices: left as a gently sloping ramp
context: Uluru's arkose is about 550–530 million years old. The Alice Springs Orogeny (~400–300 million years ago) tilted its once-horizontal layers to a dip of about 85° — almost straight up and down. Source: Wikipedia, 'Uluru'.

question: Cruise ships bound for Antarctica fill up with passengers at the docks of Ushuaia, on Tierra del Fuego, a town whose motto reads 'fin del mundo, principio de todo', end of the world, beginning of everything. What is Ushuaia billed as among the world's cities?
context: Ushuaia (~82,000+ residents) is billed as the world's southernmost CITY and the last big port before Antarctica -- one of only five 'Antarctic gateway' cities, the closest to the Antarctic Peninsula (~1,000 km), and it handles over 90% of all tourists who visit Antarctica. Honest caveat: a smaller Chilean town, Puerto Williams, sits a little farther south across the Beagle Channel, so Ushuaia is really the southernmost city of substantial SIZE. Its own name comes from the native Yamana word for a 'bay penetrating westward.' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ushuaia; mercopress.com; earthobservatory.nasa.gov)

question: Ferdinand Magellan's ships sailed past the great island at the tip of South America in 1520, and his crew saw points of flame and smoke all along the cold, dark coast. The island takes its name, Tierra del Fuego, the Land of Fire, from that sight. In the old story, what were those fires?
context: The Yamana (Yaghan) people kept fires burning constantly against the Patagonian cold -- even on hearths inside their bark canoes -- and Magellan's crew saw them dotting the shore. A colorful retelling says Magellan first called it Tierra del Humo, 'Land of Smoke,' until King Charles V of Spain remarked that there is no smoke without fire and renamed it 'Land of Fire.' Treat it as tradition: there is no proof Magellan himself gave the name, which appears on maps only in the mid-1500s. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tierra_del_Fuego; newworldencyclopedia.org)  (Legend.)

question: In front of Ushuaia, the little Argentine port at the tip of South America, runs the Beagle Channel, a narrow strait between Tierra del Fuego and the smaller islands to its south. A British naval expedition charted these waters in the 1820s and gave the channel its name. What is the Beagle Channel named for?
context: The channel honors HMS Beagle -- the survey SHIP, not the dog breed -- which first charted southern South America in 1826-1830. On the Beagle's second voyage, Charles Darwin sailed through on 29 January 1833 and marveled at the glaciers' 'beryl-like blue' ice. The strait runs about 240 km (150 mi) east-west, narrows to only ~5 km, and links the Pacific and Atlantic around the tip of the continent. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beagle_Channel)

question: Valparaíso, on Chile's Pacific coast, spills down dozens of hills too steep for ordinary streets, and since 1883 its people have ridden little wooden cars hauled up the slopes on cables. What does the city call these hillside cars?
context: These are Valparaíso's famous ascensores — technically funiculars, cars counterbalanced on inclined tracks up the cliffs. The first, Ascensor Concepción, opened in 1883 and still runs today. At their peak about 30 climbed the cerros; today around 16 survive, protected as National Monuments of Chile. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valparaiso_funiculars.)

question: The hillside houses of Valparaíso, in Chile, wear wild, clashing colours, every wall a mismatched sheet of ribbed metal, so that a whole hill looks like a patchwork quilt. Families too poor to buy new sheets nailed up salvaged iron and painted it with leftover paint. Where did they salvage those iron sheets from?
context: Valparaíso was the great Pacific seaport of the age of sail, and its hillside walls were built from the sea itself — sheets of corrugated iron rescued from old ship hulls, then coated in leftover marine paint scrounged from the harbor's shipyards. That accidental, salvaged rainbow is part of why its 'Historic Quarter of the Seaport City' became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. (Sources: swallowsnotes.com, ecochile.travel; whc.unesco.org/en/list/959.)

question: Every ship sailing between the Atlantic and Pacific in the 1800s had to brave the storms of Cape Horn, at the tip of South America, and Valparaíso was the great harbour where tired crews rested and stocked up. Its banks and rowdy saloons boomed so wildly that seamen nicknamed it 'Little ___', after a famous California boom port. Which city fills the blank?
context: Sailors called 1800s Valparaíso 'Little San Francisco' for its gold-rush-style boom of banks, brothels, and saloons — and more grandly the 'Jewel of the Pacific.' It was then THE Pacific stop for sailing ships rounding Cape Horn. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valparaiso.)

question: For a century Valparaíso grew rich because ships crossing between the oceans had no choice but to round stormy Cape Horn and stop at its docks to rest and trade. Then in 1914 a great canal opened far to the north, handing ships a shortcut that made the long Cape Horn passage pointless. Almost overnight, they stopped coming, and the boomtown fell silent. Which canal was it?
context: The Panama Canal, opened in 1914, let ships cut straight between the Atlantic and Pacific instead of sailing all the way around Cape Horn — and Valparaíso, a port undone by a distant canal, fell quiet. A great earthquake in 1906 that killed some 3,000 people had already shaken the city hard. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valparaiso.)

question: Pablo Neruda, a poet who crammed his houses with ships' figureheads and seaside curios, bought an unfinished house high on a Valparaíso hill in 1959. He loved its wide view over the harbour's natural bowl and turned it into a writing hideaway. What name does this hillside house go by?
context: La Sebastiana takes its name from Sebastián Collado, the Spaniard who began building it and once kept an aviary of birds on the third floor. Neruda wrote that he made the house 'first of air,' then raised a flag over it. Abandoned after his death in 1973, it was restored as a museum in 1991. (Sources: chile.travel; gochile.cl.)

question: All along Varanasi's riverfront, long lines of wide stone steps run straight down into the Ganges. At dawn the whole city streams to the water's edge to bathe, pray and float little lamps. What are these stone stairways called?
context: A ghat is a flight of steps leading down to a river. Varanasi's ghats — traditionally counted as 84 — form an almost continuous stone stairway along the Ganges, the stage for the whole city's daily life at the water's edge. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varanasi, Ghats section; kashiyatra.in/84-ghats-of-varanasi)

question: Babylon and Ur crumbled to ruin long ago, but Varanasi, on the Ganges, never went silent: dug-up finds show people living there by about 800 BCE, and its lanes have stayed crowded ever since. Among which of the world's cities does that rank it?
answer: oldest cities still lived in today
choices: oldest cities still lived in today
richest cities of the spice trade
context: Most of the world's ancient cities are ruins. Varanasi is different: continuously inhabited for well over 3,000 years, it is a rare 'living' ancient city — which is why Hindus call it eternal, and Mark Twain called it older than history, tradition and legend put together. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varanasi, History; prayagsamagam.com/city/varanasi)

question: Funeral pyres of wood burn at Manikarnika, the great cremation ground on Varanasi's riverfront, where families bring their dead to the edge of the Ganges and give the ashes to the river. What is startling about these fires?
answer: they never stop, burning day and night all year
choices: they never stop, burning day and night all year
they are lit for just one week each spring
they may be kindled only after nightfall
they burn only for kings and holy men
context: Manikarnika is Varanasi's main 'burning ghat.' Roughly 200-300 cremations take place there every single day, without pause, so its fires have burned continuously for as long as anyone can remember. To Hindus this is a place of hope rather than horror: they believe cremation here can set a soul free from the cycle of rebirth. (Source: edgeofhumanity.com/2019/04/28/manikarnika; thehosteller.com/blogs/the-eternal-flames-of-manikarnika-ghat)

question: Young priests in matching robes stand on the crowded steps at Dashashwamedh, on Varanasi's riverfront, every evening at dusk, lifting tall brass lamps and swinging the flames in slow circles. Conch shells blow and bells ring while boats crowd the water to watch. Who or what is being worshipped?
context: This is the Ganga Aarti, performed each evening at Dashashwamedh Ghat. Traditionally seven priests offer the swinging lamps, conches and bells to the Ganges herself — for Hindus the river is a living goddess, Ganga. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashashwamedh_Ghat; varanasiguru.com/ganga-aarti-varanasi)

question: Hindus believe the soul is trapped in samsara, an endless wheel of dying and being born again, life after life. Hindu families bring their dead to be cremated at Manikarnika, beside the Ganges in Varanasi, believing it breaks the wheel and sets the soul free forever. What is this release from the cycle of rebirth called?
context: Moksha means release from samsara, the endless cycle of death and rebirth. Hindus believe dying and being cremated at Varanasi can grant it — the hopeful heart of the city: to be burned here is to be set free. (Buddhism's parallel goal is called nirvana.) (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manikarnika_Ghat, moksha; prayagpandits.com)  (Legend.)

question: Hindus hold Varanasi to be the earthly city of the god Shiva, who, they say, founded it at the beginning of the world and never leaves it, and they know it by an older name, Kashi. Which city does the name Kashi honour it as?
choices: the City of a Thousand Gates
context: Kashi comes from a Sanskrit root meaning 'to shine,' so Varanasi is the 'City of Light.' Hindus hold it to be Shiva's own city, which he founded and never leaves, and the holiest of all places in which to die. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varanasi, Kashi/Shiva; Diana Eck, 'Banaras: City of Light')

question: Above the tangle of Varanasi's oldest lanes stands the city's holiest shrine, the Kashi Vishwanath. It is the temple of Shiva as Lord of the Universe, one of the most sacred spots in Hinduism, thronged by pilgrims from across India. Which feature makes it blaze above the rooftops in the sun?
context: The Kashi Vishwanath Temple is the spiritual heart of Varanasi — the shrine of Shiva as Vishwanath, 'Lord of the Universe.' Its tall spire and dome are plated in gold, so it catches the sun above the crowded old city. (Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varanasi, Kashi Vishwanath Temple; oranatravel.com/visit/varanasi)

question: One family alone may kindle the funeral pyres at Manikarnika, the great Hindu cremation ground beside the Ganges in Varanasi, a sacred duty passed from father to son as far back as anyone can remember. What title does the hereditary head of this family bear?
context: The Dom, though placed outside the traditional caste hierarchy, hold an indispensable and honoured office at Manikarnika: without them no cremation can happen, and their hereditary head is the Dom Raja, a 'king' of the burning ground. The flame they tend is said to have burned for centuries. (Source: edgeofhumanity.com/2019/04/28/manikarnika; thenationalnews.com/weekend/2022/10/28/making-a-living-from-the-dead)

question: Vatnajokull, Europe's largest glacier by volume, spreads across southeastern Iceland and covers about 8% of the country in ice up to a kilometre thick. Entire mountain ranges hide beneath it, along with active volcanoes that sometimes melt their way up through the surface. What kind of glacier is Vatnajokull?
context: Vatnajokull is Iceland's largest glacier and the biggest in Europe outside the Arctic, covering roughly 7,700-8,100 km2. An ICE CAP is a mound of glacier ice that buries the land beneath it yet stays under 50,000 km2; anything larger, like the ice covering Greenland or Antarctica, is called an ice SHEET. Vatnajokull's ice averages about 380 m thick and reaches some 950 m at its deepest point. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatnajokull; Vatnajokull National Park (official).

question: At the foot of Vatnajokull, guides lead visitors into blue ice caves that meltwater carves under the outlet glacier. These crystal caves are safe to enter for only one season each year. Each year the meltwater shapes them into brand-new caves. Which season is the only safe time to go in?
context: It feels backwards, but the caves are safe only in the deep cold of winter (roughly mid-November to March), when the ice is frozen hard and stable; in the warmth they melt, weaken, and collapse. Because meltwater re-carves them every year, no two winters ever produce the same cave. Source: guidetoiceland.is/travel-iceland/drive/the-crystal-ice-cave; visitvatnajokull.is.

question: Icebergs break off Vatnajokull's outlet glacier and drift across a lagoon called Jokulsarlon. They float out to sea and are tumbled smooth by the waves. The tide then shoves the clear ice back onto a stretch of jet-black volcanic sand. What nickname have travellers given this black beach?
context: The black sand is ground-up basalt from Iceland's volcanoes; against it, the clear ice really does look like scattered diamonds. Jokulsarlon itself is Iceland's deepest lake (over 284 m) and only formed because the glacier began retreating from the sea in the 1930s; it has quadrupled in size since the 1970s. The lagoon is so cinematic it has appeared in two James Bond films and Batman Begins. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jokulsarlon.
